metadata.note: Azielon original study content; not official PMI exam questions or official PMI rule wording. Rewritten 2026-09-30: scenario-based items, teaching explanations, more matching.

questions.stem: The adaptive integration team on a hybrid claims-platform project needs daily access to a shared test environment, while the infrastructure lead, working to a fixed hardware plan, wants the environment locked for four weeks. Both leads have brought the disagreement to the project manager, and the next milestone is six weeks away. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Ask the sponsor to rule on which team gets the environment so that neither lead has to give ground on the current plan.
Meet with both leads together to explore why each needs the environment and jointly design an access schedule that works for both.
Stress how much the two leads agree on overall goals and suggest they revisit the access question once the next milestone has passed.
Decide in favor of the infrastructure lead because the hardware plan is baselined and the adaptive team can work around it.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Collaborating (problem solving) — PMI's default conflict mode. Bring the parties together, uncover each side's real need, and build a solution both can own; it fits when there is time and both needs are legitimate.
Spot it: two leads with valid but competing needs, time still available (six weeks), and no safety emergency.
In this scenario: meeting both leads together to learn why each needs the environment turns a tug-of-war into a shared scheduling problem they can solve together.
Why not the others: Asking the sponsor to rule escalates before the PM has tried to resolve it; stressing shared goals and postponing is smoothing plus withdrawing, so the conflict comes back; siding with the infrastructure lead is forcing, a win-lose move in a non-emergency.
Remember: Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act → Monitor → Escalate. Escalate is the LAST step, not the first.

questions.stem: The site engineering team on a predictive hospital-wing construction project has fallen two days behind schedule because every inspection request must wait for a signature from a busy facilities director. A client representative is pressing the project manager to get the team moving. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Require each site engineer to submit an hourly progress update so the client representative can see the team is busy.
Report the engineers' slippage to their functional manager and request a formal performance review for each person.
Take over the inspection requests personally and direct the engineers on which tasks to complete while they wait.
Work with the facilities director to set up a faster signature arrangement so the engineers are no longer held up.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Servant leadership: removing impediments — the servant leader clears obstacles the team cannot clear on its own, especially organizational bottlenecks outside the team.
Spot it: a capable team, a delay caused by something outside the team (a busy approver), and pressure on the PM to "get the team moving."
In this scenario: the engineers are waiting on signatures, so the PM works with the facilities director on a faster approval path.
Why not the others: Hourly updates add reporting burden and treat a process problem as a people problem; reporting the engineers blames them for a delay they did not cause; taking over and directing is command-and-control and leaves the signature bottleneck in place.
Remember: Coach → Facilitate → Empower → Remove Barriers. Fix the system, not the people.

questions.topic: Coaching: developing a team member through feedback
questions.stem: A newly assigned scheduler on a predictive pipeline project has twice submitted schedule updates with missing logic links, which the project manager caught before the baseline report went out. The scheduler is motivated and has asked for feedback. What is the BEST action for the project manager to take?
options: Review one flawed update together, showing how the missing links distort the critical path, and agree on a self-check to use.
Correct the logic links personally before each report goes out so the scheduler is not discouraged by a series of repeated corrections.
Reassign the scheduling work to a senior planner and give the new scheduler lower-risk administrative tasks for a while.
Note both errors in the scheduler's performance file and ask the functional manager to arrange formal scheduling training.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Coaching — building a person's capability through specific, timely feedback and a concrete way to improve. It fits a performance gap in someone who is motivated to grow.
Spot it: a new person, the same kind of error twice, motivation, and a direct request for feedback.
In this scenario: reviewing one flawed update together shows how missing links distort the critical path, and an agreed self-check lets the scheduler catch the error alone next time.
Why not the others: Quietly fixing the links hides the lesson, so the errors repeat; reassigning the work removes the person before any coaching; filing the errors and requesting formal training escalates before the PM has given direct feedback.
Remember: Training fills a skill gap, coaching grows performance, mentoring builds a career. Talk to the person FIRST, privately.

questions.stem: Match each stakeholder engagement level with its description.
matching_right: Knows about the project but neither supports nor opposes it
Does not yet know about the project or its impacts
Knows about the project and backs its changes
Actively engaged and helps drive the project to success
Knows about the project but opposes it or its changes

answer.Unaware: Does not yet know about the project or its impacts
answer.Resistant: Knows about the project but opposes it or its changes
answer.Neutral: Knows about the project but neither supports nor opposes it
answer.Supportive: Knows about the project and backs its changes
answer.Leading: Actively engaged and helps drive the project to success

questions.explanation:
Concept: The stakeholder engagement assessment matrix rates each stakeholder's current (C) and desired (D) engagement on five levels, so the PM can plan how to close the gap.
Unaware: does not know about the project yet, so the first job is to inform.
Resistant: knows about the project but opposes it; needs targeted engagement, never avoidance.
Neutral: aware, but neither for nor against; often the easiest to move toward support.
Supportive: aware and backs the changes; keep them engaged and informed.
Leading: actively engaged and helps drive success, such as a champion or sponsor.
Remember: Unaware → Resistant → Neutral → Supportive → Leading. Not everyone must reach Leading; close the gap between C and D.

questions.stem: Match each step of the sender-receiver communication model with its description.
matching_right: Receiver converts the message back into meaningful thoughts
Sender converts thoughts or ideas into a message
Receiver signals the message arrived, not necessarily agreement
Message is sent through a channel such as email or phone
Receiver replies to show understanding or agreement

answer.Encode: Sender converts thoughts or ideas into a message
answer.Transmit: Message is sent through a channel such as email or phone
answer.Decode: Receiver converts the message back into meaningful thoughts
answer.Acknowledge: Receiver signals the message arrived, not necessarily agreement
answer.Feedback/response: Receiver replies to show understanding or agreement

questions.explanation:
Concept: The sender-receiver model shows how a message travels and where misunderstanding can creep in (noise).
Encode: the sender turns thoughts into words, images, or data.
Transmit: the message travels through a channel such as email, phone, or a meeting.
Decode: the receiver turns the message back into meaning, filtered by language, culture, and noise.
Acknowledge: the receiver confirms it arrived; this is NOT agreement.
Feedback/response: the receiver replies, showing understanding or agreement, which closes the loop.
Remember: Sender owns a clear message; receiver confirms understanding. "Got it" is not "I agree."

questions.topic: Team development: storming stage and working agreements
questions.stem: Two sprints after a new agile team formed to build a fleet-tracking app, developers are openly arguing about code review practices and who should approve merges. Delivery has slowed, and one developer asks the team facilitator to just pick a rule. What should the team facilitator do?
options: Set the code review and merge rules personally so the developers can stop arguing and return to delivering stories.
Give the developers a few more sprints to settle their differences, since this stage of team growth resolves itself.
Facilitate a session where the developers agree on review and merge working agreements that they record and own.
Ask the product owner to decide on the review rules, since the product owner is accountable for the team's output.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tuckman's storming stage — conflict over roles and ways of working is a normal stage. The leader coaches the team toward norming by helping it create its own working agreements.
Spot it: a newly formed team, open arguments about how to work, slowed delivery, and someone asking the leader to "just pick a rule."
In this scenario: facilitating a session where the developers agree on and record their own review and merge rules moves them from storming to norming, with ownership.
Why not the others: Setting the rules personally ends the argument but removes team ownership; waiting it out is withdrawing, and storming does not reliably fix itself; the product owner owns value and backlog order, not the team's engineering practices.
Remember: Forming = direct, Storming = coach, Norming = reinforce, Performing = delegate, Adjourning = celebrate and release.

questions.stem: On a predictive production-line installation, each work package is led by an experienced engineer, yet every minor sequencing or purchasing decision waits for the project manager's approval. Work is stalling, and the engineers say they feel like order-takers. Which TWO actions should the project manager take to empower the work package leads?
options: Set decision limits that let each lead approve changes within the budget and float allocated to that work package.
Keep approving each minor decision personally but hold the approval meeting daily to reduce the waiting time.
Send every work package decision to the change control board so each one is formally reviewed and documented.
Give the leads direct access to the cost and schedule data they need to make and justify their own decisions.
Replace the current leads with more senior engineers who can be trusted to make the right calls on their own.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Empowerment — push decisions to the lowest competent level, with clear limits and the information needed to decide well.
Spot it: experienced leads, every minor decision waiting on the PM, stalled work, and people who feel like "order-takers."
In this scenario: decision limits tied to each work package's budget and float, plus direct access to cost and schedule data, let the leads decide and justify their own calls.
Why not the others: Daily approval meetings keep the PM as the bottleneck; sending minor in-baseline decisions to the change control board misuses change control and slows work further; replacing the leads treats a delegation problem as a people problem.
Remember: Empower = authority + boundaries + information. Only changes to APPROVED baselines go to the CCB.

questions.stem: The marketing vice president for an agile team building a smart-home app wants 12 features ready for a trade show in six weeks. Based on the team's recent sprints, about eight of those features can realistically be finished by then. What should the product owner do?
options: Share the team's delivery forecast and work with the vice president to identify which features matter most for the show.
Commit to all 12 features and ask the developers to work extra hours during the final two sprints so the gap is closed in time.
Refuse the request and state that the team will deliver only the eight features that fit its historical velocity.
Split the difference by committing to ten features so both the vice president and the team give up something.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Interest-based negotiation — separate people from the problem, focus on interests rather than positions, and use objective data to find the best-value outcome.
Spot it: a demand bigger than the team's evidence-based capacity, a fixed event date, and a stakeholder with a real business goal behind the request.
In this scenario: the team's forecast is the objective criterion, and the product owner uses it with the vice president to pick the features that matter most for the show.
Why not the others: Committing to all 12 with overtime breaks sustainable pace and ignores the data; flatly refusing is positional and ignores the VP's goal; splitting the difference at ten is an arbitrary compromise that still overcommits.
Remember: Interests, not positions. Data, not pressure. The PO trades scope; the team protects quality.

questions.topic: Organizational structures and project manager authority
questions.stem: Match each organizational structure with the project manager's typical level of authority.
matching_right: PM and functional manager share authority over resources
Team reports directly to the PM, who controls the budget
PM holds more authority, usually as a full-time role
Department managers run the work; the PM role is minimal
PM mainly coordinates; the functional manager controls resources

answer.Functional: Department managers run the work; the PM role is minimal
answer.Weak matrix: PM mainly coordinates; the functional manager controls resources
answer.Balanced matrix: PM and functional manager share authority over resources
answer.Strong matrix: PM holds more authority, usually as a full-time role
answer.Projectized: Team reports directly to the PM, who controls the budget

questions.explanation:
Concept: Organizational structure decides how much authority the project manager has over people and budget.
Functional: work runs through department managers; the PM role is part-time with little authority.
Weak matrix: the PM is mostly a coordinator or expediter; the functional manager still controls resources.
Balanced matrix: authority is shared, so the PM negotiates for resources with functional managers.
Strong matrix: the PM has more authority, usually a full-time role with more budget control.
Projectized: the team reports directly to the PM, who controls resources and budget.
Remember: Functional → Weak → Balanced → Strong → Projectized: PM authority goes from LOW to HIGH.

questions.topic: Motivation: connecting the team to purpose
questions.stem: Developers on an agile team building a grocery delivery app tell their team coach that their work feels pointless. They finish stories every sprint but never hear whether shoppers use the features, and participation in team events is dropping. What should the team coach do?
options: Offer a spot bonus to the developer who completes the most story points each sprint to raise engagement.
Ask the product owner to raise the sprint commitment so the developers feel more challenged and stretched by the work.
Cut team events down to the daily stand-up so the developers have more uninterrupted time for coding.
Arrange for customers or support staff to share real usage feedback with the developers during sprint reviews.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Intrinsic motivation — purpose, autonomy, and mastery drive knowledge workers more than extrinsic rewards. Seeing the real impact of their work restores purpose.
Spot it: "feels pointless," no word on whether users benefit, and falling participation.
In this scenario: bringing customers or support staff into sprint reviews to share real usage connects the developers to the value they create.
Why not the others: A bonus for the most story points is an extrinsic reward that pits developers against each other and invites padded estimates; raising the sprint commitment adds pressure, not meaning; cutting team events removes the very feedback loops they are missing.
Remember: Money removes complaints; purpose creates energy. Show the team who they are building for.

questions.topic: Conflict resolution: forcing/directing when safety is at stake
questions.stem: On a predictive bridge-rehabilitation project, a lift of steel girders is scheduled to begin within the hour. The site engineer and the crane subcontractor's supervisor disagree about whether current wind speeds are within the lift plan's limits, and the discussion is going in circles. What should the project manager do?
options: Halt the lift under the site safety procedures until wind readings are confirmed within limits, then address the dispute.
Ask both parties to meet halfway by lifting only half of the girders today and leaving the rest until tomorrow.
Let the crane supervisor proceed, since the subcontractor is contractually responsible for the safety of all of its own lifts.
Arrange a facilitated workshop later this week so both parties can reach a shared view of acceptable wind conditions.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Forcing (directing) — a win-lose conflict mode that is right only for emergencies, safety, or ethics, when there is no time to collaborate.
Spot it: a safety hazard, a decision needed within the hour, and a discussion "going in circles."
In this scenario: the PM halts the lift under the site safety procedures until wind readings are confirmed, then works through the disagreement.
Why not the others: Lifting half the girders is a compromise that still exposes workers to the same wind; letting the subcontractor proceed gives away the PM's safety duty; a workshop later in the week is collaborating, but there is no time and the lift is minutes away.
Remember: Collaborate is the default; FORCE only for safety, ethics, or emergencies. Safety first, discussion second.

questions.stem: Functional managers keep pulling members of a predictive data-center migration team into unrelated operational meetings. The team tells the project manager it cannot concentrate on the cutover tasks, and two schedule activities are slipping. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Increase status reporting so the functional managers can see how busy the migration team already is.
Negotiate with the functional managers to protect the migration team from nonessential operational meetings.
Tell the team to decline every meeting invitation from their functional managers without discussion.
Add the lost meeting time to the schedule baseline as a new activity so the delays are formally explained.
Ask the team which other obstacles are slowing the migration work and commit to clearing the ones they name.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Servant leadership: shielding the team — the servant leader protects the team from distractions and actively asks about and clears obstacles.
Spot it: outside managers pulling team members into unrelated work, lost focus, and slipping activities.
In this scenario: negotiating with the functional managers to protect the team's time, and asking the team what else is in the way, both remove impediments at the source.
Why not the others: More status reporting adds work without stopping the pull; telling the team to decline every invitation pushes the conflict onto team members; adding the lost time to the baseline accepts the obstacle instead of removing it.
Remember: The PM stands between the team and the noise: shield, ask, remove.

questions.stem: An agile team at an insurance company has missed its sprint goal three sprints in a row, each time pulling in more work than it finished. In the latest retrospective, team members blamed unclear stories but proposed no changes. How should the scrum master respond?
options: Set a firm cap on the stories the team may pull next sprint based on the scrum master's own analysis.
Ask the product owner to rewrite every story in full detail before the next planning event so that nothing is left unclear.
Report the missed goals to the team's functional manager so the pattern is visible outside the team.
Ask open questions that help the team examine its planning data and choose one improvement to try next sprint.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Coaching with powerful questions — the agile coach helps the team find its own insight and choose its own improvement, so the team owns the change.
Spot it: a repeated pattern (overcommitting), blame without action in the retrospective, and a self-managing team.
In this scenario: open questions that point the team to its own planning data help it pick one improvement to try next sprint.
Why not the others: Capping stories from the scrum master's own analysis is telling, not coaching; having the product owner write every story in full detail treats the symptom and slows flow; reporting to the functional manager escalates outside the team before any coaching.
Remember: Ask, don't tell. Retrospective → one small experiment → check it next sprint.

questions.topic: Stakeholder engagement: tailoring engagement to stakeholder needs
questions.stem: An agile team building an online loan application has had two increments rejected late by the bank's compliance officer, who has not attended any sprint reviews. The officer says the reviews are too long and mostly irrelevant to compliance. What should the product owner do?
options: Send the officer the full sprint review recording every sprint so the officer can watch it when convenient.
Agree with the officer on a short, focused review of compliance items each sprint and capture the officer's criteria early.
Escalate the late rejections to the sponsor and ask that the compliance sign-off step be removed from the release process.
Keep building increments as planned and schedule a full compliance review with the officer before final release.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tailored stakeholder engagement — engage each stakeholder in a way that fits their needs, early and often, so their criteria shape the work before it is built.
Spot it: late rejections, a key approver skipping reviews, and a clear reason given ("too long, mostly irrelevant").
In this scenario: a short, focused compliance review each sprint, plus capturing the officer's criteria up front, turns late rejection into early feedback.
Why not the others: Sending full recordings is push communication that ignores the officer's stated concern; removing the sign-off step bypasses a legitimate compliance control; one review before release delays feedback until change is most expensive.
Remember: Identify → Analyze → Engage → Monitor. Fit the engagement to the stakeholder, not the stakeholder to the meeting.

questions.stem: A predictive telecom tower project has a core team of 8 people, including the project manager. After a scope change is approved, 4 more engineers join the team. How many additional communication channels does the project manager now need to manage?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Communication channels = n(n−1)/2, where n is the number of people, including the project manager. Channels grow much faster than headcount.
Spot it: "how many channels," a team size that changes, and the word "additional."
In this scenario: 8 people give 8×7/2 = 28 channels; 12 people give 12×11/2 = 66 channels; the increase is 66 − 28 = 38.
Why not the others: 28 is the old total; 66 is the new total, not the increase; 48 comes from multiplying the new members by the new team size (4 × 12) instead of using the formula.
Remember: n(n−1)/2, count the PM, and read the question: "total" or "additional"?

questions.topic: Team development: team charter and ground rules
questions.stem: A hybrid retail-analytics project brings together an in-house adaptive analytics team and a vendor's infrastructure crew working to a fixed plan. In the first two weeks, handoffs are confused because each group assumes different working hours, tools, and ways to raise problems. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the vendor's account manager to require the infrastructure crew to adopt the in-house team's practices.
Facilitate a joint session where both groups agree on shared ground rules and record them in a team charter.
Keep the two groups apart and route every handoff through the project manager to prevent further confusion.
Wait until the first phase gate review to assess whether the confusion is affecting the infrastructure dates.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Team charter — the team, with the PM, agrees on values, working hours, tools, decision rules, and how to raise problems. It is created together, not imposed.
Spot it: a newly mixed team, different assumptions about hours, tools, and escalation, and confused handoffs.
In this scenario: a joint session where both groups agree on ground rules and record them in a team charter gives everyone one set of norms.
Why not the others: Having the vendor force its crew to adopt in-house practices imposes rules and cuts buy-in; routing every handoff through the PM creates a bottleneck and keeps the groups apart; waiting for the phase gate lets the confusion grow for weeks.
Remember: Team charter = created BY the team, WITH the PM. New team or new friction → revisit the charter.

questions.topic: Empowerment: self-organization in the adaptive stream
questions.stem: Developers in the adaptive stream of a hybrid banking project wait for the project manager to assign their daily tasks and ask permission for most technical choices. The predictive back-end work is on track, but the adaptive stream's progress is slow. Which TWO actions will BEST empower the adaptive team?
options: Let the developers select and sequence their own tasks from the prioritized work during planning.
Assign each developer's daily tasks personally until the team learns what good sequencing looks like.
Agree with the team on which technical decisions it can make itself and which need architecture review.
Tell the team that every decision is now theirs, including budget changes and contract amendments.
Require developers to submit written justifications for technical choices before starting any work.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Self-organization in adaptive work — the team pulls and sequences its own work and makes technical decisions within clear boundaries.
Spot it: developers waiting for daily assignments and asking permission, and a slow adaptive stream while the predictive side is fine.
In this scenario: letting developers select and sequence their own tasks, and agreeing which technical decisions they own versus which need architecture review, builds autonomy with guardrails.
Why not the others: Assigning daily tasks keeps them dependent; declaring every decision theirs, including budget and contracts, over-delegates beyond the team's authority; written justifications before any work add control, not trust.
Remember: Agile work is PULLED, not pushed. Empowered does not mean unlimited: define the boundaries.

questions.stem: Match each conflict resolution mode with its description.
matching_right: Imposes one view as win-lose; suits safety or emergencies
Emphasizes agreement and downplays differences to keep harmony
Retreats from or postpones the issue, such as for a cool-down
Each side gives up something to reach a partly satisfying deal
Works through underlying interests to reach a lasting win-win solution

answer.Collaborate/problem solve: Works through underlying interests to reach a lasting win-win solution
answer.Compromise/reconcile: Each side gives up something to reach a partly satisfying deal
answer.Smooth/accommodate: Emphasizes agreement and downplays differences to keep harmony
answer.Force/direct: Imposes one view as win-lose; suits safety or emergencies
answer.Withdraw/avoid: Retreats from or postpones the issue, such as for a cool-down

questions.explanation:
Concept: The five conflict resolution modes differ in how fully each side's concerns are met; pick the mode that fits the situation.
Collaborate/problem solve: works through underlying interests to a lasting win-win; PMI's default when time allows.
Compromise/reconcile: each side gives something up; useful when time is short, but nobody fully wins.
Smooth/accommodate: stresses agreement and plays down differences; keeps the peace only for a while.
Force/direct: one view is imposed (win-lose); reserve it for safety, ethics, or emergencies.
Withdraw/avoid: steps back or postpones; acceptable only for a cool-down or a trivial issue.
Remember: Collaborate first, force only for safety, and withdraw is the weakest choice.

questions.stem: The adaptive team on a hybrid logistics-software project includes testers in Manila who rarely speak during video calls with the Chicago developers. The project manager later learns the testers had spotted defects but felt it was impolite to contradict senior developers in a group setting. What should the project manager do?
options: Tell the testers that they must speak up in every call, because open disagreement is expected from all members of this team.
Move all defect discussions into the Chicago developers' weekly design meeting, where decisions are final.
Create other channels, such as one-on-one check-ins or a shared defect board, that suit the testers' cultural norms.
Ask the Chicago developers to review each other's code more closely so tester feedback is less necessary.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Cultural awareness and emotional intelligence — people from some cultures avoid contradicting seniors in public, so the leader adapts the channels so everyone can contribute safely.
Spot it: silence in group calls, a later discovery that people held back, and a stated cultural reason.
In this scenario: one-on-one check-ins and a shared defect board let the testers raise defects in a way that fits their norms.
Why not the others: Demanding that they speak up in every call ignores the cause of the silence; moving defects into a meeting where decisions are final shuts them out further; more peer code review among developers works around, rather than restores, the testers' input.
Remember: Don't assume your norms apply. Change the channel, not the person.

questions.topic: Motivation: Herzberg motivators vs. hygiene factors
questions.stem: A project manager on a predictive manufacturing-plant expansion has already fixed the team's complaints about the cramped site office and late expense reimbursements. The engineers are no longer complaining, but they remain unenthusiastic about their work. Which TWO actions are MOST likely to increase their motivation?
options: Upgrade the site office furniture and parking arrangements for all project team members.
Move the engineering team's salary reviews from once a year to twice a year going forward.
Give experienced engineers responsibility for leading design reviews in their areas of expertise.
Introduce stricter attendance tracking so engineers know their effort is monitored.
Recognize specific achievements publicly at the monthly project review with the client present.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Herzberg's two-factor theory — hygiene factors (pay, conditions, policies) only prevent dissatisfaction; motivators (achievement, responsibility, recognition, growth) create real motivation.
Spot it: complaints already fixed, "no longer complaining," yet still unenthusiastic.
In this scenario: giving experienced engineers responsibility for design reviews and publicly recognizing specific achievements are both motivators.
Why not the others: Better furniture and parking are hygiene factors; more frequent salary reviews are also hygiene; stricter attendance tracking signals distrust (Theory X) and lowers motivation.
Remember: Hygiene = not unhappy. Motivators = energized. Hygiene fixed? Now add responsibility and recognition.

questions.topic: Conflict resolution: using data to resolve a technical disagreement
questions.stem: Two senior developers on an agile team disagree about whether to use a message queue or direct API calls for a new payments feature. The rest of the team is split, and the argument has stalled refinement for two sessions even though both options seem viable. What should the scrum master do?
options: Help the team agree on a short, time-boxed spike to test both options and decide using the results.
Choose the option the more experienced developer prefers so that refinement can continue without delay.
Ask the product owner to make the architecture decision, since the product owner orders the backlog.
Remove the item from refinement until the two developers settle the disagreement between themselves.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Data-driven collaboration — when two technical options are both viable, let evidence decide; a time-boxed spike produces that evidence.
Spot it: two viable technical options, a split team, and refinement stalled for two sessions.
In this scenario: the scrum master helps the team agree on a short spike to test both options, keeping the decision with the developers.
Why not the others: Picking the more experienced developer's preference is forcing by seniority; the product owner owns value and ordering, not architecture; parking the item until the two settle it is withdrawing.
Remember: Opinions argue; data decides. Spike = time-boxed learning.

questions.stem: A department head keeps walking into an agile team's workspace to ask developers for status updates, often pulling them away from pairing sessions. The developers are frustrated but do not want to upset a senior leader. What should the scrum master do?
options: Tell the developers to politely refuse to answer the department head's questions and to keep working on their current tasks.
Meet with the department head to learn what information is needed and offer a way to get it without interruptions.
Ask the developers to write a status note each morning for the department head to review at any time.
Report the department head's behavior to human resources as a disruption of the team's working agreements.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Servant leadership: protecting focus — engage the interrupting stakeholder and meet the real information need through agile transparency.
Spot it: a senior leader interrupting developers for status, frustration, and reluctance to push back on a senior person.
In this scenario: the scrum master meets the department head to learn what information is needed and offers non-disruptive sources such as the team board or sprint review.
Why not the others: Telling developers to refuse puts them in conflict with a senior leader; daily status notes stop the interruptions but add non-value-adding work; reporting to human resources escalates before a simple conversation.
Remember: Talk to the person FIRST. Information radiators answer "What's the status?" without interrupting anyone.

questions.topic: Coaching: helping a new product owner work incrementally
questions.stem: On a hybrid utility-billing project, a veteran business analyst has just become product owner for the adaptive customer-portal stream. She is writing a complete 200-page specification before the team starts, and the developers are idle. What should the project manager do?
options: Let her finish the full specification first, because thorough requirements reduce rework in later phases.
Ask the sponsor to replace her with an experienced product owner from another department right away.
Have the developers start building from the draft specification's first chapter without her involvement.
Work alongside her to split the highest-value needs into small items the team can start on while details emerge.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Coaching a new product owner in progressive elaboration — in adaptive work, requirements emerge; start with the highest-value items and refine details just in time.
Spot it: a predictive habit (a 200-page specification) inside an adaptive stream, an idle team, and a person new to the role.
In this scenario: working alongside her to slice top-priority needs into small items lets the team start now while details emerge.
Why not the others: Letting her finish the specification treats the adaptive stream as predictive and keeps the team idle; asking to replace her skips coaching; building without her removes the product owner from her own role.
Remember: Adaptive = just enough, just in time. Coach first; replacing someone is never the first move.

questions.stem: A hybrid campus-housing project has a university chief financial officer who approves funding for each phase but shows little interest in project details. The adaptive app team holds monthly demos, and the predictive construction team sends weekly technical reports. How should the project manager engage the CFO?
options: Give concise updates on costs and benefits before each funding decision and consult the CFO on major financial choices.
Invite the CFO to every monthly app demo and copy the CFO on each of the weekly construction reports so nothing is missed.
Include the CFO only on the general project newsletter, since the CFO has shown little interest in details.
Ask the sponsor to handle all CFO communication so the project team can stay focused on delivery work.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Power/interest grid — a high-power, low-interest stakeholder is KEPT SATISFIED: concise, targeted information that meets their decision needs, without overload.
Spot it: approves funding (high power) but shows "little interest in project details" (low interest).
In this scenario: short cost-and-benefit updates before each funding decision, plus consultation on major financial choices, keep the CFO satisfied.
Why not the others: Every demo and every report treats the CFO as high-interest and buries the key message; the general newsletter alone under-engages the person who controls funding; handing all contact to the sponsor gives up the PM's engagement role.
Remember: Manage closely (high/high) • Keep satisfied (high power) • Keep informed (high interest) • Monitor (low/low).

questions.stem: Match each communication type with its best example.
matching_right: Quick email asking a colleague where a file is saved
Signed contract amendment sent to the supplier
Hallway conversation with a team member about progress
Presentation of project results to the steering committee

answer.Formal written: Signed contract amendment sent to the supplier
answer.Formal verbal: Presentation of project results to the steering committee
answer.Informal written: Quick email asking a colleague where a file is saved
answer.Informal verbal: Hallway conversation with a team member about progress

questions.explanation:
Concept: Communication is classified by formality (official or everyday) and by medium (written or verbal).
Formal written: official records such as contracts, amendments, and plans.
Formal verbal: structured spoken communication such as a presentation to a steering committee.
Informal written: quick everyday messages such as short emails or chats.
Informal verbal: casual conversations such as a hallway chat.
Remember: Contract or legal? Formal written. Sensitive or complex? Talk it through, then confirm it in writing.

questions.stem: Match each stage of Tuckman's team development model with its description.
matching_right: Members adjust habits and agree on working behaviors
Members meet, learn roles, and are polite and cautious
Team works interdependently and resolves issues smoothly
Members clash over approaches and compete for influence
Work is completed and team members are released

answer.Forming: Members meet, learn roles, and are polite and cautious
answer.Storming: Members clash over approaches and compete for influence
answer.Norming: Members adjust habits and agree on working behaviors
answer.Performing: Team works interdependently and resolves issues smoothly
answer.Adjourning: Work is completed and team members are released

questions.explanation:
Concept: Tuckman's ladder describes how a team develops and what the leader should do at each stage.
Forming: polite and uncertain; the PM gives clear direction and clarifies roles.
Storming: conflict over roles and approaches; the PM coaches and helps set ground rules.
Norming: working agreements take hold; the PM reinforces collaboration.
Performing: interdependent and self-directed; the PM delegates and empowers.
Adjourning: work completes; celebrate, capture lessons, and release people.
Remember: Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing → Adjourning. New members can send a team back to storming.

questions.stem: During sprint planning for a telehealth scheduling feature, nobody on the agile team volunteers for an unpopular database migration task. After a long pause, a developer asks the scrum master to assign it so planning can finish. What should the scrum master do?
options: Assign the migration to the developer with the most database experience so the right person does the work.
Ask the product owner to remove the migration from the sprint so the planning event can finish on time.
Ask the developers how they want to share the migration work, such as pairing or rotating, and let them decide.
Defer the migration to the next sprint and hope a developer volunteers once current work is complete.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Self-organization — in agile, the team decides who does which work; the scrum master facilitates rather than assigns.
Spot it: an unpopular task, silence, and a request that the scrum master "just assign it."
In this scenario: asking developers how they want to share the migration, such as pairing or rotating, keeps the decision and the ownership with the team.
Why not the others: Assigning it to the most experienced developer takes ownership away and builds dependence; removing it through the product owner dodges necessary work; deferring and hoping someone volunteers is avoiding.
Remember: Agile work is PULLED by the team, not PUSHED by a manager.

questions.topic: Negotiation: prioritizing by value and cost of delay
questions.stem: Two agile teams at a streaming company both need the same platform team's help next sprint, and the platform team can support only one. The two product owners each insist their feature is more urgent, and neither will yield. What should the agile coach facilitating the discussion do?
options: Suggest the platform team split its capacity evenly so that each product owner receives half of the support.
Escalate the disagreement to the vice president of engineering to choose which feature should go first.
Guide both product owners to compare the business value and cost of delay of each feature and agree on an order.
Let the platform team pick whichever request is technically easier so it can finish more work next sprint.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Negotiating on objective criteria — business value and cost of delay give competing product owners a shared, fair basis for ordering work.
Spot it: two firm positions, one scarce shared team, and neither side yielding.
In this scenario: the coach guides both product owners to compare value and cost of delay and agree on which feature goes first.
Why not the others: Splitting capacity evenly is a compromise that may leave both features unfinished; escalating to the vice president skips facilitation; letting the platform team choose the easier request ignores value.
Remember: Positions clash; criteria converge. Value + cost of delay = which goes first.

questions.topic: Virtual teams: choosing a richer communication medium
questions.stem: On a predictive offshore wind-farm design project, engineers in Denmark and Texas have been debating a foundation design change through a long email chain. The messages are becoming sharp, and each side believes the other is dismissing its concerns. What should the project manager do?
options: Set up a video meeting where both groups can discuss the design change directly and clear up misread intentions.
Ask both groups to keep emailing but copy the project manager so that the tone of each message can be monitored.
Instruct both groups to stop discussing the change until the next scheduled monthly design review meeting.
Send the design change to the change control board so that the board can choose between the two positions.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Choosing a rich communication medium — complex or emotionally charged topics need interactive, real-time communication where tone and intent are clear.
Spot it: a long email chain, a sharpening tone, and each side feeling dismissed.
In this scenario: a video meeting lets both groups discuss the design change directly and clear up misread intentions.
Why not the others: Copying the PM on more email keeps the weak medium and adds policing; stopping discussion until the monthly review is withdrawing; sending an unprepared change to the CCB skips the technical discussion and does not repair the relationship.
Remember: Email for facts, conversation for conflict. Interactive beats push when it is sensitive.

questions.stem: On a predictive manufacturing-plant expansion, a process engineer thrives on difficult goals, asks often for concrete feedback on her performance, and prefers solving problems on her own rather than coordinating others. Which TWO assignments would BEST motivate her?
options: Ask her to coordinate the team's social events and client relationship activities for the phase.
Assign her a challenging but achievable work package with clear targets and regular performance feedback.
Place her in a supervisory role where her success depends mainly on influencing other people.
Give her ownership of a technical problem that other engineers have so far been unable to solve.
Give her routine, low-risk tasks so that she can build confidence before taking on harder work.
questions.explanation:
Concept: McClelland's acquired needs theory — people are driven mostly by achievement, affiliation, or power; match the assignment to the dominant need.
Spot it: loves difficult goals, wants concrete feedback, and prefers solving problems alone: a high need for achievement.
In this scenario: a challenging but achievable work package with clear targets and feedback, and ownership of an unsolved technical problem, both feed achievement.
Why not the others: Social coordination fits a need for affiliation; a supervisory role fits a need for power; routine low-risk tasks give an achiever nothing to strive for.
Remember: Achievement = challenge + feedback. Affiliation = belonging. Power = influence.

questions.topic: Conflict resolution: addressing conflict early and privately
questions.stem: Two engineers on a predictive rail-signaling project have been trading tense remarks in team meetings about who caused a missed test date. Other team members are becoming uncomfortable, although the engineers' own work remains on schedule. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Raise the missed test date at the next team meeting so everyone can discuss who was responsible for it.
Talk privately with the two engineers together to address the tension and help them work it out directly.
Report both engineers to their functional managers and request that one of them be moved elsewhere.
Leave the matter alone, since their work remains on schedule and the tension will likely pass on its own.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Address conflict early and privately — conflict is normal, but the people involved should work it out directly before it harms the team.
Spot it: tense remarks, discomfort spreading to others, and work still on schedule (so it is not yet a schedule crisis).
In this scenario: a private conversation with both engineers together lets them deal with the tension directly.
Why not the others: Discussing blame in a team meeting makes it public and personal; reporting both to their functional managers escalates first; leaving it alone is withdrawing while it already affects others.
Remember: Praise in public, correct in private. Talk to the people involved FIRST.

questions.stem: Progress by the adaptive team on a hybrid manufacturing-execution-system project has slowed. Test hardware it needs is stuck in a purchasing approval queue, and the plant's operations staff keep pulling developers into unplanned support tickets. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Work with purchasing to speed up approval of the test hardware the adaptive team is waiting for.
Tell the developers to handle the support tickets after hours so project work is not affected.
Track each developer's time on support tickets and report it to their managers every week.
Re-baseline the adaptive team's release dates to absorb the delays caused by both obstacles.
Agree with the operations manager on a support rotation so developers are not pulled in at random.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Servant leadership: removing organizational impediments — some obstacles, such as approvals or other departments' demands, sit outside the team, and the leader clears them.
Spot it: hardware stuck in purchasing, random interruptions from operations, and slowed progress.
In this scenario: speeding up the purchase approval and agreeing on a support rotation with operations remove both obstacles at the source.
Why not the others: Handling tickets after hours burns the team out; tracking and reporting time exposes the problem without fixing it; re-baselining accepts the obstacles instead of removing them.
Remember: Impediment outside the team = the leader's job. Remove it before you re-plan around it.

questions.stem: On a hybrid insurance project, a newly promoted team lead now facilitates the adaptive stream's daily coordination meeting. The meetings regularly overrun by 20 minutes and turn into problem-solving sessions, and he has asked the project manager for help. Which TWO actions should the project manager take to help him?
options: Run the meetings yourself until he feels confident enough to take them back over from you.
Observe a few of his meetings and give him specific, timely feedback on what to keep and change.
Ask him what outcome he wants from the meeting and help him plan practical ways to reach it.
Tell the team to be patient, since he is new to the role and will improve with more practice.
Send him an online course link and review his progress again at the next phase gate review.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Coaching through observation and questions — watch the person in action, give specific timely feedback, and ask questions that help them own the fix.
Spot it: a newly promoted lead, a clear behavior (meetings that overrun and drift), and a request for help.
In this scenario: observing his meetings and giving specific feedback, and asking what outcome he wants and planning how to reach it, build his skill.
Why not the others: Running the meetings yourself removes his chance to learn; telling the team to be patient ignores his request for help; a course link reviewed at the next gate is too distant and generic.
Remember: Coach = observe + feedback + questions. Don't take the work back.

questions.stem: Midway through a predictive wastewater-plant expansion, a project manager learns that a regional environmental agency must review the discharge design, which nobody identified during planning. The agency has not yet contacted the project. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Submit a change request to extend the schedule baseline to allow for the agency's review period.
Proceed with the current design and respond to the agency only if it raises concerns about it.
Ask the sponsor to contact the agency directly and request that its review be waived for this particular project.
Add the agency to the stakeholder register and assess its interest, influence, and approval requirements.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stakeholder identification is iterative — a newly discovered stakeholder goes into the register and is analyzed before engagement is planned or changes are requested.
Spot it: a party with approval power that "nobody identified," discovered midway through the project.
In this scenario: the PM adds the agency to the stakeholder register and assesses its interest, influence, and approval requirements.
Why not the others: A change request is premature because the impact is not yet known; waiting for the agency to raise concerns risks a late rejection; asking the sponsor to seek a waiver sidesteps a legitimate regulator.
Remember: Identify → Analyze → Engage → Monitor, and identify again whenever someone new appears.

questions.topic: Communication methods: interactive, push, pull, osmotic
questions.stem: Match each communication method with its best example.
matching_right: Intranet dashboard that stakeholders check whenever they need it
Real-time workshop where participants exchange views and decide together
Colocated team members absorb information by overhearing nearby discussions
Weekly status report emailed to a defined distribution list

answer.Interactive: Real-time workshop where participants exchange views and decide together
answer.Push: Weekly status report emailed to a defined distribution list
answer.Pull: Intranet dashboard that stakeholders check whenever they need it
answer.Osmotic: Colocated team members absorb information by overhearing nearby discussions

questions.explanation:
Concept: Communication methods describe HOW information reaches people.
Interactive: real-time, multi-way exchange such as meetings or workshops; best for complex or sensitive topics.
Push: sent to specific recipients, such as emailed reports; no proof it was understood.
Pull: recipients fetch it when needed, such as dashboards; suits large audiences.
Osmotic: colocated members absorb information by overhearing; a benefit of agile team spaces.
Remember: Interactive = talk • Push = send • Pull = fetch • Osmotic = overhear.

questions.topic: Team development tools and their purpose
questions.stem: Match each team development tool with its purpose.
matching_right: Shows when each team member is available to work on the project
Records team values, agreements, and ground rules for working together
Places team members in one location to improve collaboration
Shows who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed per activity

answer.Team charter: Records team values, agreements, and ground rules for working together
answer.RACI chart: Shows who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed per activity
answer.Resource calendar: Shows when each team member is available to work on the project
answer.Colocation: Places team members in one location to improve collaboration

questions.explanation:
Concept: These tools help a team know how it works together, who does what, and when people are available.
Team charter: the team's own values, ground rules, and working norms, created by the team.
RACI chart: a responsibility assignment matrix: Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed for each activity.
Resource calendar: shows when each person or resource is available.
Colocation: places the team together (a tight matrix or war room) to boost communication and trust.
Remember: Charter = HOW we work • RACI = WHO does it • Calendar = WHEN available • Colocation = WHERE together.

questions.stem: A quality technician on a predictive aircraft-seating manufacturing project suggests a new fixture that could cut inspection time in half. She has the skills to design it, and the idea would not affect the scope, schedule, or cost baselines. What should the project manager do?
options: Encourage her to design and trial the fixture, offering support and agreed check-ins on the results.
Submit the fixture idea to the change control board for formal approval before any work begins.
Ask the quality manager to design the fixture instead, since process changes are a management task.
Thank her for the idea and add it to the lessons learned register for use on future projects.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Empowering team-led improvement — a capable member proposing an improvement within her competence gets ownership and support, not formal control.
Spot it: a skilled technician, a good idea, and the explicit fact that it "would not affect the scope, schedule, or cost baselines."
In this scenario: encouraging her to design and trial the fixture with agreed check-ins empowers her and captures the benefit now.
Why not the others: The CCB handles changes to approved baselines, so routing this there only adds delay; giving it to the quality manager takes ownership away; parking it in lessons learned delays a benefit available today.
Remember: Baseline = APPROVED, so only baseline changes need the CCB. Everything else: empower.

questions.topic: Negotiation: balancing technical debt and features
questions.stem: Developers on an agile claims-processing team want an entire sprint for refactoring because technical debt is slowing their work. The product owner wants to keep delivering features that customers have requested. Which TWO actions should the scrum master take?
options: Back the developers in refusing new features until the product owner approves a full refactoring sprint.
Advise the product owner to reject the refactoring, since customers only see value in new features.
Help the developers show how the technical debt is slowing delivery, using data from recent sprints.
Facilitate agreement on reserving part of each sprint's capacity for debt reduction alongside features.
Ask the team to refactor quietly inside feature estimates so the product owner does not have to agree.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Negotiating technical debt versus features — use objective data and find a solution that serves both interests, such as a steady capacity allocation.
Spot it: developers want a whole refactoring sprint, the product owner wants features, and both interests are valid.
In this scenario: showing with sprint data how debt slows delivery, and agreeing to reserve part of each sprint for debt reduction, balances both sides.
Why not the others: Backing a refusal of new features is positional; advising the product owner to reject refactoring ignores the real cost of debt; hiding refactoring inside estimates breaks transparency.
Remember: Transparency + data + shared interest. Pay down debt a little every sprint.

questions.topic: Virtual teams: adapting team events across time zones
questions.stem: An agile team split between Sydney and London has only a short overlap in working hours. The daily stand-up is held at 9:00 a.m. London time, which is late at night in Sydney, and the Sydney members have become disengaged. What should the scrum master do?
options: Keep the current time, since the London members are the majority and a change would disrupt them.
Ask the product owner to choose a new meeting time, since the product owner is the person who sets the team's priorities.
Split the team into two separate teams by location, each working from its own product backlog.
Facilitate a team discussion to redesign daily coordination, such as rotating times or adding asynchronous updates.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Team-owned adaptation for distributed teams — the team decides how to adapt its events so every location can take part fairly; the scrum master facilitates.
Spot it: a short overlap in hours, a meeting time that suits one location, and disengaged remote members.
In this scenario: facilitating a team discussion about rotating times or asynchronous updates lets the team redesign its own coordination.
Why not the others: Keeping the time favors the majority and lets disengagement continue; the product owner orders the backlog, not meeting times; splitting the team by location breaks it apart instead of fixing the practice.
Remember: The team owns its process: fair for every location, decided by the team.

questions.stem: Rumors of layoffs after a hybrid bank-merger project have spread, and team members in both the adaptive and predictive streams are distracted and anxious about their jobs. Productivity is dropping. Which TWO actions will BEST address the team's motivation?
options: Work with HR and the sponsor to share accurate information about post-project roles as soon as possible.
Announce an employee-of-the-month award to boost enthusiasm for hitting the next milestone.
Organize a team social event to lift the team's spirits during the upcoming adaptive releases.
Hold one-on-one conversations to hear each person's concerns and explain the steps being taken.
Tell the team to focus on the work and avoid speculating about the upcoming reorganization.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Maslow's hierarchy — lower needs (physiological, safety) must be met before higher needs (belonging, esteem, self-actualization) can motivate.
Spot it: layoff rumors, anxiety about jobs, and falling productivity: an unmet safety need.
In this scenario: sharing accurate information about post-project roles and holding one-on-ones to hear concerns address job security directly.
Why not the others: An employee-of-the-month award targets esteem; a social event targets belonging; telling people to stop speculating dismisses the fear and leaves the rumor unanswered.
Remember: Physiological → Safety → Social → Esteem → Self-actualization. Fix the lowest unmet need first.

questions.topic: Conflict resolution: addressing root causes of recurring conflict
questions.stem: The construction supervisor and design coordinator on a predictive hotel-renovation project have argued over late drawings for the third time. Each time the project manager calmed things down by stressing their shared goals, but the arguments keep coming back. What should the project manager do NOW?
options: Keep emphasizing their common goals, since doing so has calmed each of the previous arguments quickly.
Bring both parties together to find out why the drawings are late and agree on a fix to the release process.
Instruct the design coordinator to release every drawing a week earlier, regardless of design completeness.
Add a recurring risk entry for late drawings and accept the delays as part of the project's reserves.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Root-cause problem solving for recurring conflict — smoothing calms things for a while, but only collaborating on the underlying cause stops the conflict from returning.
Spot it: "third time," "calmed things down," and "the arguments keep coming back."
In this scenario: bringing both parties together to find why drawings are late and agree on a fix to the release process addresses the cause.
Why not the others: More emphasis on common goals is the smoothing that already failed; ordering earlier releases regardless of completeness is forcing and creates quality problems; logging and accepting the delays gives up on a solvable problem.
Remember: Smoothing is a bandage; collaborating is the cure. Recurring = find the root cause.

questions.topic: Artifact ownership: who issues, approves, and updates
questions.stem: Match each hybrid project artifact with the role that owns it or approves changes to it.
matching_right: Developers create and adapt it to meet the sprint goal
Product owner is accountable for its content and ordering
Changed only after the change control board approves a request
Living record the project manager keeps updated with risk owners
Issued by the sponsor to authorize the project and the PM

answer.Project charter: Issued by the sponsor to authorize the project and the PM
answer.Schedule baseline: Changed only after the change control board approves a request
answer.Risk register: Living record the project manager keeps updated with risk owners
answer.Product backlog: Product owner is accountable for its content and ordering
answer.Sprint backlog: Developers create and adapt it to meet the sprint goal

questions.explanation:
Concept: Knowing who owns an artifact tells you who can change it, a core exam skill on hybrid projects.
Project charter: issued and approved by the sponsor; it authorizes the project and the PM.
Schedule baseline: an APPROVED target; changes need a change request approved by the change control board.
Risk register: a living log the PM keeps updated, with a named owner for each risk.
Product backlog: the product owner is accountable for its content and order.
Sprint backlog: the developers create and adapt it to reach the sprint goal.
Remember: Charter = AUTHORITY (sponsor) • Baseline = APPROVED (CCB) • Register = TRACK (PM) • Product backlog = PO • Sprint backlog = developers.

questions.stem: Match each situational leadership style with the situation where it fits best.
matching_right: Capable member who lacks confidence and needs encouragement
New team member with little skill who needs clear instructions
Skilled, confident member who can own decisions independently
Developing member who needs guidance and encouragement to grow

answer.Directing: New team member with little skill who needs clear instructions
answer.Coaching: Developing member who needs guidance and encouragement to grow
answer.Supporting: Capable member who lacks confidence and needs encouragement
answer.Delegating: Skilled, confident member who can own decisions independently

questions.explanation:
Concept: Situational leadership (Hersey-Blanchard) adjusts direction and support to a person's competence and commitment.
Directing: high direction, low support, for a new person with little skill.
Coaching: high direction and high support, for a developing person who is still learning.
Supporting: low direction, high support, for a capable person who lacks confidence.
Delegating: low direction and low support, for a skilled, confident person who can own decisions.
Remember: Direct → Coach → Support → Delegate as competence and confidence grow.

questions.topic: Stakeholder engagement: moving unaware stakeholders to supportive
questions.stem: Three months into a hybrid HR-system replacement, a project manager discovers that two regional department heads whose teams will use the new system have never heard of the project. The adaptive configuration team is about to begin user testing in their regions. What should the project manager do?
options: Proceed with user testing in both regions and introduce the project to the department heads after the results.
Brief both department heads on the project and its effect on their teams, then plan how to involve them in testing.
Ask the sponsor to issue a directive requiring both department heads to support user testing in their regions.
Move user testing to other regions where the department heads are already aware of the project and supportive.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stakeholder engagement levels — unaware stakeholders must first be informed and engaged before they can move toward supportive.
Spot it: "never heard of the project," their teams will use the system, and testing is about to start in their regions.
In this scenario: briefing both department heads on the project and its effect on their teams, then planning their involvement in testing, moves them from unaware toward supportive.
Why not the others: Testing first and informing later surprises them and invites resistance; a sponsor directive forces compliance, not support; moving testing elsewhere avoids stakeholders whose teams will still use the system.
Remember: Unaware → Resistant → Neutral → Supportive → Leading. Close the gap between current and desired.

questions.stem: Match each type of project manager power with its source.
matching_right: Ability to impose penalties or other negative consequences
Authority that comes from the assigned role or position
Influence earned through recognized knowledge and skill
Influence earned through respect, trust, and personal relationships
Ability to give recognition, bonuses, or desirable assignments

answer.Formal (legitimate): Authority that comes from the assigned role or position
answer.Reward: Ability to give recognition, bonuses, or desirable assignments
answer.Coercive: Ability to impose penalties or other negative consequences
answer.Expert: Influence earned through recognized knowledge and skill
answer.Referent: Influence earned through respect, trust, and personal relationships

questions.explanation:
Concept: A PM's power comes either from the position (granted) or from the person (earned); PMI prefers earned power.
Formal (legitimate): authority from the assigned role; it disappears if the role changes.
Reward: ability to give recognition, bonuses, or desirable assignments.
Coercive: ability to impose penalties; the weakest long-term influence and a last resort.
Expert: influence from recognized knowledge and skill; PMI's favorite.
Referent: influence from respect, trust, and relationships.
Remember: Granted = Formal, Reward, Coercive • Earned = Expert, Referent. Earned power lasts.

questions.topic: Team development: team regression when membership changes
questions.stem: A long-standing agile team that consistently met its sprint goals has just added two developers from a merged company. Within a week, debates over coding conventions have reappeared and team meetings are running long. What should the scrum master do?
options: Ask the new developers to adopt the existing agreements unchanged, since those agreements have worked well so far.
Facilitate a session in which the full team revisits and updates its working agreements with the new members.
Exclude the new developers from team events until they have observed how the team operates for a few sprints.
Report to management that the merged-company hires are reducing performance and request replacements for them.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Team regression — adding members can send a performing team back to forming or storming, so the whole team revisits its working agreements together.
Spot it: a stable team, new members, old debates coming back, and longer meetings.
In this scenario: facilitating a session where the full team updates its agreements gives the newcomers ownership and settles the conflict.
Why not the others: Making newcomers accept the old agreements unchanged denies them a voice and prolongs storming; excluding them from events delays integration; asking for replacements blames people for a normal stage.
Remember: New member = new team. Revisit the team charter together.

questions.stem: Team leads on a predictive substation-upgrade project are hesitant to make routine decisions because nobody has told them what they are allowed to approve. Decisions are piling up for the project manager, and several activities are waiting. Which TWO actions will BEST empower the team leads?
options: Clarify each lead's decision authority in the responsibility assignment matrix and share it with the team.
Require all decisions to be logged and then approved at the weekly meeting to keep them consistent.
Ask the sponsor to issue a memo telling the leads to use their own judgment on all project matters.
Set agreed cost and schedule thresholds within which leads can approve work without further consultation.
Take on the pending decisions personally to clear the queue before any roles are clarified for leads.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Clarifying decision authority — people can only act empowered when they know what they may decide and within what limits.
Spot it: hesitant leads, "nobody has told them what they are allowed to approve," and decisions piling up.
In this scenario: documenting each lead's authority in the responsibility assignment matrix and setting cost and schedule thresholds give clear, bounded decision rights.
Why not the others: Logging every decision for weekly approval keeps the PM as the bottleneck; a memo to use judgment on all matters is over-broad and still unclear; taking the pending decisions personally clears today's queue but leaves authority undefined.
Remember: Empower = clear roles (RACI) + clear limits (thresholds).

questions.stem: The hardware vendor on a hybrid airline-kiosk project wants to raise its unit price by 15 percent before signing the next phase agreement. The project manager has confirmed that a second qualified vendor could supply comparable kiosks within the schedule. What should the project manager do?
options: Accept the price increase to protect the relationship, since a vendor switch would disrupt the adaptive software team.
Tell the vendor that the contract will be moved to the second supplier unless the original unit price is kept without any change.
Ask the adaptive software team to cut features so that the budget can absorb the vendor's higher unit price instead.
Negotiate with the current vendor knowing the second supplier is a realistic fallback, and seek terms that serve both sides.
questions.explanation:
Concept: BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) — knowing your realistic fallback strengthens your position, so you can seek a fair win-win deal without caving or issuing ultimatums.
Spot it: a supplier raising its price and a confirmed, qualified alternative that fits the schedule.
In this scenario: the PM negotiates with the current vendor, confident in the fallback, and looks for terms that serve both sides.
Why not the others: Accepting the increase gives away value when a real alternative exists; an ultimatum is positional bargaining that can close off a better deal; cutting features to absorb the price shifts the cost onto the product without negotiating.
Remember: Know your BATNA, then negotiate on interests. An alternative is leverage, not a weapon.

questions.topic: Virtual teams: shared digital information radiator
questions.stem: An agile team split between Toronto and Bogotá tracks its work on a physical board in the Toronto office. Developers in Bogotá often start tasks that Toronto colleagues have already picked up, causing duplicated effort and frustration. What should the team coach do?
options: Help the team move its task board to a shared online tool that every member updates and can see in real time.
Ask a Toronto developer to email a photo of the physical board to the Bogotá developers at the end of each day.
Have the scrum master assign every task from now on so that no two developers can ever pick the same item.
Hold a second daily stand-up only for the Bogotá developers so they can coordinate their own task choices.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Information radiator for distributed teams — a shared, real-time visual board lets everyone see the same state of work.
Spot it: a physical board in one office and remote members duplicating work.
In this scenario: moving the board to a shared online tool that every member updates and sees in real time removes the duplication.
Why not the others: A daily photo is always out of date; having the scrum master assign every task breaks self-organization; a separate stand-up for one location splits the team's coordination.
Remember: Visible work = coordinated work. One board that everyone sees.

questions.stem: On a hybrid energy-trading platform project, a new functional manager has required skilled, self-driven engineers to log their activities every 15 minutes. Morale in both the adaptive and predictive streams has dropped, and two engineers are asking for transfers. Which TWO actions will BEST restore motivation?
options: Introduce penalties for missed daily targets so that performance expectations are clear to everyone.
Discuss with the functional manager replacing minute-level logging with outcome-based progress reviews.
Add a supervisor to check each engineer's work hourly during the adaptive portion of the project.
Offer a one-time cash bonus to engineers who accept the new time-tracking rules without objection.
Give the engineers more say in how they plan and carry out the work assigned to their streams.
questions.explanation:
Concept: McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y — Theory X assumes people need close control; Theory Y assumes capable people are self-motivated and respond to trust and autonomy. PMI prefers Theory Y.
Spot it: skilled, self-driven engineers, logging every 15 minutes, falling morale, and transfer requests.
In this scenario: replacing minute-level logging with outcome-based reviews and giving engineers more say in how they do their work restore trust and autonomy.
Why not the others: Penalties for missed targets are more Theory X control; an hourly supervisor adds even closer monitoring; a one-time bonus is an extrinsic reward that leaves the demotivating control in place.
Remember: X = control, Y = trust. Measure outcomes, not minutes.

questions.topic: Conflict resolution: definition of done under deadline pressure
questions.stem: As a release deadline approaches for an agile retail app, its product owner asks developers to skip automated regression tests for one story so it can ship this sprint. The developers refuse, and the argument grows heated. What should the scrum master do?
options: Support the product owner's request, since the product owner is the person accountable for deciding what gets released each sprint.
Side with the developers and inform the product owner that the story will not be released under any circumstances this sprint.
Facilitate a discussion of the risks of releasing work that does not meet the definition of done and of options that keep quality.
Let the story ship without the tests but add a new backlog item so that the missing tests are written during the next sprint.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Definition of done — the Scrum team's shared quality commitment. Work that does not meet it is not done and is not released.
Spot it: deadline pressure, a request to skip tests, and a heated product owner–developer standoff.
In this scenario: the scrum master facilitates a discussion of the risks of releasing undone work and of options that keep quality, such as splitting the story.
Why not the others: Backing the product owner ignores that the definition of done binds everyone; siding with the developers is forcing and closes off options; shipping now and adding a tests item later knowingly releases undone work and adds debt.
Remember: Done means DONE. Negotiate scope, never quality.

questions.topic: Servant leadership: supporting an overloaded team member
questions.stem: A normally reliable electrical engineer on a predictive factory-automation project has missed two deliverable dates. In a private conversation, he mentions that his workload from another project has doubled and he feels stretched too thin. What should the project manager do?
options: Remind the engineer that the project's deliverable dates are baselined and must be met no matter what.
Document the missed dates in his performance record and notify his functional manager about the lapse.
Work with the engineer and the other project's manager to rebalance his assignments across both efforts.
Reassign all of his remaining work to other engineers without first discussing the change with him.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Servant leadership: root cause over pressure — when a reliable person slips, find out why and remove the obstacle, here a competing workload.
Spot it: "normally reliable," and a private disclosure that his other workload has doubled.
In this scenario: working with the engineer and the other project's manager to rebalance assignments fixes the capacity conflict itself.
