Why not the others: Reminding him of baselined dates adds pressure without adding capacity; documenting and notifying his manager punishes instead of helping; reassigning all his work without discussion leaves him out of a decision about his own work.
Remember: A good performer dips? Ask, listen, then fix the system.

questions.stem: Match each motivation theory with its core idea.
matching_right: Managers assume people either need control or are self-motivated
Effort rises when people expect performance to earn a valued reward
People are driven mainly by achievement, affiliation, or power
Lower needs such as safety must be met before higher needs
Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators such as recognition create satisfaction

answer.Maslow's hierarchy: Lower needs such as safety must be met before higher needs
answer.Herzberg's two-factor theory: Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators such as recognition create satisfaction
answer.McGregor's Theory X and Y: Managers assume people either need control or are self-motivated
answer.McClelland's acquired needs: People are driven mainly by achievement, affiliation, or power
answer.Vroom's expectancy theory: Effort rises when people expect performance to earn a valued reward

questions.explanation:
Concept: Motivation theories explain what drives people, so the leader can choose the right action.
Maslow's hierarchy: needs form a ladder; lower needs such as safety come before esteem and growth.
Herzberg's two-factor theory: hygiene factors (pay, conditions) prevent dissatisfaction; motivators (recognition, growth) create satisfaction.
McGregor's Theory X and Y: managers assume people need control (X) or are self-motivated (Y); PMI prefers Y.
McClelland's acquired needs: each person has a dominant need: achievement, affiliation, or power.
Vroom's expectancy theory: effort rises when people believe it leads to performance and a reward they value.
Remember: Maslow = ladder • Herzberg = hygiene vs motivators • X/Y = control vs trust • McClelland = three needs • Vroom = effort → performance → valued reward.

questions.topic: Stakeholder engagement: meeting a sponsor's information needs in agile
questions.stem: A finance director sponsoring an agile budgeting-tool project asks for a task-level schedule showing exactly when each feature will be finished over the next six months. The team plans only two sprints in detail at a time. What should the product owner do?
options: Build the requested six-month task schedule and commit the team to delivering each feature on those exact calendar dates.
Explore which decisions the director needs to make and share a release roadmap and burnup forecast that support them.
Explain that agile teams do not forecast beyond two sprints and invite the director to the next sprint review.
Ask the scrum master to handle the director's request, since reporting to sponsors is the scrum master's job.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Meeting a sponsor's information needs in agile — ask what decision the request supports, then answer with adaptive forecasting tools such as a release roadmap and burnup chart.
Spot it: a sponsor asking for a predictive-style, task-level schedule on an agile project.
In this scenario: the product owner explores the decisions the director faces and shares a roadmap and a range-based burnup forecast.
Why not the others: A six-month task schedule with exact dates creates false precision; saying agile cannot forecast beyond two sprints is untrue; handing it to the scrum master misplaces the product owner's stakeholder role.
Remember: Ask "What decision do you need to make?" Roadmap + burnup = the agile forecast.

questions.stem: Match each agile event or activity with its purpose.
matching_right: Team and stakeholders inspect the increment and discuss next steps
Team selects work and creates a plan for the sprint
Team inspects how it worked and plans process improvements
Developers inspect progress toward the sprint goal and adapt the plan
Items are clarified, split, and estimated for upcoming sprints

answer.Sprint planning: Team selects work and creates a plan for the sprint
answer.Daily scrum: Developers inspect progress toward the sprint goal and adapt the plan
answer.Sprint review: Team and stakeholders inspect the increment and discuss next steps
answer.Sprint retrospective: Team inspects how it worked and plans process improvements
answer.Backlog refinement: Items are clarified, split, and estimated for upcoming sprints

questions.explanation:
Concept: Each Scrum event has one clear purpose: plan, synchronize, inspect the product, or inspect the process.
Sprint planning: the Scrum team sets the sprint goal, selects work, and plans how to deliver it.
Daily scrum: developers check progress toward the sprint goal and adapt the plan (15 minutes).
Sprint review: the team and stakeholders inspect the increment and adapt the product backlog.
Sprint retrospective: the team inspects how it worked and chooses improvements.
Backlog refinement: an ongoing activity to clarify, split, and estimate upcoming items.
Remember: Planning = WHAT and HOW • Daily = SYNC • Review = PRODUCT • Retro = PROCESS.

questions.topic: Team development: providing direction in the forming stage
questions.stem: A project manager has just assembled engineers from three departments for a predictive water-treatment plant upgrade. At the first meetings, members are polite but hesitant, and several ask what exactly they are expected to deliver. What should the project manager do?
options: Step back and let the members work out their own roles, since teams perform best when they self-organize.
Schedule a team-building offsite after the first milestone once members have settled into their work.
Ask each department's manager to explain duties to their own staff so the department groups stay separate.
Give clear direction on project objectives and review the RACI chart so each member knows their role.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Forming stage — a new team is polite and unsure, so the leader provides clear direction on goals and roles.
Spot it: a just-assembled team, hesitant members, and questions about "what exactly they are expected to deliver."
In this scenario: giving clear direction on the objectives and reviewing the RACI chart tells each member their role.
Why not the others: Stepping back to self-organize suits a performing team, not a new one; team-building after the first milestone comes too late; keeping department groups separate blocks the team from forming at all.
Remember: Forming = DIRECT: clear goals + clear roles (RACI).

questions.stem: Match each agile role with its accountability.
matching_right: Self-manage to create a usable increment each sprint
Maximizes product value by ordering and managing the backlog
Give feedback on the increment during sprint reviews
Coaches the team and removes impediments as a servant leader

answer.Product owner: Maximizes product value by ordering and managing the backlog
answer.Scrum master: Coaches the team and removes impediments as a servant leader
answer.Developers: Self-manage to create a usable increment each sprint
answer.Stakeholders: Give feedback on the increment during sprint reviews

questions.explanation:
Concept: Scrum defines three accountabilities; stakeholders matter, but they are not part of the Scrum team.
Product owner: maximizes value by ordering the product backlog; decides WHAT and in what order.
Scrum master: a servant leader who coaches the team and removes impediments.
Developers: self-manage to decide HOW and build a usable increment every sprint.
Stakeholders: inspect the increment at the sprint review and give feedback.
Remember: PO = WHAT/value • SM = coach/impediments • Developers = HOW/increment.

questions.stem: Match each group decision-making technique with its description.
matching_right: Members signal support until everyone can live with the decision
Largest group decides when no option reaches a majority
More than half agree; quick but can leave a losing minority
Everyone agrees; slow, but builds the strongest commitment
One person decides alone; fast but low team buy-in

answer.Unanimity: Everyone agrees; slow, but builds the strongest commitment
answer.Majority: More than half agree; quick but can leave a losing minority
answer.Plurality: Largest group decides when no option reaches a majority
answer.Autocratic: One person decides alone; fast but low team buy-in
answer.Consensus (fist of five): Members signal support until everyone can live with the decision

questions.explanation:
Concept: Group decision-making techniques trade speed against commitment.
Unanimity: everyone agrees; slow, but the strongest commitment.
Majority: more than half agree; quick, but leaves a losing minority.
Plurality: the largest group wins when no option has a majority.
Autocratic: one person decides; fast, with low buy-in.
Consensus (fist of five): members show support levels until all can live with it; the agile favorite.
Remember: More voices = more buy-in and more time. Agile teams check support with a fist of five.

questions.stem: A project manager is forming a predictive supply-chain analytics team whose members work in five countries and will never meet in person. Several members have already asked how and when they should reach each other and which tools to use. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Let each member keep using whatever tools are familiar to them so that nobody has to learn anything new at the start.
Send out a detailed contact list and require members to email the project manager with every question they have.
Arrange for members in the same country to form subteams that communicate with others only through designated leads.
Hold a video kickoff where members agree on shared norms for channels, response expectations, and overlapping hours.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Communication norms for virtual teams — set explicit agreements on channels, response times, and overlapping hours early, so trust and coordination start right.
Spot it: a new team across five countries that will never meet in person, with members asking "how and when" to reach each other.
In this scenario: a video kickoff where members agree on shared norms answers their questions and starts building trust.
Why not the others: Letting everyone use different tools fragments communication; routing every question through the PM creates a bottleneck; country subteams that talk only through leads split the team.
Remember: Virtual team = over-communicate + agree on the rules early (team charter).

questions.stem: Match each step of the integrated change control flow with what happens during it.
matching_right: Plans, baselines, and the change log are revised to match
Team carries out only the change that was approved
Project manager assesses impact on scope, schedule, cost, risk, and value
Results are checked to confirm the change achieved its purpose
Change control board decides based on the impact analysis

answer.Analyze: Project manager assesses impact on scope, schedule, cost, risk, and value
answer.Approve or reject: Change control board decides based on the impact analysis
answer.Implement: Team carries out only the change that was approved
answer.Update: Plans, baselines, and the change log are revised to match
answer.Monitor: Results are checked to confirm the change achieved its purpose

questions.explanation:
Concept: Integrated change control follows a fixed flow, so no change reaches the baselines without analysis and approval.
Analyze: the PM assesses effects on scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, and value.
Approve or reject: the change control board (or defined authority) decides, using the analysis.
Implement: the team carries out only the approved change.
Update: plans, baselines, and the change log are revised to reflect the decision.
Monitor: results are checked to confirm the change delivered what was intended.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor. Logging a change is NOT approving it.

questions.topic: Agile risk management: reducing risk early with a spike
questions.stem: An agile team building a ride-sharing feature depends on a third-party mapping API that has never been tested at the expected load. If it fails at scale, much of the planned work would need to be redesigned. What should the team do?
options: Build the dependent features first and test the API at scale just before release to save early effort.
Record the API concern in a risk register and review it at the end of the release with stakeholders.
Place a short experiment to load-test the API near the top of the backlog so the risk is resolved early.
Ask the API provider for a written performance guarantee and keep building on that assumption.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile risk reduction — high-impact uncertainty is tackled early by placing risk-reducing work, such as a spike or experiment, near the top of the backlog.
Spot it: an untested external dependency and "if it fails at scale, much of the planned work would need to be redesigned."
In this scenario: a short load-test experiment near the top of the backlog resolves the risk before the team builds on it.
Why not the others: Testing just before release finds the problem when redesign is most expensive; recording it for an end-of-release review is passive; a written guarantee does not prove the API works at scale.
Remember: Fail fast, fail cheap. Risky items go FIRST.

questions.topic: Issue management: issue log vs. risk register
questions.stem: On a hybrid point-of-sale rollout, 30 of the 200 store terminals delivered by the vendor have failed their power-on test. The adaptive software team can continue its work, but store installations scheduled for next month depend on working terminals. What should the project manager do?
options: Add a new entry to the risk register describing possible hardware failures and plan a response to each of them.
Record the problem in the issue log with an owner and due date, and work with the vendor on replacement units.
Wait for the vendor's quarterly business review to raise the failed terminals and discuss replacements.
Ask the software team to pause its work until all terminals are replaced so both streams stay aligned.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Issue versus risk — a risk is an uncertain future event (risk register); an issue has already happened (issue log) and needs an owner, a due date, and a resolution.
Spot it: "have failed": the event already occurred.
In this scenario: the PM records the failures in the issue log with an owner and due date and works with the vendor on replacement units.
Why not the others: The risk register is for uncertain events, not current problems; waiting for the quarterly review delays action on next month's installs; pausing the software team stops unaffected work.
Remember: Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor → Issue. Happened? Issue log. Might happen? Risk register.

questions.topic: Quality: control chart rule of seven
questions.stem: The predictive manufacturing stream of a hybrid medical-lab project plots daily fill volumes of test cartridges on a control chart. The last eight readings are all within the control limits but are all above the mean. What should the project manager do?
options: Take no action, because every one of the readings still falls within both the upper and lower control limits on the chart.
Tighten the specification limits so that the higher readings are flagged as defects in all future production.
Stop production and scrap the last eight batches, since they may not meet the customer's requirements.
Investigate the cause, because a run of consecutive points on one side of the mean suggests the process is out of control.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Control chart rule of seven — seven or more consecutive points on one side of the mean signal a nonrandom pattern, even when every point is within the control limits.
Spot it: "all within the control limits" but "all above the mean," eight in a row.
In this scenario: the process may be out of control, so the PM investigates the cause.
Why not the others: Taking no action misses the signal; tightening specification limits confuses customer specifications with process control; scrapping batches overreacts because the readings are still within limits.
Remember: Outside the limits OR seven in a row on one side = investigate. Control limits = voice of the process; spec limits = voice of the customer.

questions.stem: Match each Scrum artifact or commitment with its description.
matching_right: Single objective for the sprint that gives the team focus
Usable, done work added to all prior work by the sprint's end
Shared quality standard the whole Scrum team commits to
Selected items plus a delivery plan that developers own and adapt
Ordered list of all product work; the product owner is accountable

answer.Product backlog: Ordered list of all product work; the product owner is accountable
answer.Sprint backlog: Selected items plus a delivery plan that developers own and adapt
answer.Sprint goal: Single objective for the sprint that gives the team focus
answer.Increment: Usable, done work added to all prior work by the sprint's end
answer.Definition of done: Shared quality standard the whole Scrum team commits to

questions.explanation:
Concept: Scrum artifacts make the work transparent, and each has a clear owner or commitment.
Product backlog: the ordered list of all product work; the product owner is accountable for it.
Sprint backlog: the sprint goal, selected items, and delivery plan; developers own and adapt it.
Sprint goal: the single objective that focuses the sprint, set by the Scrum team at planning.
Increment: the usable, done work added to all earlier increments.
Definition of done: the shared quality standard every increment must meet; the whole team commits to it.
Remember: PO owns the product backlog • Developers own the sprint backlog • Everyone owns the definition of done.

questions.topic: Schedule: total float and the critical path
questions.stem: The predictive construction stream of a hybrid clinic-renovation project shows 5 days of total float for electrical rough-in. The electrician reports a 3-day delay, and the site superintendent wants to crash the schedule. What should the project manager do?
options: Monitor the activity and absorb the delay within its float, since the project finish date is not affected.
Add another electrician right away to recover the 3 days before the delay reaches the critical path.
Submit a change request to move the project completion date by 3 days to reflect the reported delay.
Fast-track the following activities so that the electrical work and drywall installation overlap.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Total float — how long an activity can slip without delaying the project finish date. A delay within float calls for monitoring, not compression.
Spot it: "5 days of total float," a "3-day delay," and someone wanting to crash.
In this scenario: 3 days is less than 5, so the finish date is safe; the PM monitors and absorbs the delay, with 2 days of float left.
Why not the others: Adding an electrician is crashing, spending money for no schedule benefit; moving the completion date is unnecessary because the finish is not affected; fast-tracking adds rework risk for no reason.
Remember: Delay ≤ float = no project delay. Crashing = add resources ($); fast-tracking = overlap work (risk).

questions.topic: Agile cost forecasting using velocity and cost per sprint
questions.stem: An agile team costs $60,000 per two-week sprint and has averaged 30 story points per sprint. The product owner estimates that 240 points remain in the release backlog. Approximately how much more will the release cost if conditions stay the same?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile cost forecasting — remaining sprints = remaining points ÷ velocity; remaining cost = remaining sprints × cost per sprint.
Spot it: a cost per sprint, an average velocity, and remaining points.
In this scenario: 240 ÷ 30 = 8 sprints, and 8 × $60,000 = $480,000.
Why not the others: $960,000 counts the 16 weeks as 16 sprints; $240,000 treats each point as costing $1,000; $360,000 uses six sprints instead of eight.
Remember: Points ÷ velocity = sprints; sprints × burn rate = cost.

questions.topic: Procurement: selecting a time and material contract
questions.stem: A predictive hospital IT upgrade needs two network specialists for an estimated four to six weeks to support cutover, but the exact amount of work cannot yet be defined. The project manager wants to engage them quickly with a simple arrangement. Which contract type is MOST appropriate?
options: Firm fixed price contract for all cutover support
Cost plus incentive fee contract with performance targets
Fixed price with economic price adjustment contract
Time and material contract with a not-to-exceed limit
questions.explanation:
Concept: Time and material (T&M) contract — pays hourly rates plus materials and suits short staff-augmentation work whose effort cannot yet be defined; a not-to-exceed cap limits the buyer's cost risk.
Spot it: specialists for "four to six weeks," work that "cannot yet be defined," and a need to start quickly with a simple arrangement.
In this scenario: a T&M contract with a not-to-exceed limit lets the specialists start fast while capping cost.
Why not the others: Firm fixed price needs well-defined scope; cost plus incentive fee is complex and suits larger, longer work; economic price adjustment handles multi-year inflation, not short support.
Remember: Fixed price = seller cost risk • Cost reimbursable = buyer cost risk • T&M = watch the hours and cap it.

questions.stem: Late in a predictive tax-filing system project, auditors ask the project manager to show that every legal requirement is linked to a design element and a test case. Several requirements were split into smaller ones during design. Which document should the project manager use?
options: The requirements traceability matrix
The scope statement and WBS dictionary
The requirements management plan
The quality control measurements
questions.explanation:
Concept: Requirements traceability matrix (RTM) — links each requirement to its origin, design, deliverables, and tests across the life cycle.
Spot it: "show that every requirement is linked to a design element and a test case," and requirements split during design.
In this scenario: the RTM gives the auditors a requirement-by-requirement trace, including the split requirements.
Why not the others: The scope statement and WBS dictionary describe scope and work packages, not requirement-to-test links; the requirements management plan explains HOW requirements are managed; quality control measurements record results without tracing them to requirements.
Remember: WBS = STRUCTURE • WBS dictionary = DETAIL • RTM = TRACE.

questions.topic: Backlog ordering: value, risk, and deadlines
questions.stem: In a hybrid pension-administration project, a regulatory reporting change must be live by a fixed date set in the predictive plan. The adaptive team's backlog is ordered by customer value alone, and the regulatory items sit near the bottom. What should the product owner do?
options: Keep the current order, since a backlog should always be sorted by customer value and nothing else at all.
Ask the predictive team to build the regulatory items so the adaptive backlog can stay exactly as it is.
Reorder the backlog so the regulatory items finish on time, weighing deadlines and risk as well as value.
Add the regulatory items to the current sprint at once, replacing work that the team has already started.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Backlog ordering — the product owner orders by value AND by risk, dependencies, and fixed deadlines such as regulatory dates.
Spot it: a fixed regulatory date, compliance items near the bottom, and ordering by customer value alone.
In this scenario: reordering so the regulatory items finish on time protects the compliance deadline.
Why not the others: Keeping a pure customer-value order ignores a legal date; handing the items to the predictive team dodges the product owner's ordering role; adding them to the current sprint at once disrupts work already started.
Remember: Order = value + risk + dependencies + deadlines. Compliance is not optional.

questions.topic: Agile frameworks compared: Scrum, Kanban, XP, SAFe, hybrid
questions.stem: Match each delivery framework or approach with its defining feature.
matching_right: Continuous pull-based flow with WIP limits and no prescribed roles
Scales agile across many teams through program increment planning
Fixed sprints of one month or less with three defined accountabilities
Predictive planning for stable parts, adaptive delivery for evolving parts
Engineering practices such as pair programming, TDD, and continuous integration

answer.Scrum: Fixed sprints of one month or less with three defined accountabilities
answer.Kanban: Continuous pull-based flow with WIP limits and no prescribed roles
answer.Extreme Programming (XP): Engineering practices such as pair programming, TDD, and continuous integration
answer.SAFe: Scales agile across many teams through program increment planning
answer.Hybrid: Predictive planning for stable parts, adaptive delivery for evolving parts

questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile frameworks share the agile mindset but differ in cadence, roles, and practices.
Scrum: fixed sprints of one month or less; product owner, scrum master, developers; velocity and burndown.
Kanban: continuous pull flow with WIP limits and no required roles; measured by cycle time, lead time, and throughput.
Extreme Programming (XP): engineering excellence: pair programming, TDD, continuous integration, refactoring.
SAFe: agile at enterprise scale; many teams aligned through program increment (PI) planning.
Hybrid: predictive for the stable parts, adaptive for the evolving parts.
Remember: Scrum = sprints • Kanban = flow • XP = engineering • SAFe = scale • Hybrid = right approach for each part.

questions.stem: Match each flow-based (kanban) term with its description.
matching_right: Time from starting work on an item until it is done
Caps how many items can be in a workflow stage at once
Number of items completed in a given time period
Time from customer request until the item is delivered
Chart of items in each stage over time, revealing bottlenecks

answer.WIP limit: Caps how many items can be in a workflow stage at once
answer.Lead time: Time from customer request until the item is delivered
answer.Cycle time: Time from starting work on an item until it is done
answer.Throughput: Number of items completed in a given time period
answer.Cumulative flow diagram: Chart of items in each stage over time, revealing bottlenecks

questions.explanation:
Concept: Kanban manages flow; these measures show how smoothly work moves.
WIP limit: caps the items in a stage so work finishes before new work starts.
Lead time: from customer request to delivery: what the customer experiences.
Cycle time: from start of work to done: the part the team controls.
Throughput: how many items finish per time period.
Cumulative flow diagram: colored bands per stage over time; a widening band shows a bottleneck.
Remember: Lead time = request → delivery; cycle time = start → done (inside lead time). Stop starting, start finishing.

questions.topic: Rolling wave planning (tailoring a predictive plan)
questions.stem: A predictive telecom rollout has fully defined requirements for its first two regions, but the design for the remaining regions depends on a spectrum auction that ends in eight months. Leadership wants a single approved plan. How should the project manager plan the later regions?
options: Plan the first regions in detail and keep later regions at a higher level, adding detail as auction results become known.
Create detailed activity-level estimates for every region right now so that the entire project can be baselined all at once.
Delay all planning, including for the first two regions, until the spectrum auction results have become available.
Leave the later regions out of the scope baseline and start a separate project for them once the auction is over.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Rolling wave planning — a form of progressive elaboration: plan near-term work in detail and keep later work at a higher level until information arrives.
Spot it: detailed requirements for early regions, later design that depends on a future event, and a request for one approved plan.
In this scenario: the PM details the first two regions and holds later regions at a high level, elaborating them as auction results arrive.
Why not the others: Detailing every region now is guesswork and leads to repeated re-baselining; delaying all planning wastes what is already known; moving later regions into another project fragments the approved scope.
Remember: Near = detailed, far = high level. Plan the wave you can see.

questions.topic: Acceptance: acceptance criteria, definition of done, Control Quality, Validate Scope
questions.stem: Match each acceptance-related term with its description.
matching_right: Verifies deliverables are correct against quality requirements
Conditions a specific deliverable must meet to be accepted by the customer
Formalizes customer or sponsor acceptance of completed deliverables
Team checklist every increment must satisfy to be considered complete

answer.Acceptance criteria: Conditions a specific deliverable must meet to be accepted by the customer
answer.Definition of done: Team checklist every increment must satisfy to be considered complete
answer.Control Quality: Verifies deliverables are correct against quality requirements
answer.Validate Scope: Formalizes customer or sponsor acceptance of completed deliverables

questions.explanation:
Concept: Acceptance terms separate "Is it built right?" from "Does the customer formally accept it?"
Acceptance criteria: conditions a specific deliverable or story must meet to be accepted.
Definition of done: the team-wide checklist every increment must meet.
Control Quality: an internal check that deliverables are correct (verified).
Validate Scope: formal customer or sponsor acceptance of verified deliverables.
Remember: Control Quality = CORRECT (verified) → Validate Scope = ACCEPTED. Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close.

questions.topic: Reserves: contingency reserve for identified risks
questions.stem: On a predictive highway-resurfacing project, an identified risk of asphalt price increases occurs, and the planned response calls for buying from an alternate supplier at a higher cost. The budget includes both contingency and management reserves. How should the project manager fund the extra cost?
options: Ask the sponsor to release management reserve to cover the higher cost of the asphalt purchase.
Use the contingency reserve set aside for this identified risk, as the planned response specifies.
Submit a change request to raise the cost baseline by the full amount of the price increase.
Cut asphalt quantities in the remaining work packages to offset the higher unit price paid.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contingency reserve — money inside the cost baseline for identified risks (known unknowns). The PM uses it when a planned response is triggered.
Spot it: "an identified risk occurs" and "the planned response calls for" a costlier supplier.
In this scenario: the PM funds the alternate supplier from the contingency reserve set aside for this risk.
Why not the others: Management reserve is for unidentified risks and needs sponsor approval; a change request to raise the baseline is unnecessary because the money is already in it; cutting asphalt quantities reduces scope and quality.
Remember: Contingency = known unknowns (inside the baseline, PM uses) • Management reserve = unknown unknowns (outside the baseline, sponsor approves).

questions.topic: Lessons learned in agile: continuous improvement through retrospectives
questions.stem: An agile team at an insurance firm records problems in a lessons-learned document at the end of each quarterly release. While reviewing the document, a scrum master notices that the same deployment problems appear in every release. What should the scrum master do?
options: Move the lessons-learned review to the end of the project so that all problems can be analyzed together.
Send the lessons-learned document to the PMO so that other teams can avoid similar deployment problems.
Ask the deployment engineers to write a more detailed lessons-learned report after each of the quarterly releases.
Help the team pick one or two improvement actions in each retrospective and check on them the following sprint.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Continuous improvement through retrospectives — agile teams learn every sprint and turn lessons into small actions they check next time.
Spot it: the same problems every release, and lessons captured only quarterly without action.
In this scenario: the scrum master helps the team choose one or two improvements in each retrospective and follow up the next sprint.
Why not the others: An end-of-project review delays learning even further; sending the document to the PMO shares it but does not change this team's behavior; longer reports add documentation, not action.
Remember: A lesson is learned only when behavior changes. Retro → action → check.

questions.topic: Integrated change control in a hybrid project
questions.stem: A hybrid airport-signage project has a baselined hardware installation plan and an adaptive team building the display software. A stakeholder asks for new display screens with a different mounting size, which would require changing the approved hardware specifications. How should the project manager handle this request?
options: Evaluate the impact on the hardware baselines and submit a change request to the change control board.
Ask the product owner to add the new screens to the software backlog and prioritize them as usual.
Let the installation crew adopt the new screens, since the adaptive team welcomes changing requirements.
Refuse the request, because changes to baselined work are not allowed in hybrid projects at all.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Change control in a hybrid project — baselined predictive parts use integrated change control; adaptive parts use the backlog.
Spot it: a request that changes "the approved hardware specifications" on the predictive side.
In this scenario: the PM evaluates the impact on the hardware baselines and submits a change request to the change control board.
Why not the others: Putting it in the software backlog bypasses the formal control that protects the hardware baseline; letting the crew adopt new screens applies agile flexibility to baselined work; refusing outright is wrong because baselined work can change through the proper process.
Remember: Baseline = APPROVED → CCB. Backlog → PO orders it. Know which side the change lands on.

questions.topic: Risk management: implementing the planned response when a trigger occurs
questions.stem: On a predictive offshore platform project, a risk of storm delays has a documented trigger: a forecast of wind above 40 knots within 72 hours. Today the forecast crossed that threshold. What should the project manager do?
options: Perform a new qualitative risk analysis to decide whether the storm risk is still a high priority now.
Add the storm to the issue log and wait to act until the storm actually delays platform work on site.
Hold a risk workshop with the full team to brainstorm new responses to the storm that has been forecast.
Ensure the assigned risk owner carries out the planned response, and watch for any secondary risks it creates.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Implementing risk responses — when a trigger occurs, the risk owner executes the planned response and the team watches for secondary and residual risks.
Spot it: a documented trigger (wind above 40 knots within 72 hours) and "today the forecast crossed that threshold."
In this scenario: the PM makes sure the risk owner carries out the planned response now.
Why not the others: A new qualitative analysis wastes the lead time the trigger was designed to give; waiting for an actual delay throws away the plan; brainstorming new responses ignores the one already agreed.
Remember: Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor → Issue. The trigger fires = execute the plan.

questions.stem: Match each project document with its purpose.
matching_right: Lists submitted change requests and their approval status
Tracks current problems, their owners, and target resolution dates
Records conditions believed true, plus constraints, for planning
Records uncertain events, their analysis, owners, and planned responses
Captures knowledge gained for use now and on future projects

answer.Issue log: Tracks current problems, their owners, and target resolution dates
answer.Risk register: Records uncertain events, their analysis, owners, and planned responses
answer.Change log: Lists submitted change requests and their approval status
answer.Assumption log: Records conditions believed true, plus constraints, for planning
answer.Lessons learned register: Captures knowledge gained for use now and on future projects

questions.explanation:
Concept: Logs and registers are TRACK documents: living records the PM keeps updated as the project runs.
Issue log: current problems, their owners, and target dates.
Risk register: uncertain future events, their analysis, owners, and responses.
Change log: every change request and its status: approved, rejected, or deferred.
Assumption log: assumptions and constraints, rechecked as conditions change.
Lessons learned register: knowledge gained, used now and on future projects.
Remember: Register/Log = TRACK. Happened = issue log • Might happen = risk register • Requested = change log.

questions.stem: A predictive furniture-manufacturing project has logged 400 defects across 12 defect categories during its first production run. The project manager wants to focus corrective effort on the few categories that account for most of the defects. Which tool should the project manager use?
options: Scatter diagram
Pareto diagram
Control chart
Fishbone diagram
questions.explanation:
Concept: Pareto diagram — a bar chart that ranks categories by frequency, with a cumulative line, to find the "vital few" causes (the 80/20 rule).
Spot it: many defects across many categories, and a wish to focus on "the few that account for most."
In this scenario: the Pareto diagram shows which categories to attack first.
Why not the others: A scatter diagram shows the relationship between two variables; a control chart shows process stability over time; a fishbone diagram explores causes of one problem but does not rank frequency.
Remember: Pareto = prioritize • Fishbone = causes • Control chart = stability • Scatter = relationship.

questions.topic: Scope control in a hybrid project
questions.stem: Stakeholders on a hybrid clinic-network project are sending requests directly to engineers. Some target the baselined network infrastructure, and others are new ideas for the adaptive patient app. Scope is growing without anyone tracking it. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Route changes to the baselined infrastructure scope through the formal change control process.
Let engineers accept small infrastructure requests directly if they take less than a day each.
Have the product owner evaluate new app ideas and order them in the adaptive stream's backlog.
Freeze the app backlog so that no new ideas can be added after the adaptive stream has started.
Approve every stakeholder request in both streams to keep stakeholder satisfaction consistently high.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Scope control in a hybrid project — baselined scope is protected by integrated change control; adaptive scope is ordered by the product owner in the backlog.
Spot it: requests going straight to engineers, some for baselined infrastructure and some for the adaptive app, and untracked growth.
In this scenario: routing infrastructure changes through formal change control and having the product owner evaluate and order app ideas bring both streams under control.
Why not the others: Letting engineers accept small infrastructure requests is scope creep; freezing the app backlog removes agile's flexibility; approving every request is uncontrolled scope growth.
Remember: Predictive side → CCB. Adaptive side → PO and backlog. Nothing goes straight to the engineers.

questions.topic: Agile release forecasting with a velocity range
questions.stem: An agile team has completed six sprints with velocities of 18, 24, 20, 22, 19, and 23 points. The remaining release backlog is estimated at 105 points, and the sponsor asks when the release will be ready. What is the BEST response?
options: Commit to exactly five sprints, since the average velocity of 21 divides evenly into 105 points.
Ask the team to raise its velocity to 27 points so the release can be finished in four sprints.
Forecast a range of five to six more sprints based on observed velocity, and update it each sprint.
Decline to forecast until every remaining item is broken into tasks and estimated in hours.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Range-based release forecasting — velocity varies, so forecasts use the observed range and are updated every sprint.
Spot it: a list of varying velocities, remaining points, and "when will it be ready?"
In this scenario: 105 ÷ 24 ≈ 4.4, so about 5 sprints at best; 105 ÷ 18 ≈ 5.8, so about 6 at worst. Forecast five to six sprints and refine it as data arrives.
Why not the others: Committing to exactly five turns an average into a promise; demanding a velocity of 27 inflates numbers rather than improving delivery; breaking everything into hours is heavy predictive planning.
Remember: Forecast a range, not a promise. Fastest and slowest velocity give best and worst case.

questions.topic: Agile cost: burn rate and scope growth
questions.stem: An agile team's cost is steady at $40,000 per sprint, but the release burnup chart shows total scope growing by about 15 points each sprint as stakeholders add items. The sponsor asks why the forecast budget keeps rising. What should the product owner do?
options: Ask the team to lower its cost per sprint by cutting testing so that the original budget can still be kept.
Show the sponsor how added scope increases the sprints needed and agree on which additions are worth their cost.
Stop showing scope growth on the burnup chart so the forecast budget stays stable in the reports sent to the sponsor.
Request extra budget from finance for every item added so that the release can include all of them.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Burn rate and scope growth — with a steady cost per sprint, added scope adds sprints, and added sprints add cost.
Spot it: a steady cost per sprint, a burnup chart whose scope line keeps rising, and a growing budget forecast.
In this scenario: the product owner shows the sponsor how added scope drives cost and agrees which additions are worth it.
Why not the others: Cutting testing sacrifices quality; hiding scope growth breaks transparency; requesting money for every added item skips value-based prioritization.
Remember: Burnup's top line = scope. Scope up → sprints up → cost up. Make it visible and decide by value.

questions.topic: Procurement: contract types in a hybrid project
questions.stem: A hybrid retail-logistics project will buy warehouse scanners with a fully defined specification and will also hire a vendor to build a routing application whose features will evolve through frequent customer feedback. Which TWO contracting approaches are MOST appropriate?
options: Use one firm fixed-price contract covering both the scanners and the evolving app.
Require the app vendor to deliver a full detailed specification before any coding.
Use a firm fixed-price contract for the well-defined scanner supply and installation.
Use a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract for the scanners so the vendor's costs are covered.
Use a time-and-materials or incremental contract that lets the app's scope evolve.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Matching contract type to certainty — fixed price for well-defined work; time-and-materials or incremental contracts for evolving, adaptive work.
Spot it: scanners with a "fully defined specification" and an app whose features "will evolve."
In this scenario: a firm fixed-price contract for the scanners and a T&M or incremental contract for the app fit each part.
Why not the others: One fixed-price contract for both forces change orders on the evolving app; requiring a full specification before coding defeats adaptive delivery; cost-plus for a well-defined purchase leaves needless cost risk with the buyer.
Remember: Clear scope → fixed price (seller risk). Evolving scope → T&M or incremental (buyer flexibility).

questions.stem: Match each requirements-related document with its purpose.
matching_right: Describes individual requirements and how they meet business needs
Links each requirement to its origin, deliverables, and tests
Gives detailed information about each work package in the WBS
Describes how requirements will be analyzed, documented, and managed

answer.Requirements traceability matrix: Links each requirement to its origin, deliverables, and tests
answer.Requirements management plan: Describes how requirements will be analyzed, documented, and managed
answer.Requirements documentation: Describes individual requirements and how they meet business needs
answer.WBS dictionary: Gives detailed information about each work package in the WBS

questions.explanation:
Concept: Requirements documents differ in whether they describe, manage, trace, or detail the work.
Requirements traceability matrix: TRACE: links each requirement to its origin, deliverables, and tests.
Requirements management plan: HOW requirements will be collected, analyzed, documented, and managed.
Requirements documentation: WHAT: the requirements themselves and the business need each one meets.
WBS dictionary: DETAIL: description, owner, and criteria for each work package.
Remember: Plan = HOW • Documentation = WHAT • RTM = TRACE • WBS dictionary = DETAIL.

questions.stem: During planning for a predictive laboratory-information system, stakeholders submit 140 requirements, far more than the approved budget can fund. Each department head insists that every one of that department's requirements is essential. What should the project manager do?
options: Include all 140 requirements in the scope baseline and request extra funding later through change control.
Select the requirements personally based on technical ease so that the team can deliver the most items.
Fund the requirements in the order they were submitted, since that approach treats every department in the same way.
Facilitate a prioritization session, such as MoSCoW, in which stakeholders rank requirements by business value.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Requirements prioritization — when demand exceeds funding, the PM facilitates stakeholders in ranking requirements by business value, for example with MoSCoW, before the scope baseline is set.
Spot it: 140 requirements, a fixed budget, and every department claiming that everything is essential.
In this scenario: a MoSCoW session gives the group a shared, value-based basis for the scope baseline.
Why not the others: Baselining everything and seeking money later builds a known gap into the plan; picking by technical ease ignores value and the stakeholders; first-come order looks fair but is value-blind.
Remember: MoSCoW = Must, Should, Could, Won't (this time). Stakeholders rank, the PM facilitates, value decides.

questions.stem: A predictive vaccine-packaging project has reached the end of its design phase. Two of the eight exit criteria, including a validated line layout, have not been met, but the team is eager to begin procurement. What should the project manager do?
options: Begin procurement now and complete the two open criteria in parallel so that the schedule is protected.
Mark the two criteria as met, since six of the eight exit criteria have already been fully satisfied.
Present the phase results at the gate review so the sponsor and governance body can decide whether to proceed.
Restart the whole design phase from the beginning to make sure that every exit criterion is fully met.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Phase gate review — a governance decision point where the sponsor or governance body reviews results against exit criteria and decides to proceed, rework, or stop.
Spot it: "end of its design phase," unmet exit criteria, and a team eager to move on.
In this scenario: the PM presents the phase results, including the two open criteria, so the governance body can decide.
Why not the others: Starting procurement now bypasses the gate and commits funds to an unvalidated layout; marking the criteria as met misreports status; restarting the whole phase overreacts, because the gate decides the remedy.
Remember: The PM brings the facts; governance makes the go/no-go call. Never fake a gate.

questions.topic: Bottlenecks: managing the constraint in the workflow
questions.stem: On a predictive fiber-installation project, crews finish splicing faster than the single testing technician can certify segments. Uncertified segments are piling up, and the project manager is considering adding more splicing crews. What should the project manager do?
options: Increase certification capacity, such as bringing in a second technician, before adding any splicing crews.
Add more splicing crews so that more segments are ready and waiting when the technician can test them.
Ask the technician to skip some of the testing steps for each segment so certification moves faster.
Keep the current plan and report the pile of uncertified segments at the next monthly status review.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Managing the bottleneck (theory of constraints) — a system can only go as fast as its slowest step, so add capacity at the constraint first.
Spot it: work piling up in front of one step (a single tester) and a proposal to speed up the upstream work.
In this scenario: increasing certification capacity, such as adding a second technician, raises the output of finished segments.
Why not the others: More splicing crews only lengthen the queue; skipping test steps trades quality for speed; waiting for the monthly review lets the pile keep growing.
Remember: Find the constraint, fix the constraint. Speeding up anything else just builds inventory.

questions.stem: Match each development life cycle with its description.
matching_right: Delivers finished, usable portions of the product in successive pieces
Scope, time, and cost are set early; changes are carefully controlled
Combines iterative refinement with frequent incremental delivery of value
Repeated cycles refine the product based on feedback and learning
Mixes predictive and adaptive elements to suit each part of the work

answer.Predictive: Scope, time, and cost are set early; changes are carefully controlled
answer.Iterative: Repeated cycles refine the product based on feedback and learning
answer.Incremental: Delivers finished, usable portions of the product in successive pieces
answer.Agile: Combines iterative refinement with frequent incremental delivery of value
answer.Hybrid: Mixes predictive and adaptive elements to suit each part of the work

questions.explanation:
Concept: Development life cycles differ in how they handle requirements and when they deliver.
Predictive: scope, time, and cost are set early; changes go through change control.
Iterative: repeated cycles refine the product based on feedback.
Incremental: delivers finished, usable pieces one after another.
Agile: both iterative and incremental: frequent delivery of refined, usable value.
Hybrid: blends predictive and adaptive parts where each fits best.
Remember: Iterative = get it RIGHT over time • Incremental = get it BUILT in pieces • Agile = both.

questions.topic: Acceptance: Validate Scope with the customer
questions.stem: The vendor's quality team on a hybrid smart-building project has verified the installed sensors against specifications, and the product owner has accepted each software increment. The building owner's representative has not yet reviewed the integrated system. What should the project manager do before closing the project?
options: Close the project, since the sensors passed quality checks and every software increment was already accepted.
Arrange for the building owner's representative to review the integrated system and formally sign off on it.
Ask the vendor's quality team to sign the formal acceptance on behalf of the building owner's representative.
Run another full round of quality control tests on the sensors before requesting any sign-off from anyone.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Validate Scope — formal acceptance of completed deliverables by the customer or sponsor. Quality verification and acceptance of parts do not replace acceptance of the whole.
Spot it: sensors verified, increments accepted, but the building owner has not reviewed the integrated system "before closing."
In this scenario: the PM arranges for the owner's representative to review the integrated system and formally sign off.
Why not the others: Closing now confuses verification with customer acceptance; the vendor's quality team cannot accept on the owner's behalf; another full quality round repeats verification that is already done.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close. No customer sign-off, no closure.

questions.topic: Reserves: management reserve for unidentified risks
questions.stem: Midway through a hybrid library-modernization project, a new city accessibility code requires ramp changes that no one had identified as a risk. The predictive construction budget includes a contingency reserve for known risks and a management reserve held by the sponsor. How should the project manager fund the ramp work?
options: Draw on the contingency reserve, since it is available for any cost increase that occurs during construction.
Take the funds from the adaptive software team's budget, since its scope can flex more easily than construction.
Absorb the cost within existing work packages and report the resulting variance at the project closure review.
Request use of the management reserve from the sponsor and follow change control to update the cost baseline.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Management reserve — money outside the cost baseline for unidentified risks (unknown unknowns); using it needs sponsor approval and a change to the cost baseline.
Spot it: a new regulation mid-project that "no one had identified as a risk."
In this scenario: the PM requests management reserve from the sponsor and follows change control to update the cost baseline.
Why not the others: Contingency reserve is tied to identified risks, so using it leaves those unfunded; taking money from the software team robs another stream; absorbing the cost and reporting at closure hides a variance.
Remember: Identified → contingency (PM, inside the baseline). Unidentified → management reserve (sponsor, outside the baseline, baseline change).

questions.stem: An agile team building a smart-meter data platform for an energy utility notes in its retrospective that the same integration defect has reached production in three consecutive iterations. Team members agree the cause is the lack of a shared test environment. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Record the pattern in the lessons learned register and schedule a formal review of it during the project closure phase.
Help the team agree on a concrete improvement to try in the next iteration and review its results at the following retrospective.
Escalate the recurring defect to the functional manager and request that an additional tester be assigned to the team right away.
Direct the developers to double their manual testing effort before every release until the defects stop escaping.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Continuous improvement in agile — lessons are captured and applied during the project, not saved for the end. The retrospective exists to pick an improvement, try it, and inspect the result.
Spot it: a retrospective, the same problem repeating across iterations, and a cause the team already agrees on.
In this scenario: the team knows the cause, so the next step is to agree on a concrete experiment (such as a shared test environment) and check at the next retrospective whether it worked.
Why not the others: waiting for closure lets the defect escape for months; escalating to the functional manager skips the team's own improvement step; ordering double manual testing is command-and-control and treats the symptom, not the cause.
Remember: Learn → Apply → Keep learning → Archive. In agile, a lesson is only learned when the team changes how it works next iteration.

questions.stem: Match each integrated change control element with its purpose.
matching_right: Record of every change request and its current status
Controls versions and specifications of product components and documents
Formal proposal to modify a document, deliverable, or baseline
Group authorized to approve, defer, or reject proposed changes

answer.Change request: Formal proposal to modify a document, deliverable, or baseline
answer.Change control board: Group authorized to approve, defer, or reject proposed changes
answer.Change log: Record of every change request and its current status
answer.Configuration management: Controls versions and specifications of product components and documents

questions.explanation:
Concept: Integrated change control has four pieces that students often blur: the request, the decision body, the status record, and version control.
Change request: the formal proposal to change a document, deliverable, or baseline; nothing changes until it is decided.
Change control board: the group with authority to approve, defer, or reject; the PM analyzes impact, the CCB decides.
Change log: TRACK. Every request and its status (approved, rejected, deferred). Logging a change is not approving it.
Configuration management: controls which versions and specifications of the product and documents are current.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor. Change plan = HOW, change log = STATUS, configuration = WHAT version.

questions.stem: During foundation design for a predictive hospital construction project, a geotechnical consultant reports that seasonal groundwater could flood the excavation, although the test borings are inconclusive. The project manager has already added the threat to the risk register. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Draw on the contingency reserve now to install a dewatering system before any excavation work begins on site.
Submit a change request to the change control board to redesign the foundation for high groundwater levels at the site.
Assess the probability and impact of the flooding threat with the engineers so it can be prioritized against other risks.
Transfer the threat by asking the excavation subcontractor to accept liability for any flooding damage that occurs.
questions.explanation:
Concept: The risk flow — once a risk is identified and logged, it is analyzed before anyone picks a response. Qualitative analysis rates probability and impact so risks can be ranked.
Spot it: the words "could" and "inconclusive", plus "already added to the risk register"; the risk is identified but not yet analyzed.
In this scenario: the next safe step is to assess probability and impact with the engineers so the flooding threat is prioritized against the other risks.
Why not the others: using contingency for dewatering jumps to a response before analysis; a redesign change request is also a response chosen too early; transferring liability to the subcontractor picks a strategy before the threat is understood.
Remember: Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor → Issue. Identify, then analyze, then respond.

questions.stem: Match each schedule network term with its meaning.
matching_right: Time an activity can slip without delaying its successor.
Longest path through the network; sets the earliest finish.
Overlap that lets a successor start before its predecessor ends.
Time an activity can slip without delaying project finish.
Required wait added between a predecessor and its successor.

answer.Critical path: Longest path through the network; sets the earliest finish.
answer.Total float: Time an activity can slip without delaying project finish.
answer.Free float: Time an activity can slip without delaying its successor.
answer.Lag: Required wait added between a predecessor and its successor.
answer.Lead: Overlap that lets a successor start before its predecessor ends.

questions.explanation:
Concept: Network terms describe how activities connect and how much flexibility each one has, which tells the PM where schedule risk sits.
Critical path: Any delay on it delays the project; it has zero total float.
Total float: Late start − early start. Negative float means you are already late.
Free float: Protects the very next activity, not just the end date.
Lag: Example: wait three days for concrete to cure before framing.
Lead: Example: start testing two days before coding finishes; a form of fast-tracking.
Remember: Critical path = zero float = watch it daily. Lag = WAIT, Lead = HEAD START.

questions.stem: Match each quality management tool with what it is used for.
matching_right: Plots two variables to reveal a possible correlation between them
Ranks defect causes by frequency to focus on the vital few
Displays how often values fall within each range of a data set
Breaks a problem into categories of possible root causes
Shows whether a process stays stable within set limits over time

answer.Pareto chart: Ranks defect causes by frequency to focus on the vital few
answer.Fishbone diagram: Breaks a problem into categories of possible root causes
answer.Control chart: Shows whether a process stays stable within set limits over time
answer.Scatter diagram: Plots two variables to reveal a possible correlation between them
answer.Histogram: Displays how often values fall within each range of a data set

questions.explanation:
Concept: The quality tools each answer one question; the exam describes the question and you name the tool.
Pareto chart: WHICH causes matter most? Bars ranked by frequency to focus on the vital few (80/20).
Fishbone diagram: WHY might it happen? Cause-and-effect categories (people, process, materials, and so on) for root cause analysis.
Control chart: IS the process stable? Data over time against upper and lower control limits; watch for points outside limits or the rule of seven.
Scatter diagram: ARE two variables related? Plots pairs to show correlation.
Histogram: HOW are values distributed? Bars showing frequency by range for one variable.
Remember: Pareto = prioritize, fishbone = find why, control chart = stable over time, scatter = relationship, histogram = distribution.

questions.stem: Midway through an iteration on a patient-scheduling app, a clinic director approaches two developers directly and asks them to add text-message appointment reminders before the iteration ends. The request is not part of the current iteration goal. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Let the developers add the reminders now, since the clinic director is a key stakeholder and the feature is small.
Tell the director that scope is fixed and the reminder feature must wait until the entire release is finished.
Submit a formal change request to the change control board to approve adding the reminders to the scope.
Guide the director to the product owner so the reminder feature can be added to the backlog and prioritized.
questions.explanation:
Concept: New requests in agile go through the product owner, who owns the order of the product backlog. The current sprint goal is protected while new work waits its turn.
Spot it: a stakeholder going straight to developers mid-iteration, and a request outside the current iteration goal.
In this scenario: the PM redirects the clinic director to the product owner, who can add the reminder feature to the backlog and order it by value.
Why not the others: letting developers add it bypasses the product owner and disrupts the iteration commitment; saying scope is fixed until release ends is predictive thinking and ignores agile's openness to change; a CCB change request is the predictive mechanism, not the agile one.
Remember: Request → PO → Backlog → Order → Select. The backlog is where change goes; the sprint is where focus stays.

questions.stem: A hybrid customer-service initiative installs call-center hardware on a predictive schedule while an AI chatbot is built in adaptive iterations. A two-week delay in the hardware shipment now affects a critical-path activity, and the go-live date is contractually fixed. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Shorten the chatbot's testing cycles so the software team can make up the two weeks that the hardware stream lost.
Ask the sponsor to move the contractual go-live date before examining any of the schedule recovery options.
Analyze the critical path for compression options, such as overlapping installation and testing, and weigh their risks.
Add technicians to every remaining hardware activity to recover time wherever installation work is running late.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Schedule compression works only on the critical path. Crashing adds resources (more cost); fast-tracking overlaps activities (more risk). You analyze the options before choosing.
Spot it: a delay on a critical-path activity, a fixed end date, and a FIRST question.
In this scenario: the delay is in the predictive hardware stream, so the PM first analyzes that critical path and weighs compression options such as overlapping installation and testing.
Why not the others: cutting chatbot testing lowers quality on work that did not cause the delay; asking to move a contractual date skips the PM's own recovery analysis; adding technicians everywhere wastes money on non-critical work.
Remember: Late → Critical path → Options → Trade-offs → Act.

questions.stem: The midpoint cost report for a predictive state licensing portal project shows a CPI of 0.85. A department director suggests resetting the cost baseline to current actuals so the monthly report to the oversight board shows green. What should the project manager do?
options: Reset the cost baseline to current actuals as suggested, and note the change in the next monthly board report.
Investigate the causes of the overrun, forecast the estimate at completion, and propose corrective actions.
Request extra funding from the oversight board to cover the variance before its cause is understood.
Report the CPI as 1.0 this month and correct the figures once the corrective actions have taken effect.
questions.explanation:
Concept: A baseline is the APPROVED target; a forecast is the current expectation. Poor performance changes the forecast and triggers corrective action, not a new baseline.
Spot it: CPI below 1.0 and a request to "reset the baseline so the report shows green".
In this scenario: CPI 0.85 means 85 cents of value per dollar spent, so the PM finds the cause, forecasts EAC, and proposes corrective actions.
Why not the others: resetting the baseline to actuals hides the variance and would need approved change control anyway; asking for money before knowing the cause skips analysis; reporting CPI as 1.0 is dishonest reporting.
Remember: Measure → Understand → Diagnose → Forecast → Decide. Forecasts move with reality; baselines move with approval.

questions.stem: The firm-fixed-price migration vendor on a predictive data-modernization project for a state agency has missed two contractual milestones, and its latest deliverables failed acceptance testing. The agency's finance manager wants to stop paying the vendor's invoices immediately. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Stop payment on all open invoices until the vendor delivers work that passes the agreed acceptance testing.
Terminate the contract for default and begin a new solicitation to select a replacement migration vendor.
Have agency staff quietly fix the failed deliverables so that the migration stays on its planned schedule.
Review the contract's performance and remedy clauses, then send the vendor a formal notice as the contract requires.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Seller performance problems are handled through the contract. The contract is the legal source of remedies such as a notice to cure, withheld payment, or termination.
Spot it: a contracted seller missing milestones, failed acceptance, and someone wanting to act outside the contract ("stop paying immediately").
In this scenario: the PM first reviews the performance and remedy clauses and then sends formal notice as the contract requires.
Why not the others: stopping payment outside the contract terms may put the buyer in breach; termination for default is a last step, not a first; quietly fixing the seller's work hides nonperformance and wastes buyer money.
Remember: Claim → Contract → Facts → Resolve → Contract path. SELLER = contract; go to the contract first.

questions.stem: Two weeks before final acceptance of a predictive student-records system upgrade, the registrar asks for proof that each regulatory reporting requirement will be delivered and verified. The project manager suspects some of those requirements have no associated test cases. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Ask the test lead to run the full regression suite and send the registrar the overall test pass rate.
Remove any reporting requirement that has no test case from the requirements documentation.
Use the traceability matrix to link each reporting requirement to its design element and test case.
Tell the registrar that requirements will be confirmed during the post-implementation review.
questions.explanation:
Concept: The requirements traceability matrix (RTM) links each requirement to its source, design, deliverable, and test, so you can prove coverage requirement by requirement.
Spot it: "proof that each requirement will be delivered and verified" and "some requirements may have no test cases".
In this scenario: the PM uses the RTM to trace every reporting requirement to its design element and test case, exposing the gaps.
Why not the others: an overall regression pass rate cannot show per-requirement coverage; deleting untested requirements changes scope without authority; deferring to the post-implementation review is too late for acceptance.
Remember: WBS = structure, WBS dictionary = detail, RTM = TRACE. Ask → Write → Trace → Build → Check → Accept.

questions.stem: A hybrid insurance program manages its policy-administration core with a predictive plan while the customer claims portal is built adaptively. The portal's backlog is ordered mostly by the date each request arrived, and a feature needed for a fixed regulatory filing sits near the bottom. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Work with the product owner to reorder the backlog by value, risk, dependencies, and the regulatory date.
Ask the developers to pick whichever backlog items they can finish fastest to show steady visible progress.
Move the regulatory feature into the predictive core's schedule so its date is managed by baseline.
Reorder the backlog personally and inform the product owner of the new priorities afterward.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Backlog ordering is the product owner's accountability. A healthy backlog is ordered by value, risk, dependencies, and deadlines, not by arrival date.
Spot it: a backlog sorted "first come, first served" and a fixed regulatory date buried near the bottom.
In this scenario: the PM works with the product owner to reorder by value, risk, dependencies, and the regulatory date.
Why not the others: letting developers pick the fastest items ignores value; moving the feature into the predictive schedule forces adaptive work into the wrong mechanism; reordering it personally takes over the product owner's role.
Remember: PO orders the product backlog. The PM facilitates; the PO decides.

questions.stem: A predictive public-sector data modernization is ending its design phase. The phase-gate review shows that two of the phase's exit criteria have not been met, but a senior manager wants to begin the build phase anyway to protect the schedule. What should the project manager do?
options: Start the build phase as the manager asks and finish the missing design items alongside the build work.
Lower the design phase's exit criteria so that the phase gate can be passed on its planned review date.
Close the design phase as complete and record the two unmet criteria as issues for the build team.
Present the unmet exit criteria and their impacts to the governing body so it can make the phase-gate decision.
questions.explanation:
Concept: A phase gate is a governance checkpoint at the end of a phase. The governing body compares results with the exit criteria and decides to continue, change, or stop.
Spot it: "phase-gate review", unmet exit criteria, and pressure to move on to protect the schedule.
In this scenario: the PM presents the unmet criteria and their impacts to the governing body so it can make the gate decision.
Why not the others: starting the build anyway bypasses the gate; lowering the exit criteria alters approved governance to hide a gap; closing the phase and passing gaps on as issues declares "done" when it is not.
Remember: AUTHORITY = governance. The PM informs the gate decision; the governing body makes it.

questions.stem: A hybrid hotel-technology rollout uses a predictive plan for property installations and a kanban board for the guest mobile app. Cards are piling up in the testing column, which is over its WIP limit, while developers keep starting new cards. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Raise the WIP limit on the testing column so the queued cards no longer show as a violation on the board.
Encourage developers to stop starting new cards and help testers finish the work already waiting in testing.
Assign the waiting cards to individual testers with firm due dates so each tester is held personally accountable.
Move the queued cards back to development until the testers report that they have spare capacity again.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Kanban manages flow by limiting work in progress (WIP). A column over its WIP limit is a bottleneck, and the fix is to finish work, not start more.
Spot it: cards piling up in one column, a WIP limit exceeded, and people still starting new work.
In this scenario: developers stop pulling new cards and swarm to help testing clear the queue.
Why not the others: raising the WIP limit hides the bottleneck instead of fixing it; assigning cards with personal due dates is push, not pull; moving cards back to development breaks flow and hides the real queue.
Remember: See → Limit → Pull → Flow → Improve. Stop starting, start finishing.

questions.stem: A predictive university project will replace the campus network over three years. First-year work is well understood, but requirements for the later buildings depend on a renovation plan that is not yet approved. The sponsor wants a complete plan now. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Decompose first-year work into work packages, and show later buildings as planning packages in the WBS.
Estimate every later-building activity in detail now, using current assumptions, to satisfy the sponsor.
Leave the later buildings out of the WBS entirely until the renovation plan is approved by the board.
Elaborate later-building work into detailed work packages as the renovation decisions are approved.
Start the later-building work now so that any renovation conflicts are discovered as early as possible.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Rolling wave planning is progressive elaboration: plan near-term work in detail and keep later work at a higher level (planning packages) until information arrives.
Spot it: well-understood early work, later work that depends on an unapproved decision, and pressure for "a complete plan now".
In this scenario: the PM decomposes first-year work into work packages, keeps later buildings as planning packages, and elaborates them as renovation decisions are approved.
Why not the others: detailed estimates on unapproved assumptions look complete but are unreliable; leaving later buildings out of the WBS drops known scope; starting later work early commits effort before requirements exist.
Remember: Near = detailed, far = planning package. Plan in waves as the fog lifts.

questions.stem: An agile team building a telehealth platform has finished a medication-history feature, and all automated tests pass. A manager wants to release it today for a marketing announcement, but the product owner has not yet reviewed the feature against the conditions agreed for the story, which include audit logging. What should the project manager do?
options: Release the feature today, because passing automated tests show that it already meets all the acceptance criteria.
Release the feature today and ask the product owner to check the audit logging after the launch is done.
Have the product owner review the feature against its acceptance criteria and definition of done before release.
Ask the compliance officer to sign off on the audit logging in place of the product owner's own review.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Verified is not accepted. Tests verify quality internally; in agile, the product owner accepts work against its acceptance criteria and the definition of done.
Spot it: "all tests pass", a rush to release, and a product owner who has not yet reviewed the story.
In this scenario: the product owner reviews the feature against its acceptance criteria and definition of done, including audit logging, before release.
Why not the others: passing automated tests shows verification, not acceptance; releasing first and checking later exposes users to an unaccepted feature; the compliance officer cannot replace the product owner's acceptance.
Remember: Build → Check → Verify → Accept → Handoff. Verified is internal; accepted is formal.

questions.stem: Match each reserve or budget term with its description.
matching_right: Funds outside the baseline for unforeseen work, the unknown-unknowns
Time added to a release plan to absorb delivery uncertainty
Funds within the baseline for identified risks, the known-unknowns
Approved time-phased budget, excluding management reserve

answer.Contingency reserve: Funds within the baseline for identified risks, the known-unknowns
answer.Management reserve: Funds outside the baseline for unforeseen work, the unknown-unknowns
answer.Cost baseline: Approved time-phased budget, excluding management reserve
answer.Schedule buffer: Time added to a release plan to absorb delivery uncertainty

questions.explanation:
Concept: Reserves protect the project against uncertainty; the exam tests which reserve covers which kind of risk and who controls it.
Contingency reserve: inside the cost baseline, for identified risks (known-unknowns); the PM uses it per the risk plan.
Management reserve: outside the cost baseline, for unforeseen work (unknown-unknowns); management controls it, and using it needs approval.
