Cost baseline: the approved, time-phased budget (includes contingency, excludes management reserve) used to measure performance.
Schedule buffer: time placed in a release plan or schedule to absorb uncertainty and protect a date.
Remember: Cost baseline + management reserve = project budget. Known risk → contingency; unknown risk → management reserve.

questions.stem: A hybrid retail transformation runs a predictive store-fit-out stream and several adaptive e-commerce teams. One adaptive team found that inviting store managers to its reviews sharply cut rework, but the other teams and the fit-out stream are unaware of this. What should the project manager do?
options: Share the practice through the lessons learned register and a cross-team session so others can adopt it now.
Capture the practice in the final lessons learned report so it can benefit the organization's future projects.
Require every team to adopt the store-manager review format starting with its next planned deliverable.
Ask the successful team to keep the practice informal so that documentation does not slow its work down.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Lessons learned are collected and shared throughout the project so current teams benefit now, not only future projects.
Spot it: one team discovers a practice that works, while other teams in the same project do not know about it.
In this scenario: the PM records the practice in the lessons learned register and runs a cross-team session so others can adopt it right away.
Why not the others: saving it for the final report loses the benefit for the rest of this project; forcing every team to adopt it ignores each team's context and self-organization; keeping it informal means nobody else learns it.
Remember: Learn → Apply → Keep learning → Archive. The register is updated during the project, not just at the end.

questions.stem: A customer on a predictive fiber-network rollout asks to add 40 business sites to the current phase. The engineering lead has already begun revising the schedule to include the new sites, and the customer expects work on them to start next week. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Approve the additional sites and update the schedule baseline, then inform the change control board at its next meeting.
Analyze the impact of the added sites on scope, schedule, cost, and risk, and then submit a change request.
Tell the customer that the scope baseline is frozen and new sites can be added only in a later project.
Start work on the sites next week and absorb the extra effort using the project's contingency reserve.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Integrated change control — every change to approved scope is analyzed for impact and decided by the authorized body before baselines are updated or work starts.
Spot it: a customer adding scope, a team member already revising the schedule, and pressure to start next week.
In this scenario: the PM analyzes the impact of 40 new sites on scope, schedule, cost, and risk, then submits a change request.
Why not the others: approving and updating the baseline before the CCB reverses the sequence; refusing outright ignores a valid request that should be evaluated; starting work on contingency spends reserve on unapproved scope.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor. Never implement a change blindly.

questions.stem: At a supplier review for an agile telecom billing project, a vendor representative mentions that its new rating-engine API may slip by a month because of staff turnover. The team's next three iterations depend on that API. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Wait for the vendor to formally confirm the delay before spending any team capacity on response planning.
Escalate the potential delay to the sponsor and ask for direction before the team discusses it.
Note the threat in the risk register and revisit it once the team reaches its next release plan.
Work with the team and product owner to add risk-response work, such as a mock API, to the backlog.
questions.explanation:
Concept: In agile, risk responses become backlog work. A risk-adjusted backlog lets the product owner prioritize risk work alongside features.
Spot it: "may slip", a dependency affecting upcoming iterations, and an agile team.
In this scenario: the PM works with the team and product owner to add response work, such as a mock API, to the backlog so the team is not blocked if the vendor slips.
Why not the others: waiting for confirmation wastes the time a response needs; escalating first skips the team's own analysis; noting it and revisiting at the next release plan is passive when the next three iterations are exposed.
Remember: Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor → Issue. In agile, respond by putting risk work in the backlog.

questions.stem: While planning a predictive wind-farm grid connection, a project team learns that the utility regulator has returned the interconnection permit application as incomplete. Detailed design of the substation cannot proceed until an approved permit is in place. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Add the returned permit to the risk register as a threat and assess its probability of occurring.
Continue detailed substation design on current assumptions and resolve the permit gap later in the project.
Record the returned permit in the issue log, assign an owner, and agree on the steps needed to resubmit it.
Escalate the returned application to the sponsor and wait for the sponsor to contact the regulator.
questions.explanation:
Concept: An issue is a problem that has already happened. It goes in the issue log with an owner, an action, and a due date.
Spot it: "returned as incomplete" and "cannot proceed"; the event has occurred and is blocking work.
In this scenario: the PM records the returned permit in the issue log, assigns an owner, and agrees on the resubmission steps.
Why not the others: the risk register is for uncertain future events, and this is certain; designing on assumptions risks rework on a blocked path; handing it to the sponsor and waiting gives away work the PM should own.
Remember: Log → Understand → Own → Fix → Watch → Close. MAY happen = risk register; HAS happened = issue log.

questions.stem: An agile team is building a hotel check-in kiosk. An operations manager reports at the release review that defects found by guests have doubled over three releases, and a sales director wants the next release shipped early by skipping regression tests. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Skip the regression tests for this release and schedule a separate stabilization release afterward.
Facilitate a root-cause analysis with the team to find where defects enter the development process.
Add a final inspection step before each release while leaving the development process unchanged.
Ask operations to log guest-reported defects so the team can fix them at the end of the project.
Make automated regression testing part of the definition of done rather than dropping it to save time.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Quality is built in, not inspected in. Rising defects mean the process is producing them, so fix the process and make quality part of "done".
Spot it: defect trends rising over releases, plus pressure to skip regression testing for speed.
In this scenario: the PM facilitates a root-cause analysis to find where defects enter, and makes automated regression testing part of the definition of done.
Why not the others: skipping regression tests trades quality for speed and creates more escapes; a final inspection catches defects late without changing the process; fixing guest defects at the end of the project lets them pile up.
Remember: See problem → Gather facts → Find why → Fix why → Prove fix. Prevention over inspection.

questions.stem: A security architect tells the steering committee of a predictive endpoint-security rollout that engineers built an unrequested threat-hunting dashboard because they believed users would like it. The dashboard is not in the scope baseline. What should the project manager do?
options: Treat the dashboard as unapproved work and have it evaluated through change control before further effort.
Keep the dashboard in the final deliverable because it clearly adds real value and users are likely to welcome it.
Remove the dashboard quietly so the steering committee does not question the team's discipline.
Update the scope baseline to include the dashboard, since the work on it has already been done.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Gold plating is adding extras the customer did not request. Any addition to the scope baseline must go through integrated change control, even if it seems valuable.
Spot it: "unrequested", "because they believed users would like it", and "not in the scope baseline".
In this scenario: the PM treats the dashboard as unapproved work and has it evaluated through change control before any more effort goes into it.
Why not the others: keeping it for its value adds unapproved scope, cost, and risk; quietly removing it hides the event from governance; updating the baseline because work is done reverses change control.
Remember: Baseline = APPROVED. Deliver what was agreed, no more and no less; value ideas go through change control.

questions.stem: Match each estimating technique with how it produces an estimate.
matching_right: Weights optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values.
Estimates each work package and rolls the totals up.
Relies on people with relevant specialized experience.
Multiplies a unit rate by the quantity of work.
Uses the actual cost or duration of a similar past project.

answer.Analogous: Uses the actual cost or duration of a similar past project.
answer.Parametric: Multiplies a unit rate by the quantity of work.
answer.Three-point (PERT): Weights optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values.
answer.Bottom-up: Estimates each work package and rolls the totals up.
answer.Expert judgment: Relies on people with relevant specialized experience.

questions.explanation:
Concept: Estimating techniques trade speed for accuracy; the right one depends on how much detail you have at that point in the project.
Analogous: Top-down and fast but least accurate; good early when detail is thin.
Parametric: Rate × quantity, e.g. $120 per square foot × 2,000 square feet; accurate when the rate is reliable.
Three-point (PERT): (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6 builds uncertainty into the estimate.
Bottom-up: Most accurate and slowest; needs a detailed WBS.
Expert judgment: Used alongside the others, especially for unusual work.
Remember: Analogous = FAST, Bottom-up = ACCURATE, Parametric = RATE × QUANTITY, PERT = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6.

questions.stem: A predictive pharmaceutical packaging-line project has a budget at completion of $800,000. At the latest status date, earned value is $300,000 and actual cost is $375,000, and the cost variance is expected to continue at the same rate. What estimate at completion should the project manager report?
options: $875,000, which is AC plus the remaining BAC minus EV
$640,000, which is BAC multiplied by the CPI of 0.80
$1,175,000, which is AC plus the full BAC of $800,000
$1,000,000, which is BAC divided by the CPI of 0.80
questions.explanation:
Concept: Estimate at completion (EAC) forecasts the total cost. When current cost performance is expected to continue, EAC = BAC ÷ CPI.
Spot it: "variance is expected to continue at the same rate", which is the typical-variance formula cue.
In this scenario: CPI = EV ÷ AC = 300,000 ÷ 375,000 = 0.80, so EAC = 800,000 ÷ 0.80 = $1,000,000.
Why not the others: AC + (BAC − EV) = $875,000 assumes the variance was a one-time event; BAC × CPI multiplies instead of dividing; AC + BAC double-counts the work already done.
Remember: "Continues" = BAC ÷ CPI. "One-time" = AC + (BAC − EV). CPI below 1.0 means over budget, so EAC grows above BAC.

questions.stem: Match each contract type with how it pays the seller and allocates cost risk.
matching_left: Fixed price with economic price adjustment
matching_right: Set price for well-defined scope; the seller carries cost risk
Buyer pays costs plus a fee earned by beating agreed targets
Hourly rates plus materials, suited to short or undefined work
Fixed price adjusted for inflation or market indexes over years
Buyer pays allowable costs plus a fee that does not vary

answer.Firm fixed price (FFP): Set price for well-defined scope; the seller carries cost risk
answer.Cost plus fixed fee (CPFF): Buyer pays allowable costs plus a fee that does not vary
answer.Cost plus incentive fee (CPIF): Buyer pays costs plus a fee earned by beating agreed targets
answer.Time and materials (T&M): Hourly rates plus materials, suited to short or undefined work
answer.Fixed price with economic price adjustme: Fixed price adjusted for inflation or market indexes over years

questions.explanation:
Concept: The contract type decides who carries cost risk; the clearer the scope, the more risk can move to the seller.
FFP: one price for a well-defined scope; overruns are the seller's problem, so the buyer's cost risk is lowest.
CPFF: the buyer reimburses allowable costs and pays a fixed fee; used when scope is uncertain, so the buyer carries the most cost risk.
CPIF: costs are reimbursed and the seller earns an incentive fee for beating cost or performance targets.
T&M: rates per hour plus materials; fast to start for staff augmentation or unclear work, but needs a not-to-exceed cap and close monitoring.
FPEPA: a fixed price with a clause that adjusts for inflation or commodity prices on multi-year contracts.
Remember: Fixed price = seller cost risk. Cost reimbursable = buyer cost risk. T&M = watch scope and hours.

questions.stem: A hybrid student-information-system upgrade traces its predictive integration requirements to adaptive backlog items. The product owner split a financial-aid user story into three smaller stories, and one of them was moved to a later release. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Stop maintaining traceability for the adaptive work, since backlog items change too often to be tracked.
Ask the product owner to merge the three stories again so the original trace link stays accurate.
Update the traceability links so the financial-aid requirement maps to all three stories and their releases.
Submit a change request to the change control board before the product owner may split any story.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Traceability must stay current as work is refined. In a hybrid project, requirements can be traced to backlog items, even as stories are split or moved.
Spot it: a traced requirement, a story split into three, and one piece moved to a later release.
In this scenario: the PM updates the trace so the financial-aid requirement maps to all three stories and their releases.
Why not the others: dropping traceability loses sight of when the requirement will be met; forcing stories to merge overrides the product owner's refinement; requiring CCB approval to split a story applies predictive control to backlog grooming.
Remember: RTM = TRACE. When the work moves, the trace moves with it.

questions.stem: The project manager of a predictive warehouse-automation project is building the WBS with the team. A team lead proposes making the lowest level a list of tasks such as order conveyors, install scanners, and test sorting logic. What should the project manager do?
options: Accept the task list as the WBS, since it gives the team a clear sequence of steps to follow from the start.
Decompose every deliverable until each element represents one day of effort for a single team member.
Skip the WBS and build the schedule directly from the team lead's task list to save planning time.
Keep the lowest WBS level as deliverable-based work packages and define activities later during scheduling.
questions.explanation:
Concept: The WBS is a deliverable-based decomposition of scope. Its lowest level is the work package; activities (tasks) are defined later when building the schedule.
Spot it: a proposed WBS made of verbs, such as order, install, and test, which signals tasks, not deliverables.
In this scenario: the PM keeps the lowest level as deliverable-based work packages and defines the activities later during scheduling.
Why not the others: accepting a task list confuses activities with deliverables and risks missing scope; forcing one-day elements over-decomposes the WBS; skipping the WBS removes the scope structure the schedule depends on.
Remember: WBS = nouns (deliverables); schedule = verbs (activities). What → Order → How long → Schedule → Approve → Control.

questions.stem: Warehouse-integration work on a predictive logistics optimization project is forecast to finish three weeks after its baselined date. A department head asks the project manager to change the schedule baseline to the forecast date so the status report no longer shows a variance. What should the project manager do?
options: Update the schedule baseline to the forecast date, since a baseline should reflect the most current plan.
Keep the baseline, report the variance against it, and evaluate options for recovering the three weeks.
Remove the warehouse-integration dates from the status report until the three weeks are recovered.
Change the baseline now and request the change control board's formal approval at its next meeting.
questions.explanation:
Concept: The schedule baseline is the approved reference for measuring progress. Variances are reported against it; it changes only through approved change control.
Spot it: a forecast slip and a request to move the baseline so the report stops showing a variance.
In this scenario: the PM keeps the baseline, reports the three-week variance honestly, and evaluates recovery options.
Why not the others: updating the baseline to the forecast confuses forecast with baseline; removing dates from the report hides the truth; changing it now and seeking approval later reverses change control.
Remember: Forecast = current expectation; baseline = APPROVED target. Forecasts move with reality; baselines move with approval.

questions.stem: In a predictive university data-center upgrade, one network engineer is assigned to eight overlapping activities, and several of them are now late. The dean asks the project manager to keep the engineer fully loaded so that no time is wasted. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Apply resource leveling to remove the engineer's overallocation, and check the effect on the critical path.
Assign the engineer more overlapping activities so that no working hours are ever left unused.
Explore adding a qualified second engineer to the critical activities that depend on this specialist.
Ask the engineer to switch among all eight activities each day so every one shows some progress.
Shift the late activities' baseline dates so the engineer's workload no longer appears as a delay.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Resource overallocation means one person is scheduled for more work than they can do at once. Resource leveling removes it, and adding capacity at the constraint protects the critical path.
Spot it: one specialist on eight overlapping activities, activities going late, and a request to "keep them fully loaded".
In this scenario: the PM levels the engineer's workload and checks the critical path impact, and explores adding a second qualified engineer to critical activities.
Why not the others: more overlapping work deepens the overload; switching among eight activities daily causes multitasking losses; shifting baseline dates hides the problem without approval.
Remember: Check float → Smooth if possible → Level if necessary. A full calendar is not the same as progress.

questions.stem: A bank's modernization program runs its core-ledger migration with a predictive plan. The new mobile app is also being managed predictively, but its requirements keep shifting after customer testing, generating dozens of change requests each month. What should the project manager do?
options: Freeze the mobile app requirements and reject further change requests until the ledger migration is complete.
Switch the entire program to adaptive delivery, including the heavily regulated core-ledger migration work.
Add more analysts to the change control board so the growing volume of change requests is processed faster.
Tailor the approach so the mobile app uses adaptive delivery while the ledger stays predictive under shared governance.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tailoring means choosing the delivery approach per component. Adaptive suits uncertain, changing requirements; predictive suits stable, regulated work. Hybrid uses both under shared governance.
Spot it: one stable, regulated component and one with requirements shifting after every customer test, flooding change control.
In this scenario: the PM tailors the approach so the mobile app is delivered adaptively while the ledger migration stays predictive under common governance.
Why not the others: freezing requirements blocks the learning the app needs; switching everything to adaptive removes control the regulated ledger needs; adding CCB analysts speeds paperwork but not value.
Remember: Predictive for stable work, agile for evolving work, hybrid when the project needs both. Identify component → choose approach → apply its rules → integrate.

questions.stem: A vendor's adaptive team on a hybrid government benefits portal has finished the eligibility module, and internal testing shows no defects. The contract requires the agency's program office to formally accept each module before payment is released. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Arrange for the program office to review the module against the agreed acceptance criteria and sign off.
Treat the clean internal test results as formal acceptance and approve the vendor's payment for the module.
Deploy the module to citizens and consider it accepted if no complaints arrive within the first month.
Ask the vendor's product owner to sign the acceptance form on the agency's behalf to save some time.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Formal acceptance comes from the authorized customer reviewing deliverables against the agreed acceptance criteria; quality control only verifies correctness.
Spot it: "internal testing shows no defects" and "the contract requires the program office to formally accept".
In this scenario: the PM arranges for the program office to review the module against its acceptance criteria and sign off, which unlocks payment.
Why not the others: clean internal tests are verification, not acceptance; "no complaints in a month" is not formal acceptance; the vendor's product owner has no authority to accept for the agency.
Remember: Build → Check → Verify → Accept → Handoff. Verified is internal; accepted is formal, and only the authorized customer accepts.

questions.stem: An agile team is building an outage-reporting app for an energy utility. A known risk that the mapping vendor would raise its license fees has occurred, and the increase matches the amount set aside for it. The operations director wants to use part of the same funds for a new analytics feature. What should the project manager do?
options: Use the leftover contingency funds for the analytics feature, since that money is already approved and available.
Ask the sponsor to release management reserve to pay for the license increase from this identified risk.
Apply the contingency funds to the license increase and send the analytics request to backlog prioritization.
Cut features from the next release to pay the fee so the contingency funds stay available for later needs.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contingency reserve is for identified risks; management reserve is for unknown risks. New feature ideas are not risks, so they go to backlog prioritization.
Spot it: "a known risk has occurred", "the increase matches the amount set aside", and someone eyeing the same funds for a new feature.
In this scenario: the PM applies the contingency to the license increase and sends the analytics idea to the product owner to prioritize.
Why not the others: using contingency for a new feature spends risk money on scope; management reserve is for unknown risks, not this planned one; cutting features to pay the fee ignores the reserve created for exactly this.
Remember: Known risk → contingency. Unknown risk → management reserve. New idea → backlog.

questions.stem: Match each step of the project closure flow with what happens in it.
matching_right: Finalize honest lessons learned and archive them for future projects
Close contracts, release resources, and issue the final report
Confirm all planned work and exit criteria are finished
Hand the product and its knowledge over to operations
Authorized customer formally signs off on the verified deliverables

answer.Complete: Confirm all planned work and exit criteria are finished
answer.Accept: Authorized customer formally signs off on the verified deliverables
answer.Transfer: Hand the product and its knowledge over to operations
answer.Learn: Finalize honest lessons learned and archive them for future projects
answer.Close: Close contracts, release resources, and issue the final report

questions.explanation:
Concept: A project is not finished when the work stops; closure follows a sequence that protects value and knowledge.
Complete: check the closure criteria; every planned deliverable is done and verified by quality control.
Accept: the authorized customer or sponsor formally accepts. Verified is internal; accepted is formal.
Transfer: transition the product to operations with training, documentation, and support so benefits continue.
Learn: finish the lessons learned register, successes and failures, honestly and blame-free, and archive it.
Close: close procurements, release the team, issue the final report, and formally close the project.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close.

questions.stem: An adaptive portal team in a hybrid government digital service demonstrates new features at an iteration review. The agency client then asks for a change that would alter the baselined interface with the predictive payment-system integration. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Have the portal team build the change in its next iteration, since the client asked for it at the review.
Reject the request, because baselined interfaces in a hybrid project cannot be changed once approved.
Assess the change's impact on the baselined interface, schedule, and cost of the payment integration.
Submit a change request for the interface change to the change control board for a formal decision.
Update the interface specification now and tell the payment team after the change is already live.
questions.explanation:
Concept: In a hybrid project, adaptive teams welcome change inside their own backlog, but anything that alters a baselined predictive element still goes through integrated change control.
Spot it: a request raised at an iteration review that would change a baselined interface with the predictive workstream.
In this scenario: the PM assesses the impact on the interface, schedule, and cost of the payment integration, then submits a change request for the board to decide.
Why not the others: building it next iteration changes a controlled interface without approval; rejecting it because it is baselined forgets that baselines can change through approval; updating the specification first and telling the payment team later bypasses control.
Remember: Adaptive part → backlog. Baselined part → change control. Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement.

questions.stem: Match each risk response strategy with what it does.
matching_right: Reduces a threat's probability or impact to an acceptable level
Increases an opportunity's probability or positive impact
Shifts a threat's impact and ownership to a third party
Changes the plan to eliminate a threat or its cause
Acts to ensure that an opportunity definitely occurs

answer.Avoid: Changes the plan to eliminate a threat or its cause
answer.Transfer: Shifts a threat's impact and ownership to a third party
answer.Mitigate: Reduces a threat's probability or impact to an acceptable level
answer.Exploit: Acts to ensure that an opportunity definitely occurs
answer.Enhance: Increases an opportunity's probability or positive impact

questions.explanation:
Concept: Risk responses differ for threats and opportunities; each one does a different thing to probability, impact, or ownership.
Avoid: change the plan so the threat cannot happen, such as removing the risky scope.
Transfer: shift the threat's impact and ownership to a third party through insurance, warranties, or contracts; the risk still exists.
Mitigate: reduce probability or impact to an acceptable level, such as adding tests or training.
Exploit: make an opportunity certain, such as assigning the best people to secure an early finish.
Enhance: raise an opportunity's probability or impact without guaranteeing it.
Remember: Threats = avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept, escalate. Opportunities = exploit, share, enhance, accept, escalate. Exploit guarantees; enhance improves.

questions.stem: An agile team building a hospital's discharge-planning app cannot deploy to the test environment because the infrastructure group has not granted the access it promised two weeks ago. The team has raised this at the daily stand-up three days in a row. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Treat the missing access as an impediment and work directly with the infrastructure manager to resolve it.
Ask the team to keep raising the access problem at each daily stand-up until infrastructure responds.
Tell the developers to deploy to a personal cloud account until the hospital finally grants the promised access.
Log the access problem as a risk and review its probability at the next iteration retrospective.
questions.explanation:
Concept: The servant leader removes impediments the team cannot resolve itself, especially ones that depend on other parts of the organization.
Spot it: an agile team blocked for days, a dependency on another group, and the same blocker repeated at the daily stand-up.
In this scenario: the PM treats the missing access as an impediment and works directly with the infrastructure manager to resolve it.
Why not the others: repeating it at every stand-up changes nothing; a personal cloud account creates a security and compliance breach; logging it as a risk misclassifies something that has already happened.
Remember: Team raises it, servant leader removes it. HAS happened = issue or impediment; MAY happen = risk.

questions.stem: A university registrar points out at an iteration review for a course-registration app that date-handling defects have appeared in four of the last five increments. Each defect was fixed quickly, but similar ones keep returning. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Add a manual date-check inspection by the registrar's staff before each increment is released.
Ask the team to keep fixing each date defect quickly as it appears, since the fixes take little time.
Reserve an iteration near the end of the release to find and correct any remaining date defects.
Facilitate a root-cause analysis with the team and adjust its engineering practices to prevent recurrence.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Recurring defects point to a process problem. Root-cause analysis finds why defects are created, and changing practices prevents them from returning.
Spot it: "similar ones keep returning" and "each defect was fixed quickly" (symptoms fixed, cause untouched).
In this scenario: the PM facilitates a root-cause analysis and helps the team adjust its engineering practices, such as adding tests for date handling.
Why not the others: a manual inspection by the registrar's staff catches defects late; continuing to fix each one treats symptoms forever; a hardening iteration at the end lets defects build up.
Remember: See problem → Gather facts → Find why → Fix why → Prove fix. Prevention over inspection.

questions.stem: Match each scope artifact with the information it provides.
matching_right: Links each requirement to its source, deliverable, and test
Detail for each work package, such as owner and criteria
Decomposes total scope into deliverables down to work packages
Deliverables, exclusions, and acceptance criteria for the project
Approved scope statement, WBS, and dictionary, changed only via change control

answer.Project scope statement: Deliverables, exclusions, and acceptance criteria for the project
answer.Work breakdown structure (WBS): Decomposes total scope into deliverables down to work packages
answer.WBS dictionary: Detail for each work package, such as owner and criteria
answer.Requirements traceability matrix: Links each requirement to its source, deliverable, and test
answer.Scope baseline: Approved scope statement, WBS, and dictionary, changed only via change control

questions.explanation:
Concept: Scope artifacts answer different questions: what is in, how it breaks down, the detail, the trace, and what is approved.
Project scope statement: the WHAT, including deliverables, exclusions, constraints, and acceptance criteria.
WBS: STRUCTURE. A deliverable-based decomposition whose lowest level is the work package, not a task list.
WBS dictionary: DETAIL. Description, responsible group, milestones, estimates, and acceptance criteria per component.
RTM: TRACE. Requirement origin → deliverable → test → status, so nothing is dropped or slipped in.
Scope baseline: APPROVED. The scope statement, WBS, and WBS dictionary together; the PM cannot change it alone.
Remember: Structure, detail, trace. Baseline = APPROVED. Protected does not mean impossible; it means authorized.

questions.stem: A predictive AI customer-service project must now go live three weeks earlier to support a product launch. The critical path includes a data-labeling activity that added contract staff could shorten and a model-training activity that could overlap with labeling at some rework risk. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Overlap all remaining activities so that every workstream finishes about three weeks earlier than planned.
Evaluate crashing and fast-tracking of critical-path activities, comparing their cost and risk impacts.
Add contract staff to every activity in the schedule, whether or not the activity is on the critical path.
Remove the model-testing activity from the schedule, because it does not produce a customer deliverable.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Schedule compression: crashing adds resources to critical-path activities (more cost), and fast-tracking overlaps them (more risk). Only critical-path work shortens the project.
Spot it: a new earlier deadline, a labeling activity more staff could shorten (crash), and training that could overlap labeling (fast-track).
In this scenario: the PM first evaluates crashing and fast-tracking on critical-path activities and compares their cost and risk.
Why not the others: overlapping everything adds rework risk to non-critical work; adding staff to every activity spends money where float exists; removing model testing cuts quality to hit a date.
Remember: Crash = add resources, costs money. Fast-track = overlap, adds risk. Late → Critical path → Options → Trade-offs → Act.

questions.stem: A predictive pharmaceutical warehouse expansion reports a schedule performance index of 1.10 and a cost performance index of 0.90 at the monthly review. A plant director asks the project manager what these indexes mean. How should the project manager describe the project's status?
options: It is ahead of schedule and over budget for the work completed so far.
It is behind schedule and under budget for the work completed so far.
It is ahead of schedule and under budget for the work completed so far.
It is behind schedule and over budget for the work completed so far.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Performance indexes read the same way: above 1.0 is good, below 1.0 is bad. SPI = EV ÷ PV (schedule); CPI = EV ÷ AC (cost).
Spot it: two index values, one above and one below 1.0, and a request to translate them into plain words.
In this scenario: SPI 1.10 means more work done than planned (ahead of schedule), and CPI 0.90 means the work cost more than it earned (over budget).
Why not the others: behind schedule and under budget reverses both; ahead and under budget misreads the CPI; behind and over budget misreads the SPI.
Remember: Would you rather have CPI 0.80 or 1.20? Above 1 is good, below 1 is bad, for both indexes.

questions.stem: An agile pharmaceutical launch includes developers from a contracted vendor under a time-and-materials agreement. The team notes in a retrospective that the vendor's developers wait days for their own manager's approval before changing any story, slowing the whole team. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Stop approving the vendor's invoices until its developers begin changing stories without waiting.
Remove the vendor's developers from the team and give their stories to the internal developers instead.
Meet the vendor's manager to agree that its developers may act on team decisions within the contract terms.
Ask the product owner to freeze all story changes so the vendor developers no longer need approvals.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile procurement relies on collaboration with the seller. When contract working rules clash with the team's way of working, the PM aligns them with the vendor within the contract terms.
Spot it: a time-and-materials vendor, a retrospective finding, and vendor staff waiting on their own manager before acting.
In this scenario: the PM meets the vendor's manager to agree that its developers can act on team decisions within the contract.
Why not the others: withholding invoices is not a contractual remedy and damages the partnership; removing the vendor developers loses capacity instead of fixing the rule; freezing story changes breaks agile's response to change.
Remember: Customer collaboration over contract negotiation, but always within the contract. SELLER = contract.

questions.stem: A hospital compliance officer asks an agile team building a patient portal how she can confirm that each privacy regulation requirement will be built and tested. The team currently tracks only user stories, with no link back to those requirements. What should the project manager do?
options: Tell the officer that agile teams do not trace requirements and she can review the product at the end.
Help the product owner link each requirement to its user stories and acceptance tests so coverage is visible.
Create a separate predictive requirements document and freeze it until the compliance officer has formally signed it.
Ask the team to write one large user story that covers all of the compliance requirements at the same time.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile teams can keep traceability lightly by linking each requirement to its user stories and acceptance tests, which shows coverage without heavy documents.
Spot it: a compliance officer needing proof that each regulation will be built and tested, and stories with no link to those requirements.
In this scenario: the PM helps the product owner link each privacy requirement to its stories and acceptance tests so coverage is visible.
Why not the others: claiming agile teams do not trace is a myth and fails the compliance need; a frozen predictive document kills flexibility and still does not show tests; one giant story hides which requirement is covered.
Remember: RTM = TRACE, even in agile. Requirement → story → acceptance test → done.

questions.stem: A hybrid healthcare platform has a predictive hardware rollout and an adaptive telemedicine app. At a stakeholder meeting, physicians report that poor video quality is driving patients away, yet the top backlog items are cosmetic changes requested by marketing. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Tell the physicians the video fix will be scheduled after the marketing items the team already ranked.
Direct the developers to abandon the current iteration and start on the video problem right away.
Raise a change request with the change control board to reorder the items in the app's backlog.
Bring the physicians' feedback to the product owner so the backlog can be reordered by value and urgency.
questions.explanation:
Concept: The backlog must reflect current value. When new evidence arrives, the product owner reorders the backlog; the PM makes sure the information reaches the product owner.
Spot it: customer-facing pain (patients leaving) versus cosmetic items ranked at the top.
In this scenario: the PM brings the physicians' feedback to the product owner so the backlog can be reordered by value and urgency.
Why not the others: sticking with the old order ignores new evidence; telling developers to abandon the iteration bypasses the product owner and disrupts the team; a CCB change request is the wrong mechanism for adaptive backlog ordering.
Remember: Request → PO → Backlog → Order → Select. New information changes the order; the PO changes the order.

questions.stem: An agile team is building a grid-monitoring dashboard for an energy company. A regional manager asks the project manager to approve an extra $120,000 for a new data feed immediately, but the governance framework lets the project manager approve changes of up to $50,000 only. What should the project manager do?
options: Approve the $120,000 now, since agile teams are expected to respond to changing needs quickly and without delay.
Prepare the options and impacts, and take the request to the body that holds that level of approval authority.
Split the request into three smaller changes that each fall under the $50,000 approval threshold.
Decline the request outright, because the data feed was not part of the original product vision.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Governance sets decision rights and thresholds. A request above the PM's delegated authority goes to the body that holds that authority, with analysis attached.
Spot it: a dollar amount above the PM's approval limit and pressure to approve "immediately".
In this scenario: the PM prepares options and impacts and takes the $120,000 request to the body that can approve it.
Why not the others: approving it exceeds delegated authority, even in agile; splitting it into three deliberately circumvents the threshold; declining it outright makes a decision that is not the PM's to make.
Remember: AUTHORITY = governance. Within threshold, decide; above threshold, analyze and escalate.

questions.stem: Midway through a predictive school construction program, the state adopts a new seismic code that applies to any building not yet occupied. The contractor says compliance will be costly and suggests continuing as designed, since permits were issued under the old code. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Confirm with legal and code officials how the new code applies to the project and assess its impacts.
Continue under the old code, because the permits already issued protect the project from the new rule.
Hand the new code requirement to the school district's operations team to address after occupancy.
Stop all construction work until the entire design has been revised to meet the new seismic code.
questions.explanation:
Concept: New laws and regulations are mandatory. The first step is to confirm whether and how the rule applies, with legal and compliance experts, before changing the plan.
Spot it: a new code mid-project, a contractor arguing that old permits cover it, and a FIRST question.
In this scenario: the PM confirms with legal and code officials how the seismic code applies to the unoccupied buildings and assesses the impacts.
Why not the others: continuing under the old code assumes an exemption no one confirmed; handing it to operations after occupancy knowingly delivers noncompliant buildings; stopping all work acts before knowing what is affected.
Remember: Law → Applies? → Impact → Expert → Change → Comply.

questions.stem: A hybrid rollout of mobile check-in across a hotel chain delivered every planned feature on schedule. Three months after launch the benefits report shows check-in wait times are unchanged because front-desk staff still process most guests manually. What should the project manager do?
options: Work with operations to learn why guests are not using mobile check-in and adjust the solution or adoption plan.
Close the project as a success, since every planned feature was delivered on schedule and within the budget.
Revise the benefits register to remove the wait-time target so that the report reflects what was actually achieved.
Ask the adaptive team to add more mobile check-in features in the hope that guests will then use it more often.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Benefits realization — projects exist to create outcomes and benefits, not just to ship outputs. If the benefit does not appear, the PM investigates why and adjusts.
Spot it: "every feature delivered on schedule" but the business measure (wait time) has not moved because people are not using the solution.
In this scenario: the PM works with operations to learn why mobile check-in is not being used and adjusts the solution or the adoption plan.
Why not the others: declaring success confuses output with value; deleting the target from the benefits register hides the gap; adding more features builds output without fixing adoption.
Remember: Output → Outcome → Benefit → Value. Delivered is not the same as valuable.

questions.stem: An agile team is building an online course marketplace for a university's continuing-education division. The university's board has just shifted strategy to focus on degree programs and plans to phase out continuing education within two years. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Continue delivering the marketplace backlog as planned, since the division will still operate for two more years.
Stop the team's work at once and move developers to degree-program projects without consulting the sponsor.
Review the product vision and business case with the sponsor and product owner against the new strategy.
Reword the marketplace's user stories to mention degree programs so that the work appears to match the strategy.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Strategic alignment — when organizational strategy changes, the business case and product vision must be re-examined with the people who own them.
Spot it: the board shifts strategy, and the product's market is being phased out.
In this scenario: the PM reviews the product vision and business case with the sponsor and product owner against the new strategy so they can decide to pivot, reduce, or stop.
Why not the others: continuing as planned ignores that the investment may no longer be justified; stopping and reassigning people alone takes a decision that belongs to the sponsor; rewording stories fakes alignment.
Remember: WHY = business case. Outside changes → inside assessment → sponsor decides.

questions.stem: A predictive project is replacing the reservation system used by 400 agents in a hotel group's call centers. Go-live is eight weeks away, and a call-center director warns that agents are anxious and some supervisors are quietly telling staff the old system will stay. What should the project manager do?
options: Delay all communication with agents until go-live so that they are not distracted from their current work.
Ask the director to issue a memo requiring all agents to use the new system and to report anyone who resists it.
Keep the old system running indefinitely beside the new one so agents can use whichever system they prefer.
Engage supervisors as change agents and plan communication, training, and support for agents before go-live.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Organizational change management — people adopt a new system when influential people champion it and users get early communication, training, and support.
Spot it: anxious users, supervisors quietly undermining the change, and go-live weeks away.
In this scenario: the PM engages supervisors as change agents and plans communication, training, and support for agents before go-live.
Why not the others: withholding communication increases anxiety and rumors; a mandate with reporting deepens resistance; running both systems indefinitely means the change never happens.
Remember: Understand → Engage → Enable → Implement → Reinforce. Win the influencers first.

questions.stem: Match each prioritization technique with how it ranks work.
matching_right: Estimates the value lost for each week of waiting.
Divides cost of delay by job size to rank work.
Separates basic needs, performance needs and delighters.
Sorts items into must, should, could and won't have.
Stakeholders spread a fixed budget of points across items.

answer.MoSCoW: Sorts items into must, should, could and won't have.
answer.Kano model: Separates basic needs, performance needs and delighters.
answer.Cost of delay: Estimates the value lost for each week of waiting.
answer.WSJF: Divides cost of delay by job size to rank work.
answer.100-point method: Stakeholders spread a fixed budget of points across items.

questions.explanation:
Concept: Prioritization techniques help the product owner or sponsor order work by value, so the team always builds the most valuable thing next.
MoSCoW: Great for fixing scope inside a deadline; the "won't have this time" list protects the team.
Kano model: Basics must exist or customers are unhappy; delighters surprise but are optional.
Cost of delay: Puts money on time: urgent, valuable items rise to the top.
WSJF: SAFe's formula: small jobs with high cost of delay go first.
100-point method: Forces trade-offs; nobody can mark everything as top priority.
Remember: Value drives order: the product owner decides WHAT and in what order; the team decides HOW.

questions.stem: On a predictive telecom network rollout, a planner has been pasting customer site addresses and contract terms into a public generative AI tool to draft installation schedules faster. Company policy restricts sharing confidential data with external AI tools. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Stop the practice, review the AI usage policy with the planner, and assess what confidential data was exposed.
Let the practice continue because it saves time, and ask the planner to carefully double-check the AI tool's output.
Report the planner to human resources for disciplinary action before discussing the situation with them.
Ban all AI tools across the project team permanently so that no similar data exposure can ever happen.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Responsible AI use — AI tools must follow organizational policy on confidential data. A breach is stopped first and its impact assessed.
Spot it: confidential customer data pasted into a public AI tool, a policy that forbids it, and a FIRST question.
In this scenario: the PM stops the practice, reviews the AI policy with the planner, and assesses what data was exposed so it can be reported and contained.
Why not the others: letting it continue keeps leaking data; sending the planner to HR before talking to them skips understanding; banning all AI permanently overreacts and does not address this exposure.
Remember: Tool → Data → Protect → Generate → Validate → Human → Monitor. Protect the data before you gain the speed.

questions.stem: A predictive core-banking upgrade is two months from transition to operations when the central bank announces new real-time fraud-reporting rules that take effect in six months. The operations director wants to go live first and deal with the rules later to avoid delaying handover. What should the project manager do?
options: Go live as planned and leave the new reporting rules for the operations team to handle after the project closes.
Stop the transition now and redesign the system before the full impact of the new rules is understood.
Analyze the rules' impact on the solution and the handover plan, and bring options to the change control board.
Ask the central bank for an exemption so the system can go live without meeting the new reporting rules.
questions.explanation:
Concept: External change — a new regulation that affects the solution is analyzed for impact and handled through integrated change control, not pushed onto operations.
Spot it: new mandatory rules with an effective date after go-live, and pressure to "go live first and deal with it later".
In this scenario: the PM analyzes the rules' impact on the solution and the handover plan and brings options to the change control board.
Why not the others: handing a known compliance gap to operations transfers a problem the project owns; stopping the transition acts before the impact is known; asking the central bank for an exemption avoids the requirement.
Remember: Outside changes → inside assessment. Law → Applies? → Impact → Expert → Change → Comply.

questions.stem: Match each organizational work structure with its purpose.
matching_right: Unit that standardizes project governance, methods, and support
Ongoing, repetitive work that sustains the organization's business
Temporary effort that creates a unique product, service, or result
Collection of work selected and prioritized to meet strategy
Related projects coordinated together to achieve shared benefits

answer.Project: Temporary effort that creates a unique product, service, or result
answer.Program: Related projects coordinated together to achieve shared benefits
answer.Portfolio: Collection of work selected and prioritized to meet strategy
answer.Operations: Ongoing, repetitive work that sustains the organization's business
answer.Project management office (PMO): Unit that standardizes project governance, methods, and support

questions.explanation:
Concept: The exam checks that you can tell temporary work, coordinated work, strategic selection, and ongoing work apart.
Project: temporary, with a defined start and end; it delivers outputs and then transitions them to operations.
Program: groups related projects to manage their interdependencies and deliver benefits none could deliver alone.
Portfolio: selects, prioritizes, and funds programs, projects, and operations so the organization does the right work for its strategy.
Operations: ongoing, repetitive work such as support and maintenance; it receives the product at transition.
PMO: standardizes governance and provides methods, templates, and support (supportive, controlling, or directive).
Remember: Project → Program → Portfolio. Projects deliver outcomes, programs coordinate benefits, portfolios align work to strategy, and operations keep it running.

questions.stem: During a quality review on a predictive gas-pipeline replacement, inspectors find weld defects that may require re-inspecting 12 kilometers of completed pipe. Correcting them would exceed the project manager's approved cost tolerance, and the sponsor is traveling this week. What should the project manager do?
options: Approve the full re-inspection with project funds, since safety issues fall outside the normal cost tolerances.
Wait for the sponsor to return before taking any action or telling anyone else about the weld defects found.
Re-inspect only the most accessible sections so that the correction cost stays inside the approved tolerance.
Follow the escalation path in the governance plan to bring the issue and options to the authorized decision maker.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Governance sets tolerances and escalation paths. When a decision exceeds the PM's authority, it follows the defined path to the authorized decision maker, even if the sponsor is away.
Spot it: a cost beyond the PM's tolerance, a safety-related defect, and an unavailable sponsor.
In this scenario: the PM follows the escalation path in the governance plan and brings the issue and options to whoever is authorized.
Why not the others: approving it personally exceeds delegated authority; waiting silently for a week delays a safety issue; re-inspecting only easy sections to stay under tolerance hides the real risk.
Remember: AUTHORITY = governance. Within tolerance, decide; beyond tolerance, escalate through the defined path.

questions.stem: An agile team is building a pharmacy refill app. A compliance lead reports at a quality review that a new federal rule will soon require an audit trail for every prescription change. Several completed features already modify prescriptions. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Ask the customer to waive the new rule for this app, since the completed features were built before it.
Add the audit trail only to future features and leave the already completed features exactly as they are now.
Work with the product owner to add the audit-trail requirement to the backlog and the definition of done.
Pause all development until a complete compliance specification is written and formally approved.
questions.explanation:
Concept: In agile, compliance requirements become backlog work and part of the definition of done, so every feature, old and new, meets them.
Spot it: a new federal rule, completed features already affected, and an agile team.
In this scenario: the PM works with the product owner to add the audit-trail requirement to the backlog and to the definition of done.
Why not the others: asking the customer to waive a federal rule is not possible; adding it only to future work leaves completed features noncompliant; pausing everything for a full specification is a predictive reflex that stalls delivery.
Remember: Law → Applies? → Impact → Expert → Change → Comply. In agile, "change" means backlog plus definition of done.

questions.stem: Match each benefits and value term with its description.
matching_right: Today's value of future cash flows minus the initial investment
Justifies the investment by describing its expected value
Time needed to recover the initial investment from returns
Person accountable for realizing and reporting a specific benefit
Explains how and when benefits will be delivered and measured

answer.Business case: Justifies the investment by describing its expected value
answer.Benefits management plan: Explains how and when benefits will be delivered and measured
answer.Benefit owner: Person accountable for realizing and reporting a specific benefit
answer.Net present value: Today's value of future cash flows minus the initial investment
answer.Payback period: Time needed to recover the initial investment from returns

questions.explanation:
Concept: Benefits and value terms describe why a project is funded, how benefits are tracked, and how value is measured in money.
Business case: WHY. It justifies the investment and is revisited if costs or benefits change.
Benefits management plan: HOW and WHEN benefits will be delivered, measured, and sustained after the project.
Benefit owner: the business person accountable for realizing and reporting a benefit, usually after handover.
Net present value: future cash flows discounted to today minus the investment; higher is better, and above zero is worth doing.
Payback period: how long until the investment is recovered; shorter is better, but it ignores returns after payback.
Remember: Business case = WHY, benefits plan = HOW and WHEN, benefit owner = WHO. NPV higher is better; payback shorter is better.

questions.stem: An agile team is building a vehicle-registration renewal service for a state agency whose strategic goal is to cut in-person office visits by 30%. A senior official asks the team to prioritize a staff-only reporting dashboard over the remaining online renewal features. What should the project manager do?
options: Put the dashboard at the top of the backlog, since requests from senior officials take priority over others.
Refuse the official's request, because staff tools do not belong in a citizen-facing digital service.
Build the dashboard and the renewal features in parallel by asking the team to work extra hours.
Help the product owner compare both requests against the visit-reduction goal when ordering the backlog.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Backlog priorities should reflect strategic objectives; the product owner orders work by the value it adds toward those goals, not by who asks.
Spot it: a measurable strategic goal (cut office visits 30%) and a senior person asking to jump the queue.
In this scenario: the PM helps the product owner compare both requests against the visit-reduction goal when ordering the backlog.
Why not the others: putting the dashboard first rewards rank over value; refusing outright takes a decision that belongs to the product owner; extra hours for both breaks sustainable pace.
Remember: Strategy → value → backlog order. The product owner decides; strategy is the tiebreaker.

questions.stem: An agile team has released a new electronic lab notebook to a pharmaceutical company's research scientists. Usage data after two releases shows most scientists still record experiments on paper, and interviews reveal they fear losing data during regulatory audits. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Ask research leadership to require daily use of the notebook and to track each scientist's compliance rate weekly.
Address the audit concerns by involving scientists in the next releases and providing hands-on adoption support.
Keep releasing new notebook features on schedule, since adoption will rise naturally as the product matures.
Provide one comprehensive training session for all scientists and then close out the change activities.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Resistance to change has a cause. Find it, involve the affected people in the solution, and support them through adoption.
Spot it: low usage, interviews revealing a specific fear (losing data in audits), and an agile team still releasing.
In this scenario: the PM addresses the audit concern by involving scientists in the next releases and giving hands-on adoption support.
Why not the others: mandating use with weekly tracking ignores the real fear; more features will not fix a trust problem; one training session and closing out change work assumes the problem is skill, not trust.
Remember: Understand → Engage → Enable → Implement → Reinforce. Resistance is information.

questions.stem: A predictive manufacturing-automation project must select a supplier for 300 industrial robots. The company's procurement policy includes environmental criteria such as energy efficiency and end-of-life recycling, but a department head wants the decision based on purchase price alone. What should the project manager do?
options: Base the supplier selection on purchase price alone, since robots are capital equipment and cost matters most.
Postpone the environmental evaluation until the robots are installed and their energy use can be measured.
Include the policy's environmental criteria in the supplier evaluation alongside price and technical factors.
Let the department head choose the supplier directly, because procurement decisions are a functional matter.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Source selection criteria must follow organizational policy. When the procurement policy includes environmental criteria, they are weighed with price and technical merit.
Spot it: a written policy with environmental criteria, and one manager wanting price alone.
In this scenario: the PM includes the policy's environmental criteria in the supplier evaluation alongside price and technical factors.
Why not the others: price alone violates the policy and ignores lifetime energy costs; evaluating after installation is too late to influence selection; letting one department head choose bypasses the procurement process.
Remember: Plan → Define → Solicit → Evaluate → Award → Manage → Close. Policy defines the criteria before you evaluate.

questions.stem: Match each responsible AI principle with what it requires on a project.
matching_right: People and the organization stay answerable for AI-driven decisions
Being able to explain how the AI system produces its outputs
Keeping confidential and personal data out of unapproved tools
People review AI results and can override them before acting
Testing outputs so that no group is systematically disadvantaged

answer.Transparency: Being able to explain how the AI system produces its outputs
answer.Accountability: People and the organization stay answerable for AI-driven decisions
answer.Fairness: Testing outputs so that no group is systematically disadvantaged
answer.Privacy and security: Keeping confidential and personal data out of unapproved tools
answer.Human oversight: People review AI results and can override them before acting

questions.explanation:
Concept: Responsible AI means using AI tools in ways that are explainable, fair, secure, and under human control; the organization, not the tool, is accountable.
Transparency: you can explain how the model reaches its outputs and document its training data and limits.
Accountability: blaming the vendor or the model is never an answer; the deploying organization owns the result.
Fairness: check outputs for bias across groups and escalate unequal treatment to governance.
Privacy and security: follow policy on approved tools and never paste confidential or personal data into public AI.
Human oversight: a person validates AI output, especially where the model is weak or safety is involved.
Remember: Tool → Data → Protect → Generate → Validate → Human → Monitor.

questions.stem: An agile team is building a remote patient-monitoring app. Midway through the release, a major insurer announces that it will reimburse only devices that share data through a new interoperability standard. The current backlog does not include support for that standard. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Continue with the current release plan and consider the new standard once this release is finished.
Direct the team to stop current work and start building support for the new standard right away.
Bring the announcement to the product owner so its impact on value and backlog priorities can be assessed.
Submit a formal change request to freeze the backlog until the interoperability standard is final.
questions.explanation:
Concept: In agile, external change is absorbed through the product owner, who assesses its effect on value and reorders the backlog.
Spot it: a market or regulatory announcement mid-release that the current backlog does not cover.
In this scenario: the PM brings the insurer's announcement to the product owner so its impact on value and priorities can be assessed.
Why not the others: finishing the release first ignores a change that affects reimbursement; stopping everything acts before assessing and bypasses the product owner; freezing the backlog contradicts agile's response to change.
Remember: Outside changes → inside assessment. Request → PO → Backlog → Order → Select.

questions.stem: A predictive project is building a new loan-origination system as part of a bank's digital-lending program. At a benefits review the project manager learns that a sister project's credit-scoring engine, which the system depends on, will be three months late. What should the project manager do?
options: Build a temporary credit-scoring engine inside the project so it no longer depends on the sister project.
Wait until the sister project delivers its engine before telling the program manager about any impact.
Ask the portfolio board to cancel the sister project, since its delay threatens the loan system's benefits.
Raise the dependency with the program manager so the impact can be managed across both projects.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Programs manage interdependencies among related projects. A dependency on a sister project is coordinated at the program level.
Spot it: "part of a program", "a sister project the system depends on", and a known delay.
In this scenario: the PM raises the dependency with the program manager so the impact can be managed across both projects.
Why not the others: building a temporary engine duplicates work and makes a program decision at project level; waiting to tell the program manager wastes response time; asking to cancel another project is far beyond the PM's role.
Remember: Dependency → Assess Impact → Coordinate → Monitor. Projects deliver outcomes; programs coordinate benefits.

questions.stem: An agile team is delivering a benefits-application service for a government department. The department's investment board requires quarterly evidence that its funding is producing results, and a board member complains that the team's reports contain only story-point totals. What should the project manager do?
options: Give the board outcome evidence such as working increments, release forecasts, and measured user results.
Explain that agile teams are self-organizing and do not need to report their progress to investment boards.
Switch the team to a full predictive plan with detailed baselines so the board receives familiar reports.
Send the board more detailed story-point data, broken down by individual team member and by iteration.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile projects still sit inside organizational governance. Oversight bodies need evidence of value, such as working product and outcomes, not internal team metrics.
Spot it: an investment board wanting evidence of results, and reports full of story points.
In this scenario: the PM gives the board working increments, release forecasts, and measured user results.
Why not the others: saying agile teams do not report ignores governance; switching to full predictive plans changes the approach to suit a report; more story-point detail is still a team estimating tool, not value.
Remember: Story points are for the team; outcomes are for the board. Agile is not "no governance".

questions.stem: A hybrid energy-storage project builds its battery installation predictively and its monitoring software adaptively. After the latest software release, an engineer finds that safety alarms are logged in a format that does not meet the grid operator's mandatory reporting standard. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Wait until the grid operator's next audit to see whether the log format is actually flagged as a problem.
Confirm the gap with the compliance lead, notify the accountable stakeholders, and assess corrective options.
Have a developer quietly change the log format in production without telling anyone outside of the delivery team.
Roll back every software release and halt the battery installation until the logging standard is met.
questions.explanation:
Concept: A possible compliance breach is confirmed, disclosed to the accountable people, and corrected through a controlled response.
Spot it: a mandatory reporting standard, a mismatch found after a release, and a FIRST question.
In this scenario: the PM confirms the gap with the compliance lead, notifies the accountable stakeholders, and assesses corrective options.
Why not the others: waiting for the audit knowingly stays noncompliant; a quiet change in production is uncontrolled and hidden; rolling back everything and halting installation acts before the gap is confirmed and stops unaffected work.
Remember: Law → Applies? → Impact → Expert → Change → Comply. Confirm, disclose, correct.

questions.stem: An agile team has delivered six releases of a bank's small-business lending portal. Analytics show loan applications have not increased as the business case projected, and customer interviews reveal that the document-upload step causes most applicants to quit. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Work with the product owner to prioritize simplifying the document-upload step in the backlog.
Continue delivering the remaining planned features, since completing full scope will bring value.
Revise the business case to lower the projected increase so the portal's results appear on target.
Track application completion rates after each release to confirm whether the change adds value.
Wait until all planned features are delivered before measuring whether the portal produces value.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile delivery optimizes for outcomes, not output: find what blocks the benefit, fix it, and measure whether the fix works.
Spot it: releases shipped but the business case metric flat, plus evidence of one step causing drop-off.
In this scenario: the PM helps the product owner prioritize simplifying document upload, and tracks application completion after each release to confirm the value.
Why not the others: delivering remaining features adds output without fixing the barrier; lowering the business case target hides the gap; waiting until everything ships delays learning.
Remember: Output → Outcome → Benefit → Value. Build, measure, learn.

questions.stem: An agile team is building a scheduling tool for a construction company's field crews. Two vice presidents give conflicting direction: one wants features that cut overtime costs, and the other wants safety-incident reporting first. The company's published strategy names worker safety as its top priority this year. What should the project manager do?
options: Split the team's capacity evenly between both requests so that neither of the vice presidents is disappointed.
Prioritize the overtime features, since cost savings are easier to measure and to report to executives.
Ask the team to vote on which vice president's features they would prefer to build first in the release.
Help the product owner order the backlog using the published strategy, and confirm it with both vice presidents.
questions.explanation:
Concept: When stakeholders conflict over priorities, the organization's published strategy is the objective tiebreaker, applied by the product owner.
Spot it: two executives pulling in different directions, and a strategy that clearly names a top priority.
In this scenario: the PM helps the product owner order the backlog using the published safety priority and confirms it with both vice presidents.
Why not the others: an even split avoids the decision and slows the top-priority value; choosing overtime features ignores the strategy; a team vote hands a value decision to the wrong people.
Remember: Strategy decides, the PO orders, the PM facilitates. Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act.

questions.stem: An agile team is replacing paper work orders with a tablet app for a telecom company's field technicians. Early releases show that senior technicians avoid the app, and several say it was designed without asking how they actually do their jobs. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Invite senior technicians to review increments and shape upcoming features so the app fits their work.
Ask field supervisors to make app use mandatory and to report any technicians who keep using paper forms.
Keep delivering the planned features, since technicians usually accept new tools after a few months.
Schedule a formal classroom course after the final release to teach technicians how to use the app.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Involving the people affected by a change in shaping it reduces resistance and improves the product at the same time.
Spot it: users avoiding the tool, and saying it was designed without asking how they work.
In this scenario: the PM invites senior technicians to review increments and shape upcoming features so the app fits their work.
Why not the others: making it mandatory ignores a valid design concern and hardens resistance; waiting for acceptance to come naturally ignores the feedback; a classroom course after the final release is too late to shape the product.
Remember: Understand → Engage → Enable → Implement → Reinforce. Build with users, not for them.

questions.stem: A hybrid banking modernization is retiring 200 servers from its old data center as the new cloud platform goes live. The bank's sustainability policy requires certified recycling of electronic equipment, but the transition plan simply says the servers will be discarded. What should the project manager do?
options: Discard the servers as the transition plan states, since recycling is an operations concern after closure.
Leave the servers in the old data center until someone else eventually makes a decision on recycling.
Update the transition plan to include certified recycling and secure data wiping for the retired servers.
Sell the servers to the highest bidder right away to offset project costs, skipping data wiping.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sustainability and data-protection policies apply across the whole life cycle, including decommissioning. A plan that conflicts with binding policy gets fixed.
Spot it: retired equipment, a policy requiring certified recycling, and a transition plan that says "discard".
In this scenario: the PM updates the transition plan to include certified recycling and secure data wiping for the servers.
Why not the others: discarding them follows a plan that violates policy; leaving them for someone else to decide abandons a project responsibility; selling them without wiping data creates a security breach.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close, and policy applies all the way to the end.

questions.stem: A predictive project is introducing an AI tool that schedules maintenance for a factory's machines. At a compliance checkpoint, auditors ask how the tool reaches its recommendations. The team cannot explain them and has kept no record of the data used to train the model. What should the project manager do?
options: Tell the auditors that the AI vendor is responsible for explaining the tool, so the project has no duty to do so.
Document the model's training data, logic, and limitations, and set up a review of its outputs for auditors.
Apply the tool's recommendations without review, since the AI has proven accurate during the pilot so far.
Remove the AI tool from scope and return to manual maintenance scheduling for the rest of the project.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Responsible AI requires transparency and accountability: the organization must be able to explain, document, and oversee how its AI tools make recommendations.
Spot it: auditors asking "how does it decide?", no explanation, and no record of training data.
In this scenario: the PM documents the model's training data, logic, and limitations, and sets up a review of its outputs for auditors.
Why not the others: pointing to the vendor ignores that the deploying organization stays accountable; applying outputs without review removes human oversight; removing the tool overreacts when documentation and review fix the gap.
Remember: Tool → Data → Protect → Generate → Validate → Human → Monitor. If you cannot explain it, you cannot defend it.

questions.stem: An agile team is building a loyalty-program app for a resort chain. At a benefits review the marketing director reports that a sharp economic downturn has cut bookings by 40% and that the app's projected revenue is now unlikely. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Continue the current release plan, since the business case was already approved and the downturn may be brief.
Review the app's business case and priorities with the sponsor and product owner in light of the downturn.
Stop the team's work at once and close the project without consulting the sponsor or product owner.
Ask the team to increase velocity so the app launches sooner and recovers the lost bookings faster.
questions.explanation:
