Concept: When external conditions undermine the business case, the investment is re-evaluated with the people who own it, who can pivot, reprioritize, or stop.
Spot it: an economic downturn and projected revenue now unlikely.
In this scenario: the PM reviews the app's business case and priorities with the sponsor and product owner in light of the downturn.
Why not the others: continuing because the case was once approved ignores that its assumptions broke; closing the project alone takes the sponsor's decision; pushing for higher velocity misunderstands velocity and does not restore demand.
Remember: WHY = business case. External change occurs → assess impact → reassess value → decide with the sponsor.

questions.stem: During a predictive factory automation project, the plant manager asks the project manager to also take charge of the plant's routine monthly equipment maintenance, since the project team is already on site. What should the project manager do?
options: Explain that routine maintenance is ongoing operations and coordinate with the plant manager on handoffs.
Add the monthly maintenance work to the project scope, since the project team is already available on site.
Accept the maintenance work informally without changing the project's scope or budget in any way.
Ask the portfolio board to reclassify the plant's maintenance as a new project within the program.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Projects are temporary and create unique results; recurring maintenance is operations work that belongs to the operating organization.
Spot it: "routine", "monthly", and "since the team is already on site".
In this scenario: the PM explains that routine maintenance is ongoing operations and coordinates handoffs with the plant manager.
Why not the others: adding it to scope turns a temporary project into ongoing work and still needs change control; taking it on informally is unapproved scope creep; reclassifying maintenance as a project misreads what a project is.
Remember: Projects are temporary; operations are ongoing. The project hands over; it does not become operations.

questions.stem: A predictive public-sector data modernization reports to both a technology steering committee and a finance oversight board. At a risk workshop the team realizes that neither body's charter says which one approves changes to the data-retention design, and a decision is needed within a month. What should the project manager do?
options: Decide the data-retention design personally, since neither body has clear authority over this change.
Ask the sponsor to clarify decision rights between the two bodies and record the result in the governance plan.
Submit the change to both bodies and implement whichever decision is received first from either one.
Delay the data-retention design until one of the bodies takes up the issue on its own initiative.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Clear decision rights are a core part of governance. If two bodies both might own a decision, the sponsor clarifies it and the answer is documented before it is needed.
Spot it: two oversight bodies, neither charter covers this decision, and a deadline coming.
In this scenario: the PM asks the sponsor to clarify decision rights and records the answer in the governance plan.
Why not the others: deciding personally assumes authority the PM does not have; sending it to both and taking the first answer invites conflicting decisions; waiting for someone to notice risks missing the deadline.
Remember: AUTHORITY = charter and governance. Unclear authority? Clarify it with the sponsor before you act.

questions.stem: During early planning of a predictive claims-system project for an insurer, a business analyst notes that state regulations require claim records to be kept for seven years, but the requirements assume three. A manager suggests leaving it for now to keep the estimate low. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the three-year assumption to protect the estimate and address retention during the operations phase.
Ask the insurer's customers to waive the retention rule so the project can proceed with three years.
Add a note to the assumption log and revisit the retention rule only if an auditor raises the issue.
Update the requirements and estimates to reflect the seven-year retention rule before baselines are approved.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Mandatory legal requirements are captured in the requirements and estimates before baselines are approved, not left as assumptions.
Spot it: "state regulations require", a requirement that conflicts with it, and a manager wanting to keep the estimate low.
In this scenario: the PM updates the requirements and estimates to reflect the seven-year retention rule before the baselines are set.
Why not the others: keeping three years builds a known violation; customers cannot waive a state law; logging it as an assumption treats a known legal fact as uncertain.
Remember: Law → Applies? → Impact → Expert → Change → Comply. Fix it in planning; it costs the least there.

questions.stem: Match each stakeholder question with the document family that answers it.
matching_left: WHY is this investment still worth funding?
Who gave the AUTHORITY to start the project?
HOW will this area of the project be managed?
What is the APPROVED target we measure against?
Where do we TRACK what may happen or has happened?
matching_right: Registers and logs, such as the risk register and issue log
Subsidiary management plans within the project management plan
Scope, schedule, and cost baselines
Project charter and governance thresholds
Business case and benefits information

answer.HOW will this area of the project be man: Subsidiary management plans within the project management plan
answer.Where do we TRACK what may happen or has: Registers and logs, such as the risk register and issue log

questions.explanation:
Concept: Find the trigger word in the question first, then the document family, then the specific document.
WHY: the business case justifies the investment and is revisited when costs, benefits, or strategy change.
AUTHORITY: the charter, issued by the sponsor, authorizes the project and gives the PM authority to use resources.
HOW: management plans describe how scope, schedule, cost, risk, and other areas will be managed.
APPROVED: baselines are the approved targets for measuring performance; they change only through change control.
TRACK: registers and logs are living records the PM keeps current; MAY happen = risk register, HAS happened = issue log.
Remember: Plan = HOW, Baseline = APPROVED, Register/Log = TRACK, Report = COMMUNICATE. Business case → charter → plan → baselines.

questions.stem: A hybrid retail transformation is opening self-checkout stores predictively and building the checkout software adaptively. At a risk workshop, strategy staff report that leadership now plans to close half of the physical stores and expand online sales. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Continue opening all planned stores, since the store openings are already baselined and contracted.
Cancel the software work at once, since the store closures make all checkout software unnecessary.
Ask the adaptive team to add online shopping features to its backlog without involving the sponsor.
Reassess the business case with the sponsor to confirm which parts of the project still align with strategy.
questions.explanation:
Concept: A strategy shift requires re-validating the business case with the sponsor, so work continues only where it still supports the new direction.
Spot it: leadership plans to close half the stores, and the project is opening stores and building checkout software.
In this scenario: the PM reassesses the business case with the sponsor to confirm which parts still align.
Why not the others: a baseline does not guarantee strategic fit, so continuing all openings ignores the shift; cancelling the software alone makes the sponsor's call; adding online features without the sponsor redirects funded work without authority.
Remember: WHY = business case. Baselines are APPROVED targets, not strategy; when strategy moves, revisit WHY first.

questions.stem: A hybrid project is introducing a bedside charting system in a hospital, with predictive hardware installation and adaptive software releases. Nurse managers report that staff are overwhelmed because each software release changes screens they have only just learned. What should the project manager do?
options: Provide a single comprehensive training session at the very end, after all the software releases are complete.
Align release timing with nursing leaders and add support such as super-users and short guides per release.
Stop all software releases until the nurses have fully learned every screen in the current version.
Ask nurse managers to tell staff to adapt to each release, since the changes improve the system overall.
questions.explanation:
Concept: The pace of change must match the organization's capacity to absorb it; release timing and support are planned with the people affected.
Spot it: users overwhelmed because each release changes what they just learned.
In this scenario: the PM aligns release timing with nursing leaders and adds super-users and short guides for each release.
Why not the others: one session at the very end leaves staff unsupported through every release; stopping all releases loses delivered value; telling staff to adapt ignores a real capacity problem.
Remember: Understand → Engage → Enable → Implement → Reinforce. Change at the speed people can absorb.

questions.stem: Match each sustainability concept with its description.
matching_right: Keeps materials in use through reuse, repair, and recycling
Discloses environmental, social, and governance performance to stakeholders
Judges success by social, environmental, and economic results
Evaluates environmental impact from raw materials to disposal
Total greenhouse gases caused by an activity or product

answer.Triple bottom line: Judges success by social, environmental, and economic results
answer.Carbon footprint: Total greenhouse gases caused by an activity or product
answer.Circular economy: Keeps materials in use through reuse, repair, and recycling
answer.Life cycle assessment: Evaluates environmental impact from raw materials to disposal
answer.ESG reporting: Discloses environmental, social, and governance performance to stakeholders

questions.explanation:
Concept: Sustainability terms describe how an organization measures and reduces its environmental and social impact, which is now part of project value.
Triple bottom line: success judged on people, planet, and profit, not profit alone.
Carbon footprint: total greenhouse gas emissions caused by an activity, product, or organization.
Circular economy: design out waste by keeping materials in use through reuse, repair, and recycling.
Life cycle assessment: measures environmental impact from raw material to disposal, cradle to grave.
ESG reporting: discloses environmental, social, and governance performance to investors and stakeholders.
Remember: People, planet, profit. Measure it (footprint, LCA), design it (circular), report it (ESG).

questions.stem: A hybrid hospital project uses an AI model, built in adaptive releases, to recommend which patients need follow-up calls. A benefits review shows the model flags patients from rural clinics far less often than urban patients with similar conditions. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep applying the model's recommendations as they are, since it raises follow-up rates across the whole patient population.
Adjust the model's scores for rural patients manually without telling clinicians or the governance body.
Escalate the potential bias to the governance body and have the model's data and outputs reviewed for fairness.
Retire the AI model permanently and go back to manual selection of patients for every follow-up call.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Responsible AI requires monitoring for bias and involving governance when a model may treat groups unequally, even if overall results look good.
Spot it: a model that flags one group far less often than a similar group.
In this scenario: the PM escalates the potential bias to the governance body and has the model's data and outputs reviewed for fairness.
Why not the others: overall improvement does not justify unfair outcomes for a group; quietly adjusting scores hides the problem from clinicians and governance; retiring the model permanently overreacts before the cause is known.
Remember: Tool → Data → Protect → Generate → Validate → Human → Monitor. Validate means accuracy and fairness.

questions.stem: A hybrid solar-farm project procures panels under a predictive plan while its monitoring software is built adaptively. A new government tariff will raise the cost of imported panels by 25% starting next quarter, and only half the panels have been ordered. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Assess the tariff's cost and schedule impact and evaluate options such as earlier orders or other suppliers.
Continue the procurement plan unchanged and absorb the higher panel costs by using the project's management reserve.
Cancel the remaining panel orders until the government decides to reverse the tariff on imported panels.
Ask the software team to cut features so its budget can pay for the higher panel costs right away.
questions.explanation:
Concept: An external change such as a new tariff is analyzed for impact and response options before choosing a course of action.
Spot it: a future cost increase with a known start date, and half the panels still not ordered.
In this scenario: the PM assesses the tariff's cost and schedule impact and evaluates options such as ordering earlier or using other suppliers.
Why not the others: absorbing it with management reserve skips analysis and uses a reserve the PM cannot draw on alone; cancelling orders while hoping for reversal risks the schedule; cutting software features shifts the problem to another workstream.
Remember: Outside changes → inside assessment. Assess → Options → Decide.

questions.stem: An agile team is starting a route-optimization product for a logistics company. During early planning, two other initiatives compete for the same data engineers, and each sponsor insists that their initiative comes first. What should the project manager do?
options: Assign the data engineers to whichever sponsor asked first, since the earliest request has the strongest claim.
Split each data engineer's time evenly across the three initiatives so that every sponsor is satisfied.
Hire contract data engineers for the team without consulting the other sponsors or portfolio managers.
Raise the conflict with the portfolio management function so resources are allocated by strategic priority.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Portfolio management selects and prioritizes initiatives and allocates shared resources according to strategy.
Spot it: several initiatives competing for the same scarce people, and each sponsor insisting on first place.
In this scenario: the PM raises the conflict with the portfolio management function so resources are allocated by strategic priority.
Why not the others: first-come allocation ignores strategy; an even split causes multitasking losses and dodges the decision; hiring contractors alone spends money without the other sponsors or the portfolio.
Remember: Projects deliver outcomes, programs coordinate benefits, portfolios align work to strategy. Competing initiatives = portfolio decision.

questions.stem: The governance plan for a hybrid factory-automation project allows the project manager to approve schedule changes of up to two weeks that do not affect the final milestone. The team finds that a sensor firmware update will delay one installation activity by eight days, and that activity has enough float to absorb it. What should the project manager do?
options: Send the eight-day change to the steering committee, since every schedule change needs its formal review.
Leave the delay unrecorded because float absorbs it, and keep the schedule and documents unchanged.
Approve the change under the delegated authority, update the documents, and inform stakeholders as required.
Ask the sponsor to raise the approval limit to four weeks so that future changes can move faster.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Governance delegates authority within thresholds. A change inside the PM's limit is decided at project level and documented, not escalated.
Spot it: a governance rule allowing the PM to approve up to two weeks, an eight-day slip, and enough float to absorb it.
In this scenario: the PM approves the change under delegated authority, updates the documents, and informs stakeholders as required.
Why not the others: sending it to the steering committee ignores delegated authority and slows decisions; leaving it unrecorded hides a real change; asking to raise the limit is not needed for this decision.
Remember: Within threshold, decide and document; above threshold, escalate. Not all changes go to the CCB.

questions.stem: A predictive project is upgrading a university's online learning portal. At a quality review, testers find that several pages fail the accessibility standard required by federal law, and fixing them would delay go-live by three weeks. A dean suggests launching first and fixing accessibility next semester. What should the project manager do?
options: Treat the accessibility gaps as mandatory and submit a change request with options for meeting the requirement.
Launch on schedule and plan the accessibility fixes for next semester, as the dean has suggested.
Ask the testers to relax the accessibility test criteria so the failing pages can pass the review.
Ask the legal office to decide whether the law applies once the portal has already gone live.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Legal requirements are not optional. A compliance gap must be fixed, with any schedule impact handled through change control.
Spot it: "required by federal law", failing pages, and a suggestion to launch now and fix later.
In this scenario: the PM treats the accessibility gaps as mandatory and submits a change request with options for meeting the requirement.
Why not the others: launching first knowingly releases a noncompliant product; relaxing the test criteria hides the failure; asking legal after go-live is backward.
Remember: Law → Applies? → Impact → Expert → Change → Comply. Compliance is a must-have, not a nice-to-have.

questions.stem: Match each value delivery term with its description.
matching_right: Change in behavior or conditions that results from using outputs
Worth of the benefits relative to the cost of obtaining them
Smallest release that tests whether a product idea delivers value
Tangible product or deliverable that the project produces
Measurable gain the organization realizes from an outcome

answer.Output: Tangible product or deliverable that the project produces
answer.Outcome: Change in behavior or conditions that results from using outputs
answer.Benefit: Measurable gain the organization realizes from an outcome
answer.Value: Worth of the benefits relative to the cost of obtaining them
answer.Minimum viable product: Smallest release that tests whether a product idea delivers value

questions.explanation:
Concept: Value delivery is a chain: what the project builds, what changes because of it, what the organization gains, and whether it was worth the cost.
Output: the tangible deliverable, such as an app, a building, or a report.
Outcome: the change in behavior or conditions when people use the output, such as faster check-in.
Benefit: the measurable gain from the outcome, such as lower cost or higher revenue.
Value: the worth of the benefits compared with what it cost to get them.
Minimum viable product: the smallest release that tests whether an idea delivers value, so you learn early.
Remember: Output → Outcome → Benefit → Value. What you build should create a result, produce a benefit, and deliver value.

questions.stem: An agile team is building a predictive-maintenance product for a manufacturer's own plants. At a risk workshop the strategy office notes that leadership now wants to sell the product to other manufacturers, which requires multi-customer support that the current architecture lacks. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Continue the current roadmap unchanged, since the original internal goal was approved by leadership.
Review the product vision and roadmap with the sponsor and product owner against the new strategy.
Rebuild the architecture for multiple customers right away, before the new goal is analyzed or confirmed.
Add every multi-customer feature to the top of the backlog without consulting the product owner first.
Have the team run a short spike to estimate the effort needed to support multiple customer companies.
questions.explanation:
Concept: A strategy shift calls for realigning the product vision and roadmap with the sponsor and product owner, supported by evidence such as a spike.
Spot it: leadership changes the product's market, and the current architecture does not fit the new goal.
In this scenario: the PM reviews the vision and roadmap with the sponsor and product owner, and the team runs a short spike to estimate multi-customer effort.
Why not the others: continuing unchanged ignores the new direction; rebuilding now commits big effort before the goal is confirmed; stacking features on top of the backlog bypasses the product owner.
Remember: Outside changes → inside assessment. A spike buys knowledge cheaply before you buy architecture expensively.

questions.stem: A predictive project is replacing the work-management system used by a utility's line crews. At a change evaluation the project manager learns that no one has assessed whether crews, supervisors, and schedulers are ready for the new processes the system will introduce. What should the project manager do?
options: Delay change management activities until after go-live, when real user problems will be easier to see.
Perform a readiness assessment of the affected groups and plan training and support based on the results.
Assume that the crews are ready because the system's design was already approved by the steering committee.
Send an email announcement to all crews that explains the new system, and consider readiness confirmed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: An organizational readiness assessment shows how prepared each affected group is, so training, communication, and support can be targeted before go-live.
Spot it: "no one has assessed whether crews, supervisors, and schedulers are ready".
In this scenario: the PM performs a readiness assessment of the affected groups and plans training and support based on the results.
Why not the others: waiting until after go-live lets problems hit operations; design approval does not mean users are ready; an email announcement creates awareness, not ability.
Remember: Understand → Engage → Enable → Implement → Reinforce. Assess readiness before you enable.

questions.stem: A hybrid cybersecurity implementation is handing over a new log-monitoring platform to operations. The operations manager notes that the platform keeps every log at full resolution forever, which will keep growing storage and energy use, while policy requires only one year of retention. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the unlimited retention setting, since more stored security data always means stronger protection.
Delete all logs older than one week to cut storage and energy use as far as the platform will allow.
Leave the retention setting for operations to change later, since the project is already handing over.
Evaluate a retention setting that meets the one-year policy and review its effect on storage and energy use.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sustainable design avoids unnecessary resource use while still meeting policy; settings should match the real requirement, not exceed or fall short of it.
Spot it: unlimited retention driving storage and energy growth, and a policy that needs only one year.
In this scenario: the PM evaluates a retention setting that meets the one-year policy and reviews its storage and energy effect.
Why not the others: keeping everything forever wastes resources without adding required value; one week violates the retention policy; leaving it to operations hands over a known problem the project can fix now.
Remember: Meet the policy, not more and not less. Fix it before Transfer in Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close.

questions.stem: In a predictive identity-management project, developers used an AI coding assistant to generate parts of the access-control module. At a compliance checkpoint, an auditor asks how the AI-generated code was verified, and the team has no record of any review. What should the project manager do?
options: Assure the auditor that AI-generated code is reliable because the assistant was trained on secure code.
Rewrite the entire module manually and prohibit AI assistance on all future work in the project.
Have the AI-generated code reviewed and tested against security standards, and record how it was verified.
Remove any mention of AI assistance from the project records so the audit can proceed without delay.
questions.explanation:
Concept: AI-generated work is still the team's work. It must be verified to the same standard as any other deliverable, with evidence kept for audit.
Spot it: AI-written security code, an auditor asking how it was verified, and no review record.
In this scenario: the PM has the AI-generated code reviewed and tested against security standards and records how it was verified.
Why not the others: trusting the assistant's training is not verification; rewriting everything and banning AI overreacts when review and testing fix the gap; hiding AI use from records is dishonest and breaks audit trust.
Remember: Tool → Data → Protect → Generate → Validate → Human → Monitor. Generated is not validated.

questions.stem: An agile team is building a usage-based auto insurance app. At a benefits review the product manager reports that a new state privacy law will limit how driving data can be collected, starting in five months. Several planned features rely on continuous location tracking. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Work with legal advisors to determine exactly how the law affects the planned location-tracking features.
Keep building the location features as planned and revisit the law when it is about to take effect.
Help the product owner reorder the backlog so that compliant features and needed changes come first.
Stop all development until the law's final regulations are published and fully interpreted by courts.
Ask the state to exempt the app from the new privacy law because development work has already begun.
questions.explanation:
Concept: An external regulatory change is interpreted with experts first, then the product owner reprioritizes the backlog so the product stays compliant and valuable.
Spot it: a new privacy law with a start date, and planned features that depend on the data it restricts.
In this scenario: the PM works with legal advisors to find exactly how the law affects the location features, and helps the product owner reorder the backlog.
Why not the others: building as planned wastes effort on features that may be illegal; stopping all work idles the team when most impact can be planned now; asking for an exemption avoids compliance.
Remember: Law → Applies? → Impact → Expert → Change → Comply. In agile, the change lands in the backlog.

questions.stem: A hybrid project for a government agency is delivering a new online tax-filing portal that operations will run after launch. At a forecast update, operations leaders say they have not budgeted any staff for portal support in the next fiscal year. What should the project manager do?
options: Plan for the project team to support the portal indefinitely after launch without any transition.
Raise the gap with the sponsor and operations leaders so support funding is secured before transition.
Launch the portal as planned and let operations resolve its staffing gap after the project closes.
Delay the portal's launch until the next fiscal year without discussing the issue with the sponsor.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Operational readiness — the product keeps its value only if operations is funded and staffed to run it. Gaps are raised with the sponsor well before transition.
Spot it: operations leaders say no support staff are budgeted, and launch is coming.
In this scenario: the PM raises the funding gap with the sponsor and operations leaders so support is secured before transition.
Why not the others: indefinite project support turns the project into operations; launching and leaving the gap risks the benefits; delaying launch without the sponsor is a decision the PM does not own.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close. No ready receiver, no safe transfer.

questions.stem: Match each ADKAR stage with what people need at that stage.
matching_right: Understanding why the change is needed now.
Personal willingness to support and take part.
Actually performing the new behavior on the job.
Knowing how to work in the new way.
Sustaining the change so people do not slide back.

answer.Awareness: Understanding why the change is needed now.
answer.Desire: Personal willingness to support and take part.
answer.Knowledge: Knowing how to work in the new way.
answer.Ability: Actually performing the new behavior on the job.
answer.Reinforcement: Sustaining the change so people do not slide back.

questions.explanation:
Concept: ADKAR is a people-side change model: adoption happens person by person, in order, and a gap at any stage stalls the benefit.
Awareness: People first need the business reason; announce the WHY before the HOW.
Desire: Awareness does not equal buy-in; engage champions and address "what's in it for me".
Knowledge: Training and job aids belong here, after people want the change.
Ability: Practice, coaching and support turn knowledge into real performance.
Reinforcement: Recognition, measures and ownership keep adoption from fading after go-live.
Remember: Change = Adoption. A deliverable nobody uses creates no value (Deliverable → Outcome → Benefit → Value).

questions.stem: A hybrid cybersecurity implementation for a payments company combines predictive network work with adaptive tooling releases. A compliance officer reports during a change evaluation that the card industry's security standard now includes new multifactor rules that apply by year-end. What should the project manager do?
options: Assess the new rules against both workstreams and plan the changes through the backlog and change control.
Apply the new rules only to the adaptive tooling releases, since the network work has an approved baseline.
Wait until the year-end deadline approaches before assessing which parts of the project are affected.
Ask the card industry council to waive the new multifactor rules because the project is under way.
questions.explanation:
Concept: In a hybrid project, a new compliance requirement is assessed across all workstreams and then handled through each one's mechanism: backlog for adaptive work, change control for baselined work.
Spot it: an industry standard update with a deadline, predictive and adaptive streams, and a change evaluation.
In this scenario: the PM assesses the new rules against both workstreams and plans changes through the backlog and change control.
Why not the others: exempting the network because it is baselined forgets that baselines can change through approval; waiting until year-end leaves no time to comply; asking the council to waive the rules avoids compliance.
Remember: Adaptive part → backlog. Baselined part → change control. Compliance applies to all of it.

questions.stem: On a hybrid public-sector data exchange project, an adaptive integration team wants firewall ports opened now to test each increment, while the predictive infrastructure lead insists on waiting for the security accreditation gate. Both positions have merit, and the two groups must work closely for the next six months. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Bring both parties together to explore their underlying needs and find an option, such as an isolated test network, that satisfies both.
Ask the sponsor to rule on which of the two positions prevails so the integration work and the accreditation schedule can both continue.
Tell the integration team to wait for accreditation, because security governance outranks delivery speed on public-sector work.
Propose that each side concede half, opening some of the requested ports now and the remaining ports after accreditation.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Collaborate/problem solve — the conflict mode that looks past each side's stated position to the underlying need and builds a win-win solution. It fits when both concerns are valid and the relationship must last.
Spot it: "both positions have merit," a long working relationship ahead, and time to talk it through.
In this scenario: the integration team needs early testing and the infrastructure lead needs security control; an isolated test network can serve both, so bring them together to find it.
Why not the others: Asking the sponsor to rule escalates before the PM has tried to resolve it; siding with accreditation is forcing, a win-lose result; conceding half is compromise, which still opens production ports and leaves both sides partly unhappy.
Remember: Collaborate is PMI's default — confront the problem, not the people. Compromise = everyone loses a little.

questions.stem: On a predictive hospital wing construction project, site engineers spend several hours each week re-entering the same inspection data into two systems required by different departments. The engineers are falling behind on design reviews, and morale is dropping. What should the project manager do?
options: Direct the engineers to work extra hours until their design reviews are back on track with the schedule.
Report the engineers' slipping design review performance to their functional managers so they can take corrective action.
Work with both departments to agree on one shared inspection record so the engineers regain their design review time.
Tell the engineers to stop using one of the systems until the two departments sort out the duplication.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Servant leadership — the PM serves the team by removing obstacles it cannot clear itself, so people can focus on valuable work.
Spot it: time lost to duplicate or non-value work imposed from outside the team, "several hours each week," falling morale.
In this scenario: the duplication comes from two departments, so the PM works with them on one shared inspection record and gives the engineers their design time back.
Why not the others: Extra hours treat the symptom and burn out the team; reporting engineers to their managers blames people for a process problem; telling them to drop a system bypasses legitimate departmental requirements.
Remember: Servant leader = remove blockers, serve the team. "Work harder" is never the first answer.

questions.stem: A junior scheduler on a predictive utility substation project submitted a monthly update with several logic errors, which the project manager caught before the steering review. The scheduler is motivated but has never built a resource-loaded schedule, and there are three weeks before the next update. What is the BEST approach?
options: Take over the monthly schedule updates personally so that logic errors never reach the steering committee again.
Review the errors together, then have the scheduler rebuild one section with the project manager giving feedback along the way.
Send the scheduler a marked-up list of corrections and ask for all of them to be applied before the next update.
Enroll the scheduler in a formal scheduling certification course and remove the monthly schedule duties until the course is completed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Coaching — short-term, skill-focused development through guided practice and feedback. It suits a motivated person who lacks a specific skill.
Spot it: "motivated but has never," a clear skill gap, and enough time before the next deadline.
In this scenario: the scheduler wants to learn and there are three weeks, so reviewing the errors together and having him rebuild a section with feedback builds lasting skill.
Why not the others: Taking over the updates creates dependence and removes the learning; a marked-up list fixes this schedule but not the understanding; pulling duties for a course is slow when hands-on practice is possible now.
Remember: Coaching = short-term skill, one-on-one with feedback; Mentoring = long-term career. Coach first, never replace first.

questions.stem: Midway through a predictive ERP rollout at a food distributor, a project manager learns that the new warehouse director, who joined last month, is not in the stakeholder register. The director's staff will use the system every day, and he has told peers he doubts the approved design. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Schedule a detailed design walkthrough with the director to convince him that the approved warehouse design is sound and complete.
Ask the sponsor to instruct the warehouse director to support the approved design and the rollout plan.
Submit a change request to reopen the warehouse design so the director's concerns can be incorporated.
Add the director to the register, analyze his interest and influence, and plan how the project will engage him.
questions.explanation:
Concept: The stakeholder flow — Identify → Analyze → Engage → Monitor. Identification never stops, and a newly found stakeholder is recorded and analyzed before you decide how to engage.
Spot it: someone with real impact on the project who "is not in the stakeholder register."
In this scenario: the director is high-impact and skeptical, but the PM does not yet know his concerns, so add him, assess interest and influence, and plan his engagement.
Why not the others: A persuasion walkthrough engages before analyzing; asking the sponsor to instruct him uses authority instead of understanding; a change request reopens the design with no analysis of what he actually needs.
Remember: Identify → Analyze → Engage → Monitor. You cannot engage someone you have not analyzed.

questions.stem: On a predictive airport baggage system upgrade, an airline operations group complains that the weekly status report is long and they keep missing items that affect gate schedules. Other stakeholders say the report suits them well. The communications management plan specifies one report for every audience. What should the project manager do?
options: Confirm what the airline group needs to know and revise the communications plan to give them a focused gate-impact summary.
Shorten the weekly report for every audience so that the airline group finds it easier to read each week.
Explain to the airline group that the report follows the approved communications plan and cannot be tailored for a single group.
Invite the airline group to all steering committee meetings so they hear every project update firsthand.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Communications management plan — the HOW document for who needs what information, in what format, and how often. It is tailored per audience and updated when needs are not being met.
Spot it: one audience says the report is not working while others are happy, and "one report for every audience."
In this scenario: confirm what the airline group needs and revise the plan to give them a focused gate-impact summary, leaving the working report alone for everyone else.
Why not the others: Shortening the report for all breaks a format that works for others; defending the plan ignores a need the plan exists to meet; inviting them to every steering meeting adds volume, not the focused information they lack.
Remember: Plan = HOW. When the HOW stops working, update the plan — tailor by audience.

questions.stem: An agile team building a mobile banking app has worked together for three weeks. Members openly challenge each other's technical approaches, and two developers argued sharply during yesterday's daily scrum. The team's velocity is still unstable. How should the scrum master respond?
options: Ask the functional manager to move one of the arguing developers to another team so that the rest of the team can settle down.
Treat the friction as a normal stage of team growth and help the team agree on working agreements for handling disagreement.
Assign all technical decisions to the most senior developer until the arguments between members stop.
Stay out of the disagreements entirely so that the team learns to self-organize without outside help.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tuckman's storming stage — after forming, members challenge ideas and each other. This friction is normal, and the leader coaches, mediates, and helps the team set ground rules.
Spot it: a new team (three weeks together), open challenges, sharp arguments, unstable velocity.
In this scenario: the scrum master treats the friction as normal growth and facilitates working agreements for handling disagreement, moving the team toward norming.
Why not the others: Moving a developer out removes a person before any coaching; handing all decisions to one senior developer kills self-organization; staying out entirely is passive when conflict is hurting collaboration.
Remember: Forming = direct, Storming = coach and set ground rules, Norming = support, Performing = delegate, Adjourning = recognize.

questions.stem: On a predictive retail store refit program, crews are delayed because regional site leads wait for the project manager's approval on small questions. The site leads say they are unsure how far their authority goes. The project manager wants them to make more day-to-day decisions. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Define each site lead's decision limits in writing, such as spending and schedule thresholds they may approve.
Require site leads to log every decision for project manager approval by the end of each day.
Allow site leads to approve changes to the scope baseline whenever their crews recommend them.
Delegate decisions within those thresholds and back the site leads when they make reasonable calls.
Hold a daily call in which the project manager decides all open questions from every site.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Empowerment through delegation — push decisions to the lowest competent level with clear boundaries, then back people when they use that authority.
Spot it: people waiting for approval on small questions, "unsure how far their authority goes," and a leader who wants them to decide.
In this scenario: write down each site lead's decision limits, then genuinely delegate within those limits and support reasonable calls.
Why not the others: Daily logs for approval keep the bottleneck; approving scope baseline changes bypasses the change control board; a daily call where the PM decides everything centralizes decisions even more.
Remember: Clear limits + real trust = empowerment. Baseline changes always go to the CCB.

questions.stem: A product owner at a travel startup wants the team to commit to 45 story points next sprint to meet a marketing date; the team has averaged 30 points over its last six sprints. The date is fixed, but the product owner can choose which features launch. What should the scrum master encourage?
options: Accepting the 45-point commitment and planning overtime for the developers so that the fixed marketing date is protected.
Splitting the difference so the team commits to roughly 38 points for the next sprint instead of 45.
A discussion in which the product owner and team pick the most valuable features that fit the team's proven capacity.
Asking the sponsor to move the marketing date so the team is not overloaded in the next sprint.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Principled (interest-based) negotiation — separate the position ("45 points") from the interest ("a strong launch on a fixed date") and find options that serve the interest.
Spot it: a demand beyond proven capacity, a fixed date, and flexibility somewhere else ("can choose which features launch").
In this scenario: velocity has averaged 30 for six sprints, so the product owner and team pick the most valuable features that fit that capacity and still hit the date.
Why not the others: Accepting 45 with overtime breaks sustainable pace and evidence-based planning; 38 points is a compromise still beyond capacity; asking to move a fixed date ignores the lever that can flex — scope.
Remember: Agile flexes scope, not quality or pace. Velocity is for forecasting, not for pushing.

questions.stem: A hybrid telecom billing project has developers in Manila working in two-week iterations and a predictive testing vendor in Warsaw. Handoffs keep failing because the teams overlap only one hour a day and questions sit unanswered overnight. What should the project manager do?
options: Move all testing work from the Warsaw vendor to Manila so the teams no longer need to coordinate across distant time zones.
Require both teams to work identical hours so that they can collaborate live throughout each day.
Replace informal handoff questions with a weekly formal status report submitted by each of the teams.
Agree with both teams on a protected overlap window, a response-time norm, and one shared channel for handoff questions.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Virtual team norms — distributed teams need explicit agreements on overlap time, response expectations, and channels to offset time-zone gaps.
Spot it: failed handoffs, "overlap only one hour a day," questions sitting unanswered overnight.
In this scenario: agree with both teams on a protected overlap window, a response-time norm, and one shared channel for handoff questions.
Why not the others: Moving testing to Manila ignores the vendor contract and is a drastic fix for a norms problem; identical hours are unsustainable across time zones; a weekly formal report makes answers even slower.
Remember: Virtual team trouble → agree team norms (when, how fast, which channel) before restructuring.

questions.stem: An agile team at an insurance company delivers consistently, but members say the work feels routine and several have asked to learn cloud-native development. The product roadmap includes a cloud migration next quarter. What should the scrum master do?
options: Invite members to take on spikes for the cloud migration and arrange pairing with experienced cloud engineers.
Offer a cash bonus for every sprint in which the team exceeds its average velocity by a set margin.
Explain that individual learning goals must wait until all of the current roadmap commitments are fully delivered.
Bring in an external cloud team for the migration so the current team can stay on its roadmap.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Intrinsic motivation — knowledge workers are driven by autonomy, mastery, and purpose more than by extra pay; growth opportunities are true motivators.
Spot it: "work feels routine," members "asked to learn," and an upcoming chance to use the new skill.
In this scenario: the cloud migration is a real mastery opportunity, so invite members to take spikes on it and pair them with experienced cloud engineers.
Why not the others: A velocity bonus is extrinsic and invites inflated estimates; postponing learning ignores what members said they need; bringing in an outside team removes the very growth they asked for.
Remember: Growth = motivator, money = hygiene. Match the reward to the need people voiced.

questions.stem: Match each conflict resolution technique with its description.
matching_right: Push one viewpoint at the expense of others; win-lose
Retreat from the conflict or postpone it until later
Integrate multiple perspectives to reach consensus and commitment
Emphasize areas of agreement and concede to keep harmony
Find a solution that gives each party partial satisfaction

answer.Withdraw/avoid: Retreat from the conflict or postpone it until later
answer.Smooth/accommodate: Emphasize areas of agreement and concede to keep harmony
answer.Compromise/reconcile: Find a solution that gives each party partial satisfaction
answer.Force/direct: Push one viewpoint at the expense of others; win-lose
answer.Collaborate/problem solve: Integrate multiple perspectives to reach consensus and commitment

questions.explanation:
Concept: The five conflict resolution modes and the kind of outcome each one produces.
Withdraw/avoid: retreat or postpone; acceptable only as a cool-down or when the issue will fade on its own.
Smooth/accommodate: play up agreement and give ground to keep harmony; temporary and relationship-focused.
Compromise/reconcile: each side gives something up, so each gets only partial satisfaction.
Force/direct: one view wins at others' expense (win-lose); for urgent or safety-critical calls.
Collaborate/problem solve: integrate viewpoints to fix the root cause and win real commitment — PMI's default.
Remember: Collaborate first. Smoothing hides differences; compromising trades them.

questions.stem: The electrical crew on a predictive water treatment plant upgrade sits idle two hours each morning waiting for a permit sign-off from a facilities office that opens late. The crew lead has raised this twice, but nothing has changed. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Ask the crew lead to keep raising the delay with facilities until the office responds.
Meet the facilities manager to arrange an earlier sign-off time or a pre-approved daily work permit.
Record the idle time in the issue log and review it at the next monthly status meeting.
Tell the crew to start work before the sign-off so that the schedule baseline is protected.
Move the crew's first hours to preparation tasks that need no permit while the fix is arranged.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Servant leadership — actively remove impediments the team cannot clear itself, and keep the team productive while the fix is underway.
Spot it: a repeated delay outside the team's control, and "raised this twice, but nothing has changed."
In this scenario: the PM meets the facilities manager to fix the sign-off timing and, meanwhile, fills the first hours with preparation work that needs no permit.
Why not the others: Asking the crew lead to keep pushing leaves the PM passive; logging it for the monthly meeting delays action on a daily loss; starting before sign-off breaks the permit process and safety rules.
Remember: Servant leadership is active, never passive — remove the blocker, then protect the team's time.

questions.stem: Match each agile coaching stance with what the coach does in it.
matching_right: Asks powerful questions so the person finds their own answers
Guides a group process neutrally toward the group's own outcome
Shares new knowledge and skills the learner does not yet have
Offers personal experience and advice as a seasoned practitioner

answer.Teaching: Shares new knowledge and skills the learner does not yet have
answer.Mentoring: Offers personal experience and advice as a seasoned practitioner
answer.Coaching: Asks powerful questions so the person finds their own answers
answer.Facilitating: Guides a group process neutrally toward the group's own outcome

questions.explanation:
Concept: The four agile coaching stances differ in where the answer comes from.
Teaching: the coach shares knowledge or a skill the learner does not have yet.
Mentoring: the coach offers personal experience and advice from years of practice.
Coaching: the coach asks powerful questions so the person finds their own answer.
Facilitating: the coach guides a group process neutrally; the group owns the content and the outcome.
Remember: Teach = new knowledge, Mentor = my experience, Coach = your answer, Facilitate = the group's decision.

questions.stem: A clinic network's compliance officer has not attended any sprint reviews for a patient-scheduling product, and the team has just learned she may block release over data retention rules. The product owner had assumed compliance would review everything at the end. What should the product owner do?
options: Keep the current plan and schedule a formal, detailed compliance review of the whole product just before the release date.
Ask the developers to add retention controls based on their own reading of the relevant regulations.
Meet the compliance officer now to capture her retention requirements and invite her to the upcoming reviews.
Escalate to the sponsor so that the compliance officer is directed to approve the release as planned.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Continuous stakeholder engagement — agile teams bring key stakeholders into reviews early and often, so their needs shape the product while change is still cheap.
Spot it: a key stakeholder who has skipped reviews, a surprise late objection, and "assumed compliance would review everything at the end."
In this scenario: the product owner meets the compliance officer now, captures her retention requirements for the backlog, and invites her to upcoming reviews.
Why not the others: One big review before release repeats the late-feedback mistake; letting developers interpret regulations guesses at requirements she can state; escalating to force approval ignores a legitimate concern.
Remember: Identify → Analyze → Engage → Monitor. In agile, engage means invite them to the review, not the release.

questions.stem: A predictive defense logistics project has 12 stakeholders who share information with one another. The sponsor asks the project manager to add four regional liaisons to this core communication group. The project manager wants to show how the change affects coordination effort. How many communication channels will exist after the change?
options: 66 channels
120 channels
54 channels
240 channels
questions.explanation:
Concept: Communication channels — every pair of people is a channel, so the count grows fast: n(n−1)/2.
Spot it: "how many communication channels," a group size, and people being added or removed.
In this scenario: 12 + 4 = 16 people, so 16 × 15 ÷ 2 = 120 channels, up from 66 before the change.
Why not the others: 66 is the count before the liaisons join; 54 is only the number of channels added (120 − 66); 240 forgets to divide by two.
Remember: n(n−1)/2 — count the people AFTER the change, and always divide by 2.

questions.stem: Match each Tuckman team development stage with the project manager's most helpful response.
matching_right: Delegate decisions and remove obstacles for an autonomous team
Give direction and clarify goals, roles, and ground rules
Recognize contributions and support members' moves to new work
Reinforce agreed norms and step back into a supportive role
Mediate disagreements and help members agree on working norms

answer.Forming: Give direction and clarify goals, roles, and ground rules
answer.Storming: Mediate disagreements and help members agree on working norms
answer.Norming: Reinforce agreed norms and step back into a supportive role
answer.Performing: Delegate decisions and remove obstacles for an autonomous team
answer.Adjourning: Recognize contributions and support members' moves to new work

questions.explanation:
Concept: Tuckman's five stages of team development and how the leader's role shifts at each; a team can slide back a stage when membership changes.
Forming: members are polite and unsure, so the PM gives direction and clarifies goals and roles.
Storming: people push back on each other; the PM mediates and helps set ground rules.
Norming: the team adopts shared norms; the PM reinforces them and steps back to a supportive role.
Performing: the team is autonomous; the PM delegates and removes obstacles.
Adjourning: the work ends; the PM recognizes contributions and supports members' transitions.
Remember: Direct → Coach → Support → Delegate → Recognize. New member joins? Expect a step back.

questions.stem: In a hybrid insurance claims modernization, adaptive development teams need central design authority approval for every minor interface change, which adds four to six days per request. The predictive infrastructure work is unaffected. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Remove architectural review for the adaptive teams so they can work at their full speed.
Work with the design authority to set guardrails within which teams decide minor interface changes themselves.
Keep design authority review for changes that cross system boundaries or alter shared standards.
Batch the interface change requests so the design authority reviews them all monthly.
Ask the adaptive teams to fix all interface designs up front to reduce later changes.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Empowerment within guardrails — teams decide what falls inside agreed boundaries, and central governance reviews only decisions with wider impact.
Spot it: every minor decision waits for a central authority, "four to six days per request," and capable teams.
In this scenario: agree guardrails so teams decide minor interface changes themselves, and keep design authority review for cross-system or shared-standard changes.
Why not the others: Removing review entirely drops governance still needed for cross-system risk; monthly batching makes the wait longer; fixing all interfaces up front forces predictive planning onto the adaptive stream.
Remember: Guardrails, not gates, for small decisions; governance for the big ones.

questions.stem: A predictive municipal data center project needs a senior network architect for eight weeks, but the functional manager says the architect is committed to another project. The project manager learns that the other project's workload drops sharply during the weeks when this project's network design peaks. What should the project manager do?
options: Share both timelines with the functional manager and propose a split allocation that covers each project's busy period.
Ask the sponsor to order the functional manager to release the architect for the full eight weeks.
Accept the refusal and hire an external architect without discussing any alternatives with the manager.
Wait until the other project finishes, then re-plan all of the network design work around the architect's future availability.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Negotiating for resources in a matrix — the functional manager controls the people, so the PM looks for an option that serves both projects before escalating.
Spot it: a resource conflict with a functional manager, plus a fact that opens a win-win (the other project's workload drops when this one peaks).
In this scenario: share both timelines and propose a split allocation that covers each project's busy period.
Why not the others: Asking the sponsor to order a release uses positional pressure before trying a win-win; hiring externally without discussion skips the negotiation; waiting and re-planning delays the project when a better option exists.
Remember: Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act → Monitor → Escalate. Escalate comes last.

questions.stem: A hybrid e-learning platform project has a predictive content production team in Toronto and an adaptive software team spread across five cities. Recently added members of the software team say they feel disconnected and do not know whom to ask for help. What should the project manager do?
options: Require new members to work from the Toronto office for their first three months on the project.
Send new members the team charter and the integrated project plan and ask them to review both documents on their own.
Pair each new member with a remote buddy and hold a video session to introduce roles, norms, and contacts.
Create a separate chat group for new members so that they can answer each other's questions.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Onboarding virtual team members — distance must be offset by deliberate connection: a buddy, live introductions, and clarity about roles and contacts.
Spot it: new remote members who "feel disconnected" and "do not know whom to ask for help."
In this scenario: pair each newcomer with a remote buddy and hold a video session introducing roles, norms, and key contacts.
Why not the others: Requiring months in Toronto ignores a team spread across five cities; documents read alone build no relationships; a newcomers-only chat isolates them from the people who have the answers.
Remember: Virtual team → build relationships on purpose. Documents inform; people connect.

questions.stem: On a predictive highway bridge rehabilitation project, experienced inspectors complain about poor site facilities and outdated safety gear, and turnover is rising even though pay is competitive. Several inspectors also say they want more responsibility. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Offer a retention bonus, since higher pay will make inspectors satisfied with their work.
Fix the site facility and safety gear problems, because they are causing the inspectors' dissatisfaction.
Hold a team celebration to lift morale before looking into the facility problems.
Give interested inspectors responsibility for leading sections of the inspection program.
Explain that site facilities are outside the project's control and cannot be changed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Herzberg's two-factor theory — hygiene factors (pay, working conditions, safety) prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate; motivators (responsibility, growth, recognition) create satisfaction.
Spot it: complaints about conditions and gear, pay described as "competitive," and a wish for "more responsibility."
In this scenario: fix the facilities and safety gear to remove the dissatisfaction, and give interested inspectors responsibility for leading sections to motivate them.
Why not the others: A retention bonus adds more of a hygiene factor that is already fine; a celebration before fixing the problems ignores the cause; calling facilities unchangeable dismisses a real hygiene problem.
Remember: Hygiene stops the pain; motivators create the gain. You need both.

questions.topic: Scrum artifacts and who owns them
questions.stem: Match each Scrum artifact or commitment with who owns it and what it does.
matching_right: Whole Scrum team sets the quality standard every increment must meet
Single objective the Scrum team commits to at sprint planning
Product owner orders it to maximize the value of upcoming work
Usable, done work the developers create and show at the review
Developers own and update it daily as their plan for the sprint

answer.Product backlog: Product owner orders it to maximize the value of upcoming work
answer.Sprint backlog: Developers own and update it daily as their plan for the sprint
answer.Definition of done: Whole Scrum team sets the quality standard every increment must meet
answer.Increment: Usable, done work the developers create and show at the review
answer.Sprint goal: Single objective the Scrum team commits to at sprint planning

questions.explanation:
Concept: Each Scrum artifact or commitment has a clear owner, and knowing who orders, owns, or edits it is a core exam skill.
Product backlog: the product owner orders it and decides what is most valuable next; anyone may suggest items.
Sprint backlog: the developers own it and update it daily; no one outside the developers adds work to it.
Definition of done: the whole Scrum team agrees on it, and every increment must meet it.
Increment: the developers build it; only done work counts, and it is inspected at the sprint review.
Sprint goal: the Scrum team crafts it at sprint planning, and it stays fixed during the sprint.
Remember: Product owner = WHAT and the order; Developers = HOW and the sprint plan; Scrum team = done and the goal.

questions.stem: During a daily scrum, a team building a nonprofit donor app says it still lacks access to the payment sandbox after five days. The vendor's technical contact has not answered the developers' emails, and the sprint ends in six days. What should the scrum master do?
options: Contact the vendor's account manager directly to obtain sandbox access and keep the team informed.
Remove the payment stories from the sprint and replace them with unrelated items from the backlog.
Encourage the developers to keep emailing the vendor contact until someone finally responds to them.
Add the access problem to the retrospective agenda so the team can plan better for the next sprint.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Removing impediments — the scrum master resolves blockers the team cannot clear itself, especially ones outside the team.
Spot it: raised at the daily scrum, stuck "after five days," an unresponsive external contact, a sprint deadline.
In this scenario: the developers' route has failed, so the scrum master goes to the vendor's account manager for sandbox access and keeps the team informed.
Why not the others: Swapping in unrelated items abandons the sprint goal instead of removing the blocker; more emails repeat what has failed for five days; waiting for the retrospective leaves the sprint blocked.
Remember: The daily scrum surfaces the impediment; the scrum master removes it — today, not at the retro.

questions.stem: Match each motivation theory with its core idea.
matching_right: Effort follows the belief that it leads to a valued reward
Each person is driven mainly by achievement, affiliation, or power
Needs rise from basic survival and safety to self-actualization
Managers assume people either need control or are self-motivated
Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction

answer.Maslow's hierarchy of needs: Needs rise from basic survival and safety to self-actualization
answer.Herzberg's two-factor theory: Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction
answer.McClelland's acquired needs: Each person is driven mainly by achievement, affiliation, or power
answer.McGregor's Theory X and Y: Managers assume people either need control or are self-motivated
answer.Vroom's expectancy theory: Effort follows the belief that it leads to a valued reward

questions.explanation:
Concept: The motivation theories on the exam each explain what drives effort in a different way.
Maslow's hierarchy of needs: needs rise from survival and safety up to esteem and self-actualization.
Herzberg's two-factor theory: hygiene factors (pay, conditions) prevent dissatisfaction; motivators (growth, recognition) create satisfaction.
McClelland's acquired needs: each person is driven mainly by achievement, affiliation, or power; match work to the dominant need.
McGregor's Theory X and Y: X assumes people need control, Y assumes they are self-motivated; PMI prefers Y.
Vroom's expectancy theory: people put in effort when they believe it leads to a reward they value.
Remember: Maslow = ladder, Herzberg = hygiene vs motivator, McClelland = three needs, McGregor = control vs trust, Vroom = effort → reward.

questions.stem: A hybrid smart-meter rollout combines predictive field installation with an adaptive customer portal. The utility's customer service director is supportive but seldom attends portal reviews, although her agents will answer all customer questions. The engagement assessment matrix shows her desired level as leading. What should the project manager do?
options: Send her the monthly field installation status report so that she stays informed about progress.
Leave her engagement as it is, because supportive stakeholders need no further engagement effort.
Ask the sponsor to require the director's attendance at every portal review meeting for the rest of the program.
Involve the director in shaping portal features, for example by having her agents test each new increment.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stakeholder engagement assessment matrix — it compares each stakeholder's current level (Unaware, Resistant, Neutral, Supportive, Leading) with the desired level, and the gap drives your engagement actions.
Spot it: "desired level as leading" for someone who is supportive today but seldom involved.
In this scenario: moving her from supportive to leading needs an active role, such as having her agents test each new portal increment.
Why not the others: Field installation reports only inform, and about the wrong stream; leaving her as is ignores the gap the matrix shows; making attendance compulsory gets presence, not leadership.
Remember: Current vs Desired — close the gap with involvement, not just information.

questions.stem: Match each element of the basic sender-receiver communication model with its description.
matching_right: Receiver converts the message back into meaningful thoughts
Anything that interferes with sending or understanding the message
Sender converts thoughts or ideas into language or symbols
Receiver signals receipt, which does not mean agreement
Sender sends the message through a chosen medium or channel

answer.Encode: Sender converts thoughts or ideas into language or symbols
answer.Transmit: Sender sends the message through a chosen medium or channel
answer.Decode: Receiver converts the message back into meaningful thoughts
answer.Acknowledge: Receiver signals receipt, which does not mean agreement
answer.Noise: Anything that interferes with sending or understanding the message

questions.explanation:
Concept: The sender-receiver model shows where a message can be lost between two people.
Encode: the sender turns thoughts into words, symbols, or images.
Transmit: the sender sends the message through a medium such as email, phone, or a meeting.
Decode: the receiver turns the message back into meaning.
Acknowledge: the receiver signals the message arrived — this is not the same as agreeing.
Noise: anything that distorts or blocks the message, such as distance, jargon, or cultural differences.
Remember: Encode → Transmit → Decode → Acknowledge, with noise all along the way. Sender owns clarity; receiver confirms receipt.

questions.stem: Match each role on a hybrid program with what it authorizes, approves, or updates.
matching_right: Updates living documents such as the risk register and issue log
Formally accepts completed deliverables against acceptance criteria
Approves or rejects change requests that affect baselines
Issues the charter that authorizes the project and its manager
Assigns and releases staff from the home department

answer.Sponsor: Issues the charter that authorizes the project and its manager
answer.Change control board: Approves or rejects change requests that affect baselines
answer.Project manager: Updates living documents such as the risk register and issue log
answer.Functional manager: Assigns and releases staff from the home department
answer.Customer: Formally accepts completed deliverables against acceptance criteria

questions.explanation:
Concept: Authority questions test whether you know each role's lane — who authorizes, approves, updates, assigns, and accepts.
Sponsor: issues and signs the charter, which authorizes the project and names the PM.
Change control board: approves or rejects change requests that affect the baselines.
Project manager: updates living documents such as the risk register and issue log directly.
Functional manager: assigns and releases staff from the home department in a matrix organization.
Customer: formally accepts completed deliverables against the agreed acceptance criteria.
Remember: Charter = AUTHORITY (sponsor), Baseline = APPROVED (CCB), Register/Log = TRACK (PM), Acceptance = customer.

questions.stem: A department head at a media company sits in on an agile team's sprint planning and assigns specific stories to the developers she thinks are fastest. Since then, team members have stopped volunteering for work, and its estimates have become less reliable. What should the scrum master do?
options: Accept the story assignments, since the department head has formal authority over the team's members.
Ask the sponsor to bar the department head from attending any of the team's sprint planning sessions or other events.
Raise the team's estimates to reflect its lower confidence in the work the department head assigned.
Speak privately with the department head about how self-selection builds ownership, and invite her to observe instead.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Self-organizing teams — agile developers pull and choose their own work, and the scrum master protects this by coaching people outside the team.
Spot it: someone outside the team "assigns specific stories," members stop volunteering, estimates slip.
In this scenario: speak privately with the department head about how self-selection builds ownership, and invite her to observe instead.
Why not the others: Accepting the assignments lets formal authority override self-organization; asking the sponsor to bar her escalates before a respectful conversation; inflating estimates hides the problem instead of fixing it.
Remember: Agile = pull, not push. Talk to the person first, then escalate.

questions.stem: Two product owners at a retail company share one agile team, and each wants the team's full capacity next sprint for their own feature. Both features support the same quarterly goal of raising online conversion rates. What should the agile coach do?
options: Facilitate a session where both product owners weigh their features against the shared conversion goal and agree on an order.
Allocate exactly half of the team's capacity to each product owner's feature for the next sprint to keep things fair.
Let the developers choose whichever of the two features seems more technically interesting to build first.
Escalate to the portfolio manager and wait for a formal ruling before the team starts its sprint planning.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Negotiating from a shared goal — when both parties serve the same objective, compare the options against that objective to reach an order both accept.
Spot it: two product owners competing for one team, and "both features support the same quarterly goal."
In this scenario: the coach facilitates a session where both weigh their features against the conversion goal and agree on an order.
Why not the others: A half-and-half split is a compromise that may delay both features; letting developers pick by interest ignores value; escalating and waiting stalls work before the two have tried to agree.
Remember: Shared goal = shared yardstick. Collaborate on value before you split or escalate.

questions.stem: A predictive satellite ground-station project has engineers in Houston, Bangalore, and Munich. A design decision reached in a hallway conversation in Houston was never shared, and the Munich team spent a week working on the superseded design. What should the project manager do to prevent this from recurring?
options: Prohibit informal design conversations so that decisions happen only in scheduled review meetings.
Ask the Munich engineers to check with Houston every morning before they start their design work.
Require design decisions to be recorded in a shared decision log and announced on the team's common channel.
Charge the full week of rework to the Houston engineers' cost account to create clear personal accountability for sharing.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Shared decision records — distributed teams need decisions captured and announced in one visible place, so every site works from the same information.
Spot it: a decision made informally at one site that was "never shared," and rework at another site.
In this scenario: require design decisions to be logged in a shared decision log and announced on the common channel.
Why not the others: Banning informal talk kills useful collaboration; daily check-ins put the burden on the wrong team; charging rework to people blames individuals for a process gap.
Remember: Informal talk is fine — undocumented decisions are the problem. Decide → Record → Share.

questions.stem: A project manager takes over a predictive refinery shutdown project whose team has missed three milestones. The functional manager says the team is lazy and needs close supervision, but the project manager sees skilled people who were never involved in planning. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Involve the crews in re-planning the remaining milestones and in estimating their own work.
Introduce hourly check-ins so supervisors can track every crew's progress closely.
Publish a ranking of crews by milestone performance to create competitive pressure.
Warn the team that missed milestones will be reflected in their annual reviews.
Give each crew ownership of a work package with clear goals and freedom to choose methods.
questions.explanation:
Concept: McGregor's Theory X and Y — Theory X assumes people must be controlled; Theory Y assumes capable people are self-motivated when involved. PMI prefers Theory Y.
Spot it: "lazy and needs close supervision" (Theory X) versus "skilled people who were never involved" (Theory Y).
In this scenario: involve the crews in re-planning and estimating their own work, and give each crew ownership of a work package with freedom on methods.
Why not the others: Hourly check-ins apply Theory X control; a public ranking creates fear instead of commitment; threatening annual reviews is coercion.
Remember: X = control, Y = trust. Involve people in the plan and they own the plan.

questions.stem: During a site meeting on a predictive stadium lighting project, an electrical contractor and a structural engineer start arguing over who will pay for bracket rework. Tempers are high, and several urgent safety items remain on the agenda. What should the project manager do at this point?
options: Decide on the spot which party will pay for the rework so that the meeting can move on quickly.
Let both parties keep arguing until they settle the payment question between themselves.
Record the dispute as a formal contract claim and refer it to the legal department for a binding resolution.
Pause the dispute, finish the safety items, and set up a separate session with the two parties soon after.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Withdraw/avoid as a short cool-down — usually the weakest mode, but right when emotions are high, more urgent work is waiting, and the conflict is revisited soon.
Spot it: "tempers are high" and "urgent safety items remain on the agenda."
In this scenario: pause the dispute, finish the safety items, and set up a separate session with both parties soon after.
Why not the others: Deciding on the spot forces a win-lose cost decision without facts; letting them keep arguing sacrifices the safety agenda; a legal claim formalizes a dispute nobody has properly discussed yet.
Remember: Withdraw = cool-down only, and always come back. Safety first, then solve.

questions.stem: In a hybrid ERP program, members of the adaptive finance team are pulled into unplanned requests from the predictive data migration team almost every day. The finance team's delivery forecasts are slipping as a result. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Set up one intake route so migration requests reach the finance team's product owner for ordering.
Tell finance team members to decline all migration requests until their own work is done.
Agree with the migration lead on predictable support windows for migration questions.
