Ask the finance team to work evenings so both teams' demands can be met on schedule.
Report the interruptions as a risk in the next monthly status report and take no other action.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Servant leadership — shield the team from disruptive interruptions while keeping necessary collaboration flowing.
Spot it: "pulled into unplanned requests almost every day," slipping forecasts, and a real cross-stream dependency.
In this scenario: route migration requests through one intake to the finance team's product owner for ordering, and agree predictable support windows with the migration lead.
Why not the others: Declining all requests blocks the stream the program depends on; evening work breaks sustainable pace; only reporting a risk ignores a problem already happening.
Remember: Protect the team's focus, don't wall it off — one intake route, planned support windows.

questions.stem: A technically strong team lead on a hybrid medical-device program dominates discussions, and newer members of the adaptive software stream have stopped raising concerns. In a one-on-one meeting, he says he only wants the product to succeed. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Remove the lead from team meetings so that the newer members feel free to speak up again.
Give the lead specific examples of meetings where others were cut off and explain the effect on the team.
Ask the newer members to send their concerns privately to the project manager from now on.
Agree on a goal for the lead to draw out newer members' views, and review progress together regularly.
Tell the lead to stop sharing technical opinions with the team for the rest of the release.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Coaching with feedback — give specific, behavior-based feedback privately, then agree a development goal and follow up.
Spot it: a strong performer whose behavior silences others, good intentions, a one-on-one already underway.
In this scenario: show the lead concrete examples of cutting others off and the effect, then agree a goal to draw out newer members' views with regular check-ins.
Why not the others: Removing him from meetings loses his expertise and changes nothing; private routes for concerns work around the behavior; banning his opinions wastes his knowledge.
Remember: Coach privately first — specific behavior, clear impact, agreed goal, follow-up.

questions.stem: A predictive city transit fare-system project is nearing a phase gate. A council member, recorded in the register as having high influence but low interest, has suddenly started asking about vendor selection after a local news story. What should the project manager do?
options: Update the council member's assessment in the register and brief her directly on how the vendor was chosen.
Continue monitoring the council member, because the register rates her interest in the project as low.
Refer the council member to the project's public news release and website for details about the vendor selection process.
Ask the procurement officer to take over all of the council member's questions about the vendor.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Re-analyzing stakeholders — analysis is not one-and-done; when interest or influence changes, reassess and adjust engagement.
Spot it: "high influence but low interest," then sudden questions after a news story, with a phase gate coming up.
In this scenario: update her assessment in the register and brief her directly on how the vendor was chosen.
Why not the others: Continuing to monitor relies on an out-of-date rating; a news release is a one-way answer to someone who needs direct engagement; handing her off to procurement drops the PM's ownership of the relationship.
Remember: Identify → Analyze → Engage → Monitor — and re-analyze when the power/interest picture changes.

questions.stem: Match each communication method with its description.
matching_right: Sent directly to specific recipients, such as emails or memos
Information absorbed by overhearing colocated teammates' conversations
Real-time exchange among two or more parties, such as meetings
Posted in a repository for recipients to access when needed

answer.Interactive communication: Real-time exchange among two or more parties, such as meetings
answer.Push communication: Sent directly to specific recipients, such as emails or memos
answer.Pull communication: Posted in a repository for recipients to access when needed
answer.Osmotic communication: Information absorbed by overhearing colocated teammates' conversations

questions.explanation:
Concept: Communication methods differ by who starts the exchange and whether understanding is confirmed.
Interactive communication: real-time, two-way exchange such as meetings and calls; use it when understanding must be confirmed.
Push communication: sent to specific people, such as emails and memos; there is no proof it was read.
Pull communication: posted where people retrieve it when they need it, such as portals; good for large audiences.
Osmotic communication: picked up by overhearing colocated teammates; a benefit of sitting together.
Remember: Interactive = talk, Push = send, Pull = post, Osmotic = overhear.

questions.stem: The predictive and adaptive streams of a hybrid bank branch digitization program have finished delivery, and final handover is scheduled for next week. Several team members are anxious about their next assignments, and productivity is dipping. What should the project manager do?
options: Raise output targets so the handover is finished before morale falls any further across the team.
Keep all members on the project payroll until each one has found a new role elsewhere on their own initiative.
Recognize the team's contributions and work with functional managers to confirm each member's next assignment.
Concentrate on the handover documents and leave assignment questions entirely to human resources.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tuckman's adjourning stage — as the work ends, members worry about what comes next; the PM recognizes contributions and helps with transitions.
Spot it: delivery finished, handover next week, anxiety about next assignments, dipping productivity.
In this scenario: recognize the team's work and work with functional managers to confirm each member's next assignment.
Why not the others: Raising targets pressures an anxious team; keeping everyone on payroll until they find roles wastes budget and still leaves them unsupported; leaving it all to HR ignores the cause of the dip.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close — and release people with recognition.

questions.stem: On a predictive pipeline integrity project, an inspector finds a minor coating defect that can be repaired in an hour using the approved work method. Company practice requires inspectors to call the project manager about every defect, but the project manager is often unreachable in the field. What should the project manager do?
options: Require inspectors to wait for the project manager's approval so that defect decisions stay consistent.
Authorize inspectors to repair defects that meet set criteria and report them afterward in the quality log.
Tell inspectors to note each defect found and leave all repairs for discussion at the end-of-phase quality review meeting.
Ask the sponsor to hire an assistant who can approve defect repairs on the project manager's behalf.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Empowerment with clear criteria — let people act within defined limits and report afterward, keeping control through records rather than approvals.
Spot it: a routine, low-risk fix under an approved method, and an approver who is "often unreachable."
In this scenario: authorize inspectors to repair defects that meet set criteria and record them in the quality log afterward.
Why not the others: Waiting for approval adds delay without adding consistency; holding repairs until the phase review lets easy fixes sit; hiring an assistant approver just moves the bottleneck.
Remember: Push decisions to the lowest competent level — criteria up front, report after.

questions.stem: A customer's procurement lead insists that the contract for an agile hotel booking platform fix every feature and the total price up front. The development vendor wants flexibility because requirements will evolve as users give feedback. Which TWO proposals should the vendor's agile lead make?
options: A fixed price per release, with scope defined at a high level and refined each iteration.
A clause letting the customer swap unstarted features of equal size without renegotiation.
Accept the fully fixed-scope, fixed-price contract to secure the deal as quickly as possible.
Refuse to sign any contract that includes a firm price commitment from the vendor.
Offer an uncapped time-and-materials contract with no scope or budget boundaries.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile contracting — structures that give the buyer cost control while letting scope evolve, such as a fixed price per release and swapping equal-size features.
Spot it: a buyer who wants everything fixed and a vendor who expects requirements to change with user feedback.
In this scenario: propose a fixed price per release with high-level scope refined each iteration, plus a clause to swap unstarted features of equal size.
Why not the others: Accepting fixed scope and price locks in what everyone expects to change; refusing any firm price ignores the buyer's need for cost control; uncapped time and materials leaves the buyer unprotected.
Remember: Fix time and cost, flex scope — and write that flexibility into the contract.

questions.stem: A fully remote agile team at a fintech firm spans seven time zones. The daily scrum is held at 11 p.m. for the two members in Sydney, and they have begun skipping it. Their updates now reach the rest of the team late. What should the scrum master do?
options: Require the Sydney members to attend, since the daily scrum is a mandatory event for all developers.
Excuse the Sydney members from the daily scrum and have them email updates to the scrum master.
Recommend moving the Sydney members to another team located in their own time zone instead.
Work with the team to rotate the meeting time or combine a short live overlap with written updates.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Adapting practices for distributed teams — make events fair and sustainable for every time zone, using rotation or a mix of live and written updates.
Spot it: an event at 11 p.m. for some members, skipped attendance, updates arriving late.
In this scenario: the scrum master works with the team to rotate the time or pair a short live overlap with written updates.
Why not the others: Requiring attendance ignores sustainable pace and fairness; emailing the scrum master turns the daily scrum into a status report; moving members off the team is a drastic first step.
Remember: The daily scrum is for the developers, not the scrum master. Adapt the practice, keep the purpose.

questions.stem: On a hybrid aerospace maintenance-software program, one engineer thrives on challenging, measurable goals, while a data analyst works best when collaborating closely and feeling part of a group. Both are underperforming in their current assignments. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Set identical individual targets for both so their performance can be compared fairly.
Make the analyst responsible for independently auditing the engineers' work for errors.
Give the engineer a challenging component with clear success measures and regular feedback.
Offer the engineer a public role directing other members' daily assignments and tasks.
Place the analyst in a paired, team-based task on the adaptive stream with frequent interaction.
questions.explanation:
Concept: McClelland's acquired needs theory — people are driven mainly by achievement, affiliation, or power, and work motivates best when it matches the dominant need.
Spot it: "challenging, measurable goals" (achievement) and "collaborating closely and feeling part of a group" (affiliation).
In this scenario: give the engineer a challenging component with clear measures and feedback, and place the analyst in a paired, team-based task.
Why not the others: Identical targets ignore individual needs; solo auditing isolates the affiliation-driven analyst; directing others appeals to power, not achievement.
Remember: Achievement = challenge + feedback; Affiliation = belonging; Power = influence. Match the work to the need.

questions.stem: A predictive hospital IT migration faces a firm regulatory deadline in three days. The database and network leads disagree on the cutover sequence; both options meet the requirements, discussions have gone in circles, and any further delay will cause the deadline to be missed. What should the project manager do?
options: Make the sequencing decision based on the available analysis and explain the reasoning to both leads.
Schedule a facilitated workshop next week so the two leads can collaborate on a consensus cutover sequence together.
Ask each lead to give up part of their approach and combine the two sequences into one plan.
Escalate the disagreement to the sponsor and wait for guidance before starting the cutover.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Force/direct — the leader decides when time is critical, the options are equally acceptable, and more discussion adds no value.
Spot it: a firm deadline in three days, "both options meet the requirements," and talks going "in circles."
In this scenario: decide the sequence from the available analysis and explain the reasoning to both leads.
Why not the others: A workshop next week misses the regulatory deadline; merging two sequences is a compromise that may yield a worse plan; escalating and waiting burns the little time left.
Remember: Collaborate is the default; force only when the clock or safety demands it.

questions.stem: On a hybrid museum digitization project, an adaptive web team asks for relief from a PMO status template that takes a full day each week to complete. The predictive portion of the project relies on these reports for governance. What should the project manager do?
options: Explain to the web team that the PMO template is mandatory for every stream and must be completed exactly as written.
Stop sending any reports for the web team, since adaptive teams report their progress through demos.
Agree with the PMO that the web team can report from its existing boards and demos while keeping key metrics.
Ask the predictive team to prepare the web team's weekly reports in addition to its own reports.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Servant leadership plus tailoring — cut unnecessary overhead for the team while still meeting real governance needs, often by reusing information radiators.
Spot it: a template that "takes a full day each week" and a governance need that is legitimate.
In this scenario: agree with the PMO that the web team reports from its existing boards and demos while keeping the key metrics governance needs.
Why not the others: Enforcing the template as written ignores the waste; stopping reports leaves governance blind; shifting the reports to the predictive team just moves the burden.
Remember: Tailor, don't drop. Serve the team AND the governance.

questions.stem: Match each situational leadership style with when a scrum master would use it.
matching_right: Low direction, high support for a capable but hesitant member
High direction, low support for an enthusiastic but unskilled beginner
Low direction, low support for a skilled and committed member
High direction and high support for a discouraged learner

answer.Directing: High direction, low support for an enthusiastic but unskilled beginner
answer.Coaching: High direction and high support for a discouraged learner
answer.Supporting: Low direction, high support for a capable but hesitant member
answer.Delegating: Low direction, low support for a skilled and committed member

questions.explanation:
Concept: Situational leadership — the leader adjusts direction and support to each person's competence and commitment for a given task.
Directing: lots of direction, little support, for an enthusiastic beginner who lacks skill.
Coaching: lots of direction and lots of support, for a learner who has become discouraged.
Supporting: little direction, lots of support, for a capable person who lacks confidence.
Delegating: little direction and little support, for someone skilled and committed.
Remember: Directing → Coaching → Supporting → Delegating as competence and commitment grow.

questions.stem: A hybrid logistics platform program's steering committee receives only milestone reports from the predictive stream. Committee members say they cannot tell whether the adaptive stream is delivering business value, and some are proposing to cut its funding. What should the project manager do?
options: Invite committee members to demos and add value metrics from each adaptive increment to their reports.
Convert the adaptive stream into milestone plans so its reports match the predictive stream's format.
Send the committee the adaptive team's detailed task lists for each increment as they are produced.
Ask the sponsor to defend the adaptive stream's funding at the next steering committee meeting.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Engaging stakeholders with visible value — in adaptive work, demos and outcome metrics show value delivered, which milestone reports cannot.
Spot it: a steering committee that "cannot tell whether the adaptive stream is delivering business value" and a threat to funding.
In this scenario: invite committee members to demos and add value metrics from each adaptive increment to their reports.
Why not the others: Converting to milestone plans undermines the adaptive approach and still shows no value; detailed task lists show activity, not value; asking the sponsor to defend it adds no evidence.
Remember: Deliverable → Outcome → Benefit → Value. Show the value, don't just report the work.

questions.stem: The project manager on a predictive offshore wind installation emailed a critical crane-schedule change to the marine contractor. Two days later, a crane arrived on the old date because the contractor's site lead never read the email. The error created safety exposure and extra cost. What should the project manager do for future critical changes?
options: Copy more of the contractor's staff on future emails so that someone is sure to read them.
Post critical changes on the project portal for the contractor to check at its convenience.
Send a formal letter stating the contractor is responsible for missed email communications.
Communicate critical changes by phone or meeting with the site lead and confirm acknowledgment.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Choosing a communication method — urgent or safety-critical information needs interactive communication with confirmed acknowledgment.
Spot it: a critical change sent only by email, "never read the email," safety exposure and extra cost.
In this scenario: for future critical changes, communicate by phone or meeting with the site lead and confirm acknowledgment.
Why not the others: Copying more people is still push with no confirmation; posting on a portal is pull and even less reliable; a blame letter records fault but prevents nothing.
Remember: Critical = interactive + acknowledged. Push sends, pull posts, only interactive confirms.

questions.stem: An agile team at a logistics company has worked together for a year, delivers reliably, and resolves its own conflicts. Management now plans to split this team evenly to seed two new product teams next quarter. What should the agile coach advise management?
options: Split the team evenly, because its strong members will quickly form two equally high-performing new teams.
Explain that splitting will restart team development, and suggest seeding each new team with only one or two members.
Oppose any change, because a stable agile team should remain together for the life of the organization.
Split the team, then have the coach assign every role on both new teams so that storming is avoided entirely.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tuckman's model and team stability — changing a team's membership sends it back to earlier stages, so high performance does not travel with individuals when a team is split.
Spot it: a mature, high-performing team and a plan to "split this team evenly."
In this scenario: warn that splitting will restart development for both halves, and suggest seeding each new team with only one or two members.
Why not the others: Expecting two instant high performers ignores that both halves restart at forming; opposing any change is rigid; assigning every role removes self-organization, and storming cannot be skipped.
Remember: New membership = new team. Stable teams keep performing — seed, don't split.

questions.stem: A predictive manufacturing plant expansion has a highly experienced commissioning team. The team often proposes better test sequences, but every proposal must go through the project manager, and each decision now takes about a week. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Delegate test sequencing decisions to the commissioning lead within the approved test plan and safety rules.
Allow the team to change any part of the approved test plan without informing anyone else.
Agree with the team on which decisions still need escalation, such as those affecting the schedule baseline.
Keep approving each proposal personally but promise the team a response within one working day.
Route every test sequence proposal to the quality department for its review and sign-off instead.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Delegation within boundaries — give experienced people decision rights inside the approved plan, and agree which decisions still need escalation.
Spot it: a highly experienced team, a PM approval bottleneck, "each decision now takes about a week."
In this scenario: delegate test sequencing to the commissioning lead within the test plan and safety rules, and agree that decisions touching the schedule baseline still escalate.
Why not the others: Changing any part of the plan without telling anyone removes control; faster PM approvals keep the bottleneck; routing proposals to the quality department just moves it.
Remember: Push decisions down; keep baseline decisions up.

questions.stem: In a hybrid automotive program, a hardware supplier working to a predictive plan wants a full specification freeze in two weeks. The adaptive software team wants interface details left open for two more months. Both sides have real constraints, and the relationship will continue for years. What should the project manager do?
options: Freeze every specification in two weeks, because the hardware supply contract is legally binding on both sides.
Keep all interfaces open for two months and pay the supplier to absorb any resulting schedule delay.
Facilitate an agreement to freeze physical interfaces now and leave software-configurable parameters open.
Let the supplier and software team negotiate directly without any involvement from the project manager.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Interest-based negotiation — look behind each side's position to the real need and find an option that meets both.
Spot it: "both sides have real constraints," a relationship lasting years, one side needing stability and the other flexibility.
In this scenario: facilitate an agreement to freeze physical interfaces now (the supplier's tooling need) and keep software-configurable parameters open (the team's need).
Why not the others: Freezing everything is forcing and ignores the adaptive need; paying the supplier to wait is costly and dodges the real issue; stepping aside abandons the PM's integration role.
Remember: Positions clash; interests often fit. Collaborate for win-win.

questions.stem: A distributed agile team building a university admissions portal has members in four countries. Retrospectives held over video are quiet, and the scrum master suspects some members are uncomfortable criticizing processes in front of the whole group. What should the scrum master do?
options: Call on each member by name to share at least one criticism of the process during every retrospective.
Cancel retrospectives for this team, since members are not contributing anything useful during them.
Hold separate retrospectives in each country so that members only have to speak in front of their local peers.
Collect anonymous digital input before the discussion and let members contribute in writing as well as aloud.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Psychological safety in virtual teams — adapt facilitation so everyone can speak up safely, including in writing or anonymously.
Spot it: quiet video retrospectives, members "uncomfortable criticizing processes in front of the whole group," several cultures.
In this scenario: collect anonymous digital input before the discussion and let members contribute in writing as well as aloud.
Why not the others: Calling on people by name raises discomfort; canceling retrospectives drops continuous improvement; splitting by country divides the team and hides cross-site problems.
Remember: Silence is data. Change the format to make it safe — not the people.

questions.stem: Members of a hybrid energy-trading system team say they feel like order takers: the predictive regulatory module is fully specified, and even the adaptive analytics work arrives with prescribed solutions. Engagement survey scores have dropped for two quarters. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Offer gift cards to members whose tasks are completed ahead of their original estimates.
Present adaptive analytics work as problems with desired outcomes and let the team design the solutions.
Let the team redesign the approved regulatory module specification however it sees fit.
Increase status meetings so members understand exactly what is expected of them each day.
Explain how the regulatory module protects customers and the business so the team sees its purpose.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Intrinsic motivation — autonomy and purpose drive engagement; let people shape solutions where they can, and explain the "why" where they cannot.
Spot it: "order takers," "prescribed solutions," engagement dropping, and a module fixed for compliance.
In this scenario: present adaptive analytics work as problems with desired outcomes for the team to solve, and explain how the regulatory module protects customers and the business.
Why not the others: Gift cards for speed are extrinsic and encourage padded estimates; redesigning an approved compliance spec bypasses change control; more status meetings add control, the opposite of autonomy.
Remember: Autonomy where you can, purpose where you can't.

questions.stem: Match each type of power an agile coach might use with its source.
matching_right: Ability to give incentives, praise, or desired assignments
Authority granted by a formal position in the organization
Ability to impose penalties or other negative consequences
Influence from being respected, trusted, or admired by others
Influence earned through recognized knowledge and skill

answer.Legitimate: Authority granted by a formal position in the organization
answer.Expert: Influence earned through recognized knowledge and skill
answer.Referent: Influence from being respected, trusted, or admired by others
answer.Reward: Ability to give incentives, praise, or desired assignments
answer.Coercive: Ability to impose penalties or other negative consequences

questions.explanation:
Concept: The five types of power describe where a person's influence comes from.
Legitimate: formal authority granted by a position in the organization.
Expert: influence earned through recognized knowledge and skill — the best power for a PM.
Referent: influence from being respected, trusted, or admired — the second best.
Reward: the ability to give incentives, praise, or desired assignments.
Coercive: the ability to impose penalties — the weakest for long-term commitment.
Remember: PMI prefers EARNED power (expert, referent) over GRANTED power (legitimate, reward, coercive).

questions.stem: Designers on a predictive rail signaling project have been told by three department heads to attend separate status meetings that repeat the same information. The designers now lose a full day each week and have asked the project manager for help. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the designers to attend the three meetings in rotation so that only one of them loses time in any given week.
Consolidate the meetings into one status update for all three department heads, freeing the designers' time.
Tell the department heads that designers will no longer attend any status meetings for the project.
Accept the meetings as part of the job and add the lost design time to the project schedule baseline.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Servant leadership — shield the team from low-value demands on its time while still meeting stakeholders' information needs.
Spot it: duplicate meetings imposed by several managers, "lose a full day each week," and the team asking for help.
In this scenario: consolidate the three meetings into one status update for all three department heads.
Why not the others: Rotating attendance keeps the waste; refusing all meetings ignores legitimate information needs; adding lost time to the baseline accepts the waste and changes a baseline without cause.
Remember: Serve the team — remove the waste, keep stakeholders informed.

questions.stem: A former predictive project coordinator on a hybrid banking program has become scrum master for the adaptive stream. She runs the daily scrum as a status report to herself and assigns tasks afterward. The developers are frustrated. She has asked the project manager for feedback. What should the project manager do?
options: Tell the developers to ignore her task assignments and organize the daily work among themselves instead.
Send her a copy of the Scrum Guide and expect her to adjust her approach to the daily scrum on her own.
Suggest that she return to her coordinator duties, because the scrum master role does not seem to suit her style.
Observe a daily scrum with her, then discuss how to shift planning of the day's work back to the developers.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Coaching a new scrum master — observe, then give specific feedback so she shifts from directing the team to serving it.
Spot it: a former coordinator running the daily scrum as a status report, assigning tasks, and asking for feedback.
In this scenario: observe a daily scrum with her, then discuss how to hand planning of the day's work back to the developers.
Why not the others: Telling developers to ignore her undermines her instead of developing her; sending the Scrum Guide gives rules without guided reflection; suggesting she leave the role replaces before coaching.
Remember: Coach first, never replace first. The daily scrum belongs to the developers.

questions.stem: Match each stakeholder engagement level with its description.
matching_right: Aware of the project but neither supports nor resists it
Aware and actively engaged in making the project succeed
Does not know about the project or its potential impacts
Aware of the project and in favor of the change
Aware of the project but opposed to the change it brings

answer.Unaware: Does not know about the project or its potential impacts
answer.Resistant: Aware of the project but opposed to the change it brings
answer.Neutral: Aware of the project but neither supports nor resists it
answer.Supportive: Aware of the project and in favor of the change
answer.Leading: Aware and actively engaged in making the project succeed

questions.explanation:
Concept: Stakeholder engagement levels, used in the engagement assessment matrix to compare current and desired engagement.
Unaware: does not know about the project or how it will affect them.
Resistant: aware of the project but opposed to the change it brings.
Neutral: aware of it but neither supporting nor resisting.
Supportive: aware and in favor of the change.
Leading: aware and actively working to make the project succeed.
Remember: Unaware → Resistant → Neutral → Supportive → Leading. Find the gap between current and desired, then plan how to close it.

questions.stem: Match each Scrum event or activity with its purpose.
matching_right: Team inspects how it worked and identifies process improvements
Team sets the sprint goal and selects work to achieve it
Product owner and team clarify, split, and estimate upcoming items
Team shows the increment and gathers stakeholder feedback
Developers inspect progress toward the goal and adapt the day's plan

answer.Sprint planning: Team sets the sprint goal and selects work to achieve it
answer.Daily scrum: Developers inspect progress toward the goal and adapt the day's plan
answer.Sprint review: Team shows the increment and gathers stakeholder feedback
answer.Sprint retrospective: Team inspects how it worked and identifies process improvements
answer.Backlog refinement: Product owner and team clarify, split, and estimate upcoming items

questions.explanation:
Concept: Each Scrum event has one clear purpose inside the sprint.
Sprint planning: the Scrum team sets the sprint goal and selects the work to reach it.
Daily scrum: developers inspect progress toward the goal and adjust the plan for the day.
Sprint review: the team shows the increment and gathers stakeholder feedback on the product.
Sprint retrospective: the team inspects how it worked and picks process improvements.
Backlog refinement: the product owner and team clarify, split, and estimate upcoming items.
Remember: Review = the PRODUCT, Retro = the PROCESS. Planning = what and why; Daily = the next 24 hours.

questions.stem: A predictive hospital construction project has a team drawn from three contracting firms. Two months in, subgroups have formed along company lines, and design information is not being shared across them. Several coordination errors have already occurred. What should the project manager do?
options: Hold a joint session to set shared goals and ground rules, and form cross-company working groups.
Assign one contractor's lead to supervise all of the subgroups and strictly enforce information sharing.
Let each contractor manage its own people, since they report to different companies.
Wait for the team to reach norming, which will resolve the subgroup problems naturally.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Team building — deliberate activities such as shared goals, ground rules, and mixed working groups that turn separate groups into one team.
Spot it: subgroups "along company lines," design information not shared, coordination errors.
In this scenario: hold a joint session to set shared goals and ground rules, and form cross-company working groups.
Why not the others: Putting one contractor's lead over everyone creates a power imbalance; letting each firm manage its own reinforces the silos; waiting for norming assumes development happens by itself.
Remember: One project, one team — shared goals and ground rules first.

questions.stem: An agile team at an e-commerce firm wants to add automated accessibility tests to its definition of done, which will slightly reduce throughput in the short term. The team's line manager, who is not part of the Scrum team, asks the scrum master whether to allow it. What should the scrum master advise?
options: Veto the change, since throughput is the manager's main priority for the team this quarter.
Support the change, since the Scrum team owns its definition of done, and explain the quality benefits.
Have the product owner approve each quality practice before the team adds it to its process.
Postpone the change until the team's velocity has risen enough for it to absorb all of the extra testing work.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Definition of done — created and owned by the Scrum team, which is empowered to raise its own quality standard.
Spot it: the team wants a stronger definition of done, and someone outside the team asks whether to "allow it."
In this scenario: support the change, because the Scrum team owns its definition of done, and explain the quality benefits to the manager.
Why not the others: A manager veto overrides the team's ownership; product owner approval per practice confuses ordering value with owning quality; waiting for velocity to rise treats velocity as a target.
Remember: Definition of done = the Scrum team's quality bar. Stronger done now = less rework later.

questions.stem: A hybrid public-health reporting project needs a data engineer from the enterprise analytics group. The group's manager offers the engineer only on Fridays, but the adaptive stream needs daily collaboration for three weeks. The analytics group is eager for early access to this project's new data model. What should the project manager do?
options: Offer the analytics group early access to the new data model in exchange for three weeks of full-time support.
Accept the Friday-only offer and extend the adaptive stream's timeline to match the reduced support.
Escalate to the sponsor so that the analytics group is required to provide the data engineer on every single day.
Hire a contract data engineer instead, without any further discussion with the analytics group.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Trading on interests — find what the other party values and offer it in exchange for what the project needs.
Spot it: a limited offer ("only on Fridays") plus something the other side wants ("eager for early access").
In this scenario: offer the analytics group early access to the new data model in return for three weeks of full-time support.
Why not the others: Accepting Fridays only harms the adaptive stream; escalating uses positional power and strains a relationship you will need again; hiring a contractor without discussion skips an easy win-win.
Remember: Ask "what do they need?" before "who can order them?"

questions.stem: A predictive mining equipment program has design teams in Chile, Canada, and Australia who have never met. Trust between sites is low: teams recheck each other's calculations, adding weeks to the schedule. The budget allows for one trip. What should the project manager do?
options: Save the travel budget and add a formal review gate for every cross-team design calculation from now on instead.
Assign all critical calculations to a single site so fewer handoffs are needed between locations.
Tell each team to stop rechecking the others' calculations, since it is wasting schedule time.
Use the travel budget for a joint planning workshop with site leads, then continue with regular video design reviews.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Building trust in virtual teams — early face-to-face time builds relationships that regular virtual contact then keeps alive.
Spot it: sites that "have never met," low trust, duplicated checking, and budget for "one trip."
In this scenario: use the travel budget for a joint planning workshop with site leads, then continue regular video design reviews.
Why not the others: A formal review gate institutionalizes distrust and adds delay; moving all calculations to one site sidesteps the trust problem; ordering teams to stop rechecking doesn't create trust.
Remember: Trust is built person to person — meet once, then keep connecting.

questions.stem: During a predictive pharmaceutical packaging line project, a supplier reports that the approved blister-foil material will be discontinued in four months, before production validation. A qualified substitute is available at a higher unit cost. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Approve the substitute right away, since the original material will soon stop being available.
Update the cost baseline to include the substitute material and then inform the change control board afterward.
Analyze the substitute's effect on scope, cost, schedule, and validation, and then submit a change request.
Ask the supplier to keep producing the original material until the project has formally closed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Integrated change control — Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor. The PM analyzes impact first; the change control board decides.
Spot it: a change forced by an outside event (discontinued material), a higher cost, and "FIRST."
In this scenario: analyze the substitute's effect on scope, cost, schedule, and validation, then submit a change request.
Why not the others: Approving it yourself skips analysis and the board; updating the baseline first reverses the flow; asking the supplier to keep producing ignores the discontinuation.
Remember: Analyze → Approve → then Update. Baseline = APPROVED, so it never changes first.

questions.stem: Match each threat response strategy with what the agile team does.
matching_right: Pass the threat to a higher level outside project authority
Reduce probability or impact, for example with an early spike
Change the plan so the threat or its cause is eliminated
Acknowledge the threat and act only if it occurs
Shift the threat's impact and ownership to a third party

answer.Avoid: Change the plan so the threat or its cause is eliminated
answer.Transfer: Shift the threat's impact and ownership to a third party
answer.Mitigate: Reduce probability or impact, for example with an early spike
answer.Accept: Acknowledge the threat and act only if it occurs
answer.Escalate: Pass the threat to a higher level outside project authority

questions.explanation:
Concept: The five threat response strategies, from removing a threat to handing it upward.
Avoid: change the plan to eliminate the threat or its cause.
Transfer: shift the impact and ownership to a third party, for example through insurance or a contract.
Mitigate: reduce probability or impact, for example with an early spike or prototype.
Accept: acknowledge the threat and act only if it occurs, perhaps using a reserve.
Escalate: pass the threat to a higher level when it is outside the project's authority.
Remember: Avoid = remove, Transfer = shift, Mitigate = reduce, Accept = live with it, Escalate = pass it up. A spike is agile mitigation.

questions.stem: On a hybrid airline crew-scheduling project, a predictive infrastructure team reports that server delivery has slipped by two weeks. This blocks performance testing that the adaptive team planned for its next iteration. The delay has already been confirmed by the vendor. What should the project manager do?
options: Add the server delay to the risk register and plan a response based on its probability and potential impact.
Wait until the servers arrive and then re-plan the adaptive team's performance testing from there.
Tell the adaptive team to skip performance testing for this release to protect the delivery date.
Record it in the issue log with an owner and due date, and work with both teams on a testing workaround.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Risk vs issue — a risk is a future uncertainty in the risk register; an issue has already happened and goes in the issue log with an owner and an action.
Spot it: "has slipped" and "already been confirmed" — past tense means issue.
In this scenario: record the confirmed delay in the issue log with an owner and due date, and work with both teams on a testing workaround.
Why not the others: The risk register is for events that might happen; waiting for the servers leaves the adaptive team blocked; skipping performance testing trades quality for the date.
Remember: Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor → Issue. Once it happens, it is an issue — TRACK it in the issue log.

questions.stem: A hybrid medical-imaging program has a predictive hardware stream and an adaptive software stream. Integration defects have doubled over three increments, and most trace back to interface requirements that each stream interpreted differently. What should the project manager do?
options: Run root cause analysis with both streams and add concrete interface examples to the acceptance criteria.
Add more integration testers so the interface defects are found much faster before each increment is released.
Extend the integration test phase so that every defect can be fixed before the next release.
Ask the hardware stream to freeze all interfaces for the remainder of the program's duration.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Prevention over inspection — find the root cause of defects and fix it at the source instead of catching more defects later.
Spot it: rising defects that "trace back to" a common cause: requirements each stream read differently.
In this scenario: run root cause analysis with both streams and add concrete interface examples to the acceptance criteria.
Why not the others: More testers only find defects faster; a longer test phase fixes symptoms, not the cause; freezing all interfaces forces predictive rigidity onto the adaptive stream.
Remember: Quality is planned in, not inspected in. Prevention costs less than rework.

questions.stem: In a sprint review for a municipal permit app, developers show the stories they planned and completed. Planning department staff point out that the new workflow misses a mandatory inspection step. All acceptance criteria for the completed stories were met. What should the product owner do?
options: Reject the completed stories, since they do not match the planning department's real workflow.
Tell the department that the stories met their acceptance criteria and the workflow is finished.
Add the inspection step to the product backlog and order it against the other remaining work.
Ask the team to extend the current sprint by one week so the missing step can be added now.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Emergent scope in agile — new needs found at a review go into the product backlog, and the product owner orders them.
Spot it: acceptance criteria met, yet stakeholders spot something missing at the sprint review.
In this scenario: add the inspection step to the product backlog and order it against the remaining work.
Why not the others: Rejecting stories that met their criteria confuses new work with defects; declaring the workflow finished ignores valuable feedback; extending the sprint breaks the timebox.
Remember: Review = the PRODUCT. New learning → product backlog → product owner orders it.

questions.stem: A hybrid stadium ticketing program must launch by opening day. The predictive turnstile installation is on the critical path with no float, while the adaptive app team delivers in two-week iterations. A turnstile shipment has just slipped five days. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Ask the app team to accelerate its iterations so that the five-day slip is fully absorbed by the app stream's schedule.
Analyze the slip's effect on the critical path and evaluate compression options such as crashing installation.
Move the launch back by five days and notify stakeholders of the new opening-day schedule.
Overlap turnstile installation with network testing right away to fast-track the remaining work.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Schedule compression — when a critical path activity slips, first analyze the impact, then choose between crashing (add resources, more cost) and fast-tracking (overlap work, more risk).
Spot it: "critical path with no float," a fixed launch date, and "FIRST."
In this scenario: analyze the five-day slip's effect on the critical path and evaluate options such as crashing the installation.
Why not the others: The app stream is not the turnstile critical path, so speeding it absorbs nothing; moving the launch gives up a fixed date without trying compression; fast-tracking at once picks a technique before analysis.
Remember: Crash = add money; Fast-track = add risk. Analyze first, then choose.

questions.stem: An agile fitness app release planned 200 story points over 10 equal sprints with a budget of $500,000. After 4 sprints, 60 points are complete and $220,000 has been spent. The sponsor asks for the release's cost performance index (CPI). What is the CPI?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile earned value — EV = (completed points ÷ planned points) × budget; CPI = EV ÷ AC and SPI = EV ÷ PV.
Spot it: story points, a release budget, money spent so far, and a request for CPI.
In this scenario: EV = 60 ÷ 200 × $500,000 = $150,000, so CPI = 150,000 ÷ 220,000 = 0.68 — less value earned than money spent.
Why not the others: 0.75 is SPI (EV ÷ PV of $200,000 after 4 of 10 sprints); 0.91 divides planned value by actual cost; 1.47 flips the CPI formula.
Remember: EV always first. CPI = EV/AC, SPI = EV/PV — below 1 is bad news.

questions.stem: A predictive hospital IT project will purchase a clinical data archive whose requirements are fully defined and stable. The hospital's leadership wants maximum cost certainty. A prospective seller has asked for a cost-reimbursable arrangement. Which contract type should the project manager recommend?
options: Firm fixed price, because the scope is well defined and the buyer needs cost certainty.
Cost plus fixed fee, because it protects the seller against any cost overruns on the work.
Time and materials, because it lets the buyer adjust the archive's scope as work proceeds.
Cost plus incentive fee, because it motivates the seller to reduce the buyer's final costs.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contract types shift cost risk between buyer and seller. Firm fixed price puts the risk on the seller and suits well-defined, stable scope.
Spot it: "fully defined and stable" requirements and "maximum cost certainty."
In this scenario: recommend firm fixed price, even though the seller would prefer a cost-reimbursable deal.
Why not the others: Cost plus fixed fee protects the seller, not the buyer; time and materials suits unclear scope, not stable scope; cost plus incentive fee still leaves the buyer carrying cost risk.
Remember: Clear scope → Fixed Price (seller risk). Unclear scope → Cost-reimbursable (buyer risk). T&M = small or uncertain work.

questions.stem: Late in a predictive tax-filing system project, external auditors ask which test cases verify each regulatory requirement. The team cannot quickly show these links, and some requirements may never have been tested. Which project document should the project manager use to address this?
options: The issue log, to list every requirement that the auditors have raised questions about.
A requirements traceability matrix linking each requirement to its design, build, and test items.
The project scope statement, because it describes deliverables and their acceptance criteria.
The quality management plan, because it defines how all of the project's testing will be performed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Requirements traceability matrix — the TRACE document linking each requirement to its source and to the design, build, and test items that satisfy it.
Spot it: "which test cases verify each regulatory requirement" and "may never have been tested."
In this scenario: use the traceability matrix to show every requirement's test links and expose the gaps.
Why not the others: The issue log tracks problems, not requirement links; the scope statement describes deliverables, not tests per requirement; the quality management plan explains how testing is done, not which test proves which requirement.
Remember: TRACE = RTM and WBS dictionary. Plan = HOW; RTM = WHERE each requirement went.

questions.stem: A hybrid bank lending platform has a predictive core-banking integration and an adaptive customer portal. A new regulation taking effect in two months requires a disclosure screen in the portal. The portal backlog is currently ordered by revenue impact. What should the product owner do?
options: Keep the current order, since the disclosure screen adds no direct revenue for the business.
Send the disclosure screen to the predictive stream's change control board for its formal approval.
Move the disclosure screen near the top, considering the regulatory deadline and any dependencies.
Add the disclosure screen to the current sprint and drop whatever work is already in progress.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Backlog ordering — the product owner orders by value, risk, dependencies, and deadlines; compliance work carries the value of staying legal.
Spot it: a "new regulation," a date two months away, and a backlog "ordered by revenue impact."
In this scenario: move the disclosure screen near the top, considering the deadline and any dependencies.
Why not the others: Keeping the order ignores the cost of missing the regulation; the change control board governs the predictive baseline, not the portal backlog; disrupting the current sprint is unnecessary with two months left.
Remember: Product owner orders the product backlog. Value = revenue + risk reduction + compliance.

questions.stem: Midway through a sprint on the adaptive stream of a hybrid hotel-booking program, a predictive integration team requests a small change to an API field used by the current sprint's work. Developers confirm the change would not endanger the sprint goal. What should happen?
options: The team rejects the change until next sprint, because a sprint backlog cannot change after sprint planning.
The product owner cancels the sprint and restarts planning so the API change is fully included.
The team sends the change to the predictive change control board before discussing it internally.
The developers and product owner renegotiate the sprint work to include the change while keeping the goal.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sprint goal vs sprint backlog — the goal is fixed during the sprint, but the sprint backlog can be renegotiated between developers and product owner as they learn.
Spot it: a small change mid-sprint that "would not endanger the sprint goal."
In this scenario: the developers and product owner renegotiate the sprint work to include the change while keeping the goal.
Why not the others: The sprint backlog is not frozen; canceling a sprint is only for an obsolete goal; the predictive change control board does not govern the adaptive sprint.
Remember: Goal = fixed; sprint backlog = flexible. Only the product owner cancels a sprint, and only if the goal is obsolete.

questions.stem: Match each kanban flow term with its description.
matching_right: Elapsed time from starting work on an item to finishing it
Chart showing item counts in each workflow state over time
Maximum number of items allowed in a workflow state
Number of items completed per unit of time
Elapsed time from customer request to delivery

answer.WIP limit: Maximum number of items allowed in a workflow state
answer.Lead time: Elapsed time from customer request to delivery
answer.Cycle time: Elapsed time from starting work on an item to finishing it
answer.Throughput: Number of items completed per unit of time
answer.Cumulative flow diagram: Chart showing item counts in each workflow state over time

questions.explanation:
Concept: Kanban manages continuous flow, and these terms control and measure it.
WIP limit: the maximum number of items allowed in a workflow state at once.
Lead time: from customer request to delivery — what the customer experiences.
Cycle time: from starting work on an item to finishing it — what the team controls.
Throughput: the number of items finished per unit of time.
Cumulative flow diagram: item counts per state over time; a widening band reveals a bottleneck.
Remember: Lead time = order to delivery; cycle time = start to finish. Kanban = visualize, limit WIP, manage flow.

questions.stem: A predictive telecom network rollout has stable, well-understood tower construction work, but a new customer self-service portal has unclear requirements that will change as customers react. The sponsor asks how the portal should be handled within the project's governance. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Develop the portal incrementally with frequent customer feedback, reporting within the project's integrated governance.
Plan the portal in full detail now so that all of its work fits neatly into the tower construction schedule baseline and its milestones.
Remove the portal from project governance so its team can work without any reporting obligations.
Delay the portal until tower construction is finished so the project keeps one consistent lifecycle.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tailoring the delivery approach — choose the approach per component: predictive for stable work, adaptive for uncertain work, all within one integrated governance.
Spot it: "stable, well-understood" work next to "unclear requirements that will change."
In this scenario: develop the portal incrementally with frequent customer feedback and report it within the project's integrated governance.
Why not the others: Planning the portal in full detail now guarantees rework on unclear requirements; removing it from governance loses oversight; delaying it to keep one lifecycle wastes value and learning.
Remember: Predictive → Hybrid → Agile. Stable = plan it; uncertain = learn it; both = hybrid.

questions.stem: The adaptive stream of a hybrid warehouse robotics program has completed a pick-route optimization feature, and the product owner accepts it after review. The client contract, managed predictively, requires formal client sign-off on deliverables at the phase gate. What should the project manager do?
options: Treat the product owner's acceptance as the final client acceptance required under the terms of the contract.
Record the product owner's acceptance and include the feature in formal client acceptance at the phase gate.
Hold the feature back from review until the phase gate so that acceptance happens only once.
Ask the client to formally sign acceptance for every individual feature as soon as it is done.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Two levels of acceptance — product owner acceptance confirms a feature meets its criteria; contractual acceptance follows the agreement's formal validate scope process.
Spot it: "product owner accepts it" alongside a contract that "requires formal client sign-off ... at the phase gate."
In this scenario: record the product owner's acceptance and include the feature in formal client acceptance at the phase gate.
Why not the others: Treating product owner acceptance as contractual skips the required sign-off; holding the feature back loses fast feedback; demanding a signature per feature rewrites the agreed process.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close. The CONTRACT decides who signs.

questions.stem: Match each budget term with its description.
matching_right: Funds for unforeseen work, held outside the cost baseline
Cost baseline plus management reserve
Total planned value of all the work at completion
Funds for identified risks, included within the cost baseline
Approved time-phased spending plan, excluding management reserve

answer.Contingency reserve: Funds for identified risks, included within the cost baseline
answer.Management reserve: Funds for unforeseen work, held outside the cost baseline
answer.Cost baseline: Approved time-phased spending plan, excluding management reserve
answer.Budget at completion: Total planned value of all the work at completion

questions.explanation:
Concept: How reserves, the cost baseline, and the project budget stack together.
Contingency reserve: money for identified risks (known-unknowns); inside the cost baseline and used by the PM.
Management reserve: money for unidentified risks (unknown-unknowns); outside the baseline, released by management.
Cost baseline: the approved time-phased budget, including contingency but not management reserve.
Project budget: the cost baseline plus management reserve.
Budget at completion: the total planned value of all the work — the baseline's final figure.
Remember: Work estimates + contingency = cost baseline; baseline + management reserve = project budget.

questions.stem: Match each agile framework with its cadence and how it drives improvement.
matching_right: Short iterations, improved through pairing, TDD, and refactoring
Fixed one-to-four-week sprints, improved at each sprint retrospective
Many teams on program increments, improved at inspect-and-adapt events
Continuous pull flow, improved by limiting WIP and cycle time

answer.Scrum: Fixed one-to-four-week sprints, improved at each sprint retrospective
answer.Kanban: Continuous pull flow, improved by limiting WIP and cycle time
answer.Extreme Programming (XP): Short iterations, improved through pairing, TDD, and refactoring
answer.SAFe: Many teams on program increments, improved at inspect-and-adapt events

questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile frameworks share values but differ in cadence and in how they build in improvement.
Scrum: fixed sprints of one to four weeks; the retrospective at each sprint's end drives improvement.
Kanban: continuous pull flow with no timebox; improves by limiting WIP and watching cycle time.
Extreme Programming (XP): very short iterations; improves quality through pairing, test-driven development, and refactoring.
SAFe: aligns many teams on program increments of about 8–12 weeks; improves at inspect-and-adapt events.
Remember: Scrum = sprints, Kanban = flow, XP = engineering, SAFe = scale.

questions.stem: A hybrid program receives a change request that affects the budget and a contract milestone. Match each step of the change control flow with what happens in it.
matching_right: Baselines, plans, change log, and affected documents are revised
Change control board accepts or rejects the change request
Project manager verifies the change delivers the intended result
Project manager assesses impact on scope, schedule, cost, and contracts
Team carries out only the change that was approved

answer.Analyze: Project manager assesses impact on scope, schedule, cost, and contracts
answer.Approve: Change control board accepts or rejects the change request
answer.Implement: Team carries out only the change that was approved
answer.Update: Baselines, plans, change log, and affected documents are revised
answer.Monitor: Project manager verifies the change delivers the intended result

questions.explanation:
Concept: The change flow — Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor — applies to any change that touches baselines or contracts, even from an adaptive team.
Analyze: the PM assesses impact on scope, schedule, cost, risk, and contracts.
Approve: the change control board accepts or rejects the request.
Implement: the team carries out only the approved change.
Update: baselines, plans, the change log, and affected documents are revised.
Monitor: the PM verifies the change worked and delivers the intended result.
Remember: Never implement a change blindly — analyze, approve, implement, update, monitor.

questions.stem: A predictive offshore platform project identified a risk that a specialized crane might be unavailable. The risk has now occurred, and the only planned response, renting from a secondary supplier, has failed because that supplier is fully booked. What should the project manager do?
options: Develop a workaround, record it in the issue log, and review whether other planned responses remain valid.
Implement the contingency plan that is documented in the risk register for this crane risk.
Accept the resulting delay, since the planned risk response has already been attempted once.
Add a new risk to the risk register and analyze its probability and impact before taking any further action.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Workaround — an unplanned response to a risk that has occurred when the planned response fails; it is tracked as an issue.
Spot it: "the risk has now occurred" and "the only planned response ... has failed."
In this scenario: develop a workaround, record it in the issue log, and check whether the other planned responses are still valid.
Why not the others: The contingency plan is the secondary supplier that already failed; accepting the delay gives up without trying; logging a new risk treats an event that has happened as a future uncertainty.
Remember: Planned response = contingency plan; unplanned response = workaround. Risk occurred → Issue.

questions.stem: Match each project document with its purpose.
matching_right: Captures knowledge gained to improve current and future work
Lists submitted change requests and their approval status
Tracks current problems, their owners, and resolution due dates
Records uncertain events, their analysis, and planned responses
Records assumptions and constraints identified during the project

answer.Issue log: Tracks current problems, their owners, and resolution due dates
answer.Risk register: Records uncertain events, their analysis, and planned responses
answer.Change log: Lists submitted change requests and their approval status
answer.Assumption log: Records assumptions and constraints identified during the project
answer.Lessons learned register: Captures knowledge gained to improve current and future work

questions.explanation:
Concept: The TRACK family — registers and logs the PM keeps up to date.
Issue log: current problems, each with an owner and a due date for resolution.
Risk register: uncertain future events, their analysis, owners, and planned responses.
Change log: every submitted change request and its status (approved, rejected, pending).
Assumption log: assumptions and constraints, which are re-checked as conditions change.
Lessons learned register: knowledge gained during the project, used now and passed on at closure.
Remember: Register/Log = TRACK. Risk = might happen; Issue = has happened.

questions.stem: A predictive consumer-electronics assembly project monitors solder joint thickness with a control chart. The last seven consecutive measurements all fall above the mean, although each is within the control limits. What should the project manager do?
options: Take no action, because every one of the seven measurements is still inside the upper and lower control limits.
Investigate for an assignable cause, since this non-random pattern suggests the process may be out of control.
Adjust the specification limits so that they match the process's current level of performance.
Stop the line and reject every unit that was produced since this pattern of measurements began.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Control charts — a process is stable when points vary randomly within the control limits; seven points in a row on one side of the mean (the rule of seven) signals a non-random cause.
Spot it: "seven consecutive measurements," "all above the mean," yet "within the control limits."
In this scenario: investigate for an assignable cause, because the pattern is non-random.
Why not the others: Staying inside limits is not enough when the pattern is non-random; changing specification limits alters customer requirements to hide a process shift; stopping the line and rejecting all units overreacts before any cause is known.
Remember: Outside the limits OR seven in a row = investigate. Control limits = the process's voice; spec limits = the customer's voice.

questions.stem: A hybrid retail loyalty program combines a predictive point-of-sale hardware upgrade with an adaptive mobile app. The sponsor asks how scope will be defined and controlled for each part of the program. Which TWO approaches should the project manager recommend?
options: Define the hardware upgrade in a scope baseline with a WBS, controlled through change requests.
Build a detailed WBS for the entire app now so both parts share a single scope baseline.
Manage the hardware upgrade through a backlog with no baseline so changes are easier.
Manage app scope through a prioritized backlog refined continuously with the product owner.
Let each team define its scope on its own without integration at the program level.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Hybrid scope management — tailor scope control per component: a baseline with change requests for stable work, a continuously refined backlog for evolving work.
Spot it: a predictive hardware upgrade plus an adaptive app, and "how scope will be defined and controlled for each part."
In this scenario: define the hardware scope in a WBS-based baseline controlled through change requests, and manage app scope through a prioritized backlog refined with the product owner.
Why not the others: A detailed WBS for the app forces predictive planning onto uncertain needs; a backlog with no baseline loses control of stable hardware scope; letting each team go its own way loses program integration.
Remember: WBS + baseline for stable scope; backlog for evolving scope; one integrated program.

questions.stem: A product owner for an agile e-learning platform asks when 180 remaining story points will be finished. The team's last five sprints delivered 28, 32, 30, 25, and 35 points, and each sprint lasts two weeks. What should the scrum master help the team provide?
options: A firm commitment to finish exactly twelve weeks from now, since the average velocity is thirty points.
A forecast of about five sprints, based on the thirty-five points from the team's best sprint.
A forecast of about six sprints based on average velocity, shown as a range reflecting the variation.
No forecast at all, because agile teams cannot predict when a set of work will be finished.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Velocity-based release forecasting — remaining points ÷ average velocity, presented as a range because velocity varies.
Spot it: "when will ... be finished," a list of past sprint velocities, and remaining story points.
In this scenario: the average is 150 ÷ 5 = 30, so 180 ÷ 30 = about six sprints (twelve weeks), shown as a range because velocity ran from 25 to 35.
Why not the others: A firm exact date hides real variation; using the best sprint is optimistic; refusing to forecast ignores that empirical data supports forecasts.
Remember: Forecast with the average, express it as a range. Velocity is for forecasting, not for promising.

questions.stem: Halfway through a twelve-sprint release, an agile team's schedule performance index is 1.1 and its cost performance index is 0.85. Team size and sprint length have not changed, but paid cloud test environments have been used heavily. What does this indicate, and what should the product owner do?
options: The release is ahead of schedule but over budget, so review the cloud spending with the team.
The release is behind schedule and over budget, so cut scope for the rest of the release.
The release is ahead of schedule and under budget, so add more scope to the release now.
The release is behind schedule but under budget, so add a developer to recover the pace.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reading performance indexes — SPI = EV/PV and CPI = EV/AC; above 1 is favorable and below 1 is unfavorable.
Spot it: "SPI is 1.1," "CPI is 0.85," and a cost driver in the stem (heavy use of paid cloud environments).
In this scenario: SPI 1.1 means ahead of schedule and CPI 0.85 means over budget, so review the cloud spending with the team.
Why not the others: SPI above 1 is not behind schedule; CPI below 1 is not under budget; adding scope or a developer responds to a misread of the indexes.
Remember: 1 = on plan. Above 1 = good news, below 1 = bad news, for both indexes.

questions.stem: A hybrid program will outsource a well-specified data center fit-out and an exploratory AI chatbot whose requirements will evolve with user testing. The buyer wants to control cost on both while allowing the chatbot to change. Which TWO contracting approaches should the project manager recommend?
options: Firm fixed price for the chatbot, with every feature specified in detail up front.
Firm fixed price for the data center fit-out, based on its well-defined specifications.
Cost plus fixed fee for the data center fit-out to cover any unknown requirements.
One cost plus award fee contract covering both parts of the program together.
Time and materials with a not-to-exceed cap for the chatbot, reviewed each increment.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Matching contract type to scope certainty — fixed price for well-defined scope; capped time and materials or cost-reimbursable for evolving scope.
Spot it: a "well-specified" fit-out, an "exploratory" chatbot, and a buyer who wants to "control cost on both."
In this scenario: use firm fixed price for the fit-out and time and materials with a not-to-exceed cap for the chatbot, reviewed each increment.
Why not the others: Fixed price for the chatbot needs detail that does not exist and invites change orders; cost plus for the fit-out gives up cost certainty on clear scope; one award fee contract ignores how different the parts are.
Remember: Clear scope → Fixed Price. Evolving scope → T&M with a cap. One contract type rarely fits both.

questions.stem: Match each scope-related document with its description.
matching_right: Gives detailed work, owner, and milestones for each WBS component
Links each requirement to its origin and to the deliverables that satisfy it
Approved scope statement, WBS, and WBS dictionary together
Describes how individual requirements meet the business need
Describes scope, major deliverables, exclusions, and acceptance criteria

answer.Requirements traceability matrix: Links each requirement to its origin and to the deliverables that satisfy it
answer.Requirements documentation: Describes how individual requirements meet the business need
answer.Project scope statement: Describes scope, major deliverables, exclusions, and acceptance criteria
answer.WBS dictionary: Gives detailed work, owner, and milestones for each WBS component
answer.Scope baseline: Approved scope statement, WBS, and WBS dictionary together

questions.explanation:
Concept: Scope documents move from individual requirements to an approved scope baseline.
Requirements traceability matrix: the TRACE tool linking each requirement to its origin and to the deliverables and tests that satisfy it.
Requirements documentation: describes each requirement and how it meets the business need.
Project scope statement: describes scope, major deliverables, exclusions, and acceptance criteria.
WBS dictionary: the detail behind each WBS component — work, owner, and milestones.
Scope baseline: the approved scope statement, WBS, and WBS dictionary; changed only through change control.
Remember: Scope baseline = Statement + WBS + Dictionary. Baseline = APPROVED; RTM = TRACE.

questions.stem: On a predictive clinical scheduling platform, stakeholders have submitted 140 requirements, but the approved budget covers only about 100. The sponsor asks how the project manager will decide which requirements go into the scope baseline. What should the project manager do?
options: Include the 100 requirements that are simplest to build so that the project stays within its approved budget.
Ask the sponsor to request more funding so that all 140 requirements can be delivered at once.
Include requirements in the order they were submitted until the approved budget is fully used.
Work with key stakeholders to rank requirements by business value, compliance needs, risk, and dependencies.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Prioritizing requirements with stakeholders — rank by business value, compliance, risk, and dependencies so the scope baseline delivers the most value within the approved budget.
Spot it: more requirements than the budget allows, and "how the project manager will decide."
In this scenario: work with key stakeholders to rank the 140 requirements, then baseline the top ones that fit the budget.
Why not the others: Choosing the simplest ignores value; asking for more money avoids the decision the approved budget forces; first-come order is arbitrary.
Remember: Constraint = fixed. Priority = value. Decide WITH stakeholders.

questions.stem: Halfway through the design phase of a predictive HRIS implementation, a customer representative requests an additional payroll report. The phase objective is an approved system design by month-end, and the report would add two weeks of design work. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Assess the report's effect on the design phase objective and the baselines, then submit a change request.
Add the report to the current design work right away, since the customer's request clearly adds business value.
Refuse the request outright, because the design phase has already started and the scope is now fixed.
Extend the design phase by two weeks and inform the customer of the new end date afterward.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Protecting phase objectives through change control — once scope is baselined, new requests are analyzed and decided through the change process.
Spot it: a new request mid-phase, "two weeks of design work," an objective due "by month-end," and "NEXT."
In this scenario: assess the report's effect on the design objective and the baselines, then submit a change request.
Why not the others: Adding the report now is scope creep; refusing outright ignores that change control exists for valid requests; extending the phase changes the schedule baseline without approval.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor. No scope creep, no gold plating.

questions.stem: On a predictive e-commerce fulfillment redesign, 40 drawings are waiting at the document review step, while designers keep starting new drawings. Each designer shows high utilization, yet completion of the design package keeps slipping. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep all designers fully utilized on new drawings so the package moves forward faster.
Limit new drawing starts and redirect some designers to help clear the review queue.
Measure each designer's individual output to identify who is slowing the package.
Re-baseline the design package completion date to reflect the current review delay.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Bottlenecks and work in progress — a system moves only as fast as its slowest step, so starting more work just grows the queue.
Spot it: "40 drawings waiting at the document review step," everyone highly utilized, yet completion keeps slipping.
In this scenario: limit new drawing starts and redirect some designers to help clear the review queue.
Why not the others: Keeping everyone busy grows the queue further; measuring individual output blames people for a flow problem; re-baselining accepts the delay without fixing the constraint.
Remember: Stop starting, start finishing. Fix the bottleneck, not the busy people.

questions.stem: Match each development lifecycle with its description.
matching_right: Combines predictive and adaptive elements within one project
Frequent smaller deliveries, each increment built once, optimized for speed
Fixed requirements, activities done once, and one final delivery
Repeated refinement plus frequent small deliveries guided by feedback
Solution refined through repeated cycles, with one final delivery

answer.Predictive: Fixed requirements, activities done once, and one final delivery
answer.Iterative: Solution refined through repeated cycles, with one final delivery
answer.Incremental: Frequent smaller deliveries, each increment built once, optimized for speed
answer.Agile: Repeated refinement plus frequent small deliveries guided by feedback
answer.Hybrid: Combines predictive and adaptive elements within one project

questions.explanation:
Concept: The development lifecycles differ in how requirements are handled and how often value is delivered.
Predictive: requirements fixed early, activities done once, one final delivery.
