Iterative: the solution is refined through repeated cycles, then delivered once.
Incremental: small usable pieces delivered often, each built once.
Agile: both iterative and incremental — refine and deliver frequently, guided by feedback.
Hybrid: combines predictive and adaptive elements in one project.
Remember: Iterative = get it RIGHT; Incremental = get it SOONER; Agile = both.

questions.stem: In the adaptive stream of a hybrid insurance claims program, a fraud-scoring story is complete, but the client's risk manager rejects it in review because it cannot handle multi-policy claims, a case not in the acceptance criteria. The predictive contract ties payment to accepted deliverables. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the team to rework the story until the risk manager is satisfied, at no extra cost to the client.
Insist the risk manager sign acceptance now and drop the multi-policy request entirely as out of scope.
Confirm the story met its agreed criteria, and capture multi-policy handling as a new item for prioritization.
File a formal claim against the client for delaying acceptance of a story that passed its tests.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Acceptance against agreed criteria — work is judged by its agreed acceptance criteria, and new needs found at review become new backlog items.
Spot it: the story is "complete," the case was "not in the acceptance criteria," and payment is tied to accepted deliverables.
In this scenario: confirm the story met its agreed criteria and capture multi-policy handling as a new item for prioritization.
Why not the others: Free rework turns new scope into unpaid work; forcing a signature and dropping the need damages the relationship and value; a formal claim escalates before a conversation.
Remember: Met the criteria = done. New need = new backlog item, prioritized.

questions.stem: The predictive construction stream of a hybrid smart-campus program holds a contingency reserve for identified risks. Excavation uncovers an underground utility line that was never listed in the risk register, and rerouting it will cost $80,000. What should the project manager do?
options: Request use of management reserve from the sponsor, since this was an unidentified risk.
Draw the $80,000 from the contingency reserve set aside for the identified risks.
Take the needed funds from the adaptive stream's budget that is set aside for its upcoming increments.
Absorb the cost within the construction stream and report the overrun at closure.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contingency vs management reserve — contingency covers identified risks inside the cost baseline; management reserve covers unidentified risks and needs management approval.
Spot it: "never listed in the risk register" — an unknown-unknown.
In this scenario: request use of management reserve from the sponsor.
Why not the others: Contingency reserve belongs to identified risks and would leave them unfunded; taking the adaptive stream's budget starves other work; absorbing the cost hides an overrun until closure.
Remember: Known-unknown = contingency (PM). Unknown-unknown = management reserve (sponsor).

questions.stem: Halfway through the release of a supply-chain visibility app, a newly assigned logistics director notes that the team's supplier-integration defects look exactly like problems another agile team solved last quarter. The team has been saving its lessons for a report at the end of the release. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Set up a session with the other team to learn how they fixed the integration defects and apply it in the next iteration.
Add the director's observation to the lessons learned register so it is included in the end-of-release report.
Ask the PMO to require every agile team to submit its lessons learned before each quarterly portfolio review.
Keep the current integration practice until the next retrospective confirms the true root cause of the defects.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Continuous lessons learned — lessons are captured AND applied throughout the work, not saved for the end; learning from another team is one of the fastest ways to improve.
Spot it: mid-release, the same problem another team already solved, lessons being saved for an end-of-release report.
In this scenario: a proven fix already exists next door, so connecting with that team and applying its fix in the next iteration stops the defects now.
Why not the others: logging it for the end-of-release report lets the defects keep recurring; a PMO mandate is slow governance, not a fix; waiting for a retrospective delays a known solution.
Remember: Capture lesson → Analyze → APPLY IMMEDIATELY if useful → Keep updating → Archive at closure.

questions.stem: A project manager on a predictive hospital wing construction project is onboarding a new project coordinator who will support the change control process. Match each integrated change control term with its description.
matching_right: Group authorized to approve, defer, or reject proposed changes
Formal proposal to modify a document, deliverable, or baseline
Controls versions and specifications of deliverables and project documents
Record of submitted changes and their current decision status

answer.Change request: Formal proposal to modify a document, deliverable, or baseline
answer.Change control board: Group authorized to approve, defer, or reject proposed changes
answer.Change log: Record of submitted changes and their current decision status
answer.Configuration management: Controls versions and specifications of deliverables and project documents

questions.explanation:
Concept: Integrated change control has four building blocks that students often mix up: the request, the decision-maker, the record and the version control.
Change request: the formal proposal to change a baseline, document or deliverable; nothing changes without one.
Change control board: the authorized group that approves, defers or rejects requests; the PM analyzes impact, the CCB decides.
Change log: the TRACK record of every request and its status (submitted, approved, rejected, deferred).
Configuration management: controls versions and specifications of deliverables and documents so everyone uses the approved version.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor. PM analyzes, CCB approves, change log tracks.

questions.stem: The vendor on a predictive identity-access-management rollout announces during execution that its single-sign-on connector will be released three weeks late. This delay was listed as a trigger in the risk register, and the risk owner documented a contingency plan to use an interim connector. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Submit a change request to extend the schedule baseline by three weeks so it matches the vendor's new release date.
Have the risk owner carry out the documented contingency plan and track whether it keeps the rollout on schedule.
Perform a fresh qualitative analysis of the connector risk before deciding which response to put into action now.
Escalate the delay to the sponsor and request management reserve funds to cover the cost of the three-week slip.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Implement risk responses — once a planned trigger fires, the risk owner executes the response already agreed; you do not start the analysis over.
Spot it: 'listed as a trigger', 'risk owner', 'documented contingency plan'.
In this scenario: the vendor delay is exactly the trigger that was planned for, so the risk owner puts the interim connector in place and the team tracks whether it protects the schedule.
Why not the others: a change request to extend the baseline skips the plan that already protects it; re-running qualitative analysis wastes time on work already done; management reserve is for unknown risks, not a known one with a contingency plan.
Remember: Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor → Issue. Trigger fires = run the plan, then watch it work.

questions.stem: The test lab on a predictive infusion-pump development project reports that the calibration fixture needed for verification testing broke this morning. Verification tests scheduled for this week cannot start until it is repaired, and the lab manager is unsure who should handle it. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Add the fixture failure to the risk register and rate its probability and impact on the test schedule.
Submit a change request to shift the verification milestone until the fixture has been repaired and tested.
Record the fixture failure in the issue log, assign an owner, and set a target date for resolving it.
Raise the fixture failure at the next weekly status meeting so the whole team can discuss possible options.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Issue management — an issue is a problem that is happening NOW; it goes in the issue log with an owner and a due date so someone actively resolves it.
Spot it: 'broke this morning', 'tests cannot start', 'unsure who should handle it'.
In this scenario: the fixture failure is certain and current, and nobody owns it, so logging it, assigning an owner and setting a target date gets it worked on.
Why not the others: the risk register is for uncertain future events; a change request to move the milestone comes before any impact analysis; waiting for the weekly meeting leaves the issue ownerless for days.
Remember: Risk = MAY happen (register). Issue = HAS happened (log). Issue → Record → Assign owner → Resolve → Monitor.

questions.stem: A quality engineer on a predictive warehouse-routing optimization project tracks order-picking cycle time on a control chart. The last eight consecutive measurements all fall above the mean. Every point is still inside the upper and lower control limits, and no customer specification has been breached. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Take no corrective action, because every measurement is still inside the upper and lower control limits.
Recalculate the control limits using the latest measurements so the chart reflects the current process performance.
Submit a change request to widen the customer's specification limits for cycle time before a breach occurs.
Have the quality engineer investigate the run for an assignable cause, since the process may be out of control.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Control chart rule of seven — seven or more consecutive points on one side of the mean signal a nonrandom pattern, even when every point is inside the control limits.
Spot it: 'eight consecutive measurements above the mean', 'still inside the control limits'.
In this scenario: the run breaks the rule of seven, so the process may be out of control; the right move is to look for an assignable (special) cause before it turns into a breach.
Why not the others: 'inside the limits' is only one test of control; recalculating limits hides the shift; widening the customer's specification changes the requirement instead of fixing the process.
Remember: Control limits = the PROCESS voice; specification limits = the CUSTOMER voice. Out of limits OR 7 in a row on one side = investigate.

questions.stem: The product owner on an agile insurance claims platform has rejected several completed stories because they lacked the audit logging that regulators require. After the first rejection the team agreed to remember the logging, but two more stories were rejected this iteration for the same reason. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Write a detailed requirements specification for all remaining features so audit logging is spelled out in advance.
Work with the team and product owner to add audit logging to the definition of done so every story includes it.
Create one separate audit-logging story near the end of the release to add logging to every completed feature.
Personally review each story for audit logging before the team presents its completed work to the product owner.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Definition of done — the team's shared checklist that EVERY backlog item must meet before it counts as complete; it builds recurring quality needs into the work.
Spot it: the same quality gap causes repeated rejections, and 'remembering' has not worked.
In this scenario: regulators require audit logging on every story, so adding it to the definition of done makes it part of each story rather than something people must remember.
Why not the others: a big upfront specification is predictive and slow; one logging story at the end creates technical debt and undone stories; a PM personally reviewing every story is command-and-control, not team ownership.
Remember: Acceptance criteria = THIS story. Definition of done = EVERY story.

questions.stem: The branch fit-out on a hybrid customer onboarding redesign follows a predictive schedule while the onboarding portal is built in two-week iterations. The only integration specialist is overallocated in weeks 10–12 on a critical-path fit-out task and on portal integration work that has three weeks of float. Two department heads each want the specialist first. What should the project manager do?
options: Shift the specialist's portal integration work within its available float so the critical-path fit-out task keeps its dates.
Crash the critical-path fit-out task by hiring contractors so both departments can use the specialist during those weeks.
Fast-track the fit-out work by overlapping its tasks so the specialist can support both departments during weeks 10–12.
Ask the sponsor to decide which department head receives the integration specialist first during the overallocated weeks.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Resource smoothing — resolve an overallocated person by moving non-critical work within its float, so the end date and critical path do not change.
Spot it: 'overallocated', one task on the critical path, the other with 'three weeks of float'.
In this scenario: the portal integration work has float, so shifting it lets the specialist protect the critical-path fit-out task with no schedule, cost or scope impact.
Why not the others: crashing adds cost the problem does not need; fast-tracking adds rework risk and does not fix the overallocation; asking the sponsor escalates a problem the PM can solve with schedule data.
Remember: Overallocation → Review float → SMOOTH if possible → LEVEL if needed → Update schedule. Solve with data before you escalate.

questions.stem: The project controls analyst on a predictive telecommunications network rollout is preparing the monthly performance report for the steering committee. Match each earned value measure with what it tells the committee.
matching_right: Cost efficiency the remaining work must achieve to meet a target
Difference between earned value and actual cost to date
Rate of progress achieved compared with the rate planned
Value of work earned for each dollar actually spent
Expected total cost of the project when all work is complete

answer.Cost performance index (CPI): Value of work earned for each dollar actually spent
answer.Schedule performance index (SPI): Rate of progress achieved compared with the rate planned
answer.Estimate at completion (EAC): Expected total cost of the project when all work is complete
answer.To-complete performance index (TCPI): Cost efficiency the remaining work must achieve to meet a target
answer.Cost variance (CV): Difference between earned value and actual cost to date

questions.explanation:
Concept: Earned value measures compare earned value (EV) with planned value (PV) and actual cost (AC) to show performance and forecast the end.
Cost performance index (CPI): EV ÷ AC; value earned per dollar spent; below 1 = over budget.
Schedule performance index (SPI): EV ÷ PV; rate of progress vs plan; below 1 = behind schedule.
Estimate at completion (EAC): forecast of the total final cost, often BAC ÷ CPI.
To-complete performance index (TCPI): (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC); the efficiency the remaining work must hit to finish on budget.
Cost variance (CV): EV − AC; negative = over budget to date.
Remember: EV always comes FIRST. Variance = subtract, index = divide. Below 1 or negative = bad news.

questions.stem: A predictive customer onboarding redesign needs an outside firm to build an identity-verification interface. The requirements are fully defined and approved, no changes are expected, and the finance director wants the organization to carry as little cost risk as possible. The procurement plan must be finalized before the next governance meeting. Which contract type should the project manager recommend?
options: A cost-plus-fixed-fee contract, because it guarantees the seller a set fee and protects the buyer from overruns.
A time-and-materials contract, because paying for hours used gives the buyer the tightest control over total cost.
A cost-plus-incentive-fee contract, because sharing any savings with the seller keeps total cost risk with the seller.
A firm-fixed-price contract, because the scope is stable and the seller bears the risk of any cost overruns.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contract type selection — firm-fixed-price (FFP) fits well-defined, stable scope and puts the most cost risk on the seller.
Spot it: 'fully defined and approved', 'no changes expected', 'as little cost risk as possible'.
In this scenario: stable scope plus a buyer who wants minimal cost risk points straight to FFP, where the seller absorbs any overrun.
Why not the others: cost-plus-fixed-fee means the buyer pays all actual costs, so it does not protect against overruns; time-and-materials leaves the buyer paying for every hour; cost-plus-incentive-fee shares risk but the buyer still carries most of it.
Remember: Clear scope = FIXED PRICE (seller risk). Unclear scope = COST-PLUS (buyer risk). T&M sits in the middle for small or staff-augmentation work.

questions.stem: During user acceptance testing of a predictive digital permitting solution, a city inspector says no test covers the approved requirement to flag permits in flood zones. The project manager worries that other approved requirements may also have been missed during design and testing. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Submit a change request to add the flood-zone requirement to the scope baseline and to the plan for acceptance testing.
Ask the test team to rerun the full acceptance test suite so any other untested requirements come to light during execution.
Use the requirements traceability matrix to link each approved requirement to its design elements and test cases and find any gaps.
Have the business analyst rewrite the requirements document so every requirement is clearer before testing continues further.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Requirements traceability matrix (RTM) — links each requirement from its source through design, build and test so gaps show up.
Spot it: 'no test covers the approved requirement', worry that 'other approved requirements may also have been missed'.
In this scenario: one gap suggests more, and the RTM is the tool that shows, requirement by requirement, which ones lack design elements or test cases.
Why not the others: a change request is not needed because the requirement is already approved scope; rerunning existing tests cannot find requirements that no test covers; rewriting the requirements document does not reveal coverage.
Remember: TRACE = RTM. Requirement → Design → Build → Test → Accept, all linked.

questions.stem: Match each document with what it feeds into next.
matching_right: Feeds the risk report and risk-response planning.
Authorizes the project and feeds the project management plan.
Justifies the investment and feeds the project charter.
Feeds the scope statement, WBS and traceability matrix.
Is analyzed into work performance information.

answer.Business case: Justifies the investment and feeds the project charter.
answer.Project charter: Authorizes the project and feeds the project management plan.
answer.Requirements documentation: Feeds the scope statement, WBS and traceability matrix.
answer.Work performance data: Is analyzed into work performance information.
answer.Risk register: Feeds the risk report and risk-response planning.

questions.explanation:
Concept: Project documents form a chain: each one is an input that shapes the next, so an error early (business case, charter) flows all the way through.
Business case: WHY comes first; the sponsor uses it to decide whether to authorize the project.
Project charter: AUTHORITY: it names the PM and high-level scope, then planning begins.
Requirements documentation: What stakeholders need becomes defined scope and traced deliverables.
Work performance data: Raw facts (hours, % done) become meaning (CPI, trends) after comparison with the plan.
Risk register: TRACK individual risks; the report summarizes overall exposure for stakeholders.
Remember: WHY → AUTHORITY → HOW → APPROVED: Business case → Charter → PM plan → Baselines. Data → Information → Reports.

questions.stem: A predictive digital permitting solution is finishing its design phase. At its phase gate review, a project manager confirms that all exit criteria are met except the security architecture approval, which the security office expects in two weeks. The sponsor wants the build phase to begin on Monday regardless. What should the project manager do?
options: Begin the build phase on Monday as the sponsor wants and report the missing security approval at the next status review.
Record the security approval as met, with an action item to obtain the formal sign-off from the office within two weeks.
Cancel the phase gate review and reschedule it for a date after the security office has issued its formal approval.
Present the unmet exit criterion and its impacts to the gate reviewers so they can make the go, no-go, or conditional decision.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Phase gate — a governance decision point where reviewers compare results with exit criteria and decide go, no-go or go with conditions.
Spot it: 'phase gate review', 'all exit criteria met except one', a sponsor pushing to start anyway.
In this scenario: the PM's job is to give the gate honest information: the unmet criterion and its impacts. The reviewers then decide, including a possible conditional go.
Why not the others: starting the build on the sponsor's word bypasses the gate; recording an unmet criterion as met falsifies status; canceling the review removes the decision point instead of informing it.
Remember: PM PRESENTS the facts, the GATE decides. Transparency beats pressure.

questions.stem: On a hybrid claims platform, data migration follows a predictive plan while claims-rule configuration is managed on a kanban board. Items keep piling up in the testing column. The earlier corrective action, asking developers to start more rules so no one was idle, made the queue longer. What should the project manager suggest NEXT?
options: Set a work-in-progress limit on the testing column so developers help clear tested work before pulling new rules.
Add another development column to the board so developers can keep starting new rules while testing catches up.
Assign more rules to each developer so that individual utilization stays high while testers work through the queue.
Lengthen the cycle-time target for claims rules so the growing testing queue no longer appears as a flow problem.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Kanban WIP limits — limiting work in progress at a bottleneck forces the team to finish work before starting more, which improves flow.
Spot it: work 'piling up in the testing column', starting more work 'made the queue longer'.
In this scenario: testing is the bottleneck, so a WIP limit on that column stops new rules from being pulled and redirects developers to help clear testing.
Why not the others: another development column adds more unfinished work; higher individual utilization is what created the queue; loosening the cycle-time target hides the problem instead of fixing flow.
Remember: Stop starting, start finishing. Visualize → Limit WIP → Pull → Find bottleneck → Improve.

questions.stem: The baseline for a predictive cloud migration of 40 applications assumed every application could be moved as-is. A supplier assessment now shows six applications must be re-architected, and their requirements will not be clear for several months. The other 34 remain on plan. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Use rolling wave planning to detail the 34 near-term migrations and elaborate the six re-architected applications as information emerges.
Keep migrating all 40 applications as-is according to the approved baseline, because the supplier assessment is only advisory.
Ask the team to produce detailed estimates for the six applications now so the complete baseline can be finalized this month.
Submit a change request with an impact analysis of the re-architecture effort on scope, schedule, and cost to the change control board.
Remove the six applications from the project scope and notify the application owners that they will be migrated later on.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Rolling wave planning plus integrated change control — plan near-term work in detail, elaborate uncertain work later, and route any change to an approved baseline through the change control board.
Spot it: a baseline assumption proved wrong, some work is clear now and some 'will not be clear for several months'.
In this scenario: the 34 known migrations can be detailed now while the six re-architected apps are elaborated as information emerges, and the changed assumption is analyzed and sent to the CCB.
Why not the others: continuing 'as-is' ignores new facts; forcing detailed estimates on unclear requirements creates false precision; removing scope without approval bypasses change control.
Remember: Near = DETAIL, far = OUTLINE. Baseline changes → Analyze → CCB approves.

questions.stem: At an iteration review for an agile hospital analytics tool, a completed readmissions report meets all its agreed acceptance criteria. The compliance officer now wants an extra export format before accepting it, while the nursing director wants it released as is. What should happen NEXT?
options: The team keeps the report open until the export format is added so that the compliance officer's concern is fully resolved.
The product owner accepts the report against its criteria and adds the export format as a new backlog item to prioritize.
The project manager holds a vote between the compliance officer and the nursing director to decide whether to accept it.
The product owner defers acceptance until the next review so the two stakeholders can try to reach an agreement first.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile acceptance — the product owner accepts work that meets its agreed acceptance criteria; new ideas become new backlog items.
Spot it: 'meets all its agreed acceptance criteria', a stakeholder asking for something extra at the review.
In this scenario: the report is done by its criteria, so the product owner accepts it, and the export format is added to the backlog and prioritized by value against other work.
Why not the others: keeping it open adds scope to finished work; a stakeholder vote replaces the product owner's decision rights; deferring acceptance delays value that is already done.
Remember: Criteria met = ACCEPT. New need = NEW BACKLOG ITEM. The product owner decides.

questions.stem: An agile team building an airport wayfinding app has a fixed launch date and budget. In release planning, a project manager explains how the plan protects both constraints. Match each reserve concept with its description.
matching_right: Funds outside the cost baseline for unforeseen work, released by management
Extra time added to the plan to absorb delays
Lower-priority features that can be dropped to protect the date
Funds within the cost baseline for identified risks

answer.Contingency reserve: Funds within the cost baseline for identified risks
answer.Management reserve: Funds outside the cost baseline for unforeseen work, released by management
answer.Feature buffer: Lower-priority features that can be dropped to protect the date
answer.Schedule buffer: Extra time added to the plan to absorb delays

questions.explanation:
Concept: Reserves and buffers protect a plan's constraints: money for risks, and time or scope for a fixed date.
Contingency reserve: inside the cost baseline, for identified risks (known-unknowns); the PM can use it per the plan.
Management reserve: outside the cost baseline, for unforeseen work (unknown-unknowns); management releases it.
Feature buffer: lower-priority features planned so they can be dropped to protect a fixed date.
Schedule buffer: extra time added to the plan to absorb delays.
Remember: Contingency = KNOWN risks, IN the baseline. Management = UNKNOWN risks, OUTSIDE the baseline. In agile, a fixed date means SCOPE flexes.

questions.stem: The payroll configuration team on a hybrid HRIS implementation works in iterations while data migration follows a predictive plan. In a retrospective this team found that waiting for migration handoffs caused most of its delays, and a new handoff checklist fixed it. The migration team starts its next wave in two weeks. What should the project manager do?
options: Save the handoff finding for the formal lessons learned session held during closure of the whole HRIS project.
Keep retrospective findings inside the configuration team to protect the psychological safety of its members.
Ask the PMO to issue a new organizational handoff standard before the migration team adopts the configuration checklist.
Share the checklist with the migration team and update the lessons learned register so the next wave applies it.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sharing lessons across teams — a lesson that fixed one team's problem should be recorded and passed to others while it can still help them.
Spot it: a retrospective found a proven fix, and another team will hit the same handoff 'in two weeks'.
In this scenario: the migration team is about to start its next wave, so the PM shares the checklist now and updates the lessons learned register so it becomes part of the project's knowledge.
Why not the others: waiting for closure helps future projects, not this wave; psychological safety protects people, not process fixes; a PMO standard is slow when a simple checklist already works.
Remember: Capture → Share → APPLY now → Archive at closure. A lesson unused is a lesson wasted.

questions.stem: The change control board secretary on a predictive zero-trust security program is teaching new members how to classify incoming change requests. Match each type of change request with its purpose.
matching_right: Keeps future project performance from deviating from the plan
Changes a controlled document or plan to reflect new information
Realigns project performance with the plan after a deviation
Modifies a nonconforming product or product component

answer.Corrective action: Realigns project performance with the plan after a deviation
answer.Preventive action: Keeps future project performance from deviating from the plan
answer.Defect repair: Modifies a nonconforming product or product component
answer.Update: Changes a controlled document or plan to reflect new information

questions.explanation:
Concept: The four types of change requests describe WHY a change is needed.
Corrective action: performance has already drifted from the plan, so bring it back in line (fix the past).
Preventive action: a trend shows performance is likely to drift, so act before it does (protect the future).
Defect repair: fix a product or component that does not conform to requirements (fix the product).
Update: revise a controlled document or plan to reflect new information (fix the paperwork).
Remember: Corrective = ALREADY off track, Preventive = ABOUT TO go off track, Defect repair = PRODUCT, Update = DOCUMENT. All four go through change control.

questions.stem: Match each agile estimating practice with what it does.
matching_right: Rough XS to XL sizing for early, coarse planning.
Groups many backlog items into size buckets quickly.
Relative size of a story compared with other stories.
Team members reveal estimates at once, then discuss gaps.
Average points a team completes per iteration.

answer.Story points: Relative size of a story compared with other stories.
answer.Planning poker: Team members reveal estimates at once, then discuss gaps.
answer.Affinity estimating: Groups many backlog items into size buckets quickly.
answer.T-shirt sizing: Rough XS to XL sizing for early, coarse planning.
answer.Velocity: Average points a team completes per iteration.

questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile teams estimate relatively and together, then use their own history to forecast; estimates are owned by the people doing the work.
Story points: Points measure effort, complexity and uncertainty together, not hours.
Planning poker: Simultaneous reveal avoids anchoring; the discussion surfaces hidden work.
Affinity estimating: Useful for a large backlog before release planning.
T-shirt sizing: Good for epics and roadmaps; refine to points later.
Velocity: Used to forecast the team's own future work, never to compare teams.
Remember: Developers estimate; the product owner prioritizes. Velocity forecasts, it never compares teams.

questions.stem: The contract packaging vendor for a predictive pharmaceutical launch announces that its plant will close for two weeks, starting Monday, for an unplanned regulatory inspection. Packaging is on the critical path, and the launch date is committed to distributors. Which action should the project manager take FIRST?
options: Submit a change request to move the committed launch date back two weeks to match the vendor's plant closure.
Analyze how the two-week closure affects the critical path and identify recovery options, such as a backup packager.
Add the plant closure to the risk register as a threat and rate its probability and impact before responding.
Ask the vendor to postpone its regulatory inspection until after the launch packaging run has been fully completed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Issue impact analysis — when a certain problem hits the critical path, first assess the impact and develop recovery options before changing any commitment.
Spot it: the plant 'will close' (certain), 'critical path', a committed launch date.
In this scenario: the closure is an issue, not a risk, and the launch date matters, so the PM first measures the critical-path impact and looks for recovery options such as a backup packager.
Why not the others: moving the launch date before analyzing options gives up too early; the risk register is for uncertain events; asking the vendor to defy a regulator is not realistic.
Remember: Issue → Analyze → Resolve → Monitor. Understand before you act; analyze before you change the baseline.

questions.stem: At a customer demo of an agile clinical scheduling platform, users again find booking errors that escaped testing. After the last demo the team added a manual test pass at the end of each iteration, but the escaped defects have not decreased. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Add a separate testing phase after the release so a dedicated group can inspect all booking features.
Facilitate a root-cause analysis with the team, such as the five whys, to find why defects keep escaping.
Inspect each completed story personally before the demo so fewer booking defects reach the customer.
Extend the iteration length by one week so the manual test pass has more time to find the defects.
Help the team build automated booking tests into the definition of done so defects are caught during development.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Build quality in — agile teams find root causes and prevent defects during development instead of adding more inspection at the end.
Spot it: defects 'escaped testing' again, and the last fix (more end-of-iteration testing) 'has not decreased' them.
In this scenario: a root-cause session such as the five whys finds why defects escape, and automated booking tests in the definition of done catch them as the code is written.
Why not the others: a separate testing phase is predictive inspection after the fact; a PM personally inspecting stories is not team ownership; a longer iteration just gives the same weak process more time.
Remember: Prevention over inspection. Defect → Root cause → Fix the CAUSE → Verify → Prevent recurrence.

questions.stem: During an architecture review on a predictive AI customer-support platform, the customer's operations lead asks the team to add Spanish-language support. It would clearly help their call centers, but it is not in the approved scope baseline. The lead engineer says it would take about three weeks. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Document the request as a change request and analyze its impact on scope, schedule, cost, and risk for the board.
Approve the Spanish-language support now because it adds clear value and the lead engineer's estimate is small.
Decline the request because the scope baseline is approved and the customer should raise it in a future project.
Ask the team to fit the Spanish-language work into existing tasks so the approved schedule does not need to change.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Integrated change control — any request that changes the approved scope baseline is documented, analyzed and decided by the change control board.
Spot it: 'not in the approved scope baseline', a valuable request from the customer, an effort estimate.
In this scenario: the Spanish-language request may be worth doing, so the PM captures it as a change request and analyzes its impact on scope, schedule, cost and risk for the board.
Why not the others: approving it yourself is scope creep; refusing it outright ignores a legitimate request; hiding it in existing tasks bypasses control and damages the baseline.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor. PM analyzes, CCB decides.

questions.stem: A quarterly review on an agile data-governance program shows a release burnup chart on which the team is completing about 30 points per iteration. The remaining 240 points cannot be finished in the five iterations left before the fixed regulatory release date. What should the project manager do?
options: Share the forecast with the product owner and stakeholders so they can decide which lower-value features to defer.
Ask the team to work overtime for the remaining iterations so its velocity rises enough to finish all features.
Have the team re-estimate the remaining stories so the total points fit within the five iterations left before release.
Extend each of the remaining iterations by a week so that the team can complete all 240 points before release.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Empirical forecasting with a fixed date — velocity shows what can realistically be done, and when the date is fixed, scope is what flexes.
Spot it: burnup chart, about 30 points per iteration, 240 points left, five iterations, a 'fixed regulatory release date'.
In this scenario: 5 × 30 = about 150 points, so roughly 90 points will not fit; the PM shares this forecast so the product owner and stakeholders decide which lower-value features to defer.
Why not the others: overtime breaks sustainable pace; re-estimating to 'fit' games the numbers; stretching iterations breaks the timebox and the fixed date.
Remember: Fixed date + known velocity = FLEX SCOPE by value. Be transparent with the data.

questions.stem: At month six of a predictive customer-data platform rollout, a project manager reviews this performance data: planned value is $380,000, earned value is $400,000, and actual cost is $470,000. The sponsor asks for a one-line status summary before tomorrow's executive briefing. Which summary is accurate?
options: The project is behind schedule and over budget.
The project is ahead of schedule and over budget.
The project is ahead of schedule and under budget.
The project is behind schedule and under budget.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reading SPI and CPI — two indexes tell you schedule and cost status at a glance.
Spot it: PV, EV and AC given; 'one-line status summary'.
In this scenario: SPI = EV ÷ PV = 400 ÷ 380 ≈ 1.05, so ahead of schedule; CPI = EV ÷ AC = 400 ÷ 470 ≈ 0.85, so over budget. That makes 'ahead of schedule and over budget' the accurate summary.
Why not the others: 'behind schedule' flips the SPI reading; 'under budget' flips the CPI reading; comparing AC with PV directly measures neither schedule nor cost performance.
Remember: EV first, always. Above 1 = good, below 1 = bad. SPI → schedule, CPI → cost.

questions.stem: Midway through a predictive telecommunications network rollout, a new national regulation requires all network-monitoring data to be stored inside the country. The monitoring vendor, under a firm-fixed-price contract, currently hosts the data abroad. The vendor's engineers offer to switch hosting if the project manager tells them to. What should the project manager do?
options: Direct the vendor's engineers to switch the hosting location now and settle any price change with them later.
Terminate the contract for convenience and find a new vendor that already stores all of its data in the country.
Work with the contract administrator to change the contract through the procedure defined in its change clause.
Leave the contract as it is and expect the vendor to comply with the regulation on its own at its own expense.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contract change control — a procured scope changes only through the contract's change procedure, by the person with contract authority.
Spot it: 'firm-fixed-price contract', new regulation, vendor engineers ready to act 'if the project manager tells them to'.
In this scenario: the hosting change alters contract scope, so the PM works with the contract administrator to modify the contract through its change clause.
Why not the others: informal direction creates an unauthorized, constructive change and price disputes; terminating the contract overreacts before a negotiated change is tried; assuming the vendor will absorb it at its own cost ignores the contract terms.
Remember: SELLER = contract. Change need → Review contract authority → Analyze → Authorized change → Seller implements.

questions.stem: On a hybrid HRIS implementation, payroll tax rules are baselined as predictive requirements, while the employee self-service portal is built in iterations. At a customer demo, a payroll director asks for proof that every tax-withholding requirement is covered by delivered portal features before approving the next funding release. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the product owner to confirm verbally that the delivered portal stories cover all of the tax requirements.
Have the team rerun every portal acceptance test so the payroll director can watch the results during the demo.
Convert the remaining portal stories into a detailed specification that repeats each of the tax requirements.
Show how the traceability matrix links each tax requirement to the portal stories and the acceptance tests that verify it.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Traceability in hybrid delivery — baselined requirements can be traced to user stories and acceptance tests, giving evidence of coverage.
Spot it: 'baselined' tax rules, 'proof that every tax-withholding requirement is covered'.
In this scenario: the traceability matrix links each tax requirement to the portal stories that implement it and the tests that verify it, which is exactly the proof the director needs.
Why not the others: a verbal assurance is not evidence; rerunning tests shows results but not which requirement each test covers; converting stories into a specification repeats work without proving coverage.
Remember: TRACE = RTM. Requirement ↔ story ↔ test: no link, no proof.

questions.stem: Match each quality tool with what it shows.
matching_right: Shows the relationship between two variables.
Shows whether a process is stable within control limits.
Ranks causes so the vital few problems stand out.
Shows how often values fall in each range.
Groups possible root causes of one problem.

answer.Pareto chart: Ranks causes so the vital few problems stand out.
answer.Fishbone diagram: Groups possible root causes of one problem.
answer.Control chart: Shows whether a process is stable within control limits.
answer.Scatter diagram: Shows the relationship between two variables.
answer.Histogram: Shows how often values fall in each range.

questions.explanation:
Concept: Quality tools turn defect data into decisions: find the biggest causes, dig into why, and check whether the process is under control.
Pareto chart: 80/20 rule: fix the few causes behind most defects first.
Fishbone diagram: Also called cause-and-effect or Ishikawa; use it to brainstorm WHY.
Control chart: Points outside limits, or a run of seven on one side, need investigation.
Scatter diagram: Correlation, not proof of cause; e.g. training hours vs defects.
Histogram: A bar chart of distribution; spot skew or clustering at a glance.
Remember: Pareto = WHICH first, Fishbone = WHY, Control chart = STABLE?, Scatter = RELATED?, Histogram = HOW OFTEN.

questions.stem: On a predictive customer-data platform rollout, a new privacy rule requires a consent-management module that was not planned. The team is split between keeping the committed September go-live date and adding the module first. The charter lists regulatory compliance as the top success criterion. What should the project manager do?
options: Let the team vote on whether to protect the go-live date or add the consent module, then plan the choice.
Use the charter's compliance priority to add the module and submit a change request for the go-live impact.
Keep the September go-live date and schedule the consent module as a separate enhancement after the platform launches.
Add the consent module and ask the team to work overtime so the September go-live date can still be achieved.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Charter success criteria set priorities — when constraints conflict, the charter's objectives tell you which one wins, and the change is then formally controlled.
Spot it: new privacy rule, a split team, and 'the charter lists regulatory compliance as the top success criterion'.
In this scenario: compliance is both mandatory and the top success criterion, so the module is added and its go-live impact goes through a change request.
Why not the others: a team vote cannot override the charter; keeping the date and deferring the module launches a noncompliant platform; overtime is an unsustainable way to hide a real schedule impact.
Remember: AUTHORITY = Charter. Mandatory beats optional. Baseline impact → change request.

questions.stem: On a predictive claims platform, one certified team must test every configured rule. Configuration staff are fully utilized and keep finishing rules early, but completed rules wait an average of nine days for testing, and the milestone is slipping. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Keep configuration staff fully utilized on new rules so that the most work is ready for the testing team.
Fast-track testing by starting it on each rule before configuration of that rule has been fully completed.
Review the resource histogram to confirm when the certified testing team is overallocated and by how much.
Reduce the regression test scope for each claims rule so the certified testing team can clear its queue.
Level resources by staggering configuration start dates so finished rules reach testing at a rate it can handle.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Managing a resource constraint — find where the bottleneck is overloaded, then pace upstream work to match what the constraint can handle.
Spot it: 'one certified team', upstream staff 'fully utilized', work 'waits an average of nine days'.
In this scenario: a resource histogram confirms when and how much the testers are overallocated, and leveling staggers configuration so rules arrive at a rate testing can absorb.
Why not the others: keeping upstream busy lengthens the queue; fast-tracking tests before configuration is complete causes rework; cutting regression scope trades quality for speed.
Remember: The system moves at the speed of its bottleneck. Identify overallocation → review → smooth or level → update schedule.

questions.stem: A newly appointed CIO on a hybrid state-government digital service questions during an architecture review why the legacy data-center shutdown follows a predictive plan while the citizen portal is built in iterations. The shutdown has fixed regulatory steps and stable requirements. The CIO wants everything run the same way. What should the project manager do?
options: Explain to the CIO why each component's approach fits its requirement stability and regulatory needs, and invite input.
Switch the data-center shutdown to iterations as well so the whole program follows a single delivery approach.
Continue the current plan without discussion, because the delivery approach was already approved during planning.
Escalate the CIO's challenge to the sponsor so that the sponsor can reaffirm the approved delivery approach.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tailoring in hybrid delivery — each component gets the approach that fits its uncertainty, stability and regulatory needs, and stakeholders are engaged with that reasoning.
Spot it: 'fixed regulatory steps and stable requirements' vs a portal built in iterations; a new executive who wants one approach for everything.
In this scenario: the PM explains why predictive suits the shutdown and adaptive suits the portal, and invites the CIO's input, which engages a key stakeholder.
Why not the others: switching everything to iterations ignores the tailoring factors; refusing to discuss it disengages the CIO; escalating to the sponsor skips the conversation the PM should have first.
Remember: Predictive for STABLE, agile for EVOLVING, hybrid when you need both. Never force one approach everywhere.

questions.stem: On a hybrid HRIS implementation, a vendor delivered the time-tracking module under a fixed-price contract with documented acceptance criteria, while in-house reports are built in iterations. Testing shows the module meets every criterion, but at the daily coordination meeting users say its approval workflow is more awkward than they expected. What should the project manager do?
options: Reject the module until the vendor redesigns the approval workflow at no extra cost to the organization.
Ask a few users to sign off informally and hold the formal acceptance until they are satisfied with the workflow.
Delay formal acceptance until the in-house team can redesign the approval workflow during its next iteration.
Accept the module formally against its criteria and raise the workflow improvement as a change or backlog item.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Formal acceptance against criteria — a deliverable that meets its documented acceptance criteria is accepted; new expectations become changes.
Spot it: 'fixed-price contract', 'meets every criterion', users want something different afterward.
In this scenario: the vendor delivered what the contract required, so the module is accepted formally, and the workflow improvement is raised as a change or a backlog item for the in-house team.
Why not the others: rejecting a conforming deliverable creates a contract dispute; informal sign-off with formal acceptance on hold is inconsistent and unfair to the seller; delaying acceptance ties the vendor to in-house work.
Remember: Criteria met = ACCEPT. New wish = CHANGE. SELLER is judged by the contract.

questions.stem: An agile logistics analytics team has a fixed release date and planned lower-priority features as a buffer. Two experienced developers have just moved to another product, and the updated forecast shows the full release will miss the date by about one iteration. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the remaining developers to work extra hours until the lost capacity has been made up before the release.
Request that the release date move out by one iteration so every planned feature can still be delivered as promised.
Work with the product owner to remove features from the planned buffer so the fixed release date is protected.
Add two new developers to the team right away so velocity recovers during the remaining iterations before release.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Feature buffer — lower-priority features are planned as a buffer so that, when capacity drops, scope flexes to protect a fixed date.
Spot it: 'fixed release date', 'lower-priority features as a buffer', capacity loss.
In this scenario: the buffer exists for exactly this case, so the PM works with the product owner to drop buffered features and keep the date.
Why not the others: overtime is not a sustainable pace; moving the date ignores the fixed constraint the buffer protects; adding new people late usually slows the team while they onboard.
Remember: In agile, time and cost are fixed; SCOPE flexes. The product owner chooses what goes.

questions.topic: Project Closure Flow and Lessons Learned
questions.stem: A project manager on a predictive public-sector data exchange is preparing the team for the final phase, which ends with signed data-sharing agreements handed to four agencies. Match each step of the closing flow with what happens in it.
matching_right: Lessons learned are finalized and archived in the organizational repository
All planned work is finished and verified against its requirements
Contracts, records, and resources are formally closed and released
The customer formally signs off against the acceptance criteria
Accepted deliverables and knowledge are handed over to operations

answer.Complete: All planned work is finished and verified against its requirements
answer.Accept: The customer formally signs off against the acceptance criteria
answer.Transfer: Accepted deliverables and knowledge are handed over to operations
answer.Learn: Lessons learned are finalized and archived in the organizational repository
answer.Close: Contracts, records, and resources are formally closed and released

questions.explanation:
Concept: A project is not finished when the work is done; it is finished when the closing flow is complete, in order.
Complete: the team finishes the scope and Control Quality verifies it (a verified deliverable, not yet accepted).
Accept: Validate Scope; the customer or sponsor formally signs off against the agreed acceptance criteria.
Transfer: accepted deliverables, documentation and know-how move to operations or the customer, which will own them.
Learn: the lessons learned register, updated all along, is finalized and moved to the organizational repository so future projects can use it.
Close: procurements closed, final report issued, records archived, resources released.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close. Capture lessons all through the project; archive them at the end. Register = THIS project, Repository = the ORGANIZATION.

questions.stem: On a hybrid HRIS implementation, a new pay-transparency law affects both the baselined payroll module, which is delivered predictively, and the employee self-service portal, which is built in iterations. Compliance is required in five months. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Submit a change request with an impact analysis for the baselined payroll module to the change control board.
Route the portal changes through the change control board so they are approved the same way as payroll.
Have the product owner add the portal changes to the backlog and prioritize them against the compliance date.
Implement the payroll changes directly, because the law is mandatory and does not need change control approval.
Defer both sets of changes until the next major release so the current plans for each team stay stable.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Change control in hybrid projects — baselined predictive parts use formal integrated change control; adaptive parts absorb change through backlog prioritization.
Spot it: one law affecting a 'baselined payroll module' and a portal 'built in iterations'.
In this scenario: the payroll change is analyzed and sent to the change control board, while the product owner adds the portal changes to the backlog and orders them to meet the compliance date.
Why not the others: routing backlog work through the CCB adds predictive overhead; 'mandatory' still needs impact analysis and approval; deferring risks missing a legal deadline.
Remember: Baseline → CCB. Backlog → product owner. Hybrid = apply the RIGHT rule to each part.

questions.stem: At a product demonstration for an agile cloud migration of a field-service app, technicians reveal they often work without connectivity and need offline access. The team is unsure whether the chosen cloud database can synchronize offline changes reliably, and the answer affects much of the remaining work. What should the project manager encourage the team to do?
options: Defer the offline feature to the last iteration so the team can first finish the better-known work.
Commit to delivering the full offline feature in the next iteration using the existing database design.
Log the offline requirement as an assumption in the risk register and continue with the current plan.
Plan a short spike early to test whether the database can reliably synchronize offline changes.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Spike — a short, timeboxed experiment that reduces technical uncertainty early, before the team commits a lot of work to an unproven design.
Spot it: 'unsure whether', 'the answer affects much of the remaining work'.
In this scenario: offline sync is a big unknown that shapes later work, so a spike early in the plan answers the question while it is still cheap to change course.
Why not the others: deferring the risky feature pushes the biggest risk to the most expensive moment; committing to the full feature on an unproven design gambles the iteration; logging it as an assumption and carrying on leaves the risk untouched.
Remember: High uncertainty = SPIKE early. Learn fast, fail cheap, then plan.

questions.stem: An agile hotel loyalty team keeps running into the same blocked integrations, so the coach is reviewing how the team surfaces and resolves problems. Match each agile practice or role with how it helps manage issues.
matching_right: Repeatedly asks why to trace a problem to its root cause
Removes impediments that the team cannot resolve on its own
Team members raise blockers affecting progress toward the sprint goal
Team inspects its way of working and chooses improvements
Visible list of current blockers and who is resolving them

answer.Daily scrum: Team members raise blockers affecting progress toward the sprint goal
answer.Retrospective: Team inspects its way of working and chooses improvements
answer.Impediment board: Visible list of current blockers and who is resolving them
answer.Scrum master: Removes impediments that the team cannot resolve on its own
answer.Five whys: Repeatedly asks why to trace a problem to its root cause

questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile teams surface and resolve impediments through events, visible tools, a servant leader and root-cause techniques.
Daily scrum: developers inspect progress toward the sprint goal and raise blockers quickly.
Retrospective: the team inspects how it works and chooses process improvements for the next sprint.
Impediment board: a visible list of current blockers and who is working on each one.
Scrum master: servant leader who removes impediments the team cannot clear on its own.
Five whys: asks 'why' repeatedly to trace a recurring problem to its root cause.
Remember: RAISE it (daily scrum) → SHOW it (board) → REMOVE it (scrum master) → PREVENT it (five whys, retrospective).

questions.stem: An agile team building a solar-farm monitoring product notes in its retrospective that integration defects appear every time they merge code on the last day of the iteration. Their earlier fix, an extra code review meeting before merging, has not reduced the defects. What should the project manager suggest?
options: Adopt continuous integration so every change is merged and verified by automated builds and tests.
Add a hardening iteration before each release so the team can fix integration defects in one batch.
Assign one tester to approve every merge on the last day so integration defects are stopped earlier.
Reduce the iteration's planned scope so the team has more time for merging on the final iteration day.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Continuous integration (CI) — team members merge small changes often, and automated builds and tests verify each merge, so integration problems are found within minutes.
Spot it: defects 'every time they merge code on the last day', and an extra review meeting did not help.
In this scenario: the root cause is big, late merges; CI replaces them with small, frequent, automatically verified merges.
Why not the others: a hardening iteration delays defect detection even further; one tester approving merges is still late inspection; cutting scope gives more time to the same flawed practice.
Remember: XP = ENGINEERING: TDD, pairing, CI, refactoring. Integrate early and often, so pain stays small.

questions.stem: The knowledge-base module of a predictive AI customer-support platform has passed all quality control tests against its specifications. The customer's representatives have not yet reviewed it, and the contract calls for their formal sign-off on each major deliverable. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Transition the verified module to the support operations team, since it has passed all quality control tests.
Review the verified module with the customer against its acceptance criteria to obtain formal acceptance.
Begin administrative closure for the module, because quality control confirmed it meets all of its specifications.
Have the team add extra search features the customer may want before presenting the module for their review.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Control Quality vs Validate Scope — quality control VERIFIES that a deliverable is correct; Validate Scope gets the customer's formal ACCEPTANCE.
Spot it: 'passed all quality control tests', customer 'not yet reviewed', contract requires 'formal sign-off'.
In this scenario: the module is verified but not yet accepted, so the next step is reviewing it with the customer against its acceptance criteria.
Why not the others: transitioning to operations skips acceptance; closure cannot start before acceptance; adding extra features the customer did not request is gold plating.
Remember: Create → Control Quality (VERIFIED) → Validate Scope (ACCEPTED) → Transition/Close. Verified ≠ accepted.

questions.stem: A predictive core banking replacement is three weeks behind, and a key data specialist is overallocated. The project scheduler is explaining recovery and resource options to the steering committee. Match each schedule technique with what it does.
matching_right: Finds the longest path through the network and its zero-float activities
Adjusts start dates to resource limits; the end date may move
Adds resources to critical-path activities, shortening time but raising cost
Shifts activities within their float; the end date does not change
Overlaps activities planned in sequence, which increases rework risk

answer.Crashing: Adds resources to critical-path activities, shortening time but raising cost
answer.Fast-tracking: Overlaps activities planned in sequence, which increases rework risk
answer.Resource leveling: Adjusts start dates to resource limits; the end date may move
answer.Resource smoothing: Shifts activities within their float; the end date does not change
answer.Critical path method: Finds the longest path through the network and its zero-float activities

questions.explanation:
Concept: Two techniques compress the schedule, two fix overallocated people, and one tells you where time matters.
Crashing: add people, overtime or money to critical-path work; saves time, COSTS money. Choose it when budget is available.
Fast-tracking: do sequential work in parallel; no extra cost, but RISK of rework. Choose it when the budget is fixed and activities can overlap.
Resource leveling: resolve overallocation by delaying work to fit resource limits; the critical path and end date can change.
Resource smoothing: resolve overallocation only within float, so the end date stays fixed.
Critical path method: finds the longest path, which sets the shortest possible duration; its activities have zero float, so compress there first.
Remember: Crash = COST, Fast-track = RISK. Smooth before you level: smoothing stays inside float, leveling can move the finish.

questions.stem: A predictive manufacturing robotics deployment has a budget at completion of $2.0 million, an earned value of $1.2 million, and an actual cost of $1.4 million. The sponsor insists on finishing within the original budget, while the finance director doubts it is possible. What should the project manager tell both stakeholders?
options: The remaining work must achieve a cost performance index of about 0.86.
The remaining work must achieve a cost performance index of about 0.75.
The remaining work must achieve a cost performance index of about 1.33.
The remaining work must achieve a cost performance index of about 1.17.
questions.explanation:
Concept: To-complete performance index (TCPI) — the cost efficiency the remaining work must achieve to finish on a target, usually the budget at completion (BAC).
Spot it: sponsor 'insists on finishing within the original budget', BAC, EV and AC given.
In this scenario: TCPI = (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC) = (2.0 − 1.2) ÷ (2.0 − 1.4) = 0.8 ÷ 0.6 ≈ 1.33. The team must perform much better than today's CPI of about 0.86, which supports the finance director's doubt.
Why not the others: 0.86 is the current CPI, not the required one; 0.75 inverts the formula; 1.17 does not follow from the numbers.
Remember: TCPI = work LEFT ÷ money LEFT. Above 1 = must get more efficient; far above current CPI = unlikely.

questions.stem: An agile HRIS program uses a vendor team whose features are reprioritized each iteration. A newly assigned procurement lead wants to replace the current arrangement with a firm-fixed-price contract covering a fully specified feature list. The project manager expects requirements to keep changing. What should the project manager propose?
options: A firm-fixed-price contract for the full feature list, as the procurement lead has requested it.
A contract with a fixed price per increment and the option to reprioritize or exit after each one.
A time-and-materials contract with no cap, so the vendor can absorb all of the changes as they arise.
A contract that lets the vendor define the full scope, since its team knows the product best.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Agile-friendly contracts — structures such as fixed price per increment with options to reprioritize or exit let scope evolve while capping the buyer's risk.
Spot it: features 'reprioritized each iteration', 'requirements to keep changing', a push for a fully specified fixed-price deal.
In this scenario: requirements will keep moving, so pricing each increment and allowing reprioritizing or exiting after each keeps flexibility and cost control.
Why not the others: a fully specified FFP contract fights changing requirements and invites disputes; uncapped T&M gives the buyer open-ended cost risk; letting the vendor define scope gives away the buyer's control of value.
Remember: Changing scope needs a CHANGE-FRIENDLY contract. SELLER terms must match the delivery approach.

questions.stem: On an agile cloud migration, external auditors must see, before the next governance meeting, that each of 25 required security controls has been built and tested. The team manages work as user stories with automated acceptance tests in its work-tracking tool. What should the project manager do?
options: Link each security control to the stories that implement it and to their automated tests in the tool.
Stop development until a complete traceability matrix document is written for all remaining work.
Tell the auditors that agile teams do not trace requirements, since working software shows the result.
Ask the product owner to sign a statement confirming that all 25 security controls have been built.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Lightweight traceability in agile — link requirements to the stories and automated tests that implement and verify them, inside the team's tools.
Spot it: auditors need proof each control 'has been built and tested', stories with 'automated acceptance tests'.
In this scenario: linking each of the 25 controls to its stories and tests in the tool gives auditors verifiable evidence without stopping work.
Why not the others: halting development for a big matrix document is needless overhead; agile still traces requirements when compliance demands it; a signed statement is assurance, not evidence.
Remember: TRACE = link requirement ↔ story ↔ test. Agile keeps it light, not absent.

questions.stem: A hybrid data-governance program builds its metadata catalog in iterations while the policy rollout is predictive. At a risk workshop, new evidence shows the data-lineage epic at the top of the backlog is far more complex than assumed, and the team cannot estimate it. What should the project manager do?
options: Help the product owner and team split the lineage epic into smaller stories that each fit within an iteration.
Put the entire lineage epic into the next iteration and extend that iteration until all the work is complete.
Move the lineage epic into the predictive policy rollout, where it can be planned in full detail with fixed dates.
Estimate the lineage epic personally so the team can commit to it and start work in the next iteration.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Backlog refinement and splitting — large, uncertain epics are split into small stories that can be estimated and finished within one iteration.
Spot it: an epic 'at the top of the backlog', 'far more complex than assumed', 'cannot estimate it'.
In this scenario: the PM helps the product owner and team split the lineage epic so the highest-value pieces can be estimated and delivered first.
Why not the others: extending an iteration breaks the timebox; moving it into the predictive stream forces fixed plans on uncertain work; estimates come from the people doing the work, not the PM.
Remember: Too big to estimate = SPLIT it. Timeboxes stay fixed; the team estimates.

questions.stem: An agile identity-access-management team is ready to release small updates every two weeks, but each release waits up to a month for the monthly change advisory board meeting. An earlier fix of adding more release documentation did not shorten the wait. What should the project manager do?
options: Let the team release small updates without the change advisory board, since the changes are low-risk.
Work with the change advisory board to agree criteria for pre-approving low-risk, standard releases.
Combine the updates into larger quarterly releases so that fewer change advisory board reviews are needed.
Escalate the delays to the chief executive to have the change advisory board removed from the process.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tailoring governance — keep oversight but fit it to the delivery approach, for example pre-approved standard changes for low-risk, frequent releases.
Spot it: small releases every two weeks stuck behind a monthly board; more documentation did not help.
In this scenario: working with the change advisory board to agree pre-approval criteria for low-risk releases keeps control and lets value flow.
Why not the others: releasing without the board bypasses governance; batching into quarterly releases increases risk and delays value; escalating to remove the board is an overreaction.
Remember: Follow authority before acting. Don't break governance; TAILOR it together.

questions.stem: The baggage-screening supplier on a predictive airport modernization reports that its scanners may not meet the aviation security regulator's updated standard. Installation is scheduled for next month. The project manager walks the team through the organization's compliance response flow. Match each step with what happens in it.
matching_right: Engage legal, compliance, or regulatory experts to interpret the rule
Carry out the approved changes so deliverables meet the requirement
Analyze the impact on scope, schedule, cost, and risk
Revise plans and baselines through the approved change control process
Confirm that the new requirement applies to the project's deliverables

answer.Identify: Confirm that the new requirement applies to the project's deliverables
answer.Assess: Analyze the impact on scope, schedule, cost, and risk
answer.Consult: Engage legal, compliance, or regulatory experts to interpret the rule
answer.Update: Revise plans and baselines through the approved change control process
answer.Implement: Carry out the approved changes so deliverables meet the requirement

questions.explanation:
Concept: Compliance is mandatory, so the PM never ignores, postpones or trades it away; instead the PM follows a clear response flow.
Identify: recognize the new or changed requirement and confirm it really applies to this project (here, the scanners).
Assess: analyze what it does to scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk before choosing a response.
Consult: bring in the compliance office, legal or the regulator so the rule is interpreted correctly, not guessed.
Update: route the needed changes through change control and update the plans and baselines once approved.
Implement: deliver the approved changes, then document evidence that the requirement is met.
Remember: Identify → Assess → Consult → Update → Implement → Document. Mandatory beats optional: you follow the rule, then record the lesson.

questions.stem: A hybrid 5G rollout builds towers on a predictive plan and its customer app in iterations. At a vendor escalation meeting, marketing wants the next tower phase moved to high-revenue urban areas, while a state partner insists on the rural coverage promised in the business case. Tower crews can support only one plan. What should the project manager do?
options: Review both options with the sponsor against the business case and benefits management plan before deciding.
Follow the marketing team's request, because urban towers will produce revenue for the company more quickly.
Split the tower crews evenly between urban and rural sites so both groups receive part of what they asked for.
Let the adaptive app team decide the tower sequence, because it works most closely with the actual customers.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Business case and benefits management plan — the business case says WHY the investment is made; the benefits plan says how, when and by whom benefits are realized. The sponsor owns the business case.
Spot it: competing stakeholder demands, 'promised in the business case', only one plan possible.
In this scenario: urban vs rural is a value trade-off tied to committed benefits, so the PM reviews both options with the sponsor against the business case and benefits plan.
Why not the others: picking faster revenue ignores committed benefits; splitting the crews delivers neither benefit on time; the app team has no authority over tower sequencing.
Remember: WHY = Business Case. Benefits plan = what, when, how, who. Sponsor owns the WHY.

questions.stem: An agile team modernizing a university ERP system is meeting with the provost's office to confirm that its work supports the university's strategy. Match each strategic alignment artifact with its description.
matching_right: Shows planned high-level releases and capabilities over time
Justifies the investment by comparing expected benefits with costs
Describes the product's intended future and the value it creates
Defines how and when benefits are delivered and measured
Goals paired with measurable results that track strategic progress

answer.Business case: Justifies the investment by comparing expected benefits with costs
answer.Benefits management plan: Defines how and when benefits are delivered and measured
answer.Objectives and key results (OKRs): Goals paired with measurable results that track strategic progress
answer.Product vision: Describes the product's intended future and the value it creates
answer.Product roadmap: Shows planned high-level releases and capabilities over time

questions.explanation:
Concept: Strategic alignment artifacts connect a product's work to the organization's strategy, from the investment case down to the release plan.
Business case: answers WHY; justifies the investment by weighing expected benefits against costs.
Benefits management plan: how, when and by whom benefits are delivered and measured.
Objectives and key results (OKRs): goals with measurable key results that track strategic progress.
Product vision: the long-term picture of what the product will become and the value it creates.
Product roadmap: high-level releases and capabilities planned over time.
Remember: Strategy → Business case (WHY) → Vision (WHERE) → Roadmap (WHEN) → Backlog (WHAT next), measured by OKRs and benefits.

questions.stem: A predictive airport modernization will replace manual baggage sorting with an automated system in three months. The plan assumed that training at go-live would be enough, but ground-crew supervisors now tell the project manager that crews fear job losses and plan to resist. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Ask the operations director to issue a memo requiring all ground crews to use the new sorting system at go-live.
Meet with the crew supervisors to explain why the change is happening and involve them in planning the transition.
Add extra training sessions in the week of go-live so crews have more time to learn how the new system works.
Postpone the go-live date until the crews' union formally agrees to support the new automated sorting system.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Leading organizational change — people resist before processes fail, so start by building awareness of WHY and involving those affected.
Spot it: 'fear job losses', 'plan to resist', a plan that relied only on training.
In this scenario: the crews do not yet understand or accept the change, so the PM meets their supervisors to explain the reasons and involve them in planning the transition.
Why not the others: a mandate increases resistance; extra training builds skill but does not address fear; waiting for union agreement gives up leadership of the change.
Remember: Assess readiness → Understand resistance → Engage → Communicate → Train → Reinforce. Understand the cause FIRST.

questions.stem: An agile team is building a public-sector data exchange for an agency that has committed to cutting its carbon emissions by 30 percent. At a status review the sponsor asks the team to run extra cloud servers around the clock so nightly data loads finish faster. What should the project manager do?
options: Add the extra servers around the clock as the sponsor asks, since faster data loads have clear user value.
Refuse the sponsor's request, because any extra computing would conflict with the agency's carbon commitment.
Have the team propose options, such as on-demand scaling, that meet the speed need within the carbon goal.
