Defer the request until the sustainability office completes its annual review of the agency's cloud usage.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sustainability as a constraint — environmental commitments shape HOW a need is met; the PM looks for options that satisfy both value and the goal.
Spot it: an agency committed to 'cutting its carbon emissions', a request for always-on servers.
In this scenario: faster loads are a real need, so the team proposes options such as on-demand scaling that meet the speed goal within the carbon target.
Why not the others: always-on servers ignore the commitment; a flat refusal ignores a legitimate need; waiting for an annual review delays a decision the team can make now.
Remember: Sustainability = environmental + social + economic. Find the option that serves BOTH value and the goal.

questions.stem: On a predictive cloud migration, team members have started using the company's approved generative AI tool to draft migration runbooks. The project manager is briefing the team on the organization's AI policy before the next phase. Match each responsible AI term with its meaning.
matching_right: A qualified person reviews AI-assisted work and stays accountable
AI accuracy declines over time as real-world data changes
Plausible-sounding AI output that is factually wrong
Keeping sensitive data out of unapproved tools and unauthorized hands
Systematic unfairness in AI data or outputs toward certain groups

answer.Hallucination: Plausible-sounding AI output that is factually wrong
answer.Bias: Systematic unfairness in AI data or outputs toward certain groups
answer.Human oversight: A qualified person reviews AI-assisted work and stays accountable
answer.Confidentiality: Keeping sensitive data out of unapproved tools and unauthorized hands
answer.Model drift: AI accuracy declines over time as real-world data changes

questions.explanation:
Concept: Responsible AI vocabulary — AI is a decision-support tool, not an accountability escape hatch; these terms name its main risks and controls.
Hallucination: AI output that sounds right but is wrong; validate before you use it.
Bias: systematic unfairness toward certain groups in data or outputs; check and review it.
Human oversight: a qualified person reviews AI-assisted work and stays accountable; AI recommends, humans decide.
Confidentiality: protect sensitive data; never paste it into unapproved or public tools.
Model drift: accuracy degrades over time as real-world data changes; keep monitoring.
Remember: Approved tool → Protect data → Generate → Validate accuracy/bias → Human decides → Monitor drift.

questions.stem: Midway through a predictive digital permitting solution, a new state law requires all public web portals to meet accessibility standards by next year. City permit staff want the go-live date kept, while disability advocates want the portal fully accessible at launch. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Wait until the law's enforcement date is closer before assessing its impact, so the current plan is not disrupted.
Analyze what the law requires of the portal and its impact on scope, schedule, and cost with affected stakeholders.
Have the team add accessibility features right away without change control, because the new law makes them mandatory.
Ask the city attorney to seek an exemption from the law so the portal can launch on its planned date without changes.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Responding to external change — a new law is mandatory; first analyze what it requires and its impact with stakeholders, then change the plan through change control.
Spot it: 'a new state law requires', competing stakeholder wishes, a fixed go-live.
In this scenario: the PM analyzes the accessibility requirement and its scope, schedule and cost impacts with permit staff and advocates before deciding on changes.
Why not the others: waiting risks a noncompliant launch; adding features without change control bypasses governance; seeking an exemption dodges a mandatory rule.
Remember: External change → Assess impact → Reassess risk/value → Prioritize response → Change the plan → Monitor. Mandatory beats optional.

questions.stem: A predictive data-governance project depends on a master data hub being delivered by another project in the same program. At a governance review the hub's project manager reports that it will be six weeks late, which would delay the first governance release. What should the project manager do?
options: Work with the program manager to coordinate the hub dependency and adjust both projects' plans.
Have the team build a simple temporary data hub so the first release is not held up by the delay.
Escalate the delay directly to the chief data officer and ask for the other project to be accelerated.
Wait for the hub to arrive and report the resulting delay in the next monthly status update.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Program-level dependency management — the program manager coordinates dependencies among the program's projects to protect shared benefits.
Spot it: 'another project in the same program', a slipping dependency affecting your release.
In this scenario: the hub delay affects both projects, so the PM works with the program manager to coordinate the dependency and adjust both plans.
Why not the others: building a temporary hub duplicates program work; going straight to the chief data officer skips program governance; waiting and reporting later is passive.
Remember: Dependency → Assess impact → Coordinate → Monitor. Projects deliver outputs, PROGRAMS coordinate benefits.

questions.stem: The sponsor of a predictive permitting system wants a small fee-calculation fix released this week instead of waiting three weeks for the next change control board meeting. The governance framework defines an expedited approval path for low-risk changes under a set cost threshold. What should the project manager do?
options: Release the fix this week based on the sponsor's request, since the sponsor has authority over the project.
Hold the fix for the next board meeting, because every change must wait for a full change control review.
Have the team release the fix as a defect correction so that it does not need change control approval.
Check whether the fix qualifies for the expedited approval path and, if so, submit it through that path.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tiered governance approval paths — many frameworks define an expedited path for low-risk changes below a set threshold.
Spot it: a 'small fix', a 'defined expedited approval path for low-risk changes under a set cost threshold'.
In this scenario: the PM checks whether the fix meets the expedited criteria and, if it does, uses that path, which meets the sponsor's need and respects governance.
Why not the others: the sponsor's wish does not replace the approval process; waiting for the full board ignores the path governance created; relabeling a change as a defect dodges required controls.
Remember: Follow authority before acting. Use the RIGHT approval path, never NO approval path.

questions.stem: At a customer demo for an agile warehouse automation project, an autonomous forklift feature works well, and the product owner wants to pilot it next week in an active warehouse. Workplace safety rules require a documented risk assessment before robots operate near workers, and none has been done yet. What should the project manager do?
options: Run the pilot next week as the product owner planned and complete the safety assessment during the pilot.
Add the safety assessment to the backlog for a later iteration so the pilot can proceed on its planned date.
Make sure the required safety risk assessment is completed and documented before any pilot near workers.
Run the pilot next week on the night shift, when fewer workers are in the warehouse near the forklifts.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Compliance gates release — mandatory safety or legal requirements must be met before work goes live, however good the feature looks.
Spot it: 'safety rules require a documented risk assessment before', 'none has been done yet'.
In this scenario: the pilot would put workers near robots, so the required safety assessment must be completed and documented first.
Why not the others: assessing 'during' the pilot is too late; putting it in the backlog for later treats a legal rule as optional; the night shift still exposes workers to an unassessed robot.
Remember: Mandatory beats optional. Compliance is not a backlog item you can defer.

questions.stem: A hybrid HRIS implementation goes live next month. At a quarterly benefits review the finance director asks who will measure the expected 40 percent drop in payroll errors after the project team disbands. The HR operations manager assumes the project will measure it. What should the project manager do?
options: Tell the finance director that benefits are measured only after the project closes, so no action is needed.
Assign the project team to measure payroll errors each month after go-live, until the 40 percent is reached.
Confirm a benefit owner in HR operations and agree on how the error metric will be tracked after handover.
Report the expected 40 percent reduction as achieved at go-live, based on the results of acceptance testing.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Benefit ownership — benefits are usually realized after the project ends, so the benefits management plan names an owner in operations and how each benefit is measured.
Spot it: 'after the project team disbands', 'who will measure', confusion about ownership.
In this scenario: the PM confirms a benefit owner in HR operations and agrees how the payroll-error metric will be tracked after handover.
Why not the others: benefits need planning before closure, not after; a disbanded project team cannot keep measuring; acceptance testing proves outputs, not realized benefits.
Remember: Deliverable → Outcome → Benefit → Value. Transition OWNERSHIP of benefits to operations.

questions.stem: An agile smart-city program has been building parking-payment features to raise city revenue. A newly appointed city CTO announces that the city's top strategic priority is now pedestrian safety, and asks how the program will respond. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue the parking-payment features until the current release ends, then consider the new strategic priority.
Reorder the backlog personally so pedestrian-safety features are started at the beginning of the next iteration.
Ask the team to vote on whether to switch to safety features or continue the parking-payment work already planned.
Work with the product owner to reorder the roadmap and backlog around features that support pedestrian safety.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Realigning to strategy in agile — when strategy changes, the product owner reorders the roadmap and backlog so the team works on what now matters most.
Spot it: 'top strategic priority is now', a new executive asking how the program will respond.
In this scenario: pedestrian safety replaces revenue as the goal, so the PM works with the product owner to reorder the roadmap and backlog around it.
Why not the others: continuing the old plan until the release ends delays alignment; the PM reordering the backlog bypasses the product owner; a team vote is not how value priorities are set.
Remember: Strategy changes → Backlog changes. The PRODUCT OWNER orders the backlog.

questions.stem: The supplier on an agile smart-city project reports that its maintenance tablets cannot support the paper-based work orders that street-repair crews assumed they could keep using. Crews will need to change their daily routine. Several crew leads are openly skeptical. What should the project manager do?
options: Involve crew representatives in reviews and pilots of each increment and enlist skeptical leads as change champions.
Announce that crews must switch to tablets when the system launches, and have supervisors enforce the change.
Ask the supplier to rebuild its tablets to replicate the paper work orders so crews do not need to change at all.
Delay all crew training until the full system is deployed, so that crews learn the final version only one time.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Engaging users in agile change — involve affected people in increment reviews and pilots, and turn respected skeptics into change champions.
Spot it: crews must 'change their daily routine', 'openly skeptical' leads.
In this scenario: bringing crew representatives into reviews and pilots, and enlisting skeptical leads as champions, builds readiness and shapes the solution with their feedback.
Why not the others: a mandate enforced by supervisors increases resistance; asking the supplier to copy paper work orders avoids the change instead of leading it; late training leaves crews unprepared.
Remember: People resist before processes fail. Involve early; skeptics can become champions.

questions.stem: A predictive digital permitting project will replace 120 self-service kiosks at city offices. At a regulatory checkpoint the project manager learns that a new city policy requires retired electronics to go to certified e-waste recyclers. The disposal plan currently sends old kiosks to a general scrap dealer. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the scrap dealer for this project, since its contract was signed before the new recycling policy took effect.
Update the disposal plan to use a certified e-waste recycler and process any cost impact through change control.
Store the retired kiosks in a city warehouse until a later project can decide how to dispose of them properly.
Ask the scrap dealer to confirm verbally that it will recycle the kiosks in line with the city's new recycling policy.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sustainability across the full life cycle — environmental policies apply to disposal too, and changing the plan to comply goes through change control.
Spot it: 'new city policy requires', 'certified e-waste recyclers', a plan that uses a general scrap dealer.
In this scenario: the disposal plan must change to a certified recycler, and any cost impact is processed through change control.
Why not the others: an older contract does not exempt the project from policy; storing kiosks just postpones compliance; a verbal promise from an uncertified dealer does not meet a certification requirement.
Remember: Mandatory beats optional. Think beyond delivery, all the way to disposal.

questions.stem: On a predictive healthcare analytics project, validation shows the AI readmission-prediction model is much less accurate for rural patients. Clinicians want it launched on schedule next month, while the hospital's equity officer wants launch delayed. The AI policy requires bias review before deployment. What should the project manager do?
options: Launch the model on schedule with a disclaimer that its predictions are less reliable for rural patients.
Have the data scientists drop rural patients from the dataset so the model's overall accuracy looks higher.
Let the data science lead decide whether the difference in accuracy is small enough to allow the launch.
Present the bias findings to the AI governance body and require mitigation and revalidation before go-live.
questions.explanation:
Concept: AI bias and governance — when a model treats a group unfairly and policy requires a bias review, the findings go to the AI governance body and the model is fixed and revalidated before use.
Spot it: 'much less accurate for rural patients', 'policy requires bias review before deployment'.
In this scenario: the PM presents the bias findings to the governance body and requires mitigation and revalidation before go-live.
Why not the others: a disclaimer still exposes rural patients to a biased model; removing rural data hides the bias; one lead deciding alone bypasses the required governance review.
Remember: Validate accuracy/BIAS → Human decision → Monitor. Governance decides, not the schedule.

questions.stem: An agile logistics team is scanning its environment for external changes that could affect its product roadmap. Match each PESTLE category with the example that best illustrates it.
matching_right: A new data privacy law takes effect in the coming year
Customers increasingly expect same-day delivery and mobile tracking
A cloud provider retires the mapping service the product relies on
Rising interest rates increase the cost of financing new warehouses
A new government takes office and shifts infrastructure funding priorities

answer.Political: A new government takes office and shifts infrastructure funding priorities
answer.Economic: Rising interest rates increase the cost of financing new warehouses
answer.Social: Customers increasingly expect same-day delivery and mobile tracking
answer.Technological: A cloud provider retires the mapping service the product relies on
answer.Legal: A new data privacy law takes effect in the coming year

questions.explanation:
Concept: PESTLE sorts external changes into six categories so teams can scan the environment systematically.
Political: government decisions and priorities, such as a new administration shifting funding.
Economic: market and financial conditions, such as interest rates or inflation.
Social: people's expectations, behavior and demographics, such as demand for same-day delivery.
Technological: changes in technology and platforms, such as a retired mapping service.
Legal: laws and regulations, such as a new data privacy law.
Remember: PESTLE = Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental. External change → Assess impact → Reprioritize.

questions.stem: The PMO director at a manufacturer is explaining to new project managers how their robotics deployment fits into the wider organization. Match each term with its description.
matching_right: Ongoing work that sustains the organization's products and services
Collection of work managed as a group to meet strategic objectives
Unit that standardizes project governance and shares resources and methods
Temporary endeavor that creates a unique product, service, or result
Related projects managed together to obtain coordinated benefits

answer.Project: Temporary endeavor that creates a unique product, service, or result
answer.Program: Related projects managed together to obtain coordinated benefits
answer.Portfolio: Collection of work managed as a group to meet strategic objectives
answer.Operations: Ongoing work that sustains the organization's products and services
answer.Project management office (PMO): Unit that standardizes project governance and shares resources and methods

questions.explanation:
Concept: Projects, programs, portfolios, operations and the PMO are different levels of organizing work.
Project: temporary, creates a unique product, service or result.
Program: related projects managed together for benefits you could not get separately.
Portfolio: projects, programs and operations grouped to meet strategic objectives.
Operations: ongoing work that sustains the business after projects hand off.
Project management office (PMO): standardizes governance and shares resources, methods and tools.
Remember: Project → Program → Portfolio. Projects deliver OUTPUTS, programs coordinate BENEFITS, portfolios align to STRATEGY.

questions.stem: An agile team on a financial reporting modernization wants a new report released before month-end close. Audit controls require that a person other than the developer approve every production deployment. With the approver out today, a developer offers to deploy the change directly to save time. What should the project manager do?
options: Allow the developer to deploy directly this one time and record the exception in the project's issue log.
Postpone the report until after the next external audit so that no control questions come up before month-end.
Keep the separate approval for this deployment and ask the team how to build that approval into its pipeline.
Escalate the missing approver to the audit committee and ask it to waive the approval requirement this month.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Segregation of duties — an audit control where the person who builds a change does not approve its deployment. Agile teams keep the control and make it efficient.
Spot it: 'audit controls require that a person other than the developer approve', a shortcut offered.
In this scenario: the PM keeps the independent approval for this deployment and helps the team build that approval into its pipeline so it stops causing delays.
Why not the others: a 'one-time' direct deployment is still a control violation; postponing until after the audit avoids the control instead of meeting it; asking the audit committee for a waiver escalates what a backup approver or better process can solve.
Remember: Mandatory beats optional. Automate the control, don't skip it.

questions.stem: The adaptive development team on a hybrid clinical scheduling platform has been copying real patient records into its test environment to speed up testing. The hospital's privacy rules prohibit identifiable patient data outside production systems. A security analyst has just raised the concern. What should the project manager do?
options: Restrict test environment access to a few senior developers so that fewer people can see the patient data.
Stop using real patient records in testing, switch to de-identified data, and inform the privacy officer.
Keep using the copied records until the current release ends, then switch to de-identified test data.
Ask the legal team for a waiver so the development team can keep using real records for testing.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Privacy compliance — a practice that breaks privacy rules must stop at once, and the privacy officer is informed so any exposure can be assessed.
Spot it: 'real patient records' in test, 'rules prohibit identifiable patient data outside production'.
In this scenario: the PM stops using real records, switches to de-identified data and informs the privacy officer.
Why not the others: restricting access still leaves prohibited data in test; continuing until the release ends knowingly extends the violation; a waiver request tries to trade away a mandatory rule.
Remember: Mandatory beats optional. Stop → Inform → Fix → Document.

questions.stem: After a reorganization, an agile team rolling out a telecom self-service app has a new product owner. Every stakeholder group is pushing its own features as urgent, and the team is spread across too many items. Which TWO actions should the project manager take to maximize value?
options: Help the product owner rank the backlog by value and cost of delay using agreed criteria.
Plan a single large release that includes every stakeholder's features so no group is left out.
Rank the backlog by the seniority of each requesting stakeholder so that decisions stay objective.
Release a minimum viable product early to confirm with real customers which features deliver value.
Measure the value delivered by the number of story points the team completes each iteration.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Maximizing value in agile — rank work by value with clear criteria (such as cost of delay), and release early to test value with real users.
Spot it: 'every stakeholder group is pushing', 'spread across too many items', a new product owner.
In this scenario: the PM helps the product owner rank the backlog by value and cost of delay, and supports an early MVP release to confirm which features customers actually value.
Why not the others: one big release with everything delays all value; ranking by seniority replaces value with power; story points measure effort, not value.
Remember: Value first, validated early. Points = EFFORT, not VALUE.

questions.stem: After a merger, an agile customer-data platform team learns at a quarterly benefits review that the new company goals no longer include loyalty-program analytics. The loyalty analytics epic is 60 percent complete. Several stakeholders argue it should be finished because so much has already been spent. What should the project manager do?
options: Help the product owner decide on the epic based on value to the new goals, not on what has already been spent.
Complete the loyalty analytics epic first, because 60 percent of its planned budget has already been spent.
Ask the team to finish the loyalty epic in parallel with new work so that no investment is lost from the effort.
Keep the epic in progress until the annual planning cycle, when the new company goals will be formally reviewed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sunk cost and strategic alignment — decide whether to continue work based on future value to current goals, not on what has already been spent.
Spot it: goals 'no longer include' the work, '60 percent complete', 'so much has already been spent'.
In this scenario: the PM helps the product owner decide on the epic by its value to the new company goals.
Why not the others: finishing because money was spent is the sunk cost fallacy; doing it in parallel still spends capacity on unaligned work; waiting for annual planning keeps funding work that may not matter.
Remember: Spent money is GONE; decide on FUTURE value. Does this still support strategy?

questions.stem: A university is retiring its legacy student system, and an agile team is rolling out a new ERP advising module to faculty advisors in increments. The project manager is coaching the product owner on the people side of the change. Match each organizational change term with its meaning.
matching_right: A respected peer who models the change and influences others
How prepared people are to accept and use the change
Recognition and follow-up that make the new behavior last
Actual, sustained use of the new system, not just its deployment
Pushback against the new way of working whose cause must be understood

answer.Change readiness: How prepared people are to accept and use the change
answer.Resistance: Pushback against the new way of working whose cause must be understood
answer.Adoption: Actual, sustained use of the new system, not just its deployment
answer.Change champion: A respected peer who models the change and influences others
answer.Reinforcement: Recognition and follow-up that make the new behavior last

questions.explanation:
Concept: Organizational change vocabulary — deployment is not adoption; these terms describe the people side of making a change stick.
Change readiness: how prepared people are to accept and use the change; assess it early.
Resistance: pushback against the new way of working; understand its cause before acting.
Adoption: people actually and consistently using the new system; deployment alone is not success.
Change champion: a respected peer who models the change and influences others to follow.
Reinforcement: recognition, coaching and follow-up that make the new behavior last.
Remember: Assess readiness → Understand resistance → Engage → Communicate → Train → Implement → REINFORCE → Measure adoption.

questions.stem: A hybrid manufacturing robotics deployment is buying 40 welding robots. During procurement negotiation the lowest bidder's robots use 30 percent more energy than a slightly higher bid. The company has published energy-reduction goals, but the draft source selection criteria score price only. What should the project manager do?
options: Award the contract to the lowest bidder, because the published source selection criteria are based on price only.
Recommend updating the source selection criteria to include lifecycle energy cost before the contract is awarded.
Award the contract to the more efficient bidder without changing the criteria, since it fits the energy-reduction goals.
Ask the lowest bidder to lower its price further to make up for the extra energy use over the robots' lifetime.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sustainability in source selection — selection criteria should reflect organizational goals, and lifecycle cost gives a truer comparison than purchase price.
Spot it: 'published energy-reduction goals', criteria that 'score price only', a large energy difference.
In this scenario: the PM recommends updating the criteria to include lifecycle energy cost BEFORE the award, so the evaluation is fair and aligned.
Why not the others: awarding on price alone ignores the company's goals; awarding against unpublished criteria is unfair and open to challenge; squeezing the low bidder does not fix the energy use.
Remember: Cheapest upfront ≠ cheapest overall. Set the criteria first, then evaluate fairly.

questions.stem: On a predictive data-governance program, a vendor's AI tool labels records as sensitive to control who can access them. At a regulatory checkpoint the vendor admits the tool cannot explain why it labels any given record. The organization's AI policy requires human-reviewable explanations for automated access decisions. What should the project manager do?
options: Deploy the tool as planned, since its labels have been highly accurate in all of the vendor's test results.
Cancel the vendor contract today and restart the tool selection process with a new list of AI vendors.
Refer the tool to the AI governance board and propose human review of its labels until the gap is resolved.
Ask the sponsor to exempt the project from the AI policy's explanation requirement for this tool only.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Explainability and human oversight — when policy requires explainable automated decisions, a black-box tool goes to AI governance, and humans review its outputs in the meantime.
Spot it: tool 'cannot explain why', policy requires 'human-reviewable explanations'.
In this scenario: the PM refers the tool to the AI governance board and proposes human review of its labels until the gap is closed.
Why not the others: high accuracy does not meet an explainability requirement; canceling the contract acts before governance has assessed options; asking the sponsor for an exemption bypasses the policy.
Remember: AI recommends, humans decide. Explainability and auditability are governance requirements.

questions.stem: An agile team is redesigning e-commerce fulfillment. A major shipping carrier announces that its label-printing API will change in 60 days. A newly assigned operations director insists that all other work stop until the API change is finished. What should the project manager do?
options: Stop all other work as the operations director asks, so the whole team can focus on the carrier API change.
Wait until closer to the carrier's deadline to start, so the team does not have to change its current priorities.
Ask the shipping carrier to delay its API change until the team has finished the features it has already planned.
Help the product owner size the API work and rank it against other backlog items to meet the 60-day deadline.
questions.explanation:
Concept: External change in agile — assess the new demand, size it and rank it in the backlog against its deadline and value, rather than stopping everything.
Spot it: 'will change in 60 days', a stakeholder demanding that 'all other work stop'.
In this scenario: the PM helps the product owner size the API work and rank it so it is finished before the 60-day deadline while other value continues.
Why not the others: stopping all work is not needed with 60 days of notice; waiting risks missing the deadline; asking the carrier to delay is not realistic.
Remember: External change → Assess → Prioritize response → Change the backlog → Monitor.

questions.stem: A predictive financial reporting modernization will hand its new consolidation system to the finance operations group next month. During a compliance review, a new regulation adds monthly control checks that operations staff must perform on the system. What should the project manager do?
options: Hand the system over on schedule and let the finance operations group work out the new control checks on its own.
Include the new control procedures and training in the transition plan and get operations' acceptance before handover.
Keep the project open indefinitely so the project team can perform the new monthly control checks for operations.
Ask the regulator to exempt the new consolidation system from the monthly control checks for its first year of use.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Transition to operations — the handover must give operations everything it needs to run the product, including new procedures and training, and ends with their acceptance.
Spot it: 'hand its new system to the finance operations group', a new regulation adding checks 'operations staff must perform'.
In this scenario: the PM adds the new control procedures and training to the transition plan and gets operations' acceptance before handover.
Why not the others: handing over and letting operations 'work it out' leaves them unprepared; projects are temporary, so the team cannot run operational checks forever; asking for an exemption dodges a mandatory rule.
Remember: Complete → Accept → TRANSFER → Learn → Close. Operations must be ready to own it.

questions.stem: The supplier on a predictive customer onboarding redesign reports during an architecture review that its platform can no longer be hosted in-country as assumed. Moving to a compliant hosting option would add $400,000. The charter lets the project manager approve cost changes of up to $100,000. What should the project manager do?
options: Prepare the options and their impacts, then escalate the decision to the steering committee.
Approve the $400,000 from the contingency reserve, since the hosting change is clearly necessary.
Negotiate a new hosting agreement with the supplier directly and inform the sponsor once it is signed.
Continue with the current platform and revisit the hosting issue at the next scheduled phase review.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Escalation thresholds — governance sets how much the PM can approve; decisions above that limit go up with analyzed options.
Spot it: '$400,000' needed, 'the charter lets the project manager approve cost changes of up to $100,000'.
In this scenario: the change is four times the PM's authority, so the PM prepares options and impacts and escalates the decision to the steering committee.
Why not the others: approving it from contingency exceeds the charter's authority; signing a new agreement first commits the organization without approval; waiting for the phase review leaves a compliance problem open.
Remember: AUTHORITY = Charter and governance thresholds. Within limits, decide; above limits, escalate with options.

questions.stem: On a predictive insurance claims platform, compliance reviews happen only at the end of each phase. In the last two phases, reviewers found regulatory gaps late, which caused weeks of rework even though the team was fully busy. The next phase starts in two weeks. What should the project manager do?
options: Skip the end-of-phase compliance review for low-risk deliverables so the team can reduce rework time.
Add more reviewers at the end of the phase so the compliance review can be completed in less time.
Accept the rework as a normal cost of regulated work and add more time for it in the phase schedule.
Involve the compliance officer during design so regulatory requirements are built in and checked earlier.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Shift compliance left — build regulatory requirements in from design with the compliance officer's help, instead of finding gaps late.
Spot it: reviews 'only at the end of each phase', gaps 'found late', 'weeks of rework'.
In this scenario: involving the compliance officer during design prevents gaps, which removes the rework at the end.
Why not the others: skipping reviews breaks a mandatory control; more reviewers at the end still find gaps too late; accepting rework as normal ignores the root cause.
Remember: Prevention over inspection. Build compliance IN; don't inspect it on at the end.

questions.stem: A hybrid healthcare analytics project installs data infrastructure on a predictive plan and builds clinician dashboards in increments. The expected benefit of fewer readmissions depends on clinicians using the dashboards daily, but usage data from the first two increments shows only 15 percent use them. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue delivering the planned dashboards, since usage normally rises once all features are done.
Report the benefit as on track, because the dashboards were delivered as planned and passed testing.
Work with clinicians to learn why usage is low and adjust the next increments to improve adoption.
Ask hospital leaders to require that all clinicians log in to the dashboards at least once each day.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Adoption drives benefits — a benefit is realized only when people use the outputs, so low usage is an early warning about value.
Spot it: benefit 'depends on clinicians using the dashboards', only '15 percent use them'.
In this scenario: the PM works with clinicians to learn why usage is low and adjusts the next increments to improve adoption.
Why not the others: continuing as planned assumes adoption will come by itself; reporting on track confuses delivered outputs with outcomes; mandating logins creates activity, not real use.
Remember: Deliverable → Outcome → Benefit → Value. Deployment ≠ adoption.

questions.stem: A hybrid AI customer-support platform installs its infrastructure on a predictive plan and builds customer channels in iterations. It must support the company's strategic goal of cutting support costs by 20 percent. Half the team wants a new voice-assistant channel, and the other half wants to improve chat self-service. Only one can be funded this quarter. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the team to vote and fund whichever option gets the most support from the members of the project team.
Let the most senior engineer choose, because she understands the platform's technical constraints the best.
Have the team and product owner compare both options against the cost-reduction goal in the business case.
Split the funding between both options so each part of the team can begin work on its preferred approach.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Evaluating options against strategy — when only one option can be funded, compare each against the strategic objective in the business case.
Spot it: 'strategic goal of cutting support costs by 20 percent', a split team, 'only one can be funded'.
In this scenario: the team and product owner compare both channels by how much each contributes to the cost-reduction goal in the business case.
Why not the others: a vote measures popularity, not strategic fit; seniority is not a value criterion; splitting the funding may leave both options too small to deliver.
Remember: WHY = Business case. Choose by strategic value, not by votes or rank.

questions.stem: A hybrid e-commerce fulfillment redesign introduces automated picking in three warehouses. Supervisor resistance, rated low early on, has grown, and at a steering committee review supervisors say they do not understand why the company is making the change. What should the project manager do?
options: Tell the supervisors that the change is final and that performance reviews will track adoption.
Send the supervisors a detailed technical guide explaining how the automated picking system works.
Pause the automated picking rollout until every supervisor states support for the new picking process.
Ask the sponsor to explain the business reasons for the change to supervisors and to hear their concerns.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sponsor-led change communication — people need to understand WHY a change is happening, and a visible sponsor is the strongest voice for that message.
Spot it: resistance 'has grown', supervisors 'do not understand why the company is making the change'.
In this scenario: the gap is awareness of the business reasons, so the PM asks the sponsor to explain the reasons and listen to the supervisors' concerns.
Why not the others: threats about performance reviews increase resistance; a technical guide explains HOW, not WHY; pausing until every supervisor agrees gives up the change.
Remember: People resist before processes fail. Explain WHY before HOW.

questions.stem: A hybrid retail transformation team is adding sustainability measures to its business case. Match each sustainability concept with its description.
matching_right: Environmental, social, and governance criteria used to assess organizations
Keeps materials in use through reuse, repair, and recycling
Measures performance by people, planet, and profit outcomes
Indirect emissions from the supply chain and use of products
Total greenhouse gases caused directly and indirectly by an activity

answer.Triple bottom line: Measures performance by people, planet, and profit outcomes
answer.ESG: Environmental, social, and governance criteria used to assess organizations
answer.Carbon footprint: Total greenhouse gases caused directly and indirectly by an activity
answer.Circular economy: Keeps materials in use through reuse, repair, and recycling
answer.Scope 3 emissions: Indirect emissions from the supply chain and use of products

questions.explanation:
Concept: Sustainability terms let a business case measure value beyond profit.
Triple bottom line: success measured by people, planet and profit together.
ESG: environmental, social and governance criteria used to judge organizations and investments.
Carbon footprint: total greenhouse gases an activity causes, directly and indirectly.
Circular economy: keeps materials in use through reuse, repair and recycling.
Scope 3 emissions: indirect emissions across the supply chain and product use.
Remember: Sustainability = environmental + social + economic, not just 'green'. Think lifecycle, not just delivery.

questions.stem: On a hybrid financial reporting modernization, a regulatory filing is due in five days. The adaptive reporting team wants to use the company's approved AI tool to draft the filing narratives. Company policy allows AI drafting only when a qualified person reviews the content and remains accountable for it. What should the project manager do?
options: Allow AI drafting with review and sign-off by a qualified accountant, and record the AI use as policy requires.
Submit the AI-drafted narratives directly, since the tool is approved and the filing deadline is only days away.
Ban AI drafting for the filing, because regulatory documents must always be written entirely by people.
Wait for the policy team to issue new AI guidance for filings before deciding whether AI can be used.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Human accountability for AI output — approved AI tools can speed work when a qualified person reviews the content and remains accountable, as policy requires.
Spot it: 'approved AI tool', policy allows AI drafting 'only when a qualified person reviews' it.
In this scenario: the policy already covers this use, so the PM allows AI drafting with review and sign-off by a qualified accountant and records the AI use.
Why not the others: submitting unreviewed output breaks the accountability rule; banning an approved tool ignores the policy; waiting for new guidance delays work the current policy already permits.
Remember: AI recommends, humans decide. Approved tool + validation + human sign-off.

questions.stem: A hybrid state-government digital service builds its citizen portal in iterations and its identity infrastructure on a predictive plan. At a stakeholder workshop the team learns that a proposed federal rule may require stronger identity verification, but the final rule is not expected for four months. What should the project manager do?
options: Build the proposed identity requirements right away so the service is ready if the rule becomes final.
Add the rule to the risk register with an owner who tracks the rulemaking, and define response triggers.
Ignore the proposed rule until it is final, because draft rules often change before they take effect.
Submit a change request to add the proposed requirements to the identity infrastructure baseline now.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Proposed rules are risks — an uncertain future external change is managed in the risk register with an owner and triggers, not built in early.
Spot it: 'proposed federal rule', 'may require', 'final rule is not expected for four months'.
In this scenario: the PM records the rule as a risk with an owner who tracks the rulemaking and defines triggers that start the response.
Why not the others: building it now commits effort to a rule that may change; baselining it now does the same through formal control; ignoring it leaves the project unprepared.
Remember: MAY happen = Risk register. HAS happened = issue or change. Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor.

questions.stem: At a sprint review on an agile data-governance product, stakeholders want a new data-quality service released to production this week. The IT operations team that must support it has not been involved, and the organization requires operational readiness sign-off for new services. What should the project manager do?
options: Release the service this week and give IT operations the support documentation shortly after it goes live.
Have the development team support the service in production itself so that IT operations need not be involved.
Postpone the release until next quarter so IT operations can run its full formal review of the new service.
Bring IT operations in now to meet the readiness criteria and add support needs to the definition of done.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Operational readiness in agile — operations teams must be involved early, and support needs can be part of the definition of done.
Spot it: 'IT operations team that must support it has not been involved', 'requires operational readiness sign-off'.
In this scenario: the PM brings IT operations in now to meet readiness criteria and adds support needs to the definition of done so future releases are ready too.
Why not the others: releasing first and documenting later skips required sign-off; developers running production themselves avoids operations instead of preparing them; waiting a full quarter overreacts.
Remember: Done means SUPPORTABLE. Operations must be ready to own it.

questions.stem: A hybrid robotics deployment uses predictive phase gates for plant commissioning, while its control software is built in iterations. A newly assigned team lead asks who has authority over the project's key artifacts. Match each artifact with who owns or approves it.
matching_right: Set by the product owner based on value
Owned and updated by the developers doing the work
Issued and approved by the sponsor, authorizing the project manager
Maintained by the project manager together with the risk owners
Approved or rejected by the change control board

answer.Project charter: Issued and approved by the sponsor, authorizing the project manager
answer.Changes to the schedule baseline: Approved or rejected by the change control board
answer.Product backlog order: Set by the product owner based on value
answer.Iteration backlog: Owned and updated by the developers doing the work
answer.Risk register: Maintained by the project manager together with the risk owners

questions.explanation:
Concept: Artifact authority — for every artifact, know who creates it, who approves it and who can update it; this is how PMI tests governance.
Project charter: issued and approved by the sponsor; it authorizes the project and the PM.
Changes to the schedule baseline: the change control board approves or rejects; the PM cannot change a baseline alone.
Product backlog order: the product owner orders it by value.
Iteration backlog: owned by the developers; they plan and adjust it to meet the iteration goal.
Risk register: a living document the PM maintains with risk owners.
Remember: Sponsor AUTHORIZES, CCB APPROVES baselines, product owner ORDERS, developers OWN their plan, PM TRACKS registers and logs.

questions.stem: During a compliance review on a predictive healthcare analytics implementation, testing shows that audit logging captures only 80 percent of the patient-data access events the regulation requires. Go-live is four weeks away, and the business wants to keep the date. What should the project manager do?
options: Go live as planned and fix the remaining audit logging gaps in the first maintenance release.
Log the gap as a compliance nonconformance and plan corrective action to close it before go-live.
Ask the compliance office for a waiver on the missing events so that the go-live date is kept.
Accept 80 percent coverage as sufficient, since most patient-data access events are logged.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Compliance nonconformance — a regulatory requirement must be fully met; a gap is recorded and corrected before go-live.
Spot it: 'only 80 percent' of required events logged, 'the business wants to keep the date'.
In this scenario: the PM logs the gap as a nonconformance and plans corrective action to close it before go-live.
Why not the others: going live and fixing it later knowingly operates out of compliance; a waiver tries to trade away a mandatory rule; 80 percent coverage does not meet a 100 percent requirement.
Remember: Mandatory beats optional. Partly compliant = not compliant.

questions.stem: A hybrid supply-chain resilience initiative is delivering its planned outputs on schedule. At a quarterly benefits review, data shows use of the supplier-risk dashboard has dropped because market conditions changed, and the business case benefits now look overstated. What should the project manager do?
options: Present an updated benefits forecast to the sponsor so they can decide to continue, change, or stop the work.
Continue the remaining work as planned, since the project is delivering its outputs on time and on budget.
Add more dashboard features to raise usage before telling the sponsor that the benefits look overstated.
Stop the remaining dashboard work now, since the benefits in the business case no longer appear achievable.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Revisiting the business case — when expected benefits change, the sponsor, who owns the business case, decides whether to continue, change or stop.
Spot it: outputs 'on schedule' but benefits 'now look overstated' due to market change.
In this scenario: the PM presents an updated benefits forecast so the sponsor can make an informed decision.
Why not the others: delivering on time does not guarantee value; adding features before telling the sponsor delays a needed decision; stopping the work is beyond the PM's authority.
Remember: WHY = Business case, owned by the sponsor. On time ≠ valuable.

questions.stem: The software supplier for an agile customer-data platform announces at a portfolio checkpoint that its license fees will triple next year. The product's business case assumed the old fees, and the new cost would erase most of the expected return. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Continue building all planned features, since the business case was approved when the project was started.
Update the business case with the new license cost and review it with the sponsor at the portfolio checkpoint.
Sign the supplier's new license terms quickly so the team's delivery schedule is not affected by negotiations.
Leave the new license cost out of the portfolio review until the team has finished the current release cycle.
Have the product owner reorder the backlog toward features that still deliver value under the revised cost.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Business case changes in agile — a major cost change is reflected in the business case and reviewed with the sponsor and portfolio, and the backlog is reordered toward what still creates value.
Spot it: fees 'will triple', would 'erase most of the expected return', a 'portfolio checkpoint'.
In this scenario: the PM updates the business case and reviews it with the sponsor, and the product owner reorders the backlog toward features still valuable under the new cost.
Why not the others: an earlier approval does not freeze the case; signing new terms quickly gives away negotiating power; hiding the cost from the portfolio review undermines governance.
Remember: WHY changes → Business case changes → Priorities change. Transparency with governance.

questions.stem: The supplier on a predictive AI customer-support platform reports at a transition-to-operations workshop that it will not provide first-line support after go-live, which the plan had assumed. The internal service desk must take over, but its agents have never supported AI tools. Go-live is in six weeks. What should the project manager do?
options: Work with service desk managers to plan training and knowledge transfer and update the transition plan.
Delay go-live until the supplier agrees to provide first-line support as the original plan assumed.
Launch on schedule and let the service desk learn to support the platform as customer tickets arrive.
Have the project team take over first-line support permanently so the service desk is not affected.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Organizational readiness for handover — the people who will operate the product must be prepared through training and knowledge transfer built into the transition plan.
Spot it: supplier 'will not provide first-line support', internal desk 'never supported AI tools', 'six weeks'.
In this scenario: the PM works with service desk managers on training and knowledge transfer and updates the transition plan.
Why not the others: delaying go-live to force the supplier ignores the fact it has declined; learning on live tickets pushes risk onto customers; a temporary project team cannot give permanent support.
Remember: Assess readiness → Engage → Train → Implement → Reinforce. Projects are temporary; operations owns the product.

questions.stem: A hybrid cloud migration was justified partly by the energy savings of closing the company's data center. Migration waves are on schedule, but at a stakeholder workshop the sustainability lead shows that migrated workloads are heavily overprovisioned, so expected energy savings are shrinking. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue the migration waves as planned, since the benefit review is scheduled after all waves close.
Work with operations to right-size migrated workloads and track the energy metric in each later wave.
Report the energy benefit as achieved, because the workloads were moved out of the data center as planned.
Pause all remaining migration waves until the sustainability lead approves a new energy-savings target.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Managing sustainability benefits — energy savings are benefits like any other; find the cause of a shortfall, correct it and track the metric as work continues.
Spot it: 'justified partly by the energy savings', workloads 'heavily overprovisioned', savings 'shrinking'.
In this scenario: the PM works with operations to right-size migrated workloads and tracks the energy metric in each later wave.
Why not the others: waiting for the final review lets the loss grow; reporting the benefit as achieved confuses migration with savings; pausing all waves overreacts to a fixable cause.
Remember: Deliverable ≠ benefit. Measure benefits as you go and fix the cause early.

questions.stem: During usability testing on a predictive medical-device project, clinicians accepted the device's AI diagnostic suggestions without checking them, even when the suggestions were wrong. The design baseline shows suggestions without any confidence level or confirmation step. What should the project manager do?
options: Add a warning to the user manual that clinicians should check every AI suggestion before they rely on it.
Keep the design as baselined, since clinicians remain responsible for every diagnosis they make with the device.
Submit a change request to add confidence levels and a required clinician confirmation step to the design.
Remove the AI suggestions from the device entirely so that clinicians cannot rely on them in their diagnoses.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Human-in-the-loop AI design — show how reliable each AI output is and require a human confirmation step; changes to a baselined design go through change control.
Spot it: clinicians 'accepted AI suggestions without checking', no 'confidence level or confirmation step', 'design baseline'.
In this scenario: the PM submits a change request to add confidence levels and a required clinician confirmation step.
Why not the others: a manual warning does not change behavior seen in testing; keeping the design ignores a proven safety risk; removing AI entirely throws away value when the risk can be controlled.
Remember: AI recommends, humans decide. Baseline change → change request.

questions.stem: An agile smart-city team learns during a vendor escalation meeting that its traffic-sensor supplier is going out of business. Half the team wants to switch to a competitor's sensors, and the other half wants to build a sensor interface in-house. Which TWO actions should the project manager take?
options: Stop all work on the project until a replacement sensor supplier has been selected and contracted.
Let the team vote on the two options right away so work can resume without any further analysis.
Plan a short spike to compare the integration effort of competitor sensors with an in-house interface.
Keep building against the current supplier's interface until its products are no longer available.
Work with the product owner to reorder the affected backlog items based on the spike findings.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Evidence-based decisions in agile — when options are uncertain, a spike produces evidence, and the product owner reorders the backlog from what was learned.
Spot it: supplier 'going out of business', team split between two options, no data yet.
In this scenario: a short spike compares integration effort for competitor sensors vs an in-house interface, and the product owner then reorders the affected backlog items.
Why not the others: stopping all work halts unaffected value; a vote without data does not reduce uncertainty; building against a failing supplier's interface creates waste.
Remember: Uncertain? SPIKE it. Learn → reorder the backlog → deliver.

questions.stem: A hybrid HRIS implementation and an unrelated office relocation project in the same portfolio both need the company's only network architect in May. The relocation project has just moved its dates, creating the conflict. Neither project manager has authority over the other's plan. What should the project manager do?
options: Book the network architect for May right away, before the relocation project manager can request the time.
Ask the network architect to split time evenly between both projects throughout the month of May.
Delay the HRIS work that needs the architect until June without discussing it with the relocation project.
Raise the resource conflict with portfolio management so it can be resolved based on strategic priority.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Portfolio resource balancing — when unrelated projects compete for a scarce resource, portfolio management decides based on strategic priority.
Spot it: 'unrelated' projects in the 'same portfolio', 'only network architect', neither PM has authority over the other.
In this scenario: the PM raises the conflict with portfolio management so it is resolved by which project matters more strategically.
Why not the others: booking first is a race, not a decision; splitting time evenly may harm both projects; delaying without discussing it hides the impact.
Remember: Project → Program → Portfolio. Shared resource conflicts across projects go to the level that owns STRATEGY.

questions.stem: A predictive customer-data platform spans business units that use different organizational structures. The steering committee is reviewing how much decision authority each unit's project manager will have. Match each organizational structure with the project manager's typical authority.
matching_right: High to almost total authority over resources and budget
Authority shared roughly equally with functional managers
Little or no authority; the functional manager controls resources and budget
Moderate to high authority, with a full-time project manager
Limited authority; the project manager acts mainly as a coordinator

answer.Functional: Little or no authority; the functional manager controls resources and budget
answer.Weak matrix: Limited authority; the project manager acts mainly as a coordinator
answer.Balanced matrix: Authority shared roughly equally with functional managers
answer.Strong matrix: Moderate to high authority, with a full-time project manager
answer.Projectized: High to almost total authority over resources and budget

questions.explanation:
Concept: PM authority grows as the organization moves from functional to projectized, so the same decision may need a functional manager in one structure and not in another.
Functional: the functional manager controls resources and budget; the PM has little or no authority.
Weak matrix: the PM is mainly a coordinator or expediter with limited authority.
Balanced matrix: authority is shared about equally with functional managers.
Strong matrix: a full-time PM with moderate to high authority and project staff.
Projectized: the PM has high to almost total authority over resources and budget.
Remember: Functional → Weak → Balanced → Strong → Projectized = PM authority RISES.

questions.stem: Match each procurement document with its purpose.
matching_right: Asks sellers to propose a solution to a complex need.
Describes the work the seller must deliver.
Formal sealed-bid request, usually awarded on lowest price.
Gathers information about seller capabilities before buying.
Asks for a price for a well-defined item.

answer.Request for information (RFI): Gathers information about seller capabilities before buying.
answer.Request for quotation (RFQ): Asks for a price for a well-defined item.
answer.Request for proposal (RFP): Asks sellers to propose a solution to a complex need.
answer.Invitation for bid (IFB): Formal sealed-bid request, usually awarded on lowest price.
answer.Statement of work (SOW): Describes the work the seller must deliver.

questions.explanation:
Concept: Procurement documents move from research to award: learn the market, ask for prices or proposals, then bind the seller to a clear statement of work.
Request for information (RFI): Research only; you are not asking for a price or a solution yet.
Request for quotation (RFQ): Scope is clear; price is the main decision factor.
Request for proposal (RFP): You describe the problem; sellers propose HOW, with price.
Invitation for bid (IFB): Common in public sector procurement with fully defined scope.
Statement of work (SOW): Becomes part of the contract; vague SOW = disputes later.
Remember: RFI = Information • RFQ = Price • RFP = Solution • IFB = Formal bid • SOW = the work itself. SELLER artifacts are legal: change them only through the contract.

questions.stem: A sales director at a logistics software company emails two developers asking them to move her reporting feature ahead of the work planned for the next sprint. The developers ask the agile project lead what to do. The product owner has not seen the request. What should the project lead do FIRST?
options: Direct the sales director to the product owner, who decides where the reporting feature ranks.
Have the developers pull the feature into the current sprint since the director is a senior stakeholder.
Rank the reporting feature yourself against other items and inform the product owner afterward.
Ask the developers to vote on whether the reporting feature should displace their planned work.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Value ownership — in agile, the product owner is the single person who orders the backlog by value; everyone else brings requests to the product owner (Rule M3-B12-R01).
Spot it: A stakeholder goes straight to developers, "move my feature up," and the product owner "has not seen the request."
In this scenario: The lead's first job is to route the sales director to the product owner, who weighs her feature against everything else and decides where it ranks.
Why not the others: Pulling it into the sprint lets rank, not value, set priority; ranking it yourself takes over the product owner's accountability; a developer vote hands a value decision to the people who decide HOW, not WHAT.
Remember: Product owner decides WHAT and in what order; the team decides HOW.

questions.stem: During sprint planning for a hospital scheduling app, developers select five items that support the sprint goal. A newly assigned functional manager then sends them a detailed task breakdown with hour assignments for each developer. Several developers are visibly frustrated. What should the agile project manager do?
options: Adopt the manager's task breakdown because it creates clearer accountability for each developer.
Explain to the manager that the developers decide how to complete the selected work, and invite his input as needed.
Ask the product owner to review and approve the manager's hour assignments before the developers begin any work.
Use the manager's breakdown for half of the selected items and let the developers plan the others.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Self-organizing team — once developers select work for a sprint, they decide how to accomplish it within the agreed constraints (Rule M3-B12-R02).
Spot it: Someone outside the team hands developers a task breakdown with hour assignments, and the team is frustrated.
In this scenario: The agile PM acts as a servant leader: explains to the manager that the developers own the plan for the selected work and channels his knowledge in as input, not orders.
Why not the others: Adopting his breakdown is command-and-control micromanagement; the product owner owns what and in what order, not task assignments; splitting half and half still takes the how away from the team.
Remember: PO = WHAT, Team = HOW, Servant leader = protects the HOW.

questions.stem: An insurance company's agile team waits two to three days for a separate database group to approve every schema change, and items pile up in the blocked column. Some developers have started quietly working around the approval step. As the team's scrum master, what is the BEST action?
options: Let the developers continue the workarounds since they keep items moving toward completion.
Report the database group's delays to the product owner and ask for the sprint scope to shrink.
Work with the database group's lead to streamline or embed the approval so items stop queuing.
Assign one developer to chase approvals full time so the others can keep building features.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Scrum master as flow coach — the scrum master removes impediments and improves the whole system around the team, including handoffs with other groups (Rule M3-B12-R03).
Spot it: Work "piles up in the blocked column," people wait days on an outside group, and workarounds start appearing.
In this scenario: The best move is to work with the database group's lead to streamline or embed the approval, so the bottleneck disappears at its source.
Why not the others: Workarounds hide the impediment and bypass a control; shrinking sprint scope accepts the blockage instead of fixing it; a full-time approval chaser treats the symptom and burns team capacity.
Remember: Servant leader removes obstacles — never waits, never ignores.

questions.stem: Midway through a two-week sprint, a fintech team learns that the payment API it planned to use cannot process refunds. An alternative API would still let the team meet the sprint goal of letting customers request refunds online, but most of the planned tasks would change. What should the team do?
options: Cancel the sprint and restart planning since the original task plan is no longer valid.
Keep the original tasks and log the API limitation as technical debt to address in a later sprint.
Ask the product owner to replace the goal with one that fits the original list of tasks.
Replan the tasks around the alternative API while keeping the refund goal for this sprint.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stable goal, flexible plan — the sprint goal is the commitment; the detailed tasks are just the team's current best plan and may change as it learns (Rule M3-B12-R04).
Spot it: Mid-sprint, the planned approach breaks, but "an alternative would still let the team meet the sprint goal."
In this scenario: The team replans its tasks around the alternative API and keeps delivering the refund goal this sprint.
Why not the others: Cancelling is only for a goal that has become obsolete, and this one hasn't; keeping the old tasks ignores what the team just learned; rewriting the goal to fit old tasks puts the plan above the value.
Remember: Goal = WHY of the sprint (stable); Tasks = HOW (adapt).

questions.stem: A product owner for an e-learning platform wants refinement sessions to produce fully detailed, signed-off requirements for every item planned over the next six months so that nothing changes later. The developers worry this will consume most of their capacity. What should the agile coach recommend?
options: Support the six-month detail so the team can commit to a fixed release plan and date with the sponsor.
Detail the near-term items and keep later items coarse so they can still change as the team learns.
Stop refinement and let developers clarify each item on the day it enters a sprint instead.
Move refinement to a separate analyst group so the developers' capacity is not affected.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Backlog refinement — an ongoing activity that makes near-term items clear enough to start, while later items stay coarse so they can still change (Rule M3-B12-R05).
Spot it: A request to fully detail and sign off six months of work "so that nothing changes later."
In this scenario: The coach recommends progressive elaboration: detail what is coming next and keep future items rough until the team learns more.
Why not the others: Six months of signed-off detail is predictive big-design-up-front inside an agile team; dropping refinement means items arrive unclear; handing it to analysts removes developer understanding and still aims to freeze scope.
Remember: Refine to CLARIFY, not to FREEZE — just enough, just in time.

questions.stem: A retail analytics team's daily meeting, meant to last 15 minutes, now runs 45 minutes because each member gives a detailed status report to the project manager, who records hours against each task. Blockers are rarely mentioned. What should the project manager do?
options: Extend the time box to 45 minutes officially so the detailed status reports can continue without rushing.
Replace the meeting with written status reports sent to the project manager each morning.
Ask each member to report only hours spent per task so the meeting finishes on time.
Refocus the meeting on progress toward the sprint goal and blockers, and take detail offline.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Daily coordination — the daily scrum is the team's short event to inspect progress toward the sprint goal and surface blockers; it is not a status report to a manager (Rule M3-B12-R06).
Spot it: A 15-minute meeting running 45 minutes, members reporting to the PM, hours recorded, and "blockers are rarely mentioned."
In this scenario: The PM refocuses the meeting on progress toward the goal and obstacles, and takes detailed discussion offline after the time box.
Why not the others: Extending the time box legitimizes status reporting; written reports remove the team's coordination; reporting only hours keeps the focus on tracking effort instead of the goal.
Remember: Daily scrum = Goal + Blockers, 15 minutes, for the team.

questions.stem: At the end of an increment, a team building a warehouse robot control dashboard plans to show stakeholders a slide deck summarizing completed stories and percent complete. Two operations supervisors who will use the dashboard every day are attending. What should the agile lead suggest instead?
options: Have the supervisors try the working dashboard and capture their feedback for the product owner.
Keep the slides but add a detailed burndown chart so stakeholders can see progress clearly.
Cancel the session and send the supervisors a recorded video of the features to approve.
Use the session to obtain stakeholder sign-off on all remaining scope so future sprints are locked in.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sprint review / demo — stakeholders inspect the working product and give feedback that shapes what comes next (Rule M3-B12-R07).
Spot it: A plan to show slides and percent complete while real users of the product are in the room.
In this scenario: The lead suggests letting the supervisors use the working dashboard and capturing their feedback for the product owner to act on.
Why not the others: A burndown chart still reports progress rather than showing the product; a recorded video removes the live conversation; a review is for inspecting and adapting, not locking future scope with sign-off.
Remember: Review = inspect the PRODUCT; Retrospective = improve the PROCESS.

questions.stem: A mobile banking team repeatedly misses its sprint commitments because code reviews stack up in the last two days of each sprint. The product owner suggests adding a code-review status item to every sprint review with stakeholders. What should the scrum master recommend?
options: Add the status item to the sprint review so stakeholders can pressure the team to improve.
Assign a senior developer to approve every code review so the rest of the team stops waiting on each other.
Raise the review bottleneck at the retrospective so the team can agree on a change in how it works.
Report the missed commitments to functional managers so they can coach their developers.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Retrospective — the team's own event to inspect and improve how it works, the right home for a recurring process bottleneck (Rule M3-B12-R08).
Spot it: A repeating internal problem, "code reviews stack up" every sprint, and someone proposing to report it to stakeholders.
In this scenario: The scrum master brings the bottleneck to the retrospective so the team itself agrees on a change to its way of working.
Why not the others: The sprint review is for inspecting the product with stakeholders, not applying pressure; one senior approver is imposed and creates a new single point of delay; reporting to functional managers blames people for a process problem.
Remember: RETROSPECTIVE fixes agile process problems.

questions.stem: On a bridge rehabilitation project, a structural drafter has submitted three drawing packages late and with errors. The project manager has not yet discussed the problem with him. The drafter's functional manager asks whether there is anything to be concerned about. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Meet privately with the drafter to learn the cause and agree on specific support and expectations.
Tell the functional manager about the late packages and request a replacement drafter.
Reassign the remaining drawing packages to another drafter without discussing it with him.
Record the errors in the issue log and notify human resources about the drafter's declining performance.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Performance issues — the PM first gives direct, private feedback and support; escalation comes only if the problem persists after that (Rule M3-B03-R09).
Spot it: Repeated late or poor work and "the PM has not yet discussed the problem with him."
In this scenario: The first step is a private one-on-one with the drafter to learn the cause and agree on support and clear expectations.
Why not the others: Asking for a replacement escalates before the drafter had any chance; reassigning his work silently avoids the conversation; logging it and notifying HR documents instead of acting and jumps to a formal route.
Remember: Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act → Monitor → Escalate. Talk to the person first.

questions.stem: A hybrid ERP rollout team sends a weekly newsletter asking plant supervisors to test new inventory screens in a sandbox before each release. Open rates are high, but sandbox logs show almost no supervisor logins. The adaptive build team depends on their feedback. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Send the newsletter twice a week so the testing request stays more visible to supervisors.
Talk with several supervisors to learn why the newsletter is not prompting testing, then adjust.
Report the high open rates as evidence that communication with supervisors is effective.
Ask the plant manager to add sandbox testing as a requirement in each supervisor's annual objectives.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Communication effectiveness — communication is measured by whether it produces the intended action or decision, not by whether it was sent or opened (Rule M3-B07-R10).
Spot it: "Open rates are high" but the behavior you wanted (sandbox logins) is almost zero.
In this scenario: The PM talks with several supervisors to find out why the newsletter doesn't lead to testing, then adjusts the method or message.
Why not the others: Sending it more often repeats what already isn't working; reporting open rates as success confuses activity with outcome; mandating testing through objectives escalates before the cause is known.
Remember: Sent is not received; received is not acted on — check the result.

questions.stem: Two developers on a telehealth app team have argued in three consecutive planning sessions about whether to use a third-party video library. The rest of the team has gone quiet during these debates. The scrum master has not yet spoken with either developer about the disagreement. What should the scrum master do FIRST?
options: Ask the product owner to choose the video library so that the team can move on with the rest of its planning.
Suggest that each developer build half of the feature so both approaches can be compared.
Talk with both developers to understand what each is concerned about and what drives the dispute.
Set a rule that future library choices will be settled by a majority vote of the team.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Conflict diagnosis — understand the source and nature of a conflict before choosing a resolution mode (Rule M3-B01-R01).
Spot it: A repeating disagreement and "the scrum master has not yet spoken with either developer."
In this scenario: The first step is to talk with both developers to learn what each is worried about and what really drives the dispute.
Why not the others: Having the product owner pick forces an outcome on a technical how question without understanding it; building half each is a compromise chosen blind; a majority-vote rule is a process fix before the cause is known.
Remember: ASSESS before you ACT — diagnose, then pick the conflict mode.

questions.stem: The electrical lead on a data center construction project wants to delay cable tray installation until equipment layouts are confirmed. The mechanical lead wants trays installed now to protect the cooling work. Both hold useful information, tray work has two weeks of float, and both leads respect each other. What should the project manager do?
options: Decide in favor of the mechanical lead because the cooling work is on the project's critical path.
Have each lead give up part of their position by installing only half of the trays now.
