Postpone the discussion until the equipment vendor has confirmed the final layouts.
Bring both leads together to work through the layout data and agree on an approach both support.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Collaborate / problem-solve — the win-win mode, best when there is time, trust, and shared information to reach a lasting solution (Rule M3-B01-R02).
Spot it: Both sides "hold useful information," there is float (time), and they "respect each other."
In this scenario: The PM brings both leads together to work through the layout data and agree on an approach both can support.
Why not the others: Deciding for one side is forcing when there's no urgency; installing half the trays is a compromise (lose-lose) when a better answer is reachable; postponing is withdrawing from a solvable problem.
Remember: Collaborate = win-win, the default exam answer when time and trust exist.

questions.stem: The adaptive software team and the predictive hardware team on a hybrid project both need the only environmental test chamber next week. Both needs are legitimate, neither team can have the full week without hurting the other's milestone, and a second chamber arrives in three weeks. There is no time for extended problem-solving. What is the BEST approach?
options: Give the hardware team the full week because predictive milestones carry contractual commitments.
Negotiate a split of chamber time so each team covers its most critical tests until the second one arrives.
Hold a multi-day workshop to redesign both teams' test strategies before anyone is assigned the chamber.
Let the teams sort out the schedule themselves and step in only if it reaches the sponsor.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Compromise — each side gives up something; best when both needs are valid, time is short, and a temporary trade-off is acceptable (Rule M3-B01-R03).
Spot it: "No time for extended problem-solving," both needs legitimate, and the constraint ends soon (a second chamber arrives).
In this scenario: The PM negotiates a split of chamber time so each team covers its most critical tests until the extra chamber arrives.
Why not the others: Giving one team the full week is forcing; a multi-day workshop is collaboration the calendar can't afford; leaving the teams to sort it out is withdrawing from a PM coordination duty.
Remember: Compromise = both give a little, for now — short time, temporary fix.

questions.stem: A newly hired UX designer on an agile team for a nonprofit donation site prefers a teal button, while a senior developer prefers dark blue. Usability testing showed no difference between the two colors, and the designer has rarely spoken up since joining. What is the BEST way for the senior developer to handle the disagreement?
options: Ask the product owner to pick the color so that neither team member has to back down.
Run another round of usability testing with more users to find out which color performs better overall.
Propose using each color on alternate pages so each person gets part of what they want.
Go with the designer's color choice and use the moment to build trust with the new colleague.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Accommodate / smooth — yield on the issue when it matters little and the relationship matters more (Rule M3-B01-R04).
Spot it: Testing showed "no difference," and the other person is new and "has rarely spoken up."
In this scenario: The senior developer goes with the designer's color and uses the moment to build trust with a new colleague.
Why not the others: Sending it to the product owner escalates a trivial issue; more testing spends effort on a question data already answered; alternating colors is a compromise that also hurts design consistency.
Remember: Low stakes + high relationship value = accommodate.

questions.stem: During a chemical plant turnaround, two crew supervisors are arguing about who should isolate a pressurized line first. An operator reports that the pressure gauge is rising toward the relief threshold. The project manager holds site safety authority. What should the project manager do?
options: Direct the isolation sequence under site safety authority and address the dispute afterward.
Bring both supervisors together to explore their concerns until they reach a shared solution.
Suggest each supervisor isolate part of the line so both feel their approach was followed.
Escalate the disagreement to the plant manager and wait for guidance on who should proceed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Force / direct — use authority to decide when urgency, safety, or legitimate authority requires it; it is the exception, not the default (Rule M3-B01-R05).
Spot it: Safety words such as "pressure rising toward the relief threshold," plus the PM "holds site safety authority."
In this scenario: The PM directs the isolation sequence now and deals with the supervisors' dispute once the hazard is controlled.
Why not the others: Collaboration is ideal normally, but there is no time during a hazard; splitting the work is a compromise that could worsen the danger; escalating and waiting delays a decision the PM is authorized to make.
Remember: Safety or emergency = direct first, discuss later.

questions.stem: At the end of a long hybrid planning session, two leads begin arguing heatedly about a component's vendor delivery date. The vendor will confirm its revised date by email tomorrow morning, and nothing can be decided until then. Both leads are visibly tired and frustrated. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep both leads in the room tonight until they agree on an assumed date to use for all planning.
Choose a delivery date now from the vendor's last estimate to end the argument quickly.
Pause the discussion and reconvene tomorrow once the vendor has confirmed the revised date.
Ask each lead to accept a midpoint between their dates so planning can continue tonight.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Withdraw / avoid — step back when the issue can't be decided yet, information is missing, or people need to cool off (Rule M3-B01-R06).
Spot it: "Nothing can be decided until" new information arrives tomorrow, and both leads are "tired and frustrated."
In this scenario: The PM pauses the discussion and reconvenes tomorrow once the vendor confirms the date.
Why not the others: Keeping them in the room forces agreement on an assumption that will be replaced; picking a date now is forcing on stale data; a midpoint is a compromise on a number the vendor will soon supply.
Remember: Withdraw is usually the weakest mode, unless the answer is coming anyway or tempers need cooling.

questions.stem: A product owner and a tester on a travel booking team are in conflict. The product owner says the tester always blocks releases, while the tester says the product owner does not care about quality. The scrum master notices each person mixes complaints, guesses about the other's motives, and a few real defect counts. How should the scrum master approach the analysis?
options: Help both sort out what is verified, what is assumed, what each needs, and how each feels.
Focus only on the objective defect counts and set aside all of the personal complaints as irrelevant.
Ask each person to write down their grievances for their functional managers to review.
Encourage the tester to accept release decisions since the product owner sets priorities.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Conflict analysis — separate facts, assumptions, interests, and emotions so the real issue becomes visible (Rule M3-B01-R07).
Spot it: A mix of complaints, "guesses about the other's motives," and "a few real defect counts."
In this scenario: The scrum master helps both sort what is verified, what is assumed, what each actually needs, and how each feels.
Why not the others: Looking only at defect counts ignores the interests and feelings driving the conflict; writing grievances for managers escalates and hardens positions; telling the tester to accept decisions is forcing and dismisses her quality concern.
Remember: Facts, assumptions, interests, emotions — untangle before you resolve.

questions.stem: Two design engineers on an aircraft cabin retrofit project disagree about which seat-rail specification to follow. One emails the project sponsor directly asking for a ruling. The project manager has not been involved yet, and the issue does not affect any approved baseline. What should the project manager do?
options: Wait for the sponsor's ruling since the engineer has already raised the issue at that level.
Meet with both engineers to review the specification question and resolve it at the working level.
Submit the specification disagreement to the change control board so it can issue a formal decision.
Ask the engineering functional manager to decide which specification the team should use.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Resolve at the source — conflicts are handled as close to the people involved as practical before escalating (Rule M3-B01-R08).
Spot it: A working-level disagreement jumped straight to the sponsor, and "no approved baseline" is affected.
In this scenario: The PM meets both engineers and resolves the specification question at the working level.
Why not the others: Waiting for the sponsor accepts a skipped level; the change control board handles baseline changes, and none is affected; handing it to the functional manager escalates what the PM can facilitate.
Remember: Escalate LAST — team level first, then PM, then sponsor.

questions.stem: A hybrid team developing a medical device firmware update learns that a new component may fail a regulatory test, with a 30% chance of delaying market launch by four months. The team's authority covers scope trade-offs within an increment, and the sponsor accepts launch delays of no more than one month. What should the project manager do?
options: Add extra testing to the upcoming increments and continue to monitor the component risk within the team.
Record the risk in the register and revisit it once the regulatory test results are available.
Take the risk and possible responses to the sponsor, since the exposure exceeds what the team may accept.
Swap the component for an alternative now using the team's authority over scope trade-offs.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Escalation threshold — escalate uncertainty when its possible impact exceeds the team's authority or the organization's risk tolerance (Rule M3-B13-R09).
Spot it: A risk impact (four months) larger than the stated tolerance (one month), and limited team authority.
In this scenario: The PM takes the risk and response options to the sponsor, because the exposure is beyond what the team may accept.
Why not the others: Extra testing keeps inside the team a risk it can't own; recording and waiting leaves a high exposure unmanaged; swapping a regulated component exceeds the team's scope-trade-off authority.
Remember: Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor. Outside your tolerance or authority? Escalate to the owner.

questions.stem: In a sprint review, a senior stakeholder criticizes the team's new claims dashboard in front of other executives, calling it amateur work. The scrum master feels a surge of anger and starts to reply. What should the scrum master do FIRST?
options: Defend the team at once by listing the constraints that shaped the dashboard's design.
End the review early and ask to discuss the feedback privately with the stakeholder later that week.
Ask the product owner to respond since the product owner is accountable for the dashboard.
Notice the anger, pause briefly, and then ask which parts of the dashboard fall short for them.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Emotional intelligence, self-awareness — notice your own emotional reaction before you respond under pressure (Rule M3-B10-R01).
Spot it: Public criticism, and the leader "feels a surge of anger and starts to reply."
In this scenario: The scrum master notices the anger, pauses, and asks what exactly falls short, turning criticism into useful feedback.
Why not the others: Defending at once reacts emotionally and misses the feedback; ending the review early avoids the conversation; passing it to the product owner dodges the moment instead of managing yourself.
Remember: EQ starts inside — self-awareness, then self-management, then social skill.

questions.stem: A project manager leads a highway signage upgrade with engineers in the United States, Japan, and Brazil. A colleague says Japanese engineers never raise concerns in meetings, so there is no point asking. One Japanese engineer has raised issues openly by email but stays quiet on calls. What should the project manager do?
options: Stop seeking the Japanese engineers' input in meetings and rely on their managers' summaries.
Ask each engineer how they prefer to raise concerns and adjust channels based on their answers.
Require every engineer to raise concerns aloud on the calls so that the process is equal for everyone.
Move all technical discussion to written email only, since calls are not working for anyone.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Cultural awareness without stereotyping — adapt communication to cultural and individual preferences, and never assume a whole group behaves alike (Rule M3-B10-R02).
Spot it: A generalization ("they never raise concerns") contradicted by an individual who speaks up in writing.
In this scenario: The PM asks each engineer how they prefer to raise concerns and adjusts channels to fit.
Why not the others: Relying on managers' summaries acts on the stereotype; forcing everyone to speak on calls is equal but not fair; moving everything to email swaps one blanket rule for another.
Remember: Ask the person, don't assume the group.

questions.stem: In hybrid release planning for a utility billing system, a vice president and two senior architects dominate discussion. Junior developers and a customer service representative, who know the most about billing errors, rarely speak. The group must choose which defects to fix before a fixed-date regulatory release. What should the project manager do?
options: Let the vice president set the defect priorities since the regulatory release date is fixed.
Ask the junior staff to email their input after the meeting so that the live discussion stays efficient and short.
Leave the vice president out of future planning sessions so others have more room to speak.
Use a round-robin or silent input step so the developers and representative share views before debate.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Inclusive decision-making — deliberately create space for quieter or less powerful voices when their knowledge matters (Rule M3-B10-R03).
Spot it: Senior people dominate, while those who "know the most" rarely speak.
In this scenario: The PM uses a round-robin or silent input step so developers and the representative share their views before debate begins.
Why not the others: Letting the VP decide ignores the best-informed people; email afterward keeps them out of the real decision; excluding the VP loses a key stakeholder instead of balancing the room.
Remember: Balance the room — gather every voice before the loudest one decides.

questions.stem: A developer on a food delivery app team tells the agile lead she is overwhelmed because her father is seriously ill and asks to be excused from the on-call rotation for the next month. The team has a contractual 24/7 support obligation, and the rotation is already thin. What should the agile lead do?
options: Acknowledge her situation and work with the team to adjust the rotation while keeping 24/7 cover.
Explain that the support contract requires her to stay on the rotation as currently scheduled.
Excuse her from on-call duty and tell the client that support coverage will be reduced for the next month.
Suggest she take unpaid leave so the team can bring in a contractor to cover her shifts.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Empathy within constraints — understand and respond to a person's situation without dropping real obligations (Rule M3-B10-R04).
Spot it: A personal hardship request that collides with a firm constraint (a contractual 24/7 support duty).
In this scenario: The lead acknowledges her situation and works with the team to rebalance the rotation so she is relieved while 24/7 cover continues.
Why not the others: Holding her to the schedule shows no empathy; reducing coverage breaks the client contract; pushing unpaid leave is a unilateral HR decision that isn't the lead's to make.
Remember: Empathy + constraints: care for the person AND keep the commitment.

questions.stem: The senior architect on a hospital expansion project repeatedly interrupts a junior civil engineer during a design review and mocks her drainage calculations as student work. Others look uncomfortable, and the engineer stops presenting. What should the project manager do?
options: Let the comments pass because the architect is senior, and support the junior engineer privately after the meeting.
Report the architect to the sponsor and request that he be removed from future design reviews.
Step in during the meeting to restore respectful discussion, then speak with the architect privately.
Move the drainage calculations to a later review that the senior architect will not attend.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Respectful team norms — challenge disrespectful behavior promptly, whatever the person's seniority (Rule M3-B10-R05).
Spot it: Mocking in a meeting, others "look uncomfortable," and the target "stops presenting."
In this scenario: The PM steps in during the meeting to restore respect, then follows up privately with the architect.
Why not the others: Staying silent tells everyone the behavior is acceptable; going to the sponsor escalates before the PM has addressed it; moving her work avoids the problem and rewards the behavior.
Remember: Protect psychological safety in the moment; coach in private.

questions.stem: A hybrid team lead jokingly calls the testing group the department of no during a cross-team meeting. Two testers later tell the project manager they felt belittled. The lead says he meant it as friendly humor and is surprised anyone was hurt. What should the project manager do?
options: Help the lead see how the remark landed for the testers while recognizing he did not mean harm.
Accept the lead's explanation and advise the two testers not to take the remark quite so personally.
Issue a formal warning since the testers' reaction proves the remark was meant as hostile.
Keep the testers and the lead out of joint meetings for a while so tensions can settle.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Intent vs. impact — resolving interpersonal issues means recognizing both what someone meant and how it landed (Rule M3-B10-R06).
Spot it: "He meant it as friendly humor," yet the testers "felt belittled."
In this scenario: The PM helps the lead understand the impact on the testers while acknowledging he did not mean harm.
Why not the others: Accepting his explanation dismisses the real impact; a formal warning wrongly treats the impact as proof of hostile intent; separating them avoids the issue without repairing it.
Remember: Good intent doesn't erase impact — address both.

questions.stem: An agile team for a streaming service has members in Seattle, Dublin, and Bangalore. Planning always starts at 9 a.m. Seattle time, so Bangalore members join near midnight and rarely contribute. Several members also speak English as a second language and struggle with fast verbal debate. What should the scrum master do?
options: Have Bangalore members send their updates to the Seattle lead before each planning meeting.
Rotate meeting times and add shared written input so every location can contribute on fair terms.
Split the team by location so each group can plan separately at a convenient local time.
Keep the current time but record each meeting so the Bangalore members can watch it the next day.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Inclusive meeting practices — distributed and diverse teams need fair scheduling and multiple ways to contribute (Rule M3-B10-R07).
Spot it: One time zone always suffers ("near midnight"), and second-language speakers struggle with fast verbal debate.
In this scenario: The scrum master rotates meeting times and adds shared written input so every location can contribute on fair terms.
Why not the others: Sending updates to a Seattle lead makes Bangalore members reporters, not planners; splitting by location breaks one team into silos; recordings let them watch, not influence.
Remember: Share the pain of time zones; offer written and spoken channels.

questions.stem: On a pharmaceutical packaging line project, shift operators, most of them contract staff, are never included in design reviews. Several costly late design changes came from issues the operators had already noticed. A steering committee member says inclusion efforts should wait until the project is finished. How should the project manager respond?
options: Agree to defer the effort and log the operators' concerns in the lessons learned register.
Plan a separate inclusion training program for the operators to start after go-live.
Show how excluding operators has driven rework and add them to the upcoming design reviews now.
Ask human resources to handle operator inclusion separately so it does not distract from the design schedule.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Inclusion as a performance enabler — including the people who do the work improves results; it is not a side project for later (Rule M3-B10-R10).
Spot it: A group left out of reviews, "costly late design changes" they had already noticed, and a push to delay inclusion.
In this scenario: The PM shows the link between exclusion and rework and adds the operators to the upcoming design reviews now.
Why not the others: Deferring and logging a lesson documents the problem instead of acting on it; training after go-live comes too late to prevent rework; handing it to HR treats inclusion as separate from delivery.
Remember: Include the doers early — it's cheaper than rework.

questions.stem: A sponsor asks a hybrid project manager to promise a client that the fixed-scope hardware phase and three adaptive software releases will all be complete by June. A forecast based on the team's actual throughput shows the third release arriving in August at the earliest. The sponsor says to just commit and figure it out later. What should the project manager do?
options: Commit to June as requested and schedule team overtime on the software releases to close the forecast gap.
Commit to June but privately tell the team to cut testing if the date starts to slip later.
Decline to discuss any dates with the client until all three releases have been completed.
Share the forecast with the sponsor and propose options the team can realistically deliver by June.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Honesty and responsibility (PMI Code of Ethics) — do not make commitments you know cannot be met (Rule M3-B16-R08).
Spot it: Evidence says August, and the sponsor says "just commit and figure it out later."
In this scenario: The PM shares the throughput forecast with the sponsor and proposes realistic options for what can be delivered by June.
Why not the others: Committing and planning overtime still makes a promise the data says is false; committing while quietly cutting testing is dishonest and risks quality; refusing to discuss dates is unhelpful and not transparent.
Remember: Forecasts are facts, not wishes — be honest early and offer options.

questions.stem: A departing developer on a payments team has sent a 40-page wiki document on the fraud detection module to her replacement and marked the knowledge transfer item complete. The replacement says he has read it but has never worked on the module. The developer leaves in one week. What should the scrum master do?
options: Accept the item as complete since the document exists and the replacement confirmed reading it.
Have the replacement make a real fraud-module change while the departing developer observes and helps.
Ask the departing developer to expand the wiki with additional diagrams before her last day.
Schedule a recorded walkthrough of the wiki document for the whole team during her final week with the company.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Effective knowledge transfer — it is complete only when the receiver can actually perform the work, not when documents were handed over (Rule M3-B11-R09).
Spot it: A document was "sent" and "marked complete," but the receiver "has never worked on the module," and time is short.
In this scenario: The scrum master has the replacement make a real change to the module while the departing developer observes and coaches.
Why not the others: Accepting a read document confuses delivery with capability; more diagrams add more one-way material; a recorded walkthrough is still explicit knowledge only and proves no ability.
Remember: KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER when anyone leaves — and prove it by doing.

questions.stem: A project manager on a municipal water meter replacement project is asked to set up a meeting about installer delays. Twelve people have been suggested as attendees, and no one has said what the meeting should produce. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Invite all twelve suggested attendees so that no one who might have something to contribute is left out.
Send the installers' delay data to the group and ask each person to reply with comments.
Book a two-hour working session and let the agenda emerge from the group's discussion.
Clarify the decision or result the meeting must deliver before choosing attendees and an agenda.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Meeting purpose first — define what the meeting must produce before choosing attendees or an agenda (Rule M3-B14-R01).
Spot it: Many suggested attendees and "no one has said what the meeting should produce."
In this scenario: The PM first clarifies the decision or result needed; that answer then drives who attends and what goes on the agenda.
Why not the others: Inviting all twelve builds a crowd without a goal; asking everyone for comments skips defining the outcome; letting the agenda "emerge" in two hours wastes time.
Remember: Purpose → Outcome → People → Agenda.

questions.stem: A hybrid project manager needs a decision on whether to move a fixed training date for a new hotel reservation system. The decision requires the training lead and operations director plus the adaptive team's product owner. Twenty other staff have asked to attend to stay informed. What should the project manager do?
options: Invite only the three decision makers and share the outcome with the other staff afterward.
Invite all twenty-three people to show transparency and build broad staff support for the decision.
Meet with the twenty staff first to gather opinions before the decision group convenes.
Let the operations director decide alone by email so no meeting needs to be scheduled.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Right attendees — invite the people needed to reach the outcome, and keep others informed by other channels (Rule M3-B14-R02).
Spot it: A decision needs three specific people, yet twenty more want to attend "to stay informed."
In this scenario: The PM invites the three decision makers and shares the outcome with the wider staff afterward.
Why not the others: Inviting all twenty-three slows the decision without adding needed input; a preliminary opinion meeting adds a step the decision doesn't need; an email decision by one person drops the other two required roles.
Remember: Decide with the few, inform the many (push communication for the rest).

questions.stem: A product owner for a logistics app plans a one-hour session where the team and two stakeholders must choose among three architecture options for route optimization. The options involve cost models and performance benchmarks that take time to understand. In past sessions, participants spent most of the hour asking basic questions. What should the scrum master suggest?
options: Extend the session to three hours so every option can be explained fully during the meeting itself.
Let the product owner select the architecture alone since the others lack background.
Send the options, cost models, and benchmarks a few days ahead so everyone arrives prepared.
Present only the recommended option so the session avoids unproductive basic questions.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Preparation and pre-reads — send context ahead when participants need time to understand complex material before deciding (Rule M3-B14-R03).
Spot it: Dense material (cost models, benchmarks) and past sessions lost "asking basic questions."
In this scenario: The scrum master suggests sending the options and data a few days ahead so everyone arrives ready to decide.
Why not the others: A three-hour session spends everyone's time on explanation that reading would cover; a solo product-owner decision on architecture sidelines the team that owns the how; presenting one option removes the real choice.
Remember: Read before you meet, decide when you meet.

questions.stem: The chief engineer speaks first on every topic in risk identification workshops for a rail signaling upgrade, and other participants mostly echo his views. The project manager suspects that important risks are being missed. What should the project manager do in the next workshop?
options: Collect risks from each participant individually before open discussion so rank does not steer input.
Ask the chief engineer to lead the workshop since his experience makes his views most reliable.
Exclude the chief engineer from the next workshop so the other participants feel freer to speak up openly.
Review risk registers from past projects instead of holding more workshops with this team.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Balanced participation — facilitators stop rank or strong personalities from steering the group (Rule M3-B14-R04).
Spot it: The senior expert "speaks first on every topic," others "echo his views," and risks may be missed.
In this scenario: The PM collects risks from each person individually before open discussion, so everyone's input is captured first.
Why not the others: Making him the leader amplifies the domination; excluding him loses real expertise; relying only on old registers skips this team's knowledge of this project's risks.
Remember: Independent input first, group discussion second.

questions.stem: A hybrid team is generating ideas to reduce customer wait times in a bank's new branch system. The operations manager immediately explains why each suggested idea will not work, and the flow of ideas has dried up. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the operations manager to screen ideas in advance so only feasible ones reach the group.
Run an idea round with no critique allowed, then evaluate the full list against agreed criteria.
Let the operations manager continue since early critique saves time on weak suggestions.
Vote on each idea as soon as it is suggested so the weaker options are removed from the list quickly.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Diverge, then converge — generating ideas and evaluating them are separate steps, because early judgment shuts down creativity (Rule M3-B14-R05).
Spot it: A manager "immediately explains why each idea will not work," and the ideas "dried up."
In this scenario: The PM runs a no-critique idea round, then evaluates the complete list against agreed criteria.
Why not the others: Pre-screening by one person filters out ideas before anyone hears them; letting critique continue keeps the group silent; voting on each idea as it comes still mixes judgment into generation.
Remember: Brainstorm = quantity first; evaluate later against criteria.

questions.stem: An agile team meets with two marketing stakeholders to decide how to handle a pricing page defect before a product launch. The discussion is productive, but as time runs out people begin leaving without a summary. Last month, a similar meeting produced no follow-through. What should the scrum master do before the meeting ends?
options: Let everyone leave on time and send the meeting recording to all of the attendees.
Schedule another meeting next week with the same group to decide who will handle the pricing page defect.
State what was decided, confirm who will act on each item, and agree when each will be done.
Add the defect to the team's board and let whoever is available pick it up next.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Decision closure — end decision meetings with explicit decisions, owners, and due dates (Rule M3-B14-R06).
Spot it: People are "leaving without a summary," and a similar meeting last month had "no follow-through."
In this scenario: Before the meeting ends, the scrum master states what was decided, confirms who will act on each item, and agrees on when.
Why not the others: Sending a recording keeps the discussion but not the ownership; another meeting delays a decision that can be closed now; leaving it for whoever is free is exactly how follow-through failed last time.
Remember: Every decision leaves with a WHO and a WHEN.

questions.stem: A project manager on a regional hospital network upgrade holds a weekly one-hour call where six site leads read out the same status numbers already posted on the project dashboard. No decisions are made, and attendees multitask during the call. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the weekly call but require site leads to turn their cameras on so they stay engaged.
Extend the call to ninety minutes so site leads can explain each status number in detail.
Cancel the call and stop collecting status from the six site leads until an issue is formally escalated.
Replace the call with written dashboard updates and meet live only when an issue needs discussion.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Asynchronous collaboration — use written or tool-based updates when a live meeting adds little value (Rule M3-B14-R07).
Spot it: People "read out the same status numbers already posted," with no decisions and multitasking.
In this scenario: The PM replaces the call with dashboard updates and meets live only when an issue needs discussion.
Why not the others: Cameras on forces attention to a meeting that has no purpose; a longer call adds more waste; cancelling status collection entirely leaves the project blind until an escalation.
Remember: Status = async (pull); problems and decisions = live.

questions.stem: Nine months into a hybrid telecom network rollout, team members attend 14 recurring meetings a week. Several were created for early design decisions that are now complete, yet they still run with thin agendas. Team members say they have little time left for delivery work. What should the project manager do?
options: Shorten every meeting by 15 minutes so total time falls without removing any meetings.
Review each recurring meeting's current purpose with the team and drop those that no longer help.
Cancel all recurring meetings at once and let team members request new sessions as needs arise.
Ask the sponsor to approve extra staff so the team can keep attending every meeting.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Meeting hygiene — review recurring meetings regularly and remove those that no longer create value (Rule M3-B14-R10).
Spot it: Many recurring meetings whose original purpose "is now complete," thin agendas, and no time left for delivery.
In this scenario: The PM reviews each meeting's current purpose with the team and drops those that no longer help.
Why not the others: Trimming 15 minutes from every meeting keeps the useless ones alive; cancelling everything also removes meetings that still matter; adding staff to attend meetings solves the wrong problem.
Remember: Every recurring meeting must re-earn its place.

questions.stem: During tax season, a scrum master for a tax software team notices that several developers are working late nights, missing daily meetings, and introducing more defects. The product owner keeps adding urgent items mid-sprint to keep up with regulatory changes. What should the scrum master do?
options: Organize a team wellness lunch and encourage developers to take breaks when they are tired.
Ask the functional manager to add more developers so the current staff can keep up with the pace.
Recommend that each developer take personal leave once the busy tax season is over.
Work with the product owner and team to control mid-sprint additions and set sustainable limits.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sustainable pace — burnout signals point to system causes such as workload and interruptions, and those causes must be fixed (Rule M3-B15-R08).
Spot it: Late nights, missed meetings, rising defects, and "urgent items added mid-sprint."
In this scenario: The scrum master works with the product owner and team to control mid-sprint additions and set sustainable limits.
Why not the others: A wellness lunch shows care but leaves the overload in place; adding people mid-crunch slows the team further; leave "after the season" postpones the fix until after the damage.
Remember: Treat the system, not just the symptom — protect the sprint, protect the people.

questions.stem: A project manager is negotiating a change order with a concrete supplier that has delivered reliably for eight years and is expected to support the company's next three projects. The supplier requests a 3% price increase backed by documented cement cost increases, and its margin is thin. What should the project manager do?
options: Negotiate a fair adjustment based on the cost evidence that also protects the long-term relationship.
Insist that the supplier absorb the full increase since the contract price was agreed in advance.
Accept the full increase without review to avoid any friction with a trusted supplier.
Issue a competitive bid to replace the supplier as leverage to hold the original price.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Relationship-aware negotiation — weigh the value of an ongoing relationship alongside the immediate deal (Rule M3-B08-R09).
Spot it: A long, reliable supplier needed for future projects, a documented cost increase, and a thin margin.
In this scenario: The PM negotiates a fair adjustment grounded in the cost evidence that also protects the long-term partnership.
Why not the others: Insisting on the old price wins today but can break a valuable relationship; accepting without review skips due diligence; a threat-driven rebid damages trust for short-term leverage.
Remember: Negotiate for win-win — evidence plus relationship.

questions.stem: A hybrid project is replacing a manufacturer's paper-based quality inspections with tablet-based inspections. The technical design is complete, and the team has focused entirely on hardware and software so far. Go-live is four months away, and the plant manager asks what the project should tackle next. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Schedule tablet training for all plant employees in the week before the system goes live.
Complete the build and let supervisors decide later how inspectors will adopt the tablets.
Identify which roles, such as inspectors and supervisors, must change how they work and by how much.
Send a plant-wide announcement describing the new tablet features and the launch date.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Change impact assessment — organizational change starts by identifying whose behavior must change, and by how much, for the outcome to succeed (Rule M5-B05-R01).
Spot it: The technical build is done, but the people side of the change hasn't been examined, and go-live is months away.
In this scenario: The PM's next step is to identify which roles, such as inspectors and supervisors, will work differently and how deep each change is.
Why not the others: Training everyone at the last minute may train the wrong people on the wrong tasks; deferring adoption to supervisors after the build leaves it unplanned; an announcement of features says nothing about what changes for each role.
Remember: Change = Adoption — first ask "who must adopt, and what changes for them?"

questions.stem: An agile team is rolling out a new self-service claims portal. Adjusters in one region fear job losses, adjusters in another say the portal is slower than the old system, and a third group says no one asked for their input. Management labels all of them resistant. What should the agile project lead do?
options: Address each group's specific concern separately, such as job security, speed, and involvement.
Launch a single persuasion campaign explaining why the portal benefits all adjusters.
Ask regional managers to require portal use and track which adjusters fail to comply.
Delay the rollout until every adjuster group formally agrees to adopt the new portal.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Resistance drivers — resistance has different causes (fear, usability, lack of voice) that need different responses (Rule M5-B05-R02).
Spot it: Three groups with three different concerns, and management labeling them all the same: "resistant."
In this scenario: The lead addresses each group's specific concern: job security, portal speed, and involvement.
Why not the others: One persuasion campaign won't fix a speed problem or a lack of involvement; mandating use and tracking non-compliance forces adoption without listening; waiting for universal agreement stalls value.
Remember: Diagnose the WHY behind the resistance, then tailor the response.

questions.stem: A project is consolidating three regional warehouses into one automated center. Staff have heard rumors of closures, and the only communication so far is a technical specification of the new conveyor system. The sponsor asks the project manager to improve the message. What should the project manager develop?
options: A plain-language summary of the conveyor system specification written for all staff.
A message covering why the move is happening, what changes, who is affected, and the expected benefits.
A schedule of site closure dates distributed to all warehouse employees without comment.
A frequently asked questions page limited to the technical features of the new center.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Change story — a clear message explaining why the change is happening, what changes, who is affected, and what value is expected (Rule M5-B05-R03).
Spot it: Rumors are spreading, and the only communication is a technical specification.
In this scenario: The PM develops a message covering the reason, the change, its impact on people, and the benefits.
Why not the others: A plain-language spec is easier to read but still skips why and impact; bare closure dates fuel rumors instead of answering them; a technical FAQ ignores people's real questions.
Remember: WHY → WHAT → WHO is affected → VALUE.

questions.stem: A hybrid project is introducing a new electronic charting system across six hospital units. In one unit, nurses trust a veteran charge nurse far more than hospital administrators, and she has been lukewarm about the system. Adoption is lagging in that unit. What should the project manager do?
options: Have a hospital administrator send the unit a message stressing that system use is mandatory.
Bypass the charge nurse and train the unit's newest nurses first since they adapt quickly.
Engage the charge nurse, address her concerns, and invite her to help lead adoption in her unit.
Report the unit's low adoption to the sponsor and request disciplinary follow-up there.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Change champions — credible leaders and local influencers drive adoption better than distant authority (Rule M5-B05-R04).
Spot it: A trusted informal leader ("trust a veteran charge nurse far more than administrators") who is lukewarm, and lagging adoption.
In this scenario: The PM engages the charge nurse, addresses her concerns, and invites her to help lead adoption in her unit.
Why not the others: An administrator's mandate comes from a less trusted source and can deepen resistance; bypassing her risks her open opposition; requesting discipline escalates and punishes instead of engaging.
Remember: Win the influencer, win the unit.

questions.stem: An agile team has released a new analytics tool to a marketing department. Leadership expects marketers to build their own campaign reports starting next week, but most have never used the tool, and the only support is a short help page. What should the agile team recommend?
options: Keep the start date and track which marketers fail to produce their reports on time.
Have the team build every campaign report until marketers choose to learn the tool.
Expand the help page with more screenshots and email it to the marketing department.
Provide hands-on practice and coaching so marketers can build reports before the change takes effect.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Capability before behavior — people must be able to do the new thing before they can be expected to keep doing it (Rule M5-B05-R05).
Spot it: A start date is set, most users "have never used the tool," and support is only "a short help page."
In this scenario: The team recommends hands-on practice and coaching so marketers can build reports before the change takes effect.
Why not the others: Tracking failures measures a gap the organization created; building reports for them delays adoption indefinitely; a longer help page is still reading, not practicing.
Remember: Aware → Able → Adopt — build the skill before you expect the habit.

questions.stem: A project delivered a new procurement approval workflow to a government agency two months ago. Usage was high at first, but staff are gradually returning to approving purchases by email outside the system. Project closure is scheduled for next month. What should the project manager do?
options: Close the project on schedule since the workflow was delivered and accepted by the agency.
Work with agency leaders to recognize system use, follow up on bypasses, and fix points of friction.
Retrain all staff on the workflow and then block email for any approval-related messages.
Record the drop in usage in the final report as a lesson learned for future projects.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reinforcement — after launch, desired behavior must be reinforced, or people drift back to old habits (Rule M5-B05-R06).
Spot it: "Usage was high at first," but staff are "gradually returning" to the old way.
In this scenario: The PM works with agency leaders to recognize use of the system, follow up on bypasses, and remove friction points.
Why not the others: Closing on schedule ignores that the benefits depend on sustained use; retraining and blocking email forces compliance without fixing the friction; a lessons-learned note only documents the drift.
Remember: Launch is not adoption — reinforce until it sticks.

questions.stem: A hybrid project rolled out a new scheduling tool to 300 clinic staff. The status report shows 98% training attendance, and the sponsor wants to declare success. Front-desk staff, however, are still double-booking appointments at most clinics. What should the project manager do?
options: Track actual tool use, staff skill on key tasks, and double-booking rates to judge the change.
Report success to the sponsor since nearly all of the staff completed the required training sessions.
Schedule a second round of training for all 300 staff so that attendance reaches a full 100 percent.
Survey staff on whether they enjoyed the training sessions and report the satisfaction scores to the sponsor.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Measuring change success — judge a change by adoption, proficiency, and business outcomes, not by training attendance (Rule M5-B05-R07).
Spot it: A strong activity number ("98% training attendance") alongside a bad outcome (double-booking continues).
In this scenario: The PM tracks actual tool use, staff skill on key tasks, and double-booking rates to see whether the change is really working.
Why not the others: Declaring success on attendance confuses output with outcome; a second training round chases 100% attendance instead of results; satisfaction scores measure enjoyment, not performance.
Remember: Trained ≠ using ≠ getting results — measure all three.

questions.stem: An agile team is migrating a university's course registration from a legacy system to a new platform over six weeks. During that period some departments will use the old system and others the new one. Academic advisors will need to look up students in both. What should the team plan for?
options: Switching every department on a single day so that advisors never need to use both systems.
Support for advisors working in both systems during the overlap, such as extra help desk staff.
Letting each department find its own workarounds until the whole migration is complete.
Pausing all new-platform releases until every department can move off the legacy system.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Transition support — plan for the period when old and new ways of working overlap and people must operate both (Rule M5-B05-R10).
Spot it: A phased migration with "some departments on the old system and others on the new," and users who need both.
In this scenario: The team plans extra support for advisors during the overlap, such as added help desk staff and quick references.
Why not the others: A single-day switch contradicts the planned incremental migration and adds risk; leaving departments to improvise invites errors; pausing releases stops incremental value delivery.
Remember: Mind the gap — support people while old and new run side by side.

questions.stem: The lighting engineer, structural engineer, and electrical contractor on a stadium lighting project keep sending technical questions to the project manager and waiting for her to decide. She is not a lighting specialist, and decisions are slowing. Several of the decisions also affect more than one contractor's work. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue making the technical decisions so accountability for every outcome stays with one person.
Hire an outside lighting consultant to make all technical decisions on the project manager's behalf.
Clarify which specialist owns each technical decision and coordinate impacts across the work.
Ask the sponsor to make each of the technical decisions since the sponsor is funding the whole project.
questions.explanation:
Concept: PM as integrator — the project manager coordinates decisions across specialists rather than owning every technical call (Rule M3-B09-R08).
Spot it: Specialists "waiting for her to decide" technical questions outside her expertise, decisions slowing, and choices that affect more than one contractor.
In this scenario: The PM clarifies which specialist owns each technical decision and coordinates the impacts across the work.
Why not the others: Making every decision herself creates a bottleneck and risks poor calls; an outside consultant for all decisions just moves the bottleneck; the sponsor funds and governs, not specialist engineering choices.
Remember: PM integrates; experts decide within their expertise.

questions.stem: A project manager leads a hybrid effort with an experienced adaptive software group and a newly formed hardware assembly crew whose members have never worked together. A critical safety defect has just been found in a hardware component. How should the project manager adjust her leadership?
options: Use the same hands-off style with both groups to show equal trust in each of the two teams.
Direct both groups closely until the defect is resolved so that control remains consistent everywhere.
Let the new crew self-organize around the safety defect so they build independence as quickly as possible.
Guide the new crew closely on the safety defect while keeping the software group self-directed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Situational leadership — adapt style to team maturity, urgency, and context; different groups on one project may need different styles (Rule M3-B02-R09).
Spot it: One mature group, one "newly formed" crew (Tuckman forming), and an urgent "critical safety defect."
In this scenario: The PM guides the new crew closely on the safety defect while leaving the experienced software group self-directed.
Why not the others: The same hands-off style for both ignores the new crew's needs; directing both groups micromanages a mature team; letting a new crew self-organize a safety problem is too much, too soon.
Remember: New team or crisis = more direction; mature team = delegate and support.

questions.stem: The head of customer support has repeatedly declined invitations to sprint reviews for a new chatbot and has told peers the project is a waste. The product owner wants to ask the sponsor to require her attendance. What should the agile project lead do FIRST?
options: Back the product owner's plan to have the sponsor require her attendance at future reviews.
Meet with the support head to learn what concerns lie behind her objections to the chatbot.
Send her a summary of the chatbot's benefits to change her view before the next review session.
Remove her from the review invitation list to limit her negative influence on other stakeholders.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Understand resistance first — learn the reason behind a stakeholder's resistance before trying to overcome it (Rule M3-B06-R01).
Spot it: Repeated declines, negative comments to peers, and someone wanting to force attendance.
In this scenario: The lead first meets the support head to learn what concerns lie behind her objections.
Why not the others: Having the sponsor require attendance forces presence, not support; a benefits summary persuades before understanding; removing her from invitations ignores a key stakeholder and can deepen resistance.
Remember: Identify → Analyze → Engage → Monitor — listen before you persuade.

questions.stem: A stakeholder engagement assessment matrix for a courthouse renovation shows the chief judge as unaware of planned courtroom closures. Her desired engagement level is supportive. Closures begin in three months, and several trials will need to be rescheduled. What should the project manager do?
options: Add the chief judge to the monthly project newsletter distribution list for regular updates.
Rate the chief judge as a low priority since she has not expressed any concerns about the project.
Ask the court administrator to inform the judge once the closure dates have been fully finalized.
Meet directly with the chief judge to explain the closures and involve her in phasing choices.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stakeholder engagement assessment matrix — compares each stakeholder's current level (unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading) with the desired level, and engagement is tailored to close the gap (Rule M3-B06-R02).
Spot it: "Current: unaware; desired: supportive," a high-influence stakeholder, and a significant impact coming soon.
In this scenario: The PM meets the chief judge directly to explain the closures and involve her in phasing choices.
Why not the others: A newsletter is push communication that won't move her from unaware to supportive; rating her low priority ignores her influence and impact; waiting for finalized dates excludes her from choices she should shape.
Remember: Current → Desired gap sets the engagement; big gap = direct, interactive contact.

questions.stem: A hybrid project is designing a new warehouse picking system. Predictive facilities work is being baselined, and the adaptive software team is starting to define early features. Veteran pickers know where current routes break down but have not been consulted. When should the project manager involve the pickers?
options: Now, while layout and early features are still being shaped, so their knowledge improves the design.
During user acceptance testing, when the finished system is ready for the pickers to validate it fully.
After go-live, through a satisfaction survey whose results feed into the next software release.
Once facilities work is baselined, so their input cannot disturb the approved warehouse layout.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Early stakeholder involvement — involve affected people while the solution is still being shaped, when their knowledge can improve it (Rule M3-B06-R03).
Spot it: Front-line experts who "know where current routes break down" and "have not been consulted," while design is still open.
In this scenario: The PM involves the pickers now, while the layout and early features are still being formed.
Why not the others: Acceptance testing is too late to shape the design cheaply; a post-go-live survey turns insight into rework; waiting until after the baseline deliberately blocks useful input.
Remember: Involve early — cheapest time to change is before it's built.

questions.stem: An agile team is changing how field technicians log repairs, which will require them to use a new mobile app every day. The team has been sending weekly emails about the change for two months. Most technicians still use paper forms. What should the scrum master recommend?
options: Increase email frequency to daily reminders so the change stays top of mind for all technicians.
Post the app instructions on the company intranet for technicians to review on their own time.
Hold working sessions with technicians to hear concerns, demo the app, and adjust to feedback.
Ask supervisors to announce that paper forms will no longer be accepted starting next month.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Two-way communication — when you need alignment or behavior change, use interactive communication, not one-way messages (Rule M3-B06-R04).
Spot it: Two months of emails, and behavior hasn't changed ("still use paper forms").
In this scenario: The scrum master recommends working sessions where technicians raise concerns, see the app demonstrated, and have their feedback acted on.
Why not the others: Daily emails push the same one-way message harder; an intranet page is pull communication that is easy to ignore; banning paper forces the change without addressing concerns.
Remember: Push informs, pull is available, INTERACTIVE changes behavior.

questions.stem: A regional director who controls funding for a new distribution center is unhappy with the project's reporting format. She has told peers she is losing confidence in the project but has not raised the issue with the project manager. What should the project manager do?
options: Contact the director soon to understand her concerns and agree on how they will be addressed.
Continue standard reporting and wait for the director to raise concerns through formal channels.
Ask the sponsor to reassure the director about the project on the project manager's behalf.
Escalate the director's comments to the steering committee as a new stakeholder risk item.
questions.explanation:
Concept: High-power, dissatisfied stakeholders — engage them proactively before dissatisfaction grows (power/interest grid: manage closely) (Rule M3-B06-R05).
Spot it: The person "controls funding," is "losing confidence," and hasn't come to the PM yet.
In this scenario: The PM contacts the director soon to understand her concerns and agree on how to address them.
Why not the others: Waiting for formal channels lets the problem grow; asking the sponsor to reassure her is escalation instead of direct engagement; logging her as a risk documents instead of acting.
Remember: High power + unhappy = go to them, now, in person.

questions.stem: A hybrid project's key customer requests a new reporting feature almost every week and is pleased when the team agrees. These additions now threaten the fixed hardware delivery date, and none has gone through impact analysis. Today the customer asks for another addition. What should the project manager do?
options: Accept the new addition to preserve the customer's high level of satisfaction with the project team.
Review the request's impact with the customer and route it through the agreed change process.
Decline all further additions from the customer until the fixed hardware delivery date has passed.
Accept the addition but quietly reduce testing effort on the hardware work to make time for it.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Satisfaction is not saying yes — stakeholder satisfaction comes from delivering agreed value, not from approving every request; requests still go through impact analysis and change control (Rule M3-B06-R06).
Spot it: Frequent requests the team "agrees" to, no impact analysis, and a fixed date now under threat.
In this scenario: The PM reviews the new request's impact with the customer and routes it through the agreed change process.
Why not the others: Accepting to keep them happy continues uncontrolled scope creep; refusing everything ignores possibly valuable requests; quietly cutting hardware testing is dishonest and trades quality for scope.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement — even for favorite customers.

questions.stem: Two vice presidents each insist that their feature must come next for a retail app. One wants a loyalty program and the other wants faster checkout. Both argue loudly in refinement sessions, and the product owner is unsure how to decide. What should the agile coach suggest?
options: Let the more senior vice president decide, since authority settles competing requests fastest.
Build half of each feature in the next sprint so that neither vice president is disappointed.
Compare the features using data such as expected revenue, customer impact, and cost of delay.
Ask the developers to vote on which of the two features they would prefer to build first.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Evidence-based prioritization — resolve competing stakeholder priorities with data and impact analysis, not volume or rank (Rule M3-B06-R07).
Spot it: Two senior people "insist" and "argue loudly," and the product owner is unsure.
In this scenario: The coach suggests comparing the features using expected revenue, customer impact, and cost of delay, which gives the product owner a defensible order.
Why not the others: Letting seniority decide replaces value with rank; building half of each delivers two unfinished features and no value; a developer vote puts a value decision with the people who decide how.
Remember: Let the data speak — value and cost of delay, not the loudest voice.

questions.stem: A project manager is planning the rollout of a new maintenance management system for a utility's field crews. The sponsor believes a single go-live announcement and a user manual will be enough to ensure that crews use the system. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Proceed with the announcement and manual, then measure adoption levels when the project closes.
Require crews to use the system by policy and remove all paper forms from go-live onward.
Delay go-live until every crew member has read and signed an acknowledgment of the user manual.
Plan crew involvement, ongoing communication, training, and reinforcement after launch.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Adoption as an outcome — people use a new system when engagement, communication, capability building, and reinforcement work together (Rule M3-B06-R10).
Spot it: A belief that "a single announcement and a manual" will ensure use.
In this scenario: The PM recommends a plan that involves crews, communicates over time, trains them, and reinforces use after launch.
Why not the others: Measuring adoption at closure finds the problem too late to fix; a policy mandate forces use without engagement or skill; signed manual acknowledgments prove reading, not ability or willingness.
Remember: Engage + Communicate + Enable + Reinforce = Adoption.

questions.stem: While building a stakeholder register for a hybrid merger integration project, a project manager records notes that two executives strongly oppose the merger and one is likely to leave the company. A team member asks to post the full register on the shared team site so everyone can see it. What should the project manager do?
options: Post the full register on the shared team site to support transparency across the whole project team.
Limit the sensitive assessments to authorized people and share only appropriate register details.
Delete the executive notes from the register entirely so there is no risk of any disclosure.
Email the full register to the team with a note asking every member to keep it confidential.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stakeholder register confidentiality — the register can hold sensitive assessments (attitudes, influence, plans) that must be shared only with appropriate people (Rule M3-B05-R08).
Spot it: Notes about executives' opposition and a likely departure, plus a request to "post the full register" publicly.
In this scenario: The PM limits the sensitive assessments to authorized people and shares only appropriate register details with the team.
Why not the others: Posting everything harms trust and the people named; deleting the notes loses analysis the PM needs; emailing it with a "keep confidential" note still discloses it.
Remember: Stakeholder register = TRACK information; sensitive parts are need-to-know.

questions.stem: A stable, high-performing agile team is asked to build a machine-learning recommendation feature, but no one on the team has machine-learning experience. Management proposes replacing two current members with machine-learning specialists. What should the scrum master recommend?
options: Replace the two members as proposed since the new feature requires a different set of team skills.
Keep the team unchanged and have members teach themselves machine learning while they keep delivering.
Give the feature to a separate specialist team and have that team integrate the work at the very end.
Add machine-learning expertise, such as a specialist pairing with the team, and keep the core members.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Team stability vs. capability gaps — keep a high-performing team together while adding the skills it lacks (Rule M3-B04-R09).
Spot it: A "stable, high-performing" team, a new skill it doesn't have, and a proposal to swap members.
In this scenario: The scrum master recommends adding machine-learning expertise, such as a specialist pairing with the team, while keeping the core members.
Why not the others: Replacing members breaks a performing team back to forming; self-teaching while delivering risks quality and burnout; a separate team with late integration creates silos and big-bang risk.
Remember: Protect a performing team — add skills, don't break it apart (Tuckman).

questions.stem: An AI scheduling assistant on a pipeline construction project predicts that welding will finish three weeks early and recommends releasing float to other activities. The welding crew lead says recent weather delays have not yet been entered into the tool's data. What should the project manager do?
options: Check the prediction against site records and the crew lead's input before releasing float.
Release the float as recommended since the tool analyzes far more data than the crew lead can.
Stop using the AI tool on the project because one of its predictions appears to be unreliable.
Ask the tool vendor to confirm the prediction before taking any action on the welding float.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Validate AI output — AI analysis must be checked against trusted data and domain knowledge before you act on it (Rule M5-B07-R02).
Spot it: An AI recommendation plus a domain expert saying the tool's data is incomplete ("weather delays not yet entered").
In this scenario: The PM checks the prediction against site records and the crew lead's input before releasing any float.
Why not the others: Releasing float on the AI's word treats it as the final authority; dropping the tool overreacts to one data gap; asking the vendor can't fix the project's missing data.
Remember: AI recommends; humans decide — validate first.

questions.stem: A hybrid project uses an AI tool to recommend which staff should join high-visibility adaptive teams. A review shows that part-time employees are almost never recommended, even when their skill ratings are high. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue using the recommendations since the tool applies the same criteria to every employee.
Tell part-time employees to increase their hours if they want high-visibility team assignments.
Examine whether the tool disadvantages part-time staff and review assignments in the meantime.
Remove skill ratings from the tool's inputs so that its recommendations become more balanced.
questions.explanation:
Concept: AI bias in people decisions — when AI influences decisions about people, check for uneven impact on groups (Rule M5-B07-R04).
Spot it: A group (part-time staff) "almost never recommended, even when their skill ratings are high."
In this scenario: The PM examines whether the tool disadvantages part-time staff and reviews assignments manually in the meantime.
Why not the others: "Same criteria" can still produce biased outcomes; telling staff to change their hours accepts the bias as fair; removing skill ratings discards a valid input without finding the real cause.
Remember: AI = Validate + Human accountability — especially where people are affected.

questions.stem: An agile team uses an AI model to rank customer feature requests by predicted value. The team discovers that one partner submitted hundreds of near-identical requests, which pushed its preferred feature to the top of the ranking. What should the team do?
options: Add safeguards such as duplicate detection and review flagged rankings before they shape priorities.
Accept the ranking since the model reflects the real volume of requests that were submitted.
Stop accepting requests from every partner until the model has been fully rebuilt and retrained.
Have the product owner ignore the AI ranking for this particular partner's requests from now on.
questions.explanation:
Concept: AI manipulation safeguards — protect AI-driven decisions from gaming or manipulated inputs (Rule M5-B07-R07).
Spot it: "Hundreds of near-identical requests" pushing one partner's feature to the top.
In this scenario: The team adds safeguards such as duplicate detection and human review of flagged rankings before they shape priorities.
Why not the others: Accepting the ranking lets volume game value; banning all partners punishes everyone for one; a one-off exception for this partner doesn't protect against the next manipulation.
Remember: Garbage in, garbage ranked — guard the inputs, keep a human check.

questions.stem: A project uses an AI tool to draft safety inspection summaries for a nuclear plant upgrade. The quality lead finds that the tool sometimes omits noncompliant readings. Legal counsel notes that these summaries are submitted to regulators. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue using the tool but add a disclaimer that summaries were generated with help from AI.
Suspend the tool for regulatory summaries and escalate the issue to governance for a decision.
Ask the vendor for an updated model and keep using the tool while the vendor develops the fix.
Have junior staff spot-check a sample of the summaries each week while the tool remains in use.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stop or escalate AI use — when reliability, legal, or ethical risk becomes unacceptable, suspend the AI use and escalate to governance (Rule M5-B07-R10).
Spot it: Safety data, "omits noncompliant readings," and "submitted to regulators."
In this scenario: The PM suspends the tool for regulatory summaries and escalates to governance for a decision.
Why not the others: A disclaimer doesn't fix omitted safety data; waiting for a vendor fix keeps an unreliable tool in regulated use; weekly junior spot-checks are too weak a control for nuclear compliance.
Remember: Compliance = mandatory; unreliable AI + regulator = stop and escalate.

questions.stem: A client accepts the first hybrid release of a warehouse management system on condition that two minor label-printing defects are fixed within 30 days. The client signed the acceptance form, but the condition was only mentioned verbally and no one volunteered for the work. What should the project manager do?
options: Treat the release as fully accepted since the client signed off on it during the meeting.
Hold back the acceptance record until both defects have been fixed and completely retested.
Record the open conditions, 30-day deadline, and owner of each fix in the acceptance records.
Add the two defects to the team's general work board without noting the acceptance condition.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Conditional acceptance — when acceptance has open conditions, document each condition, its deadline, and its owner (Rule M4-B15-R03).
Spot it: "Accepts... on condition that" defects are fixed within 30 days, with the condition only spoken and no one responsible.
In this scenario: The PM records the open conditions, the 30-day deadline, and who owns each fix in the acceptance records.
Why not the others: Treating it as fully accepted drops the client's condition; holding back the record stalls a real acceptance; adding the defects to the board without the condition loses the contractual deadline.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close; conditional acceptance needs WHAT, WHO, and WHEN in writing.

questions.stem: An agile team is handing off a customer loyalty app to the company's support operations group. The team knows of a performance risk during holiday peaks and two open low-priority defects. The support lead has not been told about either. What should the team do before the handoff?
options: Fix both defects and resolve the performance risk completely before any handoff can take place.
Keep the risk and defects on the team's own board so the team can handle them if they occur.
Note the risk and defects in the release notes and complete the handoff as originally planned.
Brief the support lead on the peak-load risk and open defects and confirm who owns each one.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Operational handoff — known risks, open issues, and support obligations transfer explicitly to the operational owner (Rule M4-B15-R06).
Spot it: A handoff to support, known risks and defects, and "the support lead has not been told."
In this scenario: The team briefs the support lead on the peak-load risk and open defects and confirms who owns each one.
Why not the others: Fixing everything first delays the transition for low-priority items; keeping them on the team's board leaves ownership with a team that is moving on; release notes alone document without a real transfer.
Remember: Transfer = risks + issues + knowledge + ownership, handed over person to person.

questions.stem: A software implementation project is closing. The vendor has delivered all contracted items, but one final invoice is disputed, and a warranty obligation runs for 90 days. Finance wants to close all project accounts this week. What should the project manager do?
options: Close the accounts as requested and deal with the invoice dispute if the vendor raises it again.
Settle the disputed invoice under the contract and confirm warranty handling before closing accounts.
Pay the disputed invoice in full so that the project can close without any further delay.
Keep every project account open until the 90-day warranty period has completely expired for the vendor.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Procurement closure — close contracts and financial obligations according to contract terms and policy, including disputes and warranties (Rule M4-B15-R09).
Spot it: "Disputed invoice," a "warranty obligation," and pressure to close accounts this week.
In this scenario: The PM settles the dispute under the contract (negotiation first) and confirms warranty handling before closing accounts.
Why not the others: Closing with a dispute open leaves a claim unresolved; paying in full skips the contract's dispute terms; keeping every account open 90 days is overkill when warranty handling can be arranged.
Remember: Claims are settled by negotiation first; close the contract only when obligations are resolved or handed off.

questions.stem: A product owner for a smart-thermostat app orders the backlog strictly by the date each request arrived. A high-risk integration with a new utility API sits near the bottom, and two of the top items depend on it. What should the product owner do?
options: Keep the date-based order since it treats every stakeholder who submitted a request fairly.
Let the developers pick whichever items seem easiest so the team builds early momentum.
Move the API integration to a separate technical list managed only by the system architects.
Reorder the work by value, risk, dependencies, and learning, moving the API work higher.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Backlog ordering — the product owner orders the backlog by current value, risk, dependencies, and learning needs, not by arrival date (Rule M4-B11-R01).
Spot it: A risky item "near the bottom" while top items "depend on it."
In this scenario: The product owner reorders the backlog, moving the high-risk API integration up so dependencies and risk are addressed early.
Why not the others: First-come order is fair to requesters but not to value; letting developers pick the easiest items ignores risk and value; a separate technical list hides the dependency from the product backlog.
Remember: Order by Value, Risk, Dependencies, Learning — tackle risk early.

questions.stem: A product owner writes acceptance criteria for a password reset story that specify database table names, an encryption library, and exact code structure. Developers say this blocks better design options. What should the product owner do?
options: Rewrite the criteria to describe expected user behavior and results, leaving design to developers.
Keep the detailed criteria since they remove ambiguity and make the story straightforward to test.
Remove the acceptance criteria and let developers define what done means after finishing the story.
Ask the architect to approve the criteria so that developers must follow the prescribed design exactly.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Acceptance criteria — describe the expected behavior and results a story must meet, not how to implement it (Rule M4-B11-R05).
Spot it: Criteria listing "table names, an encryption library, and exact code structure," and developers blocked from better designs.
In this scenario: The product owner rewrites the criteria around user behavior and outcomes and leaves design to the developers.
Why not the others: Keeping design detail removes the team's how; removing criteria loses the testable definition of expected behavior; architect approval locks in a prescribed design.
Remember: Acceptance criteria = WHAT must be true; developers choose HOW.

questions.stem: After a release, analytics for a fitness app show that almost no users open the new social sharing feature. A small experiment with workout reminders doubled weekly engagement. Four more social sharing enhancements still sit at the top of the backlog. What should the product owner do?
options: Complete the planned sharing enhancements since stakeholders already approved their priority.
Set the analytics aside until several more months of usage data have been collected and analyzed.
Reorder upcoming work to favor reminder improvements and reconsider the remaining sharing items.
Ask the team to build both feature sets in parallel so that no stakeholder is left disappointed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Empirical reprioritization — use feedback from reviews, analytics, and experiments to reorder future work (Rule M4-B11-R08).
