Spot it: Real usage data (feature unused) and an experiment showing a better idea (reminders doubled engagement).
In this scenario: The product owner reorders upcoming work toward reminder improvements and reconsiders the remaining sharing items.
Why not the others: Following an old priority ignores new evidence; waiting months delays the value the data already shows; building both in parallel spreads effort over low-value work.
Remember: Inspect and adapt — let evidence reorder the backlog.

questions.stem: A client asks to add a second loading dock to a warehouse construction project whose scope, schedule, and cost baselines are approved. The client says the change is urgent and wants a yes or no by tomorrow. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Assess the dock's effect on scope, schedule, cost, and risk before the request goes for a decision.
Approve the dock since the client is paying for it and has marked the request as urgent.
Reject the dock request since the project baselines have already been approved by the client.
Instruct the contractor to begin site preparation for the new dock while the change is being reviewed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Impact analysis before change decisions — a material change to approved baselines is analyzed across scope, schedule, cost, and risk before anyone approves or rejects it (Rule M3-B18-R02).
Spot it: Approved baselines, a new request, and pressure ("urgent," "yes or no by tomorrow").
In this scenario: The PM first assesses the dock's impact so the decision-maker has the evidence.
Why not the others: Approving on urgency skips analysis and bypasses the change control board; rejecting because baselines exist misunderstands change control; starting site work implements an unapproved change.
Remember: Change Request → ANALYZE → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor. The CCB is the judge; you bring the evidence.

questions.stem: A lead engineer on a water treatment plant upgrade tells the project manager he has already started installing a higher-capacity pump than specified because it will obviously be approved. The change request is scheduled for the change control board next week. What should the project manager do?
options: Allow the installation to continue since the board is very likely to approve the change.
Stop the pump installation until the change control board has decided on the request.
Approve the change personally so the installation can proceed without any further delay.
Complete the installation and submit a retroactive request to update the scope baseline.
questions.explanation:
Concept: No unapproved changes — a controlled change is never implemented before it is approved (Rule M3-B18-R04).
Spot it: Work "already started" because it "will obviously be approved," with the board meeting next week.
In this scenario: The PM stops the installation until the change control board decides on the request.
Why not the others: Continuing assumes an approval that doesn't exist yet; approving personally bypasses the board's authority; a retroactive request turns change control into paperwork after the fact.
Remember: Logging a request is not approving it — no approval, no implementation.

questions.stem: On a defense electronics project, two subcontractors turn out to be building from different versions of an approved circuit board design. Neither version was formally updated after last month's approved change. What should the project manager do?
options: Let each subcontractor continue with its current version and reconcile the designs at testing.
Ask the two subcontractors to agree between themselves which design version is the correct one.
Establish one controlled version of the design and make sure every subcontractor works from it.
Submit a new change request to approve both design versions as valid alternatives for the build.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Configuration management — keep one controlled, current version of approved product components so everyone builds from the same thing (Rule M3-B18-R07).
Spot it: Two subcontractors on "different versions," and an approved change that "was not formally updated."
In this scenario: The PM establishes one controlled version that reflects the approved change and makes sure every subcontractor works from it.
Why not the others: Reconciling at testing finds the problem after rework is built in; letting subcontractors choose hands a configuration decision to the wrong people; approving both versions creates permanent divergence.
Remember: Change control approves the change; configuration control makes sure everyone builds the approved version.

questions.stem: The change log for a hospital IT system project shows 40 change requests after six months. Twenty-eight of them relate to unclear requirements in the lab module, and each has been processed individually. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep processing each change request individually through the standard change procedure.
Freeze all lab module changes for the rest of the project so that the baseline stays stable.
Increase how often the change control board meets so that requests are processed faster.
Analyze why lab module requirements keep generating changes and fix that underlying cause.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Change trend analysis — look across change requests for systemic causes instead of only processing each one (Rule M3-B18-R10).
Spot it: A pattern in the change log (28 of 40 from one module's "unclear requirements").
In this scenario: The PM analyzes why lab module requirements keep generating changes and fixes that root cause, for example by improving requirements elicitation.
Why not the others: Processing each request one by one treats symptoms; a change freeze blocks needed changes without fixing their source; more frequent board meetings just process the flood faster.
Remember: Recurring changes = root cause problem — fix the source, not just the ticket.

questions.stem: A hybrid project team identifies five improvement actions at the end of a phase, including better vendor handoffs and clearer acceptance criteria. At the previous phase review, similar actions were listed but none was implemented. What should the project manager do?
options: Record the actions in the lessons learned register for use by future projects.
Give each action an owner and due date, and review progress at upcoming checkpoints.
Email the list to all team members and ask them to apply the ideas where they can.
Implement all five actions personally to make sure they are completed this time.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Owned improvement actions — improvement ideas only happen when each has an owner, a due date, and follow-up (Rule M4-B17-R03).
Spot it: A list of actions and "similar actions were listed but none was implemented."
In this scenario: The PM gives each action an owner and due date and reviews progress at upcoming checkpoints.
Why not the others: Recording in lessons learned documents instead of acting; emailing the list gives no one ownership; doing all five personally removes team ownership and overloads the PM.
Remember: No owner + no date = no improvement.

questions.stem: After a production outage caused by a configuration error, a developer admits he made the mistake. A manager suggests naming him in the incident report to discourage carelessness. Other team members have become reluctant to report near misses. What should the scrum master do?
options: Name the developer in the report so that accountability is clear to the whole organization.
Skip the incident review since the developer has already admitted making the mistake.
Ask the developer to present the error to other teams as a warning about carelessness.
Lead a review focused on how the process allowed the error, without assigning personal blame.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Blameless review — examine how the process allowed an error, not who to blame, so people keep reporting problems honestly (Rule M4-B17-R06).
Spot it: A proposal to name someone and "members have become reluctant to report near misses."
In this scenario: The scrum master leads a review focused on how the process allowed the configuration error, without personal blame.
Why not the others: Naming him punishes honesty and silences reporting; skipping the review wastes the learning; a public "warning" presentation is blame in another form.
Remember: Blame the process, not the person — safety drives reporting.

questions.stem: A project manager wants to improve inspection pass rates on a modular home construction project. The quality team proposes changing the inspection checklist, crew training, material supplier, and work sequence all at once next month. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Test one or two changes at a time so their effect on pass rates can be clearly attributed.
Implement all four changes together to raise the pass rates as quickly as possible.
Defer any changes until the project ends and review the pass rates in lessons learned.
Change the material supplier first since supplier problems are the most common cause.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Controlled improvement experiments — change a few variables at a time so you can tell what caused the result (Rule M4-B17-R09).
Spot it: Four changes planned "all at once" to improve one measure.
In this scenario: The PM recommends testing one or two changes at a time so their effect on pass rates can be attributed.
Why not the others: Changing all four together hides which one worked or hurt; deferring to lessons learned gives up improving this project; picking the supplier first assumes a cause without data.
Remember: Plan-Do-Check-Act — one change at a time, then measure.

questions.stem: A bridge painting project has spent $400,000 to date against a planned value of $450,000, and the team lead concludes the project is under budget. The earned value of the work completed is $350,000. What is the MOST accurate assessment of cost performance?
options: The project is under budget, since actual spending is lower than the planned spending.
The project is on budget, since the gap between planned and actual cost is fairly small.
The project is over budget, since the completed work is worth less than the amount spent.
The project is ahead of schedule, since less money was spent than had been planned.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Cost variance — cost performance compares earned value (the value of work done) with actual cost; CV = EV − AC and CPI = EV / AC (Rule M4-B05-R01).
Spot it: Someone comparing actual cost with planned value, a classic trap.
In this scenario: CV = 350,000 − 400,000 = −50,000, and CPI = 0.875; the project is over budget for the work completed.
Why not the others: AC vs. PV is not a valid cost measure; a gap of −$50,000 is a real overrun, not "on budget"; schedule uses SV = EV − PV = −100,000, so it is actually behind schedule.
Remember: EV is the hero of every formula — CV = EV − AC, SV = EV − PV; negative = bad.

questions.stem: A software implementation project has a BAC of $800,000, EV of $300,000, AC of $375,000, and CPI of 0.80. The overrun came from a one-time licensing error that has been corrected, and the remaining work is expected to proceed at the budgeted rate. Which EAC approach is MOST appropriate?
options: AC + (BAC − EV), giving an EAC of $875,000
BAC ÷ CPI, giving an EAC of $1,000,000
AC + a bottom-up ETC for all remaining work
BAC − EV, giving an EAC of $500,000
questions.explanation:
Concept: Choosing an EAC formula — pick the forecast based on what you expect for the remaining work (Rule M4-B05-R05).
Spot it: "One-time" (atypical) error, "corrected," and remaining work "at the budgeted rate."
In this scenario: An atypical variance means EAC = AC + (BAC − EV) = 375,000 + 500,000 = $875,000.
Why not the others: BAC ÷ CPI assumes the 0.80 inefficiency continues, which the stem rules out; a bottom-up ETC is for when the original estimate is flawed; BAC − EV is the remaining work (ETC at budget), not the total EAC.
Remember: Typical (keeps happening) → BAC / CPI; Atypical (one-time) → AC + (BAC − EV); plan broken → AC + new ETC.

questions.stem: A project to build a new data center includes purchasing servers, constructing the building, training staff, and paying first-year software subscriptions. The CFO wants the budget structured to support the company's asset depreciation strategy. What should the project manager do?
options: Present all of the costs as one combined total so the budget is simple for the CFO to review quickly.
Separate capital costs such as servers and the building from operating costs such as training.
Classify every project cost as a capital expense to maximize the assets shown on the balance sheet.
Move the training and subscription costs to operations so they are left out of the project budget.
questions.explanation:
Concept: CAPEX vs. OPEX — capital expenses buy long-lived assets that are depreciated; operating expenses are ongoing running costs (Rule M4-B05-R08).
Spot it: "Asset depreciation strategy," with a mix of assets (servers, building) and running costs (training, subscriptions).
In this scenario: The PM structures the budget separating capital costs (servers, building) from operating costs (training, subscriptions).
Why not the others: One combined total hides the split the CFO needs; calling everything capital misstates the finances; moving costs out of the budget hides true project cost.
Remember: Buy an asset = CapEx (servers); pay to run = OpEx (subscriptions, training).

questions.stem: A hybrid project is building a customer analytics platform that will store marketing preferences, purchase history, and some payment and health insurance information. The team plans to apply identical access controls to all data. What should the project manager do?
options: Apply the strictest controls to all of the data so no sensitive information is ever missed.
Keep identical access controls for all data so the platform stays simple to maintain over its lifetime.
Classify each data type by sensitivity and apply stronger controls to payment and insurance data.
Let each adaptive team decide how to protect the data that is used in its own features.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Data classification — classify data by sensitivity so handling controls match the risk of each type (Rule M5-B15-R02).
Spot it: A mix of low-sensitivity data (preferences) and high-sensitivity data (payment, health insurance) under "identical access controls."
In this scenario: The PM classifies each data type and applies stronger controls to payment and insurance data.
Why not the others: The strictest controls on everything overburdens usage and still skips classification; identical controls underprotect sensitive data; letting each team decide creates inconsistent, ungoverned protection.
Remember: Classify first, then control — protection matches sensitivity.

questions.stem: An agile team funded by a government grant must report quarterly progress against the approved release scope and budget, although its backlog changes frequently. The funder asks how the team will show variance. What should the agile project lead do?
options: Explain that agile teams do not use baselines and share the current backlog with the funder.
Freeze the backlog so that it matches the grant scope for the remainder of the whole project.
Rebaseline the scope and budget every sprint so that reported variance is always kept at exactly zero.
Keep the approved release scope and budget as a reference point and report changes against it.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Baselines in agile — even in adaptive work, an approved release scope and budget can serve as the comparison point for reporting variance (Rule M4-B16-R04).
Spot it: A funder needing "variance" against "approved release scope and budget" while the backlog keeps changing.
In this scenario: The lead keeps the approved release scope and budget as the reference and reports changes against it.
Why not the others: "Agile has no baselines" ignores a real governance need; freezing the backlog kills adaptivity; rebaselining every sprint makes variance meaningless.
Remember: Baseline = APPROVED reference point — you measure change against it.

questions.stem: Halfway through a city transit fare system project, a new consumer advocacy group forms and begins commenting publicly on fare changes. The stakeholder register was completed during initiation and has not been updated since. What should the project manager do?
options: Leave the stakeholder register unchanged since it was reviewed and approved during initiation.
Add the advocacy group to the stakeholder register with its interests, influence, and needs.
Track the advocacy group only in the issue log rather than adding it to the stakeholder register.
Ask the city's communications office to handle the advocacy group entirely outside the project.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stakeholder register as a living document — it captures stakeholders' interests, influence, and needs and is updated as new stakeholders appear (Rule M4-B16-R07).
Spot it: A new group forming mid-project and a register "not updated since initiation."
In this scenario: The PM adds the advocacy group to the register with its interests, influence, and needs, then plans its engagement.
Why not the others: An initiation approval doesn't freeze the register; the issue log tracks current problems, not stakeholders; handing the group to communications moves it outside project engagement.
Remember: Identify stakeholders early AND continuously — the register is never done.

questions.stem: A two-year hybrid project still produces a weekly 30-page design status report that was needed during early architecture work. No one reads it anymore, but the organization's audit policy requires keeping approved design decisions on record. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue producing the weekly report since it has been part of the project since the beginning.
Stop the report and delete all of the older copies to reduce storage costs and document clutter.
Shorten the report to ten pages and keep distributing it to the full project team at the end of each week.
Stop the weekly report but keep approved design decisions archived as the audit policy requires.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Right-sized documentation — retire reports that no longer add value while keeping records that policy requires (Rule M4-B16-R10).
Spot it: "No one reads it anymore," but an "audit policy requires keeping approved design decisions."
In this scenario: The PM stops the weekly report and keeps approved design decisions archived for audit.
Why not the others: Continuing out of habit wastes effort; deleting old copies breaks the audit requirement; a shorter version still produces a report no one needs.
Remember: Compliance = mandatory records; everything else must earn its keep.

questions.stem: An executive asks an agile team for a rough estimate of a new mobile wallet product to decide whether to fund an exploration phase. The team has little detail on features, and the only decision is whether to proceed to discovery. What should the team provide?
options: A quick, coarse range based on similar past products, suited to a go or no-go funding decision.
A detailed task-level estimate for every expected feature before answering the executive.
No estimate at all until discovery has produced a fully refined backlog of product features.
A precise single-number cost so the executive has complete certainty for the upcoming funding decision.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Fit the estimate to the decision — match the technique and precision to the information available and the decision being made (Rule M4-B04-R01).
Spot it: "Rough estimate," "little detail," and a simple go or no-go decision on discovery.
In this scenario: The team provides a quick, coarse range based on similar past products, which is enough for the funding decision.
Why not the others: A task-level estimate needs detail that doesn't exist; refusing to estimate blocks a legitimate decision; a precise single number gives false certainty.
Remember: Early = rough range (analogous); later = refined (bottom-up).

questions.stem: A utility must decide within two days whether to bid on replacing 50 miles of gas pipeline. The company completed a very similar 45-mile project last year and has detailed cost records from it. Which estimating approach should the project manager use?
options: Build a bottom-up estimate from a detailed work breakdown structure covering every task.
Develop three-point estimates for each activity in a newly built pipeline schedule.
Base the estimate on last year's similar pipeline project, adjusted for the known differences.
Wait for vendor quotes on all materials before preparing any estimate for the bid.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Analogous estimating — top-down estimating from similar past work; fastest, least detailed, best when history is relevant and time is short (Rule M4-B04-R03).
Spot it: "Within two days," "very similar project last year," and "detailed cost records."
In this scenario: The PM bases the estimate on last year's pipeline project, adjusted for known differences such as extra miles.
Why not the others: Bottom-up is most accurate but needs a full WBS and far more time; three-point estimates per activity need a schedule that doesn't exist; waiting for every vendor quote misses the deadline.
Remember: Analogous = fast and historical; Parametric = per-unit rate; Three-point = uncertainty; Bottom-up = detailed and slow.

questions.stem: A hybrid project must commit to a date for a hardware integration milestone that depends on an unproven sensor. Engineers say integration could take anywhere from 4 to 14 weeks, most likely 6. The sponsor asks for a single number. What should the project manager do?
options: Present a range built from optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic values with its confidence.
Give the sponsor the most likely estimate of six weeks as the committed milestone date.
Give the pessimistic 14-week estimate so the committed milestone date will never be missed.
Average the optimistic and pessimistic values and commit to the resulting nine-week date.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Three-point / range estimating — when uncertainty is high, estimate with optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic values and communicate a range with confidence (Rule M4-B04-R06).
Spot it: "Anywhere from 4 to 14 weeks," "unproven" technology, and a sponsor asking for "a single number."
In this scenario: The PM presents a range built from O, M, and P values (for example, PERT = (4 + 4×6 + 14) ÷ 6 = 7 weeks) with its confidence level.
Why not the others: The most likely value alone hides the long tail; the pessimistic value adds hidden padding; averaging only O and P ignores the most likely value.
Remember: High uncertainty = range, not a point. PERT = (O + 4M + P) / 6.

questions.stem: An agile team's release forecast assumes 40 story points per sprint, a figure the team estimated before starting. In the last six sprints the team has actually completed between 26 and 31 points. Stakeholders are relying on the forecast. What should the scrum master do?
options: Keep the 40-point assumption and ask the team to increase its effort to reach that number.
Update the release forecast using the points the team actually completed in recent sprints.
Re-estimate all backlog items with larger point values so that velocity appears to match.
Stop forecasting until the team's velocity settles at exactly 40 points for several sprints.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Calibrate with actuals — forecasts use real historical performance (velocity) instead of initial guesses (Rule M4-B04-R09).
Spot it: A planned 40 points versus six sprints of 26 to 31 actual, and stakeholders relying on the forecast.
In this scenario: The scrum master updates the release forecast using the team's actual recent velocity.
Why not the others: Pushing the team to hit 40 creates burnout and gaming; inflating point values games the metric; waiting for "exactly 40" leaves stakeholders with a false forecast.
Remember: Velocity is measured, not promised — forecast from actuals.

questions.stem: In a hybrid smart factory project, an adaptive team builds control software while a predictive team installs equipment on a baselined schedule. The software team's next release needs interface specifications that the hardware team plans to finalize in two months. No one has linked the two plans. What should the project manager do?
options: Let the software team build against assumed specifications and rework later if needed.
Ask the hardware team to finalize the interface specifications now, regardless of its baseline.
Map the interface dependency across both plans and agree on dates and owners to manage it.
Delay the software release until the hardware installation has been fully completed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Hybrid dependency integration — dependencies between predictive and adaptive streams must be mapped and managed explicitly (Rule M4-B14-R02).
Spot it: The software release "needs" hardware specs scheduled later, and "no one has linked the two plans."
In this scenario: The PM maps the interface dependency across both plans and agrees on dates and owners to manage it.
Why not the others: Building on assumptions invites rework; forcing hardware to finish now bypasses its baseline and change control; delaying software until installation ends loses the adaptive benefit.
Remember: Dependency → Assess Impact → Coordinate → Monitor.

questions.stem: The product owner for the adaptive team on a hybrid project decides to replace a planned reporting feature with a real-time dashboard. The dashboard would require additional servers, which belong to the predictive infrastructure scope under an approved cost baseline. What should the project manager do?
options: Let the product owner proceed since feature choices belong to the adaptive team alone.
Reject the dashboard since it was not included in the originally approved project scope.
Buy the extra servers from contingency reserves without notifying the project's governance body.
Submit the server impact through change control before the dashboard work commits any budget.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Hybrid change control — when adaptive product choices affect controlled (baselined) commitments, those impacts go through change control (Rule M4-B14-R05).
Spot it: A product owner decision that needs resources from "predictive infrastructure scope under an approved cost baseline."
In this scenario: The PM submits the server impact through change control before the dashboard work commits any budget.
Why not the others: The product owner owns feature choices, not the predictive cost baseline; rejecting outright skips analysis of a possibly valuable change; spending reserves without telling governance bypasses control.
Remember: Adaptive side decides WHAT to build; baseline impacts still go Change Request → Analyze → Approve.

questions.stem: A hybrid program has three agile teams that each prioritize their own backlogs well, plus a predictive infrastructure stream. Each team delivers its own top items, but the combined release offers little customer value because key cross-team features remain unfinished. What should the project manager do?
options: Let each team keep prioritizing independently since each of their backlogs is already well managed.
Set up a shared prioritization forum that orders work across all teams and infrastructure.
Have the infrastructure stream set the priorities for all three of the program's agile teams.
Add more teams to the program so that more features can be completed in every release.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Whole-initiative value prioritization — in multi-team or hybrid programs, work must be ordered for value across all teams, not only inside each team (Rule M4-B14-R08).
Spot it: Each team prioritizes "well," yet the combined release has "little customer value" because cross-team features stall.
In this scenario: The PM sets up a shared prioritization forum that orders work across all the agile teams and infrastructure.
Why not the others: Independent prioritization is what caused the problem; letting infrastructure set everyone's priorities puts one stream above customer value; adding teams adds more uncoordinated output.
Remember: Local optimum ≠ global value — prioritize across the whole.

questions.stem: A credit union's agile team has released a self-service loan-status feature over the last three iterations. The sponsor's report lists every feature as done, yet call-center volume about loan status has not changed. The product owner asks the project manager how progress should be reported at the upcoming review. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Report the number of features completed per iteration as evidence that the team is delivering value
Raise the team's velocity target so more loan features are finished before the next review meeting
Report the change in status calls and portal usage as the test of whether the increments succeeded
Wait until the full loan platform is released before measuring any member or business results
questions.explanation:
Concept: Outcomes over outputs — a shipped feature is an output; the change it causes for users and the business is the outcome that proves value. (Rule M4-B18-R04)
Spot it: "everything is done" but the business number the work was meant to move has not moved.
In this scenario: Loan-status features shipped, yet status calls are flat. Reporting call volume and portal use tells the review whether the increments worked.
Why not the others: Feature counts measure activity, not value; raising velocity just ships more unproven work; waiting for the full platform delays the learning that incremental delivery exists to give.
Remember: Deliverable → Outcome → Benefit → Value. Done is not the same as worked.

questions.stem: An agile team is building a meal-planning add-on for a grocery app. After three releases to a pilot group, fewer than 2% of users open the add-on, and interviews show customers strongly prefer the existing shopping-list feature. Eight more add-on features remain on the product roadmap. What should the project manager encourage the product owner to do?
options: Keep delivering all eight planned features because the add-on was already approved in the product roadmap
Launch a marketing push for the add-on before examining whether customers actually need it at all
Ask the team to increase velocity so the remaining features reach pilot users before the pilot ends
Use the pilot evidence to decide whether to pivot the add-on or stop funding its remaining features
questions.explanation:
Concept: Pivot or stop on evidence — in agile, the roadmap is a hypothesis; when real user data shows the expected value is not coming, the product owner changes direction instead of finishing the plan. (Rule M4-B18-R07)
Spot it: low adoption, users preferring something else, lots of planned work still ahead.
In this scenario: Under 2% usage and clear interview feedback are strong evidence. The product owner should use it to decide to pivot the add-on or stop funding the remaining eight features.
Why not the others: "It is on the roadmap" treats a plan as a promise; marketing pushes a product customers already rejected; more velocity just builds unwanted features faster.
Remember: Data → Insight → Decision → Action. Evidence beats the roadmap.

questions.stem: Sales asks a logistics startup's agile team to release a full route-optimization module on a trade-show date six weeks away. The team's forecast shows only the core routing engine is likely to be stable by then, and an unstable demo could jeopardize two major customer deals. How should the project manager approach the release plan?
options: Commit to the full module on the trade-show date and add overtime to protect the promised scope
Facilitate a decision on which stable, high-value capabilities to release, weighing the deal risk
Postpone every release until all route-optimization features are complete and fully tested
Let the sales director set the release scope because the trade-show date is a firm business commitment
questions.explanation:
Concept: Release planning is a value-and-risk decision — you choose what to release by weighing the value delivered against the risk of releasing it, not just by hitting a date. (Rule M4-B18-R10)
Spot it: a fixed external date, a forecast showing only part of the scope will be ready, a serious downside if something unstable goes out.
In this scenario: Only the core engine will be stable, and a shaky demo could lose two deals. The PM facilitates a decision on which stable, high-value capabilities go to the trade show.
Why not the others: Overtime to force full scope raises the very instability risk at stake; holding every release wastes the date; letting sales dictate scope bypasses the product owner and the team's forecast.
Remember: Release = value + risk, not just a date. Stable and valuable goes first.

questions.stem: A water utility's project manager is starting a small, low-risk project to replace 40 identical meters with a vendor the utility has used for years. The PMO template calls for monthly steering committee reviews, a full quantitative risk analysis, and a 60-page management plan. What should the project manager do?
options: Propose a scaled-down plan and review cadence that fit the project's low risk and simple scope
Apply every PMO template element in full so the project is managed the same way as larger ones
Skip formal planning entirely because the vendor and the meters are already familiar to the utility
Move the project to an adaptive life cycle so the team can avoid the PMO's documentation demands
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tailoring — fit the amount of process, documents and oversight to the project's size, risk, complexity and context instead of applying every template in full. (Rule M3-B17-R01)
Spot it: small, simple, low-risk work facing a heavyweight standard template.
In this scenario: Forty identical meters and a trusted vendor is low risk. The PM proposes a scaled-down plan and review cadence and agrees it with the PMO.
Why not the others: Full template use wastes effort on a trivial project; dropping planning altogether is over-correcting; switching life cycles to escape paperwork is the wrong reason to change approach.
Remember: Tailor = right-size. Plan = HOW, and HOW should fit the project.

questions.stem: A project manager is planning a three-year hospital expansion. Design for phase 1 is complete, but phases 2 and 3 depend on a state licensing decision expected in 14 months. The sponsor wants a fully detailed activity schedule for all three phases by next week. What should the project manager do?
options: Build detailed activity estimates for all three phases now so the sponsor has a complete, final schedule
Delay all schedule development until the state licensing decision removes the major uncertainty
Detail phase 1 activities now and hold phases 2 and 3 at milestone level until licensing is known
Detail phases 2 and 3 using phase 1 durations and add a large buffer to cover the licensing risk
questions.explanation:
Concept: Rolling wave planning — plan near-term work in detail and keep later work at a higher level until the information needed to detail it exists. (Rule M3-B17-R03)
Spot it: a known near phase, later phases that depend on a future decision, pressure to detail everything now.
In this scenario: Phase 1 design is complete, but phases 2 and 3 hinge on a licensing decision 14 months away. Detail phase 1 now and keep the later phases at milestone level.
Why not the others: Detailing everything now creates false precision that will be reworked; waiting for licensing stalls work that is ready; copying phase 1 durations plus a big buffer is guessing, not planning.
Remember: Near = detailed, far = high level. Plan as deep as you can see.

questions.stem: While a warehouse automation project is being planned, its operations director says the conveyor installation will obviously happen during the holiday shutdown and that the existing floor can take the load. Neither statement has been verified or written down anywhere. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Build the schedule around the holiday shutdown, since the operations director knows the facility
Record both statements in the assumption log, assign owners, and plan how each will be verified
Log both statements as issues and escalate them to the sponsor for a decision on how to proceed
Hire a structural engineer to redesign the floor before any other planning work is continued
questions.explanation:
Concept: Assumptions and constraints — anything the plan takes as true without proof is an assumption and must be logged, owned and verified. (Rule M3-B17-R06)
Spot it: "obviously," "it will be fine," statements nobody has checked or written down.
In this scenario: The shutdown timing and the floor load are unverified assumptions. Record them in the assumption log, give each an owner, and plan how to verify them.
Why not the others: Scheduling around them bakes untested beliefs into the plan; nothing has gone wrong yet, so they are not issues to escalate; a floor redesign acts before assessing.
Remember: Constraint / Assumption → Assess Impact → Adjust. If it's assumed, log it and test it.

questions.stem: Two months into a baselined project to build a municipal bus depot, the city council adopts an ordinance requiring electric-bus charging infrastructure in all new depots. The approved plan does not include any charging equipment. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Continue executing the approved baseline, since the ordinance was passed after planning was done
Direct the contractor to add the charging equipment now and update all baselines at project closure
Ask the sponsor to seek an exemption so that the approved plan and baselines can stay unchanged
Analyze the ordinance's effect on scope, cost, and schedule and submit a change request for review
questions.explanation:
Concept: Replanning when material information changes — a new law or requirement that affects the approved plan triggers impact analysis and formal change control, not silent continuation. (Rule M3-B17-R09)
Spot it: a new regulation, ordinance or mandate after the baseline was approved.
In this scenario: The ordinance makes charging infrastructure mandatory, and the baseline has none. Analyze the impact on scope, cost and schedule, then submit a change request.
Why not the others: Continuing ignores a legal requirement; directing the contractor first bypasses approval; seeking an exemption dodges a valid obligation rather than managing it.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor.

questions.stem: A kanban team supporting an insurer's claims system has 23 items sitting in its test column and only two testers. Developers keep pulling new work into development, and lead times have doubled over the past month. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Ask developers to pull even more new items so throughput numbers stay high during the slowdown
Agree on a WIP limit for the test column so the bottleneck is visible and developers help clear it
Hire three contract testers right away, before examining how the work actually flows across the board
Remove the test column so items move straight from development to done and lead times shrink
questions.explanation:
Concept: WIP limits — a cap on how many items can sit in a kanban column, so a bottleneck becomes visible and the team stops starting and starts finishing. (Rule M4-B13-R02)
Spot it: a piled-up column, people pulling new work anyway, lead times growing.
In this scenario: Twenty-three items wait for two testers. A WIP limit on test stops developers from overfeeding it and prompts them to help clear the queue.
Why not the others: Pulling more work deepens the jam; hiring before understanding the flow may treat the wrong problem; removing the test column hides the constraint and skips quality.
Remember: Kanban = flow. Limit WIP, stop starting, start finishing.

questions.stem: A marketing operations team has used kanban for eight months, and its weekly throughput has stayed between 9 and 13 items. A director asks when the 60 remaining campaign items will be finished. The team does not estimate items individually. What is the BEST way for the project manager to answer?
options: Run a Monte Carlo forecast from past throughput and give a date range with confidence levels
Ask each member to estimate all 60 items in hours and total them into one fixed completion date
Divide 60 by the best week's throughput and commit to that date to show confidence in the team
Decline to forecast because kanban teams do not estimate and cannot predict completion dates
questions.explanation:
Concept: Probabilistic forecasting — when a kanban system is stable, past throughput can be run through a Monte Carlo simulation to give a completion range with confidence levels. (Rule M4-B13-R05)
Spot it: a team that does not estimate items, months of steady throughput data, a stakeholder asking "when?".
In this scenario: Throughput has held at 9–13 items a week for eight months. A Monte Carlo forecast turns that history into a date range with confidence levels for the 60 items.
Why not the others: Hour estimates add work the team does not do and imply false precision; using the best week is optimistic cherry-picking; refusing to forecast ignores that kanban data supports forecasting.
Remember: Kanban metrics: throughput, lead time, cycle time. Stable history → forecast range, not a single promise.

questions.stem: On a digital agency's kanban board, designers and developers keep arguing about whether a web page is ready for build. Some cards move forward without approved copy and then bounce back, causing rework. What should the project manager do?
options: Assign the lead developer to decide case by case which cards are allowed to move into build
Add a separate rework column so returned cards can be tracked without disrupting the board
Facilitate the team in defining and posting entry criteria a card must meet before it enters build
Tell the designers to hold every card until copy for the entire site has been approved by the client
questions.explanation:
Concept: Explicit policies — a kanban team writes down and posts the criteria for work to enter or leave each column, so everyone shares one definition of "ready". (Rule M4-B13-R08)
Spot it: arguments about whether work is ready, cards bouncing back, rework.
In this scenario: Cards move to build without approved copy and then return. Facilitate the team in agreeing and posting entry criteria for the build column.
Why not the others: One person deciding case by case keeps the rule hidden; a rework column tracks the waste instead of preventing it; waiting for all site copy destroys flow.
Remember: Make policies explicit: if it isn't written on the board, it isn't a rule.

questions.stem: A hospital is two weeks from go-live on a new pharmacy dispensing system delivered under a predictive plan. Training has covered standard dispensing only. Pharmacy technicians have not practiced handling a failed barcode scan or working through a system outage. What should the project manager do?
options: Add hands-on sessions on scan failures and outage procedures before go-live and confirm readiness
Proceed with go-live and let the vendor help desk talk technicians through exceptions as they arise
Postpone go-live until technicians have been trained on every possible function in the system
Give technicians the vendor's full user manual and ask them to read the chapters on exceptions
questions.explanation:
Concept: Operational readiness training — users must be trained on normal use and on exceptions and failures before go-live, because that is where risk sits. (Rule M5-B13-R04)
Spot it: go-live approaching, training covering only the happy path, safety-critical work.
In this scenario: Technicians cannot handle a failed scan or an outage, and patient safety depends on it. Add hands-on exception and outage sessions and confirm readiness first.
Why not the others: Relying on the help desk puts learning in the middle of a live incident; training on every function is excessive and delays value; a manual is not practice.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close. Transfer includes the ability to handle exceptions.

questions.stem: A retailer's new point-of-sale software was built in adaptive releases and rolled out to 200 stores under a predictive deployment plan. The team handed the system to IT operations last week and is preparing to close. Store managers mention occasional slow checkouts, but no one is reviewing formal data. What should the project manager do?
options: Close the project as planned, since the system has been accepted and handed over to IT operations
Roll all stores back to the previous point-of-sale software until the anecdotal complaints stop
Agree with operations on early-life measures such as incident counts and checkout times, and review them
Assign the development team to rewrite the checkout module based on the store managers' comments
questions.explanation:
Concept: Early-life support — after handover, agree measurable indicators with operations and watch them closely so problems are caught before closure. (Rule M5-B13-R07)
Spot it: a recent handover, informal complaints, nobody looking at data.
In this scenario: Slow checkouts are reported only anecdotally. Agree measures such as incident counts and checkout times with IT operations and review them.
Why not the others: Closing now ignores warning signs; a full rollback overreacts before any data; rewriting code from comments acts before analyzing.
Remember: Data → Analyze → Insight → Decision → Action → Monitor.

questions.stem: An agile team has delivered the final increment of a donor-management app for a nonprofit, and the product owner has accepted it. The support team has not received the runbook, two software licenses still need to be transferred to the client, and final invoices are open. The sponsor wants to release the team tomorrow. What should the project manager do?
options: Close the project now, since the product owner has accepted the final increment of the app
Finish the runbook handover, license transfers, and invoices before formal closure
Release the team tomorrow and ask the client's support staff to finish the transition work
Move the runbook and license tasks to the backlog so a future team can pick them up later
questions.explanation:
Concept: Formal closure — a project closes only when acceptance, transition, contract and administrative duties are all complete, not just when the last deliverable is accepted. (Rule M5-B13-R10)
Spot it: product accepted but handover documents, licenses or invoices still open, pressure to release the team.
In this scenario: The runbook, license transfers and final invoices are unfinished. Complete them before closing and releasing the team.
Why not the others: Acceptance alone is not closure; pushing transition work onto the client's staff is not a handover; moving it to a future team leaves obligations orphaned.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close.

questions.stem: A manufacturer needs a custom quality-inspection software module within nine months. The internal IT team has the skills but is fully committed to an ERP upgrade, and two vendors offer similar modules. The sponsor asks the project manager whether to build or buy. What should the project manager do?
options: Recommend building in-house because the internal IT team already has all of the required technical skills
Compare internal capacity, vendor cost, timing, risk, and strategic fit before making a recommendation
Select the lowest-priced vendor, since buying is usually faster than building custom software
Ask the ERP team to split its time across both efforts so the organization avoids any vendor costs
questions.explanation:
Concept: Make-or-buy analysis — decide to build or buy by comparing capability, capacity, cost, timing, risk and strategic fit together. (Rule M4-B09-R01)
Spot it: a team with the skills but no capacity, vendors available, a deadline.
In this scenario: Internal IT is skilled but fully committed, and vendors exist. The PM compares all the factors before recommending.
Why not the others: Skills alone ignore capacity; lowest price alone ignores fit and risk; splitting the ERP team puts another priority at risk to save cost.
Remember: Make-or-buy = capability + capacity + cost + time + risk + strategy.

questions.stem: A school district needs 1,200 identical laptops with a fully specified configuration, warranty, and delivery date. Several resellers can supply the exact model, and the district's main concern is obtaining the lowest compliant price. What should the project manager do?
options: Issue a request for proposal inviting resellers to suggest their own laptop solutions
Issue a request for information to learn which laptop models the resellers could supply
Issue a request for quotation for the exact configuration and compare the compliant prices
Negotiate directly with one reseller the district has used before to save procurement time
questions.explanation:
Concept: Procurement documents — an RFI gathers information, an RFP asks sellers to propose solutions, and an RFQ asks for a price on a clearly defined need. (Rule M4-B09-R03)
Spot it: identical items, a full specification, several sellers, price as the deciding factor.
In this scenario: The laptop configuration, warranty and delivery date are fixed, and the goal is lowest compliant price. That is an RFQ.
Why not the others: An RFP invites solutions the district does not need; an RFI is for learning what exists; a single-vendor deal skips competition the district wants.
Remember: RFI = learn, RFP = solution, RFQ = price. Clear requirement + price comparison → RFQ.

questions.stem: A county is contracting to build a standard 2,000-square-foot maintenance garage using complete, stamped drawings. The procurement officer wants to minimize the county's financial exposure to cost overruns. Which contract type BEST meets this goal?
options: Cost plus fixed fee, because the county reimburses actual costs and pays a set fee
Time and materials, because the county pays for actual labor hours and materials used
Cost plus incentive fee, because the seller shares in savings under a target cost
Firm fixed price, because the seller absorbs cost overruns on the fully defined scope
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contract types and risk — in a firm fixed price contract the seller carries the cost-overrun risk, which works when scope is fully defined. (Rule M4-B09-R06)
Spot it: complete drawings, a standard build, a buyer who wants to limit cost exposure.
In this scenario: The garage is standard and fully drawn, and the county wants to cap exposure. Firm fixed price moves overrun risk to the seller.
Why not the others: Cost plus fixed fee leaves the buyer paying actual costs; time and materials has open-ended exposure; cost plus incentive still reimburses overruns in part.
Remember: Clear scope → fixed price (seller risk). Unclear scope → cost reimbursable (buyer risk).

questions.stem: Midway through a fixed-price contract to install an office security system, a seller misses two contractual milestones. A frustrated facilities manager then tells the seller's technicians directly to work weekends and skip certain tests. What should the project manager do?
options: Stop the informal direction and address the missed milestones through the contract's remedy terms
Support the facilities manager's direction so the technicians recover the missed milestones faster
Terminate the contract and hire a new seller to finish the installation on the original schedule
Withhold all payments to the seller without notice until the missed milestones are recovered
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contract administration — seller performance is managed through the contract terms and agreed channels, and only authorized people direct the seller. (Rule M4-B09-R09)
Spot it: missed milestones, someone outside the contract giving the seller's staff orders.
In this scenario: The facilities manager is informally directing technicians and skipping tests. Stop that and use the contract's remedy terms for the missed milestones.
Why not the others: Supporting informal direction creates unauthorized changes and quality risk; termination is a last resort; withholding payment without notice breaches the process.
Remember: SELLER = contract. Manage the seller through the contract, not around it.

questions.stem: A food packaging plant project is producing seal defects that final inspectors catch at a 6% rate. The operations manager proposes adding a second inspection shift so more defective packages are caught before shipping. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Add the second inspection shift so more of the defective packages are caught before shipment
Analyze the sealing process to find and correct the causes so fewer defective seals are produced
Accept the 6% rate as a cost of quality, since the inspectors are already catching the defects
Raise the sampling rate at final inspection and report the monthly defect totals to the customer's team
questions.explanation:
Concept: Prevention over inspection — quality is planned and built in; inspection finds defects, but fixing the process stops them from being made. (Rule M4-B06-R02)
Spot it: a steady defect rate and a proposal to inspect more.
In this scenario: Seal defects run at 6%. Analyzing the sealing process and correcting the causes reduces defects at the source.
Why not the others: A second inspection shift catches more but makes no fewer; accepting 6% treats waste as normal; more sampling and reporting is still inspection.
Remember: Quality = prevention over inspection. Fix the process, not just the product.

questions.stem: A hybrid project has an adaptive team building a claims-processing tool and a predictive rollout to regional offices. Pilot processing times are plotted daily on a control chart. One day this week was above the mean, but every point is within the limits and shows no pattern. A regional director wants the team to investigate. What should the project manager do?
options: Launch a root-cause investigation into the above-average day to keep it from happening again
Explain that the data shows normal variation and keep watching for points outside limits or trends
Tighten the control limits so that smaller changes in processing time will trigger investigations
Stop charting the data, since processing times within the limits show there is no quality problem
questions.explanation:
Concept: Control charts — they separate normal (common-cause) variation from signals; points within limits with no pattern mean the process is in control. (Rule M4-B06-R05)
Spot it: one point above the mean, everything within limits, someone wanting to investigate.
In this scenario: Every point is within limits with no trend, so the high day is normal variation. Explain this and keep monitoring for out-of-limit points or runs.
Why not the others: A root-cause hunt on noise wastes effort; tightening limits manufactures false alarms; stopping the chart removes the early warning.
Remember: In limits, no pattern = leave it. Out of limits or seven in a row = investigate.

questions.stem: During a retrospective, an agile mobile app team discusses why crash reports rose after the last release. Members suggest many possible reasons, including new libraries, device fragmentation, rushed testing, and unclear acceptance criteria. The team wants to organize these ideas before choosing what to investigate. Which tool should the team use?
options: A Pareto chart that ranks the crash types by how often each occurs
A control chart that plots crash rates against statistical limits
A fishbone diagram that groups the suspected causes into categories
A scatter diagram relating crash counts to the number of downloads
questions.explanation:
Concept: Cause-and-effect (fishbone/Ishikawa) diagram — organizes many possible causes of one problem into categories before investigating. (Rule M4-B06-R08)
Spot it: one effect, a long list of suspected causes, a wish to organize ideas.
In this scenario: The team has many possible reasons for the crashes and wants to group them. A fishbone diagram does exactly that.
Why not the others: A Pareto chart ranks known frequencies but does not organize causes; a control chart shows stability; a scatter diagram tests one relationship between two variables.
Remember: Fishbone = WHY (causes). Pareto = WHICH (80/20). Control = STABLE? Scatter = RELATED?

questions.stem: A government agency is replacing its paper permit process. In requirements workshops, clerks struggle to describe what the new screens should do and keep saying they will know it when they see it. Requirements must be approved before design begins. What should the project manager do?
options: Have the business analyst write requirements from the current paper forms and request sign-off
Hold more workshops with the same clerks until they can describe their requirements in writing
Build a clickable mock-up of key screens and walk clerks through it to draw out and confirm needs
Move to design using the vendor's standard permit screens and collect the clerks' feedback after deployment
questions.explanation:
Concept: Prototyping — when stakeholders cannot describe needs but will recognize them, show them a model or mock-up to draw out and confirm requirements. (Rule M4-B01-R04)
Spot it: "I'll know it when I see it," repeated workshops that stall.
In this scenario: Clerks cannot describe screens, and requirements need approval before design. A clickable mock-up lets them react and confirm needs.
Why not the others: Writing from paper forms guesses at needs; more of the same workshops repeats what failed; waiting until after deployment finds gaps far too late.
Remember: Can't say it? Show it. Prototype to discover requirements.

questions.stem: A medical device firm uses a hybrid approach: firmware is developed adaptively in two-week iterations, while the hardware follows a baselined predictive plan with regulatory design controls. Marketing requests a change to the device's casing dimensions and a new firmware display option. How should the project manager handle the requests?
options: Add both requests to the firmware backlog so the product owner can prioritize them together
Route the casing change through formal change control and let the product owner rank the display option
Send both requests to the change control board so every change follows one consistent process
Reject both requests, since the hardware baseline and the firmware roadmap are already approved
questions.explanation:
Concept: Hybrid change handling — each change follows the governance of the part it affects: formal change control for baselined work, backlog ordering by the product owner for adaptive work. (Rule M4-B01-R07)
Spot it: a hybrid project with a regulated baseline on one side, iterations on the other, and a request touching both.
In this scenario: The casing change hits the baselined, regulated hardware, so it goes to change control. The firmware display option goes to the product owner to rank.
Why not the others: Putting hardware in the backlog bypasses design controls; sending firmware to the CCB adds needless bureaucracy; rejecting both ignores legitimate requests.
Remember: Baseline → CCB. Backlog → product owner. Route by the life cycle of the work.

questions.stem: An agile team's backlog for a hotel booking platform contains a large epic for fax-based group reservations written two years ago. Analytics show no group bookings have arrived by fax in 18 months, and the sales team now uses an online group form. What should the product owner do with the epic?
options: Keep the epic near the top because stakeholders approved it when the product was first scoped
Split the epic into smaller stories so the team can deliver it gradually over future releases
Ask the team to estimate the epic in story points before making any decision on its priority
Remove the epic or drop it to the bottom, since it no longer justifies the team's effort
questions.explanation:
Concept: Backlog refinement for value — the product owner keeps ordering by current value and removes or drops items that no longer justify the effort. (Rule M4-B01-R10)
Spot it: an old item nobody uses, data showing no demand, a better alternative already in place.
In this scenario: No fax bookings in 18 months and an online form already in use. The product owner removes or deprioritizes the epic.
Why not the others: Past approval does not make it valuable now; splitting it keeps worthless work alive; estimating it wastes effort on work that should not be done.
Remember: Product backlog = product owner orders by value. No value, no place at the top.

questions.stem: A project manager is building the resource plan for a data center migration. The plan assigns six network engineers, which matches the estimated hours. However, only one of them has experience with the software-defined networking platform the migration requires. What should the project manager do?
options: Revise the plan to secure the platform skills through training, hiring, or contracting
Keep the plan as is, because the six engineers together provide enough hours to cover the work
Assign all platform-specific tasks to the one experienced engineer to protect the work's quality
Add two more network engineers to the plan so the team has extra hours for troubleshooting
questions.explanation:
Concept: Resource planning by quantity and capability — enough hours is not enough; the plan must also cover the specific skills the work needs. (Rule M4-B10-R01)
Spot it: headcount that matches the estimate, but a skill gap for key work.
In this scenario: Six engineers cover the hours, but only one knows the platform. Revise the plan to secure the skill through training, hiring or contracting.
Why not the others: Hours alone ignore the skill gap; loading one expert creates a bottleneck and single point of failure; more generalists do not add the missing skill.
Remember: Resources = how many AND how skilled.

questions.stem: A hybrid program uses a predictive plan for a factory retrofit and an adaptive team for the control software. A functional manager insists every engineer be scheduled at 100% utilization. Since then, work waiting for the program's single integration tester has piled up, and deliveries have slowed. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Limit new work to what integration testing can absorb and let engineers help clear the queue
Keep all engineers at full utilization so that none of the program's paid engineering capacity goes unused
Ask the integration tester to work overtime until the queue of waiting handoffs is cleared
Start additional engineering tasks so the engineers stay busy while they wait for testing
questions.explanation:
Concept: Flow over utilization — matching work to the system's constraint delivers more than keeping everyone 100% busy. (Rule M4-B10-R03)
Spot it: a push for full utilization, a queue growing in front of one role, slowing deliveries.
In this scenario: Work is piling up in front of the single integration tester. Limit new work to what testing can absorb and have engineers help clear the queue.
Why not the others: Full utilization is what caused the pile-up; overtime for one person is unsustainable; starting more tasks lengthens the queue.
Remember: Busy is not the goal; finished is. Manage to the bottleneck.

questions.stem: An agile team is planning the next two iterations for a public library's mobile app. Two of the five developers will attend a mandatory week-long security course, and a national holiday falls in the second iteration. The product owner wants the same scope as the last two iterations. What should the team do?
options: Commit to the same scope as before, since the team's average velocity is already well established
Base the iteration commitments on actual availability, including the course week and the holiday
Ask the two developers to skip the security course so the team's capacity is not reduced
Plan the same scope and lengthen both iterations by a few days to make up the lost working time
questions.explanation:
Concept: Capacity-based planning — commitments reflect actual availability, including leave, training and holidays, not just past averages. (Rule M4-B10-R06)
Spot it: known absences, a holiday, pressure to keep the same scope.
In this scenario: Two developers are away for a week and a holiday falls in iteration two. Plan to real capacity for each iteration.
Why not the others: Past velocity assumed full availability; skipping mandatory training creates a compliance problem; stretching the iteration breaks the fixed timebox.
Remember: Capacity first, then commitment. Timeboxes stay fixed.

questions.stem: Priya and another project manager at an engineering firm each need the firm's only licensed structural reviewer during the same three weeks. Both have asked the reviewer directly to put their work first. The reviewer is now splitting time, and both reviews are slipping. What should Priya do?
options: Raise the conflict to the PMO or portfolio manager so priority is set based on enterprise value
Negotiate directly with the reviewer for more of their hours by offering recognition from the sponsor
Hire an outside reviewer for this project without telling the other project manager about it
Crash this project's schedule so its review finishes before the other project's review begins
questions.explanation:
Concept: Enterprise resource conflicts — when projects compete for a scarce shared resource, the PMO or portfolio level sets priority based on organizational value. (Rule M4-B10-R09)
Spot it: one scarce specialist, several projects pulling on them, both slipping.
In this scenario: Direct lobbying has made both reviews slip. Priya raises the conflict to the PMO or portfolio manager to set priority based on enterprise value.
Why not the others: Offering recognition is more lobbying; a secret hire works around governance and the other project; crashing her schedule does not solve the shared constraint.
Remember: Project → Program → Portfolio. Shared resources are prioritized at the level that sees both projects.

questions.stem: A construction firm uses a predictive plan for building work and an adaptive team for a smart-building app. The risk register lists an entry stating that a new sensor supplier may offer 30% lower prices next quarter, with a mitigation plan to reduce its likelihood. What should the project manager do?
options: Reclassify the entry as an opportunity and plan a response to enhance or exploit it
Keep the mitigation plan, since all uncertain events are handled by reducing their likelihood
Delete the entry from the register, since risks cover only events with negative effects
Transfer the entry to the sensor supplier so it owns the pricing uncertainty and its outcome
questions.explanation:
Concept: Threats vs opportunities — a risk is any uncertain event; negative ones are threats and positive ones are opportunities, each with its own responses. (Rule M4-B07-R02)
Spot it: a positive possible event (lower prices, early finish) treated with a threat response.
In this scenario: A possible 30% price drop is an opportunity, yet it has a mitigation plan. Reclassify it and plan to enhance or exploit it.
Why not the others: Mitigating an opportunity reduces a benefit; deleting it misreads what risks are; transfer is a threat response and does not fit.
Remember: Threats: avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept. Opportunities: exploit, share, enhance, accept. Both can be escalated.

questions.stem: An agile team at a payments company must decide whether to launch a new fraud-scoring engine before a regulatory deadline. Launch errors could cost millions in chargebacks, and several years of historical fraud data are available. The product owner asks how to assess the launch risk. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Rate the risk high or low on the team's risk board and decide on launch at the next planning session
Skip formal analysis, since agile teams manage their risks through short feedback loops alone
Delay the launch until all fraud-scoring defects are removed, regardless of the regulatory deadline
Model the likely loss ranges from the historical fraud data, since the stakes justify deeper analysis
questions.explanation:
Concept: Quantitative risk analysis — numerical modeling such as Monte Carlo or expected monetary value is worth doing when stakes are high and good data exists. (Rule M4-B07-R05)
Spot it: millions at stake, a hard deadline, years of historical data.
In this scenario: Chargebacks could cost millions and there is solid fraud data. Modeling likely loss ranges gives the product owner a sound launch decision.
Why not the others: A high/low rating is too coarse for this exposure; feedback loops do not replace analysis at this risk level; waiting for zero defects misses the regulatory deadline.
Remember: Qualitative = rank quickly. Quantitative = model numbers when the decision is worth it.

questions.stem: To avoid a threatened strike at its domestic steel supplier, a bridge project manager decides to source steel from an overseas mill. The response has been approved and added to the project management plan. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Close the strike risk in the register, since the response has been approved and put in place
Transfer the delivery risk to the overseas mill by adding a late-delivery penalty clause to the purchase order
Add contingency reserve for the strike in case the domestic supplier's workers walk out later
Identify new risks the overseas sourcing may introduce, such as customs delays or currency swings
questions.explanation:
Concept: Secondary risks — a risk response can itself create new risks, and these must be identified and managed. (Rule M4-B07-R08)
Spot it: a response has just been implemented or approved, a new supplier, a new location or method.
In this scenario: Overseas sourcing avoids the strike but brings customs delays and currency swings. Identify these secondary risks next.
Why not the others: Closing the entry misses the new exposure; a penalty clause is a response to risks not yet analyzed; reserving for the strike ignores that the strike risk was avoided.
Remember: Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor. Every response can breed a new risk.

questions.stem: A hybrid project is delivering a new warehouse under a predictive plan and its inventory app adaptively. A risk exists that one report layout may print poorly on a legacy printer used twice a year. The only fix is a $40,000 redesign, and the impact would be a few minutes of manual reformatting. What should the project manager do?
options: Mitigate the risk by funding the redesign so the report prints correctly on every printer
Escalate the risk to the steering committee, since the legacy printer is an asset they own
Accept the risk, record the rationale, and note a simple manual workaround in case it occurs
Delete the risk from the register because both its probability and impact are very low
questions.explanation:
Concept: Risk acceptance — when a response costs more than the impact it prevents, deliberately accept the risk, document why, and note a fallback. (Rule M4-B08-R04)
Spot it: a costly fix, a tiny impact, a rare occurrence.
In this scenario: A $40,000 redesign to avoid a few minutes of reformatting twice a year is not worth it. Accept, record the rationale, and note the manual workaround.
Why not the others: Mitigating costs far more than the impact; escalation is for risks outside the PM's authority, which this is not; deleting it loses the record and the workaround.
Remember: Accept = conscious choice, recorded, with a plan B.

questions.stem: An agile team building a travel booking app learns that a regional airline wants to offer a loyalty integration in the same market. Neither company can build the full integration alone before a tourism festival that would bring a surge of new users. What should the project manager recommend to the product owner?
options: Form a joint arrangement with the airline to co-develop the integration and split the resulting gains
Transfer the integration work to the airline and let it capture the festival traffic on its own terms
Accept the opportunity passively and benefit from the festival only if the timing happens to work out
Add the integration to the bottom of the backlog until the team finishes its currently planned work
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sharing an opportunity — partnering with a third party who can help capture a positive risk that neither could fully capture alone. (Rule M4-B08-R07)
Spot it: a partner with complementary capability, a time-limited upside, no one able to do it alone.
In this scenario: Neither company can build the integration alone before the festival. A joint arrangement that splits the gains is sharing.
Why not the others: Transferring gives the benefit away (and transfer is a threat response); passive acceptance leaves value to chance; burying it in the backlog misses the window.
Remember: Share = partner to win together. Exploit = make it certain. Enhance = make it likelier.

questions.stem: A port expansion project's risk register included the chance that a key crane would be unavailable, along with a contingency plan. This morning the crane rental firm confirmed the crane will not arrive for three weeks. What should the project manager do?
options: Raise the risk's probability rating in the register and keep monitoring the crane's status
Submit a change request to extend the schedule by three weeks before taking other action
Hold a new risk workshop to identify other equipment that might also become unavailable
Log the unavailability as an issue, carry out the contingency plan, and track it to resolution
questions.explanation:
Concept: Risk becomes issue — once a risk occurs it is no longer uncertain; log it as an issue, execute the planned contingency and track it. (Rule M4-B08-R10)
Spot it: "confirmed," "has happened," a risk with a contingency plan ready.
In this scenario: The crane is confirmed three weeks late. Log it as an issue, carry out the contingency plan, and track it to resolution.
Why not the others: Raising probability treats a fact as uncertain; a change request comes only if the contingency cannot absorb the impact; a new workshop delays action.
Remember: Risk register = dark clouds. Issue log = storm has arrived. Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor → Issue.

questions.stem: A new scheduler on an office fit-out project enters activities with dates copied from a similar past project and then tries to pull in the finish date. Several activities, such as painting before drywall, now appear in an impossible order. What should the project manager tell the scheduler to do FIRST?
options: Fast-track the activities that appear out of order to recover the sponsor's target finish date
Define the logical dependencies between activities and build the network before changing any dates
Add lead time to painting so it can start earlier and still meet the sponsor's required end date
Level resources across the schedule so the crews are evenly loaded before any dependencies are defined
questions.explanation:
Concept: Activity sequencing — build the network from real dependencies first; only then can you calculate and optimize dates. (Rule M4-B03-R01)
Spot it: dates copied from another project, impossible order, attempts to compress before logic exists.
In this scenario: Painting shows before drywall, so the logic is broken. Define dependencies and build the network before changing any dates.
Why not the others: Fast-tracking and leads are compression techniques that need correct logic first; resource leveling also works only on a valid network.
Remember: Sequence → Estimate → Schedule → Optimize. Logic before dates.

questions.stem: Reviewing a network schedule, a project manager sees that activity F is the longest single activity at 20 days but has 8 days of total float. Path A-C-E-H totals 54 days with zero float. The sponsor wants to add resources to activity F to shorten the project. What should the project manager explain?
options: Adding resources to activity F will shorten the project because it is the longest activity
Activity F is critical because the longest activities always carry the most schedule risk
Only shortening path A-C-E-H can pull in the finish date, since that path has zero float
The project cannot be shortened at all, since the network already has a zero-float path
questions.explanation:
Concept: Critical path — the longest path through the network, with zero total float; only shortening it shortens the project. (Rule M4-B03-R03)
Spot it: a long single activity with float, a separate zero-float path, a push to compress the wrong activity.
In this scenario: Activity F has 8 days of float, so shortening it changes nothing. Path A-C-E-H has zero float and drives the finish date.
Why not the others: The longest activity is not the critical path; long activities are not automatically critical; a zero-float path can still be shortened by crashing or fast-tracking.
Remember: Critical path = longest path, zero float. Float ≠ critical.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical packaging line project is four weeks behind. The team proposes starting equipment validation before installation is finished. Regulators require the validation results, and they become invalid if equipment settings change after testing. What should the project manager do?
options: Overlap validation with installation, since fast tracking adds no direct cost to the project budget
Start validation early and repeat any tests later if the equipment settings happen to change
Accept the four-week delay without evaluating any other compression or recovery options at all
Keep installation and validation in sequence, and evaluate crashing or other recovery options instead
questions.explanation:
Concept: Fast tracking — overlapping activities that were in sequence saves time but adds rework risk, so use it only where the overlap is safe. (Rule M4-B03-R06)
Spot it: a proposal to overlap, a technical or regulatory reason the later work depends on the earlier one being final.
In this scenario: Validation becomes invalid if settings change after testing, so overlapping it with installation is not acceptable. Keep the sequence and evaluate crashing or other recovery.
Why not the others: "No direct cost" ignores the rework and compliance risk; planning to repeat tests makes the risk real; accepting the delay without looking at options gives up too soon.
Remember: Crashing = more cost. Fast tracking = more risk. Check the risk before you overlap.

questions.stem: While reviewing estimates for a stadium lighting upgrade, a project manager learns that each team lead quietly added 25% to their activity durations just in case. The sponsor believes the schedule reflects most-likely durations. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the padded durations, since the extra time protects the schedule from unknown delays
