Cut every estimate by 25% and require leads to meet the shorter dates with no reserve at all
Keep the padding but present the schedule to the sponsor as the most-likely durations
Remove the hidden padding and set a visible schedule reserve based on the identified risks
questions.explanation:
Concept: Transparent reserves — uncertainty belongs in a visible, risk-based contingency reserve, not hidden padding in individual estimates. (Rule M4-B03-R09)
Spot it: "just in case" added quietly, sponsor thinks estimates are most-likely.
In this scenario: Each lead padded 25% and the sponsor does not know. Remove the hidden padding and set a visible reserve based on identified risks.
Why not the others: Keeping padding hides the truth and invites Parkinson's Law; cutting 25% with no reserve swings to the other extreme; presenting padding as most-likely is misleading.
Remember: Padding hides; reserves show. Contingency reserve = known risks, visible.

questions.stem: A WBS for a corporate headquarters relocation has a work package called Move IT, estimated at 4,500 hours over five months. The project manager cannot assign a single owner to it, estimate its cost reliably, or measure its progress. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep Move IT as one package and ask the IT director to report its percent complete monthly
Add a 20% contingency to Move IT to cover the uncertainty in its current overall estimate
Break Move IT into smaller deliverables that can each be estimated, assigned, and tracked
Decompose Move IT down to hourly tasks so that every single action is controlled directly
questions.explanation:
Concept: Decomposition to work packages — break deliverables down until each can be estimated, assigned an owner and measured, and no further. (Rule M4-B02-R02)
Spot it: a work package too big to estimate, own or track.
In this scenario: Move IT is 4,500 hours with no clear owner or progress measure. Break it into smaller deliverables that can be estimated, assigned and tracked.
Why not the others: Percent-complete reporting on a blob is guesswork; contingency covers risk, not poor decomposition; hourly tasks overshoot into micromanagement.
Remember: WBS = deliverables. Decompose until you can estimate, assign and control it.

questions.stem: While validating the WBS for a new clinic, a project manager notices that elements under Commissioning cover equipment testing and staff training but not the regulatory inspection that the scope statement requires. What should the project manager do?
options: Leave the WBS as is and track the inspection separately in the project's issue log instead
List the inspection in the WBS dictionary only, since it is a regulatory step rather than work
Add the regulatory inspection under Commissioning so its elements cover all of the parent's scope
Remove the inspection from the scope statement so it matches the approved WBS decomposition
questions.explanation:
Concept: The 100% rule — the child elements of a WBS must add up to all of the parent's scope, nothing missing and nothing extra. (Rule M4-B02-R05)
Spot it: required work in the scope statement that does not appear in the WBS.
In this scenario: The inspection is in scope but missing under Commissioning. Add it so the children cover 100% of the parent.
Why not the others: The issue log is for problems, not missing scope; the WBS dictionary describes WBS elements that already exist; changing the scope statement to fit the WBS is backward.
Remember: 100% rule: all the work, and only the work. Scope baseline = scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary.

questions.stem: A defense contractor must report monthly to the government on scope performance against the approved contract. A new team member suggests tracking scope in a simple list and updating it whenever the client asks for something new. What should the project manager explain?
options: An approved scope baseline is needed so performance and changes can be measured against it
A simple list is fine as long as the team updates it promptly after each client conversation
Scope does not need a baseline, because the contract already defines the work in detail
The schedule baseline alone is enough to measure both scope and schedule performance
questions.explanation:
Concept: Scope baseline — the approved scope statement, WBS and WBS dictionary, used to measure performance and control changes on predictive work. (Rule M4-B02-R08)
Spot it: contractual reporting, formal measurement, requests to use an informal list.
In this scenario: Monthly reporting against the contract needs an approved reference point. The scope baseline provides it and changes go through change control.
Why not the others: An informal list changes silently; the contract defines obligations but is not the project's control baseline; the schedule baseline cannot measure scope.
Remember: Plan = HOW, Baseline = APPROVED. You measure against the baseline.

questions.stem: Midway through an iteration, a team building a clinic's patient portal has eight stories in progress and none done. Each developer has started two or three stories to avoid being blocked. The iteration ends in four days. What should the project manager encourage?
options: Start the remaining stories now so every item gets some progress before the iteration ends
Extend the iteration by one more week so the team can finish all eight of the stories now in progress
Ask the product owner for smaller stories that can be started and finished within four days
Swarm on the stories closest to done and hold off starting new ones until those are finished
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stop starting, start finishing — limiting work in progress and swarming on nearly done items delivers value sooner than spreading effort thin. (Rule M4-B12-R04)
Spot it: many items in progress, none done, the timebox ending soon.
In this scenario: Eight stories are started and none are done with four days left. Swarm on the ones closest to done and start nothing new.
Why not the others: Starting more spreads the team thinner; extending breaks the timebox; asking for new small stories still adds work in progress.
Remember: Done beats started. Swarm to finish.

questions.stem: An agile team building a utility's outage-reporting app is preparing for its iteration review. The team lead wants to present slides summarizing completed stories because stakeholders are busy. Two field supervisors who will use the app are attending. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Present the slides so the review stays short and respects the stakeholders' limited time
Email the completed story list to stakeholders and cancel the review to save everyone time
Use the review to plan the next iteration's tasks and assign them to individual members
Demonstrate the working features to the supervisors and gather their feedback on real use
questions.explanation:
Concept: Iteration (sprint) review — the team shows working product to real stakeholders and gathers feedback to shape the backlog. (Rule M4-B12-R07)
Spot it: a review being turned into a slide show or status email, real users attending.
In this scenario: Field supervisors who will use the app are in the room. Demonstrate working features and collect their feedback.
Why not the others: Slides show claims, not product; cancelling loses the feedback loop; task planning and assignment belong to iteration planning, and the team self-assigns.
Remember: Review = inspect the product. Retrospective = inspect the process. Planning = plan the next iteration.

questions.stem: Three days into a two-week sprint, a product owner learns that one planned story needs a small change to its acceptance criteria. The sprint goal is still valid. A stakeholder suggests canceling the sprint and starting over with a new plan. What should the project manager advise?
options: Continue the sprint and have the product owner and team adjust the story within the sprint goal
Cancel the sprint and start a new one so the revised acceptance criteria can be fully planned
Stop work on the story until the next sprint planning meeting to avoid any mid-sprint change
Escalate the change to the sponsor, who must formally approve any modification to the sprint's content
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sprint cancellation — only the product owner can cancel a sprint, and only when the sprint goal becomes obsolete; normal adjustments happen inside the sprint. (Rule M4-B12-R10)
Spot it: a small change, a sprint goal that is still valid, someone suggesting restart.
In this scenario: The goal is intact and only one story's acceptance criteria change slightly. Continue and have the product owner and team adjust the story.
Why not the others: Cancelling is for an obsolete goal, not a tweak; freezing the story wastes the sprint; the sponsor does not approve sprint content — the product owner and team manage it.
Remember: Cancel only if the sprint goal is dead. Product owner owns the what; developers own the sprint backlog.

questions.stem: A hybrid project delivered a hospital network's patient-scheduling system, with software built in adaptive releases and a predictive rollout to clinics. The business case promises a 20% drop in missed appointments within a year, but the project closes next month. What should the project manager do to support the benefit?
options: Report the benefit as achieved at closure, since the system was delivered on scope and on schedule
Agree with the clinics' operations director on who will measure missed appointments and sustain the gain
Keep the project team in place for a year so it can track and report the appointment data itself
Remove the benefit from the closure report because it cannot be measured before the project ends
questions.explanation:
Concept: Benefits transition — many benefits appear after the project ends, so the PM hands benefit ownership and measurement to the operational owner. (Rule M5-B04-R06)
Spot it: a benefit target due after closure, no one assigned to track it.
In this scenario: The 20% drop in missed appointments will show up within a year, after closure. Agree with the clinics' operations director on who measures and sustains it.
Why not the others: Delivery on time is not benefit realized; keeping the team for a year is costly and not their role; deleting the benefit loses accountability for the business case.
Remember: Output → Outcome → Benefit → Value → Owner. Benefits need an owner after the project.

questions.stem: An agile team's automated loan-approval feature cut approval time by 40%, and the product owner wants to report it as a clear success. However, manual review costs for wrongly declined applicants have risen sharply, and complaints to the regulator have doubled. How should the value of the feature be reported?
options: Report the time savings together with the added review costs, complaints, and regulatory exposure
Report the 40% time savings, since it was the primary metric in the feature's original hypothesis
Report the feature as a failure, since complaints to the regulator doubled after its release
Delay any value reporting until the regulator has completed its review of all the complaints
questions.explanation:
Concept: Net value — true value counts benefits minus the costs, risks and harms the solution creates. (Rule M5-B04-R09)
Spot it: a headline metric improved while costs, complaints or regulatory exposure rose.
In this scenario: Approval time fell 40%, but review costs and regulator complaints rose. Report both sides so leaders see the net value.
Why not the others: Reporting only the win is misleading; calling it a failure ignores a real gain; delaying all reporting hides a live risk from decision makers.
Remember: Value = benefits minus costs and harm. Report the whole picture.

questions.stem: A utility's two-year billing system replacement is approaching its phase 2 gate. Since approval, its vendor's license cost has doubled, and a cheaper cloud service now meets most of the requirements. The steering committee asks the project manager to prepare for the gate review. What should the project manager do?
options: Present phase 2 progress against the approved baselines, since the business case was already approved at initiation
Update the business case with the new costs and alternatives so the committee can reconfirm the investment
Switch to the cloud service and inform the steering committee after the new contract has been signed
Negotiate a lower license cost with the vendor before telling the steering committee about the change
questions.explanation:
Concept: Business case as a living test — the business case (the WHY) is re-checked at gates to confirm the investment still makes sense when costs or alternatives change. (Rule M5-B03-R01)
Spot it: a phase gate, costs that have jumped, a new cheaper alternative.
In this scenario: License costs doubled and a cloud option now exists. Update the business case so the committee can reconfirm, change or stop the investment.
Why not the others: Reporting only baseline progress ignores that the WHY has changed; switching before approval bypasses governance; negotiating first delays telling decision makers.
Remember: WHY = business case. Revisit the WHY at every gate.

questions.stem: A retailer's program is installing in-store kiosks, with hardware rolled out under a predictive plan and kiosk software built adaptively. The board has just announced a strategic shift from physical store growth to online sales and canceled three planned stores. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the sponsor to reassess how well the kiosk program fits the new online-first strategy
Continue the kiosk rollout as approved, since the program's funding has not been withdrawn
Redesign the kiosks as online-order pickup points without consulting the sponsor or board
Speed up the rollout so the program finishes before any strategic review can affect it
questions.explanation:
Concept: Strategic alignment — projects exist to serve strategy; when strategy shifts, the sponsor reassesses whether the work still fits. (Rule M5-B03-R02)
Spot it: a board announcement, a new direction, planned sites cancelled.
In this scenario: The retailer moved from store growth to online sales. The PM asks the sponsor to reassess the kiosk program's fit.
Why not the others: "Still funded" is not the same as still aligned; redesigning without the sponsor exceeds the PM's authority; rushing to beat the review defeats governance.
Remember: Portfolio aligns work to strategy. Strategy changes → re-check the fit.

questions.stem: An agile team building a city parking app reports success after delivering 14 features, including mobile payment. The city's goals were to reduce meter collection costs and downtown congestion. A council member asks the project manager whether the project has delivered value. What is the BEST response?
options: Confirm success, since 14 features were delivered and accepted by the product owner on schedule
Report that value was delivered because mobile payment was the top-priority item in the backlog
Present the team's rising velocity trend as evidence that value delivery is steadily increasing
Explain that features are outputs and propose measures of adoption, collection cost, and congestion
questions.explanation:
Concept: Outputs vs outcomes vs benefits — features are outputs; the outcomes and benefits are the changes in cost, behavior or conditions the project was funded to create. (Rule M5-B03-R03)
Spot it: "we delivered N features," goals stated as business results.
In this scenario: The city wanted lower collection costs and less congestion. Explain that features are outputs and propose measures of adoption, collection cost and congestion.
Why not the others: Accepted features prove delivery, not value; backlog priority is not evidence of results; velocity measures team throughput, not business value.
Remember: Deliverable → Outcome → Benefit → Value.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical firm's lab automation project must cut 15% of its remaining budget. Options include dropping an analytics dashboard requested by a senior manager or delaying an automated sample tracker that supports the firm's top strategic goal of faster regulatory submissions. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Propose reductions ranked by their contribution to faster submissions and their expected value
Cut both features by an equal share so neither stakeholder group is disadvantaged by the decision
Preserve the dashboard, since it was requested by the most senior stakeholder on the project
Delay the sample tracker, since it is the larger item and cutting it saves the most money
questions.explanation:
Concept: Value-based trade-offs — when something must be cut, rank options by contribution to strategic goals and expected value, not by who asked loudest. (Rule M5-B03-R04)
Spot it: a forced cut, one item tied to the top strategic goal, another requested by a senior person.
In this scenario: The sample tracker supports faster submissions, the firm's top goal. Propose cuts ranked by contribution to that goal and expected value.
Why not the others: Equal cuts treat unequal value as equal; seniority is not value; cutting the biggest item may destroy the most value.
Remember: Strategy first, then value, then cost. Seniority is not a prioritization method.

questions.stem: A bank is launching a digital onboarding app built in adaptive releases, with a predictive rollout to branches. The business case says only that the app will improve customer experience and efficiency. The PMO asks how the program's benefits will be tracked. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the benefit statement broad so the program can claim success across a wider range of results
Track the number of app features released per quarter as the program's main benefit measure
Wait to define any benefit measures until the branch rollout is complete and the app has fully stabilized
Restate the benefits as testable targets, such as onboarding time and drop-off rate, with baselines
questions.explanation:
Concept: Measurable benefit hypotheses — express benefits as testable targets with a baseline and a measure so realization can be tracked. (Rule M5-B03-R07)
Spot it: vague benefits like "improve experience" or "efficiency," a request for tracking.
In this scenario: The business case is vague. Restate benefits as targets such as onboarding time and drop-off rate, with baselines.
Why not the others: Broad statements cannot be proven or disproven; feature counts are outputs; waiting loses the baseline you need to show change.
Remember: If you can't measure it, you can't claim it. Benefit = metric + baseline + target.

questions.stem: At an e-commerce firm using scaled agile, the checkout team has doubled its deployment frequency. However, its fulfillment team now receives unvalidated order changes, and customer delivery errors have risen 18%. Leadership is praising the checkout team's speed. What should the project manager do?
options: Review the end-to-end flow with both teams and adjust practices to improve delivery accuracy
Make the checkout team's deployment frequency the target for every other team to match
Ask the fulfillment team to add staff so it can absorb the higher volume of order changes
Report the checkout team's gains to leadership and handle the delivery errors as a separate item
questions.explanation:
Concept: Systems thinking and local optimization — improving one team's metric can hurt the end-to-end result; optimize the whole flow. (Rule M5-B17-R05)
Spot it: one team's metric soaring while downstream quality falls.
In this scenario: Faster checkout deployments are sending unvalidated changes to fulfillment, and delivery errors rose 18%. Review the end-to-end flow with both teams.
Why not the others: Spreading checkout's metric spreads the problem; adding fulfillment staff treats the symptom; reporting gains and splitting off errors hides the cause.
Remember: Optimize the whole, not the part. One team's win can be the customer's loss.

questions.stem: A project team is designing power distribution for a new hospital. To cut cost, its engineering lead proposes one switchgear unit feeding the operating rooms, intensive care unit, and data center, with no backup path. A single failure would shut down all three areas. What should the project manager do?
options: Retain a backup power path for the critical loads, since one failure there could be catastrophic
Approve the single-unit design, since switchgear failures are rare and the cost savings are certain
Accept the design but add the switchgear failure to the risk register for regular monitoring
Defer the redundancy decision to hospital operations after the building has been handed over
questions.explanation:
Concept: Resilience in tightly coupled systems — where one failure can cascade into catastrophe, keep redundancy even at extra cost. (Rule M5-B17-R08)
Spot it: life-safety or critical operations, no backup path, cost-cutting proposals.
In this scenario: One switchgear feeding operating rooms, ICU and the data center could stop all three at once. Keep a backup power path for these critical loads.
Why not the others: "Failures are rare" ignores catastrophic impact; logging and monitoring does not reduce impact; handing it to operations after handover is too late to design it in.
Remember: High impact + tight coupling = build in resilience. Safety before savings.

questions.stem: A bank's database migration uses a predictive cutover plan while an adaptive team updates the mobile app. The project manager discovers that four other enterprise programs depend on the same database schema and plan schema changes in the same quarter. Their managers have not coordinated. What should the project manager do?
options: Coordinate informally with each program manager and adjust only this project's own plan
Proceed with the migration, since each program is responsible for its own dependencies
Raise the shared dependency to the portfolio body that can coordinate all five efforts
Freeze the schema for every program until this project's migration has been completed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Escalating enterprise dependencies — when an interdependency spans several programs, raise it to the body that can coordinate them all. (Rule M5-B17-R10)
Spot it: several programs sharing a component, overlapping changes, no one coordinating.
In this scenario: Four other programs plan schema changes on the same database in the same quarter. Raise it to the portfolio body that can coordinate all five.
Why not the others: Informal side deals cannot align five plans; ignoring shared dependencies invites collisions; freezing others' work exceeds the PM's authority.
Remember: Dependency → Assess Impact → Coordinate → Monitor. Escalate to the level that can see all of it.

questions.stem: An agile team at a medical software firm must pass an external audit of its design controls at release. The team has been delivering working increments but plans to write all traceability and test evidence during the last two weeks before the audit. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Keep the plan and assign a technical writer to compile all evidence in the final two weeks
Ask the auditor to accept working software as enough evidence instead of documentation
Capture traceability and test evidence as part of each increment's definition of done
Pause feature work for one iteration so the team can write all documentation at once
questions.explanation:
Concept: Compliance evidence as you go — audit and approval evidence is built into each increment, typically through the definition of done. (Rule M5-B02-R06)
Spot it: a regulated product, an audit ahead, a plan to document everything at the end.
In this scenario: Design-control evidence is needed for the audit. Put traceability and test evidence in each increment's definition of done.
Why not the others: End-loading documentation is risky and inaccurate; auditors decide what evidence they accept; a documentation-only iteration still batches the work.
Remember: Definition of done is set by the Scrum team — put compliance in it.

questions.stem: A state agency's project uses a prime vendor that subcontracts the processing of citizens' tax records. The agency's contract with the prime vendor includes data protection obligations, but the prime's subcontract does not. What should the project manager do?
options: Rely on the prime vendor's contract, since the subcontractor is the prime vendor's responsibility
Terminate the prime vendor's contract for leaving the obligations out of its subcontract
Require the data protection obligations to flow down to the subcontractor and verify compliance
Ask the subcontractor to sign a confidentiality statement directly with the project team
questions.explanation:
Concept: Flow-down of obligations — compliance duties in the prime contract must be passed on to subcontractors whose work creates the exposure. (Rule M5-B02-R09)
Spot it: a subcontractor handling sensitive data, obligations in the prime contract but not the subcontract.
In this scenario: The subcontractor processes tax records without data-protection terms. Require the obligations to flow down and verify compliance.
Why not the others: Relying on the prime leaves the real exposure uncovered; termination is out of proportion; a side confidentiality note bypasses the contract chain.
Remember: SELLER = contract. Obligations flow down the whole supply chain.

questions.stem: A chemical plant's control system project has predictive field installation and adaptively developed software. During testing, a sensor fault causes a small toxic gas release. No one is hurt, and a key milestone is due in two days. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Continue testing the other components so that the milestone date can still be met in two days
Ask the software team to patch the sensor code quickly and resume testing later that same day
Halt the affected testing, secure the area, and follow the site's safety and reporting procedures
Notify the sponsor that the milestone is at risk and request a revised date for the testing
questions.explanation:
Concept: Safety first in a crisis — protect people, legal obligations and critical operations before schedule or milestones. (Rule M5-B18-R01)
Spot it: a release, injury risk, hazard, and a looming deadline.
In this scenario: A toxic gas release occurred. Halt the affected testing, secure the area and follow site safety and reporting procedures first.
Why not the others: Continuing testing puts the milestone above safety; a quick patch skips investigation; asking for a new date comes after the area is safe.
Remember: People → Legal → Operations → Project targets.

questions.stem: An agile team's release for an online pharmacy caused some prescription orders to show incorrect pickup times. Executives want an update in 30 minutes. The team has confirmed that about 400 orders are affected but does not yet know whether any patients missed doses. What should the project manager communicate?
options: Share the confirmed facts, state what is still unknown, and give the time of the next update
Hold the update until the team confirms whether any patients actually missed their doses
Report the issue as minor, since only 400 orders were affected and no harm is confirmed
Give an estimate of patient harm from the team's best guess so executives see the full picture
questions.explanation:
Concept: Crisis communication — share confirmed facts fast, label what is unknown, and commit to the next update time. (Rule M5-B18-R02)
Spot it: executives want an update soon, some facts confirmed, others unknown.
In this scenario: About 400 orders are confirmed affected; patient impact is unknown. Share the facts, state the unknowns and give the next update time.
Why not the others: Waiting leaves leaders blind; calling it minor downplays a possible patient-safety issue; guessing harm presents speculation as fact.
Remember: Facts + unknowns + next update time. Honest, fast, clear.

questions.stem: During a data center migration, a project manager discovers that customer payment data may have been exposed on a misconfigured server. The organization has a documented security incident response process with an on-call response team. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Investigate the server logs personally to confirm the exposure before telling anyone
Report the possible exposure to the on-call team through the incident response process
Email all affected customers to warn them their payment data may have been exposed
Have the migration team quietly reconfigure the server and continue on the migration schedule
questions.explanation:
Concept: Use established incident channels — when a formal incident process exists, report through it first rather than improvising. (Rule M5-B18-R03)
Spot it: a possible breach, a documented response process, an on-call team.
In this scenario: Payment data may be exposed and there is an incident process. Report to the on-call team through that process first.
Why not the others: Investigating alone delays the experts; notifying customers is the incident team's decision; quietly fixing it hides the breach and destroys evidence.
Remember: Follow the playbook: report first, then help.

questions.stem: A program's new warehouse management system went live last night. Its software was built adaptively and deployed under a predictive cutover plan. Order picking is failing for 30% of orders, and trucks are waiting. The development team proposes using the outage to refactor the picking module for future growth. What should the project manager do?
options: Restore order picking first through a rollback or workaround, and defer the refactoring
Approve the refactoring, since fixing the underlying design now will prevent later outages
Hold a full lessons-learned session with all teams before deciding on any corrective action
Ask the vendor to redesign the system architecture while the warehouse works orders manually
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stabilize before optimize — in an outage, restore critical operations first; improvement work comes after. (Rule M5-B18-R04)
Spot it: a live failure hurting customers, a proposal to redesign during the crisis.
In this scenario: Picking fails for 30% of orders and trucks are waiting. Restore picking through rollback or a workaround and defer refactoring.
Why not the others: Refactoring mid-outage prolongs the outage; lessons learned come after recovery; a vendor redesign leaves operations on manual work.
Remember: Stabilize → Recover → Learn → Improve.

questions.stem: A flood shut down a factory construction site for six weeks. The site is now safe, crews have returned, and immediate repairs are complete. Project reports still show the original completion date and budget. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Keep reporting against the original date and budget, since the flood was entirely outside the team's control
Reassess the objectives, baselines, and constraints with the sponsor in light of the flood's impact
Crash all remaining activities to recover the six weeks and meet the original completion date
Close the project and open a new one, since the flood has invalidated the original business case
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reassess after the crisis — once the immediate emergency is under control, revisit objectives, baselines and constraints with the sponsor. (Rule M5-B18-R07)
Spot it: the crisis is contained, reports still show pre-crisis targets.
In this scenario: Six weeks were lost, but reports still show the original date and budget. Reassess objectives and baselines with the sponsor.
Why not the others: Reporting old targets is misleading; crashing everything before replanning may waste money; closing assumes the business case failed without analysis.
Remember: Crisis → Stabilize → Reassess → Replan.

questions.stem: A transit agency's trip-planning app is released adaptively within a predictive agency program. In surveys, riders asked for detailed route maps. Beta usage data shows most riders only check next-bus arrival times, often on older phones with limited data plans. What should the project manager recommend to the product owner?
options: Weigh the survey requests against usage data and device limits when prioritizing the next features
Prioritize the detailed maps, since riders explicitly requested them in the agency's survey
Disregard the survey entirely, since analytics are more objective than stated preferences
Build both features at full detail so that every single rider gets exactly the experience they asked for
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stated vs observed needs — balance what users say they want with what they actually do and the constraints they face. (Rule M5-B12-R05)
Spot it: survey requests that conflict with usage data and device limits.
In this scenario: Riders asked for maps but mostly check arrival times on older phones. Weigh both inputs and the device limits when prioritizing.
Why not the others: Following the survey alone ignores behavior; discarding it ignores real voice; building everything at full detail ignores capacity and device limits.
Remember: Listen to what users say, watch what they do.

questions.stem: A health insurer's project is launching a wellness program and must show whether members' activity levels improve. The analytics team proposes collecting full GPS location histories from members' fitness trackers to support the analysis. What should the project manager do?
options: Approve the full GPS collection, since more data will make the outcome analysis more accurate
Cancel outcome measurement, since any member data collection creates unacceptable risk
Collect the GPS data now and consult the privacy office once the analysis is complete
Collect only the data needed to measure activity outcomes, with consent and privacy safeguards
questions.explanation:
Concept: Privacy by minimization — collect only the data needed for the purpose, with consent and safeguards. (Rule M5-B12-R08)
Spot it: sensitive personal data, a proposal to collect more than needed.
In this scenario: Measuring activity does not require full GPS histories. Collect only what is needed, with consent and safeguards.
Why not the others: "More data is better" breaks minimization; cancelling measurement loses the outcome evidence; asking privacy later is backward.
Remember: Protect data → Validate output → Human decides. Minimum data, maximum care.

questions.stem: An online learning platform adds content features adaptively while migrating its platform under a predictive plan. The program's main success metric is daily page views, which rose 60%. Course completions and paid renewals, which the business case promised, are flat, and analysis shows page views do not track completions. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Keep page views as the key metric, since the 60% rise shows strong engagement
Add more engagement metrics, such as clicks and session length, to the dashboard
Report page views to executives and track completions within the team only
Replace page views with measures linked to completion and renewal outcomes
questions.explanation:
Concept: Vanity metrics — a metric that rises without predicting the outcomes you care about should be replaced. (Rule M5-B12-R10)
Spot it: a big rise in a surface metric, flat business results, no link between them.
In this scenario: Page views rose 60% while completions and renewals stayed flat. Replace page views with measures tied to those outcomes.
Why not the others: Keeping page views celebrates noise; adding more engagement metrics adds more vanity; reporting one thing and tracking another is misleading.
Remember: Measure what matters: metrics must predict outcomes.

questions.stem: A project team is migrating a law firm's case files to a new document system. To avoid delays, its technical lead requests that all 25 team members receive full administrator access to the production repository during the migration. What should the project manager do?
options: Approve administrator access for all members, since it is needed only during the migration
Deny all production access and require the firm's own IT staff to carry out every migration step
Grant each role only the access its migration tasks require and review permissions regularly
Share one administrator account across the team to limit the number of privileged accounts
questions.explanation:
Concept: Least privilege — each person gets only the access their role needs, reviewed regularly. (Rule M5-B15-R03)
Spot it: requests for broad admin rights "to save time," sensitive data.
In this scenario: Twenty-five people asking for full admin on confidential case files is excessive. Grant role-based access and review it regularly.
Why not the others: Blanket admin access creates big exposure; denying all access blocks the work; a shared account removes accountability.
Remember: Least privilege = need to do, not nice to have.

questions.stem: A patient-intake app project approves requirements and architecture in a predictive phase and then builds features adaptively. The architect plans to address encryption and data-retention rules after the first release, once the team knows what it is building. What should the project manager do?
options: Accept the plan, since adaptive teams can add security controls in later releases
Build encryption and retention needs into the architecture and acceptance criteria now
Schedule a penetration test before go-live to detect any privacy issues in the app
Ask the security team to own privacy separately so the project team can focus on features
questions.explanation:
Concept: Privacy and security by design — build security and privacy requirements in from the start, not after release. (Rule M5-B15-R04)
Spot it: a plan to add encryption or retention rules later, sensitive data.
In this scenario: Patient data is involved and architecture is being approved now. Build encryption and retention into architecture and acceptance criteria.
Why not the others: Adding controls later means costly rework; a penetration test finds gaps instead of preventing them; splitting ownership leaves design without privacy.
Remember: Secure by design, not by patch.

questions.stem: A retailer's CRM project plans to send customer purchase histories to an external analytics vendor for segmentation. The vendor stores data in subcontracted data centers in two countries. Contract signing is scheduled for next week. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Sign the contract on schedule and review the vendor's data handling in the first quarter
Rely on the vendor's marketing materials stating that it complies with all data laws
Assess the vendor's data handling, subprocessors, and storage locations before signing
Cancel the analytics initiative, since sharing customer data with vendors is too risky
questions.explanation:
Concept: Third-party data risk — before sharing data with a vendor, assess how it handles, stores and subcontracts that data. (Rule M5-B15-R05)
Spot it: outside vendors, subprocessors, cross-border storage, a signing deadline.
In this scenario: The vendor uses subcontracted data centers in two countries. Assess its data handling and locations before signing.
Why not the others: Signing first loses leverage; marketing claims are not evidence; cancelling assumes all sharing is unsafe without assessment.
Remember: Assess before you share. Contract after due diligence.

questions.stem: A health system uses an adaptively built analytics dashboard to choose which of 40 rural clinics to close under a predictive restructuring plan. The dashboard combines patient-visit data from three legacy systems, and one clinic manager says her visit counts look far too low. What should the project manager do?
options: Proceed with the closure decisions, since the product owner has already reviewed and accepted the dashboard
Trace the visit data to its sources and verify its quality before any closure decisions are made
Exclude that clinic from the analysis and finalize closure decisions for the other 39 clinics
Replace the dashboard figures with visit counts submitted by the clinic manager herself
questions.explanation:
Concept: Data lineage and quality — when analytics drive a big decision, trace the data to its sources and verify it first. (Rule M5-B15-R08)
Spot it: combined legacy data, a credible report that numbers look wrong, a high-stakes decision.
In this scenario: Clinic closures depend on visit data from three legacy systems, and one manager flags low counts. Trace and verify the data before deciding.
Why not the others: Product owner acceptance does not validate data; excluding one clinic ignores that the whole data set may be flawed; taking one manager's numbers swaps one unverified source for another.
Remember: Data → Analyze → Insight → Decision. Garbage in, closures out.

questions.stem: During a merger integration project, a project manager learns from confidential steering committee materials that the company will announce a major acquisition next month. A friend asks whether now is a good time to buy the company's stock. What should the project manager do?
options: Hint that it may be a good time, as long as no specific details about the deal are shared
Buy company stock personally, since no one else was told and the project is not affected
Decline to share or act on the information and keep it confidential under company policy
Tell the friend to wait until next month, which avoids revealing any details of the deal
questions.explanation:
Concept: Confidential information and personal gain — the PMI Code of Ethics forbids using privileged information for personal or others' advantage. (Rule M5-B16-R04)
Spot it: inside information, stock or financial questions, friends or family asking.
In this scenario: The PM knows about an unannounced acquisition. Decline to share or act on it and keep it confidential.
Why not the others: Hinting still discloses insider information; buying stock is insider trading; advising to wait is acting on the information too.
Remember: Responsibility, Respect, Fairness, Honesty. Confidential means confidential.

questions.stem: A program reports green status to the board. Its adaptive team's velocity has doubled, but the team recently halved the size of a story point, and hardware milestones on the predictive side are three weeks late. The sponsor wants to feature velocity in the board report. What should the project manager do?
options: Include the velocity increase in the report, since it is an accurate number from team data
Report velocity without comment and discuss the hardware milestone delays privately with the sponsor
Explain that the velocity rise reflects a changed scale and report the milestone delays accurately
Remove all metrics from the board report to avoid any misunderstanding of program status
questions.explanation:
Concept: Honest reporting — the PM must challenge metrics or narratives that mislead decision makers. (Rule M5-B16-R07)
Spot it: a metric that changed because its scale changed, a green report hiding delays.
In this scenario: Velocity doubled only because points were halved, and hardware is three weeks late. Explain the scale change and report the delays accurately.
Why not the others: A true number in a misleading context still misleads; private discussion leaves the board uninformed; removing all metrics hides status.
Remember: Honesty is a PMI value. Green must mean green.

questions.stem: A mining company's project manager learns that a local permit condition requires public disclosure of water testing results, while a customer contract clause requires those results to stay confidential. Company policy on the conflict is unclear. What should the project manager do?
options: Seek guidance from legal and compliance advisors before deciding which obligation governs
Follow the customer contract, since the customer is funding the project and owns the test data
Publish the results to satisfy the permit and inform the customer after the disclosure
Delay the water testing until the permit expires so that no disclosure obligation arises
questions.explanation:
Concept: Conflicting obligations — when legal, contractual and policy duties clash, get qualified legal and compliance advice before acting. (Rule M5-B16-R09)
Spot it: a permit and a contract that point opposite ways, unclear policy.
In this scenario: The permit requires disclosure while the contract requires confidentiality. Seek legal and compliance guidance first.
Why not the others: Siding with the funder may break the law; publishing first may breach the contract; delaying testing to dodge the permit is evasive.
Remember: Legal conflict? Get legal advice. Don't be your own lawyer.

questions.stem: A connected-car program develops its hardware under a predictive plan and its software adaptively. A regulator has published a draft rule on in-vehicle data sharing that may take effect in 18 months, close to launch. What should the project manager do?
options: Wait until the rule is final before considering it, since draft rules often change significantly
Redesign the product now to meet the strictest possible reading of the proposed regulation
Monitor the proposal's progress and assess its likely effects on design choices and launch timing
Delay the entire program until the regulator publishes the final version of the regulation
questions.explanation:
Concept: Monitoring emerging regulation — track draft rules and assess their likely effects so design and timing can adapt early. (Rule M5-B08-R05)
Spot it: a draft rule, an effective date near launch.
In this scenario: A draft data-sharing rule may take effect near launch. Monitor it and assess its effects on design and launch timing.
Why not the others: Waiting for the final rule risks late redesign; redesigning to the strictest reading over-reacts; delaying the program is too drastic.
Remember: External change → Assess Impact → Adjust. Watch the horizon.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A solar farm project's baseline assumed panels from one overseas supplier. A newly imposed tariff has raised panel costs by 35%, making the approved budget unachievable, and the supplier cannot absorb any of the increase. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue with the current supplier and report the cost variance at the next phase gate
Evaluate alternate suppliers, scope, and schedule options and submit changes for approval
Reduce the number of panels installed without informing the sponsor or the change board
Wait for the tariff to be repealed before purchasing panels or updating any of the plans
questions.explanation:
Concept: External constraints and feasibility — when an outside change makes the baseline unachievable, evaluate options and submit changes for approval. (Rule M5-B08-R08)
Spot it: a tariff, market or regulation change that breaks the approved budget.
In this scenario: A 35% tariff makes the budget unachievable. Evaluate other suppliers, scope and schedule options and submit changes.
Why not the others: Continuing and reporting later delays a known problem; cutting panels quietly bypasses change control; waiting for repeal is not a plan.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A company will deliver a new product using adaptive software releases and a predictive hardware build, and must choose between two designs. Design A returns $500,000 spread evenly over five years; Design B returns $500,000 in year five only. Both cost the same, and the cost of capital is 10%. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Treat both designs as equal, since each returns the same $500,000 in total over five years
Choose Design B, since a single large payment is easier to track and report to leadership
Use payback period alone, since it fully accounts for the time value of money in both cases
Compare the designs' net present values, which favor the earlier cash flows of Design A
questions.explanation:
Concept: Net present value (NPV) — discounts future cash flows to today's value, so money received earlier is worth more. (Rule M5-B10-R01)
Spot it: equal totals but different timing, a stated cost of capital.
In this scenario: Both designs return $500,000, but A pays earlier. At 10%, A's NPV is higher.
Why not the others: Equal totals ignore time value; ease of tracking is not a financial criterion; payback does not account for time value.
Remember: NPV = value in dollars today. Money now beats the same money later.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A steering committee is choosing between two warehouse sites with similar risk, schedule, and strategic fit. Site 1 has an NPV of $2.1 million; Site 2 has an NPV of $1.4 million and a payback period four months shorter. Assumptions for both have been validated. Which site should the project manager recommend?
options: Site 2, because a shorter payback period indicates the better overall investment
Site 1, because it has the higher NPV and the options are otherwise comparable
Site 2, because its lower NPV indicates lower risk and a more cautious investment
Either site, because both have positive NPVs and so they provide equal value
questions.explanation:
Concept: NPV selection — when options are otherwise comparable and assumptions are sound, choose the higher positive NPV. (Rule M5-B10-R02)
Spot it: similar risk and fit, different NPVs, payback as a distractor.
In this scenario: Site 1 has $2.1 million NPV versus $1.4 million, with everything else similar. Recommend Site 1.
Why not the others: Payback measures speed, not total value; lower NPV does not mean lower risk; both positive does not make them equal.
Remember: ROI = Return • NPV = Value • IRR = Rate • Payback = Time. Higher positive NPV wins.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A program delivering a customer platform in adaptive releases, with a predictive data center build, must choose one of two mutually exclusive options. Option X has an IRR of 28% and an NPV of $300,000; Option Y has an IRR of 19% and an NPV of $1.2 million. A finance analyst wants to pick X based on IRR alone. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Choose Option X, since the higher IRR shows it will create the most total value
Use IRR alongside NPV, since IRR ignores project scale and Option Y creates more value
Choose Option X, since IRR is the only measure that reflects the time value of money
Reject both options, since conflicting IRR and NPV results make the analysis unreliable
questions.explanation:
Concept: IRR's limits — IRR is a percentage return; it ignores project size, so for mutually exclusive options NPV shows which creates more value. (Rule M5-B10-R03)
Spot it: a high IRR on a small option, a large NPV on another, mutually exclusive choice.
In this scenario: X has the higher IRR but Y creates $1.2 million versus $300,000. Use IRR alongside NPV; Y creates more value.
Why not the others: Higher IRR is not more total value; NPV also reflects time value; conflicting results are expected, not a reason to reject both.
Remember: IRR is a percentage; NPV is money. When they conflict, NPV decides.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A company has spent $3 million on a custom inventory system that is 60% complete. Finishing it will cost another $2.5 million, while a commercial product meeting all needs would cost $1 million to implement with similar benefits. A director argues that stopping would waste the money already spent. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Finish the custom system, since abandoning it would waste the $3 million that was already invested
Add the $3 million to the commercial option's cost so the total investment is compared fairly
Compare only the future costs and benefits of each option and exclude the $3 million already spent
Finish the custom system but trim its scope so that the remaining cost falls below $1 million
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sunk cost — money already spent cannot be recovered and must not drive future choices; compare only future costs and benefits. (Rule M5-B10-R06)
Spot it: "we've already spent," "wasting the investment".
In this scenario: Finishing costs $2.5 million; the commercial option costs $1 million for similar benefits. Compare only future costs and benefits.
Why not the others: Finishing to justify past spending is the sunk-cost trap; adding sunk cost to one option distorts the comparison; trimming scope sacrifices benefits to stay attached.
Remember: Sunk cost = gone money. Opportunity cost = lost alternative.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A subscription meal service was approved assuming 3% interest rates and 50,000 subscribers. Its app is released adaptively while kitchens are built under a predictive plan. Rates have since risen to 7%, and early releases show demand closer to 20,000 subscribers. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the original financial model, since the investment committee approved it at initiation
Increase marketing spend to reach 50,000 subscribers so the original model stays valid
Cancel the program now, since the original financial assumptions are no longer accurate
Update the financial model with the new rates and demand and review the results with the sponsor
questions.explanation:
Concept: Revisiting financial assumptions — when rates, demand or costs change materially, update the financial model and review it with the sponsor. (Rule M5-B10-R10)
Spot it: interest rates or demand far from what was assumed at approval.
In this scenario: Rates went from 3% to 7% and demand looks like 20,000, not 50,000. Update the model and review results with the sponsor.
Why not the others: Initiation approval does not freeze assumptions; spending more to force old numbers is wishful; cancelling before re-analysis jumps to a conclusion.
Remember: Constraint / Assumption → Assess Impact → Adjust.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A wind farm project manager must escalate a supplier's six-week turbine delay that threatens a grid-connection deadline. The steering committee meets tomorrow, and the project manager has only 15 minutes on its agenda. How should the project manager prepare?
options: Present a detailed timeline of the supplier's failures so the committee understands the history
Describe the problem in general terms and ask the committee how it wants the delay handled
Wait to escalate until the supplier confirms a new delivery date and the full impact is known
Present the delay's impacts, two or three recovery options, and the specific decision needed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Effective escalation — bring impacts, options and a clear decision request, not just the problem. (Rule M5-B01-R04)
Spot it: limited meeting time, a problem beyond the PM's authority.
In this scenario: A six-week turbine delay threatens the grid deadline with only 15 minutes on the agenda. Present impacts, a few options and the decision needed.
Why not the others: A detailed history of failures wastes the time; a vague problem pushes analysis onto executives; waiting loses time to recover.
Remember: Escalate with options, not just problems.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: In one company program, an adaptive team is refreshing a low-risk internal intranet while a predictive team upgrades regulated financial reporting systems. The PMO applies identical monthly steering reviews and 40-page gate documents to both. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Keep identical governance for both teams so that oversight stays consistent across the program
Remove gate documents for both teams, since lighter governance speeds up delivery for everyone
Apply lighter governance to the intranet work and keep stronger controls on the reporting systems
Apply the reporting controls only at the end of the program to reduce the overall review workload
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tailoring governance — oversight should match risk: light for low-risk work, strong for regulated or high-risk work. (Rule M5-B01-R07)
Spot it: one-size-fits-all reviews applied to very different risk levels.
In this scenario: The intranet is low risk; financial reporting is regulated. Apply lighter governance to the intranet and keep strong controls on reporting.
Why not the others: Identical governance burdens low-risk work; removing controls on regulated work is dangerous; controls only at the end come too late.
Remember: Tailor governance to risk. Tailor = right-size.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: At a phase gate, a transit authority's steering committee verbally approved a lower-cost signaling system after a long debate about safety trade-offs. No minutes were taken. Auditors will review major decisions later in the year. What should the project manager do?
options: Record the decision, its rationale, and the trade-offs considered, and have the committee confirm it
Rely on committee members' memories, since the decision was made openly in the meeting
Update the procurement documents for the new system without recording the committee's reasoning
Ask the committee to repeat the debate at the next gate so that it can be recorded in full
questions.explanation:
Concept: Decision records — material governance decisions and their rationale must be documented and confirmed. (Rule M5-B01-R09)
Spot it: verbal approvals, no minutes, auditors coming.
In this scenario: A major safety trade-off was approved verbally with no minutes. Record the decision, rationale and trade-offs and have the committee confirm.
Why not the others: Memories fade and are not auditable; acting without recording the reasoning leaves no trail; repeating the debate wastes time.
Remember: If it isn't written, it didn't happen. Decisions go in the decision log.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: An insurer's customer chatbot was developed adaptively, and its call-center rollout followed a predictive plan. The project team treats go-live as the end of its responsibility, and no one in operations has been assigned to maintain the bot's content or performance. What should the project manager do?
options: Plan the chatbot's handover to an operational owner with support, training, and funding in place
Close the project at go-live, since the chatbot was delivered and accepted by the sponsor
Keep the project team in place indefinitely to maintain the chatbot's content and performance
Have the vendor maintain the bot's content without involving the insurer's operations team
questions.explanation:
Concept: Transition to operations — projects create capabilities that need an operational owner with support, training and funding to deliver value after go-live. (Rule M5-B09-R05)
Spot it: go-live treated as the end, no one owns the product in operations.
In this scenario: No one in operations maintains the chatbot. Plan the handover to an operational owner with support, training and funding.
Why not the others: Closing at go-live leaves an orphan; keeping the project team forever turns a project into operations; handing it to the vendor alone skips internal ownership.
Remember: Project → Transition → Operations. Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: Three separate projects (a new ERP system, a warehouse expansion, and a supplier portal) must all be ready for a company's planned move to next-day delivery. Each has its own manager and schedule, and no one tracks handoffs between them. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Set up explicit tracking and joint coordination of cross-project links toward the delivery goal
Let each project manage its own schedule, since each has its own manager and approved baseline
Merge the three projects into one project with a single schedule and one project manager
Ask the sponsor to delay the next-day delivery launch until all three projects have closed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Program-level dependency management — when several projects feed one outcome, the links between them must be tracked and coordinated explicitly. (Rule M5-B09-R08)
Spot it: several projects, one business goal, no one managing handoffs.
In this scenario: The ERP, warehouse and portal all must be ready for next-day delivery, but no one tracks handoffs. Set up explicit tracking and joint coordination.
Why not the others: Separate schedules leave gaps between them; merging into one project is disruptive and unnecessary; waiting for all to close delays the outcome.
Remember: Programs coordinate benefits across projects. Dependency → Coordinate → Monitor.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A data center is being built under a predictive plan while its monitoring software is built adaptively. The proposed water-cooling design would draw heavily from a drought-prone local aquifer, and community groups have raised concerns. The business case covers only construction costs and revenue. What should the project manager do?
options: Proceed with the current design, since the approved business case shows a strong financial return
Expand the analysis to cover water, community, and long-term cost effects before the design is final
Issue a public statement to the community groups that the design meets all current regulations
Switch to an air-cooled design right away without analyzing its energy and cost trade-offs
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sustainability in value — when environmental and social effects are material, the analysis must include them alongside financial results. (Rule M5-B06-R01)
Spot it: drought, community concerns, a business case covering only money.
In this scenario: The cooling design draws on a drought-prone aquifer. Expand the analysis to cover water, community and long-term cost effects before finalizing.
Why not the others: A strong financial return does not cover material environmental risk; a statement without analysis dismisses stakeholders; switching designs without analysis acts blindly.
Remember: Evaluate lifecycle impact → Balance value, cost, risk → Think long term.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A city is choosing lighting for a new sports complex. Option A costs 20% less to install but uses more energy and contains materials that are costly to dispose of. Option B costs more upfront but lasts twice as long. The project budget covers installation only. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Choose Option A, since the project budget covers only installation and it costs 20% less
Choose Option B, since longer-lasting products are always the more sustainable choice
Leave the choice to facility operations, since operating costs fall outside the project
Compare both options on total lifecycle cost and impact, including energy use and disposal
questions.explanation:
Concept: Lifecycle thinking — compare total lifecycle cost and impact (install, operate, dispose), not just the upfront price. (Rule M5-B06-R02)
Spot it: cheaper to install but costlier to run or dispose of, a budget that covers only installation.
In this scenario: Option A is cheaper upfront but uses more energy and costs more to dispose of. Compare total lifecycle cost and impact.
Why not the others: Choosing on install cost ignores operations; "always" statements replace analysis; operations are part of the value the project creates.
Remember: Look past go-live: build, run, retire.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A food distributor is automating its warehouse, installing robotics under a predictive plan and releasing software adaptively. To meet a noise-reduction target near the warehouse, a revised design reroutes all night deliveries through a residential school zone. What should the project manager do?
options: Approve the route change, since it meets the noise target set for the area around the warehouse
Assess the route's effect on the school zone and seek an option that does not relocate the harm
Move deliveries to daytime hours without assessing the traffic effects on nearby neighborhoods
Keep the new route and ask the school to adjust its hours to reduce contact with delivery trucks
questions.explanation:
Concept: Avoid shifting harm — a solution should not solve one group's problem by moving the harm to another. (Rule M5-B06-R03)
Spot it: a fix that meets a target by pushing impact to a different community or lifecycle stage.
In this scenario: Rerouting trucks meets the noise target but moves harm into a school zone. Assess that impact and seek an option that does not relocate the harm.
Why not the others: Meeting one target is not success if harm just moves; daytime deliveries without assessment may create new harm; asking the school to adapt shifts the burden.
Remember: Fix the problem, don't move it.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A highway widening project will require relocating a farmers' market that has operated for 40 years and serves a low-income neighborhood. The design is approved, and a state agency selected the relocation site without community input. What should the project manager do?
options: Engage market vendors and neighborhood residents to understand impacts and shape relocation plans
Proceed with the chosen relocation site, since the design was approved through the formal process
Post a relocation notice at the market and on the agency website two weeks before construction
Pay each vendor relocation compensation and consider the social impact to be fully addressed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stakeholder engagement for social impact — when a project materially affects a community, engage the affected people to understand and shape the response. (Rule M5-B06-R06)
Spot it: a long-standing community asset, no community input, a decision already made.
In this scenario: The 40-year market serves a low-income neighborhood, and the site was chosen without input. Engage vendors and residents to shape the relocation.
Why not the others: Following the approved process alone ignores the affected people; a notice is one-way communication; compensation alone does not address the social impact.
Remember: Identify Stakeholder → Analyze → Engage → Monitor.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: Three years ago, a program designed a delivery fleet around diesel-hybrid trucks; vehicle procurement follows a predictive plan and routing software is built adaptively. Since then, electric trucks have become cost-competitive, and the city has announced low-emission zones. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue procuring diesel-hybrid trucks, since the fleet design was approved three years ago
Revisit the fleet's sustainability assumptions against current technology, rules, and expectations
Switch the entire order to electric trucks without analyzing charging needs or total costs
Ask the routing software team to optimize delivery routes around the low-emission zones
questions.explanation:
Concept: Revisiting sustainability assumptions — technology, regulation and expectations change, so earlier design assumptions must be re-checked. (Rule M5-B06-R10)
Spot it: a years-old design, new technology, new regulations.
In this scenario: Electric trucks are now competitive and low-emission zones are coming. Revisit the fleet's assumptions against current conditions.
Why not the others: Old approval does not keep assumptions valid; switching everything without analysis is hasty; rerouting avoids the question instead of answering it.
Remember: Constraint / Assumption → Assess Impact → Adjust.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A new chemical plant's viability depends on whether a novel catalyst performs at scale. The current plan tests the catalyst in month 14, after site preparation and most equipment purchases. A failed test would make much of that spending worthless. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Keep the current sequence, since site preparation is on the critical path and must come first
Buy the remaining equipment sooner to lock in prices before the catalyst test takes place
Add a contingency reserve for the catalyst risk and keep the original sequence of the work
Move the catalyst scale test earlier so major spending follows proof that the process works
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sequencing to reduce uncertainty early — test the biggest unknowns first so major spending follows proof. (Rule M5-B11-R04)
Spot it: a make-or-break technical unknown scheduled late, big spending before it.
In this scenario: Plant viability depends on the catalyst, yet the test is at month 14. Move the test earlier so spending follows proof.
Why not the others: Keeping the sequence risks wasted spending; buying sooner raises exposure; a reserve funds a failure instead of preventing it.
Remember: Fail fast, fail cheap. Retire the biggest uncertainty first.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A regional hospital network is ranking options for a new patient portal (built adaptively) and a clinic consolidation (planned predictively). The top-ranked option maximizes total savings but would end evening clinic hours used mainly by shift workers with no other access to care. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Adopt the top-ranked option, since it produces the greatest total savings for the network
Rank all options equally until every patient group agrees on the preferred approach
Keep evening hours only for patients who pay an extra fee to cover the added costs
Include who gains and who loses in the ranking and assess the effect on shift workers
questions.explanation:
Concept: Distribution of value and harm — look at who gains and who loses, not only the total. (Rule M5-B11-R07)
Spot it: the highest total value option removes access for a vulnerable group.
In this scenario: The top option saves the most but ends evening hours for shift workers with no alternative. Include who gains and who loses in the ranking.
Why not the others: Total savings ignores who bears the cost; waiting for everyone to agree stalls the decision; a fee restricts access further.
Remember: Value for whom? Look at the winners and the losers.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A software company's portfolio board scores initiatives on ROI and risk, then checks strategic fit only after the ranking is final. A high-ROI on-premises upgrade ranks first, although the strategy is to move all customers to cloud services. Adaptive product teams and predictive infrastructure projects await direction. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Fund the on-premises upgrade first, since it has the highest ROI and strategy can come later
Let each adaptive team choose its own priorities based on customer feature requests
Drop ROI from the scoring and rank initiatives only on alignment with the cloud strategy
Score strategic fit alongside ROI and risk so the ranking reflects the move to cloud services
questions.explanation:
Concept: Strategic fit as a criterion — strategic alignment belongs in portfolio scoring from the start, not as an afterthought. (Rule M5-B11-R09)
Spot it: fit checked only after ranking, a top item that contradicts strategy.
In this scenario: An on-premises upgrade ranks first although strategy is cloud. Score strategic fit alongside ROI and risk.
Why not the others: Funding first and checking strategy later is the problem itself; letting each team choose loses portfolio alignment; dropping ROI throws away financial discipline.
Remember: Portfolio = align work to strategy. Strategy is a score, not a footnote.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: For the past four sprints, a fintech team has worked late nights to finish every committed item, and the sponsor now cites that output as the team's normal capacity. Two developers have quietly asked to transfer, and defect counts are climbing. As the team's agile coach, what should you do FIRST?
options: Offer compensatory time off after the release so the team can hold its current commitment
Ask the sponsor for two contractors so the late-night workload is spread across more people
Extend the sprint length to three weeks so the same committed scope fits without late nights
Plan the next sprint around the capacity the team can sustain during normal working hours
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sustainable pace — An agile team commits only to what it can deliver week after week in normal hours. Heroic overtime is borrowed capacity, and it gets paid back later as burnout, turnover and defects. (Rule M3-B12-R10)
Spot it: "late nights," "every sprint," "treated as normal capacity," rising defects, people asking to leave.
In this scenario: Four sprints of overtime are now being mistaken for the team's real capacity. The first fix is to reset planning to what the team can sustain, so the next commitment is honest.
Why not the others: Comp time accepts the overtime and just pays for it afterward; contractors add people without fixing the inflated commitment; a longer sprint keeps the same overloaded scope and only hides it.
Remember: Velocity comes from normal hours, not heroics. Overtime means planning is wrong.

questions.stem: A construction project's document controller has submitted three drawing transmittals that the site manager calls incomplete. She says she followed the procedure she was given at onboarding, and no one has shown her the site manager's checklist. The site manager wants her replaced. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Issue the controller a written warning and set a thirty-day deadline for her to improve
Ask the functional manager to reassign her and provide a more experienced replacement
Meet with both of them to agree on what a complete transmittal must contain and record it
Enroll the controller in a document management course before her next set of transmittals is due
questions.explanation:
Concept: Clarify expectations first — Before you call someone's performance poor, make sure they were told clearly what "good" looks like. A lot of so-called performance problems are really expectation gaps. (Rule M3-B03-R01)
Spot it: "followed the procedure I was given," "no one showed her the checklist," someone quick to say "replace her."
In this scenario: The controller and the site manager are using two different standards. Getting both of them to agree on, and write down, what a complete transmittal contains fixes the root cause.
Why not the others: A written warning punishes her before the expectation was ever shared; replacing her hands the same unclear standard to the next person; a course assumes a skill gap that nothing in the facts shows.
Remember: Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act. Talk to the person before you judge them.

questions.stem: On a hybrid ERP rollout, a configuration analyst on the adaptive reporting stream has missed three delivery commitments. She was previously a top performer, and her manager suggests advanced reporting training. You learn she was recently assigned to support the predictive data migration stream as well. What should you do FIRST?
options: Talk with her about what is blocking delivery, including her workload across both streams
Enroll her in the advanced reporting training that her manager recommended for early next month
Reassign her reporting work to another analyst until her delivery record improves again
Add her missed commitments to the status report so leadership can see the delivery risk
questions.explanation:
Concept: Diagnose the cause of a performance gap — A drop in performance can come from skill, knowledge, motivation, capacity or environment. The remedy has to match the cause. (Rule M3-B03-R02)
Spot it: A former top performer suddenly slipping, a new extra assignment, and a manager who jumps straight to "send her to training."
In this scenario: Her skills haven't changed, but her workload has doubled across two streams. A conversation about what is blocking her will confirm the capacity problem before anyone picks a fix.
Why not the others: Training treats a skill gap the facts don't support; moving her work away acts before diagnosing and punishes her; putting it in the status report escalates before you understand it.
Remember: Diagnose, then prescribe. Skill gap = train, capacity gap = rebalance.

questions.stem: A junior tester on an agile healthcare app team writes acceptance tests that pass but miss edge cases, and reviewers keep catching gaps late. He is eager to get better at the tests he is writing now and asks the team's agile coach for help. Which approach is BEST?
options: Pair with him on upcoming tests, asking questions that help him find edge cases himself
Connect him with a senior QA director who can guide his long-term career path in testing
Have a senior tester write the edge-case tests for his stories until his skills improve
Send him the team's testing standards and ask him to review them before next week
questions.explanation:
Concept: Coaching — Coaching builds someone's current skills on their current work. It uses guided questions and practice so the person finds the answer themselves. (Rule M3-B03-R03)
Spot it: "Wants to get better at what he does now," hands-on skill, eager learner, the immediate task.
In this scenario: His gap is edge-case thinking on the tests he is writing today. Pairing with him and asking questions builds that skill in the flow of real work.
Why not the others: A career mentor is for long-term growth, not today's tests; having a senior write the tests for him removes the learning; handing him a standards document is passive and doesn't build judgment.
Remember: Coaching = current skill, now. Mentoring = career, later. Training = new knowledge.

questions.stem: A high-performing scheduler on a power plant outage project tells the project manager she wants to become a project manager within three years. Her technical scheduling work is excellent, but she is unsure which experiences, credentials, and relationships would prepare her. What is the BEST way to support her?
options: Arrange for a seasoned program manager to advise her regularly on her career path
Set up scheduling software coaching so she can sharpen her current technical skills
Advise her to earn a certification first, since credentials matter most for promotion
Refer her to human resources to review the posted requirements for project managers
questions.explanation:
