Concept: Mentoring — Mentoring pairs someone with a more experienced person who guides their long-term career. It covers experiences, credentials and relationships, not just one skill. (Rule M3-B03-R04)
Spot it: "Wants to become a PM in three years," "unsure which experiences," career path, a strong performer.
In this scenario: Her technical work is already excellent. What she needs is someone who has walked the path and can guide her growth, and a seasoned program manager is that mentor.
Why not the others: Software coaching sharpens a skill that is already strong; a single credential tip is narrow advice, not guidance; a referral to HR gives her a list of requirements, not a relationship.
Remember: Mentoring: career development → pair with a senior mentor.

questions.stem: During a hybrid warehouse automation project, a vendor liaison interrupted a client demo twice this morning to dispute the adaptive team's findings, which unsettled the client. You plan to address it with him. Which approach is BEST?
options: Note the issue for his quarterly review so it can be discussed along with his other results
Meet him today, describe both interruptions and their effect on the client, and agree on next steps
Tell the whole team at the next meeting that everyone must act more professionally in client demos
Tell him privately that his attitude has been a problem and that he needs to be more positive
questions.explanation:
Concept: Effective feedback — Good feedback is timely, specific and about behavior. It names what the person did and its impact while it is still fresh, and it ends with next steps. (Rule M3-B03-R05)
Spot it: "This morning," a specific incident, visible impact on a client, and a PM planning how to respond.
In this scenario: Meeting him today, naming both interruptions and how they unsettled the client, and agreeing on next steps gives him something concrete he can change.
Why not the others: Waiting for a quarterly review loses the timing; scolding the whole team is vague and misdirected; talking about his "attitude" labels his character instead of describing what he did.
Remember: Feedback = Soon, Specific, Behavior, Impact, Next step. Criticize in private, praise in public.

questions.stem: In a one-on-one, a developer on an agile logistics team and the team's coach agree that her code reviews are too superficial, and she wants to improve. The talk has been positive, but a similar conversation last quarter produced no change. What should the coach do before the meeting ends?
options: Agree with her on one concrete practice to try in her next reviews and a date to check progress
Thank her for being open and trust her to improve her code reviews at her own pace this time
Ask the lead developer to monitor her reviews and report any shallow ones back to the coach
Recommend a book on code review practices and ask her to share notes when she is ready
questions.explanation:
Concept: Development action and follow-up — A development conversation isn't finished until you have one agreed action and a date to check progress. Without both, good intentions fade. (Rule M3-B03-R06)
Spot it: A positive talk, an agreed weakness, and "last time nothing changed."
In this scenario: Last quarter's talk had no concrete practice and no check-in. Agreeing on one specific review practice and a follow-up date closes that loop.
Why not the others: Trusting her to improve at her own pace repeats last quarter's failure; asking the lead to monitor her turns development into surveillance; a book with no deadline leaves the action open-ended.
Remember: No action + no date = no change. Agree → Act → Follow up.

questions.stem: A civil engineer on a bridge rehabilitation project found a load calculation error in a subcontractor's design and worked with them to correct it before fabrication, avoiding costly rework. The project manager has recently held several corrective conversations with others about late submittals. What should the project manager do?
options: Wait until project closeout to recognize the engineer along with other contributors
Focus on the late submittals, since good work is already expected from the engineers
Add a note to the engineer's personnel file and let the functional manager decide on recognition
Acknowledge the engineer's specific catch and its cost impact at the next team meeting
questions.explanation:
Concept: Deliberate recognition — Strong performance deserves the same attention as weak performance. Specific, timely recognition reinforces the exact behavior you want to see again. (Rule M3-B03-R07)
Spot it: A clear, valuable contribution happening while the PM is busy with corrective conversations.
In this scenario: The engineer's catch prevented costly rework. Naming that specific catch and its cost impact at the next team meeting reinforces it and shows the team what good looks like.
Why not the others: Waiting until closeout breaks the link between the action and the praise; focusing only on problems means good work goes unnoticed; a quiet note in his file hands off something the PM should do personally.
Remember: Praise in public, specific and soon. What gets recognized gets repeated.

questions.stem: A bank is introducing a new cloud-based testing tool for its hybrid payments program. The adaptive teams are motivated and have capacity, but in the first two weeks several testers set up environments incorrectly because none of them had used the tool before. What is the BEST response?
options: Set up individual coaching to explore what is lowering the testers' motivation levels
Borrow testers from another program so configuration errors can be caught earlier in each cycle
Tell the sponsor the tool was a poor choice and request a return to the legacy tool
Arrange hands-on sessions on the new tool for the testers before the next release cycle
questions.explanation:
Concept: Training for knowledge gaps — Training is the right tool when people lack knowledge or a skill. It isn't the fix for problems with motivation or capacity. (Rule M3-B03-R08)
Spot it: "Never used the tool before," plus people who are motivated and have capacity: a pure know-how gap.
In this scenario: The testers want to do the work and have time for it. They just don't know the new tool yet, so hands-on sessions close exactly that gap.
Why not the others: Coaching on motivation targets a problem that doesn't exist; borrowing testers treats a capacity gap they don't have; asking to drop the tool jumps to a conclusion after two weeks.
Remember: Training = new knowledge. Coaching = current skill. Mentoring = career.

questions.stem: Every week, three business units separately ask an agile e-commerce team for delivery status, and different developers answer with slightly different information. The interruptions pull developers off their work, and one unit recently acted on outdated dates. What should the team's agile coach do?
options: Ask each developer to copy the coach on replies so every status answer can be checked for accuracy
Work with the product owner to set one owner and a regular schedule for delivery updates
Tell the business units to stop contacting the team and wait for the sprint review only
Have developers log each status request so the coach can report interruption volume
questions.explanation:
Concept: Communication ownership and cadence — Recurring information needs should get one owner, one source and a predictable schedule. Otherwise ad hoc requests fragment the message and interrupt the team. (Rule M3-B07-R09)
Spot it: The same question every week, several people answering differently, and someone acting on outdated information.
In this scenario: Setting one owner and a regular update schedule with the product owner gives the business units consistent status and protects developer focus.
Why not the others: Copying the coach adds a bottleneck but keeps the interruptions; limiting them to the sprint review shuts stakeholders out; logging requests only measures the problem.
Remember: Recurring need → one owner + one cadence + one source of truth.

questions.stem: Two weeks ago, a project manager on a hospital renovation settled a dispute between the electrical and HVAC foremen over shared ceiling space by agreeing on a work-sequencing arrangement. Both foremen accepted it at the time. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Check with both foremen and review site progress to see whether the sequencing is working
Close the issue in the issue log, since both foremen formally accepted the agreed arrangement
Schedule conflict resolution training for all foremen to prevent similar site disputes
Ask the general superintendent to enforce the arrangement and report any violations
questions.explanation:
Concept: Verify the resolution — A conflict is resolved only when the underlying situation actually improves, not when both sides say yes. Following up confirms that the fix works. (Rule M3-B01-R10)
Spot it: "Two weeks ago," "both agreed at the time," and a question asking what to do NEXT.
In this scenario: Now it's time to check that the sequencing arrangement works on site: talk with both foremen and look at the progress.
Why not the others: Closing the log on agreement alone skips the check; training everyone is broad prevention, not verification; handing enforcement to the superintendent turns a fix into policing.
Remember: Issue → Analyze → Resolve → Monitor. Agreement is not the same as resolution.

questions.stem: A government agency with a long tradition of sign-offs at every level wants its new benefits portal built with adaptive delivery for the user interface and predictive delivery for the back-end integration. Early planning assumes business staff will make quick decisions on interface features. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Start the adaptive interface work and let frequent reviews reveal any decision-making delays
Switch the interface work to predictive delivery so it matches the agency's sign-off tradition
Ask the sponsor to issue a directive requiring business staff to decide within two workdays of a request
Assess whether the agency's approval norms will let business staff make fast feature decisions
questions.explanation:
Concept: Assess cultural fit — Before you rely on a way of working, check whether the organization's culture will support it or resist it. Approval habits, risk tolerance and decision speed all matter. (Rule M5-B14-R01)
Spot it: A "long tradition of sign-offs," a plan that assumes "quick decisions," an adaptive approach entering a hierarchical organization.
In this scenario: The adaptive plan depends on fast business decisions, but the agency's norms say otherwise. Assess that gap first so you can plan around it.
Why not the others: Starting and waiting to see finds the barrier only after the delays have happened; switching the interface to predictive gives up on a good fit without assessing it; a sponsor directive forces behavior before you understand the culture.
Remember: Culture first, then method. Assess before you adapt.

questions.stem: A family-owned manufacturer is adopting agile practices in its product engineering group. Engineers already meet informally on the shop floor each morning to solve problems together, a habit employees value highly. Leadership asks the agile coach how to introduce daily team coordination. What should the coach recommend?
options: Replace the morning floor meeting with a standard daily stand-up held in a nearby conference room
Pause the morning floor meetings until the team finishes formal agile training next month
Build the daily coordination on the existing morning floor meeting, adding focus on team goals
Keep the morning meeting and add a separate daily stand-up so both habits can be compared
questions.explanation:
Concept: Build on cultural strengths — Change sticks when it grows out of habits people already value. Look for existing practices that already serve the goal. (Rule M5-B14-R02)
Spot it: "Already meet each morning," "a habit employees value," and a new practice that does the same job.
In this scenario: The floor meeting already does daily coordination. Making it the team's daily coordination, with sharper focus on team goals, keeps the goodwill and adds the agile purpose.
Why not the others: Swapping in a textbook stand-up discards a valued habit and invites resistance; pausing the meeting for training breaks something that works; running two parallel meetings wastes time and confuses people.
Remember: Adapt the practice to the people. Keep what works, add the purpose.

questions.stem: A telecom company is deploying a new fiber network under a predictive plan with a quality target of fewer than two percent failed installations. The project manager learns at the midpoint that field crews receive bonuses based on installations completed per day. Failure rates are rising. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Add more quality inspectors to catch failed installations before customers are affected
Analyze whether the per-day bonus is leading crews to trade installation quality for speed
Submit a change request to raise the failure-rate target to match current field results
Hold a quality briefing reminding crews that workmanship standards still fully apply to every job
questions.explanation:
Concept: Conflicting incentives — Incentive systems drive behavior. If a reward pays for something that works against the project's goal, people will follow the reward. (Rule M5-B14-R03)
Spot it: A bonus for speed or volume, a quality target, and quality getting worse.
In this scenario: Crews are paid per installation while the project needs fewer failures. The first step is to analyze whether that bonus is driving the failures before choosing a response.
Why not the others: More inspectors catch the symptom while the cause keeps producing it; raising the failure target lowers the goal to match the bad behavior; a reminder briefing is outweighed by money.
Remember: Follow the incentive to find the behavior. Assess before you act.

questions.stem: In a hierarchical pharmaceutical firm, a senior vice president routinely bypasses the hybrid program's prioritization forum and gives adaptive team members new requests directly. Team members feel they cannot refuse someone of her rank, and planned work is slipping. What should the project manager do?
options: Tell team members to accept her requests, since her rank gives her the final say on work
Meet the vice president privately, show the impact, and offer her a seat in prioritization
Report her behavior to the CEO as a governance violation that is undermining the program
Direct team members to decline her requests and send her a copy of the intake policy
questions.explanation:
Concept: Working within power structures — A PM respects how power works in the organization but does not reinforce behavior that harms the project. Give powerful people a legitimate channel for their influence. (Rule M5-B14-R04)
Spot it: A senior leader bypassing the process, a team afraid to say no, planned work slipping.
In this scenario: A private, respectful meeting that shows her the impact and offers her a seat in prioritization channels her rank into the process instead of around it.
Why not the others: Telling the team to comply rewards the bypass; reporting her to the CEO escalates before talking to her; having the team refuse her puts them in the line of fire.
Remember: Talk to the person first, then escalate. Channel influence, don't fight it.

questions.stem: An agile team at an insurance company needs production-like data refreshed weekly for testing, but corporate policy allows refreshes only quarterly. The team and its coach have already raised it with the data operations manager, who says only the chief information officer can grant an exception. What should the coach do NEXT?
options: Ask the project sponsor to take the exception request to the chief information officer
Ask a data operations engineer to run the refresh informally outside the approved policy
Accept the quarterly refresh and have the team test against aging data in the meantime
Email the chief information officer directly on the team's behalf to demand an exception
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sponsor removes barriers — When an obstacle is bigger than the team's authority, the sponsor is the right person to take it up the chain. Removing organizational impediments is part of the sponsor's job. (Rule M5-B14-R05)
Spot it: "Corporate policy," "only the CIO can approve," and the team has already tried the manager it can reach.
In this scenario: The team already went to data operations. The next step is to ask the sponsor to take the exception request to the CIO.
Why not the others: An informal workaround breaks policy; accepting stale data gives up on quality testing; emailing the CIO directly skips the sponsor and has little leverage.
Remember: Team solves team problems; sponsor clears organizational walls.

questions.stem: A retail chain's store managers are being asked to adopt a new inventory system under a predictive rollout plan. In the same quarter, they are also absorbing a new scheduling tool and a revised pricing process. Training attendance is falling, and managers say they feel overwhelmed. What should the project manager do?
options: Make training attendance mandatory and report the store managers who miss their assigned sessions
Keep the rollout on schedule, since the other initiatives are outside this project's control
Send store managers more frequent emails explaining the benefits of the new inventory system
Ease the load on managers by shortening training modules and phasing store cutovers gradually
questions.explanation:
Concept: Change fatigue — When several changes land on the same people at once, their capacity to adopt anything drops. The project has to reduce and pace what it asks of them. (Rule M5-B14-R06)
Spot it: "Same quarter," several new systems, falling attendance, people saying they feel "overwhelmed."
In this scenario: The store managers are saturated. Shortening the training modules and phasing store cutovers lowers the load so adoption can actually happen.
Why not the others: Mandatory attendance forces compliance and deepens the fatigue; pressing on ignores the people the rollout depends on; more emails add even more to their overload.
Remember: Adoption needs capacity. Too many changes at once means no change sticks.

questions.stem: A hybrid project is rolling out a new patient portal, with adaptive teams building features and a predictive plan for go-live. The project manager discovers that another project plans to retrain the same clinic front-desk staff on a new phone system during the two weeks set aside for portal training. What should the project manager do?
options: Move portal training earlier so that it is completed before the phone system training period begins
Proceed as planned, since each project is responsible for managing its own training plan
Ask the sponsor to delay the phone system project until the patient portal has gone live
Meet the phone system project manager to align training dates and messages for front-desk staff
questions.explanation:
Concept: Coordinate overlapping initiatives — When several projects affect the same stakeholders, the projects should align their timing and messages. The staff experience them all at once. (Rule M5-B14-R07)
Spot it: "Another project," "the same staff," "the same two weeks."
In this scenario: Meeting the phone system PM to align dates and messages protects the front-desk staff and both projects.
Why not the others: Moving your training earlier on your own may just create a new clash; proceeding as planned ignores the collision; asking the sponsor to delay the other project escalates before the two PMs have talked.
Remember: Dependency → Assess impact → Coordinate → Monitor.

questions.stem: An agile team at a regional airline must decide within two days how its crew-scheduling app applies overnight rest rules. The product owner and developers are ready to decide, but the rule interpretations come from the union safety representative, and crew members will live with the outcome. What should the team do?
options: Include the safety representative and a crew member in the decision session within two days
Decide with the product owner now and share the outcome with crews at the sprint review
Postpone the decision until a full crew survey can be completed over several weeks
Let the developers pick the most conservative rule reading to minimize safety exposure
questions.explanation:
Concept: Involve who knows and who is affected — Good decisions include the people who hold critical information and the people who will live with the result. This matters even more when time is short. (Rule M3-B13-R08)
Spot it: Someone outside the team holds the rule knowledge, and a group bears the outcome, but there is a firm deadline.
In this scenario: The safety representative has the rule interpretations and crews bear the impact. Both can join the session within the two days.
Why not the others: Deciding without them and informing crews later leaves out the key knowledge; a survey that takes weeks misses the deadline; picking the most conservative reading guesses instead of asking.
Remember: Knowledge + impact = a seat at the table. Collaborate before you act.

questions.stem: During a weekly status meeting for a chemical plant upgrade, a project engineer realizes that a specification error he made caused a vendor to deliver incorrect valves. Several stakeholders and the vendor are on the call. How should the project manager handle the mistake?
options: Explain on the call that the engineer's error caused the delay so stakeholders understand the root cause
Keep the meeting on the recovery plan and discuss the specification error with the engineer privately
Ask the engineer to walk the group through his mistake so everyone learns from what happened
Tell stakeholders the vendor misread the specification to protect the engineer's reputation
questions.explanation:
Concept: No public blame — Mistakes are handled in private and processes are fixed in public. Blame kills psychological safety and stops people from raising problems early. (Rule M3-B10-R09)
Spot it: A mistake surfacing in front of stakeholders or a vendor, and a PM deciding how to respond.
In this scenario: Keep the meeting on the recovery plan and talk with the engineer privately about the specification error.
Why not the others: Naming him on the call shames him publicly; making him walk everyone through his error is public blame dressed up as learning; blaming the vendor is dishonest.
Remember: Praise in public, correct in private. Fix the problem, not the person.

questions.stem: On a hybrid data center migration, adaptive application teams are on track while the predictive network cutover is six weeks late because of a hardware shortage. The sponsor has told the board the migration is on schedule, and a colleague suggests reporting it as amber and recovering. What should the project manager do?
options: Report amber status and work on a recovery plan before disclosing the full length of delay
Report the six-week network delay and its cause to the sponsor before the next board update
Report only the application teams' progress, since the hardware shortage is not controllable
Ask the network lead to present the delay so the bad news does not come from the manager
questions.explanation:
Concept: Truthful status reporting — Report status honestly, even when the news is bad. Leaders can only act on information they actually have. (Rule M3-B16-R01)
Spot it: A known large delay, a sponsor telling the board all is well, and pressure to "soften" the color.
In this scenario: The six-week network delay is a fact. The sponsor needs it, and its cause, before the next board update.
Why not the others: Reporting amber hides a known delay; reporting only the good news is selective reporting; having someone else deliver it avoids the PM's own duty.
Remember: Honesty is a PMI value. Bad news early beats bad news late.

questions.stem: An agile team is evaluating three vendors for a payment gateway, and its product owner will make the final recommendation. The product owner's brother-in-law is a senior account executive at one of the vendors. No one else on the team knows. What should the product owner do?
options: Keep the relationship private and apply identical scoring criteria to all three competing vendors
Exclude that vendor from consideration so there is no appearance of favoritism at all
Disclose the relationship to the sponsor and team and agree how the evaluation will proceed
Hand the decision to the team without saying why, so no one feels pressured by the link
questions.explanation:
Concept: Disclose conflicts of interest — A personal relationship that could influence a decision must be disclosed. Then others can decide how to manage it. (Rule M3-B16-R02)
Spot it: A family member or friend at a vendor, someone who decides or recommends, and "no one else knows."
In this scenario: The product owner discloses the relationship to the sponsor and the team and agrees on how the evaluation will be handled.
Why not the others: Keeping it private conceals the conflict even if the scoring is fair; excluding the vendor is a unilateral call that may be unfair; handing off the decision silently still hides it.
Remember: Conflict of interest = Disclose first, then let others decide how to manage it.

questions.stem: A project coordinator on a merger integration project receives a request from a friendly analyst in another department for the employee retention list, which includes salary data. The analyst says his manager needs it for workforce planning, but he is not on the project's approved distribution list. What should the coordinator do?
options: Send only the names without salary data, since workforce planning is a legitimate purpose
Send the list with a confidentiality reminder, since the analyst works for the same parent company
Decline to send it and refer the request to the data owner to confirm authorization and need
Ask the analyst to get verbal approval from his manager and then share the full list
questions.explanation:
Concept: Protect confidential information — Sensitive data is shared only under policy with verified authorization and a legitimate need. Friendliness or a plausible reason is not approval. (Rule M3-B16-R03)
Spot it: Salary or personal data, a requester not on the distribution list, a "my manager needs it" reason.
In this scenario: The coordinator declines and refers the request to the data owner, who can confirm authorization and need.
Why not the others: Sending only the names is still an unauthorized release; a confidentiality reminder doesn't make sharing legitimate; a verbal OK from his manager isn't the data owner's authorization.
Remember: Confidential = need-to-know + authorized. When in doubt, route to the data owner.

questions.stem: Ahead of a funding review for a hybrid logistics program, its director asks the project manager to restate the adaptive teams' forecast using their most optimistic throughput from the past year, instead of their recent average. The recent average shows a three-month slip. What should the project manager do?
options: Present the forecast based on recent throughput and explain the assumptions behind the slip
Present the optimistic forecast as requested, noting the recent average in an appendix
Blend the two figures into a single midpoint forecast that softens the reported slip
Decline to present any forecast until the adaptive teams improve their throughput
questions.explanation:
Concept: Honest estimates and metrics — Forecasts must reflect the real evidence. Cherry-picking data to look better misleads decision makers. (Rule M3-B16-R04)
Spot it: "Most optimistic," "instead of the recent average," and a funding review coming up.
In this scenario: Recent throughput is the evidence-based basis. Present it with its assumptions and explain the slip.
Why not the others: The optimistic forecast with the truth in an appendix still leads with a misleading number; blending the figures deliberately shrinks the slip; refusing to forecast leaves the funders with nothing.
Remember: Forecast from actuals, not wishes. Transparency is a PMI value.

questions.stem: During a sprint, a developer on an agile health insurance team notices that a senior manager has been exporting member medical records to a personal cloud account. The developer tells the scrum master privately and is afraid of retaliation. What should the scrum master do?
options: Confront the senior manager directly and ask him to delete the exported records right away
Raise it at the next retrospective so the whole team can agree on how to handle the situation together
Tell the developer to collect more evidence before anyone reports the behavior formally
Report it through the company's compliance or ethics channel and protect the developer's identity
questions.explanation:
Concept: Escalate unethical or illegal behavior — Suspected misconduct goes through formal channels such as compliance, ethics or legal. Those channels can investigate and protect the reporter. (Rule M3-B16-R05)
Spot it: Possible data theft or illegal activity, someone senior involved, a reporter afraid of retaliation.
In this scenario: Reporting it through the compliance or ethics channel while protecting the developer's identity is the proper path.
Why not the others: Confronting the manager can destroy evidence and invite retaliation; a retrospective exposes the reporter and isn't an investigation; asking for more evidence puts the developer at risk and delays the report.
Remember: Illegal or unethical = report through proper channels. Don't investigate it yourself.

questions.stem: Near the end of a predictive office relocation project, a team lead asks whether she can use the project's surplus laptops and the reserved moving truck over the weekend to help a friend's nonprofit move offices. The equipment is company property charged to the project. What should the project manager do?
options: Approve it, since the nonprofit is a good cause and nothing is needed that weekend
Decline and handle the surplus equipment according to company disposal procedures
Allow the truck but not the laptops, since the truck rental is already paid for
Approve it informally as long as the team lead covers any fuel costs herself
questions.explanation:
Concept: Use resources only for project purposes — Company property and funds serve legitimate project and business purposes. They are not for personal favors, even for good causes. (Rule M3-B16-R06)
Spot it: "Surplus," "over the weekend," "for a friend," and company property charged to the project.
In this scenario: Decline the request and handle the surplus equipment through the company's disposal procedures.
Why not the others: Approving because the cause is good is still personal use; lending only the truck is still company property used for a favor; asking her to pay for fuel doesn't make it legitimate.
Remember: Company resources = company purposes. Good intent doesn't equal authorization.

questions.stem: A business analyst on the adaptive stream of a hybrid claims project designed a workflow change that cut processing time by 30 percent. During the steering committee presentation, a grateful sponsor thanks the project manager personally for the idea. What should the project manager do?
options: Tell the committee that the business analyst designed the change and describe her contribution
Accept the thanks on behalf of the team and mention the analyst in the next team newsletter
Say nothing now and send the analyst a private thank-you note after the steering meeting
Credit the adaptive team as a whole, since singling out one analyst might discourage others
questions.explanation:
Concept: Give appropriate credit — Credit goes to the people who actually did the work, in the forum where it matters. Correcting a misattribution is a duty, not modesty. (Rule M3-B16-R07)
Spot it: Praise landing on the wrong person, in front of leadership.
In this scenario: Right there in the steering committee, tell them the business analyst designed the change and describe what she contributed.
Why not the others: Accepting on the team's behalf leaves the wrong impression; a private note later misses the audience that matters; crediting only the team hides her individual contribution.
Remember: Give credit where it's due, where it's seen.

questions.stem: An agile team building a hiring platform found that one screening feature could disadvantage older applicants. The product owner and team consulted legal and the ethics office and decided to remove and redesign the feature. A new product owner will join next month. What should the team do?
options: Remove the feature quietly so the concern does not alarm any future stakeholders
Brief the incoming product owner verbally and leave decision records to legal
Record the ethical concern, who was consulted, and the rationale for removing the feature
Add a backlog item to revisit the feature later, since the concern may be unfounded
questions.explanation:
Concept: Document ethical decisions — Material ethical decisions, and who was consulted, should be recorded. The reasoning then survives role changes and later questions. (Rule M3-B16-R10)
Spot it: A significant ethical call, legal or ethics consulted, a handover or new role holder coming.
In this scenario: Record the concern, who was consulted and why the feature was removed, so the new product owner and future teams understand the decision.
Why not the others: Removing it quietly hides a material decision; a verbal briefing leaves no durable record; a backlog item to revisit it reopens a settled ethical risk.
Remember: If it mattered ethically, write it down: concern, consulted, decision, rationale.

questions.stem: A defense contractor's project is transitioning a radar maintenance system to a support vendor. The vendor needs operating procedures to take over, but some design documents contain export-controlled data that the vendor is not licensed to receive. What should the project manager do?
options: Share all documents under a nondisclosure agreement so the vendor has full knowledge
Withhold all technical documents and let the vendor learn the system by observation
Provide procedures with the controlled data removed and confirm the version with security
Delay the transition until the vendor obtains an export license covering every controlled document
questions.explanation:
Concept: Protected knowledge transfer — Hand over what the receiver needs while keeping controlled or confidential content protected. Security and transition must both succeed. (Rule M3-B11-R08)
Spot it: "Export-controlled," "not licensed," and the receiving team needs procedures to take over.
In this scenario: Give the vendor sanitized procedures and confirm the version with security. The vendor can operate the system and the controlled data stays protected.
Why not the others: An NDA can't authorize export-controlled release; withholding everything blocks the transition; waiting for a full license delays a handover that doesn't need the controlled data.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close. Transfer what's needed, protect what's controlled.

questions.stem: A hybrid ERP program's weekly integration meeting between the adaptive teams and the predictive infrastructure team keeps revisiting the same unresolved items. Actions are agreed verbally each week, but no one can confirm later whether they were completed. What should the project manager do?
options: Shorten the meeting so participants focus only on decisions rather than follow-up actions
Ask each team lead to email the sponsor when their team finishes an action from the meeting
Record each action with an owner and due date and review its status at the start of each meeting
Replace the weekly meeting with ad hoc calls between the teams whenever issues come up
questions.explanation:
Concept: Track meeting actions — Every action agreed in a meeting needs an owner and a due date, and it should be reviewed until it's closed. Otherwise meetings just loop. (Rule M3-B14-R09)
Spot it: "The same items keep coming back," "agreed verbally," "no one can confirm."
In this scenario: Record each action with an owner and due date, and review its status at the start of every meeting.
Why not the others: Shortening the meeting drops follow-up entirely; emailing the sponsor pulls leadership into routine tracking; ad hoc calls remove the shared forum.
Remember: Action = owner + date + status, tracked until closed.

questions.stem: An agile team's delivery has plateaued, and the department head offers the scrum master a budget for team gift cards to lift morale. Team members have recently complained about frequent reprioritization and a lack of time for technical improvements. What should the scrum master do FIRST?
options: Hand out the gift cards at the next sprint review to show that leadership values the team
Tie the gift cards to velocity goals so the team has a clear incentive to deliver more
Talk with team members about what would increase their engagement before using the budget
Return the budget, since agile teams are motivated by autonomy, not external rewards
questions.explanation:
Concept: Diagnose motivation before rewarding — Rewards only work when they match what people actually value. Find out what's driving disengagement before spending money on it. (Rule M3-B15-R01)
Spot it: A reward offered for a morale problem, alongside specific team complaints about how work is run.
In this scenario: The team's complaints are about constant reprioritization and no time for technical work. Asking them what would raise engagement comes before using the budget.
Why not the others: Gift cards at the review ignore the real complaints; tying them to velocity invites gaming; returning the budget assumes the answer without asking.
Remember: Ask before you reward. Intrinsic problems need intrinsic fixes.

questions.stem: A quality inspector on a shipbuilding project stayed late to re-inspect welds after noticing an irregular pattern, preventing costly hull rework. The project values proactive quality ownership. The project manager wants to recognize her. Which approach is BEST?
options: Include her in the year-end award nominations with other strong performers
Send a team-wide email thanking everyone for their hard work on quality
Thank her this week, naming the re-inspection and the rework it prevented
Give her a gift card and tell her it is for being such a dedicated worker
questions.explanation:
Concept: Meaningful recognition — Recognition works when it's timely, specific and tied to the behavior the project values. It tells people exactly what to repeat. (Rule M3-B15-R02)
Spot it: A specific valuable act, a value the project wants to reinforce, and a PM choosing how to recognize it.
In this scenario: Thanking her this week and naming the re-inspection and the rework it prevented reinforces proactive quality ownership.
Why not the others: A year-end nomination is too late; a team-wide thank-you is too generic; a gift card for being "dedicated" misses the specific behavior.
Remember: Recognition = Soon + Specific + linked to the Value.

questions.stem: A hybrid program has four adaptive teams working on shared components and one predictive integration team. Leadership proposes a monthly bonus for the team that completes the most features. Integration problems already arise when teams optimize their own work. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Adopt the monthly bonus but exclude the integration team, since its work is measured differently
Tie recognition to shared program outcomes, such as integrated releases that work end to end
Adopt the bonus and have team leads verify feature counts to stop teams from inflating them
Replace the bonus with individual awards for the top contributor on each of the four teams
questions.explanation:
Concept: Avoid rewards that pit teams against each other — Rewards that favor one team's output can create local optimization and unhealthy competition. The whole system then suffers. (Rule M3-B15-R03)
Spot it: Teams sharing components, integration problems, and a proposed "team with the most" bonus.
In this scenario: Tying recognition to shared outcomes like integrated, working releases rewards the collaboration the program needs.
Why not the others: Excluding the integration team still rewards local output; verifying counts only polices the gaming; individual awards shift the competition onto people.
Remember: Reward the whole system, not the silo.

questions.stem: A product owner at a media startup wants her agile team to take on a surprise partner integration in the current sprint on top of its full commitment. Team members say they could do it by working the weekend, as they did last month. What should the scrum master do?
options: Support the weekend work, since the team volunteered and the partner deal is important to the company
Refuse the integration outright and tell the product owner to wait for the next sprint
Help the product owner decide what to defer so the integration fits the team's capacity
Ask the team to estimate the extra work more aggressively so it fits in normal hours
questions.explanation:
Concept: Protect workload — When new work arrives, trade it off against existing commitments instead of adding hours. Repeated weekend work is a warning sign, not a solution. (Rule M3-B15-R04)
Spot it: "On top of a full commitment," "work the weekend again," "as they did last month."
In this scenario: The scrum master helps the product owner decide what to defer so the integration fits the team's real capacity.
Why not the others: Backing weekend work normalizes overtime; refusing outright ignores the business need and the product owner's priorities; estimating "more aggressively" fakes capacity.
Remember: New work in = something out. Capacity is fixed; priority is the lever.

questions.stem: On a predictive hospital equipment upgrade, a biomedical technician has deep expertise in the imaging systems being replaced. The project manager currently assigns her individual tasks each week with detailed instructions, and her engagement has dropped. What should the project manager do?
options: Provide more detailed instructions so she can complete weekly tasks with less effort
Give her ownership of the imaging work package, including planning how the work gets done
Ask her functional manager to raise the engagement drop in her next performance review
Move her to a different work package to give her variety and renew her interest
questions.explanation:
Concept: Meaningful ownership — Experts engage when they own an outcome and decide how the work gets done, not when they're handed step-by-step instructions. (Rule M3-B15-R05)
Spot it: An expert getting detailed task instructions, and engagement dropping.
In this scenario: Giving her ownership of the imaging work package, including planning how it's done, uses her expertise and restores engagement.
Why not the others: More detailed instructions deepen the micromanagement; handing it to her functional manager avoids the PM's role; moving her wastes her expertise.
Remember: Autonomy + mastery + purpose = motivation. Manage the what, trust the how.

questions.stem: Developers on the adaptive stream of a hybrid public health program are building data-entry screens for vaccination clinics. They describe the work as tedious form-building and see little point to it. Clinic nurses have said slow data entry creates long waits for patients. What should the project manager do?
options: Invite clinic nurses to a demo to explain how quicker screens will affect patients and staff
Rotate developers between the screens and more interesting features to reduce boredom
Offer developers a bonus for completing the screens ahead of the clinic go-live date
Remind developers that the screens are in the approved scope and must be delivered on schedule as planned
questions.explanation:
Concept: Connect work to purpose — People stay motivated when they see who their work helps and why it matters. Hearing directly from stakeholders makes that real. (Rule M3-B15-R06)
Spot it: "Tedious," "see little point," and a clear real-world impact the team hasn't seen.
In this scenario: Inviting the clinic nurses to a demo shows the developers how faster screens cut patient wait times.
Why not the others: Rotating people treats boredom but not meaning; a bonus buys speed, not purpose; reminding them of scope uses authority instead of meaning.
Remember: Show the why. Purpose beats pressure.

questions.stem: A mid-level developer on an agile team tells the scrum master she is bored and considering leaving because she always gets the same database tasks. The team is about to start a new event-streaming service that no one on the team has built before. What should the scrum master do?
options: Recommend a raise to her manager so she has a financial reason to stay on the team
Assign her the streaming work alone so she can prove she is ready for harder tasks
Keep her on database work, since changing roles now would slow team delivery
Encourage the team to let her take on streaming work, paired with an experienced peer
questions.explanation:
Concept: Growth through stretch work — Stretch assignments with support, such as pairing, coaching and learning time, keep people engaged and build team capability. (Rule M3-B15-R07)
Spot it: "Bored," "always the same tasks," "thinking of leaving," and a new technology coming up.
In this scenario: Encourage the self-organizing team to let her take on the streaming work, paired with an experienced peer, so she grows safely.
Why not the others: A raise treats a growth problem with money; assigning her alone is the scrum master directing work and leaves her unsupported; keeping her on database work ignores why she wants to leave.
Remember: Stretch + support = growth. Teams self-assign; the servant leader enables.

questions.stem: Three months ago, a project manager on a highway expansion introduced flexible start times and a monthly recognition lunch after survey scores showed low morale. The actions were well received when announced. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Add another benefit, such as team outings, to keep the momentum from the first actions
Compare current engagement and performance measures with the earlier survey results
Close the morale concern in the issue log, since the team welcomed the changes
Continue both actions for the rest of the project, since they were well received
questions.explanation:
Concept: Measure motivation actions — A motivation initiative succeeds only if engagement and performance actually improve. Compare the measures before and after. (Rule M3-B15-R10)
Spot it: Actions taken months ago, "well received," and a question asking what to do NEXT.
In this scenario: Compare current engagement and performance data with the earlier survey results to see whether the actions worked.
Why not the others: Adding more perks assumes success; closing the concern on goodwill skips the check; continuing because people liked it confuses a warm reaction with results.
Remember: Act → Monitor. Well received does not mean it worked.

questions.stem: A project manager on a hybrid customer portal needs a skeptical operations director to support moving fraud-review features into the adaptive stream. A colleague suggests getting the director's staff excited first by showing only the benefits and leaving out the added testing load. What should the project manager do?
options: Follow the colleague's advice, since the benefits will outweigh the testing load over time
Ask the sponsor to direct the operations director to support the change without debate
Present both the benefits and the added testing load to the director and discuss concerns
Wait until the director's staff are enthusiastic, then present the testing load as settled
questions.explanation:
Concept: Ethical influence — Influence means persuading with the full picture, costs as well as benefits. Hiding downsides or going around people destroys trust. (Rule M3-B08-R08)
Spot it: Advice to "show only the benefits" or build pressure before the decision maker sees the facts.
In this scenario: Present both the benefits and the added testing load to the director and discuss the concerns openly.
Why not the others: Following the colleague hides the costs; a sponsor mandate forces compliance instead of earning support; building staff enthusiasm first manipulates the director.
Remember: Influence = transparency + trust. Earn support, don't engineer it.

questions.stem: A bank is adopting agile delivery in its lending division, and teams are asked to collaborate on shared goals. However, annual reviews still rate individuals on personal task completion, and procurement requires fixed-scope contracts for every tool purchase. Adoption is stalling. What should the agile coach recommend?
options: Work with HR and procurement to align reviews and purchasing rules with team delivery
Run more agile training so staff understand the benefits of working on shared goals
Ask teams to follow agile practices anyway and treat the review system as a separate HR matter
Pause the agile adoption until the next annual review cycle has been completed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Align the system with the change — Incentives, policies and processes must support the new way of working. If they don't, they quietly pull people back to the old one. (Rule M5-B05-R09)
Spot it: "Reviews still rate individuals," "procurement requires fixed scope," adoption stalling.
In this scenario: Working with HR and procurement to align reviews and purchasing rules with team-based delivery removes what's rewarding the old behavior.
Why not the others: More training doesn't fix misaligned rewards; calling reviews someone else's problem leaves the conflict in place; pausing adoption loses momentum.
Remember: People do what the system rewards. Change the system, not just the slides.

questions.stem: On a predictive water treatment plant project, four engineers each prepared a portion of the commissioning plan. When the plan fails client review, each engineer points to another's section, and no one is sure who should fix the overall document. What should the project manager do?
options: Make all four engineers jointly accountable so the team shares ownership of the plan
Rewrite the commissioning plan personally so it meets the client's standards this time
Ask the client to specify which engineer should revise each section of the plan
Assign one person accountable for the complete plan while the engineers keep their sections
questions.explanation:
Concept: Responsible vs accountable — Many people can be responsible for doing parts of the work, but only one person is accountable for the whole result. (Rule M3-B09-R01)
Spot it: Several contributors, finger-pointing, and "no one is sure who should fix it."
In this scenario: Name one person accountable for the complete plan while the engineers stay responsible for their sections.
Why not the others: Joint accountability is what caused the finger-pointing; the PM rewriting it personally takes over the team's work; asking the client to assign fixes hands internal roles to an outsider.
Remember: RACI: many R's, only one A.

questions.stem: Three weeks into a hybrid retail loyalty program, a marketing lead, an IT architect, and a product owner have each overruled one another on feature priority, platform choice, and whether releases are accepted. Work is stalling while people wait for a final answer. What should the project manager do?
options: Facilitate agreement on who decides priority, technical design, and acceptance, and record it
Escalate each disputed decision to the sponsor as it arises so the work can keep moving
Make the pending decisions personally to keep the program moving until disputes settle
Ask the three leaders to reach consensus on every decision before any work continues
questions.explanation:
Concept: Decision rights — Everyone should know who decides priority, scope, funding, acceptance and technical design. Unclear rights cause overruling and stalls. (Rule M3-B09-R02)
Spot it: Leaders overruling each other on different decision types, and work waiting for a "final answer."
In this scenario: Facilitate agreement on who decides priority, technical design and acceptance, and record it so decisions stick.
Why not the others: Escalating every dispute keeps the confusion alive; the PM making decisions personally takes rights that aren't hers; requiring consensus on everything freezes the work.
Remember: Clear rights, fewer fights. Decide who decides.

questions.stem: An agile program with three teams created a RACI chart for release activities. It shows no one responsible for performance testing and two groups accountable for release approval. A manager proposes emailing the chart to everyone as the final word. What should the agile coach do?
options: Email the chart as proposed and ask each group to raise any objections within one week
Bring the teams together to discuss the gaps and overlaps the chart revealed and agree on roles
Assign performance testing to the team with the most capacity and update the chart directly
Discard the chart, since self-organizing agile teams should not rely on role matrices
questions.explanation:
Concept: RACI as a conversation starter — A RACI chart exposes gaps and overlaps. The people involved still have to talk and agree on the roles. (Rule M3-B09-R03)
Spot it: The chart shows a gap (no R) or an overlap (two A's), and someone wants to email it out as final.
In this scenario: Bring the teams together to discuss the gaps and overlaps and agree on roles, then update the chart.
Why not the others: Emailing it with an objection window treats the chart as the decision; assigning testing yourself skips the teams' agreement; discarding the chart throws away a useful tool.
Remember: RACI shows the gap; conversation closes it. One A per activity.

questions.stem: During planning for a predictive airport baggage system upgrade, a steering committee proposes making all six department heads jointly accountable for achieving the system's reliability target to build shared commitment. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Accept joint accountability, since shared ownership encourages all six departments to engage
Make the project manager accountable for the target, since the project delivers the system
Split the reliability target into six equal parts and give each department head one part
Name one leader accountable for the reliability target, with others responsible for their parts
questions.explanation:
Concept: Don't spread accountability too thin — When everyone is accountable, no one is. Shared commitment comes from clear roles, not a shared A. (Rule M3-B09-R04)
Spot it: "Jointly accountable," several leaders, one outcome.
In this scenario: Name one leader accountable for the reliability target, with the other department heads responsible for their parts.
Why not the others: Joint accountability diffuses ownership; making the PM own an operational target misplaces it; splitting the target into six pieces means no one owns the integrated result.
Remember: One outcome, one A. Everyone else is R, C or I.

questions.stem: A hybrid insurance claims program's designated product owner has ranked a fraud-detection feature above a reporting dashboard for the adaptive team. A regional manager asks the project manager to move the dashboard ahead because her team finds it more urgent. What should the project manager do?
options: Swap the two items, since the regional manager represents the users who need the dashboard
Submit a change request to the change control board to reorder the two features formally
Ask the adaptive team to build both features in parallel so neither stakeholder is delayed
Refer the regional manager to the product owner, who sets the ranking, and help them discuss it
questions.explanation:
Concept: Product owner prioritizes — In adaptive work, the designated product owner has authority to order the backlog. Other stakeholders influence the order through the product owner. (Rule M3-B09-R05)
Spot it: A stakeholder asking the PM to reorder adaptive work that the product owner has already ranked.
In this scenario: Refer the regional manager to the product owner and help them discuss her need. The ranking decision stays with the product owner.
Why not the others: Swapping items yourself overrides the product owner; the CCB is for baseline changes, not ordering adaptive work; building both in parallel dodges the priority decision and overloads the team.
Remember: Product backlog: the product owner orders it; the team pulls from it.

questions.stem: An agile team at a logistics firm chose a message queue library that fits the company's approved architecture standards. A senior manager who prefers a different library asks the scrum master to have the team switch before the next release. What should the scrum master do?
options: Explain that the choice meets approved standards and invite the manager to share concerns with the team
Ask the team to switch libraries, since the senior manager has more experience with messaging tools overall
Hold a vote between the team and the manager to settle which library the team will use going forward
Escalate the disagreement to the enterprise architect and ask for a binding decision on the library
questions.explanation:
Concept: Team technical autonomy — Within agreed constraints such as architecture standards, the agile team decides how to build. Managers influence by sharing concerns, not by dictating. (Rule M3-B09-R06)
Spot it: A choice that already meets approved standards, and a manager who "prefers" something else.
In this scenario: The library fits the approved architecture. The scrum master explains that and invites the manager to share his concerns with the team, which keeps the decision with the team.
Why not the others: Switching because of seniority overrides team autonomy; a vote with the manager turns a technical choice into politics; escalating for a binding ruling treats a preference as a dispute.
Remember: Constraints set the box; the team decides inside it. The scrum master shields the team.

questions.stem: A project manager on a predictive ERP upgrade is frustrated that two team members keep arriving late to design workshops, and she considers asking the sponsor, a senior vice president, to speak with them. A budget decision that exceeds her authority is also pending. How should she use the sponsor?
options: Ask the sponsor to address the lateness, since a senior leader's message carries more weight
Bring both matters to the sponsor together so the sponsor has a complete view of the project
Handle the lateness herself and bring the sponsor the budget decision beyond her authority
Resolve both matters herself, since sponsors should stay out of project-level decisions entirely
questions.explanation:
Concept: Right use of the sponsor — The sponsor provides strategic support, funding and escalation for decisions above the PM's authority. Day-to-day team management is the PM's job. (Rule M3-B09-R07)
Spot it: A routine people issue next to a decision that "exceeds her authority."
In this scenario: The PM handles the lateness herself and brings the sponsor only the budget decision she can't make.
Why not the others: Sending the sponsor after latecomers misuses the sponsor; bringing both muddies the escalation; keeping the budget decision oversteps her authority.
Remember: Sponsor = funding, authority, escalation. PM = running the team.

questions.stem: On a hybrid manufacturing systems project, a predictive work package is running two days late, which can be absorbed within its float. The project manager has authority to adjust task sequences within approved float. A team lead suggests raising the delay with the steering committee. What should the project manager do?
options: Resequence tasks within the available float and record the adjustment in the project records
Raise the delay with the steering committee so leadership is aware of every schedule movement
Submit a change request to revise the schedule baseline to reflect the two-day slippage
Ask the adaptive teams to absorb some of the predictive work to recover the two lost days
questions.explanation:
Concept: Authority at the right level — Act on what is within your authority and escalate only what exceeds it. Unneeded escalation wastes leadership time. (Rule M3-B09-R10)
Spot it: "Absorbed within float," "PM has authority," and a suggestion to go to the steering committee.
In this scenario: A two-day slip inside approved float is within the PM's authority. Resequence the tasks and record the adjustment.
Why not the others: Going to the steering committee escalates what doesn't need it; a baseline change request isn't needed when float absorbs the slip; pulling in the adaptive teams disrupts other work for no reason.
Remember: Understand → Assess → Act → Monitor → Escalate only if it's beyond you.

questions.stem: An empowered agile team at a software company chose to skip automated security scans to meet a demo date, and a vulnerability reached a customer environment. A team member says that because the team was trusted to decide, no one should be held responsible. What should the scrum master do?
options: Help the team own the outcome, analyze the decision, and agree how to prevent a repeat
Remove the team's authority over quality decisions and have management approve them instead
Agree that no one is responsible, since the team made the decision together in good faith
Identify which developer proposed skipping the scans and report that person to management
questions.explanation:
Concept: Empowerment includes accountability — An empowered team owns its decisions and their consequences. The response is to learn and improve, not to blame. (Rule M3-B02-R08)
Spot it: "We were trusted to decide, so no one is responsible," after a harmful outcome.
In this scenario: Help the team own the outcome, analyze why they decided to skip the scans, and agree how to prevent it happening again.
Why not the others: Taking away their authority punishes empowerment itself; agreeing no one is responsible drops accountability; hunting for the individual is blame, not learning.
Remember: Empowered = owns the choice AND the result.

questions.stem: A predictive project to consolidate three hospital laboratories has just received approval to close one site six months earlier than planned. Lab staff and referring physicians were informed by memo last week. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Proceed with the revised schedule, since the decision has been approved and communicated
Send a second memo repeating the closure date to make sure the message was fully received by all
Ask the sponsor to hold a town hall that defends the decision against expected objections
Gauge how staff and physicians are reacting to the earlier closure and adjust engagement plans
questions.explanation:
Concept: Monitor stakeholder sentiment — After a major decision, check how stakeholders are actually reacting and adjust engagement to match. Communicating something is not the same as it being accepted. (Rule M3-B06-R09)
Spot it: A big change, a one-way memo, and a question asking what to do NEXT.
In this scenario: Gauge how staff and physicians are reacting to the earlier closure, and adjust the engagement plans based on what you learn.
Why not the others: Proceeding assumes the memo worked; a second memo repeats one-way push communication; a town hall built to defend the decision argues before it listens.
Remember: Identify → Analyze → Engage → Monitor. Keep monitoring after big news.

questions.stem: Eight months into a hybrid smart-meter program, a city council passes an ordinance requiring customer data to be stored in-state. The program's stakeholder register was completed during initiation and has not been updated since. What should the project manager do?
options: Leave the register as it is, since stakeholder identification was already completed at initiation
Ask the adaptive teams to add the ordinance as a feature so the city's needs are covered
Update the stakeholder register to add parties affected by or enforcing the new ordinance
Notify the sponsor and wait for direction before changing any stakeholder documentation
questions.explanation:
Concept: Continuous stakeholder identification — New stakeholders appear throughout a project, through regulation, reorganizations or new markets. Identification never finishes at initiation. (Rule M3-B05-R01)
Spot it: A new law, ruling or organization appearing mid-project, and a register "not updated since initiation."
In this scenario: Update the stakeholder register to add the parties who enforce or are affected by the new ordinance, then plan how to engage them.
Why not the others: Leaving the register as is assumes identification is a one-time task; making the ordinance a feature skips stakeholder analysis; waiting for the sponsor delays a routine PM duty.
Remember: The stakeholder register is a TRACK document: living and always updated.

questions.stem: An agile team building a farm equipment rental app learns that a regional dealers' association wants a say in pricing features. The product owner proposes inviting the association to every sprint review. No one on the team knows how much sway the association has with dealers or what worries it. What should the team do FIRST?
options: Invite the association to every sprint review as the product owner has proposed
Add the association to the monthly newsletter so it gets regular product updates
Ask the association to submit all of its pricing requests to the team in writing
Analyze the association's influence, interests, attitude, and information needs
questions.explanation:
Concept: Analyze before engaging — Before choosing how to engage a stakeholder, understand their influence, interest, impact, attitude and information needs. The strategy follows from the analysis. (Rule M3-B05-R02)
Spot it: A new stakeholder group, a proposed engagement plan, and "the team knows little about them."
In this scenario: Nobody yet knows how much sway the association has or what it cares about. Analyze that first, then decide whether reviews, updates or something else fits.
Why not the others: Inviting them to every review picks a strategy blind; a newsletter might under-engage a powerful group; written-only requests may alienate them before you understand them.
Remember: Identify → Analyze → Engage → Monitor. Analysis comes before strategy.

questions.stem: A predictive factory automation project's plant manager formally approves all changes. The project manager notices that line supervisors consistently defer to a senior machinist with 30 years of experience, whose opinion often shapes how new equipment is received. How should the project manager treat the machinist?
options: Engage the machinist early as an informal influencer whose views shape equipment adoption
Route all communication through the plant manager, since he holds the formal authority
Treat the machinist as a low-priority stakeholder, since he has no approval authority
Ask the plant manager to give the machinist formal approval rights over equipment changes
questions.explanation:
Concept: Formal authority vs informal influence — Power doesn't only come from titles. Respected experts often shape how change is received, and you should engage them early. (Rule M3-B05-R03)
Spot it: "Others defer to him," long experience, and "his opinion shapes" adoption without formal authority.
In this scenario: The machinist is an informal influencer. Engaging him early turns his credibility into support for the new equipment.
Why not the others: Routing everything through the plant manager ignores real influence; treating him as low priority misreads the power map; asking for formal approval rights for him changes governance for no reason.
Remember: Titles approve; influencers adopt. Map both.

questions.stem: A hybrid telehealth program's stakeholder analysis ranked the marketing department as highly interested and the compliance office as low interest. A new federal rule on remote prescribing has just been issued, and a merger has shifted marketing's focus elsewhere. What should the project manager do?
options: Reassess stakeholder interest and influence and adjust the engagement plans to match
Keep the original rankings until the next scheduled quarterly stakeholder review
Increase communication with marketing so its interest in the program does not decline
Ask the compliance office to send its new requirements through the adaptive team intake
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reassess stakeholders when conditions change — Stakeholder priorities shift with new rules, mergers or market changes. Update the analysis and engagement to match. (Rule M3-B05-R04)
Spot it: A new regulation, a reorganization or merger, and rankings made "before."
In this scenario: The new federal rule raises compliance's stake and the merger lowers marketing's. Reassess interest and influence and adjust the engagement plans.
Why not the others: Waiting for the quarterly review leaves the plan stale; courting marketing's fading interest spends effort in the wrong place; routing compliance through feature intake mistakes a key stakeholder for a request queue.
Remember: Constraint/assumption changes → Assess impact → Adjust.

questions.stem: An agile team is starting an internal expense app for a global company. The team has a product owner, but no one knows where money comes from after this quarter, whose sign-off finance policy compliance requires, or which regional leaders the rollout depends on. What should the team do FIRST?
options: Start building features and let funding and adoption questions surface at sprint reviews
Ask the product owner to make the funding and compliance decisions as well as prioritizing work
Identify who funds, accepts, and drives adoption of the app, and how to engage each of them
Send an announcement to all regional leaders describing the app and its planned features
questions.explanation:
Concept: Identify the key decision roles — Early on, find out who funds, who accepts, who prioritizes and who drives adoption. Missing one of these can stall or sink the work later. (Rule M3-B05-R05)
Spot it: Unknown money source, unknown sign-off, unknown rollout champions, and a project just starting.
In this scenario: The team has a product owner for ordering but gaps in funding, compliance sign-off and adoption. Identifying those people and how to engage them comes first.
Why not the others: Building first and waiting for questions to surface lets critical gaps surprise you; loading the product owner with every decision confuses roles; a blanket announcement informs people without identifying who decides.
Remember: Know who pays, who approves, who uses and who prioritizes, before you build.

questions.stem: A predictive project is replacing a utility's outage-management system. The stakeholder register lists only the sponsor, IT director, and vice president of operations. Dispatchers and field crews, who will use the system daily during storms, are not listed. What should the project manager do?
options: Add dispatchers and field crews to the register and plan how to involve them in requirements
Rely on the vice president of operations to represent the needs of dispatchers and field crews
Engage dispatchers and field crews during user acceptance testing near the end of the project
Send dispatchers and field crews a project newsletter so they are aware of the new system
questions.explanation:
Concept: Include affected users — Stakeholders include the people who use the result every day and operational groups, not just sponsors and executives. Their needs shape requirements. (Rule M3-B05-R06)
Spot it: A register listing only executives, and daily users who are missing from it.
In this scenario: Add dispatchers and field crews to the register and plan how to involve them in gathering requirements.
Why not the others: Relying on a VP to speak for the users filters their real needs; involving them only at UAT is too late to shape requirements; a newsletter informs but doesn't involve them.
Remember: Users are stakeholders. Engage them early, not at the end.

questions.stem: A hybrid project will automate invoice matching, removing much of the manual work done by the accounts payable team. The project manager's stakeholder analysis so far lists only supporters, such as the CFO and internal audit. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Proceed with the supporters, since the CFO's backing will be enough to carry the change through
Wait to see which groups raise objections during the first adaptive releases and respond then
Ask human resources to announce the automation to accounts payable staff later this month
Extend the analysis to groups likely to resist, such as accounts payable, and plan for their concerns
questions.explanation:
Concept: Anticipate resistance — Good stakeholder analysis looks for likely resisters as well as supporters, especially the people whose work the change affects. (Rule M3-B05-R07)
Spot it: A change that removes someone's work, and an analysis that lists "only supporters."
In this scenario: Extend the analysis to groups likely to resist, such as accounts payable, and plan how to address their concerns.
Why not the others: Relying on the CFO's backing ignores the people who have to change; waiting for objections is reactive; an HR announcement is one-way news, not engagement.
Remember: Map resisters and supporters alike. Whoever loses the most resists the most.

questions.stem: An agile team building a warehouse picking app meets with warehouse supervisors weekly, and stakeholder satisfaction surveys are high. However, pick rates, which the product was meant to improve, have not risen after three releases. What should the product owner do?
options: Use supervisor sessions to explore why pick rates have not improved and adjust priorities
Increase the meetings to twice weekly so supervisors feel even more involved in the work
Report the high satisfaction scores as evidence that stakeholder engagement is effective
Add more supervisors to the weekly meetings so a wider range of views is represented there
questions.explanation:
Concept: Engagement for value, not activity — Stakeholder engagement is measured by outcomes, whether the product delivers the intended value. Meeting frequency and satisfaction scores don't prove it. (Rule M3-B05-R10)
Spot it: High satisfaction and regular meetings, but the business outcome isn't improving.
In this scenario: The goal was higher pick rates. Use the supervisor sessions to learn why they haven't risen and adjust priorities.
Why not the others: More meetings increases activity, not value; reporting satisfaction scores confuses happiness with outcomes; adding attendees widens the talk without focusing on results.
Remember: Deliverable → Outcome → Benefit → Value. Measure outcomes, not meetings.

questions.stem: Midway through a predictive courthouse construction project, three new site engineers join the team. Previous new hires took weeks to learn the team's reporting conventions, safety escalation practices, and the history of key design decisions. What should the project manager do?
options: Give the engineers access to the project files and ask them to read the documents on their own
Pair the engineers with a senior colleague and let them absorb the norms through everyday work
Have the engineers start on low-risk tasks until they pick up the team's ways of working
Plan a structured onboarding covering team norms, escalation practices, and key decision history
questions.explanation:
Concept: Deliberate onboarding — New members need context, norms and decision history transferred on purpose. Leaving them to absorb it wastes weeks. (Rule M3-B04-R08)
Spot it: New joiners mid-project, and past newcomers taking weeks to learn how things work.
In this scenario: Plan a structured onboarding covering team norms, escalation practices and the history of key decisions.
Why not the others: Self-reading files is passive and slow; learning by osmosis from a buddy repeats the weeks-long ramp-up; parking them on low-risk tasks delays their contribution.
Remember: Onboard on purpose: norms, escalation paths, decision history.

questions.stem: A hybrid infrastructure program uses an AI tool to score vendor proposals. It recommends the lowest-priced vendor, but the evaluation committee notes that this vendor has had recent safety incidents the tool did not weigh. A committee member suggests following the score to keep the decision objective. What should the project manager do?
options: Accept the tool's recommendation, since algorithmic scoring removes bias from the evaluation
Have the committee weigh the safety record and make the award, using the score as one input
Retrain the AI tool to include safety data and rerun the scoring before any award is made
Set the AI score aside and have the committee rescore all proposals manually from scratch
questions.explanation:
Concept: AI as decision support — AI can inform a decision, but accountable humans make it. People weigh what the tool can't see. (Rule M5-B07-R01)
Spot it: An AI score, a factor the tool ignored (safety), and pressure to "follow the score to stay objective."
In this scenario: The committee weighs the safety record and makes the award, using the AI score as one input.
Why not the others: Accepting the score treats AI as the authority; retraining the tool delays and still hands it the call; scrapping the score throws away useful input.
Remember: AI is a decision-support tool, not an accountability escape hatch.

questions.stem: An agile team uses an AI assistant both to draft acceptance criteria for user stories and to propose changes to medication-dosage calculation logic in a pharmacy app. The team currently gives all AI output the same quick peer glance. What should the team do?
options: Keep the same quick review for all AI output so the team's process stays consistent
Stop using the AI assistant for any work until all of its outputs can be fully verified
Apply deeper expert review to AI-generated dosage logic than to drafted acceptance criteria
Require full expert review of all AI output, including routine acceptance criteria drafts
questions.explanation:
Concept: Proportionate human review — The depth of review for AI output should match how much damage an error could do. High-impact output gets expert scrutiny; routine drafts get a light check. (Rule M5-B07-R05)
Spot it: AI used for both low-risk and safety-critical work, with "the same quick glance" for all of it.
In this scenario: Dosage logic can harm patients, so it gets deeper expert review. Acceptance-criteria drafts can keep a lighter check.
Why not the others: One quick review for everything under-checks the critical logic; stopping AI entirely throws away its value; full expert review of everything wastes experts on low-risk drafts.
Remember: Generate → Validate. Validation depth = impact.

questions.stem: A predictive project delivered an AI model that routes insurance claims to adjusters, and it passed acceptance testing six months ago.
