The insurer has since entered a new region with different claim types. Operations asks the project manager to finish the remaining closure items. What should the project manager do?
options: Finish the closure items, since the model passed acceptance testing when it was delivered
Confirm that operations has monitoring in place to detect model drift on new claim types
Retrain the model on the new region's claims before completing any remaining closure items
Record the new region as out of scope in the final report and complete project closure
questions.explanation:
Concept: Monitor AI after deployment — AI models can drift when the data or context changes. Someone must be watching for drift and unexpected outcomes. (Rule M5-B07-R08)
Spot it: A model that "passed testing months ago" and a changed context (a new region, new data types).
In this scenario: Before closing, confirm that operations has monitoring in place to detect drift on the new claim types.
Why not the others: Closing on old test results ignores the changed context; retraining is operations' decision after monitoring shows a need; calling the region out of scope sidesteps a known operational risk.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close. Transfer includes who watches the model.

questions.stem: A hybrid project delivering a new payroll module has a charter stating that the finance director formally accepts deliverables. At the final adaptive release demo, a payroll supervisor says the module looks great and tells the team it is accepted. What should the project manager do?
options: Record the supervisor's approval as acceptance, since she uses the module daily
Ask the supervisor to email her approval so there is a written acceptance record
Obtain formal acceptance from the finance director as the charter specifies
Proceed to closure, since the demo showed the module meets acceptance criteria
questions.explanation:
Concept: Acceptance by the right authority — Deliverables are formally accepted by the person or group given that authority, often named in the charter. Other users' approval is valuable feedback, not acceptance. (Rule M4-B15-R02)
Spot it: The charter names an approver, and someone else says "it's accepted."
In this scenario: The charter names the finance director, so formal acceptance comes from her.
Why not the others: Recording the supervisor's approval uses the wrong authority; an email from her is still the wrong person in writing; going to closure skips acceptance entirely.
Remember: Complete → Accept (by the named authority) → Transfer → Learn → Close.

questions.stem: An agile team's final product increment for a donor-management system has just been accepted by the product owner. The sponsor says the project is therefore complete. Vendor contracts, team release, and lessons-learned archiving remain open. What should the scrum master point out?
options: The project is complete, since the product owner's acceptance ends all of its remaining obligations
The team should hold one more sprint to add features before any closure work begins
The vendor contracts will close on their own once the product is in production use
Product acceptance is done, but contract, team release, and archiving tasks still remain
questions.explanation:
Concept: Product validation vs administrative closure — Accepting the product validates the deliverable. The project still needs administrative closure: contracts, releasing people and archiving lessons. (Rule M4-B15-R04)
Spot it: "The product is accepted, so we're done," with contracts, people or records still open.
In this scenario: Product acceptance is complete, but the vendor contracts, team release and lessons archiving still have to be closed.
Why not the others: Treating acceptance as the end skips closure; adding a sprint of features is scope creep; contracts don't close themselves and need formal closure.
Remember: Accept ≠ Close. Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close.

questions.stem: A predictive project is about to hand over a new building management system to a facilities team. The system passed all acceptance tests, but the facilities technicians have not been trained and have no support procedures. The sponsor wants to hand over on Friday. What should the project manager do?
options: Complete the handover on Friday, since the system passed all of its acceptance tests
Verify that technicians are trained and support procedures exist before completing handover
Keep project engineers operating the system indefinitely until facilities feels ready
Hand over on Friday and send the technicians the user manual to read afterward on their own
questions.explanation:
Concept: Readiness of the receiving team — A handover is complete only when the receiving team can operate and support the result, with training and procedures in place. (Rule M4-B15-R07)
Spot it: "Passed all tests" but "not trained," "no support procedures," and a date pressure.
In this scenario: Verify that the technicians are trained and support procedures exist before completing handover.
Why not the others: Handing over on test results alone ignores operational readiness; engineers running it indefinitely never transfers it; sending a manual afterward leaves the team unprepared.
Remember: Transfer = the receiver can run it. Tested is not the same as transitioned.

questions.stem: A hybrid project's charter makes the team responsible for delivering a new online booking service and for a 60-day stabilization period with a target of 40 percent fewer phone bookings. The service went live two weeks ago. What should the project manager do?
options: Close the project now, since the booking service went live successfully two weeks ago
Hand benefits tracking to the call center, since outcomes are an operational concern
Wait until day 60 to measure results so that short-term swings in booking volume are ignored
Track phone and online booking volumes during stabilization against the stated target
questions.explanation:
Concept: Measure early outcomes — When the charter makes the project responsible for stabilization or early benefits, the team measures those results during that period. (Rule M4-B15-R10)
Spot it: A charter with a stabilization window and a benefit target, and "went live two weeks ago."
In this scenario: Track phone and online booking volumes during stabilization against the 40 percent target, so you can act early.
Why not the others: Closing now abandons a chartered responsibility; handing tracking to the call center shifts a duty the project owns; waiting until day 60 removes any chance to correct course.
Remember: Deliverable → Outcome → Benefit. If you own the benefit, measure it.

questions.stem: A product owner for an agile e-learning platform spends most refinement sessions writing detailed acceptance criteria for features planned eight months out. Items planned for the next two sprints remain vague, and sprint planning keeps running over. What should the scrum master advise?
options: Keep refining all items in detail so the team has a complete view of the roadmap
Extend sprint planning to allow time to clarify vague items at the start of each sprint
Ask the team to refine upcoming items on its own while the product owner plans ahead
Focus refinement on upcoming items and keep distant items at a coarse, high level
questions.explanation:
Concept: Progressive refinement — Near-term backlog items are refined in detail; distant items stay coarse. Detail is added just in time as they come closer. (Rule M4-B11-R03)
Spot it: Deep detail on far-future items, vague near-term items, and planning running over.
In this scenario: Focus refinement on the next few sprints' items and keep the distant items at a high level.
Why not the others: Refining everything wastes effort on work that will change; longer sprint planning treats the symptom; leaving refinement to the team alone removes the product owner's role in clarifying value.
Remember: Rolling wave: near = detailed, far = coarse.

questions.stem: A product owner for an agile payments app ranks only customer-facing features in the backlog. The team warns that an expiring encryption library and new card-industry compliance requirements are not represented and could block releases next quarter. What should the product owner do?
options: Add the library upgrade and compliance work to the backlog and rank it against features
Keep ranking by customer value and let the team handle technical work in its spare time
Create a separate technical backlog run by the team so customer features stay the priority
Ask the sponsor to fund a separate project for the library and compliance work later on
questions.explanation:
Concept: Holistic prioritization — The backlog includes technical risk, compliance and enabling work, ranked against features. Hidden technical work becomes blocked releases. (Rule M4-B11-R06)
Spot it: A backlog of only customer features, plus expiring technology or new compliance rules.
In this scenario: Add the library upgrade and compliance work to the backlog and rank it against features so the trade-offs are visible.
Why not the others: Doing it in "spare time" guarantees it slips; a separate technical backlog splits priorities; a later separate project arrives too late for next quarter.
Remember: One backlog, all the work: features, risks, compliance, enablers.

questions.stem: An agile team delivers under a contract with a fixed release date and a regulator-approved feature list. The product owner wants to reorder backlog items and also drop one regulator-approved feature to make room for a new idea. What should the scrum master advise?
options: Reorder the backlog freely, but take dropping the approved feature through formal change approval
Make both changes, since the product owner has full authority over the backlog and its content
Freeze the backlog order until the release date, since the contract fixes the scope of the work
Drop the feature now and inform the regulator after release so that the work is not delayed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reprioritization vs controlled change — The product owner can reorder the backlog freely. Changing a contractually or regulator-controlled commitment still needs formal change approval. (Rule M4-B11-R09)
Spot it: Reordering work alongside dropping something that is "approved," "contracted" or "regulated."
In this scenario: Reordering is within the product owner's authority; removing the regulator-approved feature goes through formal change approval.
Why not the others: Making both changes ignores the controlled commitment; freezing the order removes agility the contract allows; dropping the feature and telling the regulator later bypasses control.
Remember: Order = product owner. Controlled commitment = change control. Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement.

questions.stem: On a predictive hospital IT project, a department head submitted a change request to add a reporting module. A project engineer heard about it at lunch and has started designing the module and editing the schedule. The change control board has not yet reviewed the request. What should the project manager do?
options: Let the design continue, since the department head's request will most likely be approved
Approve the change personally so the engineer's early design work is not wasted effort
Stop the design work and schedule edits until the change control board decides on the request
Log the work as a preventive action so the board can review it along with the request
questions.explanation:
Concept: Change request vs approved change — A change request is only a proposal. No work starts until the change control board approves it. (Rule M3-B18-R01)
Spot it: "Submitted," "not yet reviewed," and someone already doing the work.
In this scenario: Stop the design and schedule edits until the CCB decides.
Why not the others: Letting the design continue on a likely approval bypasses control; the PM approving it personally usurps the CCB; relabeling it a preventive action misuses the term to hide unapproved work.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor. No approval, no work.

questions.stem: The change control board for a predictive pipeline project has just approved adding a second pumping station, extending the schedule by six weeks and increasing the budget by 8 percent. The approval is recorded in the change log. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Begin building the second pumping station, since the change has now been approved
Keep the original baselines to track how far the project has moved from its first plan
Notify the sponsor and leave baseline updates until the next quarterly plan review
Update the baselines, risk register, forecasts, and plans, and inform stakeholders
questions.explanation:
Concept: Update after approval — Once a change is approved, update the affected baselines, plans, risks and forecasts, and tell stakeholders. Then carry out the work against the new baseline. (Rule M3-B18-R05)
Spot it: "Just approved," and a question asking what to do NEXT.
In this scenario: Update the baselines, risk register, forecasts and plans, and inform stakeholders. That sets up the work to be done against accurate plans.
Why not the others: Building immediately skips updating the plans; keeping the old baselines measures against an outdated plan; deferring the updates to a quarterly review leaves the records wrong.
Remember: Approve → Implement → UPDATE → Monitor. Baseline = APPROVED, so update it when the approval changes.

questions.stem: On a predictive road resurfacing project, inspectors find that one completed lane section does not meet the compaction specification. Separately, compaction readings on current work have been trending downward over the last week, though still within specification. What should the project manager do?
options: Treat both as scope changes and submit them to the change control board for approval
Treat the failed section as preventive action and the downward trend as corrective action
Treat the failed section as defect repair and the downward trend as needing preventive action
Treat both as corrective actions, since each involves compaction below the specification
questions.explanation:
Concept: Change types — Defect repair fixes a nonconforming product. Corrective action brings performance back in line. Preventive action reduces the chance of a future problem. A scope change alters what is delivered. (Rule M3-B18-R08)
Spot it: "Does not meet spec" means the product is nonconforming. "Trending toward" the limit while still within spec means it hasn't failed yet.
In this scenario: The failed lane section needs defect repair. The downward trend, still within spec, calls for preventive action.
Why not the others: Neither is a scope change, since the specification isn't changing; calling the failed section preventive swaps the two concepts; the trend hasn't breached the spec, so it isn't corrective.
Remember: Broken product = defect repair; drifting = preventive; off-plan now = corrective; new what = scope change.

questions.stem: For three retrospectives in a row, an agile team has noted that code reviews are slowing delivery. Each time it agrees to try to review faster, and nothing changes. What should the scrum master help the team do at the next retrospective?
options: Record the same observation again and trust the team to improve review speed on its own
Ask the lead developer to set a review deadline and enforce it across the whole team
Drop code reviews from the workflow for one sprint to see whether delivery speeds up
Define a specific experiment, such as a review time limit, and how its effect will be measured
questions.explanation:
Concept: Actionable retrospectives — Retrospective insights must become specific experiments with a way to measure them. Vague intentions like "try harder" don't change anything. (Rule M4-B17-R02)
Spot it: The same problem across several retrospectives, and "agreed to try" with nothing changing.
In this scenario: Define a specific experiment, such as a time limit for reviews, and how its effect will be measured.
Why not the others: Recording it again repeats the loop; a lead-imposed deadline replaces team ownership with command; dropping reviews for a sprint trades quality for speed.
Remember: Inspect → Adapt → Measure. One experiment, one metric.

questions.stem: After repeated late deliveries of steel components, a predictive construction project introduced a weekly supplier coordination call two months ago. The call is well attended, and participants say it is helpful. What should the project manager do to evaluate the improvement?
options: Compare on-time steel delivery rates before and after the coordination call started
Survey participants on how useful they find the weekly coordination call so far
Continue the weekly call, since strong attendance shows it is working as intended
Add a second weekly call with the supplier to strengthen coordination even further
questions.explanation:
Concept: Measure improvement outcomes — An improvement works only if the intended outcome changes. Attendance and satisfaction measure activity, not results. (Rule M4-B17-R04)
Spot it: "Well attended," "helpful," and a question about evaluating it.
In this scenario: The goal was on-time steel delivery. Compare delivery rates before and after the call started.
Why not the others: A usefulness survey measures opinion; continuing because attendance is strong confuses activity with results; adding a second call assumes success.
Remember: Measure the outcome you set out to change.

questions.stem: An adaptive team on a hybrid banking program found a reliable way to test integrations with a third-party credit bureau, cutting defect leakage by half. Two other programs in the bank will integrate with the same bureau next year. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the approach within the program, since other programs may have different requirements
Add the testing approach to the organization's lessons repository and brief the other programs
Record the approach in the team's own notes so it can be reused on the program's later releases
Wait until program closeout and include the approach in the final lessons-learned report
questions.explanation:
Concept: Share lessons beyond the team — Reusable lessons should reach others who can use them now, through the organization's repository and direct sharing. (Rule M4-B17-R07)
Spot it: Other programs facing "the same" situation soon, and a proven approach.
In this scenario: Add the approach to the organization's lessons repository and brief the other programs directly.
Why not the others: Keeping it inside the program wastes a proven fix; team-only notes limit reuse to one program; waiting for closeout delays value others need soon.
Remember: The lessons learned register is a living artifact. Share it while it still helps.

questions.stem: An agile team is starting a mobile app for a new retail client. A year ago, a different team in the company built a similar app and recorded lessons about app store approval delays and offline sync issues. What should the team do as it plans its first releases?
options: Plan the releases from scratch, since each client and team context is somewhat different
Wait to see whether the same issues come up and then consult the earlier team if needed
Review the earlier team's recorded lessons and factor them into release plans and risks
Ask the earlier team's lead to join the new team full time for the entire engagement
questions.explanation:
Concept: Use past lessons — When planning similar work, review lessons already recorded so you don't repeat known problems. (Rule M4-B17-R10)
Spot it: "Similar app," "a year ago," "recorded lessons" about specific risks.
In this scenario: Review the earlier team's lessons and factor them into the release plans and the risk register.
Why not the others: Planning from scratch ignores known risks; waiting for the issues to appear turns avoidable risks into problems; borrowing their lead full time is costly when the written lessons already hold the knowledge.
Remember: Before you plan, read what was learned. Lessons feed the risk register.

questions.stem: A predictive school construction project's midpoint report shows a cost performance index of 0.92 and a schedule performance index of 0.85. The superintendent tells the sponsor that both numbers are close to 1.0 and nothing is wrong. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The project is under budget and ahead of schedule for the work completed so far
The project is over budget and behind schedule for the work completed so far
The project is over budget but ahead of schedule for the work completed so far
The project is on track, since both indexes are within ten percent of 1.0
questions.explanation:
Concept: CPI and SPI — Performance indexes above 1.0 are favorable and below 1.0 are unfavorable. CPI measures cost efficiency and SPI measures schedule progress. (Rule M4-B05-R03)
Spot it: Index values below 1.0, and someone saying "close to 1.0, nothing's wrong."
In this scenario: A CPI of 0.92 means about 92 cents of value for every dollar spent, so the project is over budget. An SPI of 0.85 means it is behind schedule.
Why not the others: Under budget and ahead needs indexes above 1.0; over budget and ahead would need SPI above 1.0; "close to 1" is still unfavorable, and a 15 percent schedule gap is significant.
Remember: CPI/SPI < 1 = BAD. "I" is for index: 1 or above is good.

questions.stem: A predictive project has spent $4 million building a custom warehouse control system. Finishing it will cost another $3 million, while a commercial system meeting all requirements can be implemented for $1.5 million with lower risk. A director argues the team cannot abandon a $4 million investment. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Finish the custom system, since abandoning it would waste the $4 million already invested
Compare only the future costs and benefits of each option, setting aside the money already spent
Add the $4 million spent to the commercial option's cost before comparing the two alternatives
Finish the custom system at a reduced scope to recover part of the value already invested
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sunk cost — Money already spent can't be recovered, so it shouldn't drive future choices. Compare only future costs and benefits. (Rule M4-B05-R06)
Spot it: "Already spent," "can't abandon our investment," and a cheaper, lower-risk alternative.
In this scenario: Finishing costs $3 million; the commercial system costs $1.5 million with lower risk. Comparing only future costs and benefits points to the better option.
Why not the others: Finishing to protect the $4 million is sunk-cost thinking; adding the $4 million to the commercial option distorts the comparison; a reduced-scope finish still chases gone money.
Remember: Sunk cost = gone money. "But we already paid" is not a strategy.

questions.stem: A predictive tunnel project's risk register identified the chance of encountering unstable soil, and a contingency reserve was set aside for it. The risk has now occurred, and the planned response requires additional ground support. What should the project manager do?
options: Request management reserve from the sponsor, since the soil condition is now an issue
Use the contingency reserve to fund the planned ground-support response as documented
Submit a change request to increase the cost baseline for the added ground support
Cut other work package budgets to cover the ground support and keep the reserve intact
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contingency reserve — Contingency reserve funds planned responses to identified risks (known-unknowns). Management reserve is for unidentified risks (unknown-unknowns). (Rule M4-B05-R09)
Spot it: "Identified in the risk register," "contingency set aside," "the risk occurred."
In this scenario: The soil risk was identified and funded. Use the contingency reserve to carry out the planned ground-support response.
Why not the others: Management reserve is for unknown risks only; a baseline change request isn't needed when contingency covers it; cutting other work packages robs planned work instead of using the planned reserve.
Remember: Contingency = known risks; management reserve = unknown risks. Only if contingency runs short → change request.

questions.stem: A predictive project is building a visitor registration system for a corporate campus. The business analyst proposes capturing visitors' home addresses, dates of birth, and phone numbers in case they are useful later, though only name, host, and visit time are needed for security. What should the project manager do?
options: Collect all the proposed fields but restrict access to them to the corporate security team
Limit captured data to what campus security needs and document why each field is required
Collect all the proposed fields and delete the extra ones if no use is found within a year
Ask visitors to consent to all proposed fields so that the extra collection is permitted
questions.explanation:
Concept: Data minimization — Collect only the personal data needed for a legitimate purpose, and document why each field is needed. "Might be useful later" is not a purpose. (Rule M5-B15-R01)
Spot it: Extra personal fields captured "in case," and a smaller set that's actually required.
In this scenario: Capture only what campus security needs and document the reason for each field.
Why not the others: Restricting access still over-collects; deleting later still collects needlessly; consent doesn't justify data with no purpose.
Remember: Need it? Collect it. Don't need it? Don't touch it.

questions.stem: A new hybrid program to modernize a port's cargo tracking has an enthusiastic sponsor, but department heads keep asking who authorized the work and what it is meant to achieve. Teams have already started planning adaptive releases. What should the project manager do?
options: Obtain a charter that authorizes the program and states its objectives and direction
Share the adaptive release plan with department heads to show what will be delivered
Ask the sponsor to email department heads confirming personal support for the work
Continue planning, since the department heads' questions will fade as releases ship
questions.explanation:
Concept: The charter — The charter formally authorizes the project or program, gives the PM authority, and sets high-level objectives and direction. (Rule M4-B16-R02)
Spot it: "Who authorized this?" "What is it meant to achieve?" and work already starting on enthusiasm alone.
In this scenario: Get a charter that authorizes the program and states its objectives, which answers the department heads' questions.
Why not the others: A release plan shows the HOW, not the authority; an informal sponsor email isn't formal authorization; continuing leaves the mandate unclear.
Remember: WHY = business case, AUTHORITY = charter, HOW = plans.

questions.stem: During a sprint, an agile team learns that a key API vendor's service went down yesterday, blocking two stories. The team also hears the vendor may raise its prices next quarter. Where should the scrum master help the team record these items?
options: Record the outage in the risk register and the possible price increase in the issue log
Record the outage in the issue log and the possible price increase in the risk register
Record both items in the risk register, since each involves the same external vendor
Record both items in the issue log, since each one could affect the team's delivery plans
questions.explanation:
Concept: Risk register vs issue log — The risk register tracks uncertain future events. The issue log tracks problems that have already happened. (Rule M4-B16-R05)
Spot it: "Went down yesterday" or "blocking" means an issue. "May" or "next quarter" means a risk.
In this scenario: The outage has already happened, so it goes in the issue log. The possible price increase is uncertain, so it goes in the risk register.
Why not the others: Swapping the two reverses the definitions; putting both in the risk register hides a live blocker; putting both in the issue log treats an uncertainty as a fact.
Remember: Dark clouds = risk register; the storm is here = issue log.

questions.stem: A predictive hospital wing project team documented valuable lessons about coordinating medical gas contractors at closeout. The lessons are stored in the project's own folder, which will be archived. The company plans three more hospital projects. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the lessons in the archived project folder, where future teams can request them
Email the lessons to current team members so they can apply them on their next jobs
Add the lessons to the organization's lessons-learned repository for future projects
Include the lessons in the final report to the sponsor and close the project as planned
questions.explanation:
Concept: Organizational lessons repository — Lessons become organizational knowledge when they're stored where future projects will look, not buried in one project's archive. (Rule M4-B16-R08)
Spot it: Valuable lessons, "stored in the project's own folder," and similar future projects.
In this scenario: Add the lessons to the organization's lessons-learned repository so the three upcoming hospital projects can find them.
Why not the others: An archived folder is effectively lost; emailing current members limits reuse to those people; a sponsor report isn't a searchable knowledge base.
Remember: Project lessons register → organizational repository (OPA) at close.

questions.stem: A hybrid telecom program must estimate its predictive portion: installing 1,200 cell-site antennas. The company has reliable historical data showing each installation takes about 14 crew-hours regardless of site. Which estimating approach is BEST for the installation work?
options: Base the estimate on the total duration of one similar past program taken as a whole
Multiply the number of antenna sites by the historical crew-hours per installation
Ask each crew lead for optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic estimates for every site
Have the adaptive teams size the installation work using relative estimation instead
questions.explanation:
Concept: Parametric estimating — Parametric estimating multiplies a reliable unit rate by a quantity. It's accurate when the historical relationship is stable. (Rule M4-B04-R04)
Spot it: A reliable per-unit figure ("about 14 crew-hours each") and a known quantity (1,200 sites).
In this scenario: 1,200 sites × 14 crew-hours is the parametric estimate the reliable data supports.
Why not the others: Using one past program as a whole is analogous, which is less precise; three-point for every site is heavy when the rate is stable; relative estimation is for adaptive work, not the predictive installations.
Remember: Analogous = similar past project. Parametric = rate × quantity.

questions.stem: An agile team originally forecast delivering a claims portal in six sprints based on an assumed velocity of 40 points. After four sprints, its average velocity is 28 points, and 150 points remain. The sponsor asks for an updated delivery forecast. What should the scrum master do?
options: Forecast from the team's average of 28 points against the 150 points still remaining
Keep the original six-sprint forecast, since velocity may recover in the later sprints
Forecast using 40 points, since that was the velocity agreed on during initial planning
Ask the team to commit to 40 points per sprint so the original forecast can still hold
questions.explanation:
Concept: Empirical reforecasting — Forecasts are updated using actual performance against the remaining work, not the original assumptions. (Rule M4-B04-R07)
Spot it: An original assumption, an actual average that differs, and "remaining" work.
In this scenario: 150 points ÷ 28 per sprint is roughly six more sprints. Forecast from actual velocity and remaining work.
Why not the others: Keeping the original forecast hopes for recovery with no evidence; using the planned 40 ignores the actuals; asking the team to commit to 40 pressures them instead of forecasting.
Remember: Forecast = remaining work ÷ actual rate. Evidence over hope.

questions.stem: An executive tells a project manager that a new distribution center must open by March 1 to meet holiday demand. Bottom-up estimates from the construction and systems teams indicate a realistic opening in May. The executive asks why the schedule does not show March. What should the project manager do?
options: Update the schedule to show March 1, since that is the executive's required opening date
Ask the teams to rework their estimates until the schedule supports a March opening date
Explain the basis of the estimate and present options for meeting March with their trade-offs
Tell the executive that March is impossible and the May date cannot be changed at all
questions.explanation:
Concept: Target vs estimate — A required date or budget is a target. An estimate is evidence-based. When they differ, show the gap and the options. (Rule M4-B04-R10)
Spot it: "Must open by," a bottom-up estimate saying later, and pressure to make the schedule show the target.
In this scenario: Explain the basis of the May estimate and present options for meeting March, with their trade-offs (scope, resources, cost).
Why not the others: Changing the schedule to March misrepresents the estimate; making teams rework their numbers to fit is manipulation; a flat "impossible" shuts down problem solving.
Remember: Target = wish; estimate = evidence. Present the gap, then the options.

questions.stem: A healthcare company is building a new clinic. The building design and permits are well defined, but the patient check-in software is new and its user needs are unclear. The steering committee asks how delivery should be structured. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Use a predictive approach for both so the whole project follows a single baseline schedule
Use an adaptive approach for both so the whole project can respond quickly to changing needs
Plan the software with a predictive approach and handle the building work adaptively instead
Plan the building with a predictive approach and develop the check-in software adaptively
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tailoring by component — Use predictive delivery where requirements are stable and adaptive delivery where they are uncertain. A hybrid fits when a project has both. (Rule M4-B14-R01)
Spot it: Well-defined work (permits, construction) sitting next to unclear, new work (user needs).
In this scenario: The building is stable, so plan it predictively. The check-in software is uncertain, so develop it adaptively.
Why not the others: All predictive locks unclear software requirements too early; all adaptive fits permits and construction poorly; the reversed pairing mismatches each approach to its work.
Remember: Stable = predictive, evolving = agile, both = hybrid.

questions.stem: In a hybrid defense logistics program, adaptive teams report progress through release demos while predictive teams report earned value monthly. The steering committee complains that it receives two unrelated reporting packages and cannot judge overall program health. What should the project manager do?
options: Require the adaptive teams to adopt earned value reporting so all teams report the same way
Create separate steering committees for adaptive and predictive teams to simplify reviews
Set up one program-level governance view that combines both teams' measures for decisions
Send the committee both packages with a cover note explaining how each team measures work
questions.explanation:
Concept: One governance model — Teams can use different delivery approaches, but leadership needs one coherent view to govern the whole program. (Rule M4-B14-R03)
Spot it: Two unrelated reporting packages, and a committee that "can't judge overall health."
In this scenario: Set up one program-level governance view that combines both teams' measures for decision making.
Why not the others: Forcing earned value on the adaptive teams misfits their way of working; two steering committees fragment oversight; sending both packages with a cover note leaves leadership to integrate them.
Remember: Many delivery modes, one governance lens.

questions.stem: A hybrid project combines a predictive hardware build for smart kiosks with adaptive software development. The hardware prototype is due in month five, but the software teams have not agreed when they will need hardware for testing. What should the project manager do?
options: Let the software teams request hardware when they are ready, since their plans keep evolving
Delay software work until the hardware prototype is finished and fully tested in month five
Plan integration testing for the final month so that both components are fully complete first
Define integration milestones with both teams now, aligning software testing to hardware dates
questions.explanation:
Concept: Plan integration points early — When components run on different life cycles, agree the integration milestones up front so each side can plan to them. (Rule M4-B14-R06)
Spot it: Hardware on fixed dates, software on evolving plans, and "not agreed when."
In this scenario: Define integration milestones with both teams now, aligning software testing to the hardware dates.
Why not the others: Letting software ask when it's ready risks a late mismatch; delaying software wastes months of adaptive progress; integrating only at the end finds problems too late.
Remember: Dependency → Assess impact → Coordinate → Monitor.

questions.stem: In a hybrid airline program, predictive teams track risks in a formal register while adaptive teams discuss risks informally in their daily meetings. A delayed data interface that both sides depended on surprised everyone last month. What should the project manager do?
options: Require the adaptive teams to adopt the predictive teams' formal risk register process
Establish a shared view of cross-team risks and dependencies that all teams maintain
Ask each team to email the project manager whenever one of its dependencies might slip
Assign a coordinator to attend all team meetings and relay risks between the teams
questions.explanation:
Concept: Shared risk and dependency visibility — In hybrid work, cross-team risks and dependencies need one shared view that every team maintains, whatever each team's own method. (Rule M4-B14-R09)
Spot it: Different risk practices per team, and a shared dependency that "surprised everyone."
In this scenario: Set up a shared view of cross-team risks and dependencies that all teams keep up to date.
Why not the others: Forcing the formal register process on adaptive teams misfits them; emailing the PM hides risks from peers; a relay coordinator becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure.
Remember: Shared dependencies need shared visibility. One view, many teams.

questions.stem: A fintech startup's agile team is planning the first release of a budgeting app. The product owner proposes shipping only a login screen and a settings page because they are the quickest features to build. Leadership's real question is whether young professionals will trust a new app enough to link their bank accounts. What should the team do FIRST?
options: Design the first release as a test of whether real users will connect their bank
Release the login and settings screens first, since they need the least development effort
Build the complete feature set first so users judge the app on its full experience
Run a six-month market survey before writing any production code for the app
questions.explanation:
Concept: Minimum viable product (MVP) — the smallest release that tests the most important value or learning hypothesis, not simply the least work (Rule M4-B18-R02).
Spot it: "First release," "quickest to build," and a big open question about whether customers will actually use or trust the product.
In this scenario: Leadership's real unknown is trust with bank data, so the first release must be designed to measure whether real users connect their bank.
Why not the others: Login and settings are small but teach nothing about the hypothesis; the full feature set delays learning; a six-month survey measures opinions, not real behavior.
Remember: MVP = Minimum work to learn the MOST — Build → Measure → Learn.

questions.stem: A hospital's agile team has finished a new medication-ordering feature that passed all acceptance tests. Because it changes how nurses on 14 wards enter orders, an undetected defect could affect patient care, and ward workflows differ slightly. The sponsor wants the feature live this quarter. What is the BEST release approach?
options: Release to one or two wards first, monitor the results, then expand to the other wards
Switch all 14 wards over on the same day so that every nurse follows one consistent process
Hold the release until every ward's workflow is redesigned to match a single standard
Delay the release until automated tests cover every conceivable ward scenario
questions.explanation:
Concept: Pilots and staged rollouts — releasing to a small group first so that hidden defects or workflow surprises hurt few users and teach the team before scaling (Rule M4-B18-R05).
Spot it: High-impact release, safety or money at stake, users whose conditions differ, "passed all tests" but not yet proven in the real world.
In this scenario: Patient safety plus ward-to-ward differences make a one- or two-ward pilot, monitored and then expanded, the lowest-risk way to meet the quarter.
Why not the others: A same-day big bang exposes all 14 wards at once; standardizing every ward first is a separate change that stalls value; testing "every conceivable scenario" is impossible and delays learning.
Remember: Risky release? Pilot → Monitor → Expand.

questions.stem: An agile team building a restaurant reservation service expects to learn over the next few releases whether diners also want table-side payment. An architect proposes designing now for multi-country tax rules, twelve languages, and franchise billing, none of which appear on the product roadmap. How should the team BEST approach the architecture?
options: Build the multi-country, multilingual, franchise-ready platform now to avoid costly rework later
Keep the payment area loosely coupled for later addition, and defer the unplanned features
Hard-code the reservation logic tightly for speed and redesign fully if payment is wanted
Pause development until the product owner confirms a five-year roadmap for all markets
questions.explanation:
Concept: Emergent, "just enough" architecture — keep the design flexible where the team expects to learn, but do not build for futures nobody has asked for (Rule M4-B18-R08).
Spot it: An expected change on the horizon, plus proposals for features "not on the roadmap" to "avoid rework later."
In this scenario: Table-side payment is a likely next learning, so leave that area loosely coupled; multi-country tax, twelve languages and franchise billing are speculative and should wait.
Why not the others: Building everything now is over-engineering (YAGNI); tight hard-coding makes the expected payment change expensive; waiting for a five-year roadmap blocks value delivery.
Remember: Design for what you EXPECT to learn, not for what you IMAGINE might happen.

questions.stem: A project manager is planning a three-year predictive project to build a manufacturing plant. Site preparation and foundation work for the first eight months are well understood, but equipment installation for later phases depends on a supplier technology decision due next year. How should the project manager plan the schedule?
options: Detail the first eight months to work-package level; keep later phases high level until the decision
Decompose all three years to activity level now, using best available guesses for the equipment choices
Delay baselining any part of the schedule until the supplier technology decision is made
Plan only the site preparation work and leave later phases out of the schedule entirely
questions.explanation:
Concept: Rolling-wave planning — a form of progressive elaboration: plan near-term work in detail and keep distant work at a higher level until information arrives (Rule M3-B17-R04).
Spot it: Long project, "first months well understood," later work "depends on a decision due next year."
In this scenario: Decompose the eight months of site and foundation work to work packages now, and hold equipment phases as planning packages until the supplier technology is chosen.
Why not the others: Detailing all three years creates false precision and rework; refusing to baseline anything leaves no basis for control; leaving later phases out hides known scope from the plan.
Remember: Near = Detailed, Far = High level — plan the wave you can see.

questions.stem: The project manager planning a regional highway resurfacing project learns that a similar project lost two weeks last year because an emergency design change sat unapproved while nobody knew who could authorize it. The current project has a tight paving window before winter. What should the project manager do NOW?
options: Wait until an emergency change actually arises and then identify the right approver at that moment
Give the site foreman authority to approve any design change so crews never have to wait
Define decision authority levels and an expedited approval path in the plan before work begins
Add two weeks of schedule buffer to absorb whatever approval delays may occur later
questions.explanation:
Concept: Governance by design — decide who can approve what, and how fast, before an urgent decision arrives (Rule M3-B17-R07).
Spot it: A past delay because "nobody knew who could authorize it," a tight window, and the word "planning."
In this scenario: Build decision authority levels and an expedited change path into the plan now, so an emergency design change on the paving job gets a same-day answer.
Why not the others: Waiting for the emergency repeats last year's failure; giving a foreman unlimited authority bypasses change control; extra buffer treats the symptom, not the unclear authority.
Remember: Know WHO decides before you NEED the decision.

questions.stem: During planning for a data-center relocation, sponsor approval moves the cutover from March to a single weekend in January. The project manager then notices that the procurement plan still schedules server deliveries for February and the communications plan still announces a March outage. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Ask the sponsor to return the cutover to March so the current subsidiary plans stay valid
Revise the procurement and communications plans so they align with the January cutover
Leave the subsidiary plans as they are and let functional leads adjust during execution
Update only the communications plan, since delivery timing belongs to the vendor
questions.explanation:
Concept: Integrated planning — every subsidiary plan (procurement, communications, schedule, and so on) must stay consistent with the approved overall direction (Rule M3-B17-R10).
Spot it: A sponsor-approved change to a key date, and subsidiary plans that still show the old date.
In this scenario: The January cutover is approved, so the PM revises the procurement plan (servers before January) and the communications plan (announce the January outage).
Why not the others: Asking the sponsor to reverse an approved decision puts the hierarchy upside down; leaving plans for leads to fix in execution guarantees conflict; fixing only communications leaves servers arriving after cutover.
Remember: One project, one direction — the PM plan leads, subsidiary plans follow.

questions.stem: An IT operations team handles requests through email and a shared spreadsheet. Managers complain they cannot tell which requests are waiting for approval, which are being worked on, and where requests pile up. The team has agreed to adopt a flow-based agile method. What should the team do FIRST?
options: Set strict WIP limits for each person before mapping how requests actually move through work
Create a board with a column for each workflow state so every request's status and queue is visible
Assign a coordinator to email managers a weekly status summary of every open request
Switch to two-week timeboxes and commit to a fixed set of requests at the start of each
questions.explanation:
Concept: Kanban practice 1, visualize the workflow — make every work item, its state and its queue visible before optimizing flow (Rule M4-B13-R01).
Spot it: "Cannot tell where requests are," "piling up," work hidden in email or spreadsheets, and a team adopting a flow-based method.
In this scenario: The first move is a board with a column per workflow state so waiting, active and blocked requests are visible to everyone.
Why not the others: WIP limits come after you can see the flow; a weekly email summary is push reporting, not visualization; fixed two-week timeboxes are Scrum, not a flow method.
Remember: Kanban order = Visualize → Limit WIP → Manage flow → Improve.

questions.stem: A marketing team uses a Kanban board with a WIP limit of four in its Design column. Design currently holds four items, and a stakeholder urges a designer to start a fifth banner right away because it is "quick." Nothing on the board is marked as an expedite item. What should the designer do?
options: Start the banner now, because small items do not meaningfully affect overall flow
Raise the Design WIP limit to five so that quick requests can always be accepted
Finish or unblock a current design item, then pull the banner when a slot opens
Decline the banner and ask the stakeholder to resubmit it at quarterly planning
questions.explanation:
Concept: Pull system and WIP limits — in Kanban new work is pulled only when a slot frees up, which keeps flow smooth and cycle time short (Rule M4-B13-R03).
Spot it: A column at its WIP limit, pressure to "just start" something small, and no expedite class of service.
In this scenario: The designer helps finish or unblock a current design item, then pulls the banner when Design drops below four.
Why not the others: Starting it now breaks the limit and adds multitasking; raising the limit on demand defeats its purpose; sending it to quarterly planning ignores that a slot will open soon.
Remember: Stop starting, start finishing — PULL, don't PUSH.

questions.stem: A claims-processing team tracks its work with a cumulative flow diagram. During the past three weeks the "Awaiting review" band has steadily widened while the slope of the "Done" band has flattened, even though new claims arrive at a steady rate. The agile coach asks what the chart shows. What is the MOST likely interpretation?
options: Work is queuing at review, creating a bottleneck that is slowing completed claims
The team is finishing more work than before, since more claims are now in progress
Arrivals have surged, so the wider band only reflects higher incoming demand
Flow is healthy, because the total number of claims in the system keeps rising
questions.explanation:
Concept: Cumulative flow diagram (CFD) — each colored band is a workflow state; a widening band means a growing queue, and a flat Done line means little is being finished (Rule M4-B13-R06).
Spot it: "Band widening," "slope flattening," steady arrivals.
In this scenario: Arrivals are steady, yet "Awaiting review" grows while Done stalls, so work is piling up at review, a bottleneck.
Why not the others: More work in progress is not more work finished; a demand surge would steepen the arrivals line, and the stem says arrivals are steady; a rising total in the system signals a problem, not health.
Remember: CFD — Wide band = Queue, Flat Done = Stuck.

questions.stem: A software support team's Kanban system has an expedite lane. Over the past month, sales managers labeled nearly 60 percent of new tickets as expedite, and ordinary tickets now wait twice as long. Few of the expedited tickets involved outages or contractual deadlines. What should the team do?
options: Remove all classes of service so that every ticket is handled strictly first in, first out
Accept every expedite label, since sales managers understand customer urgency best
Agree on explicit criteria for the expedite class, such as outages or contract deadlines
Add a second expedite lane so more urgent tickets can be processed at the same time
questions.explanation:
Concept: Classes of service — explicit policies (such as expedite, fixed date, standard) that give faster handling only to work whose urgency truly differs (Rule M4-B13-R09).
Spot it: An expedite lane used for most tickets, ordinary work waiting longer, and few tickets actually urgent.
In this scenario: The team should agree explicit expedite criteria, such as outages or contract deadlines, so the lane serves real urgency again.
Why not the others: Removing all classes leaves real outages waiting; accepting every label lets the loudest requester win; a second expedite lane just makes more work "urgent."
Remember: If everything is urgent, nothing is — make policies EXPLICIT.

questions.stem: A utility's hybrid project built an outage-reporting portal through agile releases, with go-live governed by a predictive phase gate. Two days before the gate, service desk staff report that they have no runbook, monitoring alerts are not configured, and escalation contacts are undefined. The code has passed all tests. What should the project manager do?
options: Launch on schedule, since the code passed all testing and support staff can catch up after release
Hand the portal to the service desk and let staff write the runbook from user tickets
Treat the support, monitoring, and escalation gaps as go-live criteria to close before launch
Postpone go-live indefinitely until a full redesign of IT service processes is complete
questions.explanation:
Concept: Operational readiness — before go-live, support, monitoring, access, documentation and escalation must be in place, not just working code (Rule M5-B13-R02).
Spot it: "Code passed all tests," but the service desk has no runbook, alerts or escalation contacts, with a go-live gate coming.
In this scenario: The PM treats the missing runbook, monitoring and escalation paths as go-live criteria and closes them before the phase gate.
Why not the others: Launching anyway leaves outages undetected on day one; writing the runbook from tickets means learning from failures; an indefinite redesign of IT service processes goes far beyond this release.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close — "Transfer" means operations can RUN it.

questions.stem: An agile team is closing out a customer-loyalty app and handing it to a separate operations team. Three known defects remain open, a vendor's warranty on the payment module expires in 90 days, and one security risk still needs monitoring. The operations lead says she has received only the source code. What should the project team do?
options: Fix all three open defects before handover, even if the transition slips by several months
Assume operations will discover the defects and warranty terms through normal service monitoring
Hand over a documented list of open defects, the warranty terms, and the risk with its owner
Keep the open risk in the project register, since the operations team did not raise it
questions.explanation:
Concept: Explicit transition — at handover, open risks, known defects, warranties and vendor obligations are transferred on purpose, each with an owner (Rule M5-B13-R05).
Spot it: A separate operations team receiving "only the source code," plus open defects, a warranty clock and a risk still being watched.
In this scenario: The project hands over a documented list of the three defects, the 90-day warranty terms and the security risk with its new owner.
Why not the others: Fixing every defect first delays handover for months when transfer is enough; hoping operations "discovers" items is not a handover; keeping the risk in a closing project's register leaves it with nobody.
Remember: Complete → Accept → TRANSFER → Learn → Close — nothing important leaves in someone's head.

questions.stem: A manufacturer has completed its migration to a new inventory system, meeting the acceptance criteria and a two-month parallel run. Several departments still update the old system "just in case," creating conflicting stock counts. The old system's license renews next month. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Keep both systems running indefinitely so each department can use the one it prefers
Shut the old system down tonight without notice so users are forced onto the new one
Renew the old license for another year while departments decide when they are ready to switch
Decommission as planned: freeze old-system updates, archive its data, and end the license
questions.explanation:
Concept: Deliberate retirement of legacy systems — once transition criteria are met, the old system is frozen, archived and switched off as planned so benefits can flow (Rule M5-B13-R08).
Spot it: Acceptance and parallel run complete, users still updating the old system "just in case," conflicting data, a renewal date.
In this scenario: Criteria are met, so the PM executes the decommissioning plan: freeze old-system updates, archive the data, let the license end.
Why not the others: Running both systems keeps conflicting counts forever; a surprise shutdown tonight ignores communication and data archiving; renewing the license pays to delay the benefits.
Remember: New system LIVE → Old system RETIRED — two sources of truth = no truth.

questions.stem: A county government needs to reduce traffic congestion at five intersections. It has not decided whether adaptive signals, roundabouts, or sensor networks would work best and wants sellers to recommend and price their own approach. The procurement management plan has been approved. Which procurement document should the project manager use?
options: A request for proposal inviting sellers to describe their solution, approach, and pricing
A request for quotation asking sellers to price a specified signal system per intersection
A request for information used as the final basis for awarding the contract
A purchase order issued to the seller that offered the lowest price on the last project
questions.explanation:
Concept: Procurement documents — RFI gathers information, RFQ gets prices for a defined product, and RFP asks sellers to propose a solution and approach (Rule M4-B09-R04).
Spot it: The buyer "has not decided" what solution fits and wants sellers to recommend and price their own approach.
In this scenario: The county needs sellers' ideas plus pricing, so an RFP is the right bid document.
Why not the others: An RFQ assumes a specified product, which the county does not have; an RFI is for information, not contract award; reusing a past purchase order skips competitive selection entirely.
Remember: RFI = INFO, RFQ = PRICE, RFP = SOLUTION + price.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company is contracting for an experimental manufacturing process whose scope cannot yet be well defined. Procurement recommends a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract. The sponsor asks the project manager what this means for the company's financial exposure. How should the project manager respond?
options: The seller carries most of the cost risk, since its fee stays fixed regardless of actual final cost
The company carries most of the overrun risk, since it reimburses the seller's allowable costs
Cost risk is shared equally, because the contract combines fixed and variable parts
The company has no cost exposure, because the fee cannot change once it is agreed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contract types and risk — in fixed-price contracts the seller carries cost risk; in cost-reimbursable contracts (CPFF, CPIF, CPAF) the buyer pays allowable costs and carries most of it (Rule M4-B09-R07).
Spot it: Scope "cannot yet be well defined," a cost-plus contract, and a question about the buyer's financial exposure.
In this scenario: With cost-plus-fixed-fee, the company reimburses all allowable costs, so overruns land on the company; only the seller's fee is fixed.
Why not the others: The fixed fee fixes profit, not total cost, so the seller does not carry most risk; CPFF is not an equal-share arrangement; the buyer clearly has cost exposure.
Remember: Fixed Price = SELLER risk; Cost-plus = BUYER risk; T&M = in between.

questions.stem: During construction of a warehouse under a fixed-price contract, a site engineer working for the buyer verbally asked the contractor to upgrade the loading-dock doors. The contractor completed the work and has invoiced the extra cost. The project manager finds no change order or contract amendment. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Pay the invoice in full, since the buyer's own site engineer did verbally request the upgrade
Reject the invoice outright and tell the contractor to remove the new doors
Ask the site engineer to sign the invoice so it can be paid as a normal expense
Route the claim through the contract change control process and document the outcome
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contract change control — any change to a contract goes through the formal change process so it is authorized, priced and traceable (Rule M4-B09-R10).
Spot it: A verbal request, work already done, an invoice for extra cost, and no change order.
In this scenario: The PM routes the contractor's claim through contract change control, gets it evaluated and decided, and documents the result.
Why not the others: Paying in full rewards an unauthorized change; rejecting and ordering removal ignores that the buyer's own engineer asked for it; having the engineer sign the invoice disguises a change as an expense.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor — contracts too.

questions.stem: A hybrid team is delivering a warehouse scanning app; hardware integration follows a predictive plan, while the screens are built in short adaptive cycles. The app meets every documented requirement, but pickers wearing gloves cannot press the small buttons reliably. A stakeholder says quality is fine because all tests pass. How should the project manager view the situation?
options: Quality has been achieved, because every documented requirement passed its test
This is a grade issue, so it should be recorded as low grade but still acceptable
The app falls short on quality, because it is not fit for use by gloved pickers
This is a training gap, so pickers should be shown how to work without gloves
questions.explanation:
Concept: Quality = conformance to requirements AND fitness for use; grade is a separate category of features (Rule M4-B06-R01).
Spot it: "All tests pass," yet real users cannot use the product in real conditions.
In this scenario: Gloved pickers cannot press the buttons, so the app is not fit for its intended use and quality falls short, even though documented requirements passed.
Why not the others: Passing tests shows the requirements missed a usage need, not that quality is achieved; grade is about feature level, not a usability failure; asking pickers to remove gloves changes the job to fit the tool.
Remember: Quality = Meets requirements + Fit for use. Low grade can be OK; low quality never is.

questions.stem: An agile team building a travel booking site has fixed date-format defects in four of its last five sprints. Each time, a developer patched the specific screen that failed. The product owner is frustrated that similar defects keep returning. What should the team do NEXT?
options: Keep patching each failing screen quickly as users report new date defects
Investigate the shared cause behind the repeated date defects and correct it at the source
Add a manual date check at the end of each sprint to catch these defects before each release
Assign the developer who wrote the date code to fix all future date defects alone
questions.explanation:
Concept: Root-cause analysis — when the same defect keeps coming back, find and remove its common cause instead of patching symptoms (Rule M4-B06-R03).
Spot it: "Fixed in four of five sprints," "patched the specific screen," "keeps returning."
In this scenario: Date defects recur across screens, which points to a shared cause, such as a common date library or missing standard, that should be fixed at the source.
Why not the others: More quick patches repeat the cycle; an end-of-sprint check is inspection that catches defects after they occur; assigning one developer turns a system problem into blame.
Remember: Prevention over inspection — Recurring defect → 5 Whys / fishbone → fix the ROOT.

questions.stem: A quality engineer on a medical-device project reviews a control chart for tube diameters. All recent measurements lie within the customer's specification limits of 4.90 to 5.10 mm, but three consecutive points fall above the upper control limit. The production supervisor says no action is needed. What should the project manager conclude?
options: No corrective action is needed, because every part remains within the customer's specifications
The specification limits should be widened to reflect where the process now runs
The control limits are wrong and should be recalculated to include the new points
The process is out of control and needs investigation even though parts meet specifications
questions.explanation:
Concept: Control limits vs specification limits — control limits show the process's natural variation (the voice of the process); specification limits show what the customer accepts (the voice of the customer) (Rule M4-B06-R06).
Spot it: Points outside the control limits but still inside specifications, and someone saying "no action needed."
In this scenario: Points above the upper control limit mean the process is out of control and must be investigated, even though today's parts still meet spec.
Why not the others: Being within spec does not make an unstable process safe; widening specs moves the customer's goalposts; recalculating control limits to hide the points erases the signal.
Remember: Control limits = PROCESS, Spec limits = CUSTOMER. Outside control = investigate.

questions.stem: On a hybrid project, a contact-center team changed its call-routing script after root-cause analysis showed misrouted calls were driving complaints. The change went live three weeks ago, and the team lead wants to close the issue in the issue log. What should the project manager do BEFORE closing it?
options: Compare misrouting and complaint data before and after the change to confirm improvement
Close the issue now, since both the root-cause analysis and the script change are complete
Start a new root-cause analysis to look for other reasons behind the complaints
Ask agents at a team meeting whether they feel the new script is working better
questions.explanation:
Concept: Verify corrective action — a fix is complete only when data shows the defect or variation actually went down (Rule M4-B06-R09).
Spot it: A change already deployed, someone wanting to "close the issue," and a measurable problem such as complaints.
In this scenario: Before closing, the PM compares misrouting and complaint data before and after the script change to confirm the improvement.
Why not the others: Closing now assumes the fix worked; a new root-cause analysis is premature before checking this one; agents' feelings are opinion, not evidence.
Remember: Issue → Analyze → Resolve → MONITOR — close with data, not hope.

questions.stem: A product owner at a logistics firm wants the team to build an automated route-planning feature estimated at three months of work. The requirement came from one executive's conversation with a single customer, and the dispatchers who would use the feature daily have not been consulted. What should the team do BEFORE committing to the work?
options: Begin building now, since a senior executive has already personally endorsed the requirement
Write a full specification for the feature and obtain the executive's formal sign-off
Survey all customers about route planning and wait for results before any discussion
Review the route-planning need with dispatchers using a quick prototype or walkthrough
questions.explanation:
Concept: Validate requirements early — confirm important needs with the people affected before committing significant effort (Rule M4-B01-R02).
Spot it: A large feature, a requirement from one executive and one customer, and actual users "not consulted."
In this scenario: A quick prototype or walkthrough with dispatchers tests whether route planning solves their real problem before three months of work is committed.
Why not the others: An executive's endorsement is not user validation; a full specification signed by the executive still excludes the dispatchers; surveying every customer first is slow and indirect.
Remember: Validate BEFORE you build — ask the users, not just the loudest voice.

questions.stem: A project manager for an ERP upgrade has 40 approved requirements but budget for only 30 in the first release. The finance director wants her reports first, IT notes that data-migration requirements must be finished before any reporting work, and a regulatory filing is due in four months. How should the project manager prioritize?
options: Deliver the finance reports first, since the finance director is the most senior requester
Choose the 30 cheapest requirements so the largest number of items can be delivered
Rank the requirements by value, risk, dependencies such as migration, and the filing deadline
Implement requirements in the order they appear in the requirements traceability matrix
questions.explanation:
Concept: Requirements prioritization — rank requirements by value, risk, dependencies and urgency, not by seniority or ease (Rule M4-B01-R05).
Spot it: More requirements than budget, a senior requester, a prerequisite ("must be finished before"), and a fixed deadline.
In this scenario: The PM ranks the 40 requirements on value, risk, the migration dependency and the regulatory filing date, then picks the top 30.
Why not the others: Seniority ignores that reports depend on migration; the cheapest items may miss the filing; RTM order is a tracing tool, not a priority list.
Remember: Prioritize = Value + Risk + Dependency + Urgency — never "who shouts loudest."

questions.stem: In a hybrid insurance project, approved scope includes "customers can upload claim documents." During an adaptive build cycle, developers ask whether this covers photos taken on phones, and the business analyst confirms phone photos were always intended. The sponsor separately asks to add video uploads. How should the project manager handle these?
options: Treat both phone photos and video uploads as scope changes that each need formal approval
Clarify phone photos as existing scope, and send video uploads through change control
Add both items to the current build, since both relate to uploading claim documents
Treat both as clarifications and let the developers decide how much to build
questions.explanation:
Concept: Clarification vs scope change — explaining what approved scope always meant is clarification; adding something new is a change that needs change control (Rule M4-B01-R08).
Spot it: An ambiguous approved requirement, the business analyst confirming what was "always intended," and a separate request for something new.
In this scenario: Phone photos were always part of "upload claim documents," so the team clarifies and builds them; video uploads are new and go through change control.
Why not the others: Treating both as changes adds needless bureaucracy; adding both slips video in without approval; treating both as clarifications lets developers change scope.
Remember: Was it ALWAYS meant? Clarify. Is it NEW? Change Request → Analyze → Approve.

questions.stem: Two agile teams at a retailer both need the company's only database specialist for the next two sprints. Each product owner insists their release is more important, and the specialist is splitting her time and finishing neither task. What should the agile coach do?
options: Let the specialist decide which team to support, since she understands the technical work best
Split the specialist exactly 50-50 between both teams for the next two sprints as agreed
Escalate to the CIO for a ruling before discussing the conflict with either product owner
Bring both product owners to the portfolio priorities and explore options such as pairing or a contractor
questions.explanation:
Concept: Resource conflicts — resolve them with agreed priorities, creative alternatives and governance only when needed (Rule M4-B10-R04).
Spot it: One scarce specialist, two teams each claiming priority, and work that is stuck because effort is split.
In this scenario: The agile coach brings both product owners to the portfolio priorities and explores options such as pairing to spread knowledge or a short-term contractor.
Why not the others: The specialist should not have to pick between teams; a 50-50 split is exactly what is failing now; going to the CIO first skips the collaboration step.
Remember: Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act → Monitor → Escalate.

questions.stem: A construction software project is three weeks behind schedule. The sponsor proposes adding four new engineers next week and expects the delay to disappear within a month. Existing engineers would need to train the newcomers on the proprietary codebase and safety standards. What should the project manager do?
options: Add all four engineers next week and update the schedule to show full recovery within one month
Estimate ramp-up time and the training load on current staff before setting a recovery date
Reject adding engineers, since new people always slow down a project that is already late
Add the engineers but exclude them from training so that current staff are not distracted
questions.explanation:
Concept: Adding resources has a cost — onboarding and training reduce output before it improves, a lesson known as Brooks's Law (Rule M4-B10-R07).
Spot it: A late project, "add people," a promised quick recovery, and existing staff who must train newcomers.
In this scenario: The PM estimates ramp-up time and the training load on current engineers before committing to any recovery date.
Why not the others: Promising one-month recovery ignores the productivity dip; "new people always slow down" is too absolute; skipping training leaves newcomers unsafe and unproductive.
Remember: More people ≠ instant speed — plan the ramp-up.

questions.stem: A hybrid program's software teams work in adaptive cycles, while hardware milestones are planned predictively. In each of three planning cycles the teams committed to about 30 items but completed around 20 each time, forcing repeated replanning of hardware integration dates. What should the project manager do to improve the next plan?
options: Keep committing to 30 items to maintain pressure and motivate higher performance
Base the next commitments on the teams' observed completion rate rather than earlier targets
Push every hardware milestone out by a fixed six months to protect against any slippage
Ask team members to work overtime until completions reach the 30-item target
questions.explanation:
Concept: Plan with actual capacity — use observed throughput (or velocity) from past cycles to set realistic commitments (Rule M4-B10-R10).
Spot it: Repeated overcommitment ("committed 30, completed 20"), and replanning that hurts dependent work.
In this scenario: The teams reliably finish about 20 items, so the next commitments should be based on that rate, which stabilizes hardware integration dates.
Why not the others: Keeping 30 repeats the error; a blanket six-month push is arbitrary padding; overtime is unsustainable and hides the real capacity.
Remember: Yesterday's weather — plan with what you ACTUALLY deliver.

questions.stem: During a risk workshop, an agile team building a ride-sharing app lists four items: an expired office lease, a possible API vendor price change next quarter, a five-developer team, and a competitor's similar app launched last year. Which item should the team record as a risk?
options: The office lease that expired last month and must now be renewed
The fact that five developers are currently assigned to the team
The chance that the API vendor changes its pricing next quarter
The rival app that a competitor launched in the market last year
questions.explanation:
Concept: Risk vs issue vs fact — a risk is an uncertain future event or condition that could affect objectives; an issue has already happened; a fact is simply a known condition (Rule M4-B07-R01).
Spot it: Words like "possible," "may," "next quarter" signal a risk; "expired," "last year," "currently" signal issues or facts.
In this scenario: Only the possible API vendor price change next quarter is uncertain and future, so only it belongs in the risk register.
Why not the others: The expired lease has already happened, so it is an issue; team size is a known fact; the rival app launched last year is a known condition, not an uncertain event.
Remember: Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor → ISSUE — once it happens, it's an issue.

questions.stem: A project manager reviewing the risk register for a hospital renovation finds an entry that reads only "contractor problems." Team members interpret the entry differently and cannot agree on a response. Which rewrite would BEST support response planning?
options: Because the electrical subcontractor is understaffed, inspections may slip, delaying occupancy
Contractor problems are a high-priority risk and must be monitored closely at every weekly meeting
Contractors may cause problems that could have a significant effect on the overall project
Poor contractor performance, owned by procurement, with a high probability rating
questions.explanation:
Concept: Risk statements — a clear risk names the cause, the uncertain event and the effect on objectives, so a response can target it (Rule M4-B07-R03).
Spot it: A vague entry like "contractor problems" and a team that cannot agree on a response.
In this scenario: "Because the subcontractor is understaffed (cause), inspections may slip (event), delaying occupancy (effect)" gives the team something specific to act on.
Why not the others: Adding "high priority" still does not say what could go wrong; "may cause problems" is just as vague; an owner and rating without a cause and effect still leave nothing to target.
Remember: Cause → Event → Effect — "Because X, Y may happen, causing Z."

questions.stem: A hybrid bank-branch rollout's risk register lists a high-impact risk that the card-printer vendor may miss delivery dates. The response plan is sound, but at the last three status meetings no one could say whether the vendor's shipment tracking had been checked. What should the project manager do?
options: Raise the risk's probability rating so it receives more attention at status meetings
Ask the whole team to share responsibility for watching the vendor's shipments
Add a penalty clause to transfer the risk to the vendor and then remove it from the register
Name one person responsible for monitoring the vendor risk and carrying out its response
questions.explanation:
Concept: Risk ownership — every material risk needs one named owner who watches the triggers and carries out the response (Rule M4-B07-R06).
