Spot it: A good plan that nobody is executing, and "no one could say" whether monitoring happened.
In this scenario: The PM names one person to track the vendor's shipments and trigger the response, closing the accountability gap.
Why not the others: A higher rating adds attention but still no action; "everyone" watching means no one watches; a penalty clause transfers only money, and a transferred risk still needs monitoring.
Remember: A risk without an OWNER is a risk nobody manages.

questions.stem: An agile team moved payment processing to a certified third-party gateway to reduce the risk of storing card data insecurely. The product owner now proposes closing all payment-security risks. The gateway still depends on the team's integration code and correct handling of API keys. What should the team do?
options: Record the remaining integration and key-handling exposure as residual risk and monitor it
Close all payment-security risks, since the certified gateway now holds full responsibility
Reverse the gateway decision and store card data internally under the team's own controls
Move the payment risks to the issue log, since the response has already been carried out
questions.explanation:
Concept: Residual risk — the risk that remains after a response is implemented; it stays in the register and is monitored (Rule M4-B07-R09).
Spot it: A response already in place (here, transfer to a gateway) and someone wanting to "close all" related risks.
In this scenario: The gateway removed card storage, but the team's integration code and API-key handling are still exposed, so that part is recorded as residual risk and monitored.
Why not the others: Closing everything assumes transfer removed all exposure; taking card data back internally reverses a sound response; the issue log is for things that have happened, not remaining uncertainty.
Remember: Respond → what's LEFT = residual; what the response CREATES = secondary.

questions.stem: A bridge construction project faces a threat that spring flooding could damage the temporary cofferdam and halt work for weeks. The project manager wants to keep the work where it is but lower both the chance and the severity of flood damage. Which response is MOST appropriate?
options: Raise the cofferdam height and install pumps to reduce flood likelihood and damage
Buy flood insurance so that the insurer pays for any repair costs if flood damage occurs
Relocate the bridge to a site outside the floodplain to remove the threat entirely
Record the threat and handle any damage only if flooding actually happens
questions.explanation:
Concept: Threat responses — avoid (remove the threat), transfer (shift impact to a third party), mitigate (reduce probability and/or impact), accept (acknowledge), escalate (outside authority) (Rule M4-B08-R02).
Spot it: "Keep the work where it is" but "lower both the chance and severity."
In this scenario: A higher cofferdam and pumps reduce both the likelihood and the damage of flooding, which is mitigation.
Why not the others: Insurance transfers repair cost but not the work stoppage; relocating the bridge is avoidance, which the PM ruled out; waiting to react is passive acceptance.
Remember: Avoid = remove, Transfer = shift, MITIGATE = reduce, Accept = live with it.

questions.stem: A hybrid project launching a mobile banking feature learns that the national regulator will fast-track approval for products submitted by June 1. Meeting that date would put the bank months ahead of competitors, and the sponsor says capturing this advantage is the top priority. Which response should the project manager take?
options: Partner with another bank so that both banks share the benefits of the fast-track window
Assign the best specialists and reorder work so the June 1 submission is certain
Note the opportunity and benefit from it only if June 1 happens to be met
Add a few testers to improve the chance of meeting June 1 where possible
questions.explanation:
Concept: Opportunity responses — exploit (make sure it happens), enhance (raise its probability or impact), share (partner with a third party), accept (take it if it comes) (Rule M4-B08-R05).
Spot it: "Top priority" to "capture" an opportunity, with a clear date that must be met.
In this scenario: Putting the best specialists on it and reordering work makes the June 1 submission certain, which is exploiting.
Why not the others: Partnering with another bank is sharing, which gives away the advantage; noting it and hoping is acceptance; adding a few testers only enhances the odds.
Remember: Exploit = MAKE it happen; Enhance = HELP it happen; Share = PARTNER; Accept = LET it happen.

questions.stem: An agile team is running a public ticket sale for a concert on its new platform. Load tests suggest the site may slow if concurrent users exceed 50,000. The team agrees not to add servers in advance but wants a ready response if that threshold is reached. What should the team prepare?
options: Extra servers bought and provisioned now to absorb any possible spike in ticket traffic
A decision to review slowdowns at the sprint review after the ticket sale ends
A risk entry noting the threshold, with no action defined until it is reached
A plan to switch on a virtual waiting room automatically once users pass 50,000
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contingency plan — a response agreed in advance and carried out only when a defined trigger occurs; also called active acceptance (Rule M4-B08-R08).
Spot it: "Not in advance," "ready response," and a clear threshold or trigger.
In this scenario: The team prepares a virtual waiting room that switches on when concurrent users pass 50,000, the trigger.
Why not the others: Buying servers now is proactive mitigation, which the team declined; reviewing after the sale is too late; a threshold with no action is passive acceptance.
Remember: Trigger → Contingency plan → Act. No trigger, no action.

questions.stem: A hospital IT migration is two weeks behind its go-live date. Schedule analysis shows the delay is in the data-conversion activities, which have zero float, while the training-material activities are also late but have 15 days of float. Limited overtime funding is available. Where should the project manager focus it?
options: On the training materials, since they are late and easier to accelerate
Split evenly between both late groups so each team is treated fairly
On the data-conversion activities, since they drive the go-live date
On whichever activities team members volunteer to work extra hours on
questions.explanation:
Concept: Critical path and float — activities with zero float drive the finish date; activities with float can slip without moving it (Rule M4-B03-R04).
Spot it: Limited recovery money, several late activities, and float values given for each.
In this scenario: Data conversion has zero float and drives go-live, so overtime goes there; training has 15 days of float.
Why not the others: Training is late but not driving the date; an even split wastes half the money; volunteer-driven choice ignores schedule logic.
Remember: Recover on the CRITICAL path — float = breathing room.

questions.stem: A factory expansion has a contractual milestone for equipment installation on May 15. The steel structure that must be finished first is running three weeks late. The site manager suggests redefining the milestone as "installation started" so the dashboard stays green. What should the project manager do?
options: Redefine the milestone as suggested so the customer's status report stays green
Move the milestone date to June 5 in the schedule without informing the customer
Work to recover the steel-structure delay and report the milestone's true forecast
Begin installing equipment on unfinished steel so the milestone can still be claimed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Protect milestones honestly — manage the upstream work that drives a milestone and report its true forecast; do not redefine or move it cosmetically (Rule M4-B03-R07).
Spot it: A late predecessor, a contractual milestone, and a suggestion to change the definition "so the dashboard stays green."
In this scenario: The PM works to recover the steel delay and gives the customer a truthful forecast for installation.
Why not the others: Redefining the milestone hides the delay; moving the date without telling the customer is dishonest and breaks the contract baseline; installing on unfinished steel is unsafe.
Remember: Fix the DRIVER, not the dashboard — watermelon status (green outside, red inside) is a trap.

questions.stem: A project manager's network diagram for a museum exhibit shows three parallel activities, lighting, display cases, and signage, each on a path that can finish before opening day. However, all three require the same certified electrician, who can work on only one activity at a time. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Keep the schedule as it is, since the logic network already shows that opening day can be met
Level the electrician's assignments and then recheck the critical path and finish date
Fast-track the three activities further so that they overlap even more than now
Add float to each path without checking whether the electrician can do the work
questions.explanation:
Concept: Resource-constrained scheduling — a network can look fine on logic alone, but shared resources can make it unachievable; resource leveling then rechecks the critical path (Rule M4-B03-R10).
Spot it: Parallel paths that "can finish in time," all needing the same person who can do only one thing at a time.
In this scenario: The PM levels the electrician's assignments, then rechecks the critical path and finish date.
Why not the others: Trusting the logic network assumes one electrician can work in three places; more fast-tracking adds overlap the resource cannot support; adding float without checking the resource hides the conflict.
Remember: Logic + Resources = real schedule. Leveling can LENGTHEN the critical path.

questions.stem: A project to renovate a school gymnasium has started, and contractors keep asking whether the locker rooms, parking-lot lighting, and bleacher replacement are part of the job. The project charter mentions only "gym upgrades," and the team is giving inconsistent answers. What should the project manager do?
options: Let each contractor decide based on its own reading of "gym upgrades" in the charter
Include all three items to keep the school community satisfied with the renovation
Wait for the first change request to reveal what the sponsor actually expects
Confirm boundaries with the sponsor and record inclusions and exclusions in the scope statement
questions.explanation:
Concept: Scope boundaries — the scope statement lists what is in and what is explicitly out, so everyone gives the same answer (Rule M4-B02-R01).
Spot it: A vague charter phrase ("gym upgrades"), repeated "is this included?" questions, inconsistent answers.
In this scenario: The PM confirms the boundaries with the sponsor and records inclusions and exclusions in the scope statement, so locker rooms, lighting and bleachers are clearly in or out.
Why not the others: Letting contractors decide gives inconsistent scope; including everything is gold plating without approval; waiting for change requests lets confusion cause rework.
Remember: Charter = AUTHORITY (high level); Scope statement = what's IN and what's OUT.

questions.stem: A new project coordinator on a warehouse automation project drafts a WBS that lists work in time order: week 1 tasks, week 2 tasks, and so on. Several deliverables, such as operator training, are missing because they happen "later." What should the project manager advise?
options: Keep the weekly structure, since it helps the team see clearly what to do next
Add missing deliverables at the end of the weekly list when their time comes
Replace the WBS with a Gantt chart, since sequence is what matters most here
Organize the WBS by deliverables so all work is captured, and handle order in the schedule
questions.explanation:
Concept: WBS — a deliverable-oriented breakdown of 100% of the project scope; sequence and timing belong in the schedule, not the WBS (Rule M4-B02-R03).
Spot it: A WBS organized by week, and deliverables missing because they happen "later."
In this scenario: The PM advises building the WBS by deliverables (including operator training) so all work is captured, then sequencing it in the schedule.
Why not the others: A weekly structure is already dropping scope; tacking items on later still leaves gaps; a Gantt chart shows timing but does not replace the scope breakdown.
Remember: WBS = WHAT (100% rule); Schedule = WHEN.

questions.stem: A sponsor reviewing a mobile banking app project asks why the scope includes training call-center staff, writing a deployment runbook, and conducting a security audit, since "none of these are app features." How should the project manager explain this?
options: Those items are optional extras that can be removed without changing the scope baseline
Those items are product scope, since they describe characteristics of the finished app
Those items belong to operations and should be moved to a separate operating budget
Those items are project scope, the work needed to deliver, while app features are product scope
questions.explanation:
Concept: Product scope vs project scope — product scope is the features and functions of the result; project scope is all the work needed to deliver it (Rule M4-B02-R06).
Spot it: A stakeholder questioning training, runbooks or audits because "they are not features."
In this scenario: Training call-center staff, writing a runbook and running a security audit are project scope, the work to deliver; app features are product scope.
Why not the others: They are in the approved scope, so they are not optional extras; they are activities, not characteristics of the app; moving them to operations leaves required delivery work unfunded.
Remember: Product scope = WHAT it IS; Project scope = WORK to deliver it.

questions.stem: Partway through construction of an office fit-out, a client asks the project manager to add a server room, saying the change is "small, just one room." The change control board meets next week. What should the project manager do BEFORE the meeting?
options: Approve the room directly, since the client is paying and considers it minor
Reject the request, because changes are not allowed once construction begins
Assess the room's effects on schedule, cost, risk, quality, and building permits
Tell the contractor to start the room now so it does not delay other work
questions.explanation:
Concept: Impact analysis of scope changes — before a decision, assess how the change ripples into schedule, cost, risk, quality and value (Rule M4-B02-R09).
Spot it: "Small" change request, a change control board meeting coming up, and the word "BEFORE."
In this scenario: The PM assesses the server room's effects on schedule, cost, risk, quality and permits so the board can make an informed decision.
Why not the others: The PM cannot approve directly when a board exists; changes are allowed with control, so blanket rejection is wrong; starting work before approval bypasses change control.
Remember: Change Request → ANALYZE → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor.

questions.stem: Midway through a sprint, a sales director asks a developer to add a custom export feature for a prospect demo next month. The feature would take about half of the team's remaining capacity, and the sprint goal is to finish a checkout redesign. What should the developer do?
options: Build the export feature now, since the sales director outranks the team's product owner
Work on the feature at night so that the sprint goal is not affected by the request
Ask the team to cancel the sprint and start over with the export feature included
Refer the request to the product owner to weigh against the goal and the next sprint
questions.explanation:
Concept: Protecting the sprint goal — mid-sprint requests that threaten the goal or capacity go to the product owner, who owns priorities and the product backlog (Rule M4-B12-R02).
Spot it: An outside stakeholder asking a developer directly for new work in the middle of a sprint.
In this scenario: The developer refers the export request to the product owner, who weighs it against the checkout goal and likely orders it for the next sprint.
Why not the others: Rank does not override the product owner's authority; secret night work hides the cost and burns people out; only the product owner can cancel a sprint, and this does not justify it.
Remember: New request? → Product owner → Product backlog. The sprint goal is protected.

questions.stem: A team using Kanban says it "feels busy," but stakeholders complain that delivery dates are unpredictable. The team does not use timeboxes or estimates. The manager asks how the team can understand how work is flowing and forecast delivery. Which measures should the team use?
options: Cycle time per item and throughput per week to see flow and forecast delivery
Hours logged by each team member per week to see who is the most productive
Story points completed per sprint compared against other teams' velocity
Number of meetings held each week to judge how well the team coordinates
questions.explanation:
Concept: Flow metrics — cycle time (how long one item takes) and throughput (how many items finish per period) show flow and support forecasting without estimates (Rule M4-B12-R05).
Spot it: Kanban, no timeboxes or estimates, unpredictable delivery, and a request to forecast.
In this scenario: Tracking cycle time per item and throughput per week lets the team see flow and forecast delivery dates with data.
Why not the others: Hours logged measure activity, not delivery; story points and velocity need sprints and estimates, and comparing velocity across teams is misleading; meeting counts say nothing about flow.
Remember: Kanban = Cycle time + Throughput + WIP; Scrum = Velocity + Burndown.

questions.stem: During a retrospective, a team lead plans to display each developer's defect count and ask the lowest performers to explain themselves. Several team members have grown quiet in recent retrospectives. What should the scrum master do?
options: Refocus the retrospective on process causes of defects and agree on team improvements
Display the defect counts so accountability is clear and performance can improve
Suspend retrospectives until the team feels more comfortable speaking openly
Hold private meetings with each low performer in place of the retrospective
questions.explanation:
Concept: Retrospectives — the team inspects and improves its own process in a psychologically safe setting; they are not performance reviews (Rule M4-B12-R08).
Spot it: Individual metrics shown publicly, "explain themselves," and team members going quiet.
In this scenario: The scrum master refocuses the retrospective on process causes of the defects and helps the team agree on improvements.
Why not the others: Displaying individual defect counts creates blame and silence; suspending retrospectives removes the improvement loop; private meetings with "low performers" still target people instead of the process.
Remember: Retro = improve the PROCESS, not judge the PEOPLE.

questions.stem: A state agency's predictive project to modernize tax filing just had its budget cut by 25 percent. Remaining scope includes online filing for individuals, which drives most of the expected benefits, plus a redesigned internal reporting dashboard and new marketing videos. The sponsor asks for a revised plan. What should the project manager propose?
options: Protect individual online filing and defer the dashboard and videos to fit the new budget
Cut every remaining deliverable by 25 percent so that all stakeholders share the reduction evenly
Keep the dashboard and videos, since they are cheaper and quicker to complete first
Suspend the project until the legislature can restore the full original budget
questions.explanation:
Concept: Value-based prioritization under constraints — when money or time is cut, protect the deliverables that create most of the benefits and defer lower-value work (Rule M5-B04-R05).
Spot it: A budget cut, one deliverable that "drives most of the expected benefits," and lower-value extras.
In this scenario: The PM proposes keeping individual online filing whole and deferring the dashboard and videos to fit the reduced budget.
Why not the others: An even 25% cut could leave the key deliverable unfinished; doing cheap items first spends money on low value; suspending the project delivers nothing while waiting.
Remember: Output → Outcome → Benefit → Value — protect what creates the VALUE.

questions.stem: In a hybrid program, an adaptive workstream is building a loyalty-points feature. New analysis shows the remaining build would cost $1.2 million, while expected benefits have fallen to $400,000 because a partner withdrew. The team lead suggests simply stopping work on Monday. What should the project manager do?
options: Stop the workstream on Monday as suggested and inform the sponsor afterward
Present the updated cost-benefit analysis to the steering committee and recommend stopping
Continue building, since the program has already invested heavily in this feature
Halve the team and continue at a slower pace to limit the program's losses
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stopping low-value work through governance — when the cost to continue exceeds the expected benefit, recommend stopping, but let the proper governance body decide (Rule M5-B04-R08).
Spot it: Updated numbers (cost $1.2M vs benefit $400K), and someone suggesting to "just stop" without authority.
In this scenario: The PM takes the updated cost-benefit analysis to the steering committee with a recommendation to stop.
Why not the others: Stopping first and telling the sponsor later bypasses governance; "we already invested" is the sunk-cost trap; halving the team still spends money on negative value.
Remember: Sunk cost is SUNK — decide on future value, through GOVERNANCE.

questions.stem: An agile team released a meal-kit subscription upgrade expecting 20 percent of users to buy it. After three months only 6 percent did, while an unplanned gift-card option proved unexpectedly popular. The product owner is now preparing plans for next quarter. What should the team do?
options: Record which value assumptions held or failed and use the findings in future planning
Move on to the next roadmap feature, since the release is already live and running stably
Report only the gift-card success, since highlighting the miss could hurt team morale
Blame the marketing messaging and plan a larger campaign for the same upgrade feature
questions.explanation:
Concept: Value learning — after release, compare actual results with the value assumptions and record which held and which failed, so future plans get smarter (Rule M5-B04-R10).
Spot it: Expected vs actual adoption (20% vs 6%), an unexpected success, and planning for the next period.
In this scenario: The team records that the upgrade assumption failed and the gift-card demand was a surprise, and feeds both into next quarter's plans.
Why not the others: Moving on skips the learning; reporting only good news hides the miss; blaming marketing and doubling down assumes the cause without evidence.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → LEARN → Close — lessons learned include VALUE lessons.

questions.stem: Six months into a predictive project to build a regional distribution center, new environmental rules add $8 million in costs and delay expected benefits by a year. The original business case showed only a modest return. The project team has already absorbed several smaller cost increases. What should the project manager do?
options: Update the business case with the new costs and timing and take it to the sponsor for a decision
Absorb the added cost from the management reserve and continue under the original approved business case
Cancel the project on her own authority, since the original margin of return has now disappeared
Log the new rules as an issue and leave the business case unchanged until project closure
questions.explanation:
Concept: Living business case — the business case (the WHY) must be updated when major new costs, risks or benefits could change the investment decision (Rule M5-B03-R06).
Spot it: A large new cost, delayed benefits, a business case that was already marginal, and "several smaller increases" absorbed.
In this scenario: The PM updates the business case with the $8M cost and one-year delay and brings it to the sponsor to decide whether to continue.
Why not the others: The PM cannot draw on management reserve without approval, and it hides a changed decision; cancelling alone exceeds her authority; logging an issue while leaving the business case stale defeats its purpose.
Remember: Business case = WHY. If the WHY changes, the SPONSOR decides.

questions.stem: A hybrid team is building a hospital patient portal; records-system integration follows a predictive plan while portal features are built adaptively. Stakeholders are debating a video-visit module that would consume a third of the budget. The business case names the portal's main goal as reducing missed appointments. What should the project manager do?
options: Include the module, since video visits are a popular feature in competitors' patient portals
Exclude the module, since it would consume a large share of the total project budget
Evaluate how much the video module would help reduce missed appointments before deciding
Let the developers decide based on their technical interest and the module's complexity
questions.explanation:
Concept: Value-driven scope — every major scope choice should be tied to the value or objective in the business case (Rule M5-B03-R09).
Spot it: An expensive optional feature, stakeholders debating, and a business case that names a specific goal.
In this scenario: The PM evaluates how much video visits would actually reduce missed appointments, the portal's stated goal, before deciding.
Why not the others: Competitor popularity is not this project's objective; cost alone ignores the possible benefit; developer interest is not a value criterion.
Remember: Business Need → Business Case → Project → Benefits → Value — scope serves the WHY.

questions.stem: An agile team added a "fast lane" that lets premium customers skip the support queue. Premium response times improved, but standard customers now wait longer and complain more, and some upgrade just to escape delays, which in turn lengthens the fast lane. What should the team do FIRST?
options: Hire more agents for the fast lane, since demand for premium support keeps rising fast
Declare success, since premium response times met the original improvement target
Map how the fast lane feeds back into queue lengths and upgrades before adjusting it
Remove the fast lane at once and restore the original single support queue for all
questions.explanation:
Concept: Systems thinking and feedback loops — a fix in one place can cause secondary effects that loop back and change the original problem (Rule M5-B17-R01).
Spot it: "Improved here but worse there," people changing behavior because of the fix, and the effect feeding back into the cause.
In this scenario: The fast lane lengthens standard waits, which pushes upgrades, which lengthens the fast lane, so the team first maps that loop before changing anything.
Why not the others: Hiring more agents feeds the loop; declaring success ignores the side effects; removing the lane at once acts before understanding.
Remember: Data → Analyze → Insight → Decision → Action — see the LOOP before you fix it.

questions.stem: A predictive airport terminal project has separate contractors for baggage handling, security screening, and building controls. At a design review each contractor's work looks on track, but no one has defined how the baggage system will receive alarms from security screening. What should the project manager do?
options: Let each contractor settle interfaces directly with the other contractors during installation
Wait for integration testing near completion to reveal any interface problems that exist
Add the interface definition and integration testing to the plan as owned, scheduled work
Give the interface work to whichever contractor finishes its own scope first on the job
questions.explanation:
Concept: Interface management — handoffs between contractors, teams or systems are real work that must be planned, owned and scheduled (Rule M5-B17-R02).
Spot it: Several contractors each "on track," and an undefined connection between their systems.
In this scenario: The PM adds the security-to-baggage interface definition and integration testing to the plan with an owner and dates.
Why not the others: Letting contractors sort it out during installation leaves nobody accountable; waiting for integration testing finds problems too late; giving it to whoever finishes first is random ownership.
Remember: Dependency → Assess Impact → Coordinate → Monitor — interfaces are WORK, not assumptions.

questions.stem: A city transit agency plans to introduce dynamic bus fares using a hybrid approach: fare equipment is procured predictively and pricing rules are rolled out adaptively. How riders will respond to price changes is highly uncertain, and some could shift to driving. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Apply the pricing rules citywide at once so that results are not distorted by route differences
Commission an econometric forecast and apply the model's optimal fares on every route
Trial the pricing rules on a few routes, measure rider behavior, and adjust before scaling
Drop dynamic pricing, since unpredictable rider behavior makes the change too risky
questions.explanation:
Concept: Experiments and staged implementation — when people's behavior is hard to predict, try a small change, measure, and adjust before scaling (Rule M5-B17-R03).
Spot it: "Highly uncertain" response, possible unintended effects, and a change that could be rolled out in pieces.
In this scenario: The PM recommends trialing dynamic fares on a few routes, measuring rider behavior, and adjusting before a citywide rollout.
Why not the others: A citywide launch bets everything on an unknown; a forecast model cannot remove behavioral uncertainty; dropping the idea throws away the potential value without learning.
Remember: Uncertain behavior? Probe → Sense → Respond. Small bets first.

questions.stem: An agile organization runs two initiatives: migrating payroll to a new server cluster, which experts can plan precisely from known specifications, and designing a new service for gig workers whose needs and uptake are unclear. Leadership wants one management approach for both. What should the agile coach advise?
options: Plan the migration through expert analysis and develop the gig service through short learning experiments
Run both initiatives through short experiments, since experimentation suits every kind of initiative equally
Plan both fully upfront, since expert analysis can resolve any uncertainty in either initiative
Let each team choose any approach it likes freely without considering the nature of its work
questions.explanation:
Concept: Complicated vs complex (Cynefin) — complicated work can be analyzed and planned by experts; complex work has unknowns that only experiments reveal (Rule M5-B17-R04).
Spot it: One initiative with "known specifications" and expert planning; another where needs and uptake are "unclear."
In this scenario: The payroll migration is complicated, so plan it through expert analysis; the gig-worker service is complex, so develop it through short learning cycles.
Why not the others: Experiments for everything waste effort on known work; full upfront planning cannot resolve real unknowns; letting teams choose freely ignores the nature of the work.
Remember: Complicated = ANALYZE; Complex = EXPERIMENT. Tailor to the work.

questions.stem: A predictive project to build a solar farm faces several linked uncertainties: tariffs on imported panels, a pending change to grid-connection rules, and possible interest-rate increases. The sponsor wants to understand how these factors could combine to affect the investment. What should the project manager do?
options: Develop a few scenarios combining these uncertainties and assess the plan's response to each
Build the plan on the most likely value of each factor and report one single forecast to the sponsor
Analyze each uncertainty on its own and add the separate impacts together for a total
Delay planning until the tariff, grid, and interest-rate decisions have all been announced
questions.explanation:
Concept: Scenario planning — when several uncertainties interact, build a few coherent future scenarios and test the plan against each (Rule M5-B17-R07).
Spot it: "Several linked uncertainties" and a sponsor asking how they "could combine."
In this scenario: The PM develops a few scenarios combining tariffs, grid rules and interest rates and shows how the investment performs in each.
Why not the others: One most-likely forecast hides the combinations; adding separate impacts ignores how factors interact; waiting for every decision delays planning indefinitely.
Remember: Many uncertainties that INTERACT → scenarios, not a single number.

questions.stem: A hybrid team is delivering a consumer lending platform; compliance controls are planned predictively, while customer features are built adaptively. Government regulators announce new disclosure rules that take effect in five months. The team is midway through a planned release. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Continue the plan as it stands and deal with the new rules once the current release has shipped
Halt all development until legal counsel rewrites the entire compliance framework
Analyze how the new disclosure rules affect scope, schedule, controls, and upcoming releases
Add a generic disclosure page now and assume it will meet the new requirements in full
questions.explanation:
Concept: Regulatory change impact — when laws, policies or standards change, first analyze the effect on scope, schedule, controls and releases, then act (Rule M5-B02-R05).
Spot it: New rules announced, an effective date in the future, work in progress, and the word "FIRST."
In this scenario: The PM analyzes how the disclosure rules affect scope, the schedule, compliance controls and upcoming releases before replanning.
Why not the others: Continuing unchanged risks noncompliance; halting everything overreacts when there are five months; a generic page assumes compliance without analysis.
Remember: Understand → ASSESS → Collaborate → Act — never act on a law you haven't analyzed.

questions.stem: An agile team building a clinic scheduling app wants to copy production patient records into its test environment to reproduce a hard-to-find bug. Test environments are shared with outside contractors and lack production security controls. What should the team do?
options: Copy the production records, since all the contractors signed nondisclosure agreements
Copy only a small sample of real records and delete them after the bug is fixed
Give contractors direct production access so the patient data never leaves production
Use masked or synthetic data in testing so that real patient records stay protected
questions.explanation:
Concept: Protecting sensitive data across the lifecycle — regulated data such as health records must stay protected in design, testing, operations and disposal, not just in production (Rule M5-B02-R08).
Spot it: Real patient records, a test environment with weaker controls, and outside contractors.
In this scenario: The team reproduces the bug with masked or synthetic data, keeping real patient records out of the insecure test environment.
Why not the others: NDAs do not replace security controls; a "small sample" is still real patient data exposed; giving contractors production access widens exposure.
Remember: Sensitive data? Minimize, Mask, Protect — in EVERY environment.

questions.stem: An audit of a predictive food-processing plant upgrade found that temperature logs were not being retained for the required two years. The team has corrected the logging configuration and wants the audit finding closed. A regulator will reinspect in three months. What should the project manager do?
options: Close the audit finding now, since the team has already corrected the logging configuration
Test that logs are now captured and retained as required and keep evidence for the regulator
Wait for the regulator's reinspection to find out whether the configuration fix works
Add a note to the lessons learned register and then close the audit finding as resolved
questions.explanation:
Concept: Verify compliance fixes — a corrective action is closed only after evidence shows compliance is actually restored (Rule M5-B02-R10).
Spot it: An audit finding, a fix "already made," a wish to close it, and a future reinspection.
In this scenario: The PM tests that temperature logs are captured and retained as required and keeps the evidence ready for the regulator.
Why not the others: Closing now assumes the fix works; waiting for the regulator makes the inspection your test; a lessons-learned note does not prove compliance.
Remember: Issue → Analyze → Resolve → MONITOR — evidence before closure.

questions.stem: During a ransomware attack on a hybrid project's staging environment, crisis leaders decide within an hour to restore from a three-day-old backup, accepting some data loss. Everyone is exhausted, and the team lead says documentation can wait until next week. What should the project manager ensure?
options: That documentation waits until the crisis is over and the team has had some rest
That every member writes a detailed incident report before any restoration begins
That the decision, its rationale, and key assumptions are briefly recorded now
That the decision is shared only verbally to keep the sensitive details private
questions.explanation:
Concept: Decision records under pressure — even in a crisis, briefly capture critical decisions, rationale and assumptions while they are fresh (Rule M5-B18-R06).
Spot it: A fast, high-impact decision, exhausted people, and "documentation can wait."
In this scenario: The PM makes sure the restore decision, why it was chosen and the accepted data loss are recorded now in a short entry, such as a decision log.
Why not the others: Waiting a week loses details and reasons; full reports before restoring slow the recovery; verbal-only sharing leaves no audit trail.
Remember: Fast decision + short record = accountable decision. Brief now beats perfect later.

questions.stem: A regional cloud outage took an agile team's delivery app offline for six hours. Afterward the team discovered that its failover procedure depended on a manual step no one on shift knew how to perform. Service has now been restored. What should the team do NEXT?
options: Close the incident, since service was restored and the cloud provider has formally apologized
Revise the continuity and contingency plans and the risk register based on the outage lessons
Switch cloud providers so that a similar regional outage cannot happen to the delivery app again
Discipline the engineers on shift for not knowing how to perform the manual failover step
questions.explanation:
Concept: Learning after a crisis — update continuity, contingency and risk plans with what the incident revealed (Rule M5-B18-R09).
Spot it: Service restored, a hidden weakness discovered (a manual step nobody knew), and "what NEXT."
In this scenario: The team revises the failover and continuity plans and the risk register, for example by automating or documenting and training the manual step.
Why not the others: Closing without learning leaves the weakness in place; switching providers is a large reaction that does not fix the failover step; disciplining engineers blames people for a process gap.
Remember: Risk → Respond → Monitor → Issue → LEARN → update the plans.

questions.stem: A predictive project is restructuring a bank's back-office operations. Staff in design workshops stopped raising concerns after a manager remarked that "negative people may not have a place in the new structure." The project manager needs honest input about process risks. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue the workshops as planned, since the silence suggests that staff now accept the changes
Work with the sponsor to reaffirm that raising concerns is welcome and will not be penalized
Collect input only from managers, since staff are reluctant to contribute in workshops
Report the manager to HR and exclude him from all future workshops without discussion
questions.explanation:
Concept: Psychological safety during change — people must feel safe to raise concerns, especially when a transformation threatens their jobs (Rule M5-B14-R08).
Spot it: Staff who "stopped raising concerns" after a threatening remark, and a PM who needs honest input.
In this scenario: The PM works with the sponsor to openly reaffirm that concerns are welcome and will not be penalized, restoring honest input.
Why not the others: Silence is not acceptance; asking only managers loses frontline risk knowledge; reporting and excluding without discussion escalates before addressing the climate.
Remember: No safety → no truth → hidden risks. Leaders set the tone.

questions.stem: A hybrid project has built and tested a new field-service app, and the technical team is ready to deploy it to all 2,000 technicians. Readiness surveys show only 30 percent of technicians have completed training, and supervisors have not yet updated work procedures. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Deploy to all technicians now and let them learn the new app on the job instead
Postpone deployment until every technician scores 100 percent in training
Deploy now and require supervisors to update their procedures within a week
Phase the rollout by region as training and procedure updates are completed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Organizational readiness vs technical readiness — a system can be ready while people and processes are not; adjust the rollout pace to the lower of the two (Rule M5-B14-R09).
Spot it: "Technical team ready," but low training completion and procedures not updated.
In this scenario: The PM recommends phasing the rollout by region as training and procedure updates are completed.
Why not the others: Full deployment now sets 70% of users up to fail; waiting for 100% training scores is unrealistic; a one-week procedure deadline pushes change without support.
Remember: Understand → Engage → Communicate → Train → Reinforce — people ready = go live.

questions.stem: An organization adopted agile ways of working a year ago, and every team now holds all of the prescribed events. However, leaders suspect teams still wait for managers to make decisions and avoid experimenting. What should the agile coach do?
options: Measure indicators such as decision wait times and experiment frequency to check real change
Report success, since every team now holds all of the prescribed agile events on schedule
Mandate that every team runs a set number of experiments in each quarter going forward
Replace team leads who have not adopted the new behaviors quickly enough this year
questions.explanation:
Concept: Measure real change — cultural change is proven by changed behavior, not by holding the prescribed ceremonies (Rule M5-B14-R10).
Spot it: "All events held," yet leaders suspect old behaviors such as waiting for managers and avoiding experiments.
In this scenario: The agile coach measures behavior indicators such as decision wait time and experiment frequency to see whether change is actually happening.
Why not the others: Ceremony counts are output, not outcome; mandating experiment quotas forces the form without the mindset; replacing leads blames individuals before understanding.
Remember: Doing agile ≠ Being agile — measure BEHAVIOR, not ceremonies.

questions.stem: A predictive project delivered a new electronic expense system on time and within budget. Its benefits depend on employees filing expenses online instead of on paper. The sponsor asks how the project's value should be judged at the six-month benefits review. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Track the share of expenses filed online versus on paper over time
Confirm that the system passed all acceptance tests before go-live
Report that the project met its schedule and cost baselines at close
Count how many employees attended the system training sessions
questions.explanation:
Concept: Adoption metrics — when value depends on people actually using the product, measure adoption and behavior, not delivery success (Rule M5-B12-R04).
Spot it: Delivered "on time and within budget," benefits that depend on employees changing how they work, and a benefits review.
In this scenario: The PM recommends tracking the share of expenses filed online versus on paper over time, which shows whether benefits are being realized.
Why not the others: Passing acceptance tests shows the output works, not that people use it; schedule and cost success is project performance, not value; training attendance is activity, not adoption.
Remember: Output → Outcome → Benefit — value is USE, not delivery.

questions.stem: A hybrid project for a university's student portal collected 300 suggestions through a survey. Some were implemented in adaptive releases, and others were deferred because of the fixed integration schedule. Students now say their feedback "went into a black hole." What should the project manager do?
options: Run another survey to show students that their opinions are still highly valued
Tell students which suggestions were adopted, which were deferred, and why
Implement the most-requested deferred items even if integration dates slip
Publish only the adopted suggestions so that the message stays positive
questions.explanation:
Concept: Closing the feedback loop — tell stakeholders what was done with their input, including what was not done and why (Rule M5-B12-R07).
Spot it: Feedback collected, some acted on, some deferred, and complaints of a "black hole."
In this scenario: The PM tells students which suggestions were adopted, which were deferred, and the reason (the fixed integration schedule).
Why not the others: Another survey deepens the frustration; implementing deferred items by slipping integration dates ignores the constraint; sharing only good news hides the deferrals.
Remember: Identify → Analyze → Engage → Monitor — engagement means "you said, we did, and here's why."

questions.stem: During a sprint, a developer discovers that a misconfigured storage bucket has exposed customer email addresses publicly for two days. The developer has already locked the bucket. Team members want to quietly confirm the scope of the exposure before telling anyone. What should the team do?
options: Report the exposure now through the company's security incident and legal process
Investigate privately first and report it only if actual misuse of the data is confirmed
Email the affected customers directly from the team to apologize for the exposure
Delete the access logs to limit any further exposure of which data was accessed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Data incident response — suspected data exposures are reported at once through the organization's security and legal procedures (Rule M5-B15-R07).
Spot it: Exposed personal data, a quick fix already made, and a temptation to "quietly confirm" first.
In this scenario: The team reports the exposure now through the security incident and legal process, which handles investigation and any required notifications.
Why not the others: Investigating privately delays legally time-bound reporting; emailing customers from the team bypasses legal and communications controls; deleting logs destroys evidence.
Remember: Data incident? REPORT through the process — contain, don't conceal.

questions.stem: During a predictive CRM implementation, a data governance council approved an exception allowing marketing to retain customer contact data for five years instead of the standard three. The approval was given verbally in a meeting and never written down. What should the project manager do?
options: Rely on the meeting attendees to recall the approval if questions arise later on
Apply the three-year standard anyway, since the exception was never put in writing
Tell marketing to keep the data indefinitely, since an exception has been granted
Record the exception, its rationale, approver, and conditions in the governance log
questions.explanation:
Concept: Documenting governance decisions — significant data-governance decisions and exceptions are recorded with rationale, approver and conditions (Rule M5-B15-R10).
Spot it: An approved exception, given "verbally" and "never written down."
In this scenario: The PM records the five-year retention exception, why it was granted, who approved it and its conditions in the governance or decision log.
Why not the others: Memory is not an audit trail; ignoring a valid approval undermines governance; "indefinitely" goes beyond what was approved.
Remember: Not written = not governed. Decision + Why + Who + Conditions.

questions.stem: A hybrid project will automate a city's building-permit reviews, cutting approval times for large developers. Analysis shows the new online-only process could disadvantage small contractors who lack digital tools. The sponsor wants to proceed quickly. What should the project manager do?
options: Proceed as planned, since the faster approvals benefit the large majority of permit applicants
Assess the impact on each affected group and propose ways to reduce harm to small contractors
Cancel the automation to avoid disadvantaging any stakeholder group in the city
Let small contractors raise complaints after launch through the city's help desk
questions.explanation:
Concept: Ethical impact — consider who benefits and who may be harmed by a project decision, and look for ways to reduce harm (Rule M5-B16-R01).
Spot it: A change that helps one group (large developers) but may disadvantage another (small contractors), plus pressure to go fast.
In this scenario: The PM assesses the impact on each group and proposes mitigations for small contractors, such as assisted or offline options.
Why not the others: "Most people benefit" ignores harm to a vulnerable group; cancelling throws away real value; waiting for complaints makes harm the detection method.
Remember: PMI Code — Responsibility, Respect, Fairness, Honesty. Ask: who WINS, who PAYS?

questions.stem: Before a funding review, a product owner asks the team to change the analytics dashboard so it shows 50,000 active users instead of the actual 18,000, saying investors "just need to see momentum." What should the scrum master do?
options: Decline to alter the figures and escalate the request through appropriate channels
Make the change but add a small footnote describing exactly how the users were counted
Comply, since the product owner is accountable for how the product is presented
Resign from the team to avoid any association with the misleading dashboard
questions.explanation:
Concept: Refusing unethical requests — a PM or team member declines requests that are fraudulent or clearly misleading and escalates through proper channels (Rule M5-B16-R02).
Spot it: A request to show false numbers to investors, justified as "they just need to see momentum."
In this scenario: The scrum master declines to alter the user figures and raises the request through appropriate channels.
Why not the others: A footnote does not fix a false headline number; product owner accountability does not extend to misrepresentation; resigning walks away without addressing the problem.
Remember: Honesty is non-negotiable — Refuse → Escalate, never "fudge and footnote."

questions.stem: A predictive project to build a water treatment plant has a point cost estimate of $42 million. Analysis shows a 40 percent chance that cost could exceed $50 million because soil conditions are still unknown. The sponsor wants a single number for the board. What should the project manager do?
options: Report $42 million only, since the sponsor asked for a single number to share with the board
Report $50 million to be safe, without explaining how the figure was derived
Delay the board report until soil tests have removed all of the uncertainty
Present the estimate with its range and explain the soil uncertainty behind it
questions.explanation:
Concept: Honest disclosure of uncertainty — present estimates with their range and the reasons behind it, rather than false precision (Rule M5-B16-R03).
Spot it: A point estimate, a significant chance of a much higher cost, and a request for "a single number."
In this scenario: The PM presents the estimate with its range and explains the unknown soil conditions so the board can decide with open eyes.
Why not the others: $42M alone hides a 40% chance of overrun; $50M without explanation is unexplained padding; waiting for zero uncertainty delays the decision.
Remember: Estimate = Number + Range + Assumptions. Honest, not hopeful.

questions.stem: A hybrid program must select 5 of 20 community health clinics for a telehealth pilot. Clinic directors are lobbying the project manager, and several suspect the choice will favor politically connected sites. What should the project manager do?
options: Select the clinics privately to avoid lobbying and then announce the final results
Publish objective selection criteria and scoring, then apply them to every clinic
Pick the clinics whose directors lobbied hardest, since they show strong commitment
Choose the clinics at random to avoid any appearance of favoritism in the process
questions.explanation:
Concept: Transparent selection criteria — high-impact choices affecting many stakeholders should use published, objective criteria applied equally (Rule M5-B16-R06).
Spot it: Lobbying, suspicion of favoritism, and a limited number of slots.
In this scenario: The PM publishes objective criteria and scoring, then applies them to all 20 clinics, which makes the choice fair and defensible.
Why not the others: A private selection feeds suspicion; rewarding lobbying is unfair; random choice avoids bias but ignores which clinics best fit the pilot's goals.
Remember: Impact → Alternatives → CRITERIA → Balance → Monitor — fair AND visible.

questions.stem: A predictive project installing a smart-meter system could meet its deadline by skipping the planned privacy notices to residents; the notices are not legally required in this region. Residents have protested earlier utility projects over data concerns. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Keep the privacy notices, since resident trust affects the system's long-term value
Skip the notices, since they are not legally required and would put the deadline at risk
Send the notices only after meters are installed to protect the project schedule
Let the installation contractor decide whether notices should go to residents
questions.explanation:
Concept: Trust as value — long-term stakeholder trust is part of project value, even when a shortcut is legal (Rule M5-B16-R10).
Spot it: A legal-but-risky shortcut to meet a deadline, and a stakeholder group with a history of protest over the same issue.
In this scenario: The PM recommends keeping the privacy notices because resident trust affects adoption and the smart-meter system's long-term value.
Why not the others: "Not legally required" ignores the value at risk; notices after installation defeat their purpose; handing the decision to the contractor gives away a stakeholder-trust decision.
Remember: Legal ≠ enough. Short-term speed vs long-term TRUST — PMI picks trust.

questions.stem: A hybrid project is building a parking-reservation app for downtown garages, with garage hardware installed predictively. Since planning began many office workers have moved to hybrid schedules, and garage occupancy has fallen 35 percent. The business case assumed full garages. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue as planned, since the hardware contracts have already been signed with vendors
Revalidate demand assumptions and assess their effect on features and the business case
Add more features to attract drivers back to the downtown garages in greater numbers
Cancel the project, since lower occupancy makes the reservation app unnecessary
questions.explanation:
Concept: Revalidating assumptions — when customer or market behavior shifts, revisit demand assumptions and their effect on the product and business case (Rule M5-B08-R04).
Spot it: A market shift since planning (hybrid work, 35% lower occupancy) and a business case built on the old assumption.
In this scenario: The PM revalidates demand and assesses the effect on features and the business case, then brings the results to the sponsor.
Why not the others: Signed contracts do not make the assumption true; adding features guesses at a solution; cancelling without analysis overreacts.
Remember: Constraint / Assumption → Assess Impact → Adjust.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A predictive project is building a factory to produce gasoline-engine components. National lawmakers announce that sales of new gasoline vehicles will be banned in eight years. The factory's payback period is ten years. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue construction, since the ban is eight years away and outside the project's scope
Forward the news to the sponsor quickly without any analysis of its likely impact
Redesign the factory for electric-vehicle parts without consulting the sponsor
Escalate to the sponsor with an analysis of the ban's effect on payback and options
questions.explanation:
Concept: Escalating strategic external change — when an external event affects the investment itself, escalate to the sponsor with analysis that supports a decision (Rule M5-B08-R07).
Spot it: A law or market change affecting the project's long-term payoff, and the payback period longer than the change horizon.
In this scenario: A ban in eight years undercuts a ten-year payback, so the PM escalates with an analysis of the financial effect and options, such as redesign or phasing.
Why not the others: "Outside our scope" ignores the business case; forwarding news without analysis gives the sponsor nothing to decide on; redesigning alone exceeds the PM's authority.
Remember: Escalate with DATA and OPTIONS, not just news.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid e-commerce project assumes that a key carrier's shipping costs will stay below $8 per order; any higher cost makes the free-shipping model lose money. Fuel prices have become volatile. What should the project manager do?
options: Record the assumption in the assumption log and review it at project closure
Lock in free shipping permanently, since customers now expect it on every order
Drop free shipping now in case the carrier's costs rise at some point later
Monitor shipping cost per order and set a threshold that triggers a pricing review
questions.explanation:
Concept: Monitoring critical assumptions — protect key assumptions with indicators and thresholds that trigger a review when they are breached (Rule M5-B08-R09).
Spot it: An assumption the model depends on (cost below $8), and a volatile driver (fuel prices).
In this scenario: The PM tracks shipping cost per order and sets a threshold that triggers a pricing review before losses build up.
Why not the others: Reviewing at closure is too late; locking in free shipping ignores the risk; dropping it now gives up value before any trigger.
Remember: Assumption log + TRIGGER = early warning.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A portfolio committee must choose one of two predictive projects with similar risk profiles. Project A costs $2 million and delivers $3 million in benefits in present value terms. Project B costs $5 million and delivers $6 million. Funds are limited. Based on benefit-cost ratio, which should the project manager recommend?
options: Project B, since it produces more total benefit than Project A does overall
Project B, since its larger budget signals greater strategic importance
Either project, since both deliver an equal $1 million net benefit
Project A, since it returns 1.5 per dollar spent versus 1.2 for Project B
questions.explanation:
Concept: Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) — benefits divided by costs; above 1 is worth doing, and the higher the ratio, the more value per dollar (Rule M5-B10-R05).
Spot it: Limited funds, two projects with similar risk, and costs and benefits in present-value terms.
In this scenario: Project A: 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5; Project B: 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2. With scarce funds, Project A returns more per dollar.
Why not the others: Bigger total benefit ignores the ratio being asked about; a larger budget does not mean greater value; equal net benefit ignores that A needs far less money.
Remember: BCR = Benefit ÷ Cost — higher is better (NPV and IRR: higher; payback period: shorter).
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: An investment board is comparing two hybrid initiatives. Initiative X projects $4 million in returns if unproven technology works, which experts rate at 50 percent likely. Initiative Y projects $3 million using proven technology with a 90 percent success likelihood. What should the project manager advise?
options: Choose Initiative X, since its projected return is the higher of the two
Fund both, splitting the money evenly to balance the risk between them
Compare the options on risk-adjusted value, which favors Initiative Y
Choose Initiative X, since innovation matters more than predictable returns
questions.explanation:
Concept: Risk-adjusted value — weigh each option's return by its probability of success (expected monetary value) rather than comparing headline returns (Rule M5-B10-R08).
Spot it: Different returns with very different success probabilities, and "unproven" vs "proven" technology.
In this scenario: X = $4M × 50% = $2.0M; Y = $3M × 90% = $2.7M, so risk-adjusted value favors Initiative Y.
Why not the others: The higher headline return ignores the 50% risk; splitting funds evenly avoids the decision; "innovation matters more" is not a value comparison.
Remember: EMV = Probability × Impact — compare the RISK-ADJUSTED number.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A predictive project is building a hospital wing. Soon the contractor may request a structural design change that could affect both the occupancy date and cost. The charter does not state who approves changes above $500,000. What should the project manager do NOW?
options: Confirm with the sponsor who holds approval authority for major changes before one arises
Wait until a major change arrives and then ask the sponsor who should approve it at that time
Assume the change control board can approve any change regardless of its size or cost
Approve major changes personally to prevent delays and inform the sponsor afterward
questions.explanation:
Concept: Decision authority — know who can approve high-impact decisions before one is needed (Rule M5-B01-R01).
Spot it: A likely big change coming, thresholds not defined in the charter, and the word "NOW."
In this scenario: The PM confirms with the sponsor who holds approval authority for changes above $500,000 and records it in the change management plan.
Why not the others: Waiting until the change arrives causes delay; assuming the board's authority has no limit may be wrong; approving personally exceeds the PM's authority.
Remember: Who decides? Charter → Sponsor → CCB — settle it BEFORE the decision.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid project's steering committee is being asked to decide screen colors and minor field labels for the adaptive user-interface work, and each decision waits weeks for its next meeting. These choices have no budget, schedule, or compliance impact. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep sending the choices to the steering committee so it maintains full oversight of the design
Make every interface design decision personally to speed up the work for the team
Delegate these minor interface decisions to the product owner and team within agreed limits
Freeze all interface design work until the steering committee clears its decision queue
questions.explanation:
Concept: Lowest appropriate decision level — push decisions down to those closest to the work, within agreed limits; escalate only what needs higher authority (Rule M5-B01-R02).
Spot it: A senior body deciding trivial items, weeks of waiting, and "no budget, schedule, or compliance impact."
In this scenario: The PM delegates minor interface choices to the product owner and team within agreed limits, freeing the steering committee.
Why not the others: Sending trivia upward slows work without adding control; the PM taking every decision just creates a new bottleneck; freezing work waits on a queue that should not exist.
Remember: Decide LOW, escalate HIGH — only what exceeds the mandate goes up.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A predictive pipeline project team finds that meeting the deadline would require accepting a safety risk above the organization's stated risk threshold. The team lead suggests simply accepting the risk to stay on schedule. What should the project manager do?
options: Accept the risk within the team, since staying on schedule is the project's highest priority
Document the risk and continue the work without informing leadership about it
Stop the project indefinitely until the safety risk has been fully eliminated
Escalate the trade-off to the sponsor, since it exceeds the organization's risk threshold
questions.explanation:
Concept: When to escalate — escalate when a decision exceeds the team's authority, the organization's risk tolerance, or requires a strategic trade-off (Rule M5-B01-R03).
Spot it: A safety risk "above the organization's stated threshold," and a suggestion to just accept it.
In this scenario: The risk exceeds the stated threshold, so the PM escalates the schedule-versus-safety trade-off to the sponsor.
Why not the others: The team cannot accept a risk above tolerance; documenting without telling leadership hides it; an indefinite stop is a decision the PM does not own either.
Remember: Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act → Monitor → ESCALATE — above threshold = escalate.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid project's team lead has built a pricing rule that changes customer discounts, a change that requires pricing-committee approval. He wants to deploy it this week and "get the paperwork signed afterward," since the committee meets next month. What should the project manager do?
options: Deploy the rule now and request committee approval at next month's scheduled meeting
Hold deployment and request committee approval, using an expedited review if available
Deploy the rule to a few customers and seek approval only if the results look good
Cancel the pricing rule, since the committee may decide not to approve it at all
questions.explanation:
Concept: Governance before implementation — changes that need approval are approved first; do not implement and ask for ratification later (Rule M5-B01-R06).
Spot it: "Deploy this week and get the paperwork signed afterward," and a committee that must approve.
In this scenario: The PM holds deployment and requests committee approval, using an expedited review if the process allows.
Why not the others: Deploy-then-approve bypasses governance; a limited release is still unapproved implementation; cancelling assumes rejection without asking.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → APPROVE → Implement — never Implement → Approve.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: On a predictive program, change control board decisions take an average of six weeks per change request, and teams have started making changes without submitting them. The sponsor is concerned about both the delays and the uncontrolled changes. What should the project manager do?
options: Discipline the teams that bypassed the change control board to restore compliance
Allow teams to make changes freely, since the board is simply too slow to be useful
Review the board's process, thresholds, and membership to find why decisions stall
Add more approval steps so that every change the teams make is caught and reviewed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Governance effectiveness — when decisions are repeatedly delayed or bypassed, review the governance process itself (Rule M5-B01-R10).
Spot it: Slow decisions (six weeks), teams working around the process, and a sponsor worried about both.
In this scenario: The PM reviews the change control board's process, thresholds and membership to find why decisions stall, for example by delegating small changes.
Why not the others: Discipline treats the symptom; letting teams change freely abandons control; more approval steps make the bottleneck worse.
Remember: Bypassing is a SYMPTOM — fix the process, then enforce it.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid project has delivered a new customer-onboarding platform. The sponsor, pleased with the team's work, proposes keeping the project team in place indefinitely to process daily onboarding requests and routine updates. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Keep the project open indefinitely so the team can handle daily requests
Start a new project each month to cover that month's onboarding requests
Transition daily processing to an operations team and close the project
Shut the platform down until a permanent project team can be funded
questions.explanation:
Concept: Projects vs operations — a project is temporary and creates something unique; operations sustain ongoing, repetitive business work (Rule M5-B09-R04).
Spot it: A delivered product, and a proposal to keep the project team doing "daily" and "routine" work "indefinitely."
In this scenario: The PM recommends transitioning daily processing to an operations team and formally closing the project.
Why not the others: Keeping the project open forever violates its temporary nature; monthly projects are just operations in disguise; shutting the platform down throws away the value.
Remember: Project = Temporary + Unique; Operations = Ongoing + Repetitive. Complete → Accept → Transfer → Close.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A portfolio office reports that all eight predictive projects in a digital-transformation program finished on time and on budget. Yet the program's goal of reducing customer churn by 15 percent has not moved. The board asks whether the program succeeded. What should the project manager say?
options: The program succeeded, since all eight projects met their schedule and cost baselines
Program success depends on achieving the churn benefit, not only project delivery metrics
The program failed, since the individual projects must have been poorly managed
Program success cannot be judged until every future project is also completed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Program success — programs are judged by the benefits they deliver, not only by whether their projects met schedule and budget (Rule M5-B09-R07).
Spot it: All projects "on time and on budget," but the program's business goal has not moved.
In this scenario: Churn has not dropped, so the program has not yet achieved its purpose, even though project delivery succeeded.
Why not the others: Project metrics alone miss the benefit; blaming project management assumes a cause without evidence; success can be judged now against the target benefit.
Remember: Project = OUTPUTS; Program = BENEFITS; Portfolio = STRATEGY.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid project will deliver a new warehouse routing system expected to cut picking time by 20 percent within a year. The project closes next month, and no one has been named to track or deliver that benefit after handover. What should the project manager do?
options: Confirm a business owner accountable for realizing and measuring the picking-time benefit
Continue tracking the benefit personally as project manager after the project has closed
Assume the warehouse will realize the benefit automatically once the system goes live
Delay project closure until the full 20 percent improvement has been achieved
questions.explanation:
Concept: Benefit ownership — someone in the business must own realizing and measuring benefits after the project closes (Rule M5-B09-R09).
Spot it: A benefit expected after handover, and "no one has been named" to track it.
In this scenario: The PM confirms a business owner, such as the warehouse operations manager, who is accountable for delivering and measuring the picking-time benefit.
Why not the others: The PM's role ends at closure; benefits do not happen automatically; delaying closure keeps the project open for work that belongs to operations.
Remember: Output → Outcome → Benefit → Value → OWNER.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A predictive project is selecting a heating system for a new school. Option 1 has the lowest purchase price but high energy use and a 10-year life; Option 2 costs 15 percent more upfront but uses 40 percent less energy and lasts 25 years. What should the project manager do?
options: Compare lifecycle cost, energy use, waste, and resilience rather than upfront price alone
Select Option 1, since it has the lowest purchase price and fits within the project budget
Select Option 2, since sustainability should override every cost consideration
Defer the choice to the heating contractor, who knows the available systems best
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sustainable trade-offs — compare options on lifecycle cost, resource use, waste and resilience, not only on upfront price (Rule M5-B06-R05).
Spot it: The cheapest purchase with higher running costs and shorter life vs a pricier, efficient, longer-lived option.
In this scenario: The PM compares total lifecycle cost, energy use, waste and resilience for both heating systems before recommending one.
Why not the others: Lowest purchase price ignores decades of operating cost; "sustainability overrides everything" is not a balanced trade-off; the contractor should not own the owner's value decision.
Remember: Impact → Alternatives → Criteria → Balance → Monitor — think LIFECYCLE, not price tag.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid project is redesigning a food company's packaging. The team's sustainability review lists only threats, such as new plastic regulations. A marketing analyst notes that major retailers are offering premium shelf space for recyclable packaging. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the review focused on threats, since regulatory compliance is the main concern
Treat the retailer offer as a marketing matter and leave it out of the risk register
Adopt recyclable packaging now without first assessing its cost or feasibility
Add the premium shelf-space offer to the risk register as an opportunity to assess
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sustainability opportunities — sustainability can create positive risks (opportunities) as well as threats, and both belong in risk management (Rule M5-B06-R08).
Spot it: A review listing "only threats," and a clear upside (premium shelf space for recyclable packaging).
In this scenario: The PM adds the shelf-space offer to the risk register as an opportunity and assesses it for a response such as exploit or enhance.
Why not the others: Threat-only reviews miss value; calling it "just marketing" ignores a project opportunity; adopting it without assessment skips analysis.
Remember: Risk = uncertainty, UP or DOWN — Threats and Opportunities both go in the register.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A predictive project upgrading an airline's crew-scheduling system has funding for 5 of 9 remaining work packages this year. The operations vice president wants her team's packages first and others want the easiest ones done. Some packages reduce major compliance risks, and two are prerequisites for others. How should the project manager prioritize?
options: Complete the operations vice president's packages first, since she is the most senior requester
Complete the easiest packages first to show stakeholders quick and visible progress
Score each package on value, risk reduction, dependencies, and strategic fit, then rank them
Complete the packages in the order in which they appear in the WBS dictionary
questions.explanation:
Concept: Value-based prioritization — rank work by expected value, risk reduction, learning, dependencies and strategic importance (Rule M5-B11-R01).
Spot it: More work than funding, a senior requester, pressure for "easy wins," compliance risks and prerequisites.
In this scenario: The PM scores each work package on value, risk reduction, dependencies and strategic fit, then funds the top five.
Why not the others: Seniority is not value; easy work may not reduce risk or unlock others; WBS dictionary order is a description tool, not a ranking.
Remember: Prioritize by VALUE, RISK, DEPENDENCY — not by rank or ease.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: On a hybrid project, marketing wants a March launch, legal requires full accessibility compliance before launch, and finance has capped the budget. The team has shown that all three cannot be met together. What should the project manager do?
options: Commit to all three goals and ask the team to find some way to deliver them all
Present options showing what each choice gains and gives up, and obtain a decision
Quietly drop accessibility work, since it is the hardest to notice at launch
Let each stakeholder negotiate privately with the team for their own priority
questions.explanation:
Concept: Explicit trade-offs — when not every goal can be met, make the choices visible and get a decision from the right authority (Rule M5-B11-R02).
Spot it: Conflicting demands (date, compliance, budget), and evidence that "all three cannot be met."
In this scenario: The PM presents options showing what each choice gains and gives up, and obtains a decision from the sponsor or governance body.
Why not the others: Committing to the impossible sets up failure; quietly dropping legally required accessibility is unethical and noncompliant; private negotiations create hidden, conflicting deals.
Remember: Impossible triangle? Show the OPTIONS → the sponsor DECIDES.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice
