questions.stem: A predictive project upgrading a chemical plant's control system is running short of budget. Remaining work includes a legally required emergency-shutdown upgrade, a new operator dashboard requested by management, and cosmetic control-room renovations. What should the project manager prioritize?
options: The operator dashboard, since management requested it and it is highly visible
The emergency-shutdown upgrade first, then discretionary items as funds allow
All three equally, reducing each one's scope to fit the remaining budget
The renovations, since they are the cheapest and can be finished quickly
questions.explanation:
Concept: Mandatory before discretionary — legal, compliance and safety requirements are protected before nice-to-have enhancements (Rule M5-B11-R03).
Spot it: Budget shortfall plus one item that is "legally required" or safety-related.
In this scenario: The PM prioritizes the emergency-shutdown upgrade first, then the dashboard and renovations as funds allow.
Why not the others: The dashboard is visible but optional; an equal cut could leave the safety upgrade incomplete; cheap cosmetic work first spends money on low value.
Remember: MUST (legal/safety) → SHOULD → COULD.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A predictive project is 70 percent through building a proprietary document system. A vendor now offers an equivalent product at one-tenth of the remaining cost, and updated analysis shows that finishing the build no longer justifies the investment. The team argues that most of the money is already spent. What should the project manager do?
options: Complete the build, since most of the budget has already been spent on it
Switch to the vendor product without consulting the governance board
Pause the project quietly and wait for the sponsor to notice the change
Recommend to the governance board that the build be stopped or redirected
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stopping or redirecting through governance — when future value no longer justifies continued investment, recommend stopping or redirecting to the proper governance body (Rule M5-B11-R06).
Spot it: A cheaper alternative, updated analysis showing poor value, and "most of the money is already spent."
In this scenario: The PM recommends to the governance board that the build be stopped or redirected to the vendor product.
Why not the others: "Already spent" is the sunk-cost fallacy; switching without the board bypasses governance; pausing quietly hides key information.
Remember: Decide on FUTURE value, not past spending — Sunk cost is SUNK.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A predictive project last year delivered a self-service kiosk system that was prioritized over other work because it was expected to cut in-store wait times by 30 percent. The portfolio committee is now setting next year's priorities. What should the project manager provide?
options: A report confirming the kiosks were delivered on time and on budget
A list of new kiosk features that stakeholders have requested since launch
Project team satisfaction survey results about the delivery experience
Data comparing actual wait-time reductions with the 30 percent expected
questions.explanation:
Concept: Benefits tracking — check whether prioritized work actually delivered its expected value, and use that evidence in future prioritization (Rule M5-B11-R10).
Spot it: Work prioritized for a specific expected benefit, and a new round of prioritization.
In this scenario: The PM provides data comparing actual wait-time reduction with the 30% target so the committee can calibrate future choices.
Why not the others: On-time, on-budget delivery is output, not value; new feature requests are not evidence of value; team satisfaction measures the process, not the benefit.
Remember: Output → Outcome → Benefit → Value — measure the BENEFIT you promised.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: The test environment for an agile payments team has gone down three times in the last two sprints. Each time, a developer quietly borrowed another team's environment and kept working, so the outages never came up in any team event. The servant leader has just learned about the pattern. What should the servant leader do NEXT?
options: Ask the developer who borrowed the environment to own all future environment workarounds for the team.
Put the outages on the team's impediment board and work with the platform group on the recurring cause.
Have the team lower its sprint commitments so environment outages no longer threaten the sprint goal.
Escalate the outages to the CIO and request funding for a dedicated environment for the team this quarter.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Impediment visibility — a servant leader makes blockers visible to the whole team and fixes the recurring cause, not just today's symptom (Rule M3-B12-R09).
Spot it: An outage or blocker that keeps coming back; quiet workarounds; the problem never shows up at stand-up or retrospective.
In this scenario: Three outages in two sprints is a pattern. Putting it on the impediment board makes it visible, and working with the platform group attacks the root cause of the unstable environment.
Why not the others: Making one developer own the workarounds normalizes a hidden problem; lowering commitments hides the impediment instead of removing it; jumping to the CIO for funding escalates before the cause is even understood.
Remember: Hidden impediments never get fixed. See it, show it, solve the cause. Servant leader removes obstacles — never waits, never ignores.

questions.stem: On a hospital construction project, a site engineer's drawings have missed the review deadline four times, delaying two work packages. During the weekly status meeting with 12 people present, a senior client representative asks the project manager who is responsible for the delays. How should the project manager respond?
options: Name the engineer in the meeting so the client representative knows exactly where the accountability sits.
Add a note about the engineer's missed deadlines to the status report sent to all project stakeholders.
Quietly reassign the engineer's drawings to a colleague without discussing the performance issue at all.
Report the schedule impact to the group and address the engineer's performance in a private conversation.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Dignity in performance management — praise in public, correct in private; the group needs the project impact, the individual gets a confidential conversation (Rule M3-B03-R10).
Spot it: A performance problem raised in a big meeting; a senior person asking "who is to blame?"; a temptation to name names.
In this scenario: The client deserves the facts about the schedule impact and recovery, so the PM reports that openly. The engineer's missed deadlines are handled one-on-one, where the PM can learn the cause and agree on support.
Why not the others: Naming the engineer in front of 12 people shames him and damages trust; putting it in a widely distributed status report does the same in writing; quietly reassigning his work avoids the conversation and fixes nothing.
Remember: Problem with ONE person = ONE-ON-ONE conversation, never a public announcement.

questions.stem: A consumer electronics program uses a predictive plan for hardware and adaptive teams for the companion app. A supplier delay means two features must be cut from the first release, which will break commitments sales directors made to key retailers. The sales directors are already frustrated and the retail announcements go out in ten days. How should the project manager communicate the change?
options: Hold a live video session with the sales directors to explain the trade-off and work through their concerns.
Include the revised release scope in the weekly status email so every stakeholder gets the same message.
Post the revised feature list on the program wiki and let the sales directors know that it is available there.
Ask the app teams to show the feature cut at their next review so sales hears it directly from the builders.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Choosing the communication method — match the method to urgency, complexity, sensitivity and audience; sensitive, emotional news needs interactive, live communication (Rule M3-B07-R01).
Spot it: Bad news, frustrated senior stakeholders, broken commitments, a trade-off to explain, a short deadline.
In this scenario: The sales directors are upset, the change affects promises they made to retailers, and they have only ten days. A live session lets the PM explain the trade-off, hear concerns and agree on how to handle the retailers.
Why not the others: A weekly status email is push communication — too impersonal for upset senior stakeholders; a wiki post is pull communication and they may never read it; having the teams reveal the cut at a review delegates hard news to the builders.
Remember: Sensitive or complex = INTERACTIVE. Must reach known people = PUSH. Big reference library = PULL.

questions.stem: Two developers on an agile team have traded increasingly terse comments on a pull request about whether to adopt an event-driven design. The thread is now 40 messages long with no resolution, and three user stories are blocked until the design question is settled. What should the team facilitator do NEXT?
options: Ask each developer to write a formal position paper so the lead architect can review both and then decide.
Post a reminder in the thread asking both developers to keep their written comments professional.
Bring both developers together for a short whiteboard session to work through the design options live.
Let the thread continue so the two developers reach consensus on their own without any facilitation.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Interactive communication for conflict and complex decisions — when written back-and-forth is stuck, bring people together to talk it through live (Rule M3-B07-R02).
Spot it: Long email or comment threads, terse tone, no resolution, work blocked while people argue.
In this scenario: Forty messages and three blocked stories show that text has stopped working. A short whiteboard session lets the two developers explore the design options together and reach a decision the team can act on.
Why not the others: Position papers add more writing and hand the decision away from the team; a reminder to be professional addresses tone, not the stalled decision; letting the thread run on leaves the stories blocked.
Remember: Conflict or ambiguity? Stop typing, start talking — interactive beats push and pull.

questions.stem: The project manager for a clinic renovation receives a revised fire-inspection date from the city. The six subcontractor leads must adjust their crew schedules by Friday or the inspection will fail and the occupancy permit will slip. Which communication approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Upload the revised date to the project document repository for subcontractor leads to check.
Hold a full-day workshop with every subcontractor crew to walk through the complete revised schedule.
Email the revised date directly to the six subcontractor leads and ask each one to confirm receipt.
Raise the revised date at the monthly steering committee so sponsors can pass it to subcontractors.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Push communication — information sent directly to specific, known recipients who must act on it; confirming receipt closes the loop (Rule M3-B07-R03).
Spot it: A short, specific message; named recipients; a hard deadline; consequences if someone misses it.
In this scenario: Six known subcontractor leads must change crew schedules by Friday. Emailing them directly and asking for confirmation makes sure each one actually got the new inspection date in time to act.
Why not the others: A document repository is pull communication, so leads may never check it; a full-day workshop is far too heavy for one date change; routing it through the monthly steering committee is slow and indirect.
Remember: Known people + must act = PUSH it to them and confirm receipt.

questions.stem: A company is rolling out a new ERP system, with predictive deployment waves and adaptive configuration teams. The project has produced over 300 configuration guides, test scripts, and training videos. Super-users at 14 sites need different pieces at different times as their sites go live over the next nine months. What is the BEST way to make these materials available?
options: Publish the materials in a searchable knowledge portal that super-users can open whenever they need.
Email the full set of guides and videos to every super-user each time a new site prepares to go live.
Walk through all of the materials with super-users on a weekly two-hour live training call.
Have super-users request specific documents from the project coordinator when a question comes up.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Pull communication — a large body of reference information stored where people can get what they need, when they need it (Rule M3-B07-R04).
Spot it: Hundreds of documents; many users; different needs at different times; a long time span.
In this scenario: Super-users at 14 sites go live over nine months and each needs different guides at different times. A searchable knowledge portal lets each one pull exactly the material they need when their site is ready.
Why not the others: Emailing the whole set each time floods people with material they don't need; weekly two-hour calls cannot cover 300 items for 14 different timelines; routing requests through one coordinator creates a bottleneck.
Remember: Big library + many users + "as needed" = PULL (portal, repository, wiki).

questions.stem: In a refinement session, a product owner tells the agile team that the new invoicing feature must handle "the updated tax rules." An incorrect implementation would expose the company to regulatory penalties. Team members nod and move to the next item without asking questions. What should the agile coach encourage the team to do?
options: Start building and rely on the review at the end of the sprint to catch any misunderstanding.
Ask the product owner to send an email repeating the requirement to all members of the team.
Have the most senior developer interpret the tax rules on the team's behalf during development.
Restate the tax requirements as acceptance criteria and check them with the product owner.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Confirming understanding — when a misunderstanding would be costly, check that the message was received as intended instead of assuming silence means agreement (Rule M3-B07-R05).
Spot it: Vague wording ("the updated tax rules"), high stakes such as regulatory penalties, people nodding without questions.
In this scenario: The team has not shown it understands which tax rules apply. Turning the requirement into acceptance criteria and reviewing them with the product owner exposes gaps before any code is written.
Why not the others: Waiting for the sprint review finds the misunderstanding only after the work is built; an email repeating the same vague phrase confirms nothing; letting one senior developer interpret the rules replaces the product owner's intent with a guess.
Remember: Silence is not understanding. High stakes = restate it, confirm it, then build it.

questions.stem: The project manager for a data center migration learns from a vendor that a critical network switch will arrive four weeks late. The delay will push cutover past the date the sponsor committed to a major client. The next scheduled steering committee meeting is three weeks away. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Wait for the steering committee meeting so the delay can be presented along with a full recovery plan.
Tell the sponsor about the delay and its impact now so options can be weighed before the client date.
Ask the vendor to try expediting the shipment before telling the sponsor anything about the delay.
Update the schedule baseline to the new arrival date and mention the change in the next report.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Early bad news — share bad news as soon as it is known so stakeholders still have time to choose options (Rule M3-B07-R06).
Spot it: A known delay, a commitment to an external client at risk, the next scheduled meeting is weeks away.
In this scenario: The switch is four weeks late and the steering committee meets in three weeks. Telling the sponsor now gives the sponsor time to talk with the client and weigh recovery options while they still matter.
Why not the others: Waiting for the meeting wastes three weeks of decision time; asking the vendor to expedite first delays the sponsor's awareness; changing the schedule baseline without approval skips change control.
Remember: Bad news does not improve with age. Tell early, tell the decision-maker, then work the options.

questions.stem: A hybrid program's monthly report stated, "Integration will finish in June." Executives later learned that the date depended on a vendor delivering an API in April, which had never been confirmed. The sponsor asks the project manager to prevent this kind of confusion in future reports. What should the project manager change?
options: Drop forward-looking dates from the report so executives see only work that is complete.
Add task-level detail for every team so executives can derive the forecasts on their own.
Label each report item as a confirmed fact, a forecast, a pending decision, or an assumption.
Report only the most conservative date for each milestone so that executives are never surprised.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Transparent status reporting — separate what is a confirmed fact, a forecast, a pending decision and an assumption so readers know how much to trust each statement (Rule M3-B07-R07).
Spot it: Executives surprised by a hidden dependency; a date stated as certain that rested on an unconfirmed assumption.
In this scenario: The June date looked like a fact but depended on an unconfirmed vendor API. Labeling each report item by type lets executives see immediately which dates are solid and which rest on assumptions.
Why not the others: Dropping forward-looking dates removes what executives need for decisions; task-level detail buries them in data; reporting only the most conservative dates distorts the truth in the other direction.
Remember: Fact, forecast, decision, assumption — label it so nobody mistakes a hope for a promise.

questions.stem: An agile team's release has a fixed date, and two key features are only about 60 percent complete, putting the date at risk. The delivery lead has five minutes on the board's agenda tomorrow and will give the product stakeholders a full walkthrough at the review later in the week. What should the delivery lead tell the board?
options: Give a short summary stating that the release date is at risk and naming the two features affected.
Report that the release is on track because the team still hopes to recover in the final sprint.
Walk the board through the full burndown data and the story-level detail the team reviewed last week.
Leave the risk out of the board update and share it only with stakeholders attending the review.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tailoring the message — adjust the level of detail to the audience, but never change the underlying truth (Rule M3-B07-R08).
Spot it: A short slot with executives, a fuller review later with working-level stakeholders, a real risk to report.
In this scenario: The board has five minutes, so it needs a brief, honest summary: the date is at risk and these two features are behind. The full detail belongs in the review later in the week.
Why not the others: Saying "on track" because the team hopes to recover hides a known risk; a full burndown walkthrough is the wrong depth for a five-minute board slot; leaving the risk out for the board withholds the truth from the people who fund the work.
Remember: Shorter for executives, deeper for the team — but the same truth for both.

questions.stem: After a heated disagreement, a project manager mediates between the mechanical and electrical leads on a factory expansion over who owns cable tray installation. They agree that the electrical crew will install the trays and the mechanical crew will provide the supports by week 12. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Rely on the verbal agreement, since written notes might reopen the disagreement between the leads.
Send the agreement to the sponsor for approval before either lead begins any cable tray activity.
Schedule another mediation session in two weeks to check that both leads still accept the deal.
Record who owns each task and the week 12 date, and share it with both leads and affected crews.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Documenting agreements from conflict resolution — once a conflict is settled, write down who owns what and by when, and share it with everyone affected (Rule M3-B01-R09).
Spot it: A dispute just resolved verbally, ownership of a task, a specific date commitment, crews who depend on the outcome.
In this scenario: The leads agreed on ownership of the cable trays and the week 12 support date. Recording it and sharing it with both leads and their crews turns a verbal deal into a clear commitment nobody can later remember differently.
Why not the others: Relying on a verbal agreement invites the same argument later; sending a within-authority team decision to the sponsor escalates without need; another mediation session reopens a question already settled.
Remember: Resolved + recorded + shared = it stays resolved.

questions.stem: A hybrid team faces two decisions this month: choosing the color scheme for a pilot web app built adaptively, and signing a five-year data hosting contract with heavy exit penalties. The team is spending the same amount of analysis effort on both. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Use the same formal evaluation for both decisions so the team applies a consistent process.
Settle the color scheme quickly and adjust it later, and give the hosting contract deeper analysis.
Defer both decisions until the pilot ends so that real usage data can inform each of them equally.
Sign the hosting contract quickly to lock in pricing and run extended tests on the color scheme.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reversible vs hard-to-reverse decisions — spend analysis effort in proportion to how costly a decision is to undo (Rule M3-B13-R01).
Spot it: One easily changed choice and one locked-in commitment; long contracts with exit penalties; equal effort spent on both.
In this scenario: A color scheme in an adaptive pilot can change next sprint, so decide it fast and learn. A five-year hosting contract with heavy penalties is hard to exit, so it deserves careful analysis.
Why not the others: One formal evaluation for both wastes effort on the trivial choice; deferring both delays even the easy decision; rushing the contract while over-testing colors gets the balance exactly backwards.
Remember: Two-way door: decide fast. One-way door: slow down and analyze.

questions.stem: An agile team must choose between two caching libraries. A one-day spike showed both meet the performance targets, and either library could be swapped out within a single sprint if needed. One developer wants two more weeks of benchmarking before the team commits. What should the team do?
options: Pick one library based on the spike and revisit the choice if production metrics show problems.
Complete two more weeks of benchmarking so the team can be fully certain it picks the best library.
Ask the product owner to select the library since the choice affects the delivery timeline.
Build the feature with both libraries in parallel so they can be compared in real conditions.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Enough information, not perfect information — decide once the evidence is good enough and the choice is cheap to reverse (Rule M3-B13-R02).
Spot it: A spike already answered the key question; the option can be swapped in one sprint; someone wants weeks more analysis.
In this scenario: Both libraries met the performance targets and either can be replaced within a sprint. The team should choose, move on, and watch production metrics in case it needs to revisit the choice.
Why not the others: Two more weeks of benchmarking buys certainty the team does not need; handing a technical choice to the product owner confuses WHAT with HOW; building with both libraries doubles the work for little learning.
Remember: Good enough + easy to reverse = decide and inspect. Product owner decides WHAT, team decides HOW.

questions.stem: Managers on a warehouse redesign project have debated for three weeks whether a new conveyor arrangement will reduce picking time. Building a physical mock-up in an unused bay with rented equipment would cost about $4,000 and take three days. Detailed design is on hold until the question is settled. What should the project manager do?
options: Schedule another facilitated meeting so each manager can present their arguments one more time.
Ask the sponsor to choose a layout so the detailed design phase can proceed without more delay.
Propose building the low-cost mock-up to measure picking time before the detailed design is final.
Hire an outside consultant to prepare a detailed written study comparing the two conveyor arrangements.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Learning by experiment — when a cheap prototype or test can answer a question, build it instead of debating opinions (Rule M3-B13-R03).
Spot it: Weeks of debate, a question that data could settle, a low-cost and quick way to test it, work stalled waiting for the answer.
In this scenario: A $4,000, three-day mock-up can measure picking time directly. That ends the three-week debate with evidence before detailed design locks in the layout.
Why not the others: Another meeting repeats the same opinions; asking the sponsor to pick a layout decides without evidence; a consultant's paper study is slower and still does not test the real arrangement.
Remember: When learning is cheaper than arguing — prototype it, measure it, decide.

questions.stem: A hybrid team is planning a mobile app release for a retail chain. The go-live plan depends on store Wi-Fi upgrades that the facilities department says "should be done" by March, but nobody has confirmed the date. The project manager must present the release plan to leadership tomorrow. What should the project manager do?
options: Present the plan as final, since facilities indicated the Wi-Fi upgrades should finish by March.
Postpone the presentation until facilities gives written confirmation of the Wi-Fi completion date.
Remove the Wi-Fi dependency from the plan because another department is responsible for that work.
Present the plan with Wi-Fi readiness shown as an assumption, with an owner and a date to validate it.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Making assumptions explicit — when evidence is incomplete, state the assumption openly, give it an owner and set a date to validate it (Rule M3-B13-R04).
Spot it: "should be done," nobody has confirmed, a plan depends on another group's work, a presentation is due soon.
In this scenario: The release depends on unconfirmed Wi-Fi upgrades. Showing that as a labeled assumption with an owner and a validation date gives leadership an honest plan and makes the dependency visible.
Why not the others: Presenting the plan as final hides an unconfirmed dependency; postponing the presentation stalls leadership over one open item; deleting the dependency because another department owns it ignores a real risk.
Remember: Unconfirmed = ASSUMPTION. Log it, own it, validate it. Assumptions must be reassessed when conditions change.

questions.stem: Three months ago, an agile team decided to build its own reporting module because the only commercial product was far too expensive. A new vendor now offers a comparable product at about a quarter of that price. The team is roughly halfway through building the module. What should the team do?
options: Keep building, since the choice was already made and significant effort has been invested.
Reassess the build-or-buy choice with the product owner using the new vendor's pricing.
Stop building right away and buy the new vendor's product to capture the lower price.
Record the new vendor in the lessons learned so it can be considered on later projects.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Revisiting decisions — when the facts behind a decision change significantly, reassess the decision instead of defending it (Rule M3-B13-R05).
Spot it: A new vendor, a big price drop, conditions different from when the choice was made, work already halfway done.
In this scenario: The build choice rested on the commercial product being too expensive. That assumption changed, so the team and product owner should reassess build versus buy with the new pricing, including what has already been built.
Why not the others: Continuing because effort is already spent is the sunk cost trap; stopping at once and buying skips the analysis; filing it as a lesson for later projects ignores a decision that matters now.
Remember: Constraint or assumption changes → assess impact → adjust. Sunk cost is not a reason.

questions.stem: A project manager must recommend a site for a new regional distribution center. Three site proposals have arrived, and each senior stakeholder is championing a different one based on a single feature they happen to like. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Agree on weighted selection criteria with the stakeholders before the proposals are compared.
Compare the three proposals side by side and let stakeholders vote for the one they prefer.
Select the proposal favored by the most senior stakeholder to shorten the decision process.
Request more detail from all three bidders so stakeholders have additional data to review.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Decision criteria first — agree on how options will be judged before comparing them, so the choice is objective rather than a contest of favorites (Rule M3-B13-R06).
Spot it: Several stakeholders each backing a different option for one feature they like; no agreed basis for comparison.
In this scenario: Each stakeholder is judging by a different single feature. Agreeing on weighted criteria first gives everyone the same yardstick, and then the three sites can be compared fairly.
Why not the others: Comparing and voting without criteria just counts favorites; picking the most senior person's choice is decision by power; asking bidders for more detail adds data but still gives no way to weigh it.
Remember: Criteria BEFORE comparison — agree on the ruler, then measure.

questions.stem: A hybrid program's architecture board decided during a meeting to host all customer data in a single region instead of the proposed multi-region design, mainly to cut cost. The choice will affect disaster recovery and compliance for years. The only record is informal meeting chat. What should the project manager do?
options: Treat the meeting chat as the record, since every board member attended and agreed.
Ask the adaptive teams to capture the decision in their user stories as they build it.
Record the decision, the alternatives considered, and the cost reasoning in the decision log.
Email the teams a brief note announcing the single-region choice and move ahead.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Decision log — record high-impact decisions with the alternatives considered and the reasoning so future teams understand why (Rule M3-B13-R07).
Spot it: A long-lasting architecture or compliance choice; the only record is informal chat; cost was the main driver.
In this scenario: Single-region hosting will affect disaster recovery and compliance for years. Recording the decision, the multi-region alternative and the cost rationale in the decision log keeps it traceable when someone later asks why.
Why not the others: Informal chat gets lost and holds no rationale; user stories describe what to build, not why an architecture was chosen; a brief email announces the choice without the alternatives or reasoning.
Remember: Big decision → log it with WHAT, WHY and WHAT ELSE was considered.

questions.stem: Although user research was inconclusive, a product owner decided to replace a five-step onboarding flow with a single-page form. The agile team will release the change this week. The product owner asks how the team will know quickly whether the decision was a good one. What should the team recommend?
options: Wait for the quarterly revenue report to judge whether the new onboarding flow succeeded.
Treat the decision as validated once the release passes all acceptance tests in staging.
Ask team members at the next retrospective whether they believe the new flow was right.
Track early signals such as sign-up completion and drop-off rates in the days after release.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Leading indicators — after an uncertain decision, watch early signals that show quickly whether it is working (Rule M3-B13-R10).
Spot it: Inconclusive research, a decision just released, "how will we know quickly?"
In this scenario: Sign-up completion and drop-off rates show within days whether the single-page form helps users. The team can then adapt fast instead of waiting months for lagging results.
Why not the others: Quarterly revenue is a lagging indicator that arrives far too late; passing acceptance tests proves it works, not that users like it; asking the team for opinions replaces data with guesses.
Remember: Lagging tells you what happened; LEADING tells you in time to change it.

questions.stem: A project manager overseeing a plant upgrade must choose between shutting down a production line for 10 days or spreading the work across weekends for three months. The engineering lead strongly favors the shutdown. Operations, safety, and sales have not yet been consulted. What should the project manager do?
options: Approve the shutdown, since the engineering lead knows the upgrade work better than anyone.
Get input from operations, safety, and sales on both options before the decision is made.
Choose weekend phasing because it avoids disrupting production during the upgrade work.
Ask the sponsor to decide based on the engineering lead's recommendation and rationale.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Seeking diverse perspectives — before a high-impact decision, hear from every group the decision will affect, not just the loudest expert (Rule M3-B10-R08).
Spot it: One strong recommendation; major groups not consulted; big trade-offs such as downtime versus a long disruption.
In this scenario: The shutdown affects operations, safety and sales, and none of them has been asked. Getting their input on both options gives the PM a complete picture of impact before choosing.
Why not the others: Approving the engineer's choice ignores other impacts; choosing weekend phasing without input is just as one-sided; passing it to the sponsor with only the engineer's view escalates with half the facts.
Remember: Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act. Collaborate means everyone affected.

questions.stem: A hybrid program requires every change to its regulated reporting module to pass a formal impact assessment. A senior vice president asks the project manager to have an adaptive team add a field to the module next week without the assessment, saying the change is tiny. Similar requests from junior managers have gone through the assessment. What should the project manager do?
options: Send the request through the same impact assessment that every other module change receives.
Allow the change this once, since the vice president has authority and the change looks small.
Have the team add the field quietly and complete the impact assessment after it is released.
Refuse the request outright and report the vice president to the ethics office for misconduct.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Consistent rules — apply the same process to everyone regardless of their rank or power; fairness is a core ethical duty (Rule M3-B16-R09).
Spot it: A senior person asking for an exception, "it's tiny," a regulated area, juniors already following the rule.
In this scenario: Every change to the regulated module gets an impact assessment. The PM routes the vice president's request through the same assessment — respectfully and without delay.
Why not the others: Allowing it "this once" makes the rule depend on rank; adding the field quietly bypasses control on a regulated module; refusing and reporting the vice president for misconduct is an overreaction to a request.
Remember: Same rule, every rank. Assess the change — no matter who asks.

questions.stem: On an agile team, only one developer understands the legacy billing integration, and she picks up every story that touches it. In a recent conversation she mentioned she is considering a transfer to another department next quarter. What should the team facilitator do FIRST?
options: Ask her manager to block the transfer until the billing integration is replaced by the team.
Wait for the transfer to be confirmed and then ask her to write documentation during notice.
Work with the team to identify what billing knowledge only she holds and plan how to spread it.
Route all remaining billing stories to her so the work is done before she might leave the team.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Knowledge single points of failure — find knowledge that only one person holds and spread it before that person leaves (Rule M3-B11-R01).
Spot it: Only one person understands a system; they take every related task; they may be leaving.
In this scenario: The developer might transfer next quarter. Identifying what only she knows and planning pairing, rotation and documentation now protects the team before the risk becomes an issue.
Why not the others: Blocking her transfer harms her career and does not fix the risk; waiting for confirmation leaves too little time; sending her every billing story deepens the single point of failure.
Remember: Someone may leave = KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER now. Never negotiate to retain them.

questions.stem: On a power plant maintenance project, a retiring technician is the only person who can calibrate a legacy turbine control system. He says the job depends on judgment built over 30 years that the manuals do not capture. His replacement starts next month, and they will overlap for six weeks. What is the BEST knowledge transfer approach?
options: Ask the retiring technician to write a detailed calibration manual before the new hire arrives.
Have the new technician observe calibrations, then perform them under the veteran's supervision.
Send the new technician to the manufacturer's general training course on turbine control systems.
Record an interview with the retiring technician describing his methods for the new hire to review.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Transferring tacit knowledge — skills built from experience and judgment transfer best through shadowing, demonstration and supervised practice (Rule M3-B11-R02).
Spot it: "judgment built over 30 years," manuals do not capture it, an overlap period with the replacement.
In this scenario: Calibration depends on the veteran's judgment. Six weeks of watching and then doing the work under supervision lets the new technician build that judgment with feedback.
Why not the others: A written manual captures explicit steps but not judgment; a general manufacturer course does not cover this legacy system's quirks; a recorded interview is passive and cannot give feedback on real work.
Remember: Explicit knowledge → document it. Tacit knowledge → show it, shadow it, practice it.

questions.stem: A hybrid team created a vendor onboarding checklist and a data migration playbook that several other programs could reuse. Right now the files sit in the team's private chat channel and on individual laptops. The project closes in two months, and the team will then disband. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the files in the team channel so anyone who needs them can ask a team member for access.
Attach the files to the final project report that is archived with the closed project records.
Email the checklist and playbook to program managers the team knows are starting similar work.
Move the checklist and playbook into the organization's shared knowledge repository with clear tags.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Organizational knowledge repository — store reusable assets where future teams can find them, not in private channels or personal laptops (Rule M3-B11-R03).
Spot it: Reusable checklists or playbooks, files scattered in chats and laptops, the team about to disband.
In this scenario: Other programs could reuse the checklist and playbook. Moving them into the shared repository with clear tags makes them organizational process assets that survive after the team is gone.
Why not the others: Keeping them in the team channel depends on people who are leaving; burying them in an archived final report makes them hard to find; emailing a few known managers misses everyone else.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close. Learn means stored where others can find it.

questions.stem: Midway through a nine-month effort, an agile team discovered that a third-party API has undocumented rate limits that caused a production outage. Working out a fix took three days. Two other teams in the organization are starting to use the same API next month. What should the team do?
options: Record the lesson now, while details are fresh, and share it with the teams adopting the same API.
Add the issue to a list for review at the project's final lessons learned session in nine months.
Wait until the fix has proven stable across several releases before recording anything about it.
Let the developer who found the fix decide whether the issue is worth recording as a lesson.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Capturing lessons as they happen — record lessons while details are fresh and share them while they can still help others (Rule M3-B11-R04).
Spot it: A discovery in the middle of the project, other teams about to hit the same problem, a costly lesson.
In this scenario: The API rate-limit lesson cost a production outage and three days. Recording it now and sharing it with the two teams starting next month helps them avoid the same outage.
Why not the others: Waiting nine months for the final session loses details and helps no one in time; waiting for several stable releases delays useful knowledge; leaving it to one developer's discretion makes capture optional.
Remember: Lessons learned register is updated THROUGHOUT the project, not just at closure.

questions.stem: A PMO audit found that "late procurement of long-lead items" appears in the lessons learned registers of four consecutive construction projects. Each project recorded the lesson at closure. A project manager is now planning the next construction project for the same organization. What should the project manager do?
options: Add the same lesson to this project's register so the recurring pattern is formally documented.
Review the four registers with the team at the kickoff meeting and then proceed as already planned.
Build long-lead ordering tasks into this project's plan and verify during planning that they occur.
Ask the PMO to send all project managers a reminder about long-lead items at each project start.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Lessons identified vs lessons applied — a lesson is only learned when it changes how the next project is planned and run (Rule M3-B11-R05).
Spot it: The same lesson appears on project after project; everyone writes it down, nobody acts on it.
In this scenario: Late long-lead procurement has recurred four times. Building long-lead ordering into this project's plan and checking it during planning turns the lesson into action.
Why not the others: Recording the lesson again repeats what already failed four times; reviewing registers at kickoff and then carrying on unchanged is learning in name only; a PMO reminder is passive and has not stopped the pattern.
Remember: Written down ≠ learned. A lesson is learned when the plan changes.

questions.stem: A vendor built the analytics component of a hybrid program using adaptive methods. Its contract ends in four months, after which internal staff must maintain the component. Neither the contract nor the project plan includes any knowledge transfer activities. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the vendor to hand over all source code and documents on the last day of the contract.
Work with procurement to add structured knowledge transfer sessions with the vendor before exit.
Extend the vendor contract indefinitely so internal staff never have to maintain the component.
Have internal staff learn the component on their own after the vendor leaves, using the code.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Vendor knowledge transfer — plan structured handover from a vendor before the contract ends, while there is still time and contract leverage (Rule M3-B11-R06).
Spot it: A vendor contract ending, internal staff taking over, no handover in the contract or the plan.
In this scenario: Four months remain. Working with procurement to add knowledge transfer sessions gives internal staff time to learn the component while the vendor is still engaged.
Why not the others: A last-day code dump gives no time to learn; extending the contract indefinitely avoids the problem at ongoing cost; self-teaching from code after exit is slow and risky.
Remember: Vendor leaving = plan the handover BEFORE the exit, through procurement.

questions.stem: Eight agile teams in a scaled program each solve accessibility testing problems on their own, often duplicating effort and applying different standards. Several people across the teams have said they are interested in the topic and would like to learn from each other. What is the BEST approach?
options: Assign one team to own all accessibility testing so the other seven teams can set the topic aside.
Publish a mandatory accessibility policy and have each team's lead enforce it within their own team.
Ask each team to document its accessibility approach in its own wiki space for its own later use.
Help interested members from all teams form an accessibility community of practice that meets regularly.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Communities of practice — voluntary groups that share knowledge on one topic across many teams (Rule M3-B11-R07).
Spot it: Several teams solving the same problem separately, inconsistent standards, people interested in learning from each other.
In this scenario: Eight teams are duplicating accessibility work and want to learn from each other. A community of practice spreads good ideas across teams and builds a shared standard without taking ownership away from any team.
Why not the others: One team owning all accessibility creates a bottleneck and lets others lose the skill; a mandatory policy enforced by leads is top-down and ignores the people who want to collaborate; separate wikis keep the knowledge in silos.
Remember: Knowledge across many teams = COMMUNITY OF PRACTICE.

questions.stem: A project manager is planning the handover of a new building management system to the facilities operations group. The transition plan covers equipment handover and occupant training, but it says nothing about how operations staff will keep the system running after the project team leaves. What should the project manager do?
options: Add fault response, escalation contacts, and upkeep procedures for operations staff to the plan.
Proceed with the current plan, since operations staff can contact the vendor when issues occur.
Defer support topics until after handover, once operations staff have used the system for a while.
Ask occupants to report system problems to the project team for the first several months.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Operational transition — the handover plan must include what operations needs to run and support the result after the project leaves (Rule M3-B11-R10).
Spot it: Transition plan, handover to operations, nothing about keeping it running after the team leaves.
In this scenario: The plan covers equipment and training but not ongoing support. Adding fault response, escalation contacts and upkeep procedures gives operations what it needs on day one after handover.
Why not the others: Relying on the vendor alone leaves operations with no internal knowledge; deferring support until after handover means learning through failures; routing problems to the project team keeps a closing project running operations.
Remember: Complete → Accept → TRANSFER → Learn → Close. Transfer includes how to support it.

questions.stem: The adaptive software team and the predictive hardware team in a hybrid program have argued for two weeks in cross-team meetings about whether to delay the hardware design freeze. Discussion keeps drifting between scope, cost, and staffing. The project manager believes the sponsor will have to decide. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Escalate the dispute now and ask the sponsor to attend the next cross-team meeting in person.
Keep holding cross-team meetings until both teams agree without involving the sponsor at all.
Frame the specific choice, the options, and their impacts for the sponsor before escalating.
Send the sponsor two weeks of meeting notes so the sponsor can work out what to decide next.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Framing the decision before escalating — escalate only once you have defined exactly what needs to be decided, the options and their impacts (Rule M3-B14-R08).
Spot it: A long unresolved argument, discussion drifting across topics, a decision above the team's authority.
In this scenario: The debate keeps wandering among scope, cost and staffing. Framing the specific choice — delay the freeze or not — with options and impacts lets the sponsor decide quickly and well.
Why not the others: Escalating now hands the sponsor an unfocused argument; more cross-team meetings have already failed for two weeks; sending two weeks of notes makes the sponsor do the PM's analysis.
Remember: Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act → Monitor → ESCALATE — and escalate with a clear decision to make.

questions.stem: An agile team just shipped a release that required close collaboration among testers, developers, and designers, and morale has been rising. Leadership plans to present an award only to the lead developer at the next all-hands meeting. The team coach hears about the plan beforehand. What should the coach do?
options: Support the plan, since honoring the lead developer will motivate others to perform at that level.
Suggest that leadership recognize the whole team's achievement along with any standout contributions.
Ask leadership to cancel the award because recognizing one individual always undermines teamwork.
Tell the team privately that the award reflects everyone's work even though it names one person.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Team recognition — in collaborative work, recognize the team's shared achievement along with any standout individual contribution (Rule M3-B15-R09).
Spot it: Success that came from close collaboration; an award planned for one person; the team's morale is rising.
In this scenario: The release needed testers, developers and designers together. Suggesting that leadership recognize the whole team, while still noting standout work, reinforces the collaboration that produced the result.
Why not the others: Rewarding only the lead developer suggests others' work did not count; canceling the award because individual recognition "always" hurts teamwork is too absolute; privately reassuring the team leaves the public message unfair.
Remember: Team results → team recognition. Celebrate the WE, then the ME.

questions.stem: A project manager on a bridge project will meet a steel fabricator next week to negotiate a change order. The fabricator is asking for a 15 percent price increase, citing rising material costs. The project manager has the cost baseline and knows how much contingency remains. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Meet the fabricator right away to learn why the increase is needed before planning any position.
Plan to open with a 7 percent offer so the two parties can meet somewhere in the middle quickly.
Hand the negotiation to the procurement department since pricing disputes are outside the PM role.
Set a target price, a budget limit, fallback suppliers, and the highest increase the project can accept.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Negotiation preparation — before negotiating, know your target, your limits, your alternatives and your walk-away point (Rule M3-B08-R01).
Spot it: A negotiation scheduled for next week, a price increase demand, cost baseline and contingency information available.
In this scenario: The PM has a week and knows the remaining contingency. Setting a target, a limit, fallback suppliers and a maximum acceptable increase means the PM enters the meeting prepared, not reacting.
Why not the others: Meeting right away gives up preparation time; planning to split the difference is a tactic without a plan behind it; handing it all to procurement ignores that the PM owns the project's cost impact.
Remember: Prepare before you negotiate: target, limit, BATNA, walk-away.

questions.stem: In a hybrid retail program, a marketing director insists the adaptive team's mobile app must launch by October 1. The operations manager insists it cannot launch until it is fully integrated with the predictive warehouse system, which will not be ready until December. Both are senior and firm. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Ask each manager what the date and the integration need to achieve before proposing trade-offs.
Propose a November launch as a compromise so that each manager gives up part of the request.
Side with the operations manager since full integration protects the stability of operations.
Escalate the disagreement to the sponsor because the two positions directly conflict with each other.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Interests vs positions — find out why each side wants what it wants before trading concessions (Rule M3-B08-R02).
Spot it: Two firm, conflicting demands; "insists"; senior stakeholders; a date or condition stated with no reason.
In this scenario: Marketing wants October 1 and operations wants full integration. Asking what each needs to achieve may reveal a solution — such as a limited launch — that meets both underlying interests.
Why not the others: A November compromise splits the difference without knowing what matters; siding with operations ignores marketing's real need; escalating to the sponsor skips direct problem-solving.
Remember: Positions are WHAT they say; interests are WHY. Ask why first.

questions.stem: Two stakeholders each want their feature placed first in the next release, and each insists theirs matters more. The product owner has data on customer usage, projected revenue impact, and related support tickets for both features. The agile coach is asked for advice. What should the coach recommend?
options: Suggest the product owner alternate between the stakeholders so each gets priority every other release.
Advise the product owner to favor the more senior stakeholder to protect the key working relationship.
Help the product owner rank both requests against agreed measures such as usage and revenue impact.
Advise splitting team capacity evenly between both features so neither stakeholder feels shortchanged.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Objective criteria — use agreed, measurable standards to decide between competing requests so the outcome is fair and explainable (Rule M3-B08-R03).
Spot it: Stakeholders each insisting theirs matters more; data available (usage, revenue, support tickets).
In this scenario: The product owner already has usage, revenue and support data. Ranking both features against agreed measures makes the priority call fair, explainable and hard to dispute.
Why not the others: Alternating priority ignores which feature brings more value; favoring the senior stakeholder decides by power; splitting capacity evenly delays both features.
Remember: Data beats volume. Objective criteria → fair trade-offs.

questions.stem: A project manager is negotiating with a contractor on a school renovation that must be complete before classes resume in September. The contractor wants to change the payment milestones, substitute an equivalent paint brand, and finish two weeks after the current completion date. What should the project manager do?
options: Accept all three requests, since keeping a good relationship with the contractor is the priority.
Hold firm on the completion date while accepting reasonable terms on payments and paint brand.
Reject all three requests so the contractor does not see the project as willing to give ground.
Accept the two-week delay in exchange for the contractor dropping its payment milestone request.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Protecting critical constraints — hold firm on what the project cannot give up and stay flexible on lower-priority terms (Rule M3-B08-R04).
Spot it: A hard deadline (school opening), several requests of different importance.
In this scenario: Classes resume in September, so the completion date is critical. Reasonable payment changes and an equivalent paint brand are low-risk concessions that build goodwill.
Why not the others: Accepting everything gives up the one thing the project cannot move; rejecting everything wastes easy goodwill; trading the deadline for payment terms sacrifices the most critical constraint.
Remember: Know your non-negotiables. Firm on the critical, flexible on the rest.

questions.stem: A cloud provider supporting the adaptive workstream of a hybrid program has announced a 30 percent rate increase at contract renewal in 60 days. The project manager will meet the provider next week to negotiate but has not yet looked at any other options. What should the project manager do before the meeting?
options: Accept the 30 percent increase early to avoid any risk of disruption during the renewal period.
Tell the provider the program has other options to gain leverage, even though none are verified.
Ask the sponsor for extra budget so the program can absorb whatever increase the provider sets.
Identify and price a realistic alternative provider in case acceptable terms cannot be reached.
questions.explanation:
Concept: BATNA — your best alternative to a negotiated agreement; knowing it tells you when to walk away and gives real leverage (Rule M3-B08-R05).
Spot it: An upcoming negotiation, a large price increase, no alternatives researched yet.
In this scenario: The PM has not looked at any other provider. Pricing a realistic alternative shows what "too expensive" really means and gives the PM honest leverage in the meeting.
Why not the others: Accepting early gives up any chance to negotiate; claiming unverified options is a bluff that is unethical and easy to call; asking the sponsor for money to absorb any increase gives up before trying.
Remember: Never negotiate without knowing your BATNA.

questions.stem: After a long conversation, a product owner and an external partner's lead agree that the partner will deliver its API changes two sprints earlier. In exchange, their agile team will lower the priority of a report the partner had requested. The agreement was made verbally on a call. What should the product owner do NEXT?
options: Confirm the trade-off in writing with the partner and adjust the backlog ordering to reflect it.
Trust the verbal agreement, since agile values individuals and interactions over documentation.
Wait to see whether the partner delivers the API changes on time before writing anything down.
Have the partner raise a formal contract amendment through legal before either side takes action.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Documenting negotiated agreements — confirm material agreements in writing and update the artifacts they affect (Rule M3-B08-R06).
Spot it: A verbal agreement, a trade-off between parties, changes to priorities or delivery dates.
In this scenario: The partner will deliver earlier and the report drops in priority. Confirming this in writing and reordering the backlog makes the trade-off clear and visible to both sides.
Why not the others: Trusting a verbal deal misreads the agile value — interactions matter but material agreements still need records; waiting for delivery first leaves the terms unclear; a formal contract amendment is heavier than this priority change needs.
Remember: Agreed verbally? Confirm in writing. Product owner owns and orders the product backlog.

questions.stem: While negotiating approval of a change request, a key client asks the project manager to commit to a 10 percent discount on future phases in return. In the performing organization, all pricing decisions belong to the account director. The client wants an answer before the meeting ends. What should the project manager do?
options: Agree to the discount to win approval and inform the account director once the change is signed.
Offer a smaller 5 percent discount as a compromise the account director will probably support.
Explain that pricing is the account director's call and arrange for that discussion to happen.
Decline firmly and tell the client that discounts are not offered on future phases of any project.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Authority limits — never promise what you do not have the authority to give; bring in the person who does (Rule M3-B08-R07).
Spot it: A request outside the PM's role (pricing, discounts), pressure to answer immediately.
In this scenario: Pricing belongs to the account director. The PM explains that openly and arranges the conversation, protecting both the client relationship and the organization's governance.
Why not the others: Agreeing now commits the organization beyond the PM's authority; offering 5 percent is still a pricing promise the PM cannot make; flatly refusing speaks for the account director in the other direction.
Remember: Know your authority. Can't approve it? Connect them to who can.

questions.stem: A supplier for a hybrid program will meet the hardware delivery date only if the program accepts a $180,000 price increase. The project manager's delegated authority for contract changes is $50,000. Three adaptive teams depend on the hardware arriving on time. What should the project manager do?
options: Accept the offer, since the adaptive teams need the hardware to arrive on the agreed date.
Bring the supplier's offer and its schedule impact to the sponsor, who can approve that amount.
Split the increase into smaller purchase orders so that each one stays under the $50,000 limit.
Reject the offer and tell the adaptive teams to replan around a later hardware delivery date.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Escalating beyond delegated authority — when a trade-off exceeds your approval limit, bring it to whoever holds that authority, with the facts (Rule M3-B08-R10).
Spot it: A dollar amount above the PM's limit, schedule pressure, dependent teams.
In this scenario: $180,000 is well over the $50,000 limit. The PM takes the offer, the schedule impact and the options to the sponsor, who can make the call quickly.
Why not the others: Accepting exceeds the PM's authority; splitting purchase orders to stay under the limit is an ethics violation; rejecting without escalating takes a decision the sponsor should make.
Remember: Budget beyond your authority → escalate with options. Never slice the PO to dodge the limit.

questions.stem: An organization is rolling out a new work-tracking tool to its customer service teams in waves as part of an agile transformation. After the first wave, surveys show agents find the training videos too long and unrelated to their daily tasks, and only 30 percent are using the tool. The second wave starts in three weeks. What should the change lead do?
options: Continue as planned, since adoption usually improves once agents get used to the new tool.
Have managers mandate daily tool usage and report agents who do not follow the new process.
Pause the rollout until leadership selects a different tool that agents may find easier to use.
Redesign the training into short, task-based sessions with agent input before the next wave.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Adapting change tactics from feedback — organizational change should listen to affected people and adjust the approach between waves (Rule M5-B05-R08).
Spot it: Low adoption, survey feedback, a next wave coming, training that doesn't fit the users' work.
In this scenario: Agents said the training is too long and not relevant. Redesigning it into short, task-based sessions with their input before wave two addresses the actual cause of low adoption.
Why not the others: Continuing as planned ignores clear feedback; mandating usage forces behavior without fixing the cause; pausing to change tools jumps to a new solution before fixing the training.
Remember: Team resisting change → engage and LISTEN first, then adapt.

questions.stem: Midway through a highway project, a client moves approval authority for design changes from its regional engineer to a new central design office. The RACI chart and communications management plan still list the regional engineer, and several contractors keep sending design requests there. What should the project manager do?
options: Update the RACI chart and communications plan, and brief contractors on the new approval route.
Ask the regional engineer to forward any design requests received to the central design office.
Update the responsibility chart in the project records so the new authority is formally recorded.
Tell contractors about the new authority at the next meeting but leave the plans unchanged for now.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Updating roles and decision rights — when authority moves, update the documents AND make sure the people affected know (Rule M3-B09-R09).
Spot it: Approval authority moved, outdated RACI and communications plan, stakeholders still using the old route.
In this scenario: The RACI and communications plan are out of date and contractors are misrouting requests. Updating both documents and briefing contractors fixes the record and the behavior.
Why not the others: Having the old engineer forward requests keeps the wrong route alive; updating only the responsibility chart fixes the record but not what contractors do; telling contractors without updating the plans leaves the documents wrong.
Remember: Role change → update the RACI AND the communications management plan, then tell people.

questions.stem: An adaptive team in a hybrid program has been blocked for a week because the predictive infrastructure group has not provisioned its test servers. The project manager, a former systems administrator, could configure the servers herself over the weekend. What should the project manager do?
options: Configure the test servers herself over the weekend so the team can resume work on Monday.
Tell the team to set up the servers themselves since they are tired of waiting on infrastructure.
Work with the infrastructure group's manager to get the team's server request prioritized.
Note the blocked work in the status report and wait for the infrastructure group to finish it.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Removing impediments without taking over — a servant leader clears the path for the team rather than doing the team's or another group's work (Rule M3-B02-R01).
Spot it: A blocked team, a dependency on another group, a leader who has the skills to do it herself.
In this scenario: The infrastructure group owns the servers. Working with its manager to prioritize the request removes the blocker through the proper channel and keeps each group accountable for its own work.
Why not the others: Configuring servers herself takes over another group's work and bypasses its controls; telling the team to do it themselves oversteps the same boundary; noting it and waiting leaves the team blocked.
Remember: Servant leader REMOVES obstacles — never waits, never takes over.

questions.stem: Members of an agile team ask their delivery lead to approve which unit testing framework they should use for a new microservice. The team has strong testing skills, and the choice will have no effect on other teams, architecture standards, or the product's users. What should the delivery lead do?
options: Evaluate the frameworks personally and tell the team which one to adopt for the microservice.
Let the team make the framework choice, since it falls within the team's expertise and scope.
Refer the choice to the architecture review board so it follows organizational standards.
Ask the product owner to pick the framework because it may affect how fast features ship.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Delegating decisions — push decisions to the lowest level that has the competence and the context (Rule M3-B02-R02).
Spot it: A choice within the team's skills, no effect on other teams or users, team asking permission.
In this scenario: The framework choice affects only this team's microservice and the team has strong testing skills. The delivery lead lets them decide, which builds ownership and speed.
Why not the others: Deciding personally undermines self-organization; the architecture board is not needed when there is no impact on standards; the product owner decides WHAT is built, not which testing tool is used.
Remember: Product owner = WHAT. Team = HOW. Leader = protect and enable.

questions.stem: On a hospital construction project, a project manager wants the procurement lead to resolve subcontractor issues without waiting for the project manager's approval. On a previous project, a similar delegation caused confusion when leads approved changes that affected the schedule baseline. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Tell the procurement lead to handle all subcontractor issues alone and report results monthly.
Keep approving every subcontractor decision personally because delegation caused confusion before.
Ask the sponsor to issue a memo granting the procurement lead full authority over subcontractors.
Define which subcontractor decisions the lead can make alone and which need PM or board approval.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Decision boundaries before delegation — empowerment works when everyone knows which decisions are theirs and which need approval (Rule M3-B02-R03).
Spot it: A past delegation that caused confusion, decisions that could affect baselines, wanting to empower a lead.
In this scenario: Last time, leads approved changes that hit the schedule baseline. Defining which subcontractor decisions the lead can make alone and which need the PM or the change control board lets the lead act without crossing into baseline changes.
Why not the others: Unlimited delegation repeats the past confusion; keeping every decision personal abandons empowerment; a memo granting full authority also gives away baseline decisions.
Remember: Empower WITH boundaries. Baseline changes go through change control.

questions.stem: In a hybrid program, executives often walk into the adaptive team's workspace to ask developers for status, interrupting their work several times a day. The executives say they need current visibility into progress because the release is strategically important. What should the project manager do?
options: Give executives a live progress dashboard and a regular demo slot, and route other questions to the PM.
Ask executives to stop contacting the team and wait for the monthly program report for updates.
Have each developer send executives a daily written update so the executives stop visiting.
Let the executives keep visiting because stakeholder engagement matters more than team focus.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Protecting team focus with transparency — give stakeholders easy visibility so they do not need to interrupt the team (Rule M3-B02-R04).
Spot it: Executives interrupting developers, a need for status, a strategically important release.
In this scenario: Executives need visibility and developers need focus. A live dashboard and a regular demo slot give executives real information, and routing other questions to the PM protects the team.
Why not the others: Telling executives to wait for a monthly report cuts off legitimate visibility; daily written updates from each developer create even more overhead; allowing constant visits keeps disrupting the work.
Remember: Information radiators + demos = transparency without interruption.

questions.stem: A developer on an agile team tells the agile coach she is frustrated because her pull requests keep coming back with many review comments. She asks the coach to simply tell her what to fix. The coach has a fairly strong opinion about the cause. What should the coach do FIRST?
options: Give her a checklist of coding practices the coach believes will resolve most of the comments.
Ask the reviewers to leave fewer comments so she does not become discouraged by the feedback.
Ask her what patterns she sees in the review comments and what she thinks is causing them.
Have a senior developer rewrite her next pull request so she can see the preferred coding style.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Coaching before prescribing — a servant leader asks questions that help people find their own answers before offering a solution (Rule M3-B02-R05).
Spot it: "just tell me what to fix," a recurring personal problem, a coach who already has an opinion.
In this scenario: Asking what patterns she sees in the comments helps the developer diagnose the cause herself. She builds a skill she can use next time, and the coach learns her view before advising.
Why not the others: A checklist fixes today's comments but keeps her dependent on the coach; asking reviewers to comment less hides useful feedback; having someone rewrite her work takes the learning away from her.
Remember: Ask before you tell. Coaching builds capability; prescribing builds dependence.

questions.stem: On a pharmaceutical packaging line installation, a technician once admitted a wiring error and was reprimanded in front of the crew by the previous project manager. Since then, team members rarely report problems until inspections uncover them, which has caused costly rework. A new project manager has just taken over. What should the new project manager do?
options: Respond to reported problems by focusing on fixes, and thank people who raise issues early.
Introduce penalties for errors found at inspection that the team did not report beforehand.
Add more inspections so hidden errors are caught before they can affect the project schedule.
Require each technician to sign a weekly form confirming no errors remain unreported.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Psychological safety — people report problems and mistakes early only when doing so is safe and valued (Rule M3-B02-R06).
Spot it: A past public reprimand, problems now hidden until inspection, a new leader taking over.
In this scenario: The team learned that admitting errors gets you punished. By focusing on fixes and thanking early reporters, the new PM makes it safe again, so problems surface before they become costly rework.
Why not the others: Penalties for unreported errors increase fear and hiding; more inspections catch problems later instead of earlier; a signed "no errors" form adds pressure without building trust.
Remember: Punish the messenger, lose the message. Safety first → problems surface early.

questions.stem: A hybrid program must choose a data migration approach for its predictive ERP cutover. Senior managers plan to decide in a closed session next week. Data engineers on the adaptive teams, who know about serious quality problems in the source data, have not been invited. What should the project manager do?
options: Let the senior managers decide and then explain the chosen approach to the data engineers afterward.
Hand the whole decision to the data engineers and exclude managers because they lack technical detail.
Send the data engineers a survey after the decision to find out whether they have any concerns about it.
Bring the data engineers into the decision so their knowledge of the source data shapes the approach.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Involving the people closest to the work — decisions that need specialist knowledge should include the people who have it (Rule M3-B02-R07).
Spot it: A decision made by managers alone, experts with key knowledge not invited, serious risks only they know about.
In this scenario: The data engineers know about serious source-data quality problems. Bringing them into the migration decision puts that knowledge where it can shape the approach before it is locked in.
Why not the others: Deciding first and explaining later loses the knowledge when it matters; excluding managers swings to the opposite extreme; a survey after the decision gathers concerns too late to use.
Remember: Understand → Assess → COLLABORATE → Act. Collaborate with those who know the work.

questions.stem: A scrum master notices that her team waits for her to facilitate every event, settle every disagreement, and contact every stakeholder. Management praises her as indispensable, and her performance review is coming up. She wants to lead in a way that truly strengthens the team. What should she do?
options: Keep doing all of these activities herself, since management values her as indispensable to the team.
Coach team members to facilitate events and handle stakeholder contact so they rely on her less.
Step back from every activity at once so the team is forced to manage everything by itself.
Document her activities in detail so another scrum master could perform them if she is away.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Servant leader success measure — a leader succeeds when the team grows more capable and less dependent on her (Rule M3-B02-R10).
Spot it: A team that waits for the leader for everything, a leader praised as indispensable.
In this scenario: The team relies on her for every event, disagreement and stakeholder contact. Coaching members to take these on step by step builds team capability, which is the true measure of her effectiveness.
Why not the others: Continuing to do everything keeps the team dependent; stepping back from everything at once leaves an unready team without support; documenting her tasks for a backup still keeps the team dependent on a scrum master.
Remember: A good servant leader works herself out of the middle of everything.

questions.stem: Two department heads disagree over whether a new HR system's leave report should run weekly or monthly. Either option fits within approved scope, budget, and schedule, and the project management plan gives the project manager authority over report formats. One department head threatens to take the issue to the sponsor. What should the project manager do?
options: Resolve the report frequency with both department heads directly, since it is within the PM's authority.
Escalate the disagreement to the sponsor first so the sponsor hears the project's view before anyone else.
Submit a change request so the change control board can decide how often the leave report should run.
Build both a weekly and a monthly version of the report so that neither department head is disappointed.
questions.explanation:
