Concept: Escalating only above your authority — if a decision is within the PM's authority and the approved baselines, resolve it at that level (Rule M3-B06-R08).
Spot it: Options that fit scope, budget and schedule; the plan grants the PM authority; a stakeholder threatening escalation.
In this scenario: Both report frequencies fit the plan, and the PM has authority over report formats. The PM brings both department heads together and settles it directly.
Why not the others: Escalating first to get ahead of the other person is a political move, not a decision need; a change request is for changes to baselines, and neither option changes one; building both reports adds cost to avoid a conversation.
Remember: Within your authority? Resolve it. Beyond it? Escalate. Don't escalate first.

questions.stem: A hybrid team building a field inspection app assumes inspectors most want offline capability, based on comments from their regional manager. Inspectors work nearby and are easy to reach. The first adaptive release is being planned this week. What should the project manager do?
options: Proceed with offline capability, since the manager supervises inspectors and knows their needs.
Send a requirements document to inspectors and treat any lack of response as agreement.
Interview or observe several inspectors to confirm which capabilities they need most.
Build every candidate capability in the first release so inspectors can pick their favorite.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Validating stakeholder needs directly — do not rely on someone else's assumption about what users need when you can ask the users (Rule M3-B05-R09).
Spot it: Needs assumed from a manager's comments, users easy to reach, planning about to start.
In this scenario: The team's belief about offline capability came from the regional manager. Interviewing or observing a few inspectors confirms what they actually need before the first release is planned.
Why not the others: Trusting the manager keeps an untested assumption; treating no response as agreement is not validation; building everything wastes effort instead of learning what matters most.
Remember: Identify → Analyze → Engage. Ask the real users, not their proxy.

questions.stem: An agile team formed six months ago agreed on core hours and code review norms that worked well. This month three new members joined from a different time zone, and friction has grown over meeting times and how quickly reviews are completed. What should the team facilitator do?
options: Ask the new members to adopt the existing agreement, since it has worked for six months.
Facilitate a session with the whole team to revisit and update its working agreement.
Have the functional manager set new rules for meeting times and review turnaround.
Let each group keep its own norms so the new members can work however they prefer.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Working agreements — a team's agreed norms; set them early and revisit them whenever the team changes (Rule M3-B04-R01).
Spot it: New members joining, a different time zone, friction over meetings and review speed.
In this scenario: The old agreement was made before three new members joined from another time zone. A whole-team session to revisit it lets everyone shape norms that work for the new team.
Why not the others: Making newcomers adopt the old agreement ignores their constraints; having the functional manager set rules removes team ownership; separate norms for each group split the team.
Remember: Team changes → revisit the working agreement together.

questions.stem: On a telecom tower installation project, two experienced site engineers left and three new engineers joined. Over the following two weeks, productivity fell about 15 percent. The sponsor asks whether the project manager should replace the new engineers with more experienced contractors. What should the project manager do?
options: Replace the new engineers with contractors who have prior experience on similar tower installations.
Revise the schedule baseline right away to treat the lower productivity as the new normal rate.
Require the new engineers to work paid overtime until team productivity returns to its previous level.
Explain that a temporary dip is expected after team changes, and support onboarding while tracking trends.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Team development after change — when membership changes, performance usually dips temporarily as the team re-forms (Tuckman) (Rule M3-B04-R02).
Spot it: New members joining, experienced people leaving, a short-term productivity drop, pressure to replace people.
In this scenario: A 15 percent dip two weeks after a major team change is normal. The PM explains this to the sponsor, supports onboarding and watches the trend before taking drastic action.
Why not the others: Replacing new engineers overreacts to a normal dip; rebaselining treats a temporary dip as permanent and skips change control; forced overtime adds strain without helping new people learn.
Remember: New members = back to Forming. Tuckman: Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing → Adjourning.

questions.stem: A hybrid program formed an integration team with members from both adaptive and predictive workstreams. Members keep arguing over who can approve interface changes, how quickly messages must be answered, and whether decisions need full consensus. Work is slowing as a result. What should the project manager do?
options: Facilitate a team charter that sets response times, decision rules, and who approves interface changes.
Assign the predictive lead to make every integration decision so that the recurring arguments stop happening.
Split adaptive and predictive members into separate teams that meet only at scheduled phase gates.
Remind members to treat each other with respect and to settle any disagreements among themselves.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Team charter — an agreement on values, behaviors, decision rules and communication norms that prevents recurring friction (Rule M3-B04-R03).
Spot it: Arguments about who approves, response times, how decisions are made; work slowing.
In this scenario: The team keeps arguing about approvals, response times and consensus. Facilitating a team charter that settles these points lets members focus on the work.
Why not the others: Giving the predictive lead every decision is directive and ignores the adaptive side; splitting the team avoids integration it needs; a reminder to be respectful doesn't answer any of the open questions.
Remember: Recurring "who decides / how fast / how" arguments = build the TEAM CHARTER.

questions.stem: A new agile team includes a UX designer, three developers, and a tester. The developers say testing is "the tester's job," so finished code piles up waiting for testing near the end of each sprint and several stories miss the sprint. What should the scrum master do?
options: Hire a second tester so the testing workload can keep pace with the developers' output.
Remove the tester role and require every developer to test only the stories they built.
Keep the tester as quality lead while coaching developers to help test so stories reach done.
Accept the pile-up, since testing is the tester's responsibility under the team's defined roles.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Clear roles with cross-functional collaboration — keep role clarity but let everyone share responsibility for getting stories done (Rule M3-B04-R04).
Spot it: "that's not my job," a bottleneck at one role, stories missing the sprint.
In this scenario: Code piles up waiting for one tester. Keeping the tester as quality lead while coaching developers to help test spreads the load and gets stories to done within the sprint.
Why not the others: Hiring another tester treats the symptom and keeps the silo; removing the tester role discards needed expertise; accepting the pile-up leaves stories failing to finish.
Remember: Roles guide you; the Definition of Done belongs to the whole team.

questions.stem: A project team's ground rules require design documents to be submitted 48 hours before each design review. A senior engineer has missed this three times, forcing reviews to be postponed, and other team members have started submitting late as well. What should the project manager do?
options: Wait for the end-of-phase performance review to raise the pattern of late submissions with the engineer.
Address the senior engineer's late submissions privately now and hold everyone to the same rule.
Relax the ground rule to 24 hours, since several team members now find 48 hours difficult.
Overlook the engineer's late submissions because the engineer's senior expertise is valuable.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Enforcing ground rules — address repeated norm violations promptly, privately and consistently, whoever breaks them (Rule M3-B04-R05).
Spot it: A rule broken repeatedly, a senior person, others starting to copy the behavior.
In this scenario: The senior engineer's late submissions are spreading to others. Addressing it privately now and holding everyone to the same rule restores the norm before it collapses.
Why not the others: Waiting for the phase-end review lets the pattern spread; relaxing the rule rewards the violation; overlooking it because of seniority applies rules by rank.
Remember: Norm broken → address it early, privately, equally.

questions.stem: A hybrid program's adaptive teams hold retrospectives every sprint. The predictive hardware team and the integration team have never reflected together on how they work, and handoffs between them keep causing rework. Each group blames the other for the problems. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the adaptive teams to add the hardware handoff problems to their own retrospectives.
Wait for the phase-end lessons learned session to discuss the handoff issues with both groups.
Assign a coordinator to inspect every handoff and reject work that does not meet standards.
Hold a joint reflection session for both groups to examine the handoffs and agree on changes.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reflection to improve how teams work together — when problems cross groups, the groups must reflect together (Rule M3-B04-R06).
Spot it: Handoff problems between groups, each blaming the other, reflection happening only within one group.
In this scenario: The rework comes from handoffs between the hardware and integration teams. A joint reflection session lets both groups examine the handoffs together and agree on changes.
Why not the others: Adding it to the adaptive teams' retrospectives leaves out the groups involved; waiting for the phase-end lessons session lets the rework continue; an inspector at every handoff treats the symptom with policing.
Remember: Problem between groups → reflect TOGETHER. Retrospective fixes process problems.

questions.stem: At the sprint review, an agile team admits it missed its sprint goal even though every developer finished all of their assigned tasks. Integration and end-to-end testing were never done because nobody considered them part of their own tasks. What should the scrum master encourage?
options: Center planning and daily coordination on the goal so members swarm on what finishes it.
Assign integration as a named task to one specific developer in every future sprint.
Track individual task completion more closely to show who contributed the most work.
Report to management that integration was missed because it was not part of anyone's tasks.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Shared ownership of outcomes — an agile team commits to the sprint goal together, not just to each person's tasks (Rule M3-B04-R07).
Spot it: Everyone finished their tasks but the goal was missed; work nobody considered theirs.
In this scenario: Integration and end-to-end testing fell between tasks. Centering planning and daily coordination on the goal leads members to swarm on whatever is needed to finish it.
Why not the others: Assigning integration to one developer patches one gap but keeps the task mindset; tracking individual completion reinforces the problem; reporting it to management assigns blame without fixing the teamwork.
Remember: Done tasks ≠ done goal. The team owns the goal together.

questions.stem: A quality report on a shipbuilding project shows welding defects concentrated in one crew's work. The site manager proposes posting defect counts by welder name on the site notice board to motivate better work. The project manager is asked to approve the idea. What should the project manager do?
options: Post the defect counts by welder name so that each welder feels personally accountable for weld quality.
Remove the crew with the highest defect rate from the project and bring in a replacement crew.
Analyze the defect data for process causes such as equipment, materials, or procedures, and fix them.
Stop collecting defect data by crew so that the welders do not feel singled out by the reporting.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Using performance data to improve the system — use defect data to find process causes, not to shame individuals (Rule M3-B04-R10).
Spot it: Defect counts, a proposal to post names publicly, one crew with more problems.
In this scenario: Defects concentrated in one crew may come from equipment, materials or procedures. Analyzing the data for causes — with a fishbone or Pareto chart, for example — fixes the process.
Why not the others: Posting names publicly shames people and discourages honest reporting; removing the crew acts before understanding the cause; stopping the data collection throws away information needed for improvement.
Remember: Most defects come from the system, not the people. Root cause, not blame.

questions.stem: A project manager on a hybrid healthcare project wants to use a free public generative AI tool to summarize patient feedback transcripts for the adaptive team's refinement sessions. The transcripts include patient names and medical details. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Delete patient names from the transcripts and then upload them to the tool for summarizing.
Check with privacy and security staff whether this data can lawfully be processed by that tool.
Upload the transcripts, since the team will review the summaries for accuracy before use.
Ask the team to vote on whether the time saved justifies the possible exposure of the patient data.
questions.explanation:
Concept: AI and data privacy — before using any AI tool, confirm that the data can lawfully and securely be processed by it (Rule M5-B07-R03).
Spot it: Patient, customer or confidential data; a free public tool; "FIRST."
In this scenario: The transcripts include names and medical details. The PM first checks with privacy and security staff whether this tool may process them.
Why not the others: Removing names still leaves medical details and other identifiers; reviewing summaries afterward does not undo exposure; a team vote cannot override legal obligations.
Remember: Sensitive data + AI = check privacy and legal rules FIRST, before anything is uploaded.

questions.stem: An agile team used an AI model to produce release date forecast ranges that the product owner will present to executives. The model was trained only on the last six months of team data and has not been checked against actual results. What should the team do?
options: Share the forecast without mentioning the AI model so that executives focus on the dates alone.
Discard the forecast and have the team re-estimate every item manually before sharing any dates.
Present the forecast as the team's own estimate, since several team members reviewed the model's output.
State that AI produced the forecast, note its data limits, and flag that it has not been validated.
questions.explanation:
Concept: AI transparency — when AI output informs decisions, disclose that AI was used, its limits and whether it has been validated (Rule M5-B07-R06).
Spot it: AI-generated forecasts, limited training data, not checked against actual results, executives relying on them.
In this scenario: The forecast came from a model trained on six months of data and never checked against actuals. Stating this lets executives judge how much to rely on the ranges.
Why not the others: Hiding the AI source misleads executives; discarding the forecast throws away useful information; calling it the team's own estimate misrepresents where it came from.
Remember: AI output = say what made it, what it knows and what it hasn't proven.

questions.stem: A project manager on a defense contract wants to use AI to help draft risk responses based on the confidential risk register. The organization provides an approved, internally hosted AI assistant with access controls. A team member recommends a free online tool that gives more polished answers. What should the project manager do?
options: Use the organization's approved, internally hosted assistant to draft the confidential risk responses.
Use the free online tool, since more polished drafts will improve the quality of the risk responses.
Paste only the highest-priority risks into the free online tool to limit the amount of sensitive data exposed.
Have the team member trial the free tool with the register before deciding which tool to adopt.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Approved AI tools for sensitive work — use the organization's approved, controlled tools when working with confidential information (Rule M5-B07-R09).
Spot it: Confidential data, an approved internal AI assistant, a public tool that seems better.
In this scenario: The risk register is confidential defense data, and an approved internal assistant with access controls exists. That tool protects the data and meets organizational rules.
Why not the others: A free online tool exposes confidential data, however polished; sending only high-priority risks still sends the most sensitive items; a trial with the register still exposes it.
Remember: Confidential data → approved tools only. Polish never outweighs protection.

questions.stem: An adaptive team in a hybrid program has finished building a customer portal. The predictive contract requires formal client sign-off at a phase gate next week. Internal testing of the portal against the agreed acceptance criteria has not been completed. What should the project manager do?
options: Present the portal at the phase gate and fix any defects the client happens to find there.
Ask the client to sign acceptance now and schedule the quality testing during the warranty period.
Finish testing the portal against the agreed criteria before presenting it for client sign-off.
Postpone the phase gate indefinitely until the portal has no remaining defects of any kind.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Verify before acceptance — the team checks deliverables against quality criteria (control quality) before the customer formally accepts them (validate scope) (Rule M4-B15-R01).
Spot it: A sign-off coming up, internal testing not finished, acceptance criteria agreed.
In this scenario: Internal testing against the acceptance criteria is not done. Finishing it before the phase gate means the client reviews a verified deliverable.
Why not the others: Presenting untested work lets the client find the defects; signing now and testing in warranty reverses the order; postponing indefinitely for zero defects sets an unrealistic standard.
Remember: Control Quality (internal, verified) → Validate Scope (customer, accepted).

questions.stem: An agile team will release a new claims processing app to the operations department in two sprints. Operations staff have not been trained, no support arrangement exists, and nobody has decided who will own the app's data after release. What should the team do?
options: Release on schedule and let operations request training and support as issues come up later.
Add operations onboarding, a support handoff, and a named data owner to the next two sprints.
Delay the release until operations writes its own complete training and support procedures.
Have the development team provide production support indefinitely so operations staff are not burdened.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Operational readiness — plan training, support, data ownership and support procedures before handing a product to operations (Rule M4-B15-R05).
Spot it: Release soon, operations not ready, no support model, unclear ownership.
In this scenario: Two sprints remain before release. Treating operations onboarding, the support handoff and naming a data owner as planned work makes the transition ready in time.
Why not the others: Releasing and reacting later leaves operations unprepared; delaying for operations to write everything shifts the team's job to them; indefinite support by developers never completes the transfer.
Remember: Complete → Accept → TRANSFER → Learn → Close.

questions.stem: A warehouse automation project is closing. It finished two weeks ahead of schedule but 8 percent over budget. Most team members will be reassigned to other projects next week, and several administrative closing tasks remain. What should the project manager do before the team disperses?
options: Archive the project files and release the team, since the final cost figures are known.
Send team members a survey next month asking them to reflect on the project's results.
Focus the final report on the early finish to present the project's outcome positively.
Hold a lessons learned session to record what drove the cost overrun and the early finish.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Final lessons learned — before the team disperses, capture what drove performance (good and bad) for organizational learning (Rule M4-B15-R08).
Spot it: Project closing, team members being reassigned, a mixed result such as ahead of schedule but over budget.
In this scenario: The project finished early but 8 percent over budget, and the team leaves next week. A lessons learned session now captures the causes of both while people remember them.
Why not the others: Archiving and releasing the team loses the lessons; a survey next month comes after people have moved on; highlighting only the early finish hides the cost story.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → LEARN → Close. Capture lessons before releasing the team.

questions.stem: Two developers disagree with the product owner's decision to place a reporting feature ahead of a performance improvement they consider more important. They ask the scrum master to override the product owner and reorder the backlog. What should the scrum master do?
options: Help the developers present their technical concerns to the product owner, who makes the final call.
Reorder the backlog to put the performance item first, since the developers know the technical system best.
Escalate the disagreement to the sponsor so a neutral party can decide which item goes first.
Have the whole team vote on the order so the decision reflects the majority view of the team.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Product owner authority — the product owner makes the final call on backlog order; others influence it through information and input (Rule M4-B11-R02).
Spot it: Developers disagree with priorities, a request to override the product owner.
In this scenario: The developers' technical concerns are valuable input. The scrum master helps them present those concerns to the product owner, who then decides.
Why not the others: Reordering the backlog directly overrides the product owner's role; escalating to the sponsor skips the product owner; a team vote replaces accountable ownership with majority opinion.
Remember: Product owner decides WHAT and the order; team decides HOW; scrum master facilitates.

questions.stem: An agile team's user story titled "complete customer self-service portal" has carried over two sprints without being finished. The product owner cannot get any customer feedback until the whole portal is done, and stakeholders are growing impatient. What should the team do?
options: Lengthen the sprint so the entire portal story can be completed within a single longer sprint.
Assign more developers to the story so the full portal can be completed in the next sprint.
Break the story into thin slices, such as viewing invoices, that can be finished and reviewed sooner.
Keep carrying the story over, since the portal only delivers value as one complete unit.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Splitting large items — break oversized stories into thin, valuable slices that can be completed and reviewed within a sprint (Rule M4-B11-R04).
Spot it: A story carrying over sprints, no feedback until the whole thing is done, impatient stakeholders.
In this scenario: The whole-portal story is too big to finish or get feedback on. Slicing it into features like viewing invoices delivers value and feedback each sprint.
Why not the others: Lengthening the sprint breaks the fixed cadence; adding developers does not fix an oversized story; carrying it over keeps delaying all feedback.
Remember: Too big to finish? Split it thin — vertical slices, INVEST stories.

questions.stem: During refinement, a product owner reviews an item to integrate the product with a legacy fax system. The company will retire all fax services in four months, and the integration would take about three sprints to build. What should the product owner do?
options: Move the fax item to the bottom of the backlog in case the retirement date slips later on.
Remove the fax integration item, since its short remaining use no longer justifies the effort.
Complete the fax integration because stakeholders requested it and it is already approved.
Ask the team to build a simplified fax integration that can be finished in a single sprint.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Removing low-value backlog items — the product owner removes items whose value no longer justifies their cost (Rule M4-B11-R07).
Spot it: An item whose value is disappearing, a system being retired, effort that outweighs benefit.
In this scenario: Fax services retire in four months and the integration takes three sprints. It would deliver almost no use, so the product owner removes it.
Why not the others: Moving it to the bottom keeps clutter for an unlikely case; building it because it was approved ignores that its value changed; a simpler version still spends effort on a retiring system.
Remember: Value < cost → remove it. The backlog is ordered by value, not history.

questions.stem: A new product owner inherits a backlog of 200 items from many stakeholders. Priorities shift weekly depending on who spoke to the team last, and developers cannot explain how their work fits together. What should the product owner do FIRST?
options: Score all 200 items with a weighted model so every stakeholder request has a numeric rank.
Freeze the backlog order for the next three months so priorities stop changing from week to week.
Ask each stakeholder to limit their requests to a top five so the backlog becomes smaller.
Establish a clear product goal with stakeholders to guide how individual items are ordered.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Product goal — a clear product goal gives direction to backlog prioritization so items fit together toward one outcome (Rule M4-B11-R10).
Spot it: Shifting priorities, many stakeholders, work that doesn't connect, a new product owner.
In this scenario: Priorities change based on whoever spoke last because there is no shared goal. Setting a product goal with stakeholders gives a basis for ordering all 200 items.
Why not the others: Scoring every item without a goal has nothing to score against; freezing priorities for three months blocks needed adaptation; limiting requests shrinks the list without giving it direction.
Remember: Goal first, then order. Without a goal, the loudest voice wins.

questions.stem: A project's change management plan lets the project manager approve changes under $10,000 that have no schedule impact; all others go to the change control board. A team lead submits a $3,000 change with no schedule impact and suggests holding it for the board's monthly meeting. What should the project manager do?
options: Evaluate and decide on the change under the PM's authority as set in the change management plan.
Hold the change for the board's monthly meeting so all changes receive the same level of review.
Approve the change informally and let the team lead implement it without recording the decision.
Forward the change to the sponsor since any change affects the project's approved cost baseline.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Defined change authority — the change management plan sets who approves which changes; use that path instead of sending everything to the top (Rule M3-B18-R03).
Spot it: Approval thresholds, a small change within the PM's limit, no schedule impact.
In this scenario: The $3,000 change has no schedule impact and is under the PM's $10,000 limit. The PM evaluates and decides it under the plan's authority and records the decision.
Why not the others: Holding it for the board ignores the delegation the plan created; approving informally without a record skips the change log; sending it to the sponsor bypasses the defined authority.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → Approve (by the RIGHT authority) → Implement → Update → Monitor.

questions.stem: The change control board rejected a regional manager's request to add a second language to a training rollout, citing budget limits and a fixed regulatory deadline. A week has passed, and the regional manager still has not been told about the decision. What should the project manager do?
options: Update the change log to show the rejection and let the regional manager check the status there.
Wait until the regional manager asks about the request before explaining the board's decision.
Tell the regional manager about the rejection, the reasons, and any option to raise it again later.
Ask the change control board to reconsider so the regional manager is not left disappointed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Communicating rejected changes — tell requesters the decision, the reasons and any next steps, even when the answer is no (Rule M3-B18-R06).
Spot it: A change rejected, the requester not told, time passing.
In this scenario: The regional manager has waited a week. The PM explains the rejection, the budget and regulatory reasons, and whether the request could be raised again later.
Why not the others: Updating the change log only waits for the requester to go looking; waiting until asked leaves a stakeholder uninformed; asking the board to reconsider undermines a proper decision.
Remember: Change decided → update the change log AND tell the requester why.

questions.stem: Late on a Saturday, a critical security vulnerability is discovered in a live payment system that a project recently deployed. The change management plan includes an emergency change procedure. The on-call engineer wants to patch production immediately without telling anyone. What should the project manager do?
options: Let the engineer patch production now and skip the paperwork, since this is an emergency.
Use the emergency procedure to get fast approval, apply the patch, and record it for later review.
Wait for the next regular change control board meeting before applying the security patch.
Shut down the payment system until the full change control board can meet and approve the fix.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Emergency change — an emergency uses a faster approval path, but the change is still approved, recorded and reviewed (Rule M3-B18-R09).
Spot it: Urgent security or safety issue, an emergency procedure exists, someone wants to skip it.
In this scenario: The vulnerability is critical and the plan includes an emergency procedure. The PM gets fast approval, applies the patch and records it for later review.
Why not the others: Patching with no approval or record creates uncontrolled change; waiting for the regular board meeting leaves the system exposed; shutting down the system is disproportionate when a fast path exists.
Remember: Emergency = FAST change control, never NO change control.

questions.stem: A hybrid program holds a single lessons learned review at each phase gate, roughly every six months. Its adaptive teams deliver every two weeks, and recurring integration problems persist for months before anyone discusses them. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the phase-gate reviews but make them longer so more issues can be covered in each one.
Ask teams to log problems in a shared register for discussion at the next phase-gate review.
Replace the phase-gate reviews with a single comprehensive lessons learned review at closure.
Add short, regular reflection points across teams so findings can shape upcoming increments.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Learning loop frequency — reflection must happen often enough for its findings to affect upcoming work (Rule M4-B17-R01).
Spot it: Reviews only every six months, teams delivering every two weeks, recurring problems persisting.
In this scenario: Integration problems persist for months between reviews. Adding short, regular cross-team reflection points lets findings shape the next increments.
Why not the others: Longer phase-gate reviews are still six months apart; logging problems for the next phase gate still delays action; one review at closure helps only future projects.
Remember: Learn at the speed you deliver.

questions.stem: An agile team's retrospectives focus only on what went wrong. Last sprint, a new pairing approach cut the defect rate in half, but nobody recorded it. Several members will rotate to other teams next month and be replaced by new people. What should the scrum master do?
options: Capture the pairing approach and its results so the practice survives the membership changes.
Keep retrospectives focused on problems, since fixing failures is where most value is found.
Wait to see whether the defect reduction lasts several more sprints before discussing it.
Mention the success informally and trust the remaining members to keep using the approach.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Capturing successes as lessons — record what worked, not only what went wrong, so good practices survive (Rule M4-B17-R05).
Spot it: A practice that clearly improved results, not recorded, people about to rotate out.
In this scenario: The pairing approach halved defects, and members are leaving next month. Capturing the practice and its results keeps it in the team's knowledge.
Why not the others: Focusing only on problems misses repeatable successes; waiting several sprints risks losing the knowledge as people leave; mentioning it informally relies on memory.
Remember: Lessons learned = what went WELL + what went wrong.

questions.stem: A PMO methodology requires a full formal design review for every change on a facilities project. Data from the last 40 minor changes shows each review added about two weeks and none found a problem. The project manager wants to improve the process. What is the BEST approach?
options: Continue full reviews for every change, because the methodology requires strict adherence.
Stop reviewing minor changes on this project without telling the PMO about the decision.
Propose a lighter review path for minor changes to the PMO, using the 40-change data as evidence.
Replace the whole methodology with an adaptive approach for all remaining project work.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Evidence-based process improvement — adapt processes using data, and work through governance to change them (Rule M4-B17-R08).
Spot it: Data showing a process adds cost without benefit, a methodology requirement, a PMO.
In this scenario: Forty minor changes each took two weeks of review with no problems found. Proposing a lighter path to the PMO with that evidence improves the process through proper governance.
Why not the others: Continuing unchanged values method purity over results; stopping reviews without telling the PMO bypasses governance; replacing the whole methodology overreacts to one process problem.
Remember: Tailor with data, through governance. Data → Analyze → Insight → Decision → Action.

questions.stem: At the end of month four on a software rollout project, planned value is $400,000, earned value is $340,000, and actual cost is $330,000. The sponsor asks whether the project is ahead of or behind schedule. What should the project manager report?
options: Ahead of schedule, because actual cost is lower than the planned value for the same period.
Behind schedule, because the value of work completed is less than the value planned to date.
On schedule, because earned value and actual cost are within about 3 percent of each other.
Schedule status cannot be judged until the project's actual finish date is finally known.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Schedule variance in EVM — compare earned value (EV) with planned value (PV): SV = EV − PV and SPI = EV ÷ PV (Rule M4-B05-R02).
Spot it: PV, EV and AC given; "ahead or behind schedule?"
In this scenario: SV = $340,000 − $400,000 = −$60,000 and SPI = 0.85. Less work has been completed than planned, so the project is behind schedule. (CPI = 340 ÷ 330 ≈ 1.03, so it is slightly under budget.)
Why not the others: Comparing actual cost with planned value mixes up cost and schedule; comparing EV with AC measures cost, not schedule; EVM measures schedule status during the project, not only at the end.
Remember: Schedule = EV vs PV. Cost = EV vs AC. EV always comes first; below 1.0 is bad.

questions.stem: The cost performance index on a pipeline project dropped from 1.0 to 0.86 over two months. The sponsor demands an immediate 15 percent cut to all remaining activity budgets to recover. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Cut all remaining activity budgets by 15 percent as the sponsor requested to restore the CPI.
Draw on the management reserve to cover the overrun on the remaining project work packages.
Submit a change request to rebaseline the cost baseline so it matches the current CPI value.
Analyze which work packages and cost drivers caused the variance before choosing a correction.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Variance analysis — find the cause of a variance before choosing corrective action (Rule M4-B05-R04).
Spot it: A CPI drop, pressure for an immediate across-the-board fix, "FIRST."
In this scenario: CPI fell to 0.86, but the cause is unknown. Analyzing which work packages and cost drivers caused it lets the PM target the correction where it will work.
Why not the others: A blanket 15 percent cut treats all work alike without knowing the cause; management reserve is for unknown risks and needs approval; rebaselining erases the variance instead of fixing it.
Remember: ASSESS before you ACT. Variance → analyze cause → then correct.

questions.stem: A project manager must choose between two HVAC systems for a new office building. System A costs $200,000 to buy and $40,000 a year to run; System B costs $260,000 and $15,000 a year. The building's expected life is 20 years. Procurement recommends System A because it is cheaper. What should the project manager do?
options: Compare the purchase, operating, and upkeep costs of both systems over the building's life.
Choose System A because its lower price keeps the project within its approved budget.
Choose the system the HVAC vendor rates higher, since vendors understand the equipment best.
Ask procurement to negotiate a lower price for System B before comparing the two options.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Total cost of ownership — compare options over their whole life, including purchase, operation and maintenance (Rule M4-B05-R07).
Spot it: Different upfront and running costs, a long asset life, a recommendation based on purchase price only.
In this scenario: Over 20 years, System A costs about $200,000 + $800,000 = $1,000,000 and System B about $260,000 + $300,000 = $560,000. Lifecycle comparison shows B is far cheaper.
Why not the others: Choosing A because of lower price ignores operating costs; relying on vendor ratings is not objective analysis; negotiating B's price first skips the comparison that matters.
Remember: Cheapest to buy ≠ cheapest to own. Compare the lifecycle.

questions.stem: A construction project has a schedule performance index of 0.78, caused by low crew productivity; scope has not changed. Ahead of an upcoming audit, a senior manager asks the project manager to rebaseline the schedule so the project appears on track. What should the project manager do?
options: Rebaseline the schedule as requested so the audit reflects achievable dates from this point on.
Rebaseline only the late activities so the overall schedule variance looks smaller to the auditors.
Keep the current baseline, report the true variance, and present a recovery plan for remaining work.
Ask for the audit to be delayed until the team has recovered enough to show a positive variance.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Rebaselining integrity — baselines change only for approved changes, never to hide poor performance (Rule M4-B05-R10).
Spot it: Poor SPI, no scope change, pressure to look good before an audit.
In this scenario: Scope has not changed; productivity has. The PM keeps the baseline, reports the true variance and presents a recovery plan.
Why not the others: Rebaselining erases real performance history; changing only the late activities hides variance selectively; asking to delay the audit avoids accountability.
Remember: Baseline = APPROVED. It changes through change control, never to hide bad news.

questions.stem: Midway through a hybrid program, a newly appointed executive asks why the organization is funding a customer data platform at all. Members of the adaptive teams also ask what value their work is supposed to create. Which document should the project manager use to answer both questions?
options: The project charter, which names the project manager and authorizes the use of resources.
The business case, which describes the need, the chosen option, and the expected benefits.
The product roadmap, which shows the planned sequence of releases for the adaptive teams.
The risk register, which lists threats and opportunities that could affect the program.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Business case — the document that explains WHY the investment exists: the business need, options considered and expected benefits (Rule M4-B16-R01).
Spot it: "why are we funding this?" and "what value should our work create?"
In this scenario: Both questions are about justification and expected value. The business case answers them.
Why not the others: The charter AUTHORIZES the project and names the PM, but it doesn't make the full value argument; the product roadmap shows release order, not justification; the risk register tracks threats and opportunities.
Remember: WHY = business case. AUTHORITY = charter. HOW = plans. APPROVED = baselines. TRACK = registers and logs.

questions.stem: An agile team is part of a larger regulated program. External auditors ask how scope, schedule, quality, and risk will be managed across the whole effort and how the program's various management approaches fit together. Which artifact BEST answers the auditors' question?
options: The product backlog, which lists and orders the work items the team intends to deliver.
The team working agreement, which describes how members collaborate from day to day.
The sprint burndown chart, which shows how much work remains in the current sprint.
The project management plan, which integrates how each area of the work will be managed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Project management plan — the integrated document describing how scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk and other areas are managed and how they fit together (Rule M4-B16-R03).
Spot it: "how will the whole effort be managed?"; auditors; regulated programs; multiple approaches.
In this scenario: The auditors want to know how the areas are managed across the program and how approaches fit. The project management plan integrates exactly that.
Why not the others: The product backlog lists work to build, not how the effort is managed; the working agreement covers team behavior; the sprint burndown shows remaining work in one sprint.
Remember: HOW = plans. The project management plan integrates all subsidiary plans and baselines.

questions.stem: A client asks the project manager which of the 14 change requests submitted this quarter were approved, which were rejected, and which are still awaiting a decision. Which project document should the project manager consult to answer?
options: The change log, which records each change request along with its status and decision.
The issue log, which records problems needing resolution and who is assigned to them.
The scope baseline, which holds the approved scope statement, WBS, and WBS dictionary.
The assumption log, which records assumptions and constraints found during the project.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Change log — the record of every change request with its status and decision (approved, rejected, pending) (Rule M4-B16-R06).
Spot it: "which changes were approved, rejected or pending?"
In this scenario: The client wants the status of 14 change requests. The change log records each one with its status and decision.
Why not the others: The issue log tracks current problems and owners; the scope baseline holds approved scope, not request status; the assumption log tracks assumptions and constraints.
Remember: TRACK = logs. Change log = requests + decisions. Issue log = current problems.

questions.stem: In a hybrid program, an adaptive team built its software against version 2.3 of an interface specification. The predictive hardware vendor used version 2.1, which had been emailed to them months earlier. Integration testing failed as a result. What should the project manager do to prevent a repeat?
options: Ask the vendor and the team to email each other whenever the interface specification changes.
Freeze the interface specification permanently so that no new versions can ever be created.
Keep interface specifications in a controlled repository that clearly marks the approved version.
Have the adaptive team rework its software to version 2.1 so it matches what the vendor used.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Configuration and version control — keep critical artifacts in a controlled repository that shows which version is approved (Rule M4-B16-R09).
Spot it: Different teams using different versions, failures from outdated specifications, email distribution.
In this scenario: One side built to version 2.3 and the other to 2.1. A controlled repository marking the approved version gives everyone one source of truth.
Why not the others: More emails is the same uncontrolled distribution that caused the problem; a permanent freeze blocks needed updates; reworking to 2.1 fixes this one mismatch without preventing the next.
Remember: One source of truth — configuration management controls versions.

questions.stem: An agile team told executives a data migration epic would take four sprints. That figure depended on a vendor supplying test data in the first sprint and on no changes to the data model. Executives are now treating four sprints as a firm commitment. What should the team do?
options: Keep the four-sprint figure but quietly add buffer sprints without explaining where they came from.
Restate the estimate as a range and record the vendor and data-model assumptions behind it.
Refuse to give any estimate for the epic until the vendor confirms the test data delivery date.
Commit to four sprints and plan for overtime in case the vendor delivers the test data late.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Estimates with assumptions and ranges — important estimates should show a range and state the assumptions they depend on (Rule M4-B04-R02).
Spot it: A single-number estimate treated as a commitment, unconfirmed dependencies.
In this scenario: The four-sprint estimate depends on vendor test data and a stable data model. Restating it as a range with those assumptions recorded helps executives see the uncertainty.
Why not the others: Hidden buffer sprints make estimates untrustworthy; refusing to estimate leaves executives without information; committing with planned overtime hides the risk.
Remember: Estimate = range + assumptions. Log the assumptions.

questions.stem: A project manager is preparing the cost estimate for an office fit-out. The WBS is decomposed to work packages, and detailed drawings and supplier quotes are available. The sponsor needs a definitive estimate to secure funding approval. Which estimating approach should the project manager use?
options: Use the total cost of a similar fit-out finished last year and adjust it for the size difference.
Apply an industry cost-per-square-foot rate to the total floor area of the office being fitted out.
Ask the most experienced team member for a single overall figure based on professional judgment.
Estimate each work package in detail and roll the costs up through the WBS to a project total.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Bottom-up estimating — estimating each work package in detail and rolling the costs up; the most accurate method when detail is available (Rule M4-B04-R05).
Spot it: A decomposed WBS, detailed drawings and quotes, a definitive estimate needed.
In this scenario: Work packages, drawings and quotes are available and funding needs accuracy. Bottom-up estimating through the WBS fits.
Why not the others: Analogous estimating (a similar past project) is fast but less accurate; a square-foot rate is parametric and too coarse here; one expert's figure is expert judgment without detail.
Remember: Analogous = similar project. Parametric = rate × unit. Three-point = O, M, P. Bottom-up = add up work packages.

questions.stem: A team lead's estimates in a hybrid program have been off by about 30 percent because of hidden legacy system issues. Each estimate used the best information available, and the assumptions were disclosed at the time. A director wants to discipline the lead for bad estimating. What should the project manager do?
options: Explain that the estimates were honest, and focus on improving the inputs and using ranges.
Support the disciplinary action so that team leads take greater care with future estimates.
Pad all of the team lead's future estimates by 30 percent to offset the observed inaccuracy.
Take over estimating from the team lead so the director sees that the issue is handled.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Estimate accuracy vs honesty — an estimate can be honest and still be wrong when facts were unknown; judge estimators by honesty and disclosed assumptions (Rule M4-B04-R08).
Spot it: Estimates off because of hidden issues, assumptions disclosed, a push to punish.
In this scenario: The lead used the best information and disclosed assumptions. The PM explains this and improves inputs, such as discovery and ranges.
Why not the others: Discipline for honest estimates teaches people to pad or hide; a blanket 30 percent pad hides the real uncertainty; taking over estimating removes the expert.
Remember: Honest + wrong = improve the inputs, not punish the person.

questions.stem: A hybrid program's steering committee receives burnup charts from the adaptive teams and percent-complete Gantt charts from the predictive team. Committee members say they cannot tell whether the program will reach its regulatory launch date. What should the project manager do?
options: Convert the adaptive teams' progress into percent complete so both streams use one metric.
Train committee members to read burnup and Gantt charts so they can interpret each report.
Report both streams against shared milestones and business outcomes the committee cares about.
Require the adaptive teams to produce Gantt charts so all progress uses a predictive format.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reporting across approaches — translate agile and predictive progress into shared milestones and outcomes stakeholders understand (Rule M4-B14-R04).
Spot it: Different charts from different teams, a committee confused, a key launch date.
In this scenario: The committee cares about the regulatory launch date. Reporting both streams against shared milestones and outcomes shows whether it will be met.
Why not the others: Converting adaptive progress into percent complete distorts it; training executives on charts adds work without answering their question; forcing Gantt charts on adaptive teams imposes the wrong tool.
Remember: Speak the audience's language — milestones and outcomes.

questions.stem: A hybrid program includes a low-risk internal dashboard built by an adaptive team and a safety-critical control module built under a predictive approach. The PMO requires identical heavy documentation for both, while an agile coach argues the adaptive team needs almost none. What should the project manager do?
options: Apply the PMO's full documentation set to both components for consistency across the program.
Set documentation depth for each component according to its risk and its users' needs.
Exempt the adaptive team from documentation, since agile values working software over documents.
Require the same minimal documentation for both so neither team is slowed by paperwork.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tailoring documentation — set documentation depth by risk and user need, not by whether a team is agile or predictive (Rule M4-B14-R07).
Spot it: High-risk and low-risk components, one-size-fits-all rules, arguments about methodology.
In this scenario: The safety-critical module needs thorough documentation; the low-risk dashboard needs little. Tailoring each by risk and need fits both.
Why not the others: Full documentation for both burdens the low-risk work; exempting agile work misreads the Agile Manifesto; minimal documentation for both endangers the safety-critical module.
Remember: Tailor to risk and need, not to the label.

questions.stem: Six months into a hybrid program, adaptive teams wait an average of three weeks for predictive design approvals. The predictive team, meanwhile, complains about frequent requirement changes coming from the adaptive side. Each group blames the other for the delays. What should the project manager do?
options: Move every team to a fully predictive approach so all teams follow the same approval process.
Ask the adaptive teams to batch their requirement changes and submit them only at phase gates.
Escalate the conflict to the sponsor and ask for a ruling on which group is causing the delays.
Review how the hybrid handoffs and approval cadence are set up with both groups, and adjust them.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Inspecting the hybrid model itself — when friction comes from how approaches connect, adjust the handoffs and cadence (Rule M4-B14-R10).
Spot it: Long waits at handoffs, both sides blaming each other, six months in.
In this scenario: Delays sit at the connection between approaches. Reviewing handoffs and approval cadence with both groups and adjusting them removes the friction.
Why not the others: Moving everyone to predictive loses the adaptive benefits; batching changes to phase gates slows the adaptive side; asking the sponsor to assign blame fixes nothing.
Remember: Inspect and adapt the process, including the hybrid setup itself.

questions.stem: An agile team plans to deliver a full inventory management system in one release after nine months. Warehouse managers' requirements are still uncertain, but stock-level tracking alone would eliminate most of their manual spreadsheets. What should the team recommend?
options: Release stock-level tracking first and use the managers' feedback to shape later features.
Keep the single nine-month release so managers get a complete and consistent system at once.
Spend another month gathering detailed requirements so the full system is specified accurately.
Release a nonworking mock-up of the whole system to warehouse managers for early approval.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Incremental delivery and MVP — release usable value in smaller increments to reduce risk and learn sooner (Rule M4-B18-R01).
Spot it: Uncertain requirements, a long single release, one feature that delivers most of the value.
In this scenario: Stock tracking alone removes most spreadsheets. Releasing it first gives value now and feedback for later features.
Why not the others: A nine-month big-bang release delays value and learning; more requirements work cannot resolve uncertainty that only use reveals; a nonworking mock-up gives feedback without delivering value.
Remember: Deliver small, learn fast. MVP = smallest thing that delivers value and learning.

questions.stem: A health-tech team is building a remote patient monitoring app. The entire business model depends on clinicians acting on automated alerts, but no one knows whether they will. Stakeholders are pressing the product owner to spend the next two sprints on polished dashboards and single sign-on. What should the product owner prioritize FIRST?
options: The polished dashboards and sign-on features that stakeholders are requesting most loudly
A thin alert-to-clinician slice that shows whether clinicians actually respond to alerts
A complete architecture design for all future features before any working code is built
The simplest low-risk features so the team can build early momentum and confidence
questions.explanation:
Concept: Test the riskiest assumption first — when uncertainty is high, the first increment should prove or disprove the belief the whole product depends on (Rule M4-B18-R03).
Spot it: "no one knows whether…", "the entire model depends on…", stakeholders pushing polish before the core idea is proven.
In this scenario: The app is worthless unless clinicians act on alerts, so a thin alert-to-clinician slice buys the most learning for the least money.
Why not the others: Dashboards and sign-on are polish on an unproven idea; full up-front architecture is predictive big design with no learning; easy low-risk features build momentum but leave the killer question unanswered.
Remember: Riskiest assumption first — learn before you polish. MVP = Minimum Viable LEARNING.

questions.stem: For three sprints, a logistics company's agile team has spent almost all capacity on database refactoring and deployment pipeline work. Stakeholders at sprint reviews see nothing new and are losing interest, yet the pipeline work will speed up future delivery. What should the product owner do?
options: Plan upcoming sprints to pair some enabler work with at least one visible customer feature
Pause all enabler work until stakeholders have seen several new customer features delivered
Finish the refactoring first and then demonstrate the completed platform to stakeholders
Ask developers to do the pipeline work after hours so sprint capacity stays on features
questions.explanation:
Concept: Balance enablers and features — technical enablers (refactoring, pipelines) protect future speed, but each iteration should still deliver something stakeholders can see and react to (Rule M4-B18-R06).
Spot it: several sprints of "invisible" technical work, reviews with nothing to show, stakeholders losing interest.
In this scenario: The pipeline work is valuable, so keep it, but mix at least one visible customer feature into each sprint so feedback and engagement keep flowing.
Why not the others: Pausing all enablers swaps one imbalance for another and grows technical debt; finishing refactoring first keeps reviews empty even longer; after-hours work breaks sustainable pace and hides real capacity.
Remember: Backlog = enablers + features, blended every sprint — not one, then the other.

questions.stem: A retail analytics team plans to spend six months building a product recommendation engine and show it to shoppers at the end. The team is unsure whether shoppers will trust machine-made suggestions, and the budget is large. What should the agile practitioner recommend?
options: Finish the complete engine first so that shoppers can judge a polished, fully working product at launch
Survey shoppers once at the end of the six months to measure their overall satisfaction
Send the sponsor monthly reports listing the technical components completed so far
Put a rough recommendation prototype in front of a small group of shoppers within two weeks
questions.explanation:
Concept: Short feedback loops — get real user feedback early and often, before large investment piles up behind an untested idea (Rule M4-B18-R09).
Spot it: long build with a big reveal "at the end," an uncertain user reaction, a large budget at stake.
In this scenario: Shopper trust is the unknown, so a rough prototype in front of real shoppers within two weeks answers it before months of spend.
Why not the others: Building the full engine first is a big-bang reveal after the money is gone; a survey at the end is feedback too late to change anything; monthly reports to the sponsor track output and never reach the users whose trust is in question.
Remember: Build a little → show real users → learn → adjust. The shorter the loop, the cheaper the lesson.

questions.stem: A project manager is assembling the project management plan for a hospital wing renovation. The scheduler's draft assumes a specialized medical gas contractor is available in March, leaves no time for state inspections, and was built without reference to the budget finance set separately. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Baseline the schedule now and resolve the budget and contractor issues through later changes
Send the schedule to the sponsor for approval because the scheduler is the subject expert
Reconcile the schedule with procurement lead times, inspection needs, risks, and the budget
Ask finance to add a standard contingency percentage to the budget to cover any gaps
questions.explanation:
Concept: Integrated planning — the project management plan is one coherent whole; scope, schedule, cost, procurement, risk, resources and quality must be reconciled before anything is baselined (Rule M3-B17-R02).
Spot it: a component plan built "without reference to" the others, assumptions about vendor availability, missing regulatory time.
In this scenario: The schedule ignores contractor lead times, inspections and the budget, so the PM reconciles it with those plans before approval.
Why not the others: Baselining now locks in known conflicts and guarantees change requests; sending it to the sponsor skips the PM's integration job; a blanket contingency percentage papers over gaps instead of fixing the plan.
Remember: Plan = HOW, Baseline = APPROVED. Integrate the HOW before you approve it.

questions.stem: A project manager is drafting the charter for a new utility billing system. The draft lists the deliverables: new software, trained billing staff, and migrated customer accounts. The sponsor explains that the real reason for the investment is to reduce costly billing disputes. What should the project manager add to the charter?
options: A more detailed list of the software modules and training sessions that will be delivered
A target such as a 30 percent drop in billing disputes within six months after go-live
A statement that the project succeeds when every deliverable is accepted on schedule
The vendor's standard performance claims taken directly from its sales proposal
questions.explanation:
Concept: Outcomes, not just deliverables — the charter should state measurable success criteria that reflect WHY the project exists, not only WHAT will be built (Rule M3-B17-R05).
Spot it: a charter listing only outputs (software, training, migration) while the sponsor describes a business reason.
In this scenario: The real purpose is fewer billing disputes, so a measurable target like a 30 percent drop within six months ties success to that purpose.
Why not the others: More module detail is still output; "all deliverables accepted on schedule" could call the project a success while disputes stay high; a vendor's sales claims are not the buyer's own success criteria.
Remember: Deliverable → Outcome → Benefit → Value. Success is measured at the outcome, not the box you shipped.

questions.stem: A project manager is finalizing the integrated plan for a new warehouse management system. The plan covers design, build, testing, and go-live, and it ends on the cutover weekend. The operations manager asks who will support floor staff on the Monday after cutover and how staff will learn the new scanning steps. What should the project manager do?
options: Add support handover, user adoption activities, and operational acceptance to the plan
Explain that support after go-live belongs to operations and is outside the project scope
Extend system testing by two weeks so that fewer defects reach operations after cutover
Plan for the project team to keep supporting warehouse users indefinitely after go-live
questions.explanation:
Concept: Transition and operational readiness — a plan is not complete until it covers handover to operations, user adoption and support; value appears only when the result is used (Rule M3-B17-R08).
Spot it: a plan that "ends at cutover," operations asking who supports users on day one, staff who must learn new steps.
In this scenario: Adding support handover, adoption activities and operational acceptance closes the gap between go-live and real use.
Why not the others: Calling it out of scope leaves the business unable to use the system; extra testing cuts defects but trains no one and assigns no support; supporting users indefinitely turns a temporary project into operations.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close. No Transfer = no value.

questions.stem: A service desk team tracks cycle time on its kanban board. Some members start the clock when a ticket is logged, while others start it when someone begins working on it. Reported cycle times swing widely, and the manager cannot tell whether flow is improving. What should the team lead do?
options: Replace cycle time with story points so that everyone reports flow in the same shared unit
Average the results of both methods to produce one combined cycle time figure
Report only the shortest cycle times to show what the team can achieve at best
Agree on one start point and one end point for cycle time and use them for every item
questions.explanation:
Concept: Cycle time — how long an item takes from when work STARTS until it is DONE; it is only useful when every item is measured with the same start and end points (Rule M4-B13-R04).
Spot it: people starting the clock at different moments, numbers swinging widely, managers unable to see a trend.
In this scenario: The team agrees one start point (work begins) and one end point (done) and applies them to every item, so the data become comparable.
Why not the others: Story points measure size, not flow time; averaging two inconsistent methods still produces a meaningless number; reporting only the best times is cherry-picking, not measurement.
Remember: Throughput = how many finished. Cycle time = how long once started. Lead time = how long since requested.

questions.stem: A product team's kanban board shows cards piling up in the code review column while coding and testing move quickly. Two senior developers perform all reviews. The engineering manager proposes hiring more developers to increase throughput. What should the agile practitioner suggest?
options: Hire more developers so the coding stage produces finished work even more quickly than today
Raise the review column's WIP limit so that more items are allowed to wait there
Relieve the review stage first, for example by training more developers to review code
Automate more of the testing stage before making any changes to the review stage
questions.explanation:
Concept: Bottleneck first — a flow system moves only as fast as its most constrained step, so improvement effort goes to the bottleneck before anything else (Rule M4-B13-R07).
Spot it: cards piling up in one column, other stages flowing fast, a step that depends on only a few people.
In this scenario: Code review is the constraint, so relieving it (for example, training more reviewers) is what actually raises throughput.
Why not the others: More developers speed up an unconstrained step and just grow the review queue; a higher WIP limit lets even more work wait; automating testing improves a stage that is not the constraint.
Remember: Visualize → Limit WIP → Pull → Monitor flow → Find the bottleneck → Fix it → Measure.

questions.stem: A compliance software team set its kanban WIP limits and expedite rules a year ago. Since then, urgent regulator requests have tripled, and the team's flow data show expedited items routinely waiting behind standard work for days. What should the team do?
options: Keep the current policies because frequent changes would confuse the team
Use the recent flow data to revisit the expedite rules and WIP limits together
Let the manager set priorities each morning instead of using written team policies
Remove all WIP limits so urgent items can start as soon as they arrive
questions.explanation:
Concept: Evidence-based flow policies — WIP limits, classes of service and expedite rules are team agreements that should be revisited when data and demand change (Rule M4-B13-R10).
Spot it: policies set long ago, demand that has shifted, flow data showing a class of work consistently stuck.
In this scenario: Urgent regulator requests tripled and expedited items wait for days, so the team uses its flow data to adjust expedite rules and WIP limits together.
Why not the others: Keeping old policies ignores the evidence; a manager setting daily priorities replaces team-owned policies with push control; removing WIP limits overloads the system and slows everything, urgent work included.
Remember: Kanban policies are explicit AND improvable — inspect the data, then adapt the policy.

questions.stem: An agile team will release a new customer self-service portal in three weeks. The developers assume IT operations will handle incidents after release, while IT operations assumes the development team will. No one has discussed monitoring or after-hours support. What should the agile project manager do FIRST?
options: Get agreement now on which group owns incidents, monitoring, and fixes after release
Release on schedule and settle support ownership after the first real incident occurs
Delay the release until operations has fully rewritten its support procedures
Have the developers quietly absorb all support work alongside new features
questions.explanation:
Concept: Operational ownership before transition — before a release, it must be clear who owns incidents, monitoring and fixes once the product is live (Rule M5-B13-R01).
Spot it: two groups each assuming the other will support it, no discussion of monitoring or after-hours coverage, release date approaching.
In this scenario: The first step is to get the developers and IT operations to agree now on who owns what after release.
Why not the others: Waiting for the first incident guarantees confusion when it hurts most; delaying for a full rewrite of procedures overreacts to a clarification problem; developers quietly absorbing support hides the gap and drains feature capacity.
Remember: Complete → Accept → TRANSFER. You cannot transfer to "nobody".

questions.stem: A project manager at a regional bank is planning an overnight upgrade of the core payments platform. If the upgrade fails, card and transfer payments stop for over two million customers. Rehearsal results have been good. What should the project manager include in the cutover plan?
options: No fallback, because the good rehearsal results show that the upgrade will succeed
A plan to fix any problems in production once customers begin reporting them
An extra week of testing in place of any rollback or fallback preparations
A tested rollback procedure with clear go/no-go decision points during cutover
questions.explanation:
Concept: Fallback and rollback planning — when the impact of failure is severe, the cutover plan needs a tested way back and clear go/no-go points (Rule M5-B13-R03).
Spot it: a high-impact cutover (payments, safety, millions of users), overnight windows, confidence based on rehearsals alone.
In this scenario: A failed upgrade would stop payments for two million customers, so a tested rollback with go/no-go decision points is essential.
Why not the others: Good rehearsals lower probability, not impact; fixing in production after customers complain is reacting too late; more testing also lowers probability but cannot restore service if the cutover still fails.
Remember: Probability down = test more. Impact covered = plan the way back.

questions.stem: A hospital is replacing its patient records system. Infrastructure is delivered through a predictive plan, while clinical screens are built in agile sprints. Regulators require proven recovery for critical clinical systems. Go-live is two months away, and the disaster recovery plan is documented but has never been exercised. What should the project manager do?
options: Accept the written recovery plan because regulators mainly review the documentation
Add recovery testing to the product backlog for a sprint after go-live
Schedule a recovery exercise that proves the documented plan works before go-live
Ask the vendor to confirm in writing that its recovery design is reliable
questions.explanation:
Concept: Test continuity and recovery — for critical capabilities, a recovery plan counts only when it has been exercised and shown to work (Rule M5-B13-R06).
Spot it: "documented but never exercised," regulators requiring proven recovery, a critical system nearing go-live.
In this scenario: The hospital schedules a recovery exercise before go-live so the plan is proven, not just written.
Why not the others: Accepting the paper plan fails the "proven" requirement; testing after go-live leaves a critical system unprotected; a vendor letter is still paper assurance, not evidence the hospital itself can recover.
Remember: Written ≠ proven. For critical systems, rehearse the recovery before you need it.

questions.stem: An agile team is migrating two million customer records from a legacy CRM in its next release. A trial load shows record counts differ from the source by several thousand, and some account balances do not match. The product owner wants to release anyway because the new features are ready. What should the team do?
options: Release as planned and ask customers to report any missing or incorrect records they find
Reconcile counts and key values against the source and resolve the gaps before release
Delete the unmatched legacy records because they are probably old duplicates
Add a story to investigate the differences in a sprint after the release
questions.explanation:
Concept: Data migration reconciliation — whenever data moves, counts and key values must be reconciled against the source and gaps resolved before the data goes live (Rule M5-B13-R09).
Spot it: record counts that don't match, balances that differ, pressure to release because "features are ready."
In this scenario: Mismatched counts and balances are defects in customer data, so the team reconciles against the source and fixes the gaps before release.
Why not the others: Asking customers to find errors pushes quality control onto them; deleting unmatched records guesses and may destroy real data; a later-sprint story knowingly ships wrong balances into production.
Remember: Moved data must match — count it, compare it, fix it, THEN release.

questions.stem: A state transportation agency needs drone-based bridge inspection services for the first time. The project manager does not know which vendors provide this service, what capabilities are typical, or how vendors usually price the work. What should the project manager issue FIRST?
options: A request for information to learn about vendor capabilities and typical market options
A request for proposal with a detailed statement of work and weighted scoring criteria
A fixed-price award to the vendor that did similar work for another state last year
A request for quotation asking vendors for their lowest price per inspection flight
questions.explanation:
Concept: Request for information (RFI) — a procurement document used to learn about the market (who can do the work, typical capabilities, pricing approaches) before a formal solicitation (Rule M4-B09-R02).
Spot it: "first time buying this," "does not know which vendors," "what is typical."
In this scenario: The agency lacks basic market knowledge, so it issues an RFI first; that knowledge then shapes a sound statement of work and solicitation.
Why not the others: An RFP needs a solid statement of work and scoring criteria the agency cannot yet write; a direct award skips competition and market research; an RFQ compares prices for work that is already clearly defined.
Remember: RFI = Information • RFQ = Price • RFP = Solution • IFB = Formal bid.

questions.stem: A utility needs a seller to design a first-of-its-kind grid control system. Requirements will evolve as testing reveals what the grid can support, and sellers say they cannot price the work responsibly up front. The utility still wants the seller motivated to control cost. Which contract type is MOST appropriate?
options: A firm-fixed-price contract so that the seller carries all of the cost risk
A time-and-materials contract with no ceiling for the complete design effort
A fixed-price contract with economic price adjustment for yearly inflation
A cost-reimbursable contract with incentive fees tied to meeting cost targets
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contract type selection — the clearer the scope, the more a fixed price fits; the less clear, the more cost-reimbursable fits, and incentive fees keep the seller focused on cost (Rule M4-B09-R05).
Spot it: "first-of-its-kind," "requirements will evolve," sellers unable to price responsibly, buyer still wanting cost discipline.
In this scenario: Scope is uncertain, so a cost-reimbursable contract with incentive fees tied to cost targets shares risk fairly and motivates cost control.
Why not the others: Firm fixed price forces sellers to price the unknown, inviting padded bids or disputes; uncapped time and materials leaves the buyer fully exposed; an economic price adjustment addresses inflation, not undefined scope.
Remember: Clear scope → Fixed price. Unclear scope → Cost-reimbursable. Want motivation → add an Incentive.

questions.stem: A project manager needs a data consultant for roughly six weeks to help clean up records whose extent will only become clear once work starts. The project manager chooses a time-and-materials contract for flexibility. What should the project manager do to manage the buyer's exposure?
options: Switch to a firm-fixed-price contract and ask the consultant to price the job
Let the consultant bill freely because T&M contracts limit cost on their own
Set a not-to-exceed ceiling and review hours and results against it each week
Prepay the full six weeks up front so that invoicing stays simple
questions.explanation:
Concept: Time-and-materials (T&M) control — T&M gives flexibility when scope is unclear, but the buyer carries cost exposure, so it needs a ceiling and close monitoring (Rule M4-B09-R08).
Spot it: short engagements, work whose size "will only become clear once work starts," a buyer who has already chosen T&M.
In this scenario: A not-to-exceed ceiling plus weekly review of hours and results keeps the flexibility while capping the buyer's risk.
