Why not the others: Switching to fixed price asks the seller to price unknown work; T&M does not limit cost on its own — the buyer must; prepaying the full period removes the leverage to stop or adjust.
Remember: T&M = flexible for the buyer, risky for the buyer. Cap it (NTE) and watch it.

questions.stem: Inspectors at a manufacturing plant keep finding the same weld defects on finished bicycle frames and rejecting them. The plant director asks the project manager for an action that prevents the defects from being introduced rather than catching them afterward. Which action BEST meets this request?
options: Increase inspection frequency so that more defective frames are caught early
Audit the welding procedures to find where in the process the defects arise
Measure each finished frame against the specification and reject failures
Add a final inspection checkpoint at the loading dock before shipment
questions.explanation:
Concept: Quality management versus quality control — managing quality (assurance) improves the PROCESS so defects are not created; quality control INSPECTS outputs to catch defects after they exist (Rule M4-B06-R04).
Spot it: "prevent rather than catch," recurring defects of the same type, inspection finding the same problem repeatedly.
In this scenario: Auditing the welding procedures finds where in the process the defect is introduced, which is prevention.
Why not the others: More frequent inspection, measuring finished frames and a final dock checkpoint are all quality control — they find defects after they are made.
Remember: Manage Quality = process, prevent. Control Quality = product, inspect. Prevention over inspection.

questions.stem: A hybrid project combines a predictive store refit with an agile rollout of new point-of-sale software. After the first rollout wave, its help desk has logged 600 software defects across 14 categories. The team has limited capacity next sprint. What should the project manager do to decide where to focus?
options: Rank the defect categories by frequency to find the few that cause most of the issues
Use a control chart to see whether daily defect arrivals fall within statistical limits
Build a fishbone diagram for each of the 14 categories before fixing any of them
Split the fix effort evenly across all 14 categories so that every group gets help
questions.explanation:
Concept: Pareto analysis — ranks problem categories by frequency so the team can focus on the "vital few" causes that create most of the issues (the 80/20 rule) (Rule M4-B06-R07).
Spot it: many defects across many categories, limited capacity, "decide where to focus."
In this scenario: Ranking the 14 categories by frequency shows which few to fix first with the limited capacity next sprint.
Why not the others: A control chart shows whether a process is stable over time, not which category matters most; fishbone diagrams for all 14 find causes but do not prioritize and waste scarce time; splitting effort evenly ignores the 80/20 reality.
Remember: Pareto = prioritize. Fishbone = root cause. Control chart = stable? Histogram = distribution. Scatter = relationship.

questions.stem: A fintech team's features regularly pass sprint review demos, but many later fail security scans and performance tests run before each quarterly release. The resulting rework is consuming a growing share of every sprint. What should the team do?
options: Plan a separate hardening phase at the end of each release for all testing work
Ask the product owner to accept features now and log the defects for later
Assign a quality team to inspect every feature after each release is deployed
Add security scans and performance thresholds to the team's definition of done
questions.explanation:
Concept: Quality in the definition of done — building quality criteria (security, performance, testing) into acceptance and the definition of done makes work truly finished every sprint (Rule M4-B06-R10).
Spot it: features that "pass the demo" but fail later checks, growing rework, quality tests run only near release.
In this scenario: Adding security scans and performance thresholds to the definition of done catches problems in the sprint where they are created.
Why not the others: A hardening phase keeps quality late, which is the cause of the rework; accepting now and logging defects knowingly ships undone work; inspecting after deployment is late quality control.
Remember: Definition of done is owned by the Scrum team — if it isn't tested, it isn't done.

questions.stem: A project manager is gathering requirements for a county building permit system. A county commissioner insists, "We need a mobile app." Interviews show applicants' real frustration is that permits take about 40 days to approve because of manual handoffs between departments. What should the project manager do?
options: Record the mobile app as a mandatory requirement because a senior commissioner personally requested it
Begin evaluating mobile app vendors to keep the commissioner engaged and supportive
Clarify the underlying need to shorten approval time before treating an app as a requirement
Tell the commissioner that solution ideas are not part of requirements gathering
questions.explanation:
Concept: Need versus solution — requirements work separates the business need, the stakeholder need, the actual requirement and a proposed solution feature (Rule M4-B01-R01).
Spot it: a stakeholder naming a solution ("we need an app") while interviews reveal a different underlying pain.
In this scenario: The real need is faster permit approval caused by manual handoffs, so the PM clarifies that need before treating an app as a requirement.
Why not the others: Recording the app as mandatory lets a solution replace the need, and it may not fix handoffs; evaluating vendors jumps to buying; telling the commissioner solutions don't count dismisses the stakeholder instead of engaging them.
Remember: Need → Requirement → Solution. Ask "what problem does this solve?" before writing it down.

questions.stem: On a hybrid insurance project, a claims portal is built in agile sprints while payments follow fixed contract milestones. One acceptance criterion reads, "The claims page should be fast and easy to use." The tester says there is no way to show whether it passes or fails. What should the project manager do?
options: Let the testers decide during testing what fast and easy mean for this particular page
Work with the product owner to restate it, such as pages load within 2 seconds 95% of the time
Keep the current wording because precise criteria reduce the team's design flexibility
Leave the criterion for the vendor to define in detail when the next contract milestone is reached
questions.explanation:
Concept: Testable acceptance criteria — every criterion must be observable and measurable, so anyone can show whether it passes or fails (Rule M4-B01-R03).
Spot it: vague words like "fast," "easy," "user-friendly"; a tester unable to prove pass or fail.
In this scenario: The PM works with the product owner, who owns the backlog items, to restate the criterion as a measurable threshold such as 2-second loads 95 percent of the time.
Why not the others: Letting testers decide makes acceptance subjective and invites disputes; keeping vague wording leaves the problem in place; handing definition to the vendor at the milestone means the buyer defines "done" too late.
Remember: If you can't test it, you can't accept it.

questions.stem: An agile team builds infusion pump software under medical device regulations. An auditor asks the team to show how each regulated safety requirement was verified. The team's user stories and automated tests exist, but nothing links the regulated requirements to them. What should the team do?
options: Link each regulated requirement to its stories, test cases, and recorded results
Explain that agile teams value working software more than documentation
Build a full traceability matrix for every item, including unregulated features
Show the auditor the burndown chart as evidence that the work was completed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Requirements traceability — linking controlled requirements to the deliverables and tests that satisfy them, applied where it adds value, such as regulated work (Rule M4-B01-R06).
Spot it: auditors, regulations, "show how each requirement was verified," stories and tests that exist but are not linked.
In this scenario: Linking each regulated safety requirement to its stories, tests and recorded results gives the auditor the evidence trail.
Why not the others: "Working software over documentation" does not waive regulatory evidence; tracing every unregulated feature adds cost without value; a burndown shows progress, not verification.
Remember: TRACE family = RTM / WBS dictionary. Requirement → Deliverable → Test → Result.

questions.stem: A project manager is gathering requirements for an airline crew scheduling system that must run around the clock. So far, only schedulers and business managers have been interviewed. The IT operations and service desk teams, who will run and support the system, have not been consulted. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Finalize requirements with the business users and brief operations at handover
Adopt the vendor's default availability settings as the system's nonfunctional requirements
Ask the schedulers to estimate the uptime and recovery targets for operations
Involve operations and support staff to define availability, recovery, and support needs
questions.explanation:
Concept: Nonfunctional requirements from operations — the people who will run and support a system help define availability, recovery, performance and support needs (Rule M4-B01-R09).
Spot it: a 24/7 system, only business users interviewed, IT operations and service desk not yet consulted.
In this scenario: Involving operations and support staff now captures uptime, recovery and support requirements while the design can still reflect them.
Why not the others: Briefing operations at handover is too late to shape the design; vendor defaults may not fit a round-the-clock operation; schedulers are business users, not the experts on uptime and recovery.
Remember: Identify Stakeholder → Analyze → Engage → Monitor. Whoever runs it must help define it.

questions.stem: A hybrid plant automation project builds control software in agile sprints and installs hardware on a predictive schedule. The company has one certified functional safety engineer, who also supports two other projects, and her sign-off is required before commissioning. Planning has just begun. What should the project manager do?
options: Set commissioning dates first and then request the safety engineer when her sign-off is due
Have a junior engineer provide the sign-off to avoid depending on one person
Secure the safety engineer's time now and plan commissioning around her availability
Add the sign-off to the backlog and pull it in whenever the team is ready
questions.explanation:
Concept: Scarce specialists as constraints — a person with rare skills or required approvals can limit the schedule, so identify and secure them early (Rule M4-B10-R02).
Spot it: "only one certified…," shared across projects, a sign-off that gates a milestone, planning just starting.
In this scenario: Securing the safety engineer's time now and planning commissioning around her availability protects the schedule.
Why not the others: Asking only when sign-off is due risks a long wait; a junior engineer cannot give a certified safety sign-off; putting it in the backlog to pull later ignores that she is a constraint, not a flexible task.
Remember: Dependency → Assess impact → Coordinate → Monitor. Scarce people are dependencies — book them first.

questions.stem: On an agile team, one developer is the only person who understands the payment gateway integration. She has announced a planned six-week leave starting next quarter, and several payment stories are on the roadmap for that period. What should the team do?
options: Ask her to write a detailed handover manual during her final week, just before the leave begins
Pair other developers with her on payment stories so the knowledge spreads before she leaves
Freeze all payment-related changes during her absence and defer the related stories
Ask management to postpone her leave until the payment roadmap work is completed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Cross-training for continuity — when critical knowledge sits with one person, spread it before it becomes a single point of failure (Rule M4-B10-R05).
Spot it: "the only person who understands," a planned absence, upcoming work in that area.
In this scenario: Pairing others with her on payment stories spreads working knowledge while she is still available.
Why not the others: A last-week manual transfers little real understanding; freezing payment work delays value; asking to postpone her leave is not the team's call and does not fix the underlying risk.
Remember: KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER when anyone leaves — start early, pair, share.

questions.stem: For four months, a test lab team on a medical imaging project has worked 60-hour weeks to hold the baseline dates. Defects escaping to the customer are rising, and two testers have resigned. The functional manager has no spare staff. What should the project manager do?
options: Propose changes to scope, sequence, or capacity through change control to fix the overload
Approve continued overtime with bonuses so the test team can keep the current baseline dates
Coach the testers on time management so they can handle the current workload better
Quietly reduce the depth of testing per release so the testers can meet current dates
questions.explanation:
Concept: Fixing persistent overload — sustained overtime is not a plan; change demand, capacity, sequence or scope, and route baseline changes through change control (Rule M4-B10-R08).
Spot it: months of long weeks, rising defects, resignations, no spare staff from the functional manager.
In this scenario: The PM proposes scope, sequence or capacity changes through change control so the plan becomes achievable again.
Why not the others: Bonuses keep an unsustainable load in place; time-management coaching blames people for a planning problem; quietly cutting test depth lowers quality without approval.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → Approve → Implement → Update → Monitor.

questions.stem: A hybrid bridge-monitoring project, with sensor software built in sprints and civil works on a fixed plan, has a risk register holding 85 identified risks. The phase gate review is in one week, and the sponsor wants the team to focus on the risks that matter most. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Run a Monte Carlo simulation on all 85 risks before ranking any of them
Write detailed response plans for all 85 risks in the order they were logged
Ask the sponsor to choose which risks the team should work on first
Rate each risk's probability and impact to rank which ones need attention first
questions.explanation:
Concept: Qualitative risk analysis — quickly rates each risk's probability and impact to rank which ones need attention first (Rule M4-B07-R04).
Spot it: a long risk register, limited time, "focus on the ones that matter most."
In this scenario: With 85 risks and one week, rating probability and impact produces a priority list fast.
Why not the others: Monte Carlo is quantitative and is normally run only on the top risks after ranking; writing full responses for all 85 in log order wastes effort on low risks; asking the sponsor to pick risks gives away the PM's analysis job.
Remember: Risk → Analyze (qualitative first, then quantitative for the top few) → Respond → Monitor.

questions.stem: An agile team identified risks during release planning four months ago, and no one has looked at the list since. A developer mentions in passing that a third-party mapping API the product relies on is scheduled to be retired in eight weeks. What should the agile project manager do?
options: Wait for the next release planning event to update the original list of risks
Treat the API retirement as the vendor's problem because it is outside the team's control
Make risk review a regular part of planning and reviews, starting with the API change
Hold a one-time risk workshop after the current release is fully complete
questions.explanation:
Concept: Continuous risk review — risk exposure changes, so risks are revisited throughout the project, not only at the start (Rule M4-B07-R07).
Spot it: a risk list untouched for months, a new threat mentioned in passing, a fixed deadline for an external change.
In this scenario: The PM makes risk review a regular part of planning and reviews, starting with the API retirement that is only eight weeks away.
Why not the others: Waiting for the next release planning may leave no time to respond; the API is external, but the impact on the product is the team's risk; a one-time workshop after the release is too late and not ongoing.
Remember: Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor → (if it happens) Issue. Monitor means every cycle.

questions.stem: A project manager on a pipeline construction project learns that a proposed state law could ban a key coating material. If passed, it would halt all of the company's pipeline projects in the state, not just this one. What should the project manager do?
options: Add a large contingency reserve to this project's budget to cover the risk
Escalate the risk to the sponsor so it can be owned at the portfolio level
Log it in the risk register and monitor it until the law is actually passed
Begin redesigning with an alternate material on the project manager's authority
questions.explanation:
Concept: Escalating risks — when a risk's ownership or impact lies beyond the project's authority, it is escalated to the level that can own it (Rule M4-B07-R10).
Spot it: "would affect all of the company's projects," legal or policy changes, impact bigger than the project.
In this scenario: A state law that halts every pipeline project is a portfolio-level threat, so the PM escalates it to the sponsor to be owned there.
Why not the others: Project contingency cannot fund an enterprise-wide threat and hides it from decision-makers; only logging and waiting leaves no owner who can act; redesigning on the PM's own authority acts outside project scope.
Remember: Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act → Monitor → ESCALATE — when it is beyond your authority.

questions.stem: A hybrid retail project plans to launch mobile payments using an unproven open-source library; security reviewers rate the chance of a serious flaw as high. The team could instead use the bank's certified SDK with a two-week delay to the agile release. The project manager wants the threat removed entirely. What should the project manager do?
options: Replace the unproven library with the bank's certified SDK in the release plan
Buy cyber insurance to cover any losses if the open-source library is breached
Add extra security testing to lower the chance of a flaw in the library
Keep the library and set aside funds to respond if a breach does occur
questions.explanation:
Concept: Avoid — a threat response that changes the plan so the threat can no longer occur (Rule M4-B08-R01).
Spot it: "remove the threat entirely," an alternative path exists, accepting a cost such as a delay to eliminate the risk.
In this scenario: Switching to the certified SDK eliminates the unproven library and its flaw risk, at the price of a two-week delay.
Why not the others: Insurance transfers financial loss but the flaw can still happen; extra testing is mitigation that only lowers probability; setting funds aside is active acceptance.
Remember: Avoid = eliminate • Mitigate = reduce • Transfer = shift • Accept = live with it • Escalate = beyond authority.

questions.stem: An agile team building an event ticketing app must accept card payments. No one on the team has payment security expertise, and storing card data would create large compliance and breach exposure. Several certified payment processors offer card handling with contractual liability terms. What is the BEST response to this threat?
options: Have the team build its own card vault and learn the security rules as it goes
Accept the exposure because breaches are unlikely for a small ticketing app
Remove online payments and have customers pay only at the venue on event day
Contract a certified payment processor to handle card data under defined terms
questions.explanation:
Concept: Transfer — shifting a defined threat and its consequences to a third party better able to own it, usually by contract (Rule M4-B08-R03).
Spot it: no internal expertise, a specialist party exists, "contractual liability terms," insurance or outsourcing.
In this scenario: A certified payment processor is built to handle card data and takes on defined liability under contract.
Why not the others: Building an in-house vault with no expertise increases the threat; accepting large compliance exposure is careless; dropping online payments avoids the threat but throws away core product value.
Remember: Transfer = someone else owns the impact (contract, insurance, warranty). The risk still exists — just not on your books.

questions.stem: A construction project will earn a contract bonus if concrete work finishes before the rainy season. The estimate gives only a 30 percent chance of that. The company has idle crews and equipment it can assign. The project manager wants to improve the chance of earning the bonus. What should the project manager do?
options: Note the opportunity and collect the bonus only if the early finish happens to occur on its own
Transfer the concrete work to a subcontractor under a firm-fixed-price agreement
Assign a second company concrete crew to raise the odds of finishing before the rains
Share the bonus with a partner firm in exchange for its help pouring the concrete
questions.explanation:
Concept: Enhance — an opportunity response that increases the probability or positive impact of the opportunity (Rule M4-B08-R06).
Spot it: a bonus or benefit at stake, a low chance of earning it, resources available to improve the odds.
In this scenario: Assigning the company's own idle crew raises the chance of finishing before the rains and earning the bonus.
Why not the others: Waiting for luck is passive acceptance; transferring the work is a threat response, not an opportunity one; sharing gives away part of the bonus when the company already has capacity itself.
Remember: Opportunities: Exploit = make it certain • Enhance = raise the odds • Share = partner • Accept = take it if it comes.

questions.stem: A hybrid project delivers software in sprints and site works under a predictive plan. It holds a contingency reserve for identified vendor price increases. A new, unforeseen regulation now requires additional reporting work. Governance rules say management reserve can be released only by the sponsor. The team suggests quietly using the contingency reserve instead. What should the project manager do?
options: Use the contingency reserve because the money is already in the project budget
Request management reserve from the sponsor to fund the unforeseen reporting work
Absorb the new work by cutting planned testing so the budget stays unchanged
Add the work to upcoming sprints without reporting its cost to governance
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reserves — contingency reserve covers identified (known-unknown) risks inside the cost baseline; management reserve covers unforeseen (unknown-unknown) work and is released through governance (Rule M4-B08-R09).
Spot it: "unforeseen," "new regulation," a reserve earmarked for specific identified risks, rules about who releases management reserve.
In this scenario: The reporting work was never identified, so the PM requests management reserve from the sponsor, as governance requires.
Why not the others: Contingency is earmarked for the vendor price risk and would leave it unfunded; cutting testing trades quality to hide cost; adding work without reporting bypasses governance.
Remember: Contingency = KNOWN risks. Management reserve = UNKNOWN risks — released only with approval.

questions.stem: A project manager is compressing the schedule for a new data center. Racks cannot be installed until the floor is poured; the utility must energize the site before power testing, and the team prefers to install cabling before painting based on past habit. Which dependency can the project manager MOST readily change?
options: Cabling before painting, because it is based only on the team's past practice
Pouring the floor before racks, because racks need a finished, level floor
Energizing before power testing, because the utility controls the timing
Testing before handover, because the contract requires signed test evidence
questions.explanation:
Concept: Dependency types — mandatory (hard logic from physics or contract), discretionary (preferred or best-practice logic) and external (driven by outside parties) (Rule M4-B03-R02).
Spot it: "based on past habit" or "team prefers" signals discretionary; "cannot until" signals mandatory; a utility, regulator or vendor signals external.
In this scenario: Cabling before painting is only the team's preference, so it is the one the PM can resequence to compress the schedule.
Why not the others: Pouring the floor before racks is physical logic (mandatory); energizing depends on the utility (external); signed test evidence before handover is a contractual requirement (mandatory).
Remember: Mandatory = must • Discretionary = prefer • External = outsiders. Only "prefer" is yours to change.

questions.stem: A project manager must shorten an office build-out by two weeks. Interior framing is on the critical path and can be split between two crews. Landscaping has 15 days of float. Concrete curing is also on the critical path, but its duration is set by chemistry. What should the project manager do?
options: Add workers to landscaping so it finishes well ahead of its plan
Add extra crews to concrete curing so it finishes in fewer days
Pay overtime on every activity so each one finishes a bit sooner
Add a second crew to the interior framing work on the critical path
questions.explanation:
Concept: Crashing — adding resources or cost to shorten critical path activities, and only those whose duration truly shrinks with more resources (Rule M4-B03-R05).
Spot it: activities on the critical path, some with float, some with fixed durations set by physics or chemistry.
In this scenario: Interior framing is critical and can be split between crews, so adding a second crew actually shortens the project.
Why not the others: Landscaping has float, so shortening it does not move the end date; concrete curing is set by chemistry and ignores extra crews; paying overtime everywhere wastes money on non-critical work.
Remember: Crashing = add cost/resources. Fast-tracking = overlap (adds risk). Only the critical path moves the finish date.

questions.stem: Nine months into an 18-month ERP rollout, the project's schedule performance index (SPI) has held steady at 0.82 for three reporting periods. The monthly status report still shows the original go-live date, and the sponsor is planning staff training around it. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep reporting the baseline date because the team may still recover the delay later on
Rebaseline the schedule without a change request to match current progress
Revise the completion forecast from actual performance and share it with the sponsor
Wait until the SPI falls below 0.75 before raising the date with the sponsor
questions.explanation:
Concept: Forecast updates — when actual performance shows the finish date has changed, the forecast is revised and shared; the baseline changes only through change control (Rule M4-B03-R08).
Spot it: a steady SPI below 1.0 across several periods, reports still showing the original date, stakeholders planning around it.
In this scenario: An SPI stuck at 0.82 signals a later finish, so the PM revises the forecast from actual performance and tells the sponsor before training plans are built on the wrong date.
Why not the others: Reporting the old date hopes rather than forecasts; rebaselining without a change request bypasses integrated change control; waiting for a worse SPI delays bad news the sponsor needs now.
Remember: SPI < 1 = behind. Forecast = where we are heading. Baseline = what was APPROVED.

questions.stem: A subcontractor assigned to work package 3.4.2, Site Drainage, asks the project manager exactly what work is included, what the acceptance criteria are, and which organization is responsible. The WBS shows only the package name and number. What should the project manager provide?
options: The project charter describing high-level objectives and sponsor authority
The WBS dictionary entry describing the package's work, criteria, and owner
The schedule baseline showing start and finish dates for every package
The risk register listing threats that could affect the drainage work
questions.explanation:
Concept: WBS dictionary — the companion to the WBS that describes each work package in detail: scope of work, acceptance criteria, responsible organization, milestones and more (Rule M4-B02-R04).
Spot it: someone asking "what exactly is included," "what are the criteria," "who is responsible" for one work package.
In this scenario: The WBS shows only the name and number, so the dictionary entry for 3.4.2 answers the subcontractor's questions.
Why not the others: The charter is high-level authority, not package detail; the schedule baseline gives dates, not content; the risk register lists threats, not the work.
Remember: WBS = WHAT (the structure). WBS dictionary = the DETAILS of each box. TRACE family: RTM + WBS dictionary.

questions.stem: A project team finishes the operator training materials for a new water treatment plant, and internal quality control confirms they meet every specification. The contract states that deliverables are accepted by the utility's designated operations director. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Review the materials with the operations director to obtain formal acceptance
Mark the deliverable complete because quality control has already verified it
Release the materials to trainees and collect their feedback after first use
Ask the team lead to sign off since the team knows the materials best
questions.explanation:
Concept: Validate Scope — formal acceptance of completed deliverables by the customer or authorized stakeholder, after quality control has verified them (Rule M4-B02-R07).
Spot it: "quality control confirms," "accepted by the designated…," a contract naming who signs off.
In this scenario: The materials are verified, so the next step is reviewing them with the operations director to obtain formal acceptance.
Why not the others: Quality control verifies correctness but is not customer acceptance; releasing to trainees first skips acceptance; the team lead is not the authorized acceptor.
Remember: Create → Control Quality (verified) → Validate Scope (accepted) → Transition. Control Quality verifies; Validate Scope accepts.

questions.stem: A developer on a fixed-scope contract plans to spend two days adding an export-to-PDF feature that is not in the requirements. He says the client will love it and the cost is small. The client has not asked for it. What should the project manager do?
options: Allow the feature because it adds value and costs the project only two days
Let the developer add it and mention it to the client after final acceptance
Add the feature and recover the two days by trimming unit testing elsewhere
Keep the developer on approved scope and route the idea through change control
questions.explanation:
Concept: Gold plating — adding features or extras the customer did not request, even with good intentions; it adds unapproved scope, risk and cost (Rule M4-B02-R10).
Spot it: "the client will love it," "it's small," work not in the requirements, the client never asked.
In this scenario: The PM keeps the developer on approved scope and sends the PDF idea through change control, where the client can decide.
Why not the others: Allowing it because it is cheap is still unapproved scope; revealing it after acceptance hides it from the customer; trimming unit tests to pay for it adds quality risk.
Remember: Good idea? → Change request, not gold plating. Deliver what was approved — no more, no less.

questions.stem: Midway through a sprint, developers find that the API approach they planned will not work, but an alternative still meets the sprint goal. A stakeholder then asks to add an unrelated feature, saying the plan is changing anyway. What should the team do?
options: Cancel the sprint and restart planning because the original tasks no longer apply
Accept the stakeholder's new feature because the plan is already being changed
Adjust the task plan to use the alternative while holding the sprint goal steady
Keep the original API approach because the sprint plan is fixed once it is set
questions.explanation:
Concept: Protect the sprint goal — the sprint goal stays fixed during the sprint, while the developers may adapt the detailed task plan to reach it (Rule M4-B12-R01).
Spot it: a technical approach failing mid-sprint, a workable alternative, a stakeholder using "the plan is changing anyway" to add new work.
In this scenario: The team changes its tasks to use the alternative approach and keeps the goal steady; the new feature goes to the product owner for a future sprint.
Why not the others: Cancelling the sprint is for when the goal becomes obsolete, not the tasks; accepting unrelated work changes the goal mid-sprint; clinging to a failed approach ignores that the task plan is meant to adapt.
Remember: Goal = fixed. Plan = flexible. New requests → product owner → product backlog.

questions.stem: On one agile team, a daily meeting has turned into each developer reporting status to the scrum master. Blockers usually surface only at the sprint review, when it is too late to act. What should the scrum master do?
options: Replace the meeting with written status updates sent directly to the scrum master each morning
Coach developers to use the meeting to raise blockers and plan the next day together
Extend the meeting to an hour so that every task can be discussed in full detail
Ask the product owner to run the meeting and assign tasks to people each morning
questions.explanation:
Concept: Daily scrum — a short event for developers to coordinate with each other, surface blockers and plan the next day; it is not a status report to a manager (Rule M4-B12-R03).
Spot it: people reporting "to" the scrum master, blockers surfacing late, the meeting feeling like a status check.
In this scenario: The scrum master coaches developers to use the time to raise blockers and plan the next day together — servant leadership, not control.
Why not the others: Written updates keep the status-report problem and remove the team conversation; an hour-long meeting breaks the short timebox; the product owner assigning tasks undermines self-management.
Remember: Daily scrum = developers, 15 minutes, plan the next 24 hours, surface blockers. Scrum master facilitates and coaches.

questions.stem: Three stories on an agile team's board are stuck waiting for a test environment that has been down for two days. To stay busy, developers keep pulling new stories, and eleven items are now in progress with none finished. What should the team do?
options: Swarm on restoring the test environment before pulling any new stories
Keep starting new stories so that no developer is idle while waiting
Move the blocked stories off the board and back into the product backlog
Report the blockers at the sprint review and keep the current approach
questions.explanation:
Concept: Stop starting, start finishing — blocked work is a signal to resolve the constraint, not to pull more work and raise work in progress (Rule M4-B12-R06).
Spot it: items stuck on one blocker, people pulling new work "to stay busy," many items in progress with none done.
In this scenario: The team swarms on restoring the test environment so the blocked stories can finish before starting anything new.
Why not the others: Starting more stories inflates WIP and delays finishing anything; moving blocked stories off the board hides the problem; waiting for the sprint review is too late to act.
Remember: Blocker = swarm and remove it. Busy ≠ done. Limit WIP.

questions.stem: For the last three sprints, an agile team worked weekends to meet its commitments. Velocity is now dropping, and escaped defects are rising. The sponsor asks for the same output every sprint next quarter. What should the agile project manager do?
options: Keep the weekend schedule until the quarterly release has been safely delivered to customers
Inflate story point estimates so the team appears to meet its commitments
Add one hardening sprint for defects and then resume the weekend work pattern
Plan upcoming sprints on sustainable capacity and share that forecast with the sponsor
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sustainable pace — agile teams work at a pace they can keep indefinitely; overtime sprints burn people out and quality drops (Rule M4-B12-R09).
Spot it: repeated weekend work, falling velocity, rising escaped defects, pressure for the same output.
In this scenario: The PM plans on sustainable capacity and shares that honest forecast with the sponsor instead of promising more overtime.
Why not the others: More weekends deepen the burnout already showing in defects; inflating estimates games the metric and deceives the sponsor; a hardening sprint followed by more weekends restarts the same cycle.
Remember: Sustainable pace = predictable delivery. Velocity is for planning, not for pushing.

questions.stem: An agile team is building self-service returns for an online retailer. The business case says only that the feature will "improve customer experience," and no one in the business has been asked to track results. The first release is two sprints away. What should the project manager do?
options: Track the team's velocity as the main indicator that the business benefits are being realized
Leave benefit definition until after release, when real usage data exists
Agree with the business on who owns each benefit, how it is measured, and by when
Have the development team own and report the business benefits each sprint
questions.explanation:
Concept: Benefit definition — each expected benefit needs an owner in the business, a measure and a timeframe so realization can be tracked (Rule M5-B04-R01).
Spot it: vague benefit wording ("improve experience"), no one assigned to track results, release approaching.
In this scenario: The PM agrees with the business who owns each benefit, how it will be measured and by when, before release creates the baseline moment.
Why not the others: Velocity measures team output, not business benefit; waiting until after release loses the "before" baseline; the development team builds the product but the business owns benefits.
Remember: Business case = WHY. Benefits need Owner + Measure + Time — or no one can prove the value arrived.

questions.stem: A public health agency project is delivering a vaccination outreach system. Its main goal is fewer flu hospitalizations, which will not be measurable for about two years. The steering committee wants evidence much sooner that the investment is on track to deliver value. What should the project manager propose?
options: Report the number of system modules delivered each month as evidence of benefit progress
Track appointment bookings and outreach response rates as early signs of benefit
Wait two years for hospitalization data before reporting any benefit status
Use staff satisfaction with the new system as the measure of health benefit
questions.explanation:
Concept: Leading indicators — early, measurable signals that predict whether a long-term benefit is on track, used when the final outcome takes years to appear (Rule M5-B04-R02).
Spot it: a final outcome measurable only far in the future, governance wanting evidence sooner.
In this scenario: Appointment bookings and outreach response rates move early and lead toward fewer hospitalizations, so they show the investment is heading in the right direction.
Why not the others: Modules delivered measure output, not progress toward the outcome; waiting two years leaves governance blind; staff satisfaction does not signal fewer hospitalizations.
Remember: Lagging = the final result. Leading = the early signal that predicts it. Track leading, confirm with lagging.

questions.stem: A hybrid safety training program uses a predictive plan for classroom rollout and agile sprints to produce e-learning modules. The team has just delivered its 120th module, and the sponsor wants to announce that the program's value has been achieved. The business case goal was a 25 percent reduction in lost-time injuries. What should the project manager do?
options: Report the 120 modules as proof that the injury reduction target has now been fully achieved
Report injury trends alongside module counts to show whether the value is actually appearing
Increase module production so that the injury reduction target is reached more quickly
Close the program because all of the planned content has been produced on schedule
questions.explanation:
Concept: Benefit versus output — output is how much was produced; benefit is the business change it causes. Counting outputs never proves value (Rule M5-B04-R03).
Spot it: celebrating a count ("120 modules"), a business case goal expressed as a result (fewer injuries), a sponsor ready to declare victory.
In this scenario: The PM reports injury trends next to module counts, so the sponsor can see whether the 25 percent reduction is actually appearing.
Why not the others: Modules prove output, not injury reduction; producing more modules pushes more output without evidence it works; closing because content is done confuses finishing with delivering value.
Remember: Deliverable → Outcome → Benefit → Value. Count results, not boxes.

questions.stem: A telecom's agile team released a chatbot that cut call center volume by 40 percent, as planned. Since then, complaints from older customers who cannot reach a person have tripled, and cancellations in that group have risen. The product owner is preparing a value report for leadership. What should the product owner do?
options: Weigh the lost older customers against the call savings when reporting overall value
Report the 40 percent call reduction as confirmation that the release delivered value
Treat the complaints as normal resistance to change that will fade over the next months
Expand the chatbot to every channel so the call savings grow even larger next quarter
questions.explanation:
Concept: Disbenefits — negative consequences of a change (lost customers, new costs, harm to a group) that must be weighed against the intended benefits when assessing value (Rule M5-B04-R04).
Spot it: a target met, but a side effect appearing in one group; complaints, cancellations or costs rising after the release.
In this scenario: The product owner weighs lost older customers against the call savings, giving leadership a true picture of net value.
Why not the others: Reporting only the 40 percent reduction hides a real disbenefit; labeling it "resistance to change" dismisses evidence of harm; expanding the chatbot would magnify the harm before it is understood.
Remember: Net value = benefits − disbenefits. Look at who is being hurt, not only what went up.

questions.stem: A city parking garage project was justified on an assumption of 90 percent occupancy. Since approval, a light rail station has opened nearby, and the largest local employer has moved most staff to remote work. Construction is 30 percent complete. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue construction because the business case was already approved
Speed up construction so the garage opens before demand drops further
Lower the planned parking fees to guarantee the original occupancy level
Ask the sponsor to revisit the occupancy assumption and the business case
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reassess assumptions — a business case rests on assumptions; when behavior or market conditions change, those assumptions go back to the sponsor for review (Rule M5-B04-R07).
Spot it: "was justified on an assumption of…," a new competitor, shifts in how people work or travel, work still in progress.
In this scenario: Light rail and remote work undermine the 90 percent occupancy assumption, so the PM asks the sponsor to revisit it and the business case.
Why not the others: Approval does not freeze reality; speeding up builds faster toward a possibly weaker case; cutting fees changes the revenue model without authority and may not restore demand.
Remember: Constraint/Assumption → Assess impact → Adjust. The business case is a living WHY.

questions.stem: A hybrid CRM project runs predictive data center work and agile feature sprints. Vendor license fees have tripled, and the customer segment the CRM was meant to serve has been sold to another company. Updated figures show remaining costs now exceed remaining benefits. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep delivering the remaining sprints because the project was already formally approved last year
Cancel the vendor contract and stop the project on the project manager's own authority
Present the updated cost and benefit figures to the sponsor for a continue-or-stop decision
Reduce planned testing to lower remaining costs so the business case looks positive
questions.explanation:
Concept: Continued justification — if a project no longer justifies its investment, the PM brings the evidence to the sponsor or governance for a continue, change or stop decision (Rule M5-B03-R05).
Spot it: costs rising sharply, the target market gone, remaining costs now greater than remaining benefits.
In this scenario: The PM presents the updated cost and benefit figures to the sponsor, who owns the business case and the go/no-go decision.
Why not the others: Past approval does not justify spending on a losing case; stopping on the PM's own authority exceeds the PM's role; cutting testing to make figures look better is dishonest and adds risk.
Remember: Business case = WHY; sponsor owns it. PM brings the data, sponsor decides continue or stop.

questions.stem: An agile team delivered a meal-planning app on time and within budget, and every feature passed acceptance. Six months after launch, few customers use it and subscription revenue is 70 percent below target. The sponsor asks whether the effort was a success. What is the BEST response?
options: Declare full success because the scope, schedule, and budget targets were all fully met
Explain that delivery goals were met but that the product and business goals were not
Declare the whole effort a failure because delivery measures do not matter at all
Attribute the low adoption to marketing since the team delivered what was asked
questions.explanation:
Concept: Project success versus product success — project success is delivering scope on time and budget; product or business success is whether the result creates the intended outcomes (Rule M5-B03-R08).
Spot it: "on time, on budget, all features accepted" alongside low adoption or missed revenue.
In this scenario: The honest answer separates the two: delivery goals were met, but the product and business goals were not.
Why not the others: Declaring full success ignores the business result; calling it a total failure ignores real delivery performance; blaming marketing deflects instead of learning.
Remember: Project success = built it right. Product success = built the right thing and it paid off.

questions.stem: A project manager is 40 percent through a factory expansion when the company announces a merger. Early statements suggest production may be consolidated at the other company's plant. The project's charter and plan assume this factory remains the main production site. What should the project manager do?
options: Brief the steering committee on how the merger may affect the project's direction
Keep executing the approved plan until someone in leadership formally cancels the expansion
Stop all work immediately until the details of the merger become fully public
Replan the project to support the other plant based on the manager's own view
questions.explanation:
Concept: Keep governance informed — when strategy shifts in a way that may affect the project's direction, the PM briefs the governing body early so it can decide (Rule M5-B03-R10).
Spot it: merger, reorganization, new strategy; a charter or plan built on an assumption that may no longer hold.
In this scenario: The merger could make the factory expansion unnecessary, so the PM briefs the steering committee on the possible impact.
Why not the others: Executing until cancelled may waste money on a dead direction; stopping all work is a decision above the PM's authority; replanning on the PM's own view pre-empts governance.
Remember: Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act → Monitor → Escalate. Big strategic change → tell governance early.
questions.block_title: Business Case & Strategic Alignment + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hospital has run three agile software releases to fix patient discharge delays, while ward process changes follow a predictive plan. Delays persist. Staff say pharmacy sign-off rules, bed-cleaning contracts, and doctors' rounding schedules also play a part. What should the project manager do?
options: Commission a fourth software release focused on speeding up the discharge screens
Replace the discharge team lead since the delays continue under current leadership
Hire additional nurses for the discharge unit so that patients are processed faster
Map the people, workflows, systems, rules, and incentives that shape discharge timing
questions.explanation:
Concept: Systems thinking — when a problem persists despite fixes, map the whole system: people, processes, technology, policies and incentives that interact to create it (Rule M5-B17-R06).
Spot it: repeated fixes in one area that don't solve the problem, staff pointing to rules, contracts and schedules in other areas.
In this scenario: Discharge delays involve pharmacy rules, cleaning contracts and rounding schedules, so the PM maps all of these before choosing the next intervention.
Why not the others: A fourth software release repeats a fix that already failed three times; replacing the lead blames a person for a system issue; hiring nurses adds capacity without addressing the real causes.
Remember: Complex problem = many causes. Map the system before you fix a piece of it.
questions.block_title: Business Case & Strategic Alignment + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A fintech team released new automated fraud-blocking rules, and fraud losses fell 60 percent in the first month. The product owner plans to move the team on to the next feature. A support lead mentions a few calls from customers whose purchases were declined. What should the team do?
options: Move to the next feature since the fraud loss target for the quarter has clearly been achieved
Tighten the fraud rules further to push losses even closer to zero next month
Monitor for side effects such as wrongly blocked customers and abandoned purchases
Report the success and close out the fraud work item in the tracking tool now
questions.explanation:
Concept: Unintended consequences — after a major intervention, keep watching for side effects, not just the target metric (Rule M5-B17-R09).
Spot it: a big early win, a team ready to move on, weak signals like "a few calls" pointing to harm elsewhere.
In this scenario: Fraud losses fell, but declined purchases may be frustrating good customers, so the team monitors for false blocks and abandoned purchases.
Why not the others: Moving on or closing the item ignores the early warning; tightening rules further would increase wrongly blocked customers; hitting the target does not mean the change is free of harm.
Remember: Act → MONITOR. Every intervention has side effects — look for them on purpose.
questions.block_title: Business Case & Strategic Alignment + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A project manager is starting a project to install a new pharmaceutical packaging line. The team plans to check the regulatory requirements during final inspection, as it did years ago. Regulators in this market updated labeling and serialization rules last year. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the current plan and address the regulations when final inspection takes place
Identify the applicable regulations during planning and set up monitoring for updates
Rely on the equipment vendor to ensure that its machines satisfy the regulations
Have the team apply the regulations used on a similar project from five years ago
questions.explanation:
Concept: Compliance early — identify applicable legal and regulatory obligations during planning and monitor for changes throughout the project (Rule M5-B02-R01).
Spot it: "check the rules at final inspection," "as we did years ago," regulations recently updated.
In this scenario: Labeling and serialization rules changed last year, so the PM identifies the current regulations now and sets up monitoring for further updates.
Why not the others: Checking at final inspection finds problems when they are most expensive to fix; the vendor's machines do not make the whole line compliant; five-year-old rules are out of date.
Remember: Compliance = CONSTRAINT. Identify it early, build it in, keep watching it.
questions.block_title: Business Case & Strategic Alignment + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid mobile app project uses sprints for features and a predictive plan for the data platform. The app will collect location data from users in several countries. The team is debating whether a new European privacy law applies, and no one on the project has legal training. What should the project manager do?
options: Engage the company's legal or privacy counsel to interpret whether the law applies
Have the team vote on the most reasonable interpretation of the law and then move forward
Search online forums for how other companies have interpreted the new law
Assume the law does not apply until a regulator raises it with the company
questions.explanation:
Concept: Use qualified expertise — when legal or compliance interpretation exceeds the team's competence, engage qualified legal or compliance experts (Rule M5-B02-R02).
Spot it: "whether the law applies," cross-border data, no one on the team with legal training.
In this scenario: The PM engages the company's legal or privacy counsel to interpret whether the European law applies.
Why not the others: A team vote is not legal interpretation; online forums are unreliable and not accountable; assuming it does not apply until a regulator objects invites fines and rework.
Remember: Expert judgment = ask the right expert. Legal question → legal counsel.
questions.block_title: Business Case & Strategic Alignment + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: An agile team is building a payroll app that must meet wage record retention and audit rules. A compliance officer will audit the app before launch. Developers say they are "aware of the rules" but nothing in the product backlog reflects them. How should the team handle these obligations?
options: Ask the compliance officer to review the finished app in detail just before launch day
List the rules in the team charter and trust developers to follow them
Defer the compliance work to a hardening sprint just before the audit
Turn each obligation into stories with acceptance tests and retained test evidence
questions.explanation:
Concept: Make compliance concrete — compliance obligations become requirements, controls, tests and retained evidence, just like any other work (Rule M5-B02-R03).
Spot it: "aware of the rules" but nothing in the backlog, an audit coming, obligations that need proof.
In this scenario: Turning each obligation into stories with acceptance tests and retained evidence builds compliance in and prepares for the audit.
Why not the others: A final review just before launch finds gaps too late; listing rules in the team charter creates no testable work or evidence; a hardening sprint pushes compliance to the end.
Remember: Obligation → Requirement → Control → Test → Evidence. If it isn't in the backlog, it won't get built.
questions.block_title: Business Case & Strategic Alignment + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: On a highway widening project, a senior stakeholder proposes skipping a legally required wetland survey to save six weeks. He says regulators rarely check and the survey is just a formality. The project manager must respond. What should the project manager do?
options: Remove the survey because the stakeholder is senior and owns the schedule targets
Put the survey to a stakeholder vote along with other schedule reduction options
Keep the survey in the plan and explain that it is a legal constraint on the project
Skip the survey but set aside reserve in case the regulator later imposes fines
questions.explanation:
Concept: Mandatory compliance is a constraint — legal requirements are not negotiable preferences; the plan must work within them (Rule M5-B02-R04).
Spot it: "legally required," "regulators rarely check," a senior person proposing to skip it to save time.
In this scenario: The PM keeps the wetland survey and explains it is a legal constraint on the project.
Why not the others: Seniority does not override the law; a vote cannot make illegal work acceptable; budgeting for fines plans to break the law knowingly.
Remember: Law = CONSTRAINT, not preference. Never trade compliance for schedule.
questions.block_title: Business Case & Strategic Alignment + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid banking project builds its app in sprints and its infrastructure on a predictive plan. The system cannot meet a data residency rule by launch. The team and the compliance officer disagree on whether a proposed workaround is acceptable, and launch is three weeks away. What should the project manager do?
options: Launch with the team's workaround since the compliance concern seems minor
Bring the unresolved compliance risk to the governance board for a decision
Postpone the launch indefinitely without informing the sponsor or the board
Let the cloud vendor decide which workaround is acceptable under its contract
questions.explanation:
Concept: Escalating compliance risk — when a compliance risk is unresolved and beyond the team's authority, bring it to the proper governance body for a decision (Rule M5-B02-R07).
Spot it: disagreement between the team and compliance, a hard rule that cannot be met by launch, a deadline close.
In this scenario: The PM brings the data residency risk and options to the governance board, which has authority to decide.
Why not the others: Launching with a disputed workaround overrides compliance; postponing without informing governance hides the problem; the vendor does not own the organization's compliance decision.
Remember: Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act → Monitor → ESCALATE — when it is beyond your authority.
questions.block_title: Business Case & Strategic Alignment + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: An online grocery platform suffers a major outage during peak evening hours. Rumors about a data breach are spreading on social media, and executives want frequent updates. The agile team is still diagnosing the cause. What should the agile project manager do?
options: Send short, confirmed updates every 30 minutes stating what is known and next steps
Share every hypothesis engineers are testing as soon as someone raises one
Say nothing publicly until the root cause is fully known and the fix is live
Forward the raw technical logs to all executives every five minutes as they update
questions.explanation:
Concept: Crisis communication — during an incident, share short, verified updates on a regular cadence: what is known, what is being done, when the next update comes (Rule M5-B18-R05).
Spot it: rumors spreading, executives wanting frequent updates, cause still unknown.
In this scenario: Short, confirmed updates every 30 minutes replace rumor with facts without speculating.
Why not the others: Sharing every hypothesis spreads unverified guesses; silence until the fix lets rumors grow; raw logs every five minutes flood executives with noise.
Remember: In a crisis: verified + concise + regular. Facts, next steps, next update time.
questions.block_title: Business Case & Strategic Alignment + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A utility's billing cutover failed overnight, and customer bills were delayed for two days before recovery. The sponsor tells the project manager to find out who made the mistake so it goes in the lessons learned. What should the project manager do?
options: Identify the engineer responsible and record the error in the lessons learned register
Skip the review because the cutover has since been completed successfully
Ask each team member to submit a written account of who caused the failure
Lead a review focused on the process and system gaps that allowed the failure
questions.explanation:
Concept: Blameless post-event review — focus on the process and system gaps that allowed the failure, so people share openly and the fix prevents recurrence (Rule M5-B18-R08).
Spot it: "find out who made the mistake," a failure that has been recovered, lessons learned to be captured.
In this scenario: The PM leads a review on the process and system gaps that allowed the cutover to fail.
Why not the others: Naming an engineer creates fear and hides future problems; skipping the review loses the lesson; written accounts of "who caused it" are still blame-seeking.
Remember: Fix the system, not the person. Lessons learned register = what to do differently, not who to blame.
questions.block_title: Business Case & Strategic Alignment + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid project was interrupted by a ransomware attack. Infrastructure recovery followed a predictive plan, and application fixes were delivered in short sprints. All systems are now restored and the executive team is eager to resume planned work. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Declare the incident closed and move the team back to planned project work
Reinstall every system again to make sure nothing remains from the attack
Keep monitoring restored systems for reinfection and for knock-on problems
Remove the extra monitoring since it slows the restored systems somewhat
questions.explanation:
Concept: Monitor recovery — after restoring from an incident, keep watching for recurrence and secondary effects before declaring it over (Rule M5-B18-R10).
Spot it: "systems are now restored," pressure to resume normal work, an incident type known to linger (malware, data issues).
In this scenario: The PM keeps monitoring the restored systems for reinfection and knock-on problems.
Why not the others: Closing immediately ignores that ransomware can return; reinstalling everything again is costly overreaction without evidence; removing monitoring for speed drops protection when risk is highest.
Remember: Issue → Analyze → Resolve → MONITOR. Restored ≠ resolved until it stays fixed.

questions.stem: A hospital's agile team reports success by counting patient portal features shipped each sprint. Leadership asks what difference the portal is making for patients. No one can answer, and the product backlog keeps growing. What should the product owner do FIRST?
options: Raise the team's velocity so that more portal features can be shipped in every sprint
Define the patient outcome the portal should change, such as fewer missed visits
Add the features competitors offer so the portal stays attractive to patients
Survey the developers about which features they believe matter most to users
questions.explanation:
Concept: Outcome before output — define the change the product should make for users before optimizing how much is produced (Rule M5-B12-R01).
Spot it: success measured by features shipped, leaders asking "what difference is it making," a growing backlog with no direction.
In this scenario: The product owner first defines the patient outcome, such as fewer missed visits, so the backlog can be ordered by it.
Why not the others: More velocity ships more of the same with no known purpose; copying competitors is output-driven; developers' opinions are not user outcomes.
Remember: Product owner orders the backlog by VALUE — and value starts with a defined outcome.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading the design of new ticket kiosks for a transit authority. The design team assumes riders prefer a touch-screen interface, based on its experience with airport kiosks. The design baseline will be approved next month. What should the project manager do before approval?
options: Test a kiosk mock-up with real riders at a busy station before approval
Finalize the design based on the team's experience with airport kiosks
Ask transit executives which interface riders are most likely to prefer
Copy another city's kiosk design because it received positive reviews
questions.explanation:
Concept: Validate assumptions with real users — test design assumptions with actual users before committing, where it is feasible (Rule M5-B12-R02).
Spot it: "the team assumes," experience from a different context, an approval coming soon.
In this scenario: Testing a kiosk mock-up with real riders at a busy station checks the touch-screen assumption before the baseline is approved.
Why not the others: Airport experience may not match transit riders; executives are not the users; copying another city's design imports assumptions without evidence.
Remember: Assumption → test with real users → decide. Evidence beats experience.

questions.stem: A hybrid banking app project delivers features in sprints under a fixed regulatory release plan. Feedback conflicts: small business owners want batch payments and multi-user approvals, while personal customers want a simpler screen with fewer options. What should the project manager do?
options: Average the feedback so the design balances both groups' preferences equally
Follow the feedback from whichever group has submitted the most comments
Design only for personal customers since they are the larger user group
Define separate user segments and tailor requirements and tests for each group
questions.explanation:
Concept: User segmentation — when user groups have materially different needs, define separate segments and tailor requirements and tests to each (Rule M5-B12-R03).
Spot it: conflicting feedback from distinct groups, one wanting power features, another wanting simplicity.
In this scenario: The PM defines business and personal segments, each with its own requirements and tests.
Why not the others: Averaging feedback satisfies neither group; following the loudest group ignores the other; designing only for the larger group drops a real customer segment.
Remember: Different needs → different segments. One size fits none.

questions.stem: A government agency is replacing its unemployment benefits website, and law requires public sites to meet accessibility standards. Many applicants use screen readers or magnification. The approved design baseline includes no accessibility requirements or testing. What should the project manager do?
options: Plan to add accessibility features in a later phase, after the initial public launch is complete
Rely on the web framework's default settings to meet the needs of these applicants
Add accessibility requirements and testing with assistive technology users to the plan
Offer a phone line instead of making the new website itself accessible to all users
questions.explanation:
Concept: Accessibility and inclusion — when accessibility materially affects intended users or is a legal obligation, it must be built into requirements and testing (Rule M5-B12-R06).
Spot it: "law requires," users with screen readers or magnification, a baseline that leaves accessibility out.
In this scenario: The PM adds accessibility requirements and testing with assistive technology users to the plan, through change control since the baseline is approved.
Why not the others: Adding it after launch breaks the law and excludes users on day one; framework defaults do not guarantee compliance; a phone line does not make the website accessible.
Remember: Accessibility = requirement + test, not an afterthought.

questions.stem: A software firm's hybrid project added a free premium support feature, built in sprints and rolled out under a fixed plan. Customers rate it 4.8 out of 5, but it costs twice what was expected and renewals have not increased. The sales director wants it offered to every customer. What should the project manager do?
options: Expand the feature to all customers because satisfaction scores are so high
Assess renewals and cost to serve along with satisfaction before expanding it
Remove the feature right away because it does not generate direct revenue
Survey customers again to confirm that satisfaction scores remain strong
questions.explanation:
Concept: Satisfaction versus long-term value — happy customers are good, but value also depends on cost, retention and business results (Rule M5-B12-R09).
Spot it: high satisfaction scores, costs above expectations, no improvement in the business metric the feature was meant to move.
In this scenario: The PM assesses renewals and cost to serve alongside satisfaction before expanding the feature.
Why not the others: Expanding on satisfaction alone scales a costly feature that isn't paying off; removing it immediately ignores possible value; another survey just repeats the one measure already known.
Remember: Satisfaction ≠ value. Value = benefit − cost, over time.

questions.stem: A project manager is planning a new recruitment system that will store applicants' names, addresses, and employment histories. The data management plan covers how data is collected, stored, and secured. It does not say what happens to applicant data after hiring decisions are made. What should the project manager add?
options: Rules for how long applicant data is kept and how it is securely deleted
Extra form fields so recruiters can collect more applicant details early
A plan to keep all applicant data indefinitely for future hiring analysis
Stronger recruiter passwords as the single additional data protection
questions.explanation:
Concept: Data lifecycle — a data plan covers the full lifecycle: collection, storage, security, retention and secure disposal (Rule M5-B15-R06).
Spot it: personal data, a plan covering only collection and storage, silence on what happens afterward.
In this scenario: The PM adds rules for how long applicant data is kept and how it is securely deleted.
Why not the others: Collecting more fields increases exposure; keeping data indefinitely breaks privacy principles; stronger passwords help security but do not address retention.
Remember: Collect → Store → Protect → Retain → Dispose. Plan the end, not just the start.

questions.stem: On a hybrid insurance project, developers work in sprints while integration testing follows a predictive test plan. To make tests realistic, a test lead has copied the full production customer database, including names and medical claims, into the shared test environment. What should the project manager do?
options: Allow the copy because the testers are employees bound by confidentiality rules
Copy only half of the production records to test so that exposure is reduced
Run all testing in production so real customer data never has to be copied
Use masked or synthetic data in test and keep real customer data in production
questions.explanation:
Concept: Separate test and production data — real personal data stays in production; test environments use masked or synthetic data (Rule M5-B15-R09).
Spot it: a full production copy in a shared test area, sensitive fields like names or medical details.
In this scenario: The PM replaces the copy with masked or synthetic data and keeps real customer data in production.
Why not the others: Confidentiality agreements do not make the exposure acceptable; copying half still exposes real data; testing in production puts live customers at risk.
Remember: Real data → production. Test data → masked or synthetic.

questions.stem: A road construction project will run heavy trucks along a route that passes an elementary school and a nursing home. The approved plan schedules peak truck traffic between 2 and 4 p.m., when children leave school and residents' visitors arrive. What should the project manager do?
options: Proceed with the plan because the road permit allows trucks on this route
Post warning signs and let the school manage student safety at dismissal
Reroute or reschedule truck traffic to avoid school dismissal and visiting hours
Pay into a local community fund in exchange for keeping the current truck schedule
questions.explanation:
Concept: Protecting vulnerable groups — where project work could harm vulnerable stakeholders, change the plan to avoid avoidable harm (Rule M5-B16-R05).
Spot it: children, elderly, patients near the work; a schedule colliding with their most exposed times.
In this scenario: The PM reroutes or reschedules truck traffic away from school dismissal and visiting hours.
Why not the others: A permit is the legal minimum, not the ethical standard; warning signs shift the burden to the school; paying a fund to keep the risk trades money for safety.
Remember: Legal is the floor, not the ceiling. Avoidable harm → change the plan.

questions.stem: A hybrid HR project is deploying an AI resume-screening tool; the model is tuned in sprints while rollout follows a fixed plan. A senior data scientist believes the tool may unfairly reject older applicants. The steering committee discussed the concern and approved deployment with added monitoring. What should the project manager do?
options: Tell the scientist to drop the issue now that the committee has made a decision
Record the scientist's concern and the committee's rationale in the decision log
Delay deployment on the project manager's authority until the scientist agrees
Leave the concern out of records so that future approvals are not slowed down
questions.explanation:
Concept: Documenting dissent — when a material ethical concern is raised and governance decides anyway, record the concern and the rationale for transparency and accountability (Rule M5-B16-R08).
Spot it: a serious ethical objection, a committee decision that goes ahead with conditions.
In this scenario: The PM records the scientist's concern and the committee's rationale in the decision log.
Why not the others: Telling the scientist to drop it silences a legitimate concern; delaying on the PM's authority overrides governance; leaving it out of records hides it.
Remember: Decide openly, record honestly. Decision log = what was decided, by whom, and why.

questions.stem: A solar farm project's business case depends on a federal investment tax credit. Legislators have begun debating a bill that could end the credit next year, before the farm is complete. Construction is proceeding on schedule. What should the project manager do?
options: Track the bill and assess its effect on the business case and project risks
Continue as planned because the tax credit is still in effect as of today
Stop all construction until the legislative debate has been fully resolved
Leave the monitoring to the finance department since it is not a project issue
questions.explanation:
Concept: Monitoring the external environment — track external factors (laws, markets, incentives) that could change assumptions, risk, value or compliance (Rule M5-B08-R01).
Spot it: a business case depending on an outside factor, legislation under debate, work still proceeding.
In this scenario: The PM tracks the bill and assesses its effect on the business case and project risks.
Why not the others: "Still in effect today" ignores a known possible change; stopping all construction overreacts to a debate; handing it to finance ignores that it threatens the project's value.
Remember: Constraint/Assumption → Assess impact → Adjust. Watch the outside world that your WHY depends on.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid e-commerce project follows a fixed plan for warehouse automation and agile sprints for the storefront. Sales dropped 15 percent last month when a competitor ran a one-week promotion. An executive wants to rebuild the entire product roadmap in response. What should the project manager do?
options: Rebuild the whole roadmap now to respond quickly and visibly to the competitor's recent promotion
Disregard the drop because monthly sales figures always vary by some amount anyway
Cut the project budget in half to protect profit margins while sales remain lower
Analyze whether the drop reflects a short-term blip or a lasting shift before replanning
questions.explanation:
Concept: Noise versus structural change — before major replanning, determine whether a change in results is a short-term blip or a lasting shift (Rule M5-B08-R02).
Spot it: a one-time event (a promotion, a holiday), a single month's drop, an executive ready to rebuild everything.
In this scenario: The PM analyzes whether the sales drop is temporary or structural before replanning the roadmap.
Why not the others: Rebuilding everything reacts to one data point; disregarding the drop ignores a possible real shift; halving the budget is a drastic move without analysis.
Remember: Data → Analyze → Insight → Decision → Action. One bad month is data, not a trend.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A project manager is planning production of a medical monitoring device. All of its specialized chips come from one supplier in a region where trade tensions are rising and export restrictions have been proposed. The supplier's price and quality have been excellent. What should the project manager do?
options: Order the full volume now and store it in the supplier's own local warehouse
Keep the current supplier because its price and quality have been excellent
Assess the single-source and regional exposure and qualify alternate suppliers
Move all sourcing at once to a new, unqualified supplier in another country
questions.explanation:
Concept: Supply-chain concentration — relying on a single supplier or region creates exposure to disruption, including geopolitical risk (Rule M5-B08-R03).
Spot it: one supplier, a region with trade tensions, proposed export restrictions, a critical component.
In this scenario: The PM assesses the single-source and regional exposure and qualifies alternate suppliers.
Why not the others: Stockpiling in the supplier's warehouse keeps the goods in the same exposed region; keeping the supplier unchanged ignores the risk; switching all at once to an unqualified supplier creates quality risk.
Remember: One source = one point of failure. Assess exposure, qualify alternates.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice
