questions.stem: A hybrid EV charging network project uses a predictive plan for site construction and agile sprints for the charging app. It is unclear whether regulators will mandate one connector standard or allow two, and demand forecasts vary widely. What should the project manager do?
options: Pick the single most likely future and plan the whole network around it
Develop plans for several plausible futures and identify the signals for each
Wait until the connector standards are final before doing any planning
Use the average of all the demand forecasts as the single planning assumption for all sites
questions.explanation:
Concept: Scenario planning — when several plausible futures could matter, plan for each and identify signals that show which one is emerging (Rule M5-B08-R06).
Spot it: unclear regulation, widely varying forecasts, long-lived investments that must be made now.
In this scenario: The PM develops plans for several plausible futures and defines the signals for each.
Why not the others: Betting on one future leaves the project exposed if it's wrong; waiting for certainty stalls progress; averaging forecasts produces a future that may never happen.
Remember: Many futures → many scenarios + signals. Don't bet the project on one guess.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A project to build a manufacturing plant abroad is closing. During execution, currency swings nearly doubled the local cost of imported equipment, and the project finished well over budget. The organization plans similar overseas investments next year. What should the project manager do?
options: Record how currency swings drove costs and how future business cases can plan for them
Leave the currency issue out of lessons learned since it was outside the team's control
Note only that the project exceeded its budget because of vendor equipment pricing
Share the currency lesson verbally with the team and skip any written documentation
questions.explanation:
Concept: Lessons learned on external change — capture how external forces affected the project so future investment decisions can plan for them (Rule M5-B08-R10).
Spot it: a project closing, a major external driver (currency, regulation, market), similar investments planned.
In this scenario: The PM records how currency swings drove costs and how future business cases can plan for them.
Why not the others: "Outside our control" is exactly the lesson future projects need; blaming vendor pricing misstates the cause; verbal-only sharing leaves no record for next year's decisions.
Remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → LEARN → Close. Lessons learned register = written, specific, reusable.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid project steering committee is choosing between two options. Option A pays back its investment in 1.5 years and has a net present value of $200,000. Option B pays back in 3 years and has a net present value of $900,000. The sponsor wants Option A because it pays back faster. What should the project manager advise?
options: Agree that Option A's faster payback makes it the higher-value investment overall
Recommend Option B mainly because its longer payback period makes it more stable
Suggest averaging the two payback periods to create one fair basis for comparison
Explain that payback shows recovery speed while NPV shows B creates more total value
questions.explanation:
Concept: Payback period versus NPV — payback shows how fast the investment is recovered; net present value shows total value created in today's money (Rule M5-B10-R04).
Spot it: a faster payback option competing with a higher-NPV option; a sponsor preferring "faster" as if it means "better."
In this scenario: The PM explains that payback measures recovery speed, while NPV shows the slower-payback option creates far more total value.
Why not the others: Faster payback does not mean higher value; a longer payback is not a sign of stability; averaging payback periods is meaningless.
Remember: Payback = HOW FAST. NPV = HOW MUCH. Higher NPV wins when comparing value.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: An organization can fund only one of two projects this year. Project X has a net present value of $1.2 million, and Project Y has a net present value of $900,000. The committee selects Project X. What is the opportunity cost of this decision?
options: $300,000, the difference between the two projects' net present values
$2.1 million, the combined value of both of the projects
$900,000, the value of the best alternative that was given up
$1.2 million, the value of the project that was selected
questions.explanation:
Concept: Opportunity cost — the value of the best alternative given up when you choose one option over another (Rule M5-B10-R07).
Spot it: "can fund only one," two options with stated values, "what is the opportunity cost?"
In this scenario: Choosing Project X gives up Project Y, so the opportunity cost is Y's NPV of $900,000.
Why not the others: The $300,000 difference is not what was given up; the $2.1 million sum adds both, but only one could be funded; $1.2 million is the value gained, not lost.
Remember: Opportunity cost = the value of the path NOT taken — the forgone option, not the difference.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid project must choose a warehouse system with a five-year life. System A costs $200,000 to buy and $150,000 a year to support. System B costs $400,000 to buy and $40,000 a year to support. The operations manager favors System A because it is cheaper. What should the project manager advise?
options: Choose System A because its purchase price is half the price of System B
Compare five-year totals, which show B at about $600,000 versus $950,000 for A
Choose System B because a higher purchase price usually means better quality
Split the purchase across both systems to balance their different cost profiles
questions.explanation:
Concept: Total cost of ownership — compare lifecycle costs (purchase + operating + support over the full life), not just the purchase price, when operating costs differ (Rule M5-B10-R09).
Spot it: one option cheap to buy but expensive to run, a multi-year life, someone favoring the lower price tag.
In this scenario: Five-year totals are about $950,000 for the cheaper-to-buy system and $600,000 for the other, so the higher purchase price is the better deal.
Why not the others: Purchase price alone ignores $750,000 of support; "more expensive means better quality" is an assumption; splitting the purchase doubles complexity without reason.
Remember: TCO = buy + run + support over the whole life.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A project manager's approved authority allows scope and cost changes of up to $50,000; larger changes go to the change control board. A supplier failure now requires a $120,000 change to keep the project on track. What should the project manager do?
options: Submit the $120,000 change to the board that holds authority for larger changes
Approve it by splitting it into three smaller changes that each fall under the $50,000 limit
Approve it because the project manager is accountable for the overall budget
Hold the change until the next quarterly budget review cycle comes around
questions.explanation:
Concept: Governance thresholds — a PM acts within approved authority limits; changes above the threshold go to the body that holds that authority (Rule M5-B01-R05).
Spot it: a stated authority limit, a change clearly above it, a change control board named.
In this scenario: The $120,000 change exceeds the $50,000 limit, so the PM submits it to the change control board.
Why not the others: Splitting it to stay under the limit games governance; accountability for the budget does not grant approval authority; waiting for the quarterly cycle delays a needed decision.
Remember: Change Request → Analyze → APPROVE (by the right authority) → Implement → Update → Monitor.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid banking project pilots a new branch system in agile releases before a predictive national rollout. The business case assumed 70 percent of branch staff would adopt the new process, but the pilot shows only 35 percent. The steering committee's next meeting is five weeks away. What should the project manager do?
options: Wait for the next scheduled meeting to present the full pilot results to the committee
Adjust the adoption target in the business case without informing the committee
Increase the training budget and report the change only after results improve
Inform the steering committee now about the lower adoption and its effect on value
questions.explanation:
Concept: Keep governance informed — when evidence materially changes assumptions or expected value, governance hears about it promptly, not at the next scheduled meeting (Rule M5-B01-R08).
Spot it: pilot results far below the business case assumption, a decision point weeks away, a rollout about to scale up.
In this scenario: Adoption is half of the assumed rate, so the PM informs the steering committee now about the effect on value.
Why not the others: Waiting five weeks lets the rollout continue on a false assumption; changing the target silently is dishonest; increasing spend and reporting later hides the problem.
Remember: Bad news early is good governance. Material change → inform now.
questions.block_title: External Environment & Market Change + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: An IT department has two pieces of work planned for next year: moving its data center to a new facility over six months, and applying security patches to all servers every month. The CIO asks which should be managed as a project. What should the project manager answer?
options: The monthly patching, because it repeats on a standard and predictable cycle
Both efforts, because each involves servers and requires technical specialists
The data center move, because it is temporary and produces a unique result
Neither effort, because each is part of the normal IT operations workload
questions.explanation:
Concept: Project versus operations — a project is temporary and creates a unique product, service or result; operations are ongoing and repetitive (Rule M5-B09-R01).
Spot it: a one-time effort with a start and end, compared with recurring work on a standard cycle.
In this scenario: The data center move is temporary and produces a unique result; monthly patching is ongoing operations.
Why not the others: Repeating work is operations, not a project; involving servers doesn't make both projects; the move is not routine operations work.
Remember: Project = temporary + unique. Operations = ongoing + repetitive.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A bank is running four related projects: a new core platform delivered predictively, an agile mobile app, branch staff retraining, and data migration. They share dependencies, and the promised benefits arrive only when all four work together. Each project manager is optimizing their own project. What should the organization do?
options: Merge all four into one large project led by a single project manager for control
Group the projects into a program to coordinate dependencies and combined benefits
Let each project manager continue independently and meet quarterly to share status
Rank the four projects in the portfolio against unrelated investments for funding
questions.explanation:
Concept: Program management — related projects are grouped into a program when their dependencies and combined benefits need coordination (Rule M5-B09-R02).
Spot it: several related projects, shared dependencies, benefits that appear only when all work together, each PM optimizing locally.
In this scenario: The organization groups the four projects into a program to coordinate dependencies and combined benefits.
Why not the others: One giant project loses the benefits-management focus and is hard to manage; quarterly status meetings don't coordinate dependencies; portfolio ranking selects investments, it doesn't coordinate related ones.
Remember: Project → Program → Portfolio. Projects deliver outcomes, programs coordinate benefits, portfolios align to strategy.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: An executive team has 12 proposed projects and funding for only 5. Leaders want the chosen set to support the three-year strategy and to balance risk across the organization. What approach should the executive team use?
options: Use portfolio management to rank and select proposals against strategic goals
Approve the five projects whose sponsors hold the most senior positions
Combine all twelve proposals into a single program to share their benefits
Fund the five least expensive projects so the most work gets completed
questions.explanation:
Concept: Portfolio management — selecting, prioritizing and balancing investments against strategy and risk, often when funding is limited (Rule M5-B09-R03).
Spot it: many proposals, limited funding, "support the strategy," "balance risk across the organization."
In this scenario: Portfolio management ranks and selects the proposals against the three-year strategy and risk balance.
Why not the others: Sponsor seniority is not strategic alignment; a program coordinates related projects, it doesn't select among unrelated ones; funding the cheapest ignores value and strategy.
Remember: Portfolio = choose the RIGHT work. Program = coordinate related work. Project = deliver the work.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: Two hybrid projects share a single test lab. Project A's sprints need frequent lab time, and its manager booked every slot for the next month. This delays Project B's predictive safety certification, and each week of delay costs the company far more than Project A would lose. What should Project A's manager do?
options: Keep the booked slots because each manager is accountable for their own project
Release half of the slots to Project B without assessing either project's impact
Ask the lab manager to decide based on which booking request was submitted first
Raise the lab conflict to the program or portfolio level for a trade-off decision
questions.explanation:
Concept: Escalating cross-project trade-offs — when one project's local choice harms the organization overall, the trade-off goes to the program or portfolio level (Rule M5-B09-R06).
Spot it: a shared resource, one project booking it all, another project's delay costing the company more.
In this scenario: The manager raises the lab conflict to the program or portfolio level, which can weigh both projects and decide.
Why not the others: Keeping all slots optimizes locally and harms the whole; releasing half without analysis is arbitrary; first-come booking ignores business value.
Remember: Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act → Monitor → ESCALATE — enterprise trade-offs go up.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A PMO requires every project, including a four-week $20,000 office reconfiguration, to pass the five stage gates and monthly board reviews used for its $40 million programs. The reconfiguration's project manager reports that gate paperwork now takes more time than the work itself. What should the PMO do?
options: Keep identical gates for all work so governance is applied consistently
Remove all governance from small projects so that they can move faster
Scale oversight so small, low-risk projects face lighter gates and reviews
Place the reconfiguration inside a large program to share its stage gates
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tailor governance to the work — oversight should match the size, risk and complexity of the work, not be identical for everything (Rule M5-B09-R10).
Spot it: a small, low-risk project forced through heavy processes built for large programs; paperwork exceeding the work.
In this scenario: The PMO scales oversight so small, low-risk projects face lighter gates and reviews.
Why not the others: Identical gates waste effort on small work; removing all governance goes too far; putting the project into a program adds complexity without value.
Remember: Tailor, don't copy. Governance fits the risk, size and value of the work.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid project is building a new office tower on a predictive plan and a tenant energy app in agile sprints. The sponsor's sustainability objective reads only, "The building should be green." Designers and contractors are interpreting it differently. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the goal broad so designers can interpret green in their own creative ways
Set measurable targets such as energy use per square meter and waste diverted
Use the number of sustainability meetings held as the project's main measure
Adopt the contractor's marketing claims as the project's green design targets
questions.explanation:
Concept: Measurable sustainability criteria — sustainability goals need measurable targets so teams can design, deliver and verify them consistently (Rule M5-B06-R04).
Spot it: vague sustainability language ("green"), different parties interpreting it differently.
In this scenario: The PM sets measurable targets such as energy use per square meter and waste diverted.
Why not the others: A broad goal leaves each designer interpreting it differently; counting meetings measures activity, not results; contractor marketing claims aren't the project's own targets.
Remember: If you can't measure it, you can't manage it — or prove it.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A mining project's environmental permit caps daily water withdrawal from a nearby river. The engineering lead proposes exceeding the cap during dry months to hold the schedule and simply paying any fines. What should the project manager do?
options: Plan the schedule within the permit's water cap and treat that cap as fixed
Exceed the cap in dry months and budget for any fines that may be imposed
Ask community stakeholders to vote on whether the cap can be exceeded
Apply the cap only during months when inspections are most likely to occur
questions.explanation:
Concept: Environmental and social requirements as constraints — mandatory permits and legal limits are fixed boundaries the plan must work within (Rule M5-B06-R07).
Spot it: a permit cap, a proposal to exceed it "and pay the fines," schedule pressure.
In this scenario: The PM plans the schedule within the permit's water cap and treats it as fixed.
Why not the others: Paying fines knowingly breaks the law; a community vote cannot override a permit; applying the cap only when inspections are likely is deliberate non-compliance.
Remember: Compliance = CONSTRAINT. Plan within it; never budget to break it.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A hybrid construction project designs building systems in agile increments and builds on a predictive schedule. The steering committee overrode its sustainability lead's objections and chose a cheaper, higher-carbon concrete mix to stay within budget. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the decision out of project records to avoid any negative publicity
Reverse the decision on the project manager's own authority to satisfy the lead
Note only the cost savings in the report because the choice is now final
Record the concrete decision, its carbon impact, and the reasons behind it
questions.explanation:
Concept: Documenting sustainability trade-offs — when a decision trades off sustainability, record the decision, its impact and its rationale for transparency (Rule M5-B06-R09).
Spot it: a steering committee overriding a sustainability objection, a cost-versus-carbon choice.
In this scenario: The PM records the concrete decision, its carbon impact and the reasons behind it.
Why not the others: Keeping it out of records hides a material decision; reversing it on the PM's own authority overrides governance; noting only savings gives an incomplete record.
Remember: Decision log = what, impact, why, who. Record the trade-off, not only the win.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: A PMO ranked five approved projects in January. In June, a customer study shows that the fifth-ranked project would deliver about twice the value previously estimated, and the market for the top-ranked project has shrunk sharply. What should the portfolio manager do?
options: Keep the January ranking because portfolio priorities should stay stable for the full year
Start the fifth project now without waiting for any formal review or approval
Re-rank the projects using the new evidence through the portfolio review process
Wait for the next annual planning cycle before considering the study's findings
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reassess priorities with new evidence — portfolio rankings are revisited when evidence materially changes expected value (Rule M5-B11-R05).
Spot it: new data showing one project is worth much more and another much less; an old ranking still in use.
In this scenario: The portfolio manager re-ranks the projects using the new evidence through the portfolio review process.
Why not the others: Keeping the January ranking ignores material evidence; starting the fifth project now bypasses review; waiting for the annual cycle delays value.
Remember: Data → Analyze → Insight → Decision. Priorities follow evidence, through governance.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

questions.stem: An investment committee is comparing two proposals. One estimates $4.37 million in value and the other $4.21 million. Both rest on untested assumptions, with ranges of plus or minus 50 percent. The committee wants to pick the higher number. What should the project manager advise?
options: Select the $4.37 million proposal because its estimated value is clearly the higher one
Treat the estimates as roughly equal and compare the proposals on other factors
Recalculate both estimates to more decimal places for a clearer comparison
Reject both proposals because neither value estimate can be shown to be exact
questions.explanation:
Concept: False precision — highly uncertain estimates should not be compared as if small differences are meaningful (Rule M5-B11-R08).
Spot it: estimates with wide ranges (plus or minus 50 percent), a small gap between them, a push to "pick the higher number."
In this scenario: The estimates are effectively equal, so the PM advises comparing the proposals on other factors.
Why not the others: The $160,000 gap is tiny against a ±50 percent range; more decimal places add precision, not accuracy; rejecting both because they aren't exact confuses uncertainty with worthlessness.
Remember: Precision ≠ accuracy. When ranges overlap, the numbers are a tie.
questions.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice

rules.text: Keep value prioritization with the designated product or value owner.
Let the delivery team determine how to accomplish selected work within constraints.
Use the Scrum Master or equivalent facilitator to improve flow, remove impediments, and coach the system.
Keep the sprint or iteration goal more stable than the detailed task plan.
Use backlog refinement to improve clarity, not to freeze future scope.
Keep daily coordination focused on progress toward the goal and obstacles.
Use reviews or demos to inspect the product and gather feedback.
Use retrospectives to improve the way of working.
Escalate persistent performance issues only after appropriate direct support and process.
Review whether communication is producing the intended behavior or decision.
Diagnose the conflict before choosing a resolution technique.
Collaborate when a durable win-win solution is feasible.
Use compromise when a balanced temporary trade-off is appropriate.
Use accommodation when the relationship matters more than the specific issue.
Use directing only when urgency, safety, or legitimate authority requires it.
Use withdrawal when the issue is trivial, information is insufficient, or a cooling-off period is useful.
Separate facts, assumptions, interests, and emotions during conflict analysis.
Resolve conflict as close to the source as practical before escalating.
Escalate uncertainty when consequences exceed team authority or risk tolerance.
Recognize your own emotional response before reacting under pressure.
Adapt communication to cultural and individual differences without stereotyping.
Create space for quieter or less powerful voices in decision discussions.
Use empathy to understand impact without abandoning project constraints.
Challenge disrespectful behavior promptly regardless of seniority.
Separate intent from impact when resolving interpersonal issues.
Use inclusive meeting practices for distributed and diverse teams.
Treat inclusion as a performance enabler, not a side initiative.
Avoid commitments you know the project cannot meet.
Verify that the receiver can perform the task, not merely that material was delivered.
Define a meeting purpose and desired outcome before inviting people.
Invite the people needed for the outcome, not everyone who might be interested.
Provide context or pre-read material when preparation is needed.
Facilitate balanced participation and prevent domination by rank or personality.
Separate brainstorming from evaluation when generating options.
End decision meetings with explicit decisions, owners, and due dates.
Use asynchronous collaboration when live discussion adds little value.
Review recurring meetings periodically and remove those that no longer create value.
Watch for burnout signals and address system causes.
Consider relationship value as well as immediate transaction value.
Assess who must change behavior for the project outcome to succeed.
Identify resistance drivers rather than treating resistance as one generic problem.
Create a clear change story that explains why, what, impact, and expected value.
Involve credible leaders and local influencers in adoption.
Build capability before expecting sustained new behavior.
Reinforce desired behavior after launch.
Measure adoption, proficiency, and outcome—not just training attendance.
Plan transition support for the period when old and new ways of working overlap.
Keep the project manager focused on integration rather than owning every specialist decision.
Adapt leadership style to team maturity, urgency, and context.
Understand the reason for resistance before trying to overcome it.
Tailor engagement to the stakeholder’s current and desired level of involvement.
Involve affected stakeholders early when their knowledge can improve the solution.
Use two-way communication when alignment or behavior change is needed.
Address high-power dissatisfied stakeholders proactively.

rules.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice
rules.text: Match governance to the level of work.

rules.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice
rules.text: Use measurable sustainability criteria where relevant.

rules.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice
rules.text: Treat mandatory environmental or social requirements as constraints.

rules.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice
rules.text: Document important sustainability trade-offs and rationale.

rules.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice
rules.text: Reassess priorities when evidence changes.

rules.block_title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations + Integrated Practice
rules.text: Avoid false precision when comparing highly uncertain value estimates.
